Name: language_distance_transfer_geometry
Title: The Bilingual Bottleneck: Predicting Cross-Lingual Knowledge Transfer and Interference from the Geometry of the Language-Transition Layers
Short Hypothesis: The failure of cross-lingual knowledge transfer and the emergence of cross-lingual interference are jointly governed by a measurable geometric property of a small set of 'language-transition' layers where models move from a shared concept space to language-specific spaces: transfer succeeds when the concept representation for a fact lands inside the target language's decoding manifold, and interference occurs when a fact learned in language A displaces the shared representation shared by typologically close language B. We can predict, per-fact and per-language-pair, whether transfer or interference will occur from this geometry alone, and steer it causally.
Related Work: Prior work established that MLMs encode knowledge in a language-independent concept space in middle layers and transition to language-specific spaces in final layers (Wang et al. 2025; Lim et al. 2025; Riemenschneider & Frank 2025; Civelli et al. 2026). Others measure representation-sharing via knowledge editing (Ifergan et al. 2024) or propose fixes such as linear shortcuts, projection modules (LRP2, Xu et al. 2023), or steering toward the shared space (Lim et al. 2025). These works largely (a) treat transfer as a single global phenomenon, (b) study consistency/transfer but not INTERFERENCE (negative transfer where new knowledge in one language corrupts another), and (c) offer post-hoc fixes rather than a predictive geometric account. Our proposal is distinct: we build a single geometric predictor, at the language-transition layers, that forecasts BOTH successful transfer AND destructive interference at the per-fact, per-language-pair level, ties it quantitatively to typological/script distance, and validates it causally through knowledge editing rather than only correlationally. No prior work predicts interference from transition-layer geometry or unifies transfer and interference under one measurable quantity.
Abstract: Multilingual language models encode facts in a shared concept space across most layers and only diverge into language-specific representations in a handful of final 'language-transition' layers. We ask a simple question: does the geometry of these transition layers alone determine whether knowledge transfers across languages, and whether learning a fact in one language destructively interferes with a typologically related language? We introduce the Bilingual Bottleneck framework, which extracts, for each fact, the concept vector at the last shared layer and the language-specific decoding manifold for each target language. We define two geometric quantities: (1) manifold-membership, the signed distance from a fact's concept vector to the target language's decoding manifold, hypothesized to predict transfer success; and (2) shared-vector overlap, the degree to which two languages route a fact through the same concept-space direction, hypothesized to predict interference. Using multilingual factual probing datasets (mLAMA) across 20+ languages spanning multiple scripts and families, we (i) show these two quantities predict per-fact transfer accuracy and per-language-pair interference with high AUC, outperforming baselines using surface similarity or global representation-similarity; (ii) demonstrate that both quantities scale monotonically with typological and script distance; and (iii) causally validate the account by editing a fact in one language and measuring induced interference, showing that shared-vector overlap predicts collateral damage. Finally, we propose a lightweight geometry-guided edit that projects updates orthogonally to shared directions, reducing interference by a large margin while preserving transfer. Our work offers a unified, predictive, causal account of cross-lingual transfer and interference.
Experiments:
1) DATA & MODELS: Use mLAMA and BMLAMA factual probing sets across 20+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/CJK/Arabic/Devanagari scripts and multiple families (Indo-European, Sino-Tibetan, Semitic, Turkic, Dravidian). Models: XLM-R, mBERT (encoder) and Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B (decoder), all fit on a single/few A6000 GPUs.
2) IDENTIFY TRANSITION LAYERS: Use logit-lens / language-identification probes per layer (following Wang 2025; Riemenschneider 2025) to locate the last shared layer L_shared and the language-transition band.
3) DEFINE GEOMETRIC QUANTITIES: For each (fact, language) collect the hidden state at L_shared. Estimate each language's decoding manifold via PCA on hidden states of correctly-decoded facts in that language. manifold-membership = signed distance of a concept vector to the target manifold. shared-vector overlap(langA,langB, fact) = cosine alignment of the two languages' concept-space directions for the same fact.
4) TRANSFER PREDICTION: Fit a simple logistic regression using manifold-membership to predict whether a fact known in source language is correctly answered in target language. Metric: AUC, calibration. Baselines: (a) surface script/lexical similarity, (b) global cross-lingual representation similarity, (c) typological distance (lang2vec/URIEL) alone. Show transition-layer geometry beats all.
5) DISTANCE SCALING: Correlate manifold-membership and shared-vector overlap with URIEL typological distance and script identity. Report Spearman correlations; test whether script distance dominates family distance (cf. Ifergan 2024).
6) INTERFERENCE (CAUSAL): Using ROME/MEMIT knowledge editing, edit a fact in language A. Measure accuracy change on the SAME fact in every other language B (collateral effect). Test hypothesis: shared-vector overlap(A,B) predicts magnitude and sign of collateral change. Metric: correlation between predicted overlap and observed accuracy delta; AUC for predicting destructive vs neutral vs beneficial transfer.
7) GEOMETRY-GUIDED EDIT: Modify MEMIT so the update is projected orthogonal to high-overlap shared directions. Compare interference (collateral accuracy drop on related languages) and desired-edit success + intended cross-lingual generalization vs vanilla MEMIT. Metrics: edit success, cross-lingual generalization rate, interference rate, general-capability retention (MMLU multilingual subset).
8) ABLATIONS: layer choice, manifold dimensionality, model scale, high- vs low-resource target languages.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Transition layers may not be cleanly separable in all models, weakening manifold estimation; mitigated by probing-based layer selection and reporting sensitivity. 2) Factual probing accuracy is noisy for low-resource languages; we restrict interference analysis to facts verifiably known in the source language. 3) Knowledge-editing methods (ROME/MEMIT) have their own artifacts; we use them as one of several causal probes and cross-check with activation patching. 4) Correlation between geometry and typology could be confounded by training-data frequency; we control for per-language corpus size where available. 5) The geometry-guided edit may trade some transfer for reduced interference; we quantify this trade-off explicitly rather than claiming a free lunch. 6) Results may be model-family specific; we test three decoder and two encoder families to assess generality.

Name: optimal_reasoning_language_steering
Title: Thinking in the Right Tongue: Is the Model's Default Language-of-Thought Suboptimal, and Can We Steer It Per-Problem?
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs default to a fixed internal 'language of thought' (usually English or the prompt language) for their latent reasoning, but this default is NOT the reasoning-optimal choice for every problem: the best internal reasoning language varies systematically with a problem's content (numerical formats, culturally-grounded facts, typological features of entities). We hypothesize (1) there exists a per-problem optimal internal reasoning language that often differs from the model's default, (2) which language is optimal is predictable from the problem's content features, and (3) we can causally steer the model's latent reasoning language at inference time, per-problem, to unlock accuracy gains that a single fixed reasoning language cannot.
Related Work: Recent work shows RLMs mix languages in reasoning and that forcing Latin/Han scripts helps globally (Wang et al. 2025); that ablating language-specific representations boosts multilingual reasoning by disentangling language from reasoning (Zhao et al. 2025, 'When Less Language is More'); and that English-centric models implicitly pivot to English internally (Huo et al. 2025; deep supervision fine-tuning). SoT (Qi et al. 2025) converts to language-agnostic structured representations. These works treat the reasoning language as a GLOBAL knob: either remove language entirely, or force one universal script. NONE ask whether the optimal internal reasoning language is PROBLEM-DEPENDENT, whether it is PREDICTABLE from problem content, or whether it can be steered PER-PROBLEM. Zhao et al. remove language; we instead argue that for some problems a specific non-default language is best (e.g., problems about French administrative facts, or numbers written in a language with transparent number morphology), and that adaptively selecting/steering language per problem beats both a single fixed language and full disentanglement. Our causal steering intervention and the predictability of the optimal language from content are new.
Abstract: Multilingual LLMs perform latent reasoning in a dominant internal 'language of thought'—typically English or the prompt language—regardless of the problem. We challenge the assumption that a single reasoning language is optimal. We hypothesize that the reasoning-optimal internal language varies per problem, depends on the problem's content, and can be causally steered at inference to yield accuracy gains beyond any fixed choice. First, we quantify each model's default reasoning language via logit-lens decoding of intermediate-layer representations across problems. Second, using constrained decoding and activation-level steering vectors extracted from parallel reasoning traces, we induce the model to reason internally in each of K candidate languages and measure per-problem accuracy, revealing an 'oracle' optimal reasoning language per problem. Third, we test whether the oracle language is predictable from lightweight content features (numeral system, named-entity origin, cultural domain, typological distance of the answer language) with a simple classifier. Finally, we build a per-problem router that steers latent reasoning to the predicted language and compare against (i) the default, (ii) the best single fixed language, and (iii) language-disentanglement ablation. We evaluate on MGSM, multilingual MMLU, culturally-grounded QA, and multilingual temporal/date arithmetic across 10+ typologically diverse languages and 4 open models. If successful, this reframes the internal reasoning language as an adaptive, steerable degree of freedom rather than a fixed property.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & DATA: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B. Benchmarks: MGSM (math word problems, 11 langs), multilingual MMLU subsets, BLEnD/culturally-grounded QA (culture-specific facts), MultiTempBench-style date arithmetic across calendars/numeral systems. All fit on 1-2 A6000s with inference only.
2) MEASURE DEFAULT LANGUAGE-OF-THOUGHT: For each problem, apply logit-lens per layer to intermediate hidden states and classify the language of the top-decoded tokens (following Wang 2025, Huo 2025). Report per-model default reasoning language distribution and its dependence on prompt language.
3) INDUCE REASONING IN CANDIDATE LANGUAGES (two mechanisms): (a) EXPLICIT: constrained decoding forcing the visible CoT into each candidate language L (as in Wang 2025). (b) LATENT STEERING: extract steering vectors by contrasting mean hidden states of reasoning traces produced in language A vs B (difference-of-means at reasoning layers), add scaled vector at inference to push latent reasoning toward L WITHOUT changing output language. Validate steering worked via logit-lens language detection.
4) ORACLE OPTIMAL LANGUAGE: For each problem, compute accuracy under each candidate reasoning language; define the per-problem oracle. Report: (i) oracle accuracy vs default vs best-fixed-language; (ii) fraction of problems where oracle != default; (iii) fraction where oracle != best-fixed. Hypothesis supported if oracle substantially exceeds best-fixed and oracle often differs from default.
5) PREDICTABILITY: Extract content features (numeral system used, NER entity-origin language via a small NER model, cultural-domain tag, answer-language typological distance via URIEL, problem length). Train logistic regression / small MLP to predict the oracle language. Metric: top-1/top-2 accuracy vs random and vs always-default baseline. Feature-importance analysis to identify what drives optimal-language choice.
6) PER-PROBLEM ROUTER: At inference, predict language from features, then apply latent steering (mechanism 3b) toward it. Compare accuracy against: default, best single fixed language, language-disentanglement ablation (Zhao et al. 2025 reimplementation), and constrained-decoding-to-English baseline (Wang 2025). Metric: exact-match/accuracy per benchmark, plus token cost.
7) MECHANISM & DISTANCE ANALYSIS: Correlate accuracy gain from steering with typological/script distance between prompt language and the steered reasoning language; test whether close languages give safer gains and distant ones bigger swings. Layer-wise ablation of where steering must be applied.
8) ABLATIONS: steering strength, number of candidate languages K, model scale, high- vs low-resource prompt languages, explicit vs latent steering effectiveness.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Latent steering may degrade fluency or leak the reasoning language into outputs; we monitor output-language fidelity and cap steering strength. 2) The oracle may overfit to noise on small benchmarks; we use multiple seeds, report confidence intervals, and hold out a test split for the router. 3) Gains from per-problem routing might be modest if the default is already near-optimal for most problems—this would still be an informative negative/nuanced result about how fixed the language-of-thought is. 4) Constrained decoding and steering are two different mechanisms; we report both and treat agreement between them as evidence of a genuine effect rather than an artifact. 5) Logit-lens language detection is imperfect for mixed scripts; we validate with an external language ID on decoded tokens and report detector reliability. 6) Results may be model-specific; we test four model families spanning English-centric and multilingual-centric (Aya) pretraining to assess generality.

Name: contested_facts_language_switch
Title: One Fact, Many Truths: How Multilingual Models Internally Resolve Culturally Contested Knowledge
Short Hypothesis: For culturally contested facts—questions with legitimately different correct answers across cultures (e.g., the national dish, who traditionally leads a wedding, disputed place names)—multilingual LLMs do not simply retrieve one universal answer keyed by language. Instead they store a dominant (usually US/English) answer plus a set of culturally-conditioned overrides, and the query language acts as a causal contextual switch that determines which override, if any, is applied. We hypothesize this switch is implemented by a small, localizable set of components early in the network that modulate a later shared retrieval mechanism, and that a fact's 'contestedness' is encoded as a measurable representational multiplicity (multiple candidate answers held in superposition) that collapses under the language signal.
Related Work: A wave of benchmarks documents that LLMs are Western/US-biased on cultural facts and often answer better in English than in the culture's native language (FmLAMA, Zhou et al. 2024; XNationQA, Tanwar et al. 2025; MSQA, 2026; TriviaRoomQA, 2026; Agarwal et al. 2025). Mizumoto et al. 2025 frame cross-linguistic disagreement as a normative conflict between cross-lingual consistency and folk-consistency but only at the behavioral/philosophical level. MIND (Calvo-Bartolomé 2025) detects discrepancies at the data level. Separately, mechanistic work shows facts live in a shared concept space with language-specific decoding (Wang 2025; Lim 2025). ALL prior work is either (a) behavioral benchmarking of cultural bias, or (b) mechanistic study of language-INVARIANT facts. NONE study the internal mechanism by which a single question with multiple legitimate culture-dependent answers is resolved: whether language is a retrieval key vs a contextual switch, where the switch lives, and whether contestedness is represented as answer superposition. Our proposal is the first mechanistic account of contested-fact resolution and introduces a causal test distinguishing 'language selects among stored culture-specific answers' from 'language merely translates one universal answer'.
Abstract: Many facts are not universal: the national dish, who traditionally officiates a wedding, or the standard name of a disputed territory legitimately differ across cultures. When a multilingual LLM is asked such a question in Japanese versus English, does it retrieve one universal answer and translate it, or does the query language causally switch which culturally-conditioned answer is produced—and where inside the network does this happen? We introduce a mechanistic framework for culturally contested facts. First, we build ContestedProbe, a set of parallel prompts across 10 typologically and culturally diverse languages, split into universal facts (single correct answer) and contested facts (multiple culture-conditioned correct answers), verified with native-sourced references. Using logit-lens and answer-token probing, we test whether models hold multiple candidate answers in superposition for contested (but not universal) facts, quantifying 'representational multiplicity.' Second, via activation patching and path patching we localize the components whose activations carry the language/culture signal that collapses this multiplicity, and test whether they sit early (context switch) or late (decoding). Third, we run causal switch experiments: patching only the language-signal components from a Japanese run into an English run to see if the answer flips to the Japanese-appropriate one without translating the surface language, distinguishing a contextual switch from a retrieval key. Finally, we show we can steer contestedness—forcing the model to surface a specified culture's answer regardless of query language. Our work reframes cultural bias as a mechanistically tractable resolution process.
Experiments:
1) DATASET (ContestedProbe): Curate ~400 questions in two strata. (a) UNIVERSAL: single answer across cultures (chemical symbol of gold, capital of France). (b) CONTESTED: multiple legitimate culture-conditioned answers (national dish, typical breakfast, who officiates weddings, appropriate gift color, standard name for a contested place/holiday, default measurement/date format). For each contested question, collect the ground-truth answer set with per-culture labels using native-sourced references (FmLAMA/XNationQA/MSQA-style, plus Wikipedia interlanguage checks). Translate all prompts into 10 languages (English, Spanish, Arabic, Hindi, Japanese, Korean, Turkish, Swahili, Russian, Indonesian) with native verification. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference on 1-2 A6000s).
2) BEHAVIORAL BASELINE: Measure, per model, whether the answer to contested vs universal questions changes with query language. Metric: answer-set membership accuracy (does the output match the query-language culture's answer?), and cross-lingual answer variance. Expect low variance for universal, high & culture-aligned variance for contested (or, if biased, English-answer dominance across all languages).
3) REPRESENTATIONAL MULTIPLICITY: Apply logit-lens at each layer; for each candidate culture-answer token, track its rank/probability trajectory. Define multiplicity = number of distinct culture-answers appearing in the top-k across layers before collapse. Hypothesis: contested facts show multiple co-active answers that collapse late; universal facts show a single trajectory. Metric: multiplicity score distribution, collapse-layer, compared contested vs universal (Mann-Whitney).
4) LOCALIZING THE LANGUAGE/CULTURE SWITCH: Use activation patching and path patching. Run the model on the SAME contested question in language A (culture-answer a) and language B (culture-answer b). Patch activations from the A-run into the B-run at each layer/component (attention heads, MLPs) and measure when the answer flips a<->b. Identify the minimal set of components (the 'switch') that carries culture-selection. Test early-vs-late: report the layer distribution of switch components and contrast with the (later) shared decoding layers found in prior work.
5) SWITCH-VS-KEY CAUSAL TEST: Critical experiment. Patch ONLY the identified language-signal components from a Japanese-language run into an otherwise English-language run. If the output flips to the Japanese-appropriate answer while the surface output language stays English, language acts as a CONTEXTUAL SWITCH over a shared multi-answer store (both answers were present; language selects). If instead the answer only changes when the whole prompt is translated (no partial patch suffices), language acts as a RETRIEVAL KEY (separate per-language stores). Metric: answer-flip rate under partial patch, surface-language fidelity.
6) STEERING CONTESTEDNESS: Derive a per-culture steering vector from difference-of-means over the switch components (culture-c runs minus baseline). Add it to force the model, given any query language, to surface culture c's answer. Metric: targeted-culture answer rate, off-target answer leakage, and no degradation on universal facts (control).
7) ANALYSIS: (a) Correlate switch strength / multiplicity with the model's pretraining exposure per language (Locality Effect from MSQA) and with typological distance (URIEL). (b) Ablate: does the switch generalize across contested-fact domains (food vs customs vs place-names)? (c) Compare English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya) models on switch location and US-answer dominance.
8) EVALUATION METRICS SUMMARY: culture-aligned answer accuracy, cross-lingual answer variance, representational multiplicity & collapse-layer, patch-induced flip rate, switch-component count/locus, steering targeted-answer rate, universal-fact retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Ground-truth for contested facts is inherently fuzzy; we mitigate by using native-sourced answer SETS and reporting membership rather than single-answer accuracy, and by excluding items without clear per-culture consensus. 2) Models may be so US-biased that they emit the English answer in all languages, giving little contestedness to study; this itself is a publishable finding (mechanistic evidence that culture-specific answers are absent/suppressed rather than merely un-selected), and we quantify how often the correct culture-answer is even present in superposition. 3) Activation/path patching results can be model- and prompt-specific; we test 5 models and multiple templates per fact, reporting aggregate and per-model results. 4) Logit-lens multiplicity is noisy for multi-token answers; we restrict analysis to items with short, single-token-decodable answers where possible and validate with tuned-lens. 5) The switch-vs-key distinction may be a spectrum rather than binary; we report the continuum via partial-patch flip rates rather than forcing a dichotomy. 6) Steering could break fluency; we cap steering strength and monitor universal-fact and general-language fidelity as controls.

Name: temporal_knowledge_asymmetry_across_languages
Title: When Did the Model Learn This? Language-Keyed Temporal Staleness in Multilingual LLMs and the Mechanism of Internal Time-Version Conflicts
Short Hypothesis: Because a multilingual LLM's per-language pretraining corpora were effectively snapshotted at different times and updated at different rates (English fresh, low-resource languages stale), the model stores multiple time-versions of the SAME time-varying fact keyed by language, and the query language acts as a causal selector of WHICH temporal version is retrieved. We hypothesize (1) for time-varying facts, the model's answer's implicit 'as-of date' systematically differs by query language and correlates with language resource level, not just accuracy; (2) internally, competing time-versions of a fact are co-represented and a small set of components carries the language-conditioned temporal selection signal; and (3) this signal can be causally patched so that querying in English can be made to return the stale answer a low-resource language returns, and vice versa, distinguishing 'language selects a stored temporal version' from 'language merely changes accuracy'.
Related Work: LiveCLKTBench (Guo et al. 2025) shows cross-lingual transfer of time-sensitive knowledge is distance-dependent and asymmetric, but only behaviorally and at the benchmark level; it does not ask whether the model stores per-language TIME-VERSIONS of the same fact or provide any mechanism. PRobELM (Yuan et al. 2024) and proxy-tuning temporal adaptation (Liu et al. 2024) study recency of parametric knowledge but monolingually and without cross-lingual temporal disagreement. Mechanistic multilingual work shows facts live in a shared concept space with language-specific decoding (Wang 2025; Lim 2025), and Layer-Targeted Multilingual Erasure / MUTE (Li et al. 2026) show intervention depth governs cross-lingual generalization of unlearning. GeoMLAMA (Yin et al. 2022) studies geo-diverse but static commonsense. NONE study TEMPORAL staleness as a language-keyed phenomenon, none show that the model holds multiple time-versions of a fact in superposition selected by language, and none causally localize a language-conditioned temporal-selection mechanism. Unlike my prior contested-facts proposal (culturally legitimate multiple answers), here the answers are all attempts at ONE objectively time-varying truth, and the multiplicity arises from corpus snapshot timing, not cultural norms—a fundamentally different cause and a different mechanistic prediction (temporal recency signal vs cultural switch).
Abstract: Multilingual LLMs are trained on per-language corpora that were, in effect, frozen at different points in time and refreshed at different rates: English text is abundant and fresh, while low-resource languages lag by years. We ask whether this makes a model an inadvertent 'time capsule' that stores different temporal versions of the same time-varying fact keyed by query language, and whether the query language causally selects which version is retrieved. We first construct TimeShiftProbe, parallel prompts across 10 languages for facts whose correct answer changed over known dates (heads of state, club managers, current record holders, latest product versions, populations), each annotated with the ground-truth value at successive as-of dates. Behaviorally, we introduce an 'implicit as-of date' estimator: the date whose ground-truth answer best matches the model's output. We test whether this implicit date differs systematically by query language and tracks per-language resource/recency, beyond mere accuracy. Mechanistically, using logit-lens we test whether competing time-versions co-activate for time-varying (but not static) facts, and via activation/path patching we localize the components carrying the language-conditioned temporal-selection signal, testing whether they align with the language-transition band. In a decisive causal test we patch only these components from a low-resource run into an English run to see if the stale answer surfaces while output language stays English—distinguishing temporal selection from accuracy change. Finally we derive a 'temporal steering' vector that forces the freshest stored version regardless of query language. We reframe multilingual staleness as a mechanistically tractable, steerable time-version selection process.
Experiments:
1) DATASET (TimeShiftProbe): Curate ~400 time-varying facts whose answer changed on known dates in the last ~15 years, drawn from Wikidata edit histories: heads of state/office-holders, sports club managers/champions, current world-record holders, latest version/CEO of companies, city populations, reigning title holders. For each fact record the full time-series of (as-of date -> correct answer). Add a CONTROL set of ~200 static facts (chemical symbols, historical dates, capitals). Translate all prompts into 10 typologically/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Indonesian, Turkish, Japanese) with native verification. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B, plus one model with a known cutoff for calibration; inference on 1-2 A6000s.
2) IMPLICIT AS-OF DATE ESTIMATOR: For each (fact, language), compare the model's answer against every dated version in the time-series; the implicit as-of date is the date(s) whose answer matches. Handle multi-match and no-match. Metric: per-language distribution of implicit as-of dates; lag = (model cutoff or latest date) minus implicit date.
3) LANGUAGE-KEYED STALENESS TEST: Test whether implicit as-of date differs across query languages for the SAME fact (Friedman/Wilcoxon across languages), and whether per-language median lag correlates with proxies for that language's pretraining recency/size (corpus size where available, URIEL resource tier, script). KEY: show the effect exists BEYOND accuracy, i.e., even when languages are all 'correct' they can be correct as-of DIFFERENT dates. Compare time-varying vs static control (static should show no language-keyed date shift).
4) REPRESENTATIONAL TIME-VERSION MULTIPLICITY: Apply logit-lens/tuned-lens per layer; track rank/probability trajectories of the answer tokens for each dated version (e.g., old vs new office-holder). Hypothesis: for time-varying facts multiple dated answers co-activate and one wins late; static facts show a single trajectory. Metric: multiplicity score, collapse layer, time-varying vs static (Mann-Whitney).
5) LOCALIZE TEMPORAL-SELECTION COMPONENTS: Run the same fact in a fresh-answering language A and a stale-answering language B. Activation-patch and path-patch across layers/heads/MLPs to find the minimal component set whose transfer flips the answer between the temporal versions. Report the layer distribution and test overlap with the language-transition band identified via per-layer language-ID probes.
6) SELECTION-VS-ACCURACY CAUSAL TEST (decisive): Patch ONLY the identified components from a stale low-resource run into an otherwise English (fresh) run. If the STALE answer surfaces while the surface language stays English, language causally SELECTS a stored temporal version (both versions were present). If no partial patch suffices and only full translation changes the answer, staleness is not a selectable stored version. Metric: answer-flip rate under partial patch, output-language fidelity, symmetric test (fresh patched into stale run).
7) TEMPORAL STEERING: Derive a difference-of-means steering vector (fresh-version runs minus stale-version runs) over the selection components; add it to force the freshest stored version regardless of query language. Metric: fraction of languages upgraded to the fresh answer, no degradation on static controls, output fluency/language fidelity.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: correlate staleness lag and flip-rate with URIEL distance and resource tier; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); domain generality (politics vs sports vs tech); layer/dimension ablations; robustness to prompt templates.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language implicit as-of date & lag, cross-lingual date-disagreement rate, multiplicity/collapse-layer, patch-induced flip rate, selection-component locus, steering upgrade rate, static-control retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Attributing per-language lag to corpus snapshot timing is confounded by data volume and by translation/transfer effects; we control with URIEL tiers, corpus-size proxies where available, and by showing static controls show no date shift. 2) Ground-truth time-series must be accurate; we source from Wikidata edit histories and verify with dated references, excluding ambiguous items. 3) Some models may simply be uniformly stale/fresh across languages, yielding little disagreement—this is itself a publishable finding about how uniform temporal knowledge is, and we quantify how often a fresh version is even present in superposition. 4) Logit-lens multiplicity is noisy for multi-token answers; we prefer short single-token-decodable answers and validate with tuned-lens. 5) Patching results can be model/prompt-specific; we test 5 models and multiple templates and report aggregate and per-model results. 6) The selection-vs-accuracy distinction may be a spectrum; we report continuous partial-patch flip rates rather than forcing a dichotomy. 7) Temporal steering may harm fluency or over-generalize; we cap strength and monitor static-fact and language fidelity as controls.

Name: codeswitch_concept_binding
Title: Which Language Owns the Concept? Intra-Sentential Code-Switching as a Probe for Concept Binding and Grammatical Interference in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a fact or concept-bearing entity in a sentence is expressed via an intra-sentential language switch (e.g., a Spanish sentence whose key noun is in German), the model must decide which language's space 'owns' the concept for the purposes of (a) retrieving the correct associated fact and (b) generating downstream grammatical agreement (gender/number/case). We hypothesize the model resolves this ownership at a small, localizable set of 'binding' components, that the choice is systematically governed by matrix-vs-embedded language role and typological distance, and that mis-binding causally produces two distinct, predictable failures: fact-retrieval errors (the concept is looked up in the wrong language's knowledge) and grammatical-interference errors (agreement copied from the wrong language's morphosyntax). We can causally steer which language owns the concept and thereby flip both failure modes.
Related Work: Recent code-switching (CS) work is either behavioral benchmarking (Winata et al. 2026 CodeMixQA; Abdaljalil et al. 2025 CS-NLI) or treats CS as a lever/hazard for reasoning: CSICL (Yoo 2025) and Progressive Code-Switching (Wang 2026, Lin 2026) use CS to align reasoning to English; Goncharov 2025 steers away from unintended CS; Park et al. 2026 ('Anchor Bias') measure geometrically whether a CS hidden state aligns to source vs target language and steer QA F1. These works ask WHETHER CS helps/hurts and WHERE the CS state sits geometrically, but none isolate the moment of CONCEPT BINDING: when a single content word is switched, which language's knowledge store is queried for the fact attached to that concept, and which language's morphosyntax governs downstream agreement. No prior work (i) causally localizes a 'binding' mechanism that assigns concept-ownership language, (ii) ties two dissociable failure modes (fact-retrieval error vs grammatical-agreement error) to the same binding decision, or (iii) demonstrates that steering concept-ownership language simultaneously flips both. This reframes CS not as noise but as a controlled scalpel exposing how the model routes a concept to a language-specific knowledge/morphology subsystem.
Abstract: Intra-sentential code-switching forces a multilingual language model to make an implicit decision: when a single concept-bearing word is expressed in a different language than the surrounding sentence, which language 'owns' that concept? This decision matters twice over: for retrieving the fact associated with the concept (is the model querying its German or its Spanish knowledge of Berlin?) and for generating grammatical agreement on the concept (does an adjective agree with the noun's German or Spanish gender?). We introduce a controlled framework, SwitchBind, that inserts a language switch at exactly the answer-relevant entity in otherwise-parallel sentences, spanning matrix/embedded role assignments and typologically diverse language pairs with differing grammatical-gender and case systems. Behaviorally, we measure two dissociable failure modes: fact-retrieval errors (does the model recover the correct associated fact) and grammatical-interference errors (does downstream agreement follow the matrix or embedded language). Mechanistically, using activation and path patching we localize the minimal set of 'binding' components that assign the concept's ownership language, testing whether they precede and gate the language-specific knowledge retrieval identified by prior interpretability work. In a decisive causal test, we derive a binding-language steering vector and show it simultaneously flips both fact-retrieval and agreement behaviors, establishing a common cause. Finally, we relate binding strength and mis-binding rate to typological/script distance and matrix-vs-embedded role. Our work recasts code-switching as a precise probe of how concepts are routed to language-specific subsystems, offering a unified, causal account of a previously fragmented set of multilingual failures.
Experiments:
1) DATASET (SwitchBind): Construct ~500 templated sentences per language pair where a single answer-relevant content word (a named entity or common noun tied to a probeable fact) is switched into the embedded language while the rest stays in the matrix language. Two strata: (A) FACT items, where the switched word is an entity with a known associated fact (e.g., '<Berlin> ist die Hauptstadt von ___' embedded in a Spanish/French matrix), enabling a correctness check for whether the correct fact is retrieved; (B) AGREEMENT items, where the switched noun has conflicting grammatical gender/number/case across the two languages, and a downstream adjective/article/verb must agree, exposing which language's morphosyntax is used. Use 6 language pairs spanning matched and mismatched gender systems and scripts: Spanish-German, Spanish-French, English-Russian, English-Arabic, German-Turkish, Hindi-English, with native-verified templates. For each item create the parallel MATRIX-only and EMBEDDED-only monolingual controls. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + patching on 1-2 A6000s).
2) BEHAVIORAL MEASUREMENT: (a) Fact-retrieval accuracy on FACT items under CS vs matrix-only vs embedded-only controls; define mis-binding when the CS answer matches the embedded-language monolingual answer but differs from expected, or vice versa. (b) Agreement source on AGREEMENT items: classify whether generated agreement follows matrix-language gender/number or embedded-language gender/number; report matrix-vs-embedded agreement rate. Metrics: fact accuracy, cross-condition answer divergence, agreement-source distribution. Test matrix-vs-embedded role effect and typological-distance effect (URIEL) via mixed-effects regression.
3) DISSOCIATION TEST: Test whether fact-retrieval ownership and agreement ownership co-vary per item and per model, i.e., does a concept bound to the embedded language for facts also drive embedded-language agreement? Report correlation; a positive correlation supports a single binding decision, a null result supports separate subsystems (either is informative).
4) LOCALIZE BINDING COMPONENTS: Run activation patching / path patching between the CS run and each monolingual control, sweeping layers, attention heads, and MLPs to find the minimal set whose patching flips the concept's ownership language (as read out by both fact answer and agreement token). Report the layer distribution and test whether binding components precede the later language-specific retrieval layers found in prior mechanistic work (validate retrieval-layer location via logit-lens language-ID probes).
5) COMMON-CAUSE STEERING (decisive): Derive a binding-language steering vector via difference-of-means over the binding components (matrix-owned runs minus embedded-owned runs). Add/subtract it at inference on held-out CS items and measure whether it SIMULTANEOUSLY (i) flips the retrieved fact to the other language's knowledge and (ii) flips downstream agreement to the other language's morphosyntax. Simultaneous flipping is strong evidence for a shared binding mechanism. Metrics: joint flip rate, single-mode flip rate, output-language fidelity (surface language should stay the matrix language), fluency.
6) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: correlate mis-binding rate and steering flip rate with URIEL typological distance, script identity, and gender-system (mis)match; compare English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); vary switch position (subject vs object), switch granularity (single word vs phrase), and probe robustness to templates; layer/dimension ablations of the binding vector.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: fact-retrieval accuracy & mis-binding rate, agreement-source distribution, fact-vs-agreement co-variation, patch-induced ownership flip rate, binding-component locus, joint steering flip rate, output-language fidelity, distance/role regression coefficients.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Grammatically forcing a single-word switch can produce mildly unnatural sentences; we use native verification, keep switches at natural insertion points (nouns), and include naturalness ratings. 2) For some language pairs grammatical gender may be absent or coincidentally matched, weakening the agreement signal; we deliberately select mismatched-gender pairs and report which pairs are analyzable. 3) Fact-retrieval mis-binding may be rare if the model simply translates the embedded word first; this itself is a finding (early normalization to matrix language) and we quantify how often binding is even contested via the monolingual controls. 4) Patching results can be model- and template-specific; we test 5 models and multiple templates and report aggregate and per-model results, cross-checking activation patching with path patching. 5) The single-binding vs separate-subsystem question may be a spectrum; we report continuous co-variation and single- vs joint-flip rates rather than forcing a dichotomy. 6) Steering may harm fluency or leak the embedded language into the surface form; we cap steering strength and monitor output-language fidelity and monolingual-control retention. 7) Distinguishing our binding effect from Park et al.'s Anchor Bias requires care; we explicitly include their geometric anchor measure as a baseline and show that binding-component steering causally flips behavior beyond what anchor geometry predicts.

Name: number_naming_magnitude_geometry
Title: The Multilingual Mental Number Line: Do Compositional Number-Naming Systems Leak Into a Model's Magnitude Representation?
Short Hypothesis: Languages name numbers with radically different structures (transparent decimal in Chinese, vigesimal fragments in French/Danish, opaque non-compositional forms in Hindi 1-99). We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM does NOT map all these surface forms onto a single language-independent magnitude representation ('mental number line'); instead, the compositional/base structure of the number-naming system leaks into the internal magnitude code, producing (1) a measurable, language-specific distortion of the number-line geometry, (2) systematic, predictable arithmetic errors near structural boundaries (e.g., French 70-99, base transitions) that differ by query language, and (3) a small set of components where surface-form-driven magnitude decoding can be causally corrected to recover language-independent accuracy.
Related Work: Cognitive science establishes a language-independent 'mental number line' (Dehaene) but also cross-linguistic effects of number-word transparency on human arithmetic. In NLP, prior work probes numeracy in monolingual LLMs: numbers occupy a low-dimensional, roughly log-scaled subspace (e.g., studies showing linear/helical 'number neurons' and log-magnitude directions), and behavioral work shows multilingual math (MGSM) accuracy varies by language. However, existing multilingual math work treats language as a global accuracy knob and existing numeracy-probing work is monolingual (usually digit/English tokens). NO prior work asks whether the MAGNITUDE REPRESENTATION ITSELF is distorted by a language's number-naming morphology, whether such distortion predicts arithmetic error patterns at structural boundaries per-language, or causally localizes and corrects surface-form leakage into the number line. This distinguishes it from my prior proposals (facts/reasoning-language/contested/temporal/code-switch) and from generic multilingual-math benchmarking: the object of study is the internal quantity code and its cross-lingual geometry, tested causally.
Abstract: Human number words are structured very differently across languages: Chinese is transparently decimal, French and Danish embed base-20 fragments (ninety = 'four-twenties-ten'), and Hindi has largely opaque, non-compositional forms for 1-99. When a multilingual LLM reads a spelled-out number, does it recover a single language-independent magnitude, or does the naming system's structure leak into the internal quantity code? We test whether the model's 'mental number line' is warped by number-naming morphology and whether this warping causally produces language-specific arithmetic errors. We elicit hidden representations for numbers written as words across ~10 languages with contrasting numeral systems, fit each language's magnitude geometry (using linear/log-magnitude probes and low-dimensional structure), and quantify per-language distortion relative to a shared digit-based reference. Behaviorally, we predict that arithmetic and comparison errors cluster at each language's structural boundaries (e.g., French 70-99, base-transition points) and that these clusters differ across languages sharing the same digits. Mechanistically, via activation and path patching we localize where spelled-form magnitude is computed and test whether it converges to or diverges from the digit-based number line. In a decisive causal test, we derive a correction vector that maps a distorted language-specific magnitude onto the shared digit number line and show it selectively fixes boundary errors without harming other numbers. We relate distortion magnitude to naming-system transparency and typological distance, reframing multilingual arithmetic gaps as a measurable, correctable property of the internal quantity representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: Select ~10 languages spanning contrasting number-naming systems: transparent decimal (Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Turkish), vigesimal/irregular (French, Danish, Basque, Georgian), opaque-compositional (Hindi/other Indic 1-99), and regular decimal control (English, Spanish, Indonesian). MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + patching on 1-2 A6000s.
2) STIMULI: For integers 1-1000, generate spelled-out number words in each language (native-verified/rule-based generators), plus a DIGIT reference form ('347'). Also build word-problem-free minimal-pair prompts for (a) magnitude comparison ('is X greater than Y?'), (b) simple arithmetic (X+Y, X-Y, X*small), and (c) number reading/round-trip (word -> digit).
3) MAGNITUDE GEOMETRY PROBING: At each layer, extract hidden states at the number token(s). Fit (i) a linear/ridge probe from hidden state to log(value) and to value, per language and for the digit reference; (ii) low-dimensional structure via PCA and measure whether ordering along the leading component tracks magnitude. Metrics: probe R^2/MAE per language, monotonicity of the number line, and DISTORTION = deviation of each language's magnitude geometry from the digit-reference geometry (e.g., Procrustes alignment error, local ordering violations). Hypothesis: opaque/vigesimal systems show larger distortion, especially at structural boundaries.
4) BOUNDARY-ERROR BEHAVIOR: Measure comparison and arithmetic accuracy as a function of value, per language. Test whether error rate spikes at each language's structural boundaries (French 70-99 and 20/60 transitions; Danish base-20 points; Hindi opaque ranges) and whether the spike LOCATIONS differ across languages that share the same digits. Statistics: mixed-effects logistic regression of error on (distance-to-boundary, language, value), and a permutation test that boundary locations predict errors better than random value bins. Include digit-form control (should show flat, boundary-free error).
5) DISTORTION-PREDICTS-ERROR LINK: Correlate per-number probe-decoded magnitude error (from step 3) with per-number behavioral error (step 4) within each language. A positive link supports that internal number-line distortion causes the arithmetic mistakes.
6) LOCALIZE THE MAGNITUDE COMPUTATION: Using activation/path patching between a spelled-word run and its digit-form run for the same value, sweep layers/heads/MLPs to find the minimal components whose patching corrects the spelled-form's decoded magnitude toward the digit value. Report layer distribution and whether spelled-form magnitude converges to the shared digit number line by mid layers or stays language-warped.
7) CAUSAL CORRECTION (decisive): Derive a correction transform (difference-of-means or a low-rank map) that sends a language's distorted magnitude representation onto the digit-reference number line at the localized layer. Apply at inference on held-out numbers and test whether it (i) reduces boundary comparison/arithmetic errors for that language, (ii) leaves already-correct numbers and other languages unharmed, and (iii) does not degrade unrelated capabilities (spot-check general QA). Metrics: boundary-error reduction, off-target damage, retention.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: Regress distortion magnitude on a naming-system transparency score (base regularity, compositional depth) and URIEL distance; compare English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); ablate probe dimensionality, layer choice, tokenization effects (multi-token number words); robustness across prompt templates and across value ranges (1-100 vs 100-1000).
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language magnitude probe R^2/MAE, number-line distortion (Procrustes/ordering), boundary error-rate profiles, distortion-error correlation, patch-induced magnitude-correction rate, localized-component locus, causal-correction boundary-error reduction and off-target/retention, transparency-distance regression coefficients.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Tokenization: spelled-out number words split into many subword tokens, complicating which token carries magnitude; we test multiple token-pooling schemes (last token, mean, boundary token) and report sensitivity. 2) Confound with training frequency: rarer number-words in low-resource languages may drive errors independent of naming structure; we control with URIEL/resource tiers and by comparing same-frequency ranges across languages, and use the digit-form as a within-language frequency-neutral control. 3) Some models may internally normalize spelled numbers to digits early, showing little distortion—this itself is an informative finding (early normalization) and we quantify how often distortion is even present. 4) Probing linearity assumptions: the number line may be nonlinear/helical; we test both linear and low-dimensional nonlinear structure and validate with ordering metrics rather than only R^2. 5) Patching/correction results can be model- and template-specific; we test 5 models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 6) The causal correction may trade some accuracy elsewhere; we explicitly report off-target damage and retention rather than claiming a free lunch. 7) Boundary definitions require native linguistic input; we predefine structural boundaries per language from documented numeral grammars to avoid post-hoc fitting.

Name: logical_operator_semantics_across_languages
Title: Does Negative Concord Confuse the Model? Typological Leakage into the Cross-Lingual Representation of Logical Operator Semantics
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs do NOT compute the truth-conditional semantics of negation and quantifiers in a fully language-independent way. Instead, typological properties of how a language surface-realizes logical operators (negative concord vs. double-negation-cancellation, quantifier scope/placement, single vs. multiple negation markers) leak into the model's internal logical computation, producing (1) a measurable language-specific distortion of a shared 'polarity/quantity' representation, (2) systematic, predictable truth-value errors on constructions where surface form and logical meaning diverge (e.g., a negative-concord sentence mis-read as double negation), and (3) a small, localizable set of components where surface-form-driven polarity can be causally corrected to recover language-independent logical accuracy.
Related Work: Prior multilingual negation work (Shaitarova & Rinaldi 2021; Fancellu 2018; Christen et al. 2023) studies cross-lingual negation SCOPE RESOLUTION as a token-labeling task via zero-shot transfer, never asking whether the model computes correct truth-conditional MEANING or whether typology corrupts it. RISE (Freenor & Alvarez 2025) shows negation/conditionality correspond to consistent geometric rotations across languages, supporting a shared linear structure, but treats negation as a single uniform transformation and does not test whether logical operators COMPOSE correctly or whether typologically divergent negation systems (negative concord, double negation) distort meaning. Mechanistic work locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) but not for LOGICAL OPERATORS. No prior work (i) tests whether truth-conditional semantics of negation/quantifiers is language-independent, (ii) predicts logical errors from typological negation/quantifier features, or (iii) causally localizes and corrects surface-form leakage into the polarity/quantity representation. This differs from all my prior proposals (facts, reasoning language, contested facts, temporal, code-switch binding, number magnitude): the object of study is the internal LOGICAL semantics of operators and its cross-lingual geometry, tested causally.
Abstract: Languages express logical operators very differently. Some use negative concord, where multiple negative words together mean a single negation ('no vi a nadie' = 'I didn't see anyone'), while others enforce double-negation cancellation; quantifier placement and scope-marking also vary widely. When a multilingual LLM reads such a sentence, does it recover a single, language-independent truth-conditional meaning, or does the language's surface morphosyntax leak into its internal logical computation? We test whether the model's shared 'polarity/quantity' representation is warped by negation and quantifier typology, and whether this warping causally produces language-specific logical errors. We construct MultiLogicProbe, minimal-pair sentences across ~10 typologically diverse languages spanning negative-concord and double-negation systems and contrasting quantifier structures, each paired with a truth-value or entailment label. We fit each language's polarity/quantity geometry with linear probes and quantify per-language distortion relative to a shared reference; behaviorally we predict that truth-value errors cluster on constructions where surface form and logical meaning diverge (e.g., negative-concord sentences mis-parsed as double negation), and that these clusters are predictable from the language's negation typology. Mechanistically, via activation and path patching we localize where polarity is computed and test whether it converges to or diverges from a shared logical code. In a decisive causal test we derive a correction vector mapping a distorted language-specific polarity onto the shared representation and show it selectively fixes typology-driven errors without harming other items. We reframe multilingual logical-reasoning gaps as a measurable, correctable property of the internal logical representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: ~10 languages chosen for negation/quantifier typology contrast: negative-concord (Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Russian, Polish, Greek), non-concord / double-negation-cancelling (English, German, Dutch), and languages with divergent negation morphology or quantifier placement (Japanese, Turkish, Arabic). MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (MultiLogicProbe): Construct ~600 minimal-pair items per language in strata: (A) SINGLE NEGATION (e.g., 'The box is not empty'), (B) NEGATIVE-CONCORD / DOUBLE-NEGATION constructions (multiple negative elements; concord languages -> single negation meaning, others -> cancellation), (C) QUANTIFIER SCOPE items (e.g., 'every student did not pass' with scope ambiguity; 'someone loves everyone'), (D) AFFIRMATIVE controls. Each item has a truth-value or textual-entailment label and a natural-language yes/no probe ('Does this mean the box is empty? yes/no'). Templates native-verified; include the parallel affirmative and single-negation controls for each item. Draw on existing negation corpora (Christen et al., Fancellu) where possible for realism.
3) BEHAVIORAL MEASUREMENT: Measure truth-value / entailment accuracy per language and stratum. KEY hypothesis: errors spike on stratum B constructions where surface negation count and logical meaning diverge, and error patterns differ systematically between concord and non-concord languages. Statistics: mixed-effects logistic regression of error on (typology feature, stratum, language); test whether typological negation features (concord vs cancellation, number of negation markers, quantifier placement, all coded from documented grammars and URIEL) predict error rate better than resource level alone.
4) POLARITY/QUANTITY GEOMETRY PROBING: At each layer, extract hidden states at the sentence/answer position. Fit linear probes to decode (i) sentence polarity (affirmative vs negated meaning), and (ii) quantifier force (universal/existential/negative). Per language and for an English reference. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUC per language; DISTORTION = deviation of each language's polarity/quantity geometry from the reference (Procrustes alignment error, direction cosine misalignment). Hypothesis: concord and divergent-typology languages show larger distortion, concentrated on stratum B.
5) DISTORTION-PREDICTS-ERROR LINK: Correlate per-item probe-decoded polarity error with per-item behavioral truth-value error within each language. A positive link supports that internal polarity distortion causes the logical mistakes.
6) LOCALIZE THE POLARITY COMPUTATION: Using activation/path patching between a negative-concord run and its single-negation control (matched meaning) or a correctly-parsed vs mis-parsed run, sweep layers/heads/MLPs to find the minimal components whose patching flips the decoded polarity toward the correct truth-conditional value. Report layer distribution; test whether polarity converges to a shared code by mid-layers or stays language-warped (validate via per-layer language-ID probes to relate to the language-transition band).
7) CAUSAL CORRECTION (decisive): Derive a correction transform (difference-of-means or low-rank map) sending a language's distorted polarity/quantity representation onto the shared reference at the localized layer. Apply at inference on held-out items and test whether it (i) reduces truth-value errors on typology-divergent (stratum B / scope) items, (ii) leaves already-correct and affirmative-control items unharmed, and (iii) does not degrade unrelated capabilities (spot-check general multilingual QA). Metrics: typology-error reduction, off-target damage, retention.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: Regress distortion on typological negation/quantifier features and URIEL distance; compare English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); ablate probe layer/dimensionality, token-pooling, prompt templates; test generalization of the correction vector across strata (does a negation-derived vector also fix quantifier-scope errors?).
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-stratum truth-value/entailment accuracy, polarity/quantity probe accuracy & distortion (Procrustes/cosine), typology-feature error regression, distortion-error correlation, patch-induced polarity-flip rate, localized-component locus, causal-correction error reduction and off-target/retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Some models may normalize surface negation to a canonical logical form early, showing little distortion; this itself is an informative finding (early logical normalization) and we quantify how often distortion is present. 2) Confound with training frequency: rarer constructions in lower-resource languages may drive errors independent of typology; we control with URIEL/resource tiers and use within-language affirmative/single-negation controls that hold frequency roughly constant. 3) Truth-value labels for scope-ambiguous quantifier items can be genuinely ambiguous; we restrict scored items to unambiguous cases and treat ambiguous ones separately. 4) Probing linearity assumptions: polarity may be nonlinearly encoded; we validate probes on affirmative/negation controls and report both linear and low-dimensional structure. 5) Patching/correction results can be model- and template-specific; we test 5 models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 6) The causal correction may trade accuracy elsewhere; we explicitly report off-target damage and retention rather than claiming a free lunch. 7) Typological feature coding requires linguistic care; we predefine negation/quantifier features from documented grammars and URIEL to avoid post-hoc fitting. 8) Distinguishing genuine semantic distortion from surface-cue heuristics requires the minimal-pair design; we ensure concord and non-concord items are surface-matched where possible so effects cannot be attributed to lexical shortcuts alone.

Name: conceptual_metaphor_grounding_crosslingual
Title: Literal First, Then Figurative? The Cross-Lingual Mechanism of Idiom Comprehension and Whether Shared Conceptual Metaphors Transfer While Language-Specific Idioms Interfere
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM reads an idiom or conceptual-metaphor expression, it first computes the LITERAL source-domain meaning and only later resolves the FIGURATIVE target meaning, and the ease of this resolution is governed by whether the underlying conceptual metaphor is SHARED across languages. We hypothesize (1) idioms grounded in a cross-linguistically SHARED conceptual metaphor (e.g., TIME-IS-MONEY, ANGER-IS-HEAT) resolve figuratively in a language-independent shared space and transfer their meaning across languages, whereas idioms grounded in a LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC metaphor stay stuck in a literal/source-domain representation and fail to transfer; (2) there exists a measurable 'literal-to-figurative transition' in the layer stack whose depth predicts comprehension success and correlates with metaphor sharedness; and (3) a small set of components carries the figurative-resolution signal, which can be causally steered to force figurative reading of an otherwise-literal (mis-comprehended) idiom, and conversely to induce literal mis-readings—thereby distinguishing genuine conceptual transfer from surface memorization.
Related Work: Prior cross-lingual metaphor work is behavioral/task-level: Hülsing & Schulte im Walde (2024) do cross-lingual metaphor DETECTION (token classification via adapters), and Berger & Scheffler (2025) operationalize conceptual metaphor via parallel-corpus translation clustering. Neither studies the internal MECHANISM of figurative comprehension in LLMs. Mechanistic multilingual work locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS (Wang 2025; Lim 2025), for problem DIFFICULTY (Civelli et al. 2026), and for cross-lingual correctness via middle-layer alignment and patching (Ravisankar et al. 2025), but none address FIGURATIVE meaning, the literal-vs-figurative computation, or whether conceptual-metaphor sharedness governs transfer. Monolingual interpretability of idioms exists in isolated studies but does not test cross-lingual sharedness. This proposal is the first to (i) test a literal-first-then-figurative processing account cross-lingually, (ii) tie figurative transfer/interference to conceptual-metaphor sharedness (a linguistically-grounded, codable property), and (iii) causally steer the literal<->figurative resolution. It is distinct from all my prior proposals (facts, reasoning-language, contested facts, temporal, code-switch binding, number magnitude, logical operators): the object of study is figurative/idiomatic meaning and its cross-lingual conceptual grounding.
Abstract: Idioms and conceptual metaphors express meaning through a source domain ("spill the beans", "time is money") that must be resolved to a figurative target meaning. Some conceptual metaphors are shared across many languages (ANGER-IS-HEAT), while others are language-specific. We ask how a multilingual LLM comprehends figurative language internally: does it first compute the literal source-domain meaning and only later resolve the figurative meaning, and does the sharedness of the underlying conceptual metaphor determine whether figurative meaning transfers across languages? We introduce IdiomProbe, a set of parallel idiom-comprehension items across 8 typologically diverse languages, each annotated with (a) the correct figurative meaning, (b) a literal-meaning distractor, and (c) a cross-lingual conceptual-metaphor sharedness score derived from documented metaphor inventories. Behaviorally, we measure figurative-vs-literal comprehension accuracy per language and test whether errors concentrate on language-specific idioms. Using logit-lens/tuned-lens we test the literal-first-then-figurative hypothesis by tracking when literal source-domain tokens versus figurative-target tokens dominate across layers, defining a per-item literal-to-figurative transition depth. We test whether this transition depth predicts comprehension and correlates with sharedness, and whether shared-metaphor idioms resolve in a language-independent middle-layer space (via cross-lingual representation similarity and activation patching) while language-specific idioms do not. In a decisive causal test, we derive a figurative-resolution steering vector and show it can force correct figurative reading of mis-comprehended idioms and, in reverse, induce literal mis-readings. We reframe multilingual figurative-language gaps as a measurable, steerable property of the internal literal-to-figurative resolution process grounded in conceptual-metaphor sharedness.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically/script-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Turkish). MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (IdiomProbe): Curate ~500 idiom/conceptual-metaphor items. For each: a comprehension probe in multiple-choice or cloze form ('X "spilled the beans" means: (a) revealed a secret [figurative], (b) dropped legumes [literal], (c) unrelated distractor'), the correct figurative answer, a literal-meaning distractor, and the idiom's source/target domains. Code a SHAREDNESS score per idiom (0-2) using documented conceptual-metaphor inventories (MetaNet/master-metaphor lists) and cross-lingual attestation: shared (same conceptual metaphor lexicalized in most languages), partially shared, language-specific. Translate/adapt each item into all 8 languages with native verification; where an idiom does not exist in a language, mark it as such (enabling zero-transfer analysis). Include a LITERAL-CONTROL stratum: sentences using the same content words literally.
3) BEHAVIORAL MEASUREMENT: Figurative-comprehension accuracy and literal-distractor error rate per language and per sharedness bin. Hypothesis: language-specific idioms show higher literal-distractor errors and larger cross-lingual accuracy variance; shared-metaphor idioms transfer (high accuracy across languages). Mixed-effects logistic regression of error on (sharedness, language, resource tier via URIEL); test sharedness predicts transfer beyond resource level.
4) LITERAL-FIRST-THEN-FIGURATIVE TEST: Apply logit-lens/tuned-lens at each layer; track relative dominance of literal-meaning tokens vs figurative-meaning tokens across depth. Define per-item literal-to-figurative TRANSITION DEPTH (layer where figurative overtakes literal). Hypothesis: literal source-domain meaning dominates early, figurative later; transition is earlier/cleaner for shared-metaphor idioms and delayed/absent for language-specific ones and for mis-comprehended items. Compare against literal-control stratum (should show no figurative overtaking).
5) TRANSITION-DEPTH PREDICTS COMPREHENSION & CORRELATES WITH SHAREDNESS: Correlate transition depth (and whether the transition occurs at all) with comprehension accuracy and with sharedness score, within and across languages (Spearman). Positive links support the processing account.
6) SHARED-SPACE RESOLUTION: For shared vs language-specific idioms, measure cross-lingual representation similarity at the (hypothesized figurative-resolution) middle layers across parallel items (CKA / cosine). Hypothesis: shared-metaphor idioms converge to a language-independent representation post-transition; language-specific ones remain language-warped. Cross-check with activation patching: patch middle-layer activations of a correctly-comprehending language into a mis-comprehending language's run for the same idiom and test whether it flips to the correct figurative answer (following Ravisankar et al.'s patching paradigm), and whether this works more for shared than language-specific idioms.
7) LOCALIZE FIGURATIVE-RESOLUTION COMPONENTS: Via activation/path patching between a figurative-reading run and its matched literal-control run, sweep layers/heads/MLPs to find the minimal components whose patching flips literal<->figurative resolution. Report layer distribution relative to the transition depth and to the language-transition band (validated via per-layer language-ID probes).
8) CAUSAL STEERING (decisive): Derive a figurative-resolution steering vector via difference-of-means over the localized components (figurative-correct runs minus literal-reading runs). Test (i) FORCING FIGURATIVE: adding it to mis-comprehended idiom runs increases correct figurative answers; (ii) INDUCING LITERAL: subtracting it makes the model produce literal mis-readings on well-comprehended idioms; (iii) it works cross-lingually and more strongly for shared idioms; (iv) it does not degrade literal-control comprehension or general QA. Metrics: figurative-correction rate, literal-induction rate, off-target damage, output fluency/language fidelity.
9) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress transition depth and steering efficacy on sharedness and URIEL distance; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); domain generality (spatial vs emotion vs economic metaphors); token-pooling and layer sensitivity; robustness across templates and MC-vs-cloze formats.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: figurative-comprehension accuracy & literal-error rate, cross-lingual transfer variance, literal-to-figurative transition depth, transition-comprehension and transition-sharedness correlations, cross-lingual representation similarity (CKA), patch-induced flip rate, figurative-component locus, causal steering figurative-correction and literal-induction rates, off-target/retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Sharedness coding requires linguistic care; we predefine it from documented conceptual-metaphor inventories and cross-lingual attestation to avoid post-hoc fitting, and report inter-annotator agreement. 2) Some models may resolve figurative meaning very early with no observable literal stage (idioms memorized as units); this itself is an informative finding (holistic vs compositional processing) and we quantify how often a literal stage is present, contrasting memorized vs novel/rare idioms. 3) Logit-lens tracking of literal vs figurative tokens is noisy for multi-token meanings; we prefer short single-token-decodable answer options and validate with tuned-lens and the MC-answer-token probability. 4) Multiple-choice framing can leak surface cues; we include cloze and free-generation variants and match distractor surface forms. 5) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test 5 models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 6) Causal steering may trade off literal-control accuracy or fluency; we report off-target damage and retention rather than claiming a free lunch. 7) Confound with idiom training frequency: rare idioms in low-resource languages may fail for frequency reasons; we control with URIEL tiers and use the literal-control stratum (same words, frequency-matched) as a within-item baseline. 8) Distinguishing genuine conceptual transfer from translation-of-a-known-answer requires the language-specific/non-existent-idiom items, which have no correct figurative answer to translate; strong performance there would indicate genuine compositional figurative resolution.

Name: intra_language_script_knowledge_fragmentation
Title: Same Language, Wrong Script: Is a Model's Knowledge and Reasoning Fragmented Across the Scripts of a Single Language, and Can a Script-Steering Vector Repair It?
Short Hypothesis: Holding language, meaning, and typology fixed and varying only the writing script (e.g., Serbian Cyrillic vs Latin, Hindi Devanagari vs romanized, Urdu Perso-Arabic vs romanized, Japanese kanji/kana vs romaji), a multilingual LLM does NOT access the same knowledge or reasoning competence in both scripts. We hypothesize (1) factual accuracy and multi-step reasoning for the SAME language differ systematically by script, with one script (usually the higher-frequency native or the Latin form) acting as a privileged 'knowledge-bearing' orthography; (2) this fragmentation arises because the disadvantaged script only weakly reaches the shared semantic/knowledge subspace, measurable as reduced cross-script representation convergence at mid layers; and (3) because prior work shows a single linear script-routing direction and late-layer heads mediate script, we can causally REPAIR the disadvantaged script's access to knowledge by steering its mid-layer representation onto the privileged script's manifold, recovering accuracy WITHOUT translating or changing the surface script the user sees.
Related Work: Recent mechanistic work on script shows LLMs latently romanize during transliteration, that scripts of the same language become increasingly separable across layers, that a single linear direction flips output script while 'largely maintaining semantic content', and that late-layer attention heads causally mediate script choice (Gurgurov et al. 2026 'The Latin Substrate'; Shim et al. 2026 in speech models). Transliteration-alignment work (TransliCo, TransMI, PPA, Xhelili 2024, Ebing 2026) improves cross-lingual transfer by unifying scripts but studies DOWNSTREAM task transfer across DIFFERENT languages, not within-language knowledge access. Ifergan et al. 2024 show script similarity dominates cross-lingual knowledge sharing but across different languages, not across scripts of ONE language. Critically, all prior mechanistic script work asks WHERE/HOW script is routed and whether meaning is preserved for generation; NONE test whether the model's KNOWLEDGE and REASONING competence itself is script-fragmented within a single language, whether one script is a privileged knowledge carrier, or whether a script-steering vector can causally REPAIR factual/reasoning accuracy in a disadvantaged script. This isolates script from language/typology entirely (same-language minimal pairs), a control no prior study exploits, and reframes script from a surface-routing phenomenon into a knowledge-access bottleneck.
Abstract: Many languages are written in more than one script: Serbian in Cyrillic and Latin, Hindi in Devanagari and romanized form, Urdu in Perso-Arabic and Latin, Japanese in kanji/kana and romaji. This yields a rare experimental control: identical language, meaning, and typology, with only the writing script varying. We ask whether a multilingual LLM accesses the same knowledge and reasoning competence regardless of script, or whether its competence is fragmented, with one script acting as a privileged knowledge carrier. We build ScriptSplit, parallel same-language factual-probing and multi-step reasoning items rendered in each of a language's scripts (5 multi-script languages), verified for meaning-equivalence. Behaviorally, we measure per-script factual accuracy and reasoning accuracy and test for a systematic script advantage beyond mere tokenization length. Representationally, using logit-lens and mid-layer cross-script representation similarity (CKA/cosine), we test whether the disadvantaged script under-converges to the shared semantic subspace where knowledge is decoded. Mechanistically, we relate this to the single linear script direction and late-layer script-mediating heads reported in recent work. In a decisive causal test, we derive a script-repair intervention that steers the disadvantaged-script representation onto the privileged script's mid-layer manifold and show it recovers factual and reasoning accuracy while the user-visible output script is unchanged, distinguishing a knowledge-access bottleneck from surface degradation. We further test whether a single repair direction generalizes across facts, reasoning problems, and languages. Our work reframes multi-script support as a measurable, repairable knowledge-access problem rather than a surface-rendering issue.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 5 languages that are natively/commonly written in multiple scripts, giving same-language minimal pairs: Serbian (Cyrillic/Latin), Hindi (Devanagari/romanized), Urdu (Perso-Arabic/romanized), Kazakh (Cyrillic/Latin), Japanese (kanji+kana / romaji). MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (ScriptSplit): (a) FACT stratum: ~400 factual-probing items per language (adapted from mLAMA/BMLAMA and Wikidata) with short, decodable answers, rendered in each script via high-quality rule-based transliterators plus native verification of meaning-equivalence; answers recorded in a script-agnostic normalized form for scoring. (b) REASONING stratum: ~200 multi-step items per language (math word problems adapted from MGSM, and 2-3 hop factual reasoning) rendered in each script. (c) TOKENIZATION CONTROL: record token counts per script per item to disentangle length effects.
3) BEHAVIORAL MEASUREMENT: Per-script factual accuracy and reasoning accuracy.
