Test for a systematic script advantage (Wilcoxon signed-rank on paired items) and identify the privileged script per language/model. Mixed-effects regression of correctness on (script, token-length, item difficulty) to show the script effect survives controlling for tokenization length. Report per-language script-accuracy gaps.
4) REPRESENTATIONAL CONVERGENCE: For meaning-equivalent script pairs of the same item, compute mid-layer cross-script representation similarity (CKA and per-item cosine) at the answer/last-content position across layers. Hypothesis: the disadvantaged script under-converges to the privileged script's mid-layer representation, and per-item convergence predicts whether the disadvantaged script answers correctly. Use logit-lens to test whether the disadvantaged script latently romanizes/normalizes toward the privileged form and how late.
5) CONVERGENCE-PREDICTS-ACCURACY LINK: Within each language, correlate per-item cross-script convergence (step 4) with the disadvantaged script's correctness (step 3). A positive link supports a knowledge-access bottleneck: knowledge is present but not reached in the weak script.
6) LOCALIZE & RELATE TO SCRIPT MECHANISM: Identify the linear script-steering direction and late-layer script-mediating heads (following Gurgurov 2026 / Shim 2026 methodology) for each model. Test whether these components are the same ones whose intervention changes knowledge access, or whether knowledge repair requires steering at EARLIER mid layers than surface script control (dissociating surface-script routing from knowledge-manifold access).
7) CAUSAL SCRIPT-REPAIR (decisive): Derive a repair transform (difference-of-means or low-rank map) that maps the disadvantaged-script mid-layer representation of an item onto the privileged script's manifold at the localized layer. Apply at inference on held-out items and test: (i) factual and reasoning accuracy in the disadvantaged script increases toward the privileged-script level; (ii) the user-visible OUTPUT script/language is unchanged (fidelity check) — showing repair is about internal knowledge access, not surface transliteration; (iii) already-correct and privileged-script items are unharmed; (iv) no degradation on unrelated general QA. Metrics: disadvantaged-script accuracy recovery, output-script fidelity, off-target damage, retention.
8) GENERALIZATION: Test whether a single repair direction estimated on FACT items transfers to REASONING items and across languages sharing a script family (e.g., a Cyrillic-to-Latin repair vector from Serbian applied to Kazakh), quantifying how language-agnostic the knowledge-access gate is.
9) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: privileged-script identity vs per-script pretraining frequency proxies and tokenization efficiency; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); layer/dimension sensitivity; transliterator-fidelity robustness; short vs long reasoning chains.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-script factual & reasoning accuracy and script-gap, tokenization-controlled regression coefficients, mid-layer cross-script convergence (CKA/cosine), convergence-accuracy correlation, localized-component locus and layer relative to surface-script gate, causal repair accuracy-recovery, output-script fidelity, off-target/retention, cross-item/cross-language repair-vector transfer.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Transliteration fidelity: automatic transliterators can introduce noise or lossy mappings (esp. Japanese kanji->romaji, Urdu vowels); we use high-fidelity rule-based transliterators, native verification of meaning-equivalence, and report sensitivity to transliterator choice; morphosyllabic scripts are analyzed separately. 2) Tokenization confound: the disadvantaged script may simply tokenize into more/rarer tokens; we control for token length in regression and treat length-matched subsets, and show the causal repair (which does not change tokenization) still recovers accuracy, dissociating length from knowledge access. 3) Some models may internally normalize both scripts to a shared form early, showing little fragmentation; this itself is an informative finding (early script-invariant knowledge access) and we quantify how often fragmentation is present. 4) Frequency confound: the privileged script is likely the higher-frequency training form; we cannot fully separate frequency from script identity, but the within-language minimal-pair design removes language/typology confounds and we report frequency proxies transparently. 5) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test 5 models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 6) The repair may trade some accuracy elsewhere or harm fluency; we explicitly report off-target damage, retention, and output-script fidelity rather than claiming a free lunch. 7) Overlap with recent script-mechanism papers (Gurgurov 2026, Shim 2026) requires clear differentiation; we include their script direction/heads as baselines and show the novel contribution is the KNOWLEDGE/REASONING fragmentation and its causal repair, which they do not study.

Name: grammatical_gender_concept_leakage
Title: Is a Bridge Masculine? Grammatical Gender Leaking Into the Conceptual Representation of Objects in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs do not represent inanimate object concepts in a fully gender-neutral, language-independent way. Instead, the grammatical gender that a language arbitrarily assigns to a noun leaks into the model's internal conceptual representation of that object, biasing (1) the associative/adjectival attributes the model ascribes to it, (2) downstream inferences and pronoun/anaphora choices about it, in ways that (3) systematically differ across languages that assign opposite genders to the same object and disappear for genderless languages, and (4) can be isolated as a low-dimensional 'gender-leakage' direction that is causally steerable and correctable without harming factual knowledge about the object.
Related Work: Classic psycholinguistics (Boroditsky et al. 2003) showed humans describe objects using attributes stereotypically consistent with their native language's grammatical gender (e.g., German 'bridge'=feminine -> 'beautiful, elegant'; Spanish 'bridge'=masculine -> 'strong, sturdy'). In NLP, gender-bias work overwhelmingly targets SOCIAL/animate gender (occupations, coreference like WinoMT/WinoBias) and mitigation of stereotypes about people. Cross-lingual representation work locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts (Wang 2025; Lim 2025). A few papers note gendered-noun agreement errors in translation, and my prior code-switch-binding proposal studied which language's morphosyntax drives AGREEMENT during code-switching. NONE test whether GRAMMATICAL (arbitrary, inanimate) gender contaminates the SEMANTIC/CONCEPTUAL representation of the object itself, whether this reproduces the Boroditsky effect inside LLMs cross-lingually, whether it is a localizable low-dimensional direction, or whether it can be causally steered/removed. This reframes a linguistic-relativity question as a mechanistic, causal probe of language-specific interference in an otherwise shared concept space, and uses genderless languages (Turkish, Finnish, Hungarian, English) and opposite-gender language pairs as clean controls no prior LLM study exploits.
Abstract: Grammatical gender assigns an arbitrary gender to inanimate nouns (German 'Bridge' is feminine, Spanish 'Puente' is masculine), a purely formal property with no semantic content. Classic psycholinguistics found that this arbitrary assignment nonetheless shapes how humans conceptualize objects. We ask whether the same leakage occurs inside multilingual LLMs: does the grammatical gender of a noun contaminate the model's internal conceptual representation of the object, and can we isolate and causally control it? We assemble GenderLeak, a set of inanimate objects with documented opposite grammatical genders across language pairs (e.g., Spanish vs German), plus genderless-language controls (English, Turkish, Finnish, Hungarian). Behaviorally, we test whether the model ascribes stereotypically masculine/feminine attributes, pronouns, and inferences to an object in a manner predicted by that language's grammatical gender, and whether the effect flips across opposite-gender languages and vanishes in genderless ones. Representationally, we probe for a 'grammatical-gender' direction at the object's hidden state and measure how strongly an inanimate concept's representation is displaced along it as a function of the noun's gender, contrasting shared-concept-space layers with language-specific ones. In a decisive causal test, we steer along the identified gender-leakage direction to flip an object's ascribed attributes and pronoun choices, and derive a corrective projection that removes the leakage while preserving factual knowledge about the object. We relate leakage strength to typological distance and to whether languages agree on a noun's gender. Our work turns a linguistic-relativity question into a mechanistic, causal account of language-specific interference in a shared concept space.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: Gendered languages with contrasting assignments (Spanish, French, Italian, German, Russian, Hindi) and GENDERLESS controls (English, Turkish, Finnish, Hungarian). MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (GenderLeak): Curate ~300 concrete inanimate objects (bridge, key, spoon, moon, sun, table, clock, apple...). For each, record the grammatical gender of its noun in every gendered language (from dictionaries), creating OPPOSITE-GENDER pairs (objects that are masculine in one language, feminine in another) and AGREE pairs (same gender across languages) as a within-item contrast. Build three probe types per object per language: (A) ATTRIBUTE elicitation: ask the model to list adjectives describing the object; score each adjective on a masculine/feminine stereotype axis using a pre-rated adjective lexicon (independently gender-rated, following Boroditsky-style norms). (B) FORCED-CHOICE: 'Is the {object} more like a warrior or a ballerina?' / gendered-attribute minimal pairs. (C) PRONOUN/ANAPHORA: in genderless-language (English) prompts about the object, measure the model's tendency to refer to it as 'he' vs 'she' vs 'it' when the object concept was primed in a gendered language. Native verification of all templates.
3) BEHAVIORAL BOR­ODITSKY TEST: For each object, test whether the masculinity/femininity of ascribed attributes (type A/B) correlates with the noun's grammatical gender in the query language. KEY within-item design: for OPPOSITE-GENDER objects, test whether the SAME object flips its ascribed gender-stereotyped attributes when queried in the masculine-assigning vs feminine-assigning language. Genderless-language controls should show no systematic shift. Statistics: mixed-effects regression of attribute-masculinity on (grammatical gender, language, object), with object as random effect; test the gender coefficient and the opposite-pair flip.
4) CROSS-LINGUAL LEAKAGE MAGNITUDE: Quantify per-object cross-lingual DISAGREEMENT in ascribed gender attributes and relate it to whether languages assign the noun opposite genders (predicted high disagreement) vs the same gender (low). Show genderless languages cluster near neutral.
5) REPRESENTATIONAL GENDER DIRECTION: Extract hidden states at the object noun/last-content position. Train a linear probe to decode grammatical gender of the noun; obtain the 'grammatical-gender direction' per layer. Measure the object concept's projection onto this direction and test whether it (i) tracks the noun's grammatical gender, (ii) is stronger in language-specific late layers than in the shared mid-layer concept space (relate to the language-transition band via per-layer language-ID probes), and (iii) per-object projection magnitude predicts the behavioral attribute shift (step 3).
6) LEAKAGE-PREDICTS-BEHAVIOR LINK: Correlate per-object representational projection onto the gender direction with per-object behavioral attribute-masculinity, within and across languages. A positive link supports genuine conceptual leakage rather than surface lexical priming.
7) CAUSAL STEERING (decisive): Derive a gender-leakage steering vector via difference-of-means (masculine-noun object states minus feminine-noun object states, controlling for the shared concept). (a) FLIP: add/subtract it on held-out objects and test whether ascribed attributes and pronoun choices flip masculine<->feminine while the object's IDENTITY and factual knowledge stay intact. (b) CORRECT: derive a projection that removes the gender direction from the object representation and test whether it neutralizes the cross-lingual attribute disagreement (making a bridge described the same way regardless of query language) WITHOUT degrading factual QA about the object (e.g., 'What is a bridge used for?'). Metrics: attribute-flip rate, pronoun-flip rate, cross-lingual disagreement reduction after correction, factual-QA retention, off-target damage.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress leakage strength on URIEL typological distance and on gender-system type (2-gender vs 3-gender vs noun-class); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); layer/dimension sensitivity; token-pooling; robustness across templates and elicitation formats; test whether a single gender direction generalizes across objects and across languages.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: attribute-masculinity gender coefficient and opposite-pair flip, cross-lingual attribute disagreement vs gender-agreement, gender-direction probe accuracy and per-object projection, projection-behavior correlation, causal flip/pronoun-flip rates, correction-induced disagreement reduction, factual-QA retention, off-target damage, typology/gender-system regression coefficients.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The effect may be driven by surface lexical priming (gendered articles/agreement in the prompt) rather than a deep conceptual representation; we mitigate with a critical control that primes the object concept in a gendered language but ELICITS attributes in a genderless language (English), removing surface gender cues, and by using the representational-projection-predicts-behavior link (step 6) as evidence beyond surface form. 2) Adjective gender-stereotype ratings are subjective; we use independently pre-rated lexicons, report inter-rater agreement, and use forced-choice minimal pairs (type B) as a rating-free complement. 3) Some models may show no leakage (gender-neutral concept space); this is itself an informative, publishable finding about the cleanliness of the shared concept space, and we quantify how often leakage is present. 4) Grammatical-gender assignment is confounded with word frequency and morphology; the within-item opposite-gender design and genderless controls remove object-identity confounds, and we report frequency proxies. 5) Probing linearity assumptions may not hold; we validate the gender direction on animate nouns with natural gender as a positive control and report low-dimensional structure. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test 5 models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) The corrective projection may harm fluency or factual knowledge; we explicitly report factual-QA retention and off-target damage rather than claiming a free lunch. 8) Distinguishing our contribution from social-gender-bias work is essential; we focus exclusively on INANIMATE arbitrary grammatical gender, which has no semantic ground truth, making any systematic effect clear evidence of leakage.

Name: crosslingual_knowledge_state_calibration
Title: Does the Model Know What It Doesn't Know in Every Language? A Shared Internal Knowledge-State Signal, Its Language-Specific Distortion, and Causal Calibration Repair
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs compute a largely language-independent internal 'knowledge-state' signal (a direction that separates facts the model actually knows from facts it does not) in their shared middle layers, but this signal is systematically DISTORTED and ATTENUATED at the language-transition/final layers for non-English queries, producing the well-documented non-English overconfidence. We hypothesize (1) a single mid-layer knowledge-state probe trained on English transfers zero-shot to predict correctness in many languages, showing the know/don't-know signal is shared; (2) the per-language calibration gap is explained by how much this shared signal is corrupted between the mid layer and the output, not by the mid-layer signal itself; and (3) we can CAUSALLY REPAIR calibration in a low-resource language by transplanting/steering the mid-layer knowledge-state direction into the language-specific decoding path, recovering calibration WITHOUT changing the produced answer.
Related Work: Recent work establishes the BEHAVIORAL multilingual calibration gap: Krause et al. 2023 and Huang et al. 2026 show non-English overconfidence and that high-resource SFT inflates confidence without accuracy gains; Zhou et al. 2025 ('Beyond the Final Layer') show non-English calibration is worse and that late-INTERMEDIATE layers carry a better-calibrated signal, proposing a training-free layer-ensemble (LACE) that adaptively picks layers per language. Broad UQ surveys (Liu et al. 2025) and self-consistency/verbalized-confidence methods treat calibration monolingually. Separately, mechanistic multilingual work shows facts live in a shared concept space with language-specific decoding (Wang 2025; Lim 2025). Our proposal is distinct: (a) we reframe calibration as a shared 'knowledge-state' (know vs not-know) signal and test cross-lingual TRANSFER of a single mid-layer probe as evidence of language-independence — Zhou et al. only ensemble per-language layers and never test a shared transferable knowledge direction; (b) we give a MECHANISTIC decomposition attributing the calibration gap to signal DISTORTION between mid and final layers (a measurable degradation), not merely to which layer is best; and (c) we provide a CAUSAL repair via activation transplant/steering of the knowledge-state direction that improves non-English calibration while leaving answers unchanged — a causal intervention absent from all prior (correlational/ensembling/prompting) work. This converts 'non-English is miscalibrated' into 'the model already knows internally; the signal is corrupted late and can be causally restored.'
Abstract: Multilingual language models are systematically overconfident in non-English languages, but why remains unclear: do they simply lack a reliable internal sense of what they know in those languages, or do they possess it and lose it before it reaches the output? We argue for the latter and make it mechanistically precise. We hypothesize that models compute a largely language-independent internal knowledge-state signal in their shared middle layers that separates facts they truly know from facts they do not, and that the multilingual calibration gap arises because this signal is distorted and attenuated in the language-specific final layers, more so for non-English queries. We test three claims. First, a single linear knowledge-state probe trained only on English mid-layer activations transfers zero-shot to predict per-fact correctness across many languages, evidencing a shared know/don't-know direction. Second, we decompose each language's calibration error into a mid-layer component and a mid-to-output distortion component, and show the distortion component, not the mid-layer signal, explains the non-English gap and correlates with typological/resource distance. Third, in a decisive causal test we transplant or steer the mid-layer knowledge-state direction into the language-specific decoding path of low-resource queries and show it restores calibration (lower ECE, higher AUROC of correctness) while leaving the produced answer and surface language unchanged. Across mLAMA-style factual probing and multilingual QA over 15+ languages and five open models, our work reframes multilingual miscalibration as a recoverable late-stage distortion of an already-present internal signal.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & DATA: Models Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + light probing/patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). Data: mLAMA/BMLAMA short-answer factual probing and multilingual QA (e.g., translated TriviaQA / MKQA-style) across 15+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/CJK/Arabic/Devanagari and multiple families/resource tiers. For each (fact, language) obtain a correctness label (answer matches gold) and the model's verbalized/token-probability confidence.
2) EXTRACT KNOWLEDGE-STATE SIGNAL: At each layer, pool the hidden state at the answer-relevant position. Train a simple logistic-regression 'knowledge-state probe' on ENGLISH data to predict correctness (know vs not-know). Select the best mid-layer via English validation.
3) SHARED-SIGNAL TRANSFER TEST (claim 1): Apply the English-trained mid-layer probe zero-shot to every other language and measure AUROC of predicting per-fact correctness. Baselines: (a) the model's own verbalized confidence, (b) max token probability, (c) final-layer probe. Hypothesis: the English mid-layer probe transfers well (high AUROC) across languages, and beats verbalized confidence and the final-layer signal, evidencing a language-independent knowledge-state direction. Also test a per-language-trained probe to bound the shared-vs-specific gap.
4) LOCATE LANGUAGE-TRANSITION BAND: Use per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens (following Wang 2025) to identify where representations move from shared to language-specific, to anchor the mid vs final decomposition.
5) CALIBRATION-GAP DECOMPOSITION (claim 2): For each language compute (i) MID calibration: reliability/ECE and AUROC using the shared mid-layer knowledge-state score; (ii) OUTPUT calibration: ECE/AUROC of the model's actual emitted confidence. Define DISTORTION = degradation from mid to output (e.g., AUROC_mid - AUROC_output, and increase in ECE). Test whether per-language DISTORTION, not MID quality, explains the cross-lingual calibration gap. Correlate DISTORTION with URIEL typological distance from English and with resource tier (Spearman). Compare English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya).
6) MECHANISM OF DISTORTION: Via activation patching between an English run and a non-English run on matched facts the model KNOWS, patch mid-layer knowledge-state components forward and measure whether the emitted confidence's calibration is restored; sweep layers to identify where the signal is lost. Cross-check with path patching.
7) CAUSAL CALIBRATION REPAIR (claim 3, decisive): Derive a knowledge-state steering/transplant operator: at the localized layer, project the non-English representation onto the shared knowledge-state direction (or transplant the mid-layer knowledge-state component). Apply at inference on held-out non-English items and measure: (i) OUTPUT calibration (ECE down, AUROC of correctness up) toward English levels; (ii) ANSWER-INVARIANCE: the produced answer token and surface language are unchanged (fidelity check) — showing we fix confidence, not content; (iii) no accuracy degradation and no harm on already-well-calibrated English items; (iv) general-capability spot check (multilingual MMLU subset). Baselines: temperature scaling per language, LACE-style layer ensemble (Zhou 2025 reimplementation), verbalized-confidence prompting. Metrics: ECE, AUROC/AURC of correctness, Brier score, selective-prediction risk-coverage, answer-change rate.
8) ABLATIONS: probe layer and dimensionality; single shared direction vs low-rank subspace; high- vs low-resource targets; short-answer vs open QA; robustness across prompt templates; whether a single repair operator generalizes across languages and across datasets (facts -> QA).
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: cross-lingual probe-transfer AUROC, per-language MID vs OUTPUT calibration and DISTORTION, distortion-vs-typology/resource correlations, patch-localized loss layer, causal repair ECE/AUROC/Brier improvement, answer-invariance rate, accuracy/general retention, comparison to temperature scaling / LACE / verbalized confidence.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Some models may genuinely lack a good mid-layer knowledge-state signal in low-resource languages (signal absent, not distorted); this is an informative outcome and we quantify per-language how much of the deficit is MID vs DISTORTION. 2) Correctness labeling for open-ended answers is noisy in low-resource languages; we anchor on short-answer factual probing with normalized matching and restrict causal-repair analysis to reliably-labeled items. 3) The English-trained probe transferring could be confounded by shared latent romanization/pivoting; we report per-language transfer and compare against per-language-trained probes to bound this. 4) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 5) Calibration repair may trade accuracy or fluency; we explicitly report answer-change rate, accuracy retention, and general-capability spot checks rather than claiming a free lunch. 6) Overlap with Zhou et al. 2025 (layer-wise multilingual calibration) requires clear differentiation; we include their LACE as a baseline and position our contribution as the shared transferable knowledge-state direction, the mid-to-output distortion decomposition, and the causal answer-preserving repair, none of which they provide. 7) A single global knowledge-state direction may be an oversimplification; we test low-rank subspace variants and report where a scalar direction is insufficient.

Name: language_modulated_context_trust
Title: Whose Word Does It Take? Query Language as a Trust Dial in Context-vs-Memory Knowledge Conflicts, and the Language-Modulation of Memory/Context Heads
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM faces a conflict between a retrieved context and its own parametric memory, the query language causally shifts WHICH source it trusts: the same 'memory heads' and 'context heads' that arbitrate conflicts operate with language-dependent gains, so a fact the model stubbornly retains from memory in English can be overridden by the same conflicting context when queried in a low-resource language (and vice versa). We hypothesize (1) context-vs-memory reliance is a systematic, predictable function of query language and language-of-context, tracking resource/typological distance; (2) this arises because query language modulates the relative activation of a small, shared set of memory vs context heads rather than creating new circuitry; and (3) we can causally equalize the trust dial across languages by rescaling those heads' contributions, without retraining, closing the cross-lingual faithfulness gap.
Related Work: Mechanistic conflict work (Jin et al. 2024 PH3; Li et al. 2025 JuICE superposition; Farahani & Johansson 2024; Wadhwa et al. 2024; Pham et al. 2026) identifies memory vs context attention heads and their arbitration, but is ENTIRELY English/monolingual and never asks whether the arbitration itself is language-dependent. Behavioral training-data work (Kim et al. 2025) and the three-regime framework (Venkata 2026) explain context-vs-memory reliance via confidence/coherence but ignore query language as a variable. Very recent multilingual conflict benchmarks (CLEAR 2026; 'When Abundance Conceals Weakness' Zhao et al. 2026; Park & Lee 2025 mRAG language preference) show BEHAVIORALLY that conflict resolution depends on language resource/affinity, but offer NO mechanism, no head-level account, and no causal intervention. Our proposal is the first to (a) frame query language as a causal 'trust dial' over the SAME memory/context heads found in monolingual mechanistic work, (b) show these heads are language-MODULATED rather than language-specific, and (c) provide a training-free head-rescaling intervention that equalizes context-trust across languages. This unifies the mechanistic conflict literature with multilingual representation and turns behavioral observations into a causal, steerable mechanism.
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented models must constantly decide whether to trust a retrieved passage or their own parametric memory. Prior mechanistic work localized this arbitration to a small set of 'memory heads' and 'context heads' in later layers, but only in English. We ask a simple question: is that decision language-dependent? We hypothesize that the query language acts as a causal 'trust dial'—the same fact the model stubbornly recalls from memory when asked in English can be overridden by an identical counterfactual context when asked in a low-resource language, because query language modulates the relative gain of shared memory versus context heads rather than invoking separate circuitry. We build CrossTrust, a set of counterfactual knowledge-conflict items (a factual question, the model's known parametric answer, and a context asserting a different answer) rendered across 12 typologically and resource-diverse languages, crossing query language with context language. Behaviorally, we measure per-language memory-recall vs context-following rates and test whether they track resource level and typological distance beyond accuracy. Mechanistically, we identify memory/context heads via path patching in English and test whether the SAME heads carry the arbitration in other languages, quantifying how their relative activation shifts with query language. In a decisive causal test, we rescale these heads' contributions to equalize the context-trust dial across languages and show it closes the cross-lingual faithfulness gap—making the model equally willing to accept correct context regardless of query language—without retraining and while preserving accuracy on non-conflict items. Our work reframes multilingual RAG unfaithfulness as a language-modulated, mechanistically tractable, and correctable arbitration process.
Experiments: 1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + path patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/CJK/Arabic/Devanagari and high/mid/low resource tiers (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili, Indonesian, Yoruba). 2) DATASET (CrossTrust): ~500 factual items with short decodable answers (from mLAMA/BMLAMA/Wikidata). For each, verify the model KNOWS the fact (correct closed-book answer) so a genuine conflict exists, then build a COUNTERFACTUAL context asserting a different plausible answer. Cross query language x context language (native-verified translations). Include a NON-CONFLICT control where context agrees with memory, and a MEMORY-UNKNOWN stratum (model does not know the fact) to separate conflict from gap-filling. 3) BEHAVIORAL TRUST-DIAL MEASUREMENT: Per (query-language, context-language) compute Memory-Recall rate (answer = parametric) vs Context-Following rate (answer = counterfactual context). Test with mixed-effects logistic regression whether query language predicts context-following controlling for item and for whether the model knew the fact; correlate per-language context-following with URIEL typological distance and resource tier. Hypothesis: low-resource query languages defer to context more; cross-language (query!=context) increases conflict differently by distance. 4) LOCATE MEMORY/CONTEXT HEADS (English): Use path patching / attention knockout (following Jin 2024, Wadhwa 2024) to identify heads that promote memory vs context on conflict items in English. 5) SAME-CIRCUIT-OR-NEW TEST: Apply the English-identified heads' knockout in every other language and measure whether context-following changes as expected. Quantify per-language the relative activation/contribution of these SAME heads on matched conflict items. Hypothesis: the heads are shared but their relative gain shifts with query language (language modulates, not replaces). Report head-contribution differences vs behavioral trust-dial shift correlation; test whether a small handful of heads explains the cross-lingual variance. Cross-check with JuICE-style superposition analysis. 6) CAUSAL EQUALIZATION (decisive): Derive a per-language head-rescaling that sets the memory/context head balance to a reference (e.g., English or a target trust level). Apply at inference and test: (i) context-following rate for CORRECT-context items rises to reference level in low-resource languages (closing the faithfulness gap); (ii) memory-recall for cases where memory is correct and context is wrong is preserved (no blind context-trust); (iii) NON-CONFLICT and MEMORY-UNKNOWN controls and general multilingual QA (MMLU subset) are unharmed; (iv) surface output language unchanged. Baselines: CK-PLUG (Bi 2025), contrastive decoding (CoCoA/AdaCAD), per-language temperature, and translate-context-to-English (CrossRAG). Metrics: context-following/memory-recall rates, cross-lingual faithfulness gap, ECE of trust decisions, accuracy retention, off-target damage. 7) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: query-language vs context-language decomposition; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); number of heads needed; whether one rescaling generalizes across items and datasets; robustness to context plausibility and templates; layer distribution of the arbitrating heads relative to the language-transition band (validated via per-layer language-ID probes). EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language memory-recall vs context-following, trust-dial regression on resource/typology, shared-head knockout effects, head-contribution vs behavior correlation, causal equalization faithfulness-gap closure, correct-vs-wrong-context asymmetry, retention/off-target, baseline comparisons.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The 'model knows the fact' precondition is noisy in low-resource languages; we restrict conflict analysis to items verified correct closed-book per language and separately report the MEMORY-UNKNOWN stratum. 2) Counterfactual contexts must be plausible and equally fluent across languages; we use native verification and control for context plausibility ratings. 3) Some models may uniformly follow context (RAG shortcut, Wadhwa 2024), leaving little memory-recall to modulate—this is itself informative and we quantify per-language how contested the trust decision is. 4) Path-patching head identification can be model/template-specific; we test 5 models, multiple templates, and cross-check path patching with attention knockout and JuICE-style superposition analysis. 5) Head rescaling may trade blind context-trust for faithfulness; we explicitly report the correct-vs-wrong-context asymmetry and retention rather than claiming a free lunch. 6) Query vs context language effects are entangled; the crossed design and separate regressions isolate each. 7) Overlap with recent multilingual conflict benchmarks (CLEAR, Zhao 2026) requires clear differentiation; we include them as behavioral baselines and position our contribution as the head-level language-modulation mechanism and the causal equalization intervention, which they lack. 8) A single scalar per-head rescaling may be too coarse; we test low-rank/per-head-vector variants and report where a scalar dial is insufficient.

Name: crosslingual_implicature_directness_leakage
Title: Reading Between the Lines Across Languages: Does a Language's Directness Typology Leak Into How Multilingual Models Compute Pragmatic Implicature?
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM interprets an utterance requiring pragmatic enrichment (scalar implicature 'some'→'not all', indirect refusals, indirect requests), it first computes the LITERAL semantic meaning and only later derives the PRAGMATIC meaning, and the ease/accuracy of this derivation is systematically distorted by the query language's directness typology: in high-directness (low-context) languages the model over-relies on literal meaning and under-derives implicatures, whereas in high-context languages it does the reverse, producing predictable cross-lingual disagreement on the SAME utterance. We further hypothesize (1) a shared, largely language-independent 'pragmatic-enrichment' signal in middle layers that transfers across languages; (2) a measurable literal-to-pragmatic transition whose depth predicts comprehension and correlates with directness distance; and (3) a small, localizable set of components carrying the enrichment signal that can be causally steered to force or suppress pragmatic reading, distinguishing genuine language-independent pragmatic computation from surface memorization.
Related Work: Recent probing work (Braun 2026, J-PragEval) shows Japanese pragmatic contrasts (honorifics, zero anaphora, indirect refusal) are partly linearly decodable and partly worked out during generation in a single small model, and proposes parameter-free pragmatic steering — but it is MONOLINGUAL (Japanese only), studies register/reference rather than truth-conditional implicature, and never tests cross-lingual transfer or directness-typology leakage. Bangla honorific datasets (Shuvo 2026, BLADE) are fine-tuning/generation resources, not mechanistic. Mechanistic multilingual work locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) and for figurative meaning in my prior metaphor proposal, but NONE address pragmatic implicature, the literal-vs-pragmatic computation, or whether a language's directness/politeness typology (high- vs low-context, documented in pragmatics literature and codable) governs implicature derivation and cross-lingual transfer/interference. Monolingual NLP work on scalar implicature (e.g., IMPPRES-style entailment tests) is English-centric and non-mechanistic. This proposal is the first to (i) test a literal-first-then-pragmatic account of implicature cross-lingually, (ii) tie implicature derivation and its cross-lingual disagreement to directness typology, and (iii) causally localize and steer the pragmatic-enrichment signal, distinct from all my prior proposals (facts, reasoning-language, contested, temporal, code-switch, numbers, logic, metaphor, script, gender, calibration, context-trust).
Abstract: Human communication routinely means more than it literally says: 'some students passed' implies not all; 'my schedule is quite full' can politely refuse an invitation. Deriving these pragmatic enrichments is essential to comprehension, yet languages differ dramatically in how directly speakers convey meaning—some are high-context, favoring indirectness, others low-context and explicit. We ask how a multilingual LLM computes pragmatic implicature internally: does it first compute literal meaning and only later derive the pragmatic reading, and does a language's directness typology leak into that derivation, making the model over- or under-enrich the same utterance depending on query language? We build ImplicProbe, parallel implicature-comprehension items across 8 typologically and pragmatically diverse languages, covering scalar implicature, indirect refusals, and indirect requests, each annotated with the literal reading, the pragmatic reading, and a language-level directness score from pragmatics inventories. Behaviorally we measure pragmatic-vs-literal comprehension per language and test whether errors track directness distance. Using logit-lens/tuned-lens we test the literal-first-then-pragmatic account by tracking when literal versus pragmatic answer tokens dominate across layers, defining a per-item literal-to-pragmatic transition depth, and test whether it predicts comprehension and correlates with directness. We probe for a shared middle-layer enrichment signal and test cross-lingual transfer via a single probe and activation patching. In a decisive causal test we derive a pragmatic-enrichment steering vector and show it can force correct enrichment on under-enriched items and, in reverse, induce literal misreadings—establishing a common, steerable mechanism. We reframe multilingual pragmatic gaps as a measurable, typology-driven, correctable property of the internal literal-to-pragmatic resolution process.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically and pragmatically diverse languages spanning documented high-context/indirect (Japanese, Korean, Arabic, Hindi) and low-context/direct (English, German, Dutch, Russian) styles, coded via pragmatics-literature directness scales (Hall high/low-context; politeness typology) plus URIEL for typological distance. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (ImplicProbe): Curate ~500 implicature items in three strata: (A) SCALAR IMPLICATURE ('The teacher said some students passed. Did all students pass?' correct pragmatic answer: no/likely-not; literal-only answer: unknown), (B) INDIRECT REFUSAL ('A: Want to join dinner? B: I have an early meeting tomorrow.' Did B accept? pragmatic: no), (C) INDIRECT REQUEST/INFERENCE ('It's cold in here.' as a request to close a window). Each item has a comprehension probe (multiple-choice or yes/no), the correct PRAGMATIC answer, a LITERAL distractor, and a LITERAL-CONTROL variant where the same words carry only literal meaning. Translate/adapt each item into all 8 languages with native verification (ensuring the indirect form is natural in each language); mark items where an indirect form is unnatural to enable transfer-limit analysis. Draw on IMPPRES-style scalar templates where useful.
3) BEHAVIORAL MEASUREMENT: Pragmatic-comprehension accuracy and literal-distractor error rate per language and stratum. KEY hypothesis: low-directness (high-context) languages show more pragmatic enrichment (fewer literal errors) and direct languages more literal errors on the SAME item, yielding systematic cross-lingual disagreement. Mixed-effects logistic regression of error on (directness score, stratum, language, resource tier via URIEL); test directness predicts enrichment beyond resource level. Compare against LITERAL-CONTROL (should show no pragmatic overtaking).
4) LITERAL-FIRST-THEN-PRAGMATIC TEST: Apply logit-lens/tuned-lens per layer; track relative dominance of literal-answer vs pragmatic-answer tokens across depth. Define per-item literal-to-pragmatic TRANSITION DEPTH (layer where pragmatic overtakes literal). Hypothesis: literal meaning dominates early, pragmatic later; transition is earlier/cleaner in high-context languages and delayed/absent in direct languages and mis-comprehended items.
5) TRANSITION-DEPTH PREDICTS COMPREHENSION & CORRELATES WITH DIRECTNESS: Correlate transition depth (and whether it occurs) with comprehension accuracy and with directness score, within/across languages (Spearman). Positive links support the processing account.
6) SHARED ENRICHMENT SIGNAL & TRANSFER: Train a linear 'pragmatic-enrichment' probe (pragmatic vs literal reading) on ENGLISH mid-layer states; apply zero-shot to other languages and measure AUROC, evidencing a language-independent enrichment direction. Compare against per-language-trained probes. Cross-check with activation patching: patch mid-layer states of a correctly-enriching language into a mis-comprehending language's run for the same item and test whether it flips to the correct pragmatic answer (following shared-space patching paradigms).
7) LOCALIZE ENRICHMENT COMPONENTS: Via activation/path patching between a pragmatic-reading run and its matched literal-control run, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose patching flips literal<->pragmatic resolution. Report layer distribution relative to transition depth and to the language-transition band (validated via per-layer language-ID probes).
8) CAUSAL STEERING (decisive): Derive a pragmatic-enrichment steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (pragmatic-correct runs minus literal-reading runs). Test (i) FORCE ENRICHMENT: adding it to under-enriched items (esp. in direct languages) increases correct pragmatic answers; (ii) INDUCE LITERAL: subtracting it makes the model produce literal misreadings on well-comprehended items; (iii) it works cross-lingually and more strongly where enrichment was weak; (iv) it does not degrade literal-control comprehension or general QA. Metrics: pragmatic-correction rate, literal-induction rate, off-target damage, output fluency/language fidelity.
9) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress transition depth and steering efficacy on directness and URIEL distance; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); stratum generality (scalar vs indirect-speech); token-pooling and layer sensitivity; MC-vs-cloze-vs-free-generation formats; whether a single enrichment vector generalizes across strata and languages.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: pragmatic-comprehension accuracy & literal-error rate, cross-lingual disagreement, literal-to-pragmatic transition depth, transition-comprehension and transition-directness correlations, cross-lingual probe-transfer AUROC and patch flip rate, enrichment-component locus, causal steering pragmatic-correction and literal-induction rates, off-target/retention, directness/typology regression coefficients.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Directness typology coding is coarse and debated; we use documented pragmatics scales (Hall high/low-context, politeness typology) plus report robustness to alternative codings and treat it as a graded predictor, not ground truth. 2) Some models may resolve implicature very early or holistically (no literal stage), especially for memorized scalar items; this is itself an informative finding and we quantify how often a literal stage is present, contrasting common vs novel items and using the literal-control stratum. 3) Ground-truth pragmatic answers can be genuinely context-dependent (indirect refusals may be polite deferrals); we restrict scored items to those with clear native-consensus pragmatic readings and analyze ambiguous ones separately. 4) Multiple-choice framing can leak surface cues; we include cloze and free-generation variants and surface-match distractors. 5) Logit-lens tracking of literal vs pragmatic tokens is noisy for multi-token meanings; we prefer short single-token-decodable options and validate with tuned-lens and MC-answer-token probability. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test 5 models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Causal steering may trade off literal-control accuracy or fluency; we report off-target damage and retention rather than claiming a free lunch. 8) Confound with training frequency of indirect forms in low-resource languages; we control with URIEL tiers and use the literal-control stratum (same words, frequency-matched) as a within-item baseline. 9) Overlap with J-PragEval (Braun 2026) requires clear differentiation; we position our contribution as cross-lingual, truth-conditional implicature (not register), directness-typology leakage, and cross-lingual transfer/steering, which it does not study, and can include its register-probing setup as a monolingual sanity baseline.

Name: evidentiality_source_representation_crosslingual
Title: How Do You Know? Whether Multilingual Models Track the Source of Information and How Evidentiality Typology Leaks Into Their Certainty
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs compute a largely language-independent internal representation of the SOURCE of a claim (directly witnessed vs. inferred vs. hearsay), but the query language's evidentiality typology—whether it grammatically forces source marking (Turkish, Bulgarian, Quechua) or leaves it optional/lexical (English, Spanish)—leaks into how strongly the model commits to and expresses certainty about the claim. We hypothesize (1) a shared 'evidential-source' direction in middle layers that transfers across languages; (2) a language-typology-dependent distortion whereby claims phrased with hearsay/inferential evidentials in obligatory-marking languages are internally down-weighted in factual commitment more than the same claims in optional-marking languages, predictably shifting the model's asserted certainty and downstream factual reliance; and (3) a small, localizable set of components carrying the source signal that can be causally steered to convert a claim's internal source (e.g., turn 'I heard X' into 'I witnessed X') and thereby flip the model's certainty/commitment, without changing the surface answer.
Related Work: Evidentiality—the grammatical marking of information source (witnessed/inferred/hearsay)—is richly studied in linguistics and typology (Aikhenvald; Willett 1988) and in bilingual psycholinguistics: Tosun & Filipovic (2025) show Turkish-English bilinguals process firsthand vs. non-firsthand information asymmetrically because the distinction is grammatically obligatory in Turkish but optional in English; children's and L2 acquisition studies confirm source-marking shapes certainty judgments. In NLP, work on uncertainty/certainty and source attribution is monolingual/English-centric, and mechanistic multilingual work locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) and a shared knowledge-state/calibration signal in my prior calibration proposal. NO prior work asks whether an LLM internally represents the SOURCE of a claim, whether that source representation is language-independent, whether a language's evidentiality typology leaks into the model's factual commitment/certainty, or causally localizes and steers an evidential-source signal. This is distinct from my calibration proposal (which concerns know/don't-know about the model's OWN knowledge, not the epistemic source attributed to a claim) and from context-vs-memory conflict (source of an answer, not grammatical evidentiality of an assertion). It turns a classic linguistic-relativity phenomenon into a mechanistic, causal probe of source representation in multilingual models, with direct implications for hallucination and certainty calibration.
Abstract: Human languages differ in how they mark the source of information: Turkish, Bulgarian, and Quechua grammatically force speakers to indicate whether a claim was directly witnessed, inferred, or heard from others, while English marks this only optionally through lexical hedges. Psycholinguistics shows this obligatory marking shapes how confidently bilinguals commit to information. We ask whether multilingual LLMs internally represent the source of a claim, whether that representation is language-independent, and whether a language's evidentiality typology leaks into the model's certainty and factual commitment. We build EvidenceProbe, parallel statements across 8 typologically diverse languages spanning obligatory-marking (Turkish, Bulgarian, Georgian, Quechua-influenced), mixed, and optional-marking (English, Spanish, German, Japanese) systems, each rendered with three source framings (direct witness, inference, hearsay) and paired with the model's certainty judgment and a downstream factual-reliance probe. Using linear probes we test for a shared middle-layer evidential-source direction that transfers across languages; using logit-lens and mixed-effects models we test whether obligatory-marking languages more strongly down-weight hearsay/inferential claims' internal commitment than optional-marking languages produce on the same content. Via activation and path patching we localize the components carrying the source signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer that signal to convert a claim's internal source (e.g., hearsay to witnessed) and show it flips the model's asserted certainty and factual reliance without changing the surface answer. We relate leakage strength to evidentiality typology and typological distance, reframing source representation as a measurable, steerable property of multilingual models with direct implications for certainty calibration and hallucination.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 languages chosen for evidentiality-typology contrast: obligatory grammatical marking (Turkish, Bulgarian, Georgian, Azerbaijani), and optional/lexical marking (English, Spanish, German, Japanese). Code each language's evidentiality system (obligatory vs. optional, number of source distinctions) from typological references (Aikhenvald/WALS) plus URIEL for typological distance. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (EvidenceProbe): Curate ~400 base propositions (verifiable and neutral factual/eventive statements, e.g., 'It rained in the capital yesterday', 'The team won the match'). For each, create three SOURCE framings—DIRECT WITNESS ('I saw that...'), INFERENCE ('It seems/apparently, from evidence...'), HEARSAY ('I heard/they say that...')—realized naturally in each language: via obligatory evidential morphology where the grammar requires it (e.g., Turkish -mis for non-firsthand) and via lexical means where optional. Native verification of naturalness and source-equivalence. Include a NO-SOURCE control (bare assertion). Add probes: (a) CERTAINTY probe ('How certain is this claim? / Is this definitely true?') yielding a certainty score; (b) FACTUAL-RELIANCE probe (use the claim in a short downstream inference and measure whether the model treats it as established); (c) SOURCE-IDENTIFICATION probe ('Did the speaker witness this directly, infer it, or hear it?').
3) SHARED EVIDENTIAL-SOURCE DIRECTION (probing + transfer): At each layer pool the hidden state at the claim/answer position. Train a linear probe on ENGLISH data to classify source (witness/inference/hearsay) and apply zero-shot to other languages; measure macro-F1/AUROC transfer as evidence of a language-independent source direction. Compare to per-language-trained probes to bound shared-vs-specific. Select best mid-layer via English validation.
4) TYPOLOGY-LEAKAGE BEHAVIORAL TEST: Measure per-(language, source-framing) certainty and factual-reliance. KEY hypothesis: obligatory-marking languages produce a LARGER drop in certainty/reliance for hearsay/inference vs. witness than optional-marking languages on the SAME base proposition. Mixed-effects regression of certainty/reliance on (source framing, evidentiality-obligatoriness, language, resource tier via URIEL), with proposition as random effect; test the framing x obligatoriness interaction. Compare against NO-SOURCE control.
5) INTERNAL COMMITMENT DISTORTION: Using logit-lens and the shared source probe, measure the internal 'factual-commitment' signal (e.g., projection onto a witnessed-vs-hearsay axis or truth-assertion direction) per language and framing, and test whether obligatory-marking languages more strongly separate framings internally. Correlate per-item internal commitment shift with behavioral certainty shift (link test). Relate leakage magnitude to typological distance and evidentiality-system richness (Spearman).
6) LOCALIZE SOURCE COMPONENTS: Via activation/path patching between a witnessed-framing run and a hearsay-framing run of the SAME proposition, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose patching flips the internal source (as read out by the source-ID probe and certainty). Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (validated via per-layer language-ID probes).
7) CAUSAL SOURCE STEERING (decisive): Derive a source-steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (witnessed runs minus hearsay runs). Test (i) UP-COMMIT: adding it to a hearsay-framed claim raises the model's asserted certainty and factual reliance toward the witnessed level; (ii) DOWN-COMMIT: subtracting it makes a witnessed claim treated as hearsay (lower certainty/reliance); (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where evidentiality is obligatory; (iv) it does NOT change the surface answer/content or output language (fidelity check) and does not harm NO-SOURCE-control or general QA. Metrics: certainty-flip rate, reliance-flip rate, source-ID-flip rate, output fidelity, off-target damage.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress leakage and steering efficacy on evidentiality-obligatoriness and URIEL distance; English-centric (Llama) vs. multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; token-pooling; robustness across templates and probe formats (verbalized vs. token-probability certainty); whether a single source vector generalizes across propositions and languages; check whether steering source spuriously changes factual accuracy (it should not, since content is fixed).
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: cross-lingual source-probe transfer F1/AUROC, per-(language,framing) certainty & factual-reliance, framing x obligatoriness interaction, internal-commitment vs. behavior correlation, leakage-vs-typology correlation, patch-localized source-flip layer, causal steering certainty/reliance/source-ID flip rates, output fidelity, off-target/retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Realizing the three source framings naturally and equivalently across languages is delicate (obligatory morphology vs. optional lexis); we use native verification, naturalness ratings, and treat obligatoriness as a graded predictor, reporting sensitivity to framing choices. 2) Some models may ignore evidential framing entirely (no source representation), especially for optional-marking languages; this is itself an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often a source signal is present via the probe transfer and source-ID accuracy. 3) Certainty judgments are noisy and prompt-sensitive; we use both verbalized certainty and token-probability measures and multiple templates, reporting agreement. 4) The leakage effect may be confounded with training frequency of evidential constructions in lower-resource languages; we control with URIEL resource tiers and use the NO-SOURCE and within-proposition witnessed-vs-hearsay contrasts as frequency-neutral baselines. 5) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test 5 models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs. path patching. 6) Causal steering may trade fluency or accuracy; we report output fidelity, accuracy retention, and off-target damage rather than claiming a free lunch. 7) Distinguishing this from generic calibration (know/don't-know about the model's own knowledge) is essential; our steering fixes the CONTENT and manipulates only the attributed SOURCE, so any certainty change is attributable to source representation, not to what the model knows. 8) A single scalar source direction may be an oversimplification; we test low-rank subspace variants and report where a scalar axis is insufficient.

Name: colexification_concept_conflation_crosslingual
Title: One Word, Two Concepts: Does a Language's Colexification Pattern Blur How Multilingual Models Represent and Distinguish Meanings?
Short Hypothesis: When two distinct concepts are colexified (expressed by a single word) in a language but lexically distinguished in another (e.g., Russian distinguishes light-blue 'goluboy' from dark-blue 'siniy' while English conflates both as 'blue'; French distinguishes savoir/connaitre where English has one 'know'; many languages colexify 'hand/arm', 'wood/forest', 'time/weather'), the colexification pattern of the QUERY language leaks into the multilingual model's internal representation: the two concepts are held closer together (less separable) when queried in a colexifying language than in a distinguishing language, even though the underlying world concepts are identical. We hypothesize (1) the internal separability of two concepts is systematically modulated by the query language's colexification status, predictable from cross-linguistic colexification databases; (2) this conflation causally produces sense-disambiguation and fine-grained-inference errors that differ by query language; and (3) a small, localizable 'sense-splitting' direction can be causally steered to force the model to distinguish colexified senses in a conflating language, recovering distinguishing-language accuracy without changing the surface answer.
Related Work: Colexification (one lexeme for multiple concepts) is a core typological phenomenon catalogued in databases like CLICS and used to study semantic universals. In NLP, colexification has been used to build multilingual semantic resources and improve embeddings (e.g., colexification-informed lexical typology), and Yavas et al. 2023 touch on polysemy/copredication cross-lingually at the classification level. Mechanistic multilingual work establishes a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS (Wang 2025; Lim 2025), high-dimensional interlingual subspaces with fragmentation (Wilie et al. 2025, ILO), and neuron-level alignment (Huang et al. 2025, NeuronXA). Disentanglement/orthogonality work (Ki et al. 2024) removes language from semantics for retrieval. However, NO prior work asks whether a query language's colexification pattern LEAKS into and blurs the internal CONCEPT-level representation, whether the separability of two world-concepts is causally modulated by whether the query language lexicalizes the distinction, whether this predicts fine-grained sense-disambiguation errors per language, or whether a causal sense-splitting steering vector can restore the distinction. This differs from all my prior proposals (facts, reasoning-language, contested facts, temporal, code-switch binding, numbers, logic, metaphor, script, gender, calibration, context-trust, pragmatics, evidentiality): the object of study is lexical CONFLATION of concepts and its cross-lingual representational geometry, grounded in colexification typology and tested causally.
Abstract: Languages carve the world into words differently: Russian obligatorily distinguishes light-blue from dark-blue with separate basic color terms, French separates 'to know a fact' (savoir) from 'to know a person' (connaitre), and many languages use a single word for 'hand' and 'arm' or 'wood' and 'forest'. When these concepts are colexified—fused into one word—in the query language but distinguished in another, does a multilingual model represent them as internally more confusable? We test whether a language's colexification pattern leaks into the model's concept-level geometry, blurring distinctions the world itself preserves. Using cross-linguistic colexification databases (CLICS) we assemble ColexProbe: concept pairs that are colexified in some of 8 typologically diverse languages and distinguished in others, each with disambiguation and fine-grained inference probes. Representationally, we measure the internal separability of the two concepts (probe accuracy, representational distance) as a function of the query language's colexification status, testing whether colexifying languages hold the senses closer. Behaviorally, we test whether sense-disambiguation and fine-inference errors cluster in colexifying languages on the same underlying items. Mechanistically, via activation and path patching we localize a 'sense-splitting' signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to force a conflating language to distinguish the two senses, measuring recovered disambiguation accuracy while the surface answer and language stay fixed. We relate conflation strength to colexification frequency and typological distance, reframing lexical relativity as a measurable, steerable property of a model's shared concept space.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically/lexically diverse languages chosen so that key concept pairs are colexified in some and distinguished in others (English, Russian, Spanish, German, French, Hindi, Japanese, Turkish). MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (ColexProbe): Using CLICS/colexification databases and curated linguistic lists, select ~120 concept pairs that are colexified in at least one target language and lexically distinguished in at least one other (e.g., light-blue/dark-blue [Russian distinguishes, English colexifies], know-fact/know-person [French/Spanish distinguish, English colexifies], hand/arm, wood/forest, finger/toe, time/weather, day/sky, tree/wood, blue/green [grue] in some languages). For each pair record per-language colexification status (from CLICS + native verification). Build three probe types, translated/native-verified into all 8 languages: (A) SENSE DISAMBIGUATION: a context uniquely selecting one sense, asking which sense is meant / choosing the correct fine-grained referent; (B) FINE-GRAINED INFERENCE: minimal-pair entailment where the two senses yield different answers (e.g., 'she knows the answer' vs 'she knows the actor' -> different downstream inference); (C) CONTRAST probe: 'are X and Y the same thing?' where colexification predicts erroneous 'yes'. Include CONTROL pairs that are distinguished in ALL languages (clearly separate concepts) and pairs colexified in ALL languages, to bound the effect.
3) REPRESENTATIONAL SEPARABILITY: For each concept pair and each query language, elicit hidden states for prompts instantiating sense-1 vs sense-2. Measure internal separability at each layer via (i) a linear probe distinguishing the two senses (accuracy/AUROC), and (ii) representational distance between the two senses' mean hidden states (cosine / Mahalanobis). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME pair, separability is LOWER in languages that colexify the pair than in languages that distinguish it, especially in the shared mid-layer concept space; controls (all-distinguished pairs) show high separability everywhere. Statistics: mixed-effects model of separability on (colexification status, language, layer) with pair as random effect.
4) BEHAVIORAL CONFLATION TEST: Measure disambiguation, fine-inference, and contrast-probe accuracy per (pair, language). Hypothesis: colexifying languages show more sense-conflation errors (lower disambiguation accuracy, more erroneous 'same thing' answers) on the SAME underlying concept pair than distinguishing languages. Mixed-effects logistic regression of error on (colexification status, language, resource tier via URIEL), test that colexification predicts errors beyond resource level; correlate error magnitude with colexification frequency (CLICS attestation strength) and typological distance.
5) SEPARABILITY-PREDICTS-BEHAVIOR LINK: Within/across languages, correlate per-pair internal separability (step 3) with per-pair behavioral disambiguation error (step 4). A positive link supports genuine representational conflation causing behavioral errors rather than surface lexical effects.
6) LOCALIZE SENSE-SPLITTING COMPONENTS: Via activation/path patching between a distinguishing-language run and a colexifying-language run for the same pair (or between correctly-disambiguated vs conflated runs), sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose patching increases sense separability / flips a conflated answer to the correct sense. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (validated via per-layer language-ID probes).
7) CAUSAL SENSE-SPLITTING STEERING (decisive): Derive a sense-splitting steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (distinguished-sense runs minus conflated runs, or a low-rank sense-separation map). Test (i) SPLIT: adding it during a colexifying-language query increases correct sense disambiguation and reduces erroneous 'same thing' answers toward distinguishing-language levels; (ii) it works cross-lingually and more strongly where colexification is strongest; (iii) a REVERSE test—projecting OUT the sense-splitting direction—induces conflation errors in a distinguishing language, confirming the direction's role; (iv) it does NOT change the surface answer language, does not harm all-distinguished CONTROL pairs, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: disambiguation-accuracy recovery, contrast-error reduction, conflation-induction rate (reverse), output-language fidelity, off-target damage, retention.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress conflation strength and steering efficacy on CLICS colexification frequency and URIEL distance; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); domain generality (color vs body-part vs epistemic-verb vs nature colexifications); probe layer/dimensionality; token-pooling; robustness across templates and MC-vs-cloze-vs-free formats; whether a single sense-splitting vector generalizes across pairs and languages.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-pair per-language separability (probe accuracy, representational distance), colexification-status effect on separability, per-language disambiguation/fine-inference/contrast accuracy, separability-behavior correlation, colexification-frequency and typology correlations, patch-localized sense-splitting layer, causal steering disambiguation recovery and conflation-induction rates, output fidelity, off-target/retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Colexification status coding requires care and can be graded (partial colexification, register-dependent); we use CLICS plus native verification, treat colexification as a graded predictor (attestation frequency), and report sensitivity to coding. 2) Effects could be driven by surface lexical priming (the colexifying word appears in the prompt) rather than deep concept conflation; we mitigate with a critical control that primes the concept in a colexifying language but ELICITS the distinction in a distinguishing language (removing the surface single-word cue), and use the separability-predicts-behavior link (step 5) as evidence beyond surface form. 3) Some models may internally distinguish colexified senses regardless of query language (clean concept space); this itself is an informative, publishable finding about lexical-relativity robustness, and we quantify how often conflation is present. 4) Confound with training frequency/rarity of the finer-grained senses in low-resource languages; we control with URIEL resource tiers and use all-distinguished and all-colexified CONTROL pairs as frequency-neutral baselines, plus within-pair contrasts. 5) Probing linearity assumptions may not hold; we validate separability metrics on all-distinguished control pairs (should be high) and report both linear-probe and distance-based measures. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test 5 models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Causal steering may trade off control-pair accuracy or fluency; we report off-target damage, control retention, and output fidelity rather than claiming a free lunch, and the reverse (conflation-induction) test guards against the steering being a generic accuracy boost. 8) The sense-splitting signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants and report where a scalar direction is insufficient. 9) Some concept pairs are genuinely fuzzy (grue color boundaries); we restrict scored items to clear cases and analyze fuzzy ones separately.

Name: spatial_frame_of_reference_leakage
Title: Left or North? Whether Multilingual LLMs Adopt a Language-Dependent Spatial Frame of Reference and How to Steer It
Short Hypothesis: When a text-only multilingual LLM resolves an underspecified spatial relation (e.g., 'the ball is to the X of the tree'), it internally commits to a default spatial frame of reference (FoR)—egocentric relative (left/right/front/back), object-centric intrinsic, or geocentric absolute (north/south)—and this default is causally shifted by the query language's habitual FoR typology: geocentric-preferring languages (e.g., Guugu Yimithirr-like, Tseltal, and, more accessibly, languages/registers favoring cardinal directions) push the model toward absolute framing, egocentric languages (English, Dutch) toward relative framing. We hypothesize (1) the model's chosen FoR for the SAME spatial scene systematically varies with query language, predictable from documented FoR typology; (2) there is a shared, largely language-independent 'FoR representation' in middle layers whose selection is language-modulated; and (3) a small, localizable set of components carries the FoR-selection signal that can be causally steered to flip the frame (relative<->absolute<->intrinsic), changing the model's spatial inference without changing the scene—distinguishing genuine frame selection from surface lexical translation.
Related Work: Classic psycholinguistics establishes cross-linguistic variation in default frame of reference and its effect on human spatial reasoning (Levinson et al. 2002; Li et al. 2011; Pederson; Majid et al.). In ML, COMFORT (Zhang et al. 2024) evaluates FoR ambiguity in VISION-language models and finds poor consistency and English dominance across languages, and VSR (Liu et al. 2022) shows VLMs struggle with reference frames—but both are (a) multimodal, (b) purely behavioral, and (c) offer no internal mechanism or intervention. Mechanistic multilingual work locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS (Wang 2025; Lim 2025), but never for spatial coordinate systems. No prior work asks whether a TEXT-ONLY multilingual LLM adopts a language-dependent FoR, whether FoR selection is a localizable, language-modulated internal signal, or whether it can be causally steered. This is distinct from all my prior proposals (facts, senses/colexification, gender, evidentiality, pragmatics, etc.): the object of study is the spatial reference frame the model reasons in, grounded in FoR typology and tested causally, in text alone (no vision).
Abstract: Languages carve space with different default coordinate systems: English typically uses egocentric relative terms (left, right, in front), some languages prefer intrinsic object-centered framing, and others habitually use absolute cardinal directions (north, south). Decades of psycholinguistics show this shapes human spatial reasoning. We ask whether a text-only multilingual LLM, when resolving an underspecified spatial relation, internally commits to a frame of reference (FoR), whether the query language causally shifts that commitment, and whether we can steer it. We build FrameProbe, a set of parallel spatial-scene descriptions and underspecified spatial questions rendered across 8 typologically diverse languages annotated with each language's habitual FoR from typological references. Behaviorally, we measure which FoR the model adopts (via forced-choice and free-inference probes whose correct answer differs across relative/intrinsic/absolute interpretations) and test whether it tracks the query language's FoR typology beyond surface translation. Using linear probes we test for a shared middle-layer FoR representation that transfers across languages; using logit-lens we track when the frame is selected. Via activation and path patching we localize the FoR-selection components, and in a decisive causal test we derive a frame-steering vector that flips the model's frame (relative<->absolute<->intrinsic), changing its spatial inference on the same scene while leaving the surface language unchanged. We relate frame-selection strength to FoR typology and typological distance. Our work reframes a classic linguistic-relativity phenomenon as a measurable, steerable property of a text-only model's internal spatial coordinate system.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 languages spanning documented FoR preferences: strongly egocentric/relative (English, Dutch, Japanese), mixed/intrinsic-leaning (Spanish, German), and absolute-cardinal-favoring registers/languages (Hausa, Tamil, and Indonesian/Balinese-style absolute usage), coded from FoR typology references (Levinson, Pederson) plus URIEL for typological distance. If a fully geocentric small language lacks LLM coverage, substitute languages/registers with strong cardinal-direction conventions and treat FoR-preference as a graded predictor. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (FrameProbe): ~400 spatial-scene items in three strata whose answer depends on the adopted FoR: (A) RELATIVE-vs-ABSOLUTE: 'You face north. A tree is ahead of you; a ball sits to your right. From the tree's perspective / in cardinal terms, where is the ball?'—the correct answer differs under relative (right) vs absolute (east) framing. (B) INTRINSIC-vs-RELATIVE: scenes with a fronted object (a car, a person) where 'in front of the car' differs under intrinsic (object's own front) vs relative (viewer-projected) framing. (C) FRAME-DIAGNOSTIC free-inference: rotation/navigation mini-problems (as in Levinson's animals-in-a-row and maze tasks, rendered in text) solvable only by consistently applying one frame. Each item has FoR-labeled correct answers per frame and, where possible, a NEUTRAL control with a unique frame-independent answer. Translate/native-verify into all 8 languages, ensuring spatial terms are natural in each.
3) BEHAVIORAL FRAME-SELECTION TEST: For each (item, language) determine which FoR the model's answer implies. KEY hypothesis: the adopted FoR distribution shifts with query language toward that language's habitual FoR. Mixed-effects multinomial regression of chosen-frame on (language FoR-preference, stratum, resource tier via URIEL), item as random effect; test that FoR-preference predicts frame choice beyond resource level and beyond surface translation (control: items where all frames agree should show no language effect). Report per-language frame-choice profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical scenes.
4) SHARED FoR REPRESENTATION & TRANSFER: At each layer pool hidden states at the answer/relation position. Train a linear 'FoR probe' (relative/intrinsic/absolute) on ENGLISH data; apply zero-shot to other languages and report macro-F1/AUROC as evidence of a language-independent FoR direction. Compare to per-language-trained probes to bound shared-vs-specific. Use logit-lens to identify when frame-diagnostic tokens (e.g., 'right' vs 'east') begin to dominate across depth (frame-selection depth).
5) FRAME-DEPTH & LEAKAGE ANALYSIS: Correlate frame-selection depth and internal FoR-probe output with behavioral frame choice within/across languages (link test), and correlate leakage magnitude (how strongly query language shifts the internal frame) with FoR-typology preference and URIEL distance (Spearman).
6) LOCALIZE FoR-SELECTION COMPONENTS: Via activation/path patching between a run that adopts frame F1 and a matched run adopting F2 on the SAME scene (induced via minimal FoR-cueing or different query languages), sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose patching flips the internal frame (read out by the FoR probe and the emitted answer). Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (validated via per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs path patching.
7) CAUSAL FRAME STEERING (decisive): Derive frame-steering vectors via difference-of-means over localized components (e.g., absolute-frame runs minus relative-frame runs).
