Test (i) FLIP: adding/subtracting the vector changes the model's spatial inference on held-out scenes from relative to absolute (and intrinsic variants), as verified by frame-diagnostic answers; (ii) it works cross-lingually and can OVERRIDE the query language's default frame; (iii) REVERSE consistency: steering toward a frame improves accuracy on items whose correct answer requires that frame; (iv) it does NOT change the surface output language or the neutral-control (frame-independent) answers, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: frame-flip rate, frame-diagnostic accuracy under target frame, output-language fidelity, neutral-control retention, general-QA retention.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress frame-selection leakage and steering efficacy on FoR-preference and URIEL distance; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; token-pooling; stratum generality (relative-vs-absolute vs intrinsic); whether a single frame-steering vector generalizes across scenes and languages; robustness across templates and forced-choice-vs-free formats.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language chosen-frame profiles and cross-lingual disagreement, FoR-preference regression coefficients, cross-lingual FoR-probe transfer F1/AUROC, frame-selection depth, internal-frame vs behavior correlation, leakage-vs-typology correlation, patch-localized frame-selection layer, causal steering frame-flip rate and target-frame accuracy, output fidelity, neutral-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) FoR-typology coding is coarse and, for some languages, register-dependent; we use documented FoR references, treat FoR-preference as a graded predictor, report sensitivity to alternative codings, and substitute cardinal-direction-favoring languages/registers where fully geocentric small languages lack LLM coverage. 2) Constructing genuinely frame-diagnostic text items is delicate; we adapt validated psycholinguistic paradigms (animals-in-a-row, rotation/maze tasks) into text, native-verify naturalness, and include frame-independent NEUTRAL controls to detect artifacts. 3) Some models may default to English relative framing regardless of query language (English dominance, as COMFORT found for VLMs); this is itself an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often the frame is even contested and whether an internal FoR signal is present via probe transfer. 4) Effects could reflect surface translation of spatial terms rather than deep frame selection; we mitigate with frame-diagnostic items whose surface wording is matched, the neutral controls, and the internal-frame-predicts-behavior link (step 5), plus steering that overrides the query language while keeping surface language fixed. 5) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test 5 models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 6) Causal steering may trade fluency or neutral-control accuracy; we report output fidelity, neutral-control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the reverse-accuracy test to ensure steering selects a frame rather than generically boosting accuracy. 7) The FoR signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants and report where a scalar direction is insufficient. 8) Distinguishing from COMFORT/VSR is essential; we position our contribution as text-only, mechanistic, and causal (internal FoR representation, localization, and steering), which they do not provide, and can include a COMFORT-style behavioral consistency measure as a baseline.

Name: grammatical_aspect_completion_leakage
Title: Did It Finish? Whether a Language's Grammatical Aspect Typology Leaks Into How Multilingual Models Represent Event Completion
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM reads a described event, it computes a largely language-independent internal representation of the event's COMPLETION/BOUNDEDNESS status (did it finish vs. is it ongoing/unbounded), but the query language's grammatical-aspect typology leaks into it: languages that obligatorily grammaticalize perfective/imperfective (e.g., Russian) push the model toward a strong completion commitment, while aspect-optional/context-dependent languages (e.g., Chinese, German) leave it underspecified, producing predictable cross-lingual disagreement on whether the SAME event completed. We hypothesize (1) a shared middle-layer 'completion' direction that transfers across languages; (2) a typology-dependent distortion of how strongly the model commits to completion, tracking aspect-obligatoriness; and (3) a small, localizable set of components carrying the completion signal that can be causally steered to flip an event from completed to ongoing (and vice versa), changing downstream telicity/entailment inferences without changing the surface answer.
Related Work: Lexical and grammatical aspect are richly studied in linguistics (Comrie; Smith; Olsen 1997) and vary sharply cross-linguistically in obligatoriness (Slavic perfective/imperfective marking vs. aspect-neutral languages). In NLP, monolingual work probes tense/aspect and telicity (e.g., aspectual classification, event-completion inference in English), but is not cross-lingual or mechanistic. Mechanistic multilingual work locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) and, in my prior proposals, for polarity, evidential source, colexified senses, and spatial frames. NO prior work asks whether a query language's grammatical-aspect typology leaks into the model's internal representation of EVENT COMPLETION/BOUNDEDNESS, whether that representation is language-independent and transferable, whether it predicts cross-lingual completion-inference disagreement, or whether a completion signal can be causally localized and steered. This is distinct from my temporal-knowledge proposal (which concerns per-language staleness of stored facts, not the aspectual completion of a described event) and from all other prior proposals: the object of study is event-completion/aspect and its cross-lingual representational geometry, grounded in aspect typology and tested causally.
Abstract: Languages differ in whether they force speakers to mark how an event unfolds in time: Slavic languages obligatorily choose perfective ('read-to-completion') versus imperfective ('was reading'), English grammaticalizes the progressive, and languages like Chinese or German leave completion largely to context. Deciding whether a described event finished or is ongoing is essential to inference, yet the grammar of the query language may bias this decision. We ask whether a multilingual LLM internally represents an event's completion/boundedness in a language-independent way, and whether a language's aspect typology leaks into how strongly the model commits to completion. We build AspectProbe, parallel event descriptions across 8 typologically diverse languages spanning obligatory-aspect, progressive-grammaticalizing, and aspect-optional systems, each with completion-inference and telicity-entailment probes and a language-level aspect-obligatoriness code from typological references. Behaviorally we test whether the model's judgment of whether the SAME event completed shifts with query language toward that language's aspect typology. Using a linear probe we test for a shared middle-layer completion direction that transfers zero-shot across languages; using logit-lens we track when completion is decided. Via activation and path patching we localize the completion signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to flip an event between completed and ongoing, changing downstream entailment inferences while leaving the surface answer and language unchanged. We relate leakage strength to aspect typology and typological distance, reframing aspectual relativity as a measurable, steerable property of the model's shared event representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 languages spanning aspect typology: obligatory perfective/imperfective (Russian, Polish, Bulgarian), progressive-grammaticalizing (English), and aspect-optional/context-dependent (German, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish), coded for aspect-obligatoriness from typological references (Comrie; Smith; WALS) plus URIEL for typological distance, treating obligatoriness as a graded predictor. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (AspectProbe): ~400 base events (e.g., 'she painted the fence', 'they built a house', 'he wrote a letter'), each realized in three aspectual framings where naturally available—COMPLETED/PERFECTIVE, ONGOING/IMPERFECTIVE-PROGRESSIVE, and NEUTRAL/context-only—using obligatory morphology where the grammar requires it and lexical/periphrastic means where optional. Native verification of naturalness and aspect-equivalence. Probes per item: (A) COMPLETION probe ('Is the fence now fully painted? / Did the event finish?') yielding a completed/ongoing/unknown judgment; (B) TELICITY-ENTAILMENT minimal pairs ('She was painting the fence' should NOT entail 'the fence is painted'; 'She painted the fence' should) with correct entailment labels; (C) DOWNSTREAM-INFERENCE probe using the event in a short continuation whose correct answer depends on completion. Include a NEUTRAL control and events that are aspectually unambiguous in all languages to bound the effect.
3) BEHAVIORAL LEAKAGE TEST: For each (event, language, framing) record the completion judgment and entailment accuracy. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME event under a NEUTRAL/underspecified framing, obligatory-aspect languages push the model to a firmer completed-vs-ongoing commitment than aspect-optional languages, and completed/ongoing framings produce sharper internal separation in obligatory-aspect languages. Mixed-effects regression of completion-commitment and entailment error on (aspect-obligatoriness, framing, language, resource tier via URIEL), event as random effect; test the framing x obligatoriness interaction and cross-lingual disagreement on identical events, controlling with aspectually-unambiguous items (should show no language effect).
4) SHARED COMPLETION DIRECTION & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the event/answer position. Train a linear 'completion probe' (completed vs. ongoing) on ENGLISH data and apply zero-shot to other languages; report AUROC/macro-F1 as evidence of a language-independent completion direction. Compare to per-language-trained probes to bound shared-vs-specific. Use logit-lens to identify the layer where completion-diagnostic tokens begin to dominate (completion-decision depth).
5) DEPTH & LEAKAGE ANALYSIS: Correlate completion-decision depth and internal completion-probe output with behavioral completion judgment within/across languages (link test), and correlate leakage magnitude (how much query language shifts the internal completion signal on neutral items) with aspect-obligatoriness and URIEL distance (Spearman).
6) LOCALIZE COMPLETION COMPONENTS: Via activation/path patching between a completed-framing run and an ongoing-framing run of the SAME event, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose patching flips the internal completion state (read out by the completion probe and the emitted answer). Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (validated via per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs. path patching.
7) CAUSAL COMPLETION STEERING (decisive): Derive a completion-steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (completed runs minus ongoing runs). Test (i) FINISH: adding it makes the model treat an ongoing/neutral event as completed, updating telicity entailments accordingly; (ii) UN-FINISH: subtracting it makes a completed event treated as ongoing; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where aspect is obligatory; (iv) it does NOT change the surface answer content/language and does not harm aspectually-unambiguous controls or general QA (fidelity + retention). Metrics: completion-flip rate, entailment-flip rate, output fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress leakage and steering efficacy on aspect-obligatoriness and URIEL distance; English-centric (Llama) vs. multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; token-pooling; robustness across templates and probe formats; whether a single completion vector generalizes across events and languages; reverse-consistency check that steering selects an aspect rather than generically boosting accuracy.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-(language,framing) completion judgment & entailment accuracy, framing x obligatoriness interaction, cross-lingual disagreement, shared completion-probe transfer AUROC/F1, completion-decision depth, internal-vs-behavior correlation, leakage-vs-typology correlation, patch-localized completion layer, causal steering completion/entailment-flip rates, output fidelity, control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Realizing the three aspectual framings naturally and equivalently across languages is delicate (obligatory morphology vs. optional periphrasis); we use native verification, naturalness ratings, and treat obligatoriness as a graded predictor, reporting sensitivity to framing choices. 2) Some models may ignore aspectual marking or resolve completion holistically (no shared signal), especially in aspect-optional languages; this is itself an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often a completion signal is present via probe transfer and completion-judgment accuracy. 3) Completion judgments and telicity entailments can be genuinely context-dependent; we restrict scored items to those with clear native-consensus readings and analyze ambiguous ones separately, using the aspectually-unambiguous control set as a within-design baseline. 4) Confound with training frequency of aspectual constructions in lower-resource languages; we control with URIEL resource tiers and use neutral and unambiguous-control items as frequency-neutral baselines plus within-event framing contrasts. 5) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test 5 models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs. path patching. 6) Causal steering may trade fluency or control accuracy; we report output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the reverse (un-finish) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure steering manipulates aspect rather than generically boosting accuracy. 7) The completion signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants and report where a scalar direction is insufficient. 8) Distinguishing from my temporal-staleness proposal is essential; here content is fixed and we manipulate only the aspectual completion of a described event, so any inference change is attributable to the completion representation, not to stored factual recency.

Name: kinship_granularity_relational_leakage
Title: Older Brother or Just Brother? Whether a Language's Kinship-Term Granularity Leaks Into How Multilingual Models Represent Family Relations
Short Hypothesis: Languages carve kinship at radically different granularities: Mandarin/Korean/Hindi obligatorily encode relative age (older vs younger sibling) and lineage (maternal vs paternal uncle/grandparent), while English collapses these ('brother', 'uncle', 'grandmother'). We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of a kin RELATION, but the query language's kinship-granularity typology leaks into it: relations that are lexically distinguished in the query language (e.g., older vs younger sibling) are held more separably and reasoned about more accurately, whereas relations collapsed by the query language are internally conflated—even though the underlying family fact is identical. We further hypothesize (1) a shared middle-layer kin-relation direction (encoding lineage, generation, relative age) that transfers across languages; (2) the internal separability and downstream relational-reasoning accuracy of a fine distinction is causally modulated by whether the query language lexicalizes it, predictable from kinship-terminology typology; and (3) a small, localizable 'relation-splitting' signal can be causally steered to force a collapsing language to distinguish a fine kin relation, recovering fine-distinction accuracy without changing the surface answer.
Related Work: Kinship terminology is a canonical domain of linguistic typology (Morgan; Murdock; the Eskimo/Sudanese/Hawaiian/Iroquois systems) that varies sharply in whether relative age, lineage (maternal/paternal), and gender are obligatorily encoded. Recent NLP work touches kinship only behaviorally and culturally: BanglaSocialBench (Sijan et al. 2026) and social-power/address-term benchmarks evaluate whether LLMs pick culturally appropriate kin address terms, and multi-hop QA datasets test relational-chain reasoning ('mother's brother's son') monolingually or in English. Mechanistic multilingual work locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS (Wang 2025; Lim 2025), and my prior colexification proposal studied lexical conflation of general concepts (colors, know-verbs, body parts). NO prior work asks whether a query language's KINSHIP-GRANULARITY typology leaks into the model's internal RELATIONAL representation of family ties, whether the separability of fine kin distinctions (relative age, lineage) is causally modulated by the query language, whether this predicts relational-reasoning errors per language, or whether a causal relation-splitting steering vector can restore a collapsed distinction. This differs from my colexification proposal because kinship involves structured RELATIONAL/compositional reasoning (multi-hop kin chains, generation/lineage/age dimensions) rather than single-concept sense disambiguation, and it is grounded in the specific, highly-structured typology of kinship-terminology systems. It differs from behavioral kinship benchmarks by providing an internal, mechanistic, causal account rather than a cultural-alignment evaluation.
Abstract: Family relations are universal, but languages name them very differently: Mandarin, Korean, and Hindi obligatorily distinguish an older from a younger brother and a maternal from a paternal uncle, while English collapses each into a single word. Deciding, tracking, and reasoning about kin relations is a structured relational task—yet the grammar and lexicon of the query language may bias which distinctions the model even represents. We ask whether a multilingual LLM internally encodes kin relations (lineage, generation, relative age) in a language-independent way, and whether a language's kinship-term granularity leaks into how separably it holds fine distinctions and how accurately it reasons about them. We build KinProbe, parallel kin-relation descriptions and multi-hop kin-chain reasoning problems across 8 typologically diverse languages spanning fine-grained (Mandarin, Korean, Hindi, Turkish) and collapsing (English, Spanish, German, Russian) kinship systems, each annotated with the fine distinctions the language lexicalizes. Representationally, we measure the internal separability of fine kin relations (e.g., older vs younger sibling, maternal vs paternal uncle) as a function of the query language's granularity, testing whether collapsing languages hold them closer. Behaviorally, we test whether fine-distinction and multi-hop kin-reasoning errors cluster in collapsing languages on identical underlying family facts. Using a linear probe we test for a shared middle-layer kin-relation direction that transfers zero-shot across languages; via activation and path patching we localize a relation-splitting signal. In a decisive causal test we steer it to force a collapsing language to distinguish a fine relation, recovering accuracy while the surface answer and language stay fixed, and reverse-project it to induce conflation. We relate leakage strength to kinship typology and typological distance, reframing kinship relativity as a measurable, steerable property of a model's relational representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 languages spanning kinship-granularity typology: fine-grained systems that obligatorily encode relative age and/or lineage (Mandarin Chinese: older/younger sibling, maternal/paternal grandparents & uncles/aunts; Korean: relative-age and speaker-gender-dependent sibling terms; Hindi: maternal/paternal distinctions and relative-age; Turkish: relative-age and paternal/maternal aunt/uncle) and collapsing systems (English, Spanish, German, Russian) that use broad terms. Code each language's kinship-granularity (which of {relative age, lineage/side, gender} are lexicalized for each relation) from kinship-typology references (Murdock; ethnographic/lexicographic sources) plus URIEL for typological distance; treat granularity as a graded per-relation predictor. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (KinProbe): (a) FINE-DISTINCTION stratum: ~250 items where a described family scenario fixes a fine relation (e.g., 'A was born before B; both are C's sons' -> A is C's OLDER son) and the probe asks a question whose correct answer depends on the fine distinction (older vs younger; maternal vs paternal). (b) MULTI-HOP KIN-CHAIN stratum: ~200 relational-reasoning problems ('X is Y's mother's younger brother's daughter; how is X related to Y?') with a unique correct kin label. (c) CONTRAST stratum: 'Given only that A and B are siblings, can you tell which is older?' probing whether the model hallucinates a distinction or correctly reports underspecification. Each item is rendered in all 8 languages with native verification, using the fine-grained kin terms where the language has them and the broad term where it collapses; answers recorded in a language-agnostic normalized relation code for scoring. Include a CONTROL stratum of relations distinguished in ALL languages (e.g., mother vs father) and relations collapsed in ALL (to bound the effect).
3) REPRESENTATIONAL SEPARABILITY: For each fine relation pair (e.g., older-brother vs younger-brother; maternal-uncle vs paternal-uncle) and each query language, elicit hidden states for prompts instantiating each member. Measure internal separability at each layer via a linear probe distinguishing the two (accuracy/AUROC) and representational distance (cosine/Mahalanobis) between mean states. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME relation pair, separability is LOWER in languages that collapse it than in languages that lexicalize it, especially in the shared mid-layer concept space; all-distinguished control pairs show high separability everywhere. Mixed-effects model of separability on (granularity status, language, layer), relation-pair as random effect.
4) BEHAVIORAL LEAKAGE TEST: Measure fine-distinction accuracy, multi-hop kin-chain accuracy, and contrast-stratum correctness (correctly reporting underspecification vs hallucinating a distinction) per (relation, language). Hypothesis: collapsing languages show more fine-distinction errors and more hallucinated-or-lost distinctions on the SAME underlying family facts than fine-grained languages. Mixed-effects logistic regression of error on (granularity status, language, resource tier via URIEL); test that granularity predicts errors beyond resource level; correlate error magnitude with typological distance.
5) SEPARABILITY-PREDICTS-BEHAVIOR LINK: Within/across languages, correlate per-relation internal separability (step 3) with per-relation behavioral fine-distinction error (step 4). A positive link supports genuine representational conflation causing behavioral errors rather than surface lexical effects.
6) SHARED KIN-RELATION DIRECTION & TRANSFER: Train linear probes on ENGLISH mid-layer states to decode kin-relation dimensions where English still marks them (generation: parent/grandparent; gender: brother/sister) and, for age/lineage, train on a fine-grained language (Mandarin); apply zero-shot cross-lingually and report AUROC/macro-F1 transfer as evidence of language-independent relational directions. Compare to per-language-trained probes to bound shared-vs-specific. Use logit-lens to identify when the fine distinction is (or fails to be) resolved across depth.
7) LOCALIZE RELATION-SPLITTING COMPONENTS: Via activation/path patching between a fine-grained-language run and a collapsing-language run for the same relation (or between correctly-distinguished vs conflated runs), sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose patching increases relation separability / flips a conflated answer to the correct fine relation. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (validated via per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs path patching.
8) CAUSAL RELATION-SPLITTING STEERING (decisive): Derive a relation-splitting steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (distinguished-relation runs minus conflated runs), or a low-rank age/lineage-separation map. Test (i) SPLIT: adding it during a collapsing-language query increases correct fine-distinction and multi-hop accuracy toward fine-grained-language levels; (ii) it works cross-lingually and more strongly where the language collapses the distinction most; (iii) REVERSE: projecting OUT the splitting direction induces conflation errors in a fine-grained language, confirming its role; (iv) it does NOT change the surface output language, does not harm all-distinguished CONTROL relations, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: fine-distinction and kin-chain accuracy recovery, hallucination/underspecification error change, conflation-induction rate (reverse), output-language fidelity, off-target damage, retention.
9) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress conflation strength and steering efficacy on kinship-granularity and URIEL distance; separate the three kin dimensions (relative age vs lineage/side vs gender) to see which leak most; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; token-pooling; robustness across templates and MC-vs-cloze-vs-free formats; whether a single relation-splitting vector generalizes across relation types and languages.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-relation per-language separability (probe accuracy, representational distance), granularity effect on separability, fine-distinction/multi-hop/contrast accuracy per language, separability-behavior correlation, granularity/typology correlations, cross-lingual kin-relation probe transfer AUROC/F1, patch-localized relation-splitting layer, causal steering fine-distinction/kin-chain recovery and conflation-induction rates, output fidelity, control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Kinship-granularity coding is intricate (systems vary within families, some distinctions are register- or dialect-dependent); we use kinship-typology references plus native verification, treat granularity as a graded per-relation predictor, and report sensitivity to coding. 2) Effects could be driven by surface lexical priming (the fine-grained kin word appears in the prompt) rather than deep relational conflation; we mitigate with a critical control that fixes the fine relation via a SCENARIO (birth-order/side facts) rather than the kin word, and with a cross-elicitation control that describes the relation in a fine-grained language but ELICITS the answer in a collapsing language, plus the separability-predicts-behavior link (step 5). 3) Some models may internally distinguish fine kin relations regardless of query language (clean relational space); this is itself an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often conflation is present via probe transfer and fine-distinction accuracy. 4) Confound with training frequency/rarity of fine kin terms in lower-resource languages; we control with URIEL resource tiers and use all-distinguished and all-collapsed CONTROL relations as frequency-neutral baselines plus within-relation contrasts. 5) Multi-hop kin-chain items conflate relational-reasoning ability with lexical granularity; we include scenario-based fine-distinction items that isolate the granularity effect and report both. 6) Probing linearity assumptions may not hold; we validate separability metrics on all-distinguished control relations (should be high) and report both linear-probe and distance-based measures. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test 5 models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Causal steering may trade off control-relation accuracy or fluency; we report off-target damage, control retention, and output fidelity rather than claiming a free lunch, and the reverse conflation-induction test guards against the steering being a generic accuracy boost. 9) The relation-splitting signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants and report where a scalar direction is insufficient. 10) Distinguishing from behavioral kinship benchmarks (BanglaSocialBench) and from my colexification proposal is essential; we position the contribution as the internal, causal account of structured RELATIONAL kinship representation and its typology-driven leakage, which neither provides.

Name: measure_system_unit_leakage_crosslingual
Title: How Many Kilometers Is a Mile? Whether a Language's Default Measurement System Leaks Into How Multilingual Models Represent and Reason About Physical Quantities
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM reasons about a physical quantity (distance, weight, temperature, volume), it computes a largely language-independent internal magnitude, but the query language's culturally-default measurement system leaks into it: the model implicitly assumes the units and the culturally-typical magnitude ranges of the query language's dominant system (metric vs imperial vs local traditional units), producing predictable cross-lingual disagreement and unit-conversion errors on the SAME physical quantity. We hypothesize (1) a shared middle-layer magnitude representation whose readout is modulated by an internally-inferred 'default unit system' tied to the query language; (2) unit-ambiguous quantities are interpreted in the query language's default system, causing systematic errors that track the language's real-world measurement convention; and (3) a small, localizable 'unit-system' signal can be causally steered to switch the assumed measurement system (e.g., make an English query default to metric or a US query default to Celsius), changing the model's numeric inference without changing the surface answer language.
Related Work: Prior multilingual numeracy work is monolingual or treats language as a global accuracy knob; my own prior number-naming proposal studied how compositional NUMBER-WORD morphology distorts the internal magnitude code, but did not touch MEASUREMENT SYSTEMS or units. Cultural-bias benchmarks (FmLAMA, BLEnD, XNationQA) document Western/US default biases behaviorally but never test measurement-system defaulting, unit interpretation of ambiguous quantities, or any mechanism. Unit-conversion is studied as a tool-use/arithmetic skill in English-centric math benchmarks, not as a language-conditioned representational default. Mechanistic multilingual work locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) and, in my prior proposals, for polarity, evidential source, colexified senses, spatial frames, aspect, and kinship. NO prior work asks whether the query language's default measurement system leaks into the model's internal magnitude/unit representation, whether unit-ambiguous quantities are silently interpreted in the language's dominant system, whether this predicts cross-lingual quantity disagreement and conversion errors, or whether a unit-system signal can be causally localized and steered. This is distinct from my number-naming proposal (surface number-word structure vs magnitude) because the object here is the assumed UNIT SYSTEM and culturally-typical magnitude ranges attached to a quantity, grounded in the real-world metric/imperial/local-unit typology of each language's speaker community, and tested causally.
Abstract: Physical quantities are universal, but the units used to express them are cultural: most of the world defaults to metric, the US to imperial, and some communities to local traditional units, while temperatures are given in Celsius in some countries and Fahrenheit in others. When a multilingual LLM reasons about a quantity described without explicit units, or converts between systems, does the query language silently impose its speakers' default measurement system on the internal magnitude? We test whether a language's measurement-system convention leaks into the model's internal representation of physical quantities. We build UnitProbe, parallel quantity-reasoning items across 8 languages whose speaker communities differ in default systems (English[US/UK split], Spanish, German, Russian, Hindi, Japanese, Chinese, Arabic), covering distance, weight, temperature, and volume, with three item types: unit-ambiguous interpretation ('the drive is about 30 units—is that far?'), explicit conversion, and culturally-typical range judgments. Behaviorally we test whether the model's interpretation of ambiguous quantities and its conversion errors track each language's default system beyond surface translation. Using a linear probe we test for a shared middle-layer magnitude direction and a separable 'assumed unit-system' direction that transfers across languages; via activation and path patching we localize the unit-system signal. In a decisive causal test we steer it to switch the assumed system (e.g., force a US-English query to default to Celsius/metric), changing the model's numeric inference while leaving the surface answer and language unchanged, and reverse-steer to induce the opposite default. We relate leakage strength to each language's real-world measurement convention and typological distance, reframing measurement-system bias as a measurable, steerable property of the model's quantity representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 languages whose speaker communities differ in default measurement systems: English (with a US-imperial vs UK/metric register split treated as two conditions), Spanish, German, Russian, Hindi, Japanese, Chinese, Arabic. Code each language's default system per quantity dimension (distance: miles vs km; weight: lb vs kg; temperature: F vs C; volume: gallons/pints vs liters) from real-world measurement-convention references, treating default-system as a graded per-dimension predictor; add URIEL for typological distance. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (UnitProbe): ~450 items across four physical dimensions (distance, weight, temperature, volume) in three strata: (A) UNIT-AMBIGUOUS INTERPRETATION: a quantity given with a generic/no unit where the reasonableness or a follow-up inference depends on which system is assumed ('A comfortable room is about 22 degrees—warm or cold?' answer differs under C vs F; 'The trip is 60 units by car—short or long?' differs under mi vs km); (B) EXPLICIT CONVERSION: 'How many kilometers is 30 miles?' etc., with exact correct answers, to measure conversion accuracy and directional bias per language; (C) CULTURALLY-TYPICAL RANGE JUDGMENT: 'Is 100 a normal highway speed here?' whose correct answer depends on the assumed unit (km/h vs mph). Each item rendered in all 8 languages with native verification, with unit words kept generic/underspecified in stratum A. Include an EXPLICIT-UNIT CONTROL (units fully specified) where the correct answer is unit-system-independent, to bound the effect. Normalize answers to a language-agnostic form for scoring.
3) BEHAVIORAL LEAKAGE TEST: For each (item, language) determine which measurement system the model's interpretation implies. KEY hypothesis: for unit-ambiguous items, the assumed system shifts with query language toward that language community's default (e.g., temperature interpreted as Fahrenheit in US-English, Celsius elsewhere; distance as miles in US-English, km elsewhere). Mixed-effects multinomial/logistic regression of assumed-system (and conversion error) on (language default-system, dimension, resource tier via URIEL), item as random effect; test that default-system predicts interpretation beyond surface translation (EXPLICIT-UNIT CONTROL should show no language effect). Report per-language assumed-system profiles, cross-lingual disagreement on identical quantities, and conversion-error directionality.
4) SHARED MAGNITUDE & ASSUMED-UNIT DIRECTIONS (probing + transfer): At each layer pool the hidden state at the quantity/answer position. (a) Fit a magnitude probe (regress to log-value) to confirm a shared magnitude code; (b) train a linear 'assumed unit-system' probe (metric vs imperial; C vs F) on data where the system is inferable, on ENGLISH, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually, reporting AUROC/F1 transfer as evidence of a language-independent unit-system direction that is SELECTED per language. Compare to per-language-trained probes to bound shared-vs-specific. Use logit-lens to identify when the assumed unit becomes decodable across depth.
5) DEPTH & LEAKAGE ANALYSIS: Correlate the internal assumed-unit probe output with behavioral interpretation within/across languages (link test), and correlate leakage magnitude (how much query language shifts the internal assumed unit on ambiguous items) with each language's real-world default-system convention and URIEL distance (Spearman).
6) LOCALIZE UNIT-SYSTEM COMPONENTS: Via activation/path patching between a run assuming system S1 and a matched run assuming S2 on the SAME quantity (induced via different query languages or minimal unit-cueing), sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose patching flips the assumed system (read out by the unit-system probe and the emitted answer). Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (validated via per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs path patching.
7) CAUSAL UNIT-SYSTEM STEERING (decisive): Derive a unit-system steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (metric-assuming runs minus imperial-assuming runs; Celsius minus Fahrenheit). Test (i) SWITCH: adding/subtracting it makes a US-English query default to metric/Celsius (and vice versa), changing the numeric interpretation and range judgments on held-out ambiguous items; (ii) it works cross-lingually and can OVERRIDE the query language's default; (iii) REVERSE-CONSISTENCY: steering toward the correct system for a given item improves accuracy on items whose correct answer requires that system; (iv) it does NOT change the surface output language and does not harm EXPLICIT-UNIT controls or general QA (fidelity + retention). Metrics: assumed-system flip rate, interpretation/range-judgment accuracy under target system, output-language fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress leakage and steering efficacy on each language's default-system convention and URIEL distance; separate dimensions (temperature vs distance vs weight vs volume) to see which leak most; the US-vs-UK English split as a clean within-language, within-typology test of convention (isolating culture from language); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; token-pooling; robustness across templates and forced-choice-vs-free formats; whether a single unit-system vector generalizes across dimensions and languages.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language assumed-system profiles and cross-lingual disagreement, default-system regression coefficients, conversion-error directionality, cross-lingual magnitude and unit-system probe transfer AUROC/F1, assumed-unit decodability depth, internal-vs-behavior correlation, leakage-vs-convention correlation, patch-localized unit-system layer, causal steering assumed-system-flip rate and target-system accuracy, output fidelity, control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Default-system coding is graded and register/context-dependent (e.g., UK mixes miles and Celsius); we use real-world convention references, treat default-system as a graded per-dimension predictor, exploit the US-vs-UK English split as a clean control, and report sensitivity to coding. 2) Effects could reflect surface translation of unit words rather than an internal assumed-system default; we mitigate by keeping units generic/underspecified in stratum A, using the EXPLICIT-UNIT control, and the internal-assumed-unit-predicts-behavior link (step 5), plus steering that overrides the query language while keeping surface language fixed. 3) Some models may default to a single system (usually metric or US) regardless of query language; this is itself an informative, publishable finding about measurement-system bias, and we quantify how often the assumed system is even contested via probe transfer and behavioral variance. 4) Confound with training frequency of unit constructions in lower-resource languages; we control with URIEL resource tiers and use EXPLICIT-UNIT controls as frequency-neutral baselines plus within-item contrasts. 5) Conversion accuracy conflates arithmetic skill with unit-default bias; we separate directional bias (which system is assumed) from raw arithmetic error and report both. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test 5 models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Causal steering may trade fluency or control accuracy; we report output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the reverse-consistency test to ensure steering selects a unit system rather than generically boosting accuracy. 8) The unit-system signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants and report where a scalar direction is insufficient. 9) Distinguishing from my number-naming proposal is essential; here number words and magnitudes are held fixed and we manipulate only the assumed UNIT SYSTEM, so any inference change is attributable to unit-system representation, not to number-word morphology.

Name: crosslingual_ripple_inference_decomposition
Title: Does an Edit Ripple Across Languages? Decomposing Cross-Lingual Propagation of Entailed Facts into a Shared Inference Step and a Language-Specific Decoding Step
Short Hypothesis: When a fact is edited in one language, the logically-entailed consequences of that edit (its 'ripple' facts) fail to appear in other languages far more often than the edited fact itself, and this cross-lingual ripple failure decomposes cleanly into two dissociable causes: (1) a SHARED INFERENCE failure, where the model never computes the entailed consequence in its language-independent middle-layer concept space, versus (2) a LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC DECODING failure, where the consequence IS computed internally but is not surfaced in the target language. We hypothesize these two failure modes are separable via probing, predictable from typological distance, and separately repairable—decoding failures by steering the internal consequence into the target language's decoding path, inference failures only by deepening the edit—so that diagnosing which mode dominates for a given ripple/language pair tells us exactly which intervention will work.
Related Work: Cross-lingual knowledge editing work (Beniwal et al. 2024 XME; Banerjee et al. 2024 ELFI/ELFO; Durrani et al. 2025 survey) shows edits to a fact propagate poorly across languages, especially across script families, but studies only whether the EDITED fact transfers—not whether its logically-entailed RIPPLE consequences transfer, and offers no mechanistic decomposition. Monolingual ripple-effect work (Cohen et al. RippleEdits; Huang et al. 2026 JNO; Rinberg et al. 2025 RippleBench) studies propagation to related facts within ONE language and treats propagation as a single quantity, never crossing languages or separating an inference step from a decoding step. Mechanistic multilingual work locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for static facts (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) but does not study edits, ripples, or inference. Our proposal is the first to (a) measure cross-lingual propagation of ENTAILED consequences of an edit, (b) decompose ripple failure into a shared-inference vs language-specific-decoding component via mid-layer probing and activation patching, (c) tie each component to typological/script distance, and (d) show the two components require different repairs, turning a monolithic 'edits don't transfer' observation into an actionable, mechanism-level diagnostic.
Abstract: Editing a fact in a language model should update not only that fact but its logical consequences: if we teach the model that a country's capital changed, questions about which city hosts that country's government should update too. In multilingual models, does this inferential closure cross language boundaries, and if it fails, why? We introduce CrossRipple, a framework and dataset that, for each edited fact, defines a set of one- and two-hop entailed 'ripple' facts and evaluates whether the edit and its ripples surface across languages spanning multiple scripts and families. We first show, behaviorally, that ripple facts transfer across languages far worse than the edited fact itself, with a gap that grows with typological and script distance. We then decompose each cross-lingual ripple failure into two dissociable causes using interpretability. Training a linear probe on the model's middle-layer 'concept space' for the post-edit consequence, we distinguish SHARED-INFERENCE failures (the model never internally derives the consequence) from LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC DECODING failures (the consequence is present internally but not surfaced in the target language), and validate the split with activation patching. Crucially, we show the two failure modes demand different fixes: decoding failures are repaired by steering the internal consequence representation into the target language's decoding path (recovering the ripple without re-editing), while inference failures require editing at deeper, shared layers. Across mLAMA-derived ripple facts, ROME/MEMIT edits, and five open models over 12 languages, our work converts 'edits don't propagate multilingually' into a per-ripple, per-language mechanistic diagnostic with matched interventions.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Decoder models Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (edits + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/CJK/Arabic/Devanagari and multiple families/resource tiers (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili, Indonesian, French).
2) DATASET (CrossRipple): Starting from mLAMA/Wikidata factual triples, select ~400 editable facts and, for each, construct its logically-entailed RIPPLE facts using Wikidata relation chains and RippleEdits-style templates: (a) ONE-HOP ripples (e.g., edit 'capital of X is Y' -> ripple 'the government of X sits in Y', 'Y is a city in X'); (b) TWO-HOP ripples (composition of two relations). Each edited fact and each ripple fact has a short, decodable gold answer, translated/native-verified into all 12 languages. Verify pre-edit that the model answers the edited fact and ripples with the OLD value (so the edit is a genuine change), and record which facts/languages the model knows pre-edit to separate genuine ripple failure from prior ignorance.
3) EDITING SETUP: Apply the edit in ENGLISH only (the canonical asymmetry setting) using ROME and MEMIT; also test editing in a non-English source language as an ablation. Evaluate post-edit: (i) EDIT SUCCESS on the edited fact in every language; (ii) RIPPLE SUCCESS on each ripple fact in every language. Metric: accuracy of producing the NEW consequence value.
4) BEHAVIORAL RIPPLE GAP: Show ripple facts transfer across languages substantially worse than the edited fact, and that the ripple-transfer gap grows with URIEL typological distance and script difference (Spearman; mixed-effects regression of ripple success on distance, hop-count, and prior-knowledge, with fact as random effect). Contrast one-hop vs two-hop ripples.
5) MID-LAYER CONSEQUENCE PROBE: For each ripple, train a linear probe (on ENGLISH post-edit hidden states at the answer position) to detect whether the NEW consequence value is internally represented in the middle-layer concept space, selecting the best layer on English held-out data. Apply this probe to the target-language runs. DECOMPOSITION: for each failed ripple in a target language, classify it as (A) SHARED-INFERENCE FAILURE if the probe says the new consequence is NOT internally present, or (B) DECODING FAILURE if the probe says it IS present but the surface answer still gives the old/wrong value. Report the proportion of A vs B per language and per hop-count.
6) CAUSAL VALIDATION OF THE SPLIT: For a sample of DECODING-classified failures, use activation patching—patch the mid-layer consequence representation from a correctly-rippling language (e.g., English) into the failing target-language run—and test whether the correct new answer surfaces (confirming the consequence was decodable if reached). For INFERENCE-classified failures, verify patching the mid-layer does NOT help (the consequence isn't there to patch). Cross-check with path patching.
7) MATCHED REPAIRS (decisive): (a) DECODING REPAIR: derive a difference-of-means steering vector at the localized layer that pushes the internal consequence into the target language's decoding path; apply on held-out DECODING failures and measure ripple recovery, while confirming surface output language is unchanged and edited-fact/unrelated-fact accuracy is preserved. (b) INFERENCE REPAIR: for INFERENCE failures, test that only editing at deeper/shared layers (or adding the consequence as a direct edit) restores the ripple, and that decoding steering alone does NOT. This demonstrates the two modes require different interventions. Metrics: per-mode ripple recovery rate, output-language fidelity, edited-fact retention, unrelated-fact (locality) retention, general-capability spot check (multilingual MMLU subset).
8) DISTANCE & MODEL ANALYSIS: test whether DECODING failures dominate for typologically close languages (inference shared, decoding weak) and INFERENCE failures dominate for distant/low-resource languages; compare English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); ablate editing method (ROME vs MEMIT), hop-count, and probe layer.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: edit success and ripple success per language, ripple-transfer gap vs typological/script distance and hop-count, proportion of shared-inference vs decoding failures, patch-confirmed classification accuracy, per-mode matched-repair recovery rates, output fidelity, edited-fact and locality retention, general-capability retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Defining logically-entailed ripples requires care to avoid facts that are not strictly entailed; we restrict to Wikidata-derivable one/two-hop consequences and native-verify templates, reporting inter-annotator agreement on entailment. 2) The mid-layer consequence probe may be inaccurate, blurring the inference-vs-decoding split; we validate the probe on English (where ground truth is available), report probe AUROC, and confirm the split causally via patching rather than relying on the probe alone. 3) Editing methods (ROME/MEMIT) have artifacts and may not cleanly install the edited fact even in English; we condition all ripple analysis on successful English edits and report edit-success rates. 4) Some ripple failures may reflect the model never knowing the intermediate relation in the target language (a prior-knowledge gap, not an edit-propagation failure); we pre-screen per-language knowledge of intermediate relations and separate these cases. 5) Decoding steering may harm fluency or leak the source language; we cap steering strength and monitor output-language fidelity and locality retention rather than claiming a free lunch. 6) Results may be model- or method-specific; we test five models and two editing methods and report aggregate and per-model results. 7) The inference/decoding dichotomy may be a spectrum for partially-computed consequences; we report probe confidence and partial-patch recovery continuously rather than forcing a binary.

Name: crosslingual_error_step_localization
Title: Where Does the Chain Break in Each Language? Decomposing Multilingual Reasoning Failure into a Shared Error-Prone Skeleton and Language-Specific Step Weaknesses
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM solves the SAME multi-step reasoning problem in different languages, its failures are not uniformly distributed: some reasoning STEPS are error-prone regardless of language (a shared, language-independent difficulty skeleton), while other steps fail only in specific languages (language-specific step weaknesses tied to that step's linguistic demands, e.g., number-word morphology, connective/negation handling). We hypothesize (1) the per-step error profile decomposes into a shared component (a step's intrinsic difficulty that transfers across languages) and a language-specific component predictable from the step's linguistic operation and typological distance; (2) an internal 'step-correctness' signal at the point of each step is largely language-independent and transferable; and (3) at language-specific failure steps, the model has already committed the error locally, so a targeted per-step intervention (re-injecting the shared correct intermediate representation into the target language's execution path at that step) repairs the chain without re-solving the whole problem.
Related Work: Recent work shows multilingual reasoning suffers cross-lingual collapse where models revert to English mid-chain (Lim et al. 2026 OSCD; Li et al. 2025 language drift/SCD) and that forcing a shared reasoning language helps globally (Wang 2025; Zhao 2025). Multi-hop mRAG work (Wang 2026 Syfer; Shen 2025) decomposes questions to limit error compounding but at the pipeline level. Benchmarks (MGSM) report per-language accuracy but treat reasoning failure as a single scalar. Mechanistic multilingual work locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS (Wang 2025; Lim 2025). NONE ask WHERE in a multi-step chain each language breaks, whether error location decomposes into a shared difficulty skeleton plus language-specific step weaknesses, whether an internal step-correctness signal transfers across languages, or whether repairing the single failing step (rather than the whole chain) fixes reasoning. Unlike prior 'force English' or 'disentangle language' approaches that treat the whole chain, and unlike my prior representational-leakage proposals, this proposal localizes failure at the STEP granularity and provides a per-step, mechanism-level decomposition and matched repair.
Abstract: Multilingual LLMs solve the same reasoning problem with very different accuracy across languages, but accuracy alone hides the crucial question: where in the reasoning chain does each language break, and is that failure point shared or language-specific? We introduce StepBreak, a framework that aligns multi-step reasoning traces of the same problem across languages at the level of individual reasoning steps, letting us build a per-step, per-language error profile. Behaviorally, we decompose each step's failure rate into a SHARED component (a step's intrinsic difficulty that fails across most languages) and a LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC component (steps that fail only in certain languages), and test whether the language-specific component is predicted by the step's linguistic operation (numerical computation, connective/negation handling, entity tracking) and by typological distance. Mechanistically, we train a linear 'step-correctness' probe on the model's hidden state at each step boundary and test whether it transfers zero-shot across languages, evidencing a language-independent notion of a step being right or wrong. Finally, in a decisive causal test, at each identified language-specific failure step we re-inject the shared correct intermediate representation (transplanted from a language that solves that step) into the target language's execution path and measure whether the downstream chain is repaired, without re-solving earlier steps. Across MGSM and multi-hop factual reasoning over 10 languages and five open models, our work reframes multilingual reasoning gaps as a structured, localizable, and step-wise-repairable phenomenon rather than a monolithic accuracy deficit.
Experiments: 1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili). 2) DATA (StepBreak): Use MGSM math word problems (which have canonical step decompositions) plus ~200 curated 2-4 hop factual-reasoning problems (Wikidata-derived), each with a gold intermediate-step decomposition. For each problem, elicit chain-of-thought in each language (native-verified prompts) and align generated steps to the gold decomposition using a step-matcher (numeric intermediate value matching for math; entity/relation matching for factual hops), yielding a per-step correctness label per (problem, language). Restrict analysis to problems the model can solve in at least one language so a shared skeleton exists. 3) PER-STEP ERROR PROFILE & DECOMPOSITION: For each step position/type, compute failure rate per language. Fit a mixed-effects model: step-failure ~ step-difficulty (random effect per step) + language + step-type x language interaction. Decompose variance into SHARED (step random effect, consistent across languages) vs LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC (significant step x language interactions). Metric: proportion of failures attributable to shared vs language-specific components; identify which step TYPES (numeric ops, negation/connective, entity tracking) drive the language-specific component and correlate with URIEL typological distance and script. 4) FIRST-ERROR LOCALIZATION: For each failed chain, identify the FIRST erroneous step. Test whether the first-error-step distribution is shared across languages (same steps break first) or shifts by language; quantify with distributional distance across languages and correlate shift with typology. 5) STEP-CORRECTNESS PROBE & TRANSFER: At each step boundary token, pool the hidden state; train a linear probe on ENGLISH to predict whether that step is correct; apply zero-shot to other languages and report AUROC, evidencing a language-independent step-correctness signal. Compare to per-language-trained probes; use logit-lens to check when the error becomes internally detectable. 6) CAUSAL PER-STEP REPAIR (decisive): For language-specific failure steps, identify a source language that solves that step correctly; via activation patching, transplant the mid-layer representation of the correct intermediate result into the target-language run AT that step boundary, then let generation continue. Measure whether the downstream chain and final answer are repaired. Compare against (a) no intervention, (b) full re-solve in English (translate-then-solve baseline), (c) forcing English CoT (Wang 2025). Metrics: chain-repair rate, final-answer accuracy gain, whether surface reasoning language is preserved, and locality (do already-correct steps/problems remain unharmed). Cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: shared-vs-language-specific split by problem type (math vs factual); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); which step types are most repairable by transplant; probe layer/dimensionality; robustness to step-matcher noise; whether a single transplant direction generalizes across problems. EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-step per-language failure rates, shared vs language-specific variance decomposition, first-error-step distribution shift vs typology, step-correctness probe transfer AUROC, causal per-step repair rate and answer-accuracy gain, comparison to translate-then-solve and force-English baselines, locality retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Step alignment across languages is noisy, especially for free-form CoT; we mitigate with numeric intermediate-value matching for math (robust) and entity/relation matching for factual hops, report matcher accuracy, and restrict to problems with clean gold decompositions. 2) Models may not emit explicit steps in some languages (collapse to English mid-chain); we detect this via per-step language-ID and treat it as a distinct failure category, quantifying how often steps are even language-native. 3) The shared-vs-language-specific decomposition depends on having enough problems solved in multiple languages; we select problem difficulty so a shared skeleton exists and report coverage. 4) The step-correctness probe may be inaccurate; we validate it on English with gold labels and confirm findings causally via patching rather than relying on the probe alone. 5) Per-step transplant may harm fluency or fail if the error is not localized to that step (compounding); we report locality retention and cross-check whether repair works only for genuinely local errors. 6) Patching/probing results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Distinguishing from 'force English' approaches is essential; we include them as baselines and position our contribution as step-level localization, the shared/language-specific decomposition, and targeted per-step repair that preserves the native reasoning language.

Name: crosslingual_computational_depth_allocation
Title: Thinking Longer in Some Languages: Does a Multilingual Model Recruit Less Internal Computational Depth for the Same Problem, and Can We Force It to Think Deeper?
Short Hypothesis: For the SAME problem, a multilingual LLM recruits systematically different amounts of internal computational depth depending on the query language: it 'commits' to an answer at an earlier layer (shallower processing) for some languages—often disadvantaged/low-resource or high-fertility ones—even when the correct answer requires deep multi-layer computation, and this premature depth-under-allocation is a distinct, measurable cause of cross-lingual accuracy gaps that is separable from tokenization fertility and knowledge gaps, and is causally repairable by forcing the model to keep computing (delaying its internal commitment) without retraining.
Related Work: Two literatures border this idea but never meet. (1) Tokenization/fertility work (Lundin et al. 2025 'Token Tax'; Regmi et al. 2026; RomanSetu 2024) shows tokens-per-word predicts multilingual accuracy, but this is about SURFACE sequence length, not internal per-forward-pass computational DEPTH; more tokens is horizontal, not vertical, compute. (2) Adaptive/dynamic-depth compute work (Mixture-of-Depths, Raposo 2024; looped/recurrent LMs, Zhu 2025; early-exit; ANIRA, Moosa 2026; 'Thinking Hard Not Smart', Fan 2026) studies per-token vertical compute allocation and test-time scaling, but is monolingual/architectural and never asks whether query LANGUAGE modulates how much internal depth a fixed model recruits for the same problem. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding but studies WHAT is represented, not the DYNAMICS/DEPTH of computation or when the model internally commits. My prior proposals concern representational leakage and step-level error localization; NONE measure per-language internal computational depth (layer of answer-commitment / early-exit agreement), tie premature shallow commitment to cross-lingual accuracy gaps as a cause separable from fertility, or causally force deeper processing. This reframes multilingual gaps as a compute-ALLOCATION problem in the depth dimension.
Abstract: Multilingual LLMs solve the same problem with very different accuracy across languages. The dominant explanation is surface tokenization: morphologically complex, low-resource languages fragment into more tokens ('token tax'), inflating cost and depressing accuracy. But token count is horizontal compute; it says nothing about how much vertical, internal computation—how many layers of processing—the model actually recruits before committing to an answer. We hypothesize that query language modulates internal computational depth: for the same problem, the model reaches a stable internal answer at an earlier layer (shallow commitment) in some languages, prematurely halting the multi-layer computation that harder items require. We measure per-item, per-language computational depth using training-free signals—the layer at which the logit-lens/tuned-lens top prediction stabilizes to the final answer (the 'commitment layer') and layer-wise answer entropy—across 10 typologically diverse languages and five open models on multi-step reasoning and multi-hop factual tasks. We test three claims: (1) commitment depth differs systematically by language and, critically, premature shallow commitment predicts errors beyond what tokenization fertility and prior-knowledge gaps explain; (2) the depth deficit concentrates on items that genuinely need deep computation, and correlates with typological distance; and (3) in a decisive causal test, we force the model to keep computing—delaying commitment via depth-recurrent looping of late layers or by suppressing the early-commitment signal—and show it recovers accuracy in shallow-committing languages without changing tokenization or retraining. This reframes multilingual gaps as an internal depth-allocation failure, distinct from and additive to the token tax.
Experiments: 1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + logit/tuned-lens + light looping on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource/fertility-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili). 2) DATA: (a) Multi-step reasoning: MGSM (parallel across languages); (b) multi-hop factual reasoning: ~250 Wikidata-derived 2-3 hop items with short decodable answers; (c) single-hop factual control (mLAMA/BMLAMA) where deep multi-layer computation is NOT required. Parallel, native-verified prompts; short single-token-decodable gold answers where possible. Record per-item tokenization fertility (tokens/word) and per-language prior-knowledge (single-hop accuracy) to control for them. 3) MEASURE COMPUTATIONAL DEPTH (training-free): For each (item, language) apply tuned-lens (and logit-lens as a cross-check) at every layer to the answer position and define: (i) COMMITMENT LAYER = earliest layer after which the top-decoded answer token stays fixed to the model's final output; (ii) layer-wise answer ENTROPY trajectory and its stabilization depth; (iii) 'early-exit agreement' = fraction of layers whose top token already equals the final answer. Validate tuned-lens fidelity per language. 4) DEPTH-DIFFERS-BY-LANGUAGE (claim 1): Mixed-effects regression of commitment layer on (language, task, item), item as random effect; test that commitment depth varies by language for matched items. KEY separability test: regress item correctness on commitment-depth-relative-to-item-need WHILE controlling for fertility and single-hop prior-knowledge; show premature shallow commitment predicts errors ADDITIVELY beyond fertility and knowledge (report incremental R^2 / likelihood-ratio tests, and partial correlations). Contrast reasoning/multi-hop (need depth) vs single-hop control (should show weak or no depth-deficit effect). 5) NEED-VS-USE & TYPOLOGY: Define per-item 'depth need' from the English commitment layer (or from item hop-count/difficulty). Show the per-language depth DEFICIT (need minus used) concentrates on high-need items and correlates with URIEL typological distance and script/fertility (Spearman), while dissociating fertility (which we also regress) from depth deficit. 6) CAUSAL DEEPER-THINKING INTERVENTIONS (decisive): (a) LATE-LAYER LOOPING: re-feed the residual stream through a block of late layers k times (a training-free depth-recurrence, inspired by looped LMs) for shallow-committing languages, delaying commitment; (b) COMMITMENT SUPPRESSION: subtract a difference-of-means 'early-commitment' direction (mean late-minus-early residual on already-committed items) to reduce premature saturation; (c) as a comparison, a simple 'add filler thinking tokens' prompt baseline. Measure accuracy change on shallow-committing languages, ensuring: (i) tokenization unchanged (interventions are internal, not longer prompts, except the prompt baseline), (ii) commitment layer actually deepens (verify via lens), (iii) no harm to already-correct items, single-hop control, or general QA (multilingual MMLU subset), (iv) output language/fluency preserved. Compare against the fertility-motivated baseline of romanization/transliteration (RomanSetu-style) to show depth-repair gains are complementary. 7) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); which languages benefit most from looping (predicted: high depth-deficit ones); number of loops / suppression strength; lens choice (tuned vs logit) robustness; whether a single looping recipe generalizes across tasks. EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language commitment depth & entropy-stabilization depth, commitment-depth vs correctness (incremental predictive power over fertility+knowledge), depth-deficit vs typology/fertility correlations, need-vs-use analysis, causal intervention accuracy recovery with verified depth-deepening, control/general-QA retention, output-language fidelity, comparison to romanization and filler-token baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Tuned/logit-lens commitment-layer estimates are noisy, especially for multi-token answers and low-resource languages; we prefer short single-token-decodable answers, validate lens fidelity per language, and cross-check tuned vs logit lens and entropy-based depth measures. 2) Commitment depth may be confounded with fertility and prior-knowledge; the whole design controls for both via regression and single-hop controls, and the causal interventions do not change tokenization, dissociating depth from the token tax. 3) Some models/languages may show NO depth deficit (already-deep processing everywhere); this is itself an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often shallow premature commitment occurs. 4) Late-layer looping can destabilize generation or degrade fluency; we cap loop count and suppression strength, verify commitment actually deepens, and report retention/fluency rather than claiming a free lunch. 5) The 'depth need' proxy (from English or hop-count) is imperfect; we triangulate with item difficulty and report sensitivity. 6) Results may be model- and lens-specific; we test five models and two lenses and report aggregate and per-model results. 7) Depth deficit and step-level error localization (a prior proposal) could overlap; here the object is the vertical layer-depth of internal commitment for the whole item, not horizontal step-wise error position, and the intervention is depth-recurrence, not step transplant—we make this contrast explicit. 8) The commitment-suppression direction may act as a generic accuracy lever; we guard against this by verifying it selectively deepens computation and does not help the single-hop control that needs no depth.

Name: moral_valence_language_weighting
Title: One Deed, Many Verdicts: A Shared Moral-Valence Axis and Its Language-Specific Reweighting in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs compute a largely language-independent internal 'moral-valence' representation of an action (how good/bad it is along shared moral dimensions), but the query language acts as a causal weighting dial that reweights this shared valence at the language-specific decoding layers, producing the documented cross-lingual variation in moral verdicts. We hypothesize (1) a single mid-layer moral-valence probe trained in one language transfers zero-shot to predict per-action moral judgments across languages, evidencing a shared moral axis; (2) the cross-lingual disagreement on the SAME action arises from a language-conditioned reweighting between mid and output layers, not from a different mid-layer valence, and this reweighting tracks the culturally-typical stance of the language's speaker community; and (3) a small, localizable set of components carries this moral-weighting signal that can be causally steered to shift a verdict toward another culture's typical judgment without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Prior multilingual moral work is almost entirely behavioral: MultiTP (Jin et al. 2024) shows large cross-lingual variance in trolley-problem judgments; Hammerl et al. 2022 show multilingual LMs capture moral norms; Mohammadi et al. 2025 and CRaFT (2025) correlate model outputs with WVS/PEW and find WEIRD-alignment and that 'cultural awareness emerges through linguistic framing'; X-Value (2026) benchmarks cross-lingual values judgment. All document THAT moral verdicts vary by language and correlate with culture, but none examine the internal MECHANISM. Mechanistic multilingual work locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) but never for MORAL VALENCE. Our proposal is the first to (a) test whether a shared, transferable moral-valence axis exists internally and cross-lingually, (b) decompose cross-lingual moral disagreement into a shared mid-layer valence versus a language-conditioned late-layer REWEIGHTING (rather than a different underlying judgment), tie that reweighting to the culturally-typical stance of each language, and (c) causally localize and steer the moral-weighting signal to shift verdicts across cultures while holding language fixed. This converts 'moral judgments vary by language' into a mechanistic, causal, and steerable account. It is distinct from my prior contested-facts proposal (which concerns factual answers with legitimately different values, e.g., national dish) because here the object is normative moral EVALUATION along shared moral dimensions, and the central claim is a shared valence axis that is language-reweighted, not multiple stored answers.
Abstract: Multilingual language models deliver systematically different moral verdicts on the same action depending on the query language, and prior work has documented this behaviorally and correlated it with cultural surveys. But why does it happen inside the model: does the model actually evaluate the action differently, or does it compute a shared sense of right and wrong and then reweight it per language before answering? We argue for the latter and make it mechanistically precise. We hypothesize that models compute a largely language-independent internal moral-valence representation of an action in their shared middle layers, and that the query language acts as a causal weighting dial at the language-specific decoding layers, shifting the emitted verdict toward the culturally-typical stance of that language's speaker community. We test three claims. First, a linear moral-valence probe trained in one language transfers zero-shot to predict per-action approval/disapproval across many languages, evidencing a shared moral axis. Second, we decompose each cross-lingual moral disagreement into a mid-layer component and a mid-to-output reweighting component and show the disagreement is driven by reweighting, not by a different mid-layer valence, and that the reweighting magnitude tracks each language's culturally-typical position (from World Values Survey-derived stances). Third, in a decisive causal test we localize the moral-weighting components via activation and path patching and steer them to shift a verdict from one culture's typical judgment toward another's while leaving the surface language and the described action unchanged. Across MultiTP- and WVS-derived moral vignettes over 12 languages and five open models, we reframe multilingual moral variation as a shared valence that is late-stage, culturally reweighted, and steerable.
Experiments: 1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/culturally/resource-diverse languages spanning WEIRD and non-WEIRD communities (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili, Indonesian, Korean). 2) DATASET (MoralWeigh): Assemble ~500 moral-evaluation items along shared moral dimensions with a per-action valence probe ('Is this action morally acceptable? yes/no' plus a graded 1-7 acceptability rating). Draw from (a) WVS/PEW justifiability topics (e.g., divorce, alcohol, specific interpersonal harms/fairness/authority scenarios) that have documented cross-cultural stance variation, and (b) MultiTP-style dilemmas for a scaling check. For each item record the culturally-typical stance per language community from WVS survey data (the ground-truth 'cultural prior'). Include a UNIVERSAL-CONSENSUS control stratum (actions judged near-uniformly across cultures, e.g., gratuitous cruelty) and a HIGH-VARIANCE stratum (topics with large cross-cultural disagreement). Translate/native-verify all items into 12 languages; keep the described action fixed across languages. 3) BEHAVIORAL BASELINE: Measure per-(action, language) verdict and rating. Confirm cross-lingual disagreement concentrates in the high-variance stratum and that per-language verdicts track the WVS cultural stance (correlation with survey data), while the consensus control shows low variance. Mixed-effects model of verdict on (language cultural-stance, stratum), action as random effect. 4) SHARED MORAL-VALENCE PROBE & TRANSFER (claim 1): At each layer pool the hidden state at the answer position; train a linear moral-valence probe (approve vs disapprove, and a regression to the graded rating) on ENGLISH mid-layer activations, select the best layer on English held-out data, and apply zero-shot to every other language. Metric: AUROC/Spearman of predicting per-action verdict/rating cross-lingually. Baselines: model's emitted verdict, final-layer probe, surface-lexical sentiment. Also train per-language probes to bound shared-vs-specific. High transfer supports a language-independent moral axis. 5) LOCATE LANGUAGE-TRANSITION BAND: Per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens (Wang 2025) to anchor the mid vs output decomposition. 6) DISAGREEMENT DECOMPOSITION (claim 2): For each action, compare the MID-layer shared-probe valence across languages (should be similar if the axis is shared) versus the OUTPUT verdict (which disagrees). Define REWEIGHTING = shift from the shared mid-layer valence to the emitted verdict per language.
