Test whether cross-lingual disagreement is explained by REWEIGHTING (mid-valence similar, output differs) rather than by differing mid-valence. Correlate per-language reweighting magnitude/direction with the WVS cultural stance and with typological/cultural distance. 7) LOCALIZE MORAL-WEIGHTING COMPONENTS: Run the same high-variance action in a language that approves vs one that disapproves; use activation and path patching across layers/heads/MLPs to find the minimal component set whose transfer flips the verdict. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) CAUSAL CULTURAL STEERING (decisive, claim 3): Derive a moral-weighting steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (approving-culture runs minus disapproving-culture runs). Test (i) SHIFT: adding/subtracting it moves the verdict toward another culture's typical judgment on held-out high-variance items; (ii) it works cross-lingually and can OVERRIDE the query language's default stance; (iii) it does NOT change the surface output language or the described action (fidelity check), and does not flip the UNIVERSAL-CONSENSUS control (a genuine moral axis should resist steering on clear-cut cases) or degrade general QA; (iv) REVERSE-consistency: the magnitude of steering needed correlates with the cultural distance between source and target stance. Metrics: verdict-shift rate, rating shift, output-language fidelity, consensus-control resistance, general-QA retention. 9) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: WEIRD vs non-WEIRD asymmetry (is English/WEIRD the default the model reweights AWAY from?); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); moral-dimension breakdown (harm/fairness vs purity/authority-type topics); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank moral subspace; robustness across templates and yes/no-vs-rating formats; whether one steering vector generalizes across topics and languages. EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: cross-lingual moral-probe transfer AUROC/Spearman, per-language verdict vs WVS-stance correlation, mid-valence-similarity vs output-disagreement (reweighting) decomposition, reweighting-vs-cultural-distance correlation, patch-localized weighting layer, causal steering verdict-shift rate, consensus-control resistance, output fidelity, general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Moral 'ground truth' is contested; we avoid claiming correctness and instead use WVS/PEW community stances descriptively as cultural priors, restrict scored items to topics with documented cross-cultural variation, and use a near-universal-consensus control to anchor a genuine axis. 2) Instruction-tuned models may refuse or hedge on moral items; we use graded acceptability ratings and log-probability-based approval scores (as in Mohammadi et al.) alongside verdicts, and report refusal rates. 3) The shared mid-layer valence might itself differ by language (no shared axis) for some topics; this is an informative outcome and we quantify per-topic how much of the disagreement is mid-valence vs reweighting rather than assuming the split. 4) Probe transfer could be confounded by latent English pivoting; we report per-language transfer, compare to per-language-trained probes, and include non-WEIRD source-language probes. 5) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 6) Causal steering raises misuse concerns (making a model endorse a target culture's stance); we frame and use it strictly as an interpretability/diagnostic tool, evaluate on non-harmful value topics, verify it does not flip clear-cut moral wrongs (consensus control), and report retention rather than deploying it. 7) WVS stance mapping to specific vignettes is imperfect; we use topics with direct WVS items and native verification, and report sensitivity. 8) A single moral-weighting direction may be an oversimplification across distinct moral dimensions; we test low-rank subspaces and per-dimension directions and report where a scalar dial is insufficient. 9) Distinguishing from my contested-facts proposal is essential; here the target is normative moral EVALUATION along a shared valence axis (not selection among multiple stored factual answers), and the core claim/intervention concerns late-layer reweighting of that axis.

Name: crosslingual_task_vector_portability
Title: Is a Learned Task Language-Independent? Cross-Lingual Portability of In-Context Function Vectors and the Abstraction-vs-Execution Decomposition of ICL Transfer
Short Hypothesis: When a NEW abstract task is taught purely in-context via demonstrations in language A, the model forms a compact, largely language-independent 'task vector' (function vector) in its middle layers that encodes WHAT to do; cross-lingual ICL transfer succeeds when this shared task vector is correctly extracted from language-A demonstrations AND correctly executed on a language-B query, and transfer failures decompose cleanly into a shared TASK-ABSTRACTION failure (the task vector is never formed or is language-entangled) versus a language-specific EXECUTION failure (the correct task vector is present but cannot be applied/decoded in the target language). We can extract the task vector from one language and inject it to drive the task in another language WITHOUT any demonstrations, and this transplant repairs execution-type failures but not abstraction-type failures.
Related Work: Two literatures border but never meet. (1) Cross-lingual ICL work is entirely behavioral: X-InSTA (Tanwar 2023), BUFFET (Asai 2023), source-language selection (Philippy 2026), multilingual-demonstration blending (Tu 2025, Kaneko 2025) all study which demonstrations/source languages maximize target-language accuracy, with no internal account. (2) Monolingual mechanistic ICL work shows tasks are summarized by a compact 'function vector' (Todd et al. 2024) or 'task vector' (Hendel et al. 2023) at a mid-layer that can be extracted and injected to trigger the task zero-shot in ENGLISH. NO work asks whether this task/function vector is language-independent, whether it can be extracted from demonstrations in one language and injected to execute the task on a query in another language, or whether cross-lingual ICL transfer failure decomposes into task-abstraction versus execution/decoding components. This is also distinct from all my prior proposals, which concern PRETRAINED knowledge or typological-feature leakage; here the object is a NEWLY acquired, purely in-context task representation and its cross-lingual portability, tested causally via function-vector transplant.
Abstract: In-context learning lets a model acquire a brand-new task from a handful of demonstrations without any weight update. Monolingual interpretability shows this learned task is compressed into a single 'function vector' at a middle layer that can be extracted and injected to trigger the task zero-shot. We ask a simple question with broad implications for multilingual AI: is a task learned in one language language-independent? Concretely, if a model infers a task from demonstrations in language A, does it form a shared task vector that it can execute on a query written in language B, and when cross-lingual in-context transfer fails, is it because the task was never abstracted or because it could not be executed in the target language? We introduce PolyTaskVec, a suite of simple, novel, non-lexical abstract tasks (e.g., 'return the antonym', 'output the last-listed item', 'apply a taught symbol-to-category mapping') instantiated with parallel demonstrations and queries across 10 typologically diverse languages, so tasks cannot be solved by memorized facts. We extract each task's function vector per language, measure its cross-lingual similarity, and test whether a function vector extracted from language-A demonstrations, injected into a demonstration-free language-B query, drives correct task execution. We decompose every cross-lingual transfer failure into a shared-abstraction failure (no transferable task vector forms) versus an execution failure (the correct vector is present but not applied) and validate the split by showing function-vector transplant repairs execution failures but not abstraction failures. We relate portability to typological distance and reframe cross-lingual ICL as a measurable, steerable interplay of a shared task abstraction and a language-specific execution step.
Experiments: 1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + activation extraction/patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili). 2) DATASET (PolyTaskVec): Build ~15 SIMPLE ABSTRACT tasks designed to be solvable from demonstrations alone and NOT from memorized facts, in three families: (a) LINGUISTIC-MAPPING tasks with parallel content (antonym-of-word, plural-of-word, capitalize-first-letter-of-answer where scripts allow, translate-to-a-fixed-third-language); (b) LIST/STRUCTURE tasks (return last item, return item at taught position, count items, sort by a taught key) whose demonstrations use language-native words but require no world knowledge; (c) TAUGHT-RULE tasks (a novel symbol-to-category or arbitrary word-to-label mapping defined entirely by the in-context demonstrations, e.g., learn that 'blicket' maps to category X from examples), which are guaranteed novel and non-parametric. Each task has k parallel demonstrations and held-out queries rendered in all 10 languages with native verification; answers scored via language-agnostic normalized matching. Include a WORLD-KNOWLEDGE-CONTAMINATION check: tasks where the answer could be recalled are excluded or flagged. 3) BEHAVIORAL CROSS-LINGUAL ICL MATRIX: For every (task, demo-language A, query-language B) pair, measure task accuracy with standard few-shot ICL (demos in A, query in B). Report the full A x B transfer matrix per task; test how transfer accuracy depends on URIEL typological/script distance between A and B via mixed-effects regression (task as random effect). Establish which (task, A, B) cells are failures. 4) EXTRACT FUNCTION VECTORS PER LANGUAGE: Following Todd et al., for each (task, language) compute the function vector as the mean over demonstration runs of a mid-layer attention/residual activation at the query position (sweep layers to find the best 'task layer' on English validation). Verify each language's own function vector, injected into a demonstration-FREE query in the same language, triggers the task (zero-shot task execution), confirming valid extraction. 5) CROSS-LINGUAL FUNCTION-VECTOR SIMILARITY: Measure cosine/CKA similarity between function vectors of the SAME task extracted from different languages, and between DIFFERENT tasks (control). Hypothesis: same-task cross-language vectors are far more similar than different-task vectors, evidencing a shared, language-independent task abstraction; similarity decreases with typological distance. 6) DECISIVE PORTABILITY TEST: Inject the function vector extracted from language-A demonstrations into a demonstration-FREE query written in language B (no demos in B at all) and measure whether the task is correctly executed on the B query. High success = the task abstraction is genuinely shared and portable. Compare against (i) same-language injection (upper bound), (ii) random/other-task vector (lower bound), (iii) standard cross-lingual ICL with demos. 7) ABSTRACTION-vs-EXECUTION DECOMPOSITION: For each cross-lingual ICL FAILURE cell (demos in A, query in B), classify it: (A) ABSTRACTION FAILURE if the A-extracted function vector, even when transplanted, fails to drive the task on B queries (the task abstraction does not transfer); (B) EXECUTION FAILURE if standard ICL fails BUT transplanting the A-function-vector into the B query succeeds (the abstraction was present/shared; the model just failed to apply it in B). Report the proportion of A vs B across tasks and language pairs; correlate the two failure types with typological distance (predict execution failures dominate for close languages, abstraction failures for distant/low-resource ones). Cross-check with activation patching of the task-layer representation from a succeeding run into a failing run. 8) MATCHED-REPAIR VALIDATION: Show the decomposition is actionable: EXECUTION failures are repaired by function-vector transplant (measured recovery rate), while ABSTRACTION failures are not and instead require demonstrations in a language closer to the query or in the query language itself. Verify transplant preserves the output language and does not harm control tasks or general QA. 9) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: task-family effects (mapping vs structural vs taught-rule); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); function-vector layer/dimensionality; number of demonstrations k; whether a single averaged multi-language function vector transfers best (blended-abstraction hypothesis, connecting to Tu 2025's multilingual-demo finding); robustness across templates. EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: full cross-lingual ICL transfer matrix and distance regression, same-task vs different-task function-vector similarity and its distance dependence, demonstration-free cross-lingual injection success vs same-language and random baselines, proportion of abstraction vs execution failures with patching validation, matched-repair recovery rates, output-language fidelity and control/general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Ensuring tasks are truly non-parametric and not solvable via memorized facts is critical; we use taught-rule tasks with novel arbitrary mappings and structural tasks requiring no world knowledge, run a contamination check, and report per-task whether zero-demo baselines already succeed. 2) Function-vector extraction quality varies across models and layers; we validate extraction via same-language zero-shot triggering before any cross-lingual claim and sweep layers on held-out data. 3) Some models may not form a clean transferable function vector for certain tasks/languages (especially low-resource); this is itself an informative finding, and we quantify how often a portable vector exists rather than assuming it. 4) The abstraction-vs-execution split may be a spectrum; we report continuous transplant-recovery rates rather than forcing a strict binary and cross-check with activation patching. 5) Cross-lingual similarity of vectors could be inflated by shared surface/format cues rather than genuine task abstraction; different-task controls and taught-rule (format-matched) tasks guard against this. 6) Transplant may harm fluency or leak the source language; we monitor output-language fidelity and cap injection strength. 7) Results may be model-specific; we test five models spanning English-centric and multilingual-centric pretraining and report aggregate and per-model results. 8) Overlap with monolingual function-vector work (Todd et al., Hendel et al.) requires clear differentiation; our contribution is the cross-lingual portability of task vectors and the abstraction-vs-execution decomposition of ICL transfer, neither of which they address.

Name: irrealis_world_separation_crosslingual
Title: If Pigs Could Fly: Does a Language's Irrealis Grammar Shape How Multilingual Models Separate the Actual World from Hypothetical Worlds?
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM reads a counterfactual/hypothetical statement, it computes a largely language-independent internal 'world-separation' representation that keeps the actual world distinct from the hypothetical world (so real-world facts do not contaminate reasoning inside the hypothetical), but the query language's irrealis/subjunctive/conditional grammar leaks into how cleanly this separation is enforced: languages that obligatorily grammaticalize counterfactuality (e.g., dedicated subjunctive/counterfactual marking) produce a sharper internal actual-vs-hypothetical split and less real-world contamination, whereas languages that mark it only optionally (e.g., English 'if...had') allow more leakage, yielding predictable cross-lingual disagreement on counterfactual inferences about the SAME scenario. We further hypothesize (1) a shared middle-layer world-separation direction that transfers across languages; (2) the amount of real-world contamination inside a hypothetical is causally modulated by the query language's irrealis grammar, predictable from typology; and (3) a small, localizable 'hypotheticality' signal can be causally steered to strengthen or weaken world-separation, fixing or inducing contamination errors without changing the surface answer.
Related Work: Counterfactual-reasoning work in NLP is monolingual/English and behavioral: Li, Yu & Ettinger (2023) show models can override real-world knowledge in counterfactual scenarios but that the effect is largely driven by lexical cues; CounterLogic (Joishy et al. 2025) shows accuracy drops ~14% when context contradicts parametric knowledge and proposes a prompting fix (Flag&Reason); Toutanova et al. (2022) probe whether world knowledge is needed for causal inference. Reasoning-as-state-transition and counterfactual-intervention interpretability work (Zhang et al. 2026; Mohanty et al. 2026) study internal states but not cross-lingual irrealis. Mechanistic multilingual work locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) and, in my prior proposals, for polarity, evidential source, aspect, etc. NONE ask whether a query language's IRREALIS/SUBJUNCTIVE/COUNTERFACTUAL grammar leaks into the model's internal separation of the actual world from hypothetical worlds, whether that separation is language-independent and transferable, whether irrealis grammaticalization predicts real-world contamination of counterfactual reasoning per language, or whether a hypotheticality signal can be causally localized and steered. This is distinct from my prior aspect/evidentiality/polarity proposals (which concern completion, information source, and negation semantics respectively): here the object is the world-status (actual vs hypothetical) representation and its cross-lingual geometry, grounded in irrealis typology and tested causally, and it converts the English-only 'lexical-cue-driven counterfactual' finding into a cross-lingual, mechanistic, causal account.
Abstract: Reasoning about what could have been requires holding two worlds apart: the actual world, where real-world facts hold, and a hypothetical world, where a counterfactual premise takes over and ordinary facts may be suspended ('If pigs could fly, they would need wings'). Languages differ sharply in how they grammatically mark this hypothetical status—some obligatorily use subjunctive or dedicated counterfactual morphology, others (like English) mark it only optionally. We ask whether a multilingual LLM internally separates the actual world from hypothetical worlds in a language-independent way, and whether a language's irrealis grammar leaks into how cleanly that separation is enforced, letting real-world knowledge contaminate counterfactual reasoning more in some languages than others. We build IrrealisProbe, parallel counterfactual and hypothetical items across 8 typologically diverse languages spanning strong and weak irrealis grammaticalization, each with a counterfactual-consequence probe, a real-world-contamination distractor (the true-in-reality but counterfactually-wrong answer), and a factual control. Behaviorally we test whether real-world-contamination errors track each language's irrealis typology on the SAME scenario. Using a linear probe we test for a shared middle-layer world-separation direction that transfers zero-shot across languages; via logit-lens we track when the hypothetical world 'takes over' across depth. Through activation and path patching we localize the components carrying the hypotheticality signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to strengthen world-separation (removing contamination in weak-irrealis languages) and to weaken it (inducing contamination), while leaving the surface answer and language unchanged. We relate leakage strength to irrealis typology and typological distance, reframing counterfactual robustness as a measurable, steerable property of a model's world-separation representation.
Experiments: 1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 languages spanning irrealis/counterfactual grammaticalization: strong obligatory marking (Spanish, French, Italian with subjunctive/conditional; Russian with the bi-particle counterfactual; Turkish with dedicated conditional-past) versus weaker/optional marking (English, German, Chinese). Code each language's irrealis grammaticalization strength (obligatory subjunctive/counterfactual morphology vs optional periphrasis) from typological references (Palmer's Mood and Modality; WALS irrealis/conditional chapters) plus URIEL for typological distance; treat grammaticalization strength as a graded predictor. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs. 2) DATASET (IrrealisProbe): ~450 items in three strata. (A) COUNTERFACTUAL-CONSEQUENCE: a counterfactual premise plus a question whose correct answer requires reasoning INSIDE the hypothetical world and DIFFERS from the real-world fact (e.g., 'If cats were reptiles, would a cat be warm-blooded?' correct: no [hypothetical]; contamination answer: yes [real-world]). (B) HYPOTHETICAL-vs-FACTUAL minimal pairs: the same content framed factually ('Cats are mammals; is a cat warm-blooded?') vs counterfactually, so the correct answer flips; used to isolate whether the model suspends the real fact. (C) FACTUAL CONTROL: purely factual items (no hypothetical) where the real-world answer is correct, to bound the effect. Each item has the counterfactual-correct answer, a real-world-contamination distractor, and (where possible) short single-token-decodable options. Realize the hypothetical framing naturally in each language—obligatory subjunctive/counterfactual morphology where the grammar requires it, optional periphrasis elsewhere—with native verification of naturalness and premise-equivalence. Draw on Li et al. (2023)/CounterLogic templates, extended cross-lingually and controlled for lexical cues (match surface wording of contamination distractors). 3) BEHAVIORAL LEAKAGE TEST: For each (item, language) record whether the model gives the counterfactual-correct answer or the real-world-contamination answer. KEY hypothesis: strong-irrealis languages show LESS real-world contamination (cleaner world-separation) on the SAME scenario than weak-irrealis languages, yielding systematic cross-lingual disagreement. Mixed-effects logistic regression of contamination-error on (irrealis grammaticalization strength, stratum, language, resource tier via URIEL), item as random effect; test the grammaticalization coefficient beyond resource level and beyond lexical cues; compare against the FACTUAL CONTROL (should show no language-driven contamination). Report per-language contamination profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical scenarios. 4) SHARED WORLD-SEPARATION DIRECTION & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the answer/premise position. Train a linear 'hypotheticality' probe (is the reasoning operating in the actual vs hypothetical world) on ENGLISH data and apply zero-shot to other languages; report AUROC/macro-F1 transfer as evidence of a language-independent world-separation direction. Compare to per-language-trained probes to bound shared-vs-specific. Use logit-lens to identify the layer where the hypothetical-consequence token overtakes the real-world token (world-takeover depth). 5) DEPTH & LEAKAGE ANALYSIS: Correlate world-takeover depth and internal hypotheticality-probe output with behavioral contamination within/across languages (link test), and correlate leakage magnitude (how much query language shifts internal world-separation on matched counterfactual items) with irrealis grammaticalization strength and URIEL distance (Spearman). 6) LOCALIZE HYPOTHETICALITY COMPONENTS: Via activation/path patching between a counterfactual-framing run and its matched factual-framing run of the SAME content, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose patching flips the internal world-status (read out by the hypotheticality probe and the emitted answer). Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (validated via per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) CAUSAL WORLD-SEPARATION STEERING (decisive): Derive a hypotheticality steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (counterfactual runs minus factual runs). Test (i) STRENGTHEN: adding it to weak-irrealis-language counterfactual queries reduces real-world contamination toward strong-irrealis levels (the model reasons inside the hypothetical); (ii) WEAKEN: subtracting it induces contamination on well-separated items (real-world facts leak in); (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where irrealis is weakly grammaticalized; (iv) it does NOT change the surface output language or the described scenario (fidelity check), does not harm the FACTUAL CONTROL, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: contamination-error reduction, contamination-induction rate (reverse), output-language fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: strengthening should only help on counterfactual items (where suspending real facts is correct) and should NOT change factual-control answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever. 8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress leakage and steering efficacy on irrealis grammaticalization and URIEL distance; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; token-pooling; robustness across templates and MC-vs-cloze-vs-free formats; whether a single hypotheticality vector generalizes across scenarios and languages; test whether the same direction generalizes from counterfactuals to other hypothetical framings (wishes, future conditionals, fiction) to probe whether world-separation is a unified representation. EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-(language,stratum) counterfactual-correct vs contamination rate, grammaticalization x framing interaction, cross-lingual disagreement, shared hypotheticality-probe transfer AUROC/F1, world-takeover depth, internal-vs-behavior correlation, leakage-vs-typology correlation, patch-localized hypotheticality layer, causal steering contamination-reduction and contamination-induction rates, output fidelity, factual-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Realizing the counterfactual/hypothetical framing naturally and equivalently across languages is delicate (obligatory subjunctive morphology vs optional periphrasis); we use native verification, naturalness ratings, and treat grammaticalization strength as a graded predictor, reporting sensitivity to framing choices. 2) Prior work (Li et al. 2023) shows counterfactual behavior is largely lexical-cue-driven; we control this by surface-matching contamination distractors, including minimal-pair factual-vs-counterfactual framings, and using the internal-hypotheticality-predicts-behavior link (step 5) as evidence beyond surface form. 3) Some models may fail to separate worlds at all (uniform real-world contamination) or resolve it very early/holistically; either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often a world-separation signal is present via probe transfer and stratum-B flip accuracy. 4) Counterfactual-consequence correct answers can be genuinely debatable for some premises; we restrict scored items to those with clear native-consensus consequences (drawing on validated psycholinguistic/CounterLogic items) and analyze ambiguous ones separately. 5) Confound with training frequency of irrealis constructions in lower-resource languages; we control with URIEL resource tiers and use the FACTUAL CONTROL and within-content factual-vs-counterfactual contrasts as frequency-neutral baselines. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Causal steering may trade fluency or factual-control accuracy; we report output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the reverse (contamination-induction) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure steering manipulates world-separation rather than generically boosting accuracy. 8) The hypotheticality signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants and report where a scalar direction is insufficient. 9) Distinguishing from my aspect/evidentiality/polarity proposals is essential; here content is fixed and we manipulate only the world-status (actual vs hypothetical) of a scenario, so any inference change is attributable to the world-separation representation, not to completion, information source, or negation semantics.

Name: prodrop_null_argument_reconstruction
Title: Filling the Silence: Does a Multilingual Model Reconstruct Dropped Arguments Into a Shared Representation, and Does Pro-Drop Typology Govern How Robustly It Tracks the Unspoken?
Short Hypothesis: When a sentence omits an argument that must be inferred (a dropped subject in a pro-drop language, a zero-anaphor in Japanese/Chinese, an omitted object), a multilingual LLM reconstructs the referent into an internal 'filled-slot' representation that is largely language-independent, but the robustness of this reconstruction is modulated by the query language's pro-drop typology: in habitually pro-drop languages the model fills the covert argument confidently from a shared referential representation, whereas in non-pro-drop languages the same omission (or a translated-equivalent gap) is more weakly reconstructed, producing predictable cross-lingual disagreement on who/what the silent argument refers to. We hypothesize (1) a shared middle-layer 'filled-argument' representation whose readout transfers across languages; (2) reconstruction robustness and referent-resolution accuracy track pro-drop typology and typological distance; and (3) a small, localizable 'argument-filling' signal can be causally steered to strengthen reconstruction (fixing dropped-argument resolution errors) or to erase the filled slot (inducing the model to lose track of the referent), without changing the surface answer.
Related Work: Zero-anaphora and null-argument resolution are long-studied in NLP as a supervised coreference/labeling task, largely monolingually (Chinese/Japanese zero-pronoun resolution) and behaviorally; recent work notes LLMs struggle with zero-anaphora in pro-drop languages but offers no mechanistic account. Mechanistic multilingual work locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS (Wang 2025; Lim 2025), and interpretability work on entity/binding tracking (e.g., binding IDs, coreference circuits) is English-only and concerns OVERT mentions. My prior proposals concern overt content: facts, typological-feature leakage into polarity/aspect/evidentiality/number/kinship/units, spatial frames, moral valence, task vectors, and edit ripples. NONE ask whether a model internally RECONSTRUCTS a COVERT (omitted, unspoken) argument into a filled representation, whether that filled-slot representation is language-independent and transferable, whether pro-drop typology modulates reconstruction robustness, or whether the argument-filling signal can be causally localized and steered. This flips the usual object of study from represented-surface-content to represented-ABSENCE, making it the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of how models track the unspoken.
Abstract: Human languages routinely leave arguments unspoken: Spanish and Italian drop subjects ('Comio' = '(he/she) ate'), Japanese and Chinese freely drop both subjects and objects, and even English omits arguments in coordination and control. Understanding such sentences requires silently reconstructing the missing referent. We ask whether a multilingual LLM internally fills these gaps by reconstructing the omitted argument into a shared representation, and whether a language's pro-drop typology governs how robustly it does so. We build DropProbe, a set of parallel sentences and referent-resolution probes across 8 typologically diverse languages spanning strong pro-drop (Spanish, Italian, Japanese, Chinese, Turkish), partial, and non-pro-drop (English, German, Russian) systems, where a subject or object is grammatically omitted and its correct referent is recoverable from context. Behaviorally, we test whether the model resolves the dropped argument correctly and whether errors track pro-drop typology on the same underlying scenario. Using a linear probe trained to decode the identity of a covert argument from hidden states, we test for a shared middle-layer 'filled-slot' representation that transfers zero-shot across languages, and compare a dropped-argument sentence against its overt-mention counterpart to test whether the model fills the gap to the same internal state. Via activation and path patching we localize the argument-filling components, and in a decisive causal test we steer that signal to strengthen reconstruction (repairing dropped-argument resolution) or to erase the filled slot (making the model lose the referent), while leaving the surface answer and language unchanged. We relate reconstruction robustness to pro-drop typology and typological distance, reframing the tracking of unspoken content as a measurable, steerable property of multilingual models.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 languages spanning pro-drop typology: strong pro-drop (Spanish, Italian, Turkish, Japanese, Chinese — the latter two also object-drop), partial (Russian), and non-pro-drop (English, German), coded from typological references (WALS pro-drop/null-subject parameter) plus URIEL for typological distance; treat pro-drop status as a graded predictor. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (DropProbe): ~450 items in three strata. (A) DROPPED-SUBJECT resolution: a short discourse establishes candidate referents, then a clause omits its subject (grammatically natural in pro-drop languages; realized via the closest natural equivalent — e.g., coordination/control gaps — in non-pro-drop languages), and a probe asks who performed the action. (B) DROPPED-OBJECT resolution (for object-drop languages) with an analogous setup. (C) OVERT-MENTION control: the identical scenario with the argument explicitly stated, giving a within-item baseline for what the 'filled' representation should be. Each item has a unique correct referent recoverable from context, a plausible distractor referent, and short single-token-decodable answer options (referent names). Translate/native-verify all items into all 8 languages, ensuring the omission is natural where the grammar allows it and the closest equivalent gap elsewhere; flag items where no natural omission exists in a language for the transfer-limit analysis.
3) BEHAVIORAL LEAKAGE TEST: For each (item, language) record whether the model resolves the covert argument to the correct referent. KEY hypothesis: on the SAME scenario, strong pro-drop languages resolve dropped arguments more accurately/confidently than non-pro-drop languages (where the omission is less habitual), and pro-drop typology predicts resolution accuracy beyond resource level. Mixed-effects logistic regression of resolution error on (pro-drop status, stratum, language, resource tier via URIEL), item as random effect; compare against the OVERT-MENTION control (should show high, language-flat accuracy). Report per-language resolution profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical scenarios.
4) SHARED FILLED-SLOT REPRESENTATION & TRANSFER: At each layer, pool the hidden state at the position where the covert argument's grammatical slot resolves (the verb/clause-final position). Train a linear probe to decode the referent identity (from a small closed candidate set per item) on ENGLISH (or a strong pro-drop language) and apply zero-shot to other languages; report AUROC/macro-F1 transfer as evidence of a language-independent filled-argument representation. Compare to per-language-trained probes to bound shared-vs-specific. CRITICAL 'gap-filling' test: measure representational similarity (cosine/CKA) between the dropped-argument hidden state and its OVERT-MENTION counterpart — high similarity indicates the model genuinely reconstructs the omitted argument to the same internal state; test whether this filling-similarity is higher in strong pro-drop languages.
5) DEPTH & LEAKAGE ANALYSIS: Use logit-lens to identify the layer where the covert referent becomes internally decodable (fill-in depth). Correlate fill-in depth and probe-decoded referent with behavioral resolution within/across languages (link test), and correlate reconstruction robustness (filling-similarity, probe confidence) with pro-drop typology and URIEL distance (Spearman).
6) LOCALIZE ARGUMENT-FILLING COMPONENTS: Via activation/path patching between a dropped-argument run and its OVERT-MENTION run of the same scenario, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose patching installs (or removes) the filled referent (read out by the referent probe and the emitted answer). Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (validated via per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs path patching. Also test whether patching the filled-slot representation FROM a strong pro-drop language's run INTO a failing non-pro-drop run repairs resolution.
7) CAUSAL ARGUMENT-FILLING STEERING (decisive): Derive an argument-filling steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (correctly-filled runs minus unfilled/failed runs, using the overt-vs-dropped contrast). Test (i) STRENGTHEN: adding it to failing dropped-argument queries (esp. in non-pro-drop languages) increases correct referent resolution toward pro-drop levels; (ii) ERASE: subtracting it makes the model lose track of the referent even on well-resolved items (referent becomes unrecoverable / distractor chosen); (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where reconstruction was weak; (iv) it does NOT change the surface output language or the described scenario (fidelity check), does not harm the OVERT-MENTION control, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: resolution-accuracy recovery, erasure-induced error rate (reverse), output-language fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: strengthening should help only where an argument is actually omitted and should not change overt-mention answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress reconstruction robustness and steering efficacy on pro-drop status and URIEL distance; subject-drop vs object-drop; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; token-pooling; robustness across templates and MC-vs-cloze-vs-free formats; whether a single argument-filling vector generalizes across scenarios and languages; whether the filled-slot representation generalizes across grammatical roles (subject vs object gaps).
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-(language,stratum) dropped-argument resolution accuracy, pro-drop x stratum interaction, cross-lingual disagreement, shared filled-slot probe transfer AUROC/F1, dropped-vs-overt filling-similarity, fill-in depth, internal-vs-behavior correlation, robustness-vs-typology correlation, patch-localized argument-filling layer, cross-lingual filled-slot transplant repair rate, causal steering resolution-recovery and erasure-induction rates, output fidelity, overt-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Constructing natural argument omissions equivalently across languages is delicate: strong pro-drop languages omit subjects freely, but non-pro-drop languages require the closest natural gap (coordination/control), which is not a perfect match; we native-verify naturalness, treat pro-drop status as a graded predictor, flag items where no natural omission exists (using them for a transfer-limit analysis), and rely on the within-item OVERT-MENTION control to anchor the comparison. 2) Some models may reconstruct dropped arguments robustly in all languages (clean shared filling) — this is itself an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often reconstruction is weak via filling-similarity and probe transfer. 3) Referent resolution can be genuinely ambiguous; we restrict scored items to those with a unique context-determined referent (native-verified) and analyze ambiguous ones separately. 4) The filled-slot probe could pick up surface distractor cues rather than a genuine reconstruction; the dropped-vs-overt filling-similarity test and the internal-predicts-behavior link (step 5) guard against this, as does patching the overt representation into the dropped run. 5) Confound with training frequency of null-argument constructions in lower-resource languages; we control with URIEL resource tiers and use the OVERT-MENTION control as a frequency-neutral within-item baseline. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Causal steering may trade fluency or overt-control accuracy; we report output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the erasure (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure steering manipulates argument-filling rather than generically boosting accuracy. 8) The argument-filling signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants and report where a scalar direction is insufficient. 9) Distinguishing this from generic coreference/binding work is essential; our object is the reconstruction of a COVERT (omitted) argument and its cross-lingual pro-drop modulation, not resolution of overt mentions, and our contribution is the mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of tracking the unspoken.

Name: crosslingual_running_state_tracking
Title: Keeping Count Across Languages: Does a Multilingual Model Maintain a Shared Running State, and Does Number/Classifier Typology Govern How Robustly It Updates the Tally?
Short Hypothesis: As a multilingual LLM reads a discourse that incrementally adds, removes, or modifies entities (e.g., 'three apples, then two more, then eat one'), it maintains a running, largely language-independent internal STATE (a set/count representation) that it updates step by step, but the ROBUSTNESS of this state-update-and-maintenance is modulated by the query language's number-marking typology: languages that obligatorily grammaticalize number/plurality (English, Russian) support sharper incremental updates, while classifier or optional-number languages (Chinese, Japanese, Turkish) allow more state drift, producing predictable, language-dependent errors in the final tally on the SAME scenario. We hypothesize (1) a shared middle-layer running-count/state representation whose value is linearly decodable and transfers across languages; (2) update robustness and final-tally accuracy track number/classifier typology and typological distance, and degrade with the number of update steps; and (3) a small, localizable 'state-update' signal can be causally steered to inject or correct a tally increment, repairing (or corrupting) the running state without changing the surface answer.
Related Work: Monolingual interpretability shows transformers build incremental world-state / entity-tracking representations (e.g., box/entity binding-ID work, state-tracking probes, arithmetic-state neurons), but this is English-only and never asks whether the running state is language-independent or whether number-marking typology modulates its maintenance. My prior number-naming proposal concerns how compositional NUMBER-WORD morphology distorts a STATIC magnitude of a single number; here the object is a DYNAMIC running tally updated across a discourse (a working-memory/state-tracking mechanism), and the modulating factor is number/classifier GRAMMAR (obligatory plural vs classifier vs optional number), not number-word spelling. Behavioral multilingual math (MGSM) reports per-language accuracy but treats reasoning as a scalar and never localizes state maintenance or ties it to number typology. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts, not for a running discourse state. No prior work (i) tests whether an incremental running-count/set state is shared and transferable across languages, (ii) ties its update robustness to number/classifier typology and step-count, or (iii) causally steers a single tally-update. This makes it the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of running-state maintenance.
Abstract: Understanding a story often requires silently keeping count: three guests arrive, one leaves, two more come. Humans maintain a running mental state and update it incrementally, but languages track number very differently—some obligatorily mark plurality, others use classifiers or leave number optional. We ask whether a multilingual LLM maintains a shared, language-independent running state as it reads such a discourse, and whether a language's number-marking typology governs how robustly it updates and maintains that tally. We build TallyProbe, parallel incremental-update narratives across 8 typologically diverse languages spanning obligatory-plural, classifier, and optional-number systems, where entities are added, removed, or modified over a controlled number of steps and the correct final count is known. Behaviorally, we measure final-tally accuracy per language and per step-count, testing whether errors track number/classifier typology on the same scenario. At each update step we train a linear probe to decode the current running count from hidden states and test whether this state representation is shared and transfers zero-shot across languages, and whether per-step decoded state tracks the ground-truth trajectory. Via activation and path patching we localize the components that carry each update, and in a decisive causal test we inject or correct a single increment by steering the state-update signal—repairing a dropped update in a drift-prone language, or inducing a miscount in a robust one—while leaving the surface answer and language unchanged. We relate update robustness to number typology, typological distance, and step-count, reframing cross-lingual reasoning gaps as a measurable, steerable property of running-state maintenance.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 languages spanning number-marking typology: obligatory plural (English, Russian, Spanish), classifier languages (Chinese, Japanese), and optional/reduced number-marking (Turkish, Indonesian, Korean), coded from typological references (WALS nominal-plurality and numeral-classifier chapters) plus URIEL for typological distance; treat number/classifier status as a graded predictor. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (TallyProbe): ~500 incremental-update narratives with a controlled number of UPDATE STEPS (2-8), each step adding, removing, or modifying a count of one or more entity types (e.g., 'There are 3 cups. Someone brings 2 more. Then 1 is taken away. How many cups are there now?'). Vary: step-count, number of distinct entity types (single-tally vs multi-entity requiring separate tallies), and operation mix. Each narrative has a known ground-truth running trajectory and final answer, with short single-token-decodable numeric answers. Translate/native-verify into all 8 languages, rendering entities and counts naturally with each language's number/classifier grammar. Include a SINGLE-STEP CONTROL (no incremental update; direct count) to bound the effect and separate state-maintenance from basic counting.
3) BEHAVIORAL LEAKAGE TEST: Measure final-tally accuracy per (narrative, language). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME scenario, classifier/optional-number languages show more tally errors than obligatory-plural languages, errors grow with step-count, and number typology predicts accuracy beyond resource level. Mixed-effects logistic regression of error on (number/classifier typology, step-count, entity-count, language, resource tier via URIEL), narrative as random effect; test typology and step-count coefficients; compare against the SINGLE-STEP CONTROL (should show small, language-flat error). Report per-language accuracy-vs-step-count curves and cross-lingual disagreement on identical narratives.
4) SHARED RUNNING-STATE REPRESENTATION & TRANSFER: At each UPDATE-STEP boundary, pool the hidden state and train a linear probe to decode the CURRENT running count on ENGLISH data; apply zero-shot to other languages and report decoding accuracy/MAE as evidence of a language-independent running-state representation. Compare to per-language-trained probes to bound shared-vs-specific. CRITICAL trajectory test: track the per-step decoded count against the ground-truth trajectory and measure where/whether the internal state diverges (the step at which drift begins), per language.
5) DRIFT & LEAKAGE ANALYSIS: Correlate the divergence step and per-step decoded-state error with behavioral final-tally error within/across languages (link test), and correlate state-maintenance robustness (trajectory-tracking accuracy) with number/classifier typology, step-count, and URIEL distance (Spearman). Test whether errors are UPDATE failures (an increment is missed at a step) vs MAINTENANCE failures (a correct count decays over subsequent steps) by examining the trajectory.
6) LOCALIZE STATE-UPDATE COMPONENTS: Via activation/path patching between two narratives that differ in a single update step (e.g., '+2' vs '+3' at step k, matched otherwise), sweep layers/heads/MLPs at that step boundary for the minimal components whose transfer changes the downstream decoded running count. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (validated via per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs path patching. Also test patching the correct post-update state FROM a robust language's run INTO a drifting language's run at the divergence step to see if it repairs the final tally.
7) CAUSAL STATE-UPDATE STEERING (decisive): Derive a per-increment steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (e.g., states after '+1' minus states before, or '+n' vs '+0' contrasts). Test (i) CORRECT: injecting the appropriate increment at a step where a drift-prone language dropped an update repairs the running state and final answer; (ii) CORRUPT: injecting a spurious increment (or subtracting a needed one) induces a miscount in a robust language; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where drift was greatest; (iv) it does NOT change the surface output language or the narrative content (fidelity check), does not harm the SINGLE-STEP CONTROL, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: tally-repair rate, miscount-induction rate (reverse), output-language fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: a +1 vector should shift the decoded state by exactly one and the final answer accordingly, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress state-maintenance robustness and steering efficacy on number/classifier typology, step-count, and URIEL distance; single-tally vs multi-entity (does the model maintain separate language-independent tallies per entity?); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; token-pooling; robustness across templates and MC-vs-free formats; whether a single increment-steering vector generalizes across narratives, magnitudes, and languages.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language final-tally accuracy and accuracy-vs-step-count curves, typology and step-count regression coefficients, cross-lingual disagreement, shared running-state probe transfer accuracy/MAE, per-step trajectory tracking and divergence step, update-vs-maintenance failure decomposition, state-drift-vs-typology correlation, patch-localized state-update layer, cross-lingual state transplant repair rate, causal steering tally-repair and miscount-induction rates, output fidelity, single-step-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Rendering counts/updates naturally and equivalently across obligatory-plural, classifier, and optional-number languages is delicate; we use native verification, treat number/classifier status as a graded predictor, and rely on the SINGLE-STEP CONTROL and identical narrative structure to isolate the state-maintenance effect from surface rendering. 2) Some models may maintain the running state robustly in all languages (clean shared state) — this is itself an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often drift occurs via per-step trajectory tracking. 3) Final-tally errors could stem from arithmetic ability rather than state maintenance; the per-step trajectory probe and update-vs-maintenance decomposition, plus the SINGLE-STEP arithmetic control, dissociate these. 4) The running-count probe could latch onto surface number tokens rather than a genuine maintained state; we probe at step boundaries where no explicit total is stated, use narratives where the running total is never surfaced until the query, and validate with the cross-lingual transplant and steering tests. 5) Confound with training frequency of numeral/classifier constructions in lower-resource languages; we control with URIEL resource tiers and use the single-step control as a frequency-neutral baseline. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Causal steering may trade fluency or control accuracy; we report output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the reverse (miscount-induction) and reverse-consistency (+1 shifts state by exactly one) tests to ensure steering manipulates the running state rather than generically boosting accuracy. 8) The state-update signal may be low-rank or magnitude-dependent rather than a single fixed direction; we test per-magnitude and low-rank variants and report where a scalar increment direction is insufficient. 9) Distinguishing from my number-naming proposal is essential; here number words/magnitudes of individual quantities are not the object — the object is the DYNAMIC running tally maintained across a discourse and its modulation by number/classifier GRAMMAR, tested causally at the level of incremental state updates.

Name: crosslingual_competence_metacompetence_gap
Title: Can the Model Describe the Rule It Obeys? The Cross-Lingual Gap Between Using a Grammatical Construction and Knowing About It
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs possess implicit procedural competence (they correctly produce a grammatical construction) that is dissociated from explicit metalinguistic competence (they cannot correctly state the rule for it), and crucially this competence-vs-metacompetence gap is language-dependent: the same underlying construction can be reliably USED yet not DESCRIBED, with the size of the gap tracking language resource level and typological distance. We further hypothesize that the implicit-competence signal is largely language-independent and shared in middle layers, that the metalinguistic-description ability draws on a separate, more English-centric pathway, and that the two can be causally dissociated—steering the metalinguistic pathway changes how the model describes a rule without changing whether it obeys it, and vice versa.
Related Work: Song, Hu & Mahowald (2025) show LLMs cannot introspect about their own linguistic knowledge, but their study is MONOLINGUAL (English), behavioral, and about self-access, not about a use-vs-description dissociation across languages. Arcon et al. (2026) benchmark metalinguistic knowledge multilingually via WALS multiple-choice questions and find it correlates with digital resource level, but they only measure explicit knowledge behaviorally and never compare it to the model's implicit USE of the same construction, never test the competence-metacompetence gap per language, and offer no mechanism. Classic linguistics distinguishes tacit competence from metalinguistic awareness; NLP grammaticality-judgment work (BLiMP/CLiMP/multilingual acceptability) measures use, and separate metalinguistic-QA work measures description, but no work JOINTLY measures both on the SAME construction, ties their DISSOCIATION to language typology/resource, or mechanistically separates an implicit-use pathway from a metalinguistic-description pathway and causally dissociates them. This is distinct from all my prior proposals (which concern factual knowledge, typological-feature leakage into semantics, reasoning dynamics, or task/state representations): here the object is the model's KNOWLEDGE-ABOUT-LANGUAGE versus its KNOWLEDGE-IN-LANGUAGE, and their cross-lingual dissociation.
Abstract: A speaker can flawlessly produce plural nouns without being able to state the pluralization rule; competence and metacompetence are dissociable. We ask whether multilingual LLMs show the same dissociation, whether it is language-dependent, and how it is implemented internally. We build UseVsDescribe, a paired benchmark that, for each of a set of grammatical constructions (plural/agreement/case/word-order/negation phenomena drawn from WALS features and minimal-pair paradigms) across 10 typologically and resource-diverse languages, measures two things on the identical construction: (1) IMPLICIT COMPETENCE—whether the model correctly produces/prefers the grammatical form (via forced-choice minimal pairs and generation), and (2) EXPLICIT METACOMPETENCE—whether it can correctly describe, identify, or apply the rule metalinguistically. Behaviorally, we quantify the per-language competence-metacompetence gap and test whether it grows with lower resource level and greater typological distance, revealing languages the model can use but not explain. Mechanistically, we train a linear probe for the implicit grammaticality signal and test whether it is shared and transfers zero-shot across languages, while the metalinguistic-description ability draws on a more English-centric pathway; via activation patching we localize the two and test their separation relative to the language-transition band. In a decisive causal test, we steer the metalinguistic pathway to change how the model describes a rule while leaving its actual usage intact (and conversely corrupt usage while descriptions persist), establishing that use and description are causally dissociable representations. We reframe multilingual metalinguistic ability as a measurable, language-dependent, and mechanistically separable competence from language use.
Experiments: 1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Turkish, Swahili, Indonesian, Japanese). 2) DATASET (UseVsDescribe): Select ~40 grammatical constructions grounded in WALS features and standard minimal-pair paradigms (noun pluralization, subject-verb agreement, case/adposition marking, adjective-noun order, negation placement, tense/aspect marking, classifier use). For each construction in each language build TWO matched probe types on the SAME phenomenon: (A) IMPLICIT-USE probes—forced-choice minimal pairs (grammatical vs ungrammatical form) scored by preference/log-prob, plus a short generation/cloze that requires producing the correct form; (B) METALINGUISTIC probes—(i) DESCRIBE: 'What is the rule for forming X in this language?' scored against native-verified rule statements; (ii) IDENTIFY: 'Is this sentence grammatical? If not, what is wrong?'; (iii) APPLY-METALINGUISTICALLY: given the rule stated explicitly, apply it to a novel item (tests whether failure is rule-knowledge vs rule-application). Native verification of all items and gold rule statements; where a construction is absent in a language, mark it. Keep answers short/scoreable. 3) BEHAVIORAL COMPETENCE-METACOMPETENCE GAP: Per (construction, language) compute IMPLICIT-USE accuracy and METACOMPETENCE accuracy; define GAP = implicit-use minus metacompetence. KEY hypothesis: a large positive gap exists (can use but not describe), and the gap GROWS with lower resource level and greater typological distance. Mixed-effects regression of the gap on (resource tier via URIEL, typological distance, construction), construction and language as random effects; test that the gap is significant and predicted by resource/distance beyond overall accuracy. Also test the reverse-direction cases (describe-but-not-use) and their frequency. Report per-language gap profiles and which constructions are usable-but-inexplicable. 4) SHARED IMPLICIT-GRAMMATICALITY SIGNAL & TRANSFER: At each layer pool hidden states at the critical (form) position on implicit-use minimal pairs; train a linear 'grammaticality' probe on ENGLISH and apply zero-shot cross-lingually, reporting AUROC as evidence of a shared implicit-competence direction. Compare to per-language-trained probes. Separately train a 'can-describe-this-rule' probe from metalinguistic-probe hidden states and test its cross-lingual transfer; hypothesis: the implicit-grammaticality signal transfers better/is more language-independent than the metalinguistic-description signal (which is more English-centric). 5) LOCATE PATHWAYS: Use per-layer language-ID probes/logit-lens (Wang 2025) to anchor the language-transition band. Via activation and path patching, localize (a) components carrying the implicit grammaticality preference (patch between grammatical vs ungrammatical runs) and (b) components carrying the metalinguistic description (patch between correct-description vs wrong-description runs). Test whether these are DISTINCT component sets and where they sit relative to the transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching. 6) CAUSAL DISSOCIATION (decisive): Derive two steering vectors—a metalinguistic-description vector and an implicit-use vector—via difference-of-means over their localized components. Test (i) DESCRIBE-ONLY: steering the metalinguistic pathway changes the model's stated rule/description WITHOUT changing its actual minimal-pair usage (usage accuracy unchanged); (ii) USE-ONLY: steering the implicit pathway flips its grammaticality preference WITHOUT changing its verbal description; (iii) these dissociations hold cross-lingually and are stronger where the behavioral gap is largest; (iv) no degradation of general QA and output-language fidelity preserved. Metrics: description-change rate with usage held fixed, usage-flip rate with description held fixed, cross-over dissociation index, general-QA retention. 7) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: DESCRIBE-vs-APPLY split (is metalinguistic failure about lacking the rule or failing to apply it?); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); construction-type breakdown; probe layer/dimensionality; robustness across templates and MC-vs-free formats; whether a single metalinguistic direction generalizes across constructions and languages. EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-(construction,language) implicit-use and metacompetence accuracy and their gap, gap-vs-resource/typology regression, describe-but-not-use vs use-but-not-describe frequencies, cross-lingual transfer AUROC of implicit-grammaticality vs metalinguistic-description probes, localized pathway loci and separation from the language-transition band, causal dissociation rates (description-change with usage fixed; usage-flip with description fixed), general-QA retention and output fidelity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Scoring free-form rule descriptions is hard and subjective; we mitigate with native-verified gold rule statements, a rubric plus an LLM-judge validated against human annotations, and complement free description with the more objective IDENTIFY and APPLY-metalinguistically probes. 2) The competence-metacompetence gap could reflect a generic verbalization/instruction-following deficit rather than genuinely separate knowledge; the APPLY-metalinguistically probe (rule given, must apply) and the causal dissociation (steering description without touching usage) guard against this, and we compare gap sizes against a non-linguistic verbalization control task. 3) Some models may show little gap or uniformly poor metacompetence; either is an informative, publishable finding about how metalinguistic ability scales with resource, and we quantify how often the gap is present. 4) Implicit-use minimal pairs can be confounded by frequency/lexical cues; we use matched minimal pairs and multiple items per construction, and validate the grammaticality probe on held-out constructions. 5) Patching/probing results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 6) Causal steering may harm fluency or leak languages; we cap strength and report output fidelity and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the cross-over (use-only vs describe-only) design to ensure the two vectors are genuinely selective rather than generic accuracy levers. 7) WALS-derived rule statements can be coarse or contested for some features; we restrict to well-documented constructions with clear native consensus and analyze contested ones separately. 8) Distinguishing from Song et al. (introspection) and Arcon et al. (WALS benchmarking) is essential; our contribution is the JOINT use-vs-describe dissociation on the SAME construction, its language-dependence, and the mechanistic/causal separation of the two pathways, none of which they provide.

Name: crosslingual_phonological_reasoning
Title: Hearing Text Without Sound: Do Multilingual LLMs Build a Shared Cross-Script Phonological Representation, and Does Orthographic Transparency Govern Its Reach?
Short Hypothesis: Despite operating purely on graphemes/subwords, multilingual LLMs recover a largely language-independent internal PHONOLOGICAL representation of words (encoding how they sound) that supports sound-based reasoning—rhyme, homophony, alliteration, and puns—across scripts; the accuracy and cross-lingual reach of this ability is systematically governed by the query language's ORTHOGRAPHIC TRANSPARENCY (how directly its script maps to sound): transparent orthographies (Spanish, Finnish, Turkish) yield sharp, transferable phonological representations, while deep/opaque orthographies (English, French) and logographic scripts (Chinese) produce weaker, more distorted ones. We hypothesize (1) a shared middle-layer phonological direction (approximating an IPA-like code) that transfers zero-shot across languages/scripts; (2) sound-reasoning accuracy and the sharpness of this representation track orthographic transparency and typological/script distance; and (3) a small, localizable 'phonology' signal that can be causally steered to fix or induce rhyme/homophone judgments without changing the surface answer.
Related Work: Phonology in LLMs is studied mostly in speech/phoneme-based models: Kim et al. (2025) analyze cross-lingual phonetic representation and phonological similarity in speech models; Goriely & Buttery (2025) use word segmentation as a phonological probe for phoneme-based LMs on child-directed speech; Zaitova et al. (2022) map phonology to semantics for spoken-word recognition. All operate on speech/phoneme inputs, not standard grapheme/subword text LLMs. Monolingual English work notes LLMs have partial phonological/rhyme ability but is not cross-lingual or mechanistic, and does not tie it to orthographic transparency. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS, and recent script work shows latent romanization during transliteration—but neither asks whether a shared PHONOLOGICAL (sound) representation exists across scripts, whether it supports cross-lingual sound-based reasoning, whether orthographic transparency governs it, or whether it is causally steerable. This is distinct from all my prior proposals (facts, typological-feature leakage into semantics, reasoning dynamics, task/state representations, metalinguistic competence): the object of study here is the model's implicit representation of how written words SOUND and its cross-script sharedness, grounded in orthographic-depth typology and tested causally.
Abstract: Large language models read text, not sound: they see graphemes tokenized into subwords, never phonemes. Yet answering whether two words rhyme, are homophones, or form a pun requires knowing how they sound. We ask whether multilingual LLMs nonetheless build a shared, language-independent phonological representation that lets them reason about sound across scripts, and whether a language's orthographic transparency—how directly its writing maps to pronunciation—governs how sharp and transferable that representation is. We build PhonoProbe, parallel sound-reasoning items across 8 languages spanning transparent (Spanish, Finnish, Turkish), deep/opaque alphabetic (English, French, Russian), and non-alphabetic (Arabic abjad, Chinese logographic) orthographies, covering rhyme judgment, homophone detection, alliteration, and pun comprehension, each with a phonology-based correct answer and an orthography-based distractor (words that look similar but sound different, and vice versa). Behaviorally we measure sound-reasoning accuracy per language and test whether errors and orthography-vs-phonology reliance track orthographic transparency on matched items. We train a linear phonological probe (predicting IPA-derived features / rhyme-class from hidden states) and test whether it is shared and transfers zero-shot across languages and scripts, and whether a cross-script pair of homophones/rhymes converge to the same internal state. Via activation and path patching we localize the phonology signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to flip rhyme/homophone judgments—repairing a phonology error hidden behind orthographic similarity, or inducing one—while leaving the surface answer and language unchanged. We relate representation sharpness to orthographic transparency and script distance, reframing latent phonology as a measurable, steerable property of text-only multilingual models.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 languages spanning orthographic depth: transparent (Spanish, Finnish, Turkish), deep alphabetic (English, French, Russian), non-alphabetic (Arabic [abjad, vowels often unwritten], Chinese [logographic]), coded for orthographic transparency from documented orthographic-depth scales plus URIEL for typological/script distance; treat transparency as a graded predictor. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (PhonoProbe): ~500 sound-reasoning items in four strata. (A) RHYME: 'Do WORD1 and WORD2 rhyme?' (B) HOMOPHONE: 'Do WORD1 and WORD2 sound the same?' (C) ALLITERATION: identify which words in a set share an initial sound. (D) PUN/HOMOPHONE-COMPREHENSION: short items whose meaning turns on a homophone. Crucially, each item includes ORTHOGRAPHY-vs-PHONOLOGY dissociating pairs: (i) words that LOOK similar but SOUND different (e.g., English 'though/tough'), where the orthography-based answer is wrong; (ii) words that look different but sound the same/rhyme, where surface form misleads. Include a CROSS-SCRIPT stratum: transliterated homophone/rhyme pairs and, where meaningful, borrowings, to test sound matching across scripts. Gold answers use IPA/pronunciation dictionaries; native verification of naturalness. Include an ORTHOGRAPHY-CONTROL stratum where surface and sound agree, to bound the effect.
3) BEHAVIORAL TEST: Sound-reasoning accuracy per (item, language, stratum). KEY hypothesis: transparent-orthography languages achieve higher accuracy and rely LESS on the orthography distractor than deep/logographic ones on the dissociating items. Mixed-effects logistic regression of error on (orthographic transparency, stratum, language, resource tier via URIEL), item as random effect; test transparency beyond resource level. Report per-language accuracy, orthography-vs-phonology reliance, and cross-lingual disagreement on matched sound relations.
4) SHARED PHONOLOGICAL REPRESENTATION & TRANSFER: At each layer, pool the hidden state at the word position; train linear probes to decode (i) rhyme class / final-syllable phonology and (ii) a small set of IPA-derived articulatory features (voicing, place, manner, vowel height) on ENGLISH data, and apply zero-shot to other languages/scripts; report AUROC/F1 transfer as evidence of a language-independent phonological direction. Compare to per-language-trained probes to bound shared-vs-specific. CRITICAL convergence test: measure representational similarity (cosine/CKA) between cross-script homophone/rhyme pairs (e.g., a word and its transliteration, or two rhyming words in different scripts); high similarity indicates a shared sound code; test whether convergence is higher for transparent orthographies.
5) DEPTH & TRANSPARENCY ANALYSIS: Use logit-lens to identify when phonological information becomes decodable (phonology depth). Correlate probe-decoded phonology and its sharpness with behavioral sound-reasoning accuracy within/across languages (link test), and correlate representation sharpness with orthographic transparency and script/typological distance (Spearman).
6) LOCALIZE PHONOLOGY COMPONENTS: Via activation/path patching between a phonology-correct run and an orthography-misled run on the SAME dissociating item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose patching flips the judgment toward the sound-based answer (read out by the phonology probe and emitted answer). Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (validated via per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs path patching. Also test patching the phonological representation FROM a transparent-orthography language's run INTO a failing deep-orthography run.
7) CAUSAL PHONOLOGY STEERING (decisive): Derive a phonology steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (sound-based-correct runs minus orthography-misled runs). Test (i) REPAIR: adding it to items where orthographic similarity misleads (esp. in deep-orthography languages) increases correct sound-based answers; (ii) INDUCE: subtracting it makes the model rely on orthography and misjudge rhyme/homophones on well-answered items; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where orthography is opaque; (iv) it does NOT change the surface output language or item content (fidelity check), does not harm the ORTHOGRAPHY-CONTROL stratum, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: sound-reasoning accuracy recovery, orthography-reliance-induction rate (reverse), output-language fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering should only change answers on phonology-dependent items, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress representation sharpness and steering efficacy on orthographic transparency and URIEL/script distance; stratum breakdown (rhyme vs homophone vs alliteration vs pun); tokenization effects (words split into many subwords) via token-pooling schemes; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single phonology vector generalizes across strata and languages; whether the shared phonological code is stronger for alphabetic than logographic scripts.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-(language,stratum) sound-reasoning accuracy and orthography-vs-phonology reliance, transparency regression coefficients, cross-lingual disagreement, shared phonological-probe transfer AUROC/F1, cross-script homophone/rhyme convergence (CKA/cosine), phonology decodability depth, internal-vs-behavior correlation, sharpness-vs-transparency correlation, patch-localized phonology layer, cross-lingual phonology transplant repair rate, causal steering repair and orthography-induction rates, output fidelity, control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Tokenization: words split into many subwords, complicating which token carries phonology and whether the model can even access sub-lexical sound; we test multiple token-pooling schemes (last token, mean, boundary), report sensitivity, and treat tokenization as an explicit covariate rather than a nuisance. 2) Gold phonology (rhyme/homophone) requires pronunciation dictionaries and dialect choices; we use standard IPA/pronunciation resources, native verification, and restrict scored items to clear cases, analyzing dialect-ambiguous ones separately. 3) Some models may lack any shared phonological representation, especially for logographic Chinese where graphemes encode sound only indirectly; this is itself an informative, publishable finding about the limits of latent phonology, and we quantify how often a phonology signal is present via probe transfer and convergence tests. 4) Effects could be driven by memorized rhyme lists rather than a compositional sound code; the ORTHOGRAPHY-vs-PHONOLOGY dissociating items (look-alike/sound-different and vice versa) and the cross-script convergence test guard against surface memorization, and steering that overrides orthography while fixing surface language provides causal evidence. 5) Confound with training frequency of sound-reasoning tasks per language; we control with URIEL resource tiers and use the orthography-control stratum as a frequency-neutral within-item baseline. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Causal steering may trade fluency or control accuracy; we report output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the reverse (orthography-induction) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure steering manipulates phonology rather than generically boosting accuracy. 8) The phonology signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants and report where a scalar direction is insufficient. 9) Distinguishing from speech/phoneme-model work (Kim 2025; Goriely 2025) is essential; our contribution is that STANDARD grapheme/subword text LLMs latently reconstruct a shared cross-script phonological code governed by orthographic transparency, tested mechanistically and causally, which prior speech-input work does not address.

Name: crosslingual_social_deixis_status_representation
Title: Who Outranks Whom? Whether Multilingual Models Track a Shared Relative-Status Representation and How Honorific Typology Governs Its Realization
