Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM processes a conversation, it infers and maintains a largely language-independent internal representation of the RELATIVE SOCIAL STATUS between interlocutors (who is higher/lower/equal in the addressee relationship), and this shared 'social-deixis' representation drives the choice of honorific/politeness register; the ROBUSTNESS and correctness of tracking status is systematically modulated by the query language's honorific typology: languages that grammatically obligate honorific/register marking (Japanese, Korean, Javanese, Hindi) support sharper status tracking and register selection, while languages that mark politeness only lexically/optionally (English, German) yield weaker, more error-prone tracking, producing predictable cross-lingual disagreement on the appropriate register for the SAME social scenario. We further hypothesize (1) a shared middle-layer relative-status direction that transfers zero-shot across languages; (2) status-tracking robustness and register accuracy track honorific typology and typological distance; and (3) a small, localizable 'relative-status' signal that can be causally steered to flip the inferred status relation (e.g., make the model treat the addressee as higher-status), changing honorific choice without altering the propositional content.
Related Work: Prior multilingual register/honorific work is behavioral or resource-oriented: LoraxBench (Aji & Cohn 2025) shows register (e.g., high-politeness Krama Javanese) affects LLM performance but offers no mechanism; Bangla honorific datasets (BLADE) and social-power/address-term benchmarks (BanglaSocialBench) evaluate whether models pick culturally appropriate honorifics; J-PragEval (Braun 2026) shows Japanese honorifics are partly linearly decodable in a single monolingual model but studies neither cross-lingual transfer nor an underlying relative-status representation. Sociolinguistics richly documents honorific systems and the T-V/relative-status distinction (Brown & Levinson politeness theory; Comrie on honorifics). Mechanistic multilingual work locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) and, in my prior proposals, for polarity, aspect, evidential source, kinship, spatial frames, etc. NO prior work asks whether an LLM internally represents the RELATIVE SOCIAL STATUS between interlocutors as a shared, language-independent variable that is realized through each language's honorific grammar, whether status-tracking robustness is modulated by honorific typology, or whether the relative-status signal can be causally localized and steered. This is distinct from my prior pragmatics proposal (which concerned truth-conditional implicature and directness, not the representation of interlocutor status/register) and from behavioral honorific benchmarks: here the object is the internal social-deixis/relative-status representation and its cross-lingual geometry, grounded in honorific typology and tested causally.
Abstract: Every conversation encodes a social relationship: is the addressee a superior, a peer, or a subordinate? Languages realize this very differently—Japanese, Korean, Javanese, and Hindi grammatically obligate honorific and politeness marking keyed to relative status, while English signals it only through optional lexical politeness. Choosing the right register requires inferring and tracking who outranks whom. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent representation of relative interlocutor status that drives honorific choice, and whether a language's honorific typology governs how robustly it tracks status. We build StatusProbe, parallel dialogue scenarios across 8 typologically diverse languages spanning obligatory-honorific and optional-politeness systems, where context establishes the relative status of speaker and addressee (e.g., employee-to-boss, teacher-to-student, peer-to-peer) and the correct register/honorific form is determined by that status. Behaviorally, we measure whether the model selects the status-appropriate register and whether errors track honorific typology on the same underlying scenario. We train a linear probe to decode the inferred relative status (higher/equal/lower) from hidden states and test whether this representation is shared and transfers zero-shot across languages, and whether the same social scenario maps to the same internal status state regardless of language. Via activation and path patching we localize the relative-status components, and in a decisive causal test we steer that signal to flip the inferred status relation—making the model address a superior as a subordinate or vice versa—changing honorific realization while the propositional content stays fixed. We relate status-tracking robustness to honorific typology and typological distance, reframing social deixis as a measurable, steerable property of multilingual models.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 languages spanning honorific typology: obligatory grammatical honorific/politeness systems (Japanese, Korean, Javanese, Hindi, Thai) and optional/lexical-politeness systems (English, German, Russian), coded for honorific-obligatoriness and number of register levels from typological/sociolinguistic references (Comrie; Brown & Levinson) plus URIEL for typological distance; treat honorific-obligatoriness as a graded predictor. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (StatusProbe): ~450 dialogue scenarios in three strata. (A) REGISTER-SELECTION: context establishes the relative status of speaker and addressee (employee-to-boss, boss-to-employee, teacher-to-student, student-to-teacher, stranger, close peer, elder-to-child), then the model must produce or choose an utterance; the correct honorific/politeness level is fixed by status. (B) STATUS-INFERENCE probe: given a short dialogue using a particular register, ask the model to infer the relative status of the interlocutors (higher/equal/lower). (C) STATUS-CONSISTENCY: a scenario where status is established early and a later turn must maintain the correct register (tests maintenance across turns). Each item has a status-appropriate correct answer, a status-inappropriate distractor (wrong register), and short scoreable options. Translate/native-verify into all 8 languages, realizing register with each language's honorific grammar where obligatory and lexical politeness where optional; flag scenarios where a language lacks a distinct register form. Include a NEUTRAL control where no status asymmetry exists (peers) to bound the effect.
3) BEHAVIORAL LEAKAGE TEST: For each (scenario, language) score whether the model selects/produces the status-appropriate register. KEY hypothesis: obligatory-honorific languages track status more accurately and select register more reliably on the SAME scenario than optional-politeness languages, and honorific-obligatoriness predicts register accuracy beyond resource level. Mixed-effects logistic regression of register error on (honorific-obligatoriness, stratum, language, resource tier via URIEL), scenario as random effect; compare against the NEUTRAL control (should show no status-driven register error). Report per-language register-accuracy profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical social scenarios.
4) SHARED RELATIVE-STATUS DIRECTION & TRANSFER: At each layer, pool the hidden state at the addressee/utterance position; train a linear probe to decode inferred relative status (higher/equal/lower) on ENGLISH (or a strong-honorific language) data and apply zero-shot to other languages; report macro-F1/AUROC transfer as evidence of a language-independent relative-status representation. Compare to per-language-trained probes to bound shared-vs-specific. CRITICAL scenario-invariance test: measure representational similarity (cosine/CKA) of the status state for the SAME social scenario across languages; high similarity indicates a shared social-deixis representation abstracted from the surface honorific realization; test whether invariance is higher for obligatory-honorific languages.
5) DEPTH & TYPOLOGY ANALYSIS: Use logit-lens to identify when relative status becomes internally decodable (status-inference depth). Correlate status-inference depth and probe-decoded status with behavioral register selection within/across languages (link test), and correlate status-tracking robustness (probe confidence, scenario-invariance) with honorific-obligatoriness and URIEL distance (Spearman).
6) LOCALIZE RELATIVE-STATUS COMPONENTS: Via activation/path patching between a higher-status-addressee run and a lower-status-addressee run of the SAME propositional scenario, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose patching flips the inferred status (read out by the status probe and the emitted register). Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (validated via per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs path patching. Also test patching the status representation FROM an obligatory-honorific language's run INTO a failing optional-politeness run to see if it repairs register selection.
7) CAUSAL RELATIVE-STATUS STEERING (decisive): Derive a relative-status steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (higher-status-addressee runs minus lower-status-addressee runs). Test (i) FLIP-UP: adding it makes the model treat the addressee as higher-status, raising the honorific/politeness level (e.g., addressing a subordinate deferentially); (ii) FLIP-DOWN: subtracting it makes the model treat a superior as a subordinate, lowering register; (iii) it works cross-lingually and can OVERRIDE the scenario's actual status relation; (iv) it changes ONLY register/honorific realization, NOT the propositional content or surface language (fidelity check), does not harm the NEUTRAL control, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: register-shift rate under steering, status-probe flip rate, propositional-content preservation, output-language fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering the status axis should change register but not factual answers, guarding against a generic lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress status-tracking robustness and steering efficacy on honorific-obligatoriness and URIEL distance; number of register levels (binary T-V vs multi-level Javanese/Korean); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; token-pooling; robustness across templates and MC-vs-generation formats; whether a single relative-status vector generalizes across scenarios and languages; whether status is tracked as an ordinal axis (higher>equal>lower) in the representation.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-(language,stratum) register-selection accuracy, honorific-obligatoriness x stratum interaction, cross-lingual disagreement, shared relative-status probe transfer F1/AUROC, cross-lingual scenario-invariance (CKA/cosine), status-inference depth, internal-vs-behavior correlation, robustness-vs-typology correlation, patch-localized relative-status layer, cross-lingual status transplant repair rate, causal steering register-shift and status-flip rates, propositional-content preservation, output fidelity, neutral-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Realizing register naturally and equivalently across languages is delicate (obligatory multi-level honorifics vs optional lexical politeness); we use native verification, treat honorific-obligatoriness and register-level count as graded predictors, flag scenarios lacking distinct register forms, and rely on the NEUTRAL control and identical propositional content to isolate the status effect. 2) Some models may track relative status robustly in all languages (clean shared representation) or fail uniformly—either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often status-tracking is weak via probe transfer and scenario-invariance. 3) The appropriate register can be genuinely context/culture-dependent; we restrict scored items to scenarios with clear native-consensus status relations and analyze culturally contested ones separately. 4) The status probe could latch onto surface honorific tokens rather than an abstract status representation; the cross-language scenario-invariance test (same status decoded from different surface realizations), the internal-predicts-behavior link, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 5) Confound with training frequency of honorific constructions in lower-resource languages (e.g., Javanese Krama); we control with URIEL resource tiers and use the NEUTRAL control as a frequency-neutral baseline. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Causal steering may trade fluency or content preservation; we report propositional-content preservation, output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the flip-down (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure steering manipulates the status axis rather than generically shifting politeness or accuracy. 8) The relative-status signal may be ordinal/low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank and ordinal-axis variants and report where a scalar direction is insufficient. 9) Distinguishing from my prior pragmatics/directness proposal is essential; here the object is the representation of interlocutor RELATIVE STATUS and its honorific realization, not truth-conditional implicature, and from behavioral honorific benchmarks by providing the internal, mechanistic, causal account.

Name: crosslingual_generic_overgeneralization_leakage
Title: Some Birds Fly, All Birds Fly: Whether a Language's Bare-Plural Generic Grammar Leaks Into How Multilingual Models Represent the Quantificational Force of Generic Claims
Short Hypothesis: Generic sentences ('Birds fly') are quantificationally weak (they tolerate exceptions: penguins don't fly), yet languages encode genericity very differently—bare plurals in English, definite plurals/marked forms in Romance, classifier-marked or aspect-marked forms elsewhere. We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal 'generic-vs-universal force' representation of a claim, but the query language's genericity-marking grammar leaks into it: languages whose generic form is more surface-similar to a universal ('all') push the model to internally OVER-STRENGTHEN generics into exceptionless universals, producing predictable cross-lingual disagreement on whether a generic tolerates exceptions about the SAME claim. We further hypothesize (1) a shared middle-layer generic-force direction that transfers zero-shot across languages; (2) over-strengthening (the 'generic overgeneralization effect' known in humans) tracks the language's genericity typology and typological distance; and (3) a small, localizable 'quantificational-force' signal that can be causally steered to weaken an over-strengthened generic (restoring exception-tolerance) or to strengthen it (inducing universal readings), without changing the surface answer.
Related Work: Generics and the human 'generic overgeneralization effect' (people erroneously accept 'all birds fly' after endorsing 'birds fly') are richly studied in psycholinguistics (Leslie; Prasada; Meyer et al.) and vary sharply cross-linguistically in surface marking (bare plural, definite plural, classifier/aspect marking). In NLP, generics work is monolingual/English and behavioral: probing whether LLMs know generics tolerate exceptions, or generating generic knowledge for commonsense; none study genericity CROSS-LINGUALLY or mechanistically. My prior proposals cover typological leakage into polarity/negation, aspect/completion, evidential source, hypotheticality/irrealis, number tracking, and quantifier SCOPE—but NONE address the quantificational FORCE of GENERIC claims (generic vs universal, exception-tolerance), the genericity-marking typology, or the human overgeneralization effect. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts, not generic force. This is the first to (i) test whether an LLM internally represents generic-vs-universal force in a language-independent way, (ii) tie cross-lingual over-strengthening of generics to genericity-marking grammar and typological distance, and (iii) causally localize and steer the quantificational-force signal, distinct from my logical-operator (negation/scope) proposal because the object is the defeasible, exception-tolerant semantics of GENERICS, not truth-functional negation or scope.
Abstract: Generic sentences like 'Birds fly' express weak, exception-tolerating generalizations—penguins exist, yet the generic is still true. Humans notoriously over-strengthen generics into exceptionless universals (the generic overgeneralization effect), and languages mark genericity very differently: English uses bare plurals, Romance languages definite plurals, and others classifier- or aspect-marked forms whose surface shape varies in how close it is to an explicit 'all'. We ask whether a multilingual LLM internally represents the quantificational force of a claim—generic (defeasible) versus universal (exceptionless)—in a language-independent way, and whether a language's genericity-marking grammar leaks into that representation, making the model over-strengthen generics in some languages more than others. We build GenericProbe, parallel items across 8 typologically diverse languages, each pairing a generic claim with an exception probe ('Birds fly. Do penguins fly?') and a universal-quantifier control ('All birds fly'), plus surface-matched distractors. Behaviorally we test whether exception-tolerance judgments on the SAME generic shift with query language toward that language's genericity typology. We train a linear 'generic-vs-universal force' probe and test its zero-shot cross-lingual transfer and whether the same generic maps to the same internal force state across languages. Via activation and path patching we localize the quantificational-force signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to weaken an over-strengthened generic (restoring exception-tolerance) or strengthen it (inducing universal readings), while leaving the surface answer and language unchanged. We relate over-strengthening to genericity typology and typological distance, reframing a classic human cognitive bias as a measurable, steerable property of a model's shared meaning representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 languages spanning genericity-marking typology: bare-plural generics (English, German), definite-plural/marked generics (Spanish, French, Italian, Russian), and classifier/aspect-marked genericity (Chinese, Japanese), coded for how surface-distinct the generic form is from an explicit universal, plus URIEL for typological distance; treat genericity-marking as a graded predictor. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (GenericProbe): ~450 items in three strata. (A) GENERIC-EXCEPTION: a generic claim ('Birds fly', 'Dogs have four legs', 'Sharks are dangerous') plus an exception probe about a known exceptional subkind ('Do penguins fly?', 'Does a three-legged dog have four legs?'); correct answer respects exception-tolerance (the generic remains acceptable, the exception is genuinely an exception). (B) UNIVERSAL CONTROL: the same content with explicit 'all'/'every', where the exception SHOULD make the universal false. (C) SURFACE-MATCHED distractor items to separate over-strengthening from lexical cues. Each item has short scoreable answers. Draw base generics from established English generics datasets and psycholinguistic overgeneralization stimuli, translate/native-verify into all 8 languages, rendering genericity with each language's natural form. Include items where the generic is true-but-exception-bearing vs items that are genuinely universal, to measure both false-universal endorsement and correct universal rejection.
3) BEHAVIORAL LEAKAGE TEST: For each (item, language) measure over-strengthening = rate of treating a generic as exceptionless (rejecting the exception / endorsing the parallel universal). KEY hypothesis: languages whose generic form is surface-closer to a universal show MORE over-strengthening on the SAME claim; genericity-marking predicts over-strengthening beyond resource level. Mixed-effects logistic regression of over-strengthening on (genericity-marking, stratum, language, resource tier via URIEL), item as random effect; the UNIVERSAL CONTROL should show correct exception-driven rejection across languages. Report per-language over-strengthening profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical generics.
4) SHARED GENERIC-FORCE DIRECTION & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the claim/answer position; train a linear probe to decode generic (defeasible) vs universal (exceptionless) force on ENGLISH data and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC/F1 transfer as evidence of a language-independent generic-force direction. Compare to per-language-trained probes to bound shared-vs-specific. CRITICAL invariance test: measure representational similarity (cosine/CKA) of the force state for the SAME generic across languages; test whether invariance is lower (more distortion toward universal) in languages whose generic form resembles a universal.
5) DEPTH & TYPOLOGY ANALYSIS: Use logit-lens to identify when generic-vs-universal force becomes decodable (force-decision depth). Correlate force-decision depth and probe-decoded force with behavioral over-strengthening within/across languages (link test), and correlate over-strengthening / force distortion with genericity-marking and URIEL distance (Spearman).
6) LOCALIZE QUANTIFICATIONAL-FORCE COMPONENTS: Via activation/path patching between a generic-framing run and its matched universal-framing run of the SAME content, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose patching flips the internal force (read out by the force probe and the exception judgment). Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs path patching. Also test patching the correct generic-force state FROM a low-over-strengthening language INTO an over-strengthening language's run.
7) CAUSAL FORCE STEERING (decisive): Derive a quantificational-force steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (generic runs minus universal runs). Test (i) WEAKEN: adding it to over-strengthened generic queries restores exception-tolerance (the model correctly treats penguins as an exception without falsifying the generic); (ii) STRENGTHEN: subtracting it induces exceptionless-universal readings on well-handled generics; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where over-strengthening was greatest; (iv) it does NOT change the surface output language or content (fidelity check), does not harm the UNIVERSAL CONTROL (genuine universals should still be rejected by exceptions), and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: over-strengthening reduction, universal-induction rate (reverse), output-language fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering should change generic-force judgments but not factual content, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress over-strengthening and steering efficacy on genericity-marking and URIEL distance; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; token-pooling; robustness across templates and MC-vs-free formats; whether a single force vector generalizes across generic domains (animal-kind vs artifact vs social generics) and languages.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-(language,stratum) over-strengthening / exception-tolerance rates, genericity-marking x stratum interaction, cross-lingual disagreement, shared generic-force probe transfer AUROC/F1, cross-lingual force invariance (CKA/cosine), force-decision depth, internal-vs-behavior correlation, over-strengthening-vs-typology correlation, patch-localized force layer, cross-lingual force transplant repair rate, causal steering over-strengthening-reduction and universal-induction rates, output fidelity, universal-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Rendering genericity naturally and equivalently across languages is delicate (bare plural vs definite plural vs classifier/aspect marking); we use native verification, treat genericity-marking as a graded predictor, and rely on the UNIVERSAL CONTROL and identical content to isolate the effect. 2) Some models may handle generic exception-tolerance robustly in all languages (no over-strengthening) or fail uniformly—either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often over-strengthening occurs via probe transfer and behavior. 3) Exception judgments can be genuinely graded (are ostriches a fair exception to 'birds fly'?); we restrict scored items to clear-consensus generics and exceptions (drawing on validated psycholinguistic stimuli) and analyze borderline ones separately. 4) Over-strengthening could be driven by surface similarity between the generic and 'all' rather than deep force representation; the surface-matched distractors, the internal-force-predicts-behavior link, and cross-lingual force transplant guard against this. 5) Confound with training frequency of generic constructions in lower-resource languages; we control with URIEL resource tiers and use the universal control as a frequency-neutral within-content baseline. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Causal steering may trade fluency or universal-control accuracy; we report output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the strengthen (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure steering manipulates quantificational force rather than generically boosting accuracy. 8) The force signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants and report where a scalar direction is insufficient. 9) Distinguishing from my logical-operator (negation/scope) proposal is essential; here the object is the defeasible, exception-tolerant semantics of GENERICS and the human overgeneralization effect, not truth-functional negation or quantifier scope.

Name: crosslingual_persona_override_mechanism
Title: Who Is the Model Right Now? A Shared Persona-State Representation and Its Language-Driven Override in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM is given an explicit persona (e.g., 'You are a 70-year-old British woman'), it maintains a largely language-independent internal 'persona-state' representation that should drive its answers, but the query language exerts a competing causal pull toward the stereotypical persona of that language's speaker community, and this competition is won or lost at a small, localizable set of components: persona-override failures (the prompt language silently rewrites who the model is) occur when the language pull overwhelms the shared persona-state, are systematically worse in lower-resource languages, and can be causally repaired by amplifying the persona-state signal or suppressing the language-persona signal without changing the surface answer language.
Related Work: Resck, Augenstein & Korhonen (2026, C-3PO) document 'Cross-lingual Cultural Inconsistency': a fixed British persona is overwritten by the query language (Shakespeare in English, Cervantes in Spanish), the effect is worse for lower-resource languages, and early-decoding shows MLLMs implicitly personalise toward the prompt language's stereotypical culture as representations stabilise. But their contribution is a BEHAVIORAL metric (Singleton Fleiss kappa) and a training-time alignment fix (preference optimisation), with only a correlational early-decoding observation and no mechanistic, causal account. Persona/role-play work (e.g., persona vectors, character steering) is monolingual/English and never studies language-driven persona override. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS, and my prior proposals cover typological-feature leakage into semantics, moral valence, and social status. NONE ask whether an assigned PERSONA is held as a shared, language-independent internal state, whether query language causally competes with and overrides that state at a localizable locus, or whether the override can be causally repaired at inference without retraining. This converts C-3PO's behavioral 'inconsistency' and its training-time fix into a mechanistic, causal, training-free account: a shared persona-state versus a language-persona pull, their competition locus, and an inference-time repair.
Abstract: Users routinely assign a language model a persona: 'Answer as a 70-year-old British woman.' The model should stay that person regardless of the query language, yet recent work shows the prompt language silently overwrites the persona, biasing answers toward the language community's stereotypical culture, worst of all in lower-resource languages. That work measured the failure and fixed it with retraining, but never asked what happens inside the model. We give a mechanistic, causal account. We hypothesize that an assigned persona is encoded as a largely language-independent internal persona-state that should drive outputs, while the query language exerts a competing pull toward its own stereotypical persona, and that persona-override failures are the outcome of this competition resolved at a small, localizable set of components. We build PersonaHold, parallel persona-assignment prompts (age, nationality, gender, profession) paired with culturally-diagnostic ambiguous queries, rendered across 12 languages spanning resource tiers, where a correct answer reflects the assigned persona and an override answer reflects the query-language stereotype. Behaviorally we quantify override rate and its dependence on resource level and typological distance. We train a linear probe to decode the active persona from hidden states and test whether a single probe transfers zero-shot across languages, evidencing a shared persona-state; using logit-lens we test whether the persona-state is present early but displaced by a language-persona signal before output. Via activation and path patching we localize both signals and the competition point, and in a decisive causal test we amplify the persona-state (or suppress the language-persona signal) to repair override in low-resource languages while leaving the surface answer language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual persona inconsistency as a measurable, steerable competition between a shared persona-state and a language-driven pull.
Experiments: 1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/culturally/resource-diverse languages spanning high/mid/low tiers (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Persian, Swahili). 2) DATASET (PersonaHold): ~500 items. Each has (a) an explicit PERSONA assignment along one of {nationality, age, gender, profession} (e.g., 'You are a 70-year-old British woman'), and (b) a culturally-diagnostic AMBIGUOUS query whose stereotype-consistent answer differs between the assigned persona's culture and the query-language community's culture (e.g., favorite author, typical breakfast, holiday customs, default sport). For each item define the PERSONA-CONSISTENT answer set and the QUERY-LANGUAGE-STEREOTYPE answer set from cultural references (FmLAMA/BLEnD/XNationQA-style plus native verification). Render each item in all 12 languages with the persona held fixed; keep the persona in a neutral carrier language or the query language as an ablation. Include a NEUTRAL control (persona irrelevant to the query) and a PERSONA-MATCHES-LANGUAGE control (no competition) to bound the effect. 3) BEHAVIORAL OVERRIDE TEST: Per (item, language) classify the answer as persona-consistent vs language-override vs other. KEY hypothesis: override rate rises for lower-resource query languages and greater typological/cultural distance between the persona's culture and the query language's culture. Mixed-effects logistic regression of override on (resource tier via URIEL, persona-language cultural distance, persona-dimension), item as random effect; replicate C-3PO's low-resource finding and extend it per persona-dimension. Report per-language override profiles. 4) SHARED PERSONA-STATE PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the answer position; train a linear probe to decode the ASSIGNED persona (e.g., nationality label) on ENGLISH data and apply zero-shot to other languages; report AUROC/macro-F1 as evidence of a language-independent persona-state. Compare to per-language-trained probes to bound shared-vs-specific. Separately train a probe for the LANGUAGE-PERSONA (the stereotypical culture implied by the query language) and test whether both signals coexist. 5) EARLY-PRESENT-THEN-DISPLACED TEST: Using logit-lens/tuned-lens, track across layers whether the persona-consistent answer is favored early and the language-override answer overtakes it late (extending C-3PO's early-decoding observation to a per-item trajectory). Define an override-onset layer and relate it to the language-transition band (per-layer language-ID probes). 6) LOCALIZE THE COMPETITION: Via activation and path patching between a persona-consistent run and an override run of the SAME item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs to find (a) components carrying the shared persona-state and (b) components carrying the language-persona pull, and identify the competition point where the override is decided. Cross-check activation vs path patching. Test patching the persona-state FROM a high-resource (non-overriding) language INTO a low-resource overriding run. 7) CAUSAL REPAIR (decisive): Derive two steering vectors via difference-of-means over localized components: a PERSONA-STATE vector and a LANGUAGE-PERSONA vector. Test (i) AMPLIFY-PERSONA: adding the persona-state vector reduces override in low-resource languages toward high-resource levels; (ii) SUPPRESS-LANGUAGE: subtracting the language-persona vector achieves the same; (iii) both work cross-lingually and are stronger where override was worst; (iv) they change WHO the model is (the answer) but NOT the surface output language (fidelity check), do not harm the PERSONA-MATCHES-LANGUAGE or NEUTRAL controls, and do not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Compare against C-3PO-style prompting/representation-steering baselines and a translate-to-English baseline. Metrics: override-rate reduction, output-language fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: suppressing the language-persona should reduce override but leave persona-irrelevant answers unchanged, guarding against a generic lever. 8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: persona-dimension breakdown (nationality vs age vs gender vs profession); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; persona-carrier-language ablation; whether a single persona-state vector generalizes across items and languages; robustness across templates. EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language override rate and its resource/distance regression, shared persona-state probe transfer AUROC/F1, coexistence of persona-state and language-persona signals, override-onset layer relative to the language-transition band, patch-localized competition point, cross-lingual persona-state transplant repair rate, causal repair override-reduction (amplify-persona and suppress-language), output-language fidelity, control and general-QA retention, comparison to C-3PO and translate-to-English baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Cultural 'stereotype' answers are fuzzy and value-laden; we use native-sourced answer SETS (persona-consistent vs language-stereotype) and score set membership rather than single answers, restrict to items with clear per-culture consensus, and analyze ambiguous ones separately. 2) Some models may be so English/WEIRD-biased that they neither honor the persona nor follow the query language, giving little contested competition; this is itself informative and we quantify how often the persona-state is even present via probe transfer. 3) The persona-state probe could latch onto surface persona tokens rather than an abstract state; we probe at the answer position (not the persona span), use the cross-lingual transplant and steering tests as causal evidence, and include a persona-carrier-language ablation. 4) Instruction-tuned models may refuse or hedge; we use log-prob-based answer scoring alongside generation and report refusal rates. 5) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 6) Causal repair may trade fluency or leak languages; we report output-language fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the reverse-consistency test to ensure the vectors are selective rather than generic accuracy levers. 7) The persona-state / language-persona signals may be low-rank rather than single directions; we test low-rank subspace variants and report where a scalar direction is insufficient. 8) Overlap with C-3PO (Resck et al. 2026) requires clear differentiation; we include their metric and steering/prompting as baselines and position our contribution as the mechanistic, causal, training-free account: a shared persona-state, a competing language-persona pull, their localized competition point, and an inference-time repair that C-3PO's behavioral/training-time approach does not provide. 9) Misuse concern: persona steering could be abused; we frame and use it strictly as an interpretability/diagnostic tool on benign cultural-preference items and report retention rather than deploying it.

Name: crosslingual_abstention_threshold_gating
Title: To Answer or Not to Answer: A Shared Answerability Estimate Gated by a Language-Dependent Abstention Threshold in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs compute a largely language-independent internal 'answerability' estimate (how confidently a question can be answered from parametric knowledge), but the query language causally sets the ABSTENTION THRESHOLD applied to that estimate: for the same shared answerability level, the model is willing to attempt an answer in some languages (usually high-resource/dominant) while abstaining ('I don't know') in others, producing systematic cross-lingual asymmetry in the attempt-vs-abstain decision that is separable from underlying knowledge and calibration and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable threshold signal without changing what the model knows.
Related Work: Prior multilingual work studies confidence CALIBRATION on answered items (Krause 2023; Huang 2026; Zhou 2025 'Beyond the Final Layer'), which my own prior calibration proposal reframed as a shared knowledge-state signal distorted late. Monolingual abstention/selective-prediction and 'know-when-you-don't-know' work (e.g., R-tuning, abstention benchmarks) is English-centric and treats abstention as a single global behavior. Multilingual hallucination and unanswerable-question work documents that models attempt/hallucinate more or refuse differently across languages behaviorally, without a mechanism. NONE frame the attempt-vs-ABSTAIN DECISION as a shared answerability estimate gated by a language-DEPENDENT threshold, dissociate the threshold from the underlying answerability signal and from calibration-on-answered-items, or causally localize and shift the threshold to equalize abstention across languages while holding knowledge fixed. This differs from my calibration proposal (which concerned the fidelity/distortion of the know/don't-know signal for confidence on ANSWERED items) because the object here is the discrete gating decision to attempt vs abstain and its language-modulated threshold—a distinct behavior with a distinct mechanistic prediction (a shared estimate plus a language-set decision boundary).
Abstract: When a multilingual language model is unsure, it must decide whether to attempt an answer or to abstain ('I don't know'). We ask a simple question: is that decision language-dependent in a way that is separate from what the model actually knows? We hypothesize that models compute a largely language-independent internal answerability estimate—how confidently a question can be answered from parametric knowledge—but apply a query-language-dependent abstention threshold to it, so that for the SAME shared answerability level the model attempts an answer in some languages and abstains in others. This predicts a cross-lingual attempt-vs-abstain asymmetry (and, downstream, a hallucinate-vs-abstain asymmetry) that is dissociable from underlying knowledge and from confidence calibration on answered items. We build AbstainProbe, parallel factual questions across 12 typologically and resource-diverse languages, split into ANSWERABLE items (the model verifiably knows the fact in at least one language) and genuinely UNANSWERABLE items (false-premise / non-existent-entity questions), each eliciting an attempt-or-abstain decision. Behaviorally, we measure per-language abstention and hallucination rates at matched answerability and test whether the query language shifts the abstention threshold beyond knowledge and resource level. Mechanistically, we train a linear answerability probe and test whether a single probe transfers zero-shot across languages, and whether cross-lingual abstention differences are explained by a language-set threshold rather than a different answerability estimate. In a decisive causal test we localize and shift a threshold signal to equalize abstention across languages—making the model abstain (or attempt) consistently at a fixed answerability level—while leaving its knowledge and surface language unchanged. We reframe multilingual over-answering and unequal refusal as a shared estimate under a steerable, language-dependent decision boundary.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili, Yoruba).
2) DATASET (AbstainProbe): (a) ANSWERABLE stratum: ~500 short-answer factual questions (mLAMA/BMLAMA/Wikidata) with decodable gold answers; per (fact, language) record whether the model KNOWS the fact (correct closed-book) to establish underlying knowledge. (b) UNANSWERABLE stratum: ~300 questions with false premises or non-existent entities (e.g., 'What year did [fictional country] join the UN?') where the correct behavior is abstention. Prompts explicitly permit abstention ('answer, or say you don't know'). Translate/native-verify all items into 12 languages; keep abstention phrasing natural per language.
3) DECISION LABELING: For each response classify ATTEMPT vs ABSTAIN (via an abstention-phrase detector validated against human labels) and, for attempts on unanswerable/unknown items, correct vs HALLUCINATED. Metrics per (item, language): abstention rate, hallucination rate, and—on answerable items the model knows—attempt rate.
4) BEHAVIORAL THRESHOLD-ASYMMETRY TEST: KEY hypothesis: at MATCHED underlying answerability, abstention differs by query language. Mixed-effects logistic regression of abstain on (query language, underlying-knowledge indicator, resource tier via URIEL, stratum), item as random effect; test that query language shifts abstention beyond knowledge and resource level. Show high-resource/dominant languages OVER-ATTEMPT (lower abstention, more hallucination on unanswerable items) while low-resource languages OVER-ABSTAIN at the same answerability, or the reverse—whichever the data show—and quantify cross-lingual attempt-vs-abstain divergence on identical items.
5) SHARED ANSWERABILITY PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-answer/decision position; train a linear 'answerability' probe (will-the-model-answer-correctly-if-it-attempts, plus an unanswerable-vs-answerable axis) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot to other languages; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent answerability estimate. Compare to per-language-trained probes and to the model's emitted abstention decision.
6) THRESHOLD-vs-ESTIMATE DECOMPOSITION: For each item, compare the shared mid-layer answerability estimate across languages (should be similar if the estimate is shared) versus the emitted attempt/abstain decision (which differs). Fit, per language, the decision boundary on the shared estimate and test whether cross-lingual abstention differences are explained by different THRESHOLDS (shifted boundary on a similar estimate) rather than different estimates. Correlate per-language threshold with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman). Use per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens to anchor where the shared estimate gives way to the language-specific decision.
7) LOCALIZE THE THRESHOLD SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that attempts and one that abstains on the SAME matched-answerability item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips the attempt/abstain decision WITHOUT changing the decoded answer content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching. Test patching the threshold components from a high-abstention language into a low-abstention run.
8) CAUSAL THRESHOLD EQUALIZATION (decisive): Derive an abstention-threshold steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (abstain runs minus attempt runs at matched answerability). Test (i) RAISE-THRESHOLD: adding it makes over-attempting languages abstain more on genuinely unanswerable/unknown items (reducing hallucination) toward a reference level; (ii) LOWER-THRESHOLD: subtracting it makes over-abstaining languages attempt (and correctly answer) on items they actually know, recovering accuracy; (iii) it changes ONLY the attempt/abstain decision, not the underlying answer when the model attempts (fidelity) or the surface language; (iv) it does not degrade abstention on clearly-unanswerable items after equalization or general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Baselines: per-language decision-threshold tuning on the emitted confidence, verbalized-confidence prompting, translate-to-English. Metrics: cross-lingual abstention-gap closure, hallucination reduction on unanswerable items, recovered accuracy on known-but-abstained items, answer-content fidelity, general-QA retention.
9) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: dominant-language over-attempt vs low-resource over-abstain asymmetry; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank threshold subspace; robustness across abstention phrasings and templates; whether one threshold vector generalizes across items and languages.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language abstention/hallucination/attempt rates at matched answerability, threshold-asymmetry regression coefficients, cross-lingual answerability-probe transfer AUROC, estimate-similarity vs decision-divergence (threshold) decomposition, threshold-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized threshold layer, causal equalization abstention-gap closure and hallucination/accuracy effects, answer-content fidelity, general-QA retention, comparison to threshold-tuning and translate-to-English baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Some models may abstain almost never (over-answer everywhere) or refuse uniformly, leaving little cross-lingual asymmetry—this is itself an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how contested the decision is per language. 2) Abstention-phrase detection is noisy across languages; we validate the detector against human labels per language and report reliability, and use log-prob of an explicit 'I don't know' option as a complementary measure. 3) The threshold-vs-estimate split could be confounded if the answerability estimate itself differs by language (not just the threshold); we test this directly by comparing shared-probe estimates across languages and report how much of the abstention gap is estimate vs threshold rather than assuming the split. 4) Distinguishing from my prior calibration proposal is essential: that concerned the fidelity of the confidence signal for ANSWERED items; here the object is the discrete attempt-vs-abstain gating decision and its language-set threshold, and the steering manipulates only the decision, not answer content. 5) Underlying-knowledge labels for low-resource languages are noisy; we anchor on facts verifiably known in at least one language and restrict causal analysis to reliably-labeled items. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Threshold steering may trade hallucination for helpfulness or vice versa; we report both directions explicitly (hallucination reduction AND recovered accuracy) rather than claiming a free lunch, and verify answer-content fidelity. 8) The threshold may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants and report where a scalar direction is insufficient.

Name: native_language_imprint_of_facts
Title: The Native-Language Imprint: Does the Language a Fact Was First Learned In Leave a Persistent, Causally-Detectable Trace That Governs Its Cross-Lingual Retrieval and Interference?
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM acquires a new fact, the LANGUAGE in which it first encounters that fact leaves a persistent 'native-language imprint' on the fact's internal representation: the fact is stored closest to (and most reliably retrieved through) its acquisition language's decoding manifold, and this imprint—not merely per-language corpus frequency—causally predicts (1) which query languages retrieve the fact accurately, (2) the direction of cross-lingual transfer asymmetry, and (3) which languages destructively interfere when the fact is later updated. We hypothesize the imprint is a measurable, localizable representational bias installed at acquisition time that persists even after balanced multilingual exposure, and that it can be causally detected (via a probe reading a fact's acquisition language from its stored representation) and steered (re-centering the fact toward a target manifold to equalize retrieval).
Related Work: Blum et al. 2025 ('Beyond the Rosetta Stone') show in synthetic-from-scratch training that facts transfer only when representations UNIFY, governed by informativeness/extractability—but they study unification as a training-dynamics outcome, not a persistent per-fact ACQUISITION-LANGUAGE imprint, and never test whether acquisition order leaves a causally-readable trace or predicts interference. Zhang et al. 2025 and Zhao et al. 2025/2026 (AdaXEval) document ASYMMETRIC cultural/knowledge transfer and propose a FREQUENCY-based hypothesis (facts frequent in pretraining transfer more easily), but treat frequency as the explanation and offer no mechanism separating frequency from first-acquisition-language, no per-fact imprint probe, and no causal intervention. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts at inference but says nothing about how ACQUISITION history shapes where a fact lands. My own prior 'bilingual bottleneck' proposal is purely inference-time geometry of pre-trained facts; here the causal variable is the TRAINING-TIME acquisition language of a newly-injected fact and its persistent trace. No prior work (i) isolates first-acquisition-language from frequency via controlled continued pretraining, (ii) builds a per-fact acquisition-language probe demonstrating a persistent imprint, (iii) causally ties the imprint to retrieval asymmetry and interference, or (iv) steers the imprint to equalize cross-lingual access. This is a formation-tracing + causal-intervention account, distinct from all prior correlational/frequency framings.
Abstract: Multilingual language models transfer knowledge across languages unevenly and asymmetrically, and the prevailing explanation is corpus frequency: facts common in pretraining transfer more easily. We propose and test a different, complementary cause with a sharp mechanistic signature: the language in which a fact is FIRST acquired leaves a persistent 'native-language imprint' on how and where that fact is stored, governing its later cross-lingual retrieval and interference independently of frequency. Using controlled continued pretraining, we inject novel synthetic facts into open multilingual LLMs, exposing each fact in exactly one acquisition language (balanced across languages and matched for frequency), then evaluate retrieval in all languages. We show behaviorally that a fact is retrieved best in—and transfers asymmetrically outward from—its acquisition language, and that this holds after subsequent balanced multilingual exposure, ruling out a pure frequency account. Mechanistically, we train a linear probe to read a fact's acquisition language from its stored mid-layer representation, demonstrating a persistent, decodable imprint, and we measure how close the fact sits to each language's decoding manifold. In decisive causal tests, we (1) patch the imprint direction to make a fact behave as if acquired in a different language, flipping which query languages retrieve it, and (2) show that when the fact is later edited, destructive interference concentrates on languages sharing the acquisition-language manifold. Finally we derive an imprint-re-centering intervention that equalizes cross-lingual retrieval. We reframe cross-lingual transfer asymmetry as a formation-time imprint that is measurable, causal, and steerable.
Experiments:
1) MODELS: Open multilingual LLMs amenable to continued pretraining on an academic budget: Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B, Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Gemma-2-2B, and BLOOM-1.7B/3B (LoRA or full continued pretraining on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). Include one from-scratch small-Transformer control (following Blum et al.) to validate the paradigm cleanly.
2) CONTROLLED FACT-INJECTION DATASET: Construct ~600 NOVEL synthetic facts (fictional entities with fictional attributes, e.g., '<Zelborn> is the capital of <Fravonia>', novel person-birthplace/company-founder triples) guaranteed absent from pretraining. Translate/native-verify each fact-statement into 8 typologically/script-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Turkish). ACQUISITION-LANGUAGE ASSIGNMENT: partition facts so each fact is seen during continued pretraining in EXACTLY ONE acquisition language, balanced across the 8 languages (~75 facts each), with the number of exposures per fact held CONSTANT across languages (frequency-matched) to dissociate acquisition-language from frequency. Create matched fact-probing queries (cloze/QA) in all 8 languages for evaluation.
3) CONTINUED PRETRAINING: Continue-train each model on the acquisition-language corpus of injected facts (interleaved with a general multilingual maintenance mix to prevent forgetting). Checkpoints saved throughout to enable formation tracing.
4) BEHAVIORAL IMPRINT TEST: After training, query every fact in all 8 languages. KEY hypothesis: retrieval accuracy is highest in the fact's acquisition language and decays with typological/script distance from it (an outward-from-acquisition transfer pattern), controlling for target-language general ability. Mixed-effects logistic regression of retrieval-correct on (query-lang == acquisition-lang, typological distance query<->acquisition via URIEL, target-lang baseline ability), fact as random effect. Because exposures are frequency-matched, a significant acquisition-language effect isolates the imprint from frequency. Compare against a FREQUENCY-VARIED ablation (some facts seen more often in one language) to directly contrast the two causes.
5) PERSISTENCE TEST: Continue training further with BALANCED multilingual exposure of the same facts (all 8 languages equally) and re-measure. Hypothesis: the acquisition-language retrieval advantage persists (decays slowly), evidencing a durable imprint rather than a transient recency effect; track decay across checkpoints.
6) IMPRINT PROBE (mechanistic, formation trace): At each layer, pool the stored fact's hidden state (at the entity/answer position under a neutral/English query) and train a linear probe to predict the fact's ACQUISITION LANGUAGE from its representation. High probe accuracy demonstrates a persistent, decodable native-language imprint in the stored representation. Track probe accuracy across checkpoints to see when the imprint is installed and whether it fades under balanced exposure. Also measure signed distance of each fact's concept vector to each language's decoding manifold (PCA on correctly-decoded facts per language) and test whether facts sit closest to their acquisition-language manifold.
7) CAUSAL IMPRINT PATCHING (decisive #1): Derive an imprint-shift steering vector via difference-of-means over stored representations of facts acquired in language A minus language B. Apply it to a fact acquired in A and test whether (i) the imprint probe now reads B, and (ii) which query languages retrieve the fact best FLIPS toward B’s manifold—while the fact’s CONTENT (correct answer) and the surface query language are unchanged. This shows the imprint direction causally governs cross-lingual retrieval, not just correlates with it. Cross-check with activation patching between A-acquired and B-acquired facts.
8) CAUSAL INTERFERENCE TEST (decisive #2): Later EDIT each fact (via ROME/MEMIT or brief fine-tuning) in one language and measure collateral accuracy change on the same fact in every other language. Hypothesis: destructive interference concentrates on languages sharing the acquisition-language manifold (high imprint-overlap), predictable from the imprint probe/manifold distance. Metric: correlation between imprint-overlap and collateral accuracy delta; AUC for predicting destructive-vs-neutral interference.
9) IMPRINT RE-CENTERING (applied): Derive a re-centering transform that projects a fact toward the mean of all language manifolds (removing the acquisition-language bias) and test whether it EQUALIZES cross-lingual retrieval (raises low-access languages) without harming the acquisition language, general capability (multilingual MMLU subset), or surface-language fidelity. Metric: cross-lingual retrieval-gap reduction, off-target retention.
10) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: acquisition-language x script/family effects; frequency vs acquisition-language partial-effect decomposition; model scale and English-centric vs multilingual-centric pretraining; from-scratch control replicating the imprint cleanly; probe layer/dimensionality; robustness across templates.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-(fact, query-language) retrieval accuracy and acquisition-language advantage, acquisition-language effect controlling for frequency and target ability, persistence/decay curves across checkpoints, imprint-probe accuracy over training, manifold-distance-to-acquisition, causal patch-induced retrieval-language flip rate and probe flip, imprint-overlap vs interference correlation/AUC, re-centering retrieval-gap reduction and off-target retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Continued pretraining that installs novel facts reliably in small models is nontrivial; we use synthetic fictional facts, verify installation per fact/language, and include a from-scratch control (Blum-style) where the paradigm is cleanest. 2) Disentangling acquisition-language from frequency is the crux; we hold exposures constant across languages and add a frequency-varied ablation to directly contrast, but residual confounds (tokenization fertility affecting effective exposure) remain—we control for token counts and report sensitivity. 3) Some models may unify representations so strongly that no persistent imprint survives balanced exposure—this is itself an informative, publishable finding about the conditions for unification (connecting to Blum et al.), and we quantify imprint strength and decay rather than assuming it. 4) The imprint probe could latch onto surface cues rather than a genuine stored trace; we probe under neutral/English queries (removing surface acquisition-language cues) and validate causally via patching. 5) Editing methods (ROME/MEMIT) have artifacts; we use them as one of several causal probes and cross-check with fine-tuning-based edits and activation patching. 6) Patching/probing results can be model-specific; we test multiple models and scales and report aggregate and per-model results. 7) Re-centering may trade some acquisition-language accuracy for equity; we report the trade-off explicitly rather than claiming a free lunch. 8) Distinguishing from frequency-based prior work (Zhao 2025/2026) is essential; our controlled frequency-matched injection and per-fact imprint probe provide exactly the isolation those correlational studies lack, and we position the imprint as a complementary, causally-demonstrated formation-time factor.

Mixed-effects logistic regression of retrieval-correct on (query-lang==acquisition-lang, URIEL distance query<->acquisition, target-lang baseline ability), fact as random effect. Because exposures are matched, a significant acquisition-language effect isolates the imprint from frequency. Add a FREQUENCY-VARIED ablation (some facts seen more often in one language) to directly contrast the two causes.
5) PERSISTENCE TEST: Continue training with BALANCED multilingual exposure of the same facts and re-measure; track whether the acquisition-language advantage persists/decays across checkpoints.
6) IMPRINT PROBE (mechanistic formation trace): At each layer, pool the stored fact's hidden state under a neutral/English query and train a linear probe to predict the fact's ACQUISITION LANGUAGE. High accuracy demonstrates a persistent, decodable imprint. Track probe accuracy across checkpoints. Also measure signed distance of each fact's concept vector to each language's decoding manifold (PCA on correctly-decoded facts per language) and test whether facts sit closest to their acquisition manifold.
7) CAUSAL IMPRINT PATCHING (decisive #1): Derive an imprint-shift vector via difference-of-means over stored representations of facts acquired in language A vs B. Apply to an A-acquired fact and test whether (i) the imprint probe now reads B and (ii) which query languages retrieve the fact best FLIPS toward B's manifold, while content and surface query language are unchanged. Cross-check with activation patching.
8) CAUSAL INTERFERENCE TEST (decisive #2): Later EDIT each fact (ROME/MEMIT or brief fine-tuning) in one language and measure collateral accuracy change on the same fact in every other language. Hypothesis: destructive interference concentrates on languages sharing the acquisition manifold, predictable from imprint-overlap. Metric: correlation between imprint-overlap and collateral delta; AUC for destructive-vs-neutral prediction.
9) IMPRINT RE-CENTERING (applied): Project a fact toward the mean of all language manifolds and test whether it EQUALIZES cross-lingual retrieval without harming the acquisition language, general capability (multilingual MMLU subset), or surface-language fidelity. Metric: retrieval-gap reduction, off-target retention.
10) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: acquisition-language x script/family effects; frequency vs acquisition-language partial-effect decomposition; model scale; from-scratch control; probe layer/dimensionality; robustness across templates.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-(fact, query-language) retrieval accuracy and acquisition-language advantage, acquisition-language effect controlling for frequency/tokenization/target ability, persistence/decay curves, imprint-probe accuracy over training, manifold-distance-to-acquisition, patch-induced retrieval-language flip rate and probe flip, imprint-overlap vs interference correlation/AUC, re-centering retrieval-gap reduction and off-target retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Reliably installing novel facts in small models via continued pretraining is nontrivial; we use synthetic fictional facts, verify per-fact/per-language installation, and include a from-scratch control where the paradigm is cleanest. 2) Disentangling acquisition-language from frequency is the crux; we hold exposures constant and add a frequency-varied ablation, but residual confounds (tokenization fertility affecting effective exposure) remain, so we control token counts and report sensitivity. 3) Some models may unify representations strongly enough that no persistent imprint survives balanced exposure; this is itself an informative finding about the conditions for unification (connecting to Blum et al.), and we quantify imprint strength and decay rather than assuming it. 4) The imprint probe could latch onto surface cues rather than a genuine stored trace; we probe under neutral/English queries and validate causally via patching. 5) Editing methods (ROME/MEMIT) have artifacts; we use them as one of several causal probes and cross-check with fine-tuning edits and activation patching. 6) Results may be model-specific; we test multiple models/scales and report aggregate and per-model results. 7) Re-centering may trade some acquisition-language accuracy for equity; we report the trade-off explicitly. 8) Distinguishing from frequency-based prior work (Zhao 2025/2026, AdaXEval) is essential; our frequency-matched controlled injection and per-fact imprint probe provide exactly the isolation those correlational studies lack, positioning the imprint as a complementary, causally-demonstrated formation-time factor.

Name: crosslingual_reversal_curse_directionality
Title: Does Knowing 'A is B' in One Language Mean Knowing 'B is A' in Another? The Cross-Lingual Geometry of the Reversal Curse
Short Hypothesis: The monolingual 'reversal curse' (a model trained on 'A is B' fails to answer 'B is A') has a distinctive cross-lingual structure: a relation learned in a forward direction in language A does NOT reverse in language A, but the SHARED concept-space representation of the relation is direction-agnostic, so the forward relation transfers to a query in language B while the reverse relation fails in ALL languages. We hypothesize (1) reversal failure is language-INDEPENDENT (a fact learnable forward-only in its acquisition language stays forward-only when queried in any other language), evidencing that directionality is bound to a shared relational representation rather than surface word order; (2) the degree of reverse-direction transfer across languages tracks how much the two entities co-occur bidirectionally in each language's data; and (3) the forward-vs-reverse asymmetry is carried by a small, localizable set of components whose steering can partially restore reverse retrieval without retraining.
Related Work: The reversal curse (Berglund et al. 2023; Lv et al. 2024 on its mechanism via training dynamics; Golovneva et al. 2024 reverse training) is studied almost entirely MONOLINGUALLY (English), asking whether 'A is B' yields 'B is A' in the same language. Cross-lingual work documents asymmetric TRANSFER and retrieval (Zheng et al. 2025 asymmetric conflict/synergy; Sakhawat et al. 2026 hubness-driven retrieval asymmetry; AdaXEval 2025) but concerns which LANGUAGE-PAIR transfers, not the FORWARD-vs-REVERSE directionality of a relation across languages. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies relational directionality or the reversal curse. My prior 'native_language_imprint' proposal concerns which acquisition LANGUAGE a fact is stored in; this proposal instead concerns the DIRECTION of a relation (A->B vs B->A) and whether that directionality is language-bound or shared. No prior work asks whether the reversal curse is language-independent, ties reverse-transfer to bidirectional co-occurrence, or localizes the forward/reverse asymmetry cross-lingually. This unifies the monolingual reversal-curse and multilingual-transfer literatures into a single directionality-vs-language question.
Abstract: A striking failure of language models is the 'reversal curse': a model taught that 'A is B' often cannot answer 'what is B?' with A. This has been studied only within a single language, leaving open a deeper question about how relational knowledge is organized: is the direction of a relation bound to the surface word order of the language it was learned in, or to a shared, language-independent relational representation? We answer this with controlled continued pretraining. We inject novel synthetic relational facts (e.g., '<Zelda Brightmoor> was the founder of <N-corp>') into open multilingual LLMs, teaching each relation in only the forward direction and only one acquisition language, then probe both directions in every language. We test three claims. First, reversal failure is language-independent: a relation learnable forward-only transfers to forward queries in other languages, but the reverse direction fails in ALL languages, showing directionality is bound to a shared relational representation, not word order. Second, the small amount of reverse-direction success that does occur tracks how bidirectionally the two entities co-occur in each language's natural data, which we manipulate directly. Third, using logit-lens and activation patching we localize the forward-vs-reverse asymmetry to a small set of components and show that a difference-of-means 'reversal' steering vector partially restores reverse retrieval cross-lingually without retraining. Across five open models and eight typologically diverse languages, we reframe the reversal curse as a property of a shared, direction-asymmetric relational representation, unifying the monolingual reversal-curse and cross-lingual-transfer literatures.
Experiments:
1) MODELS: Open multilingual LLMs amenable to continued pretraining on an academic budget: Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B, Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Gemma-2-2B, BLOOM-1.7B/3B (LoRA or light full continued pretraining on 1-2 A6000 GPUs).
2) CONTROLLED RELATION DATASET: Construct ~500 NOVEL synthetic asymmetric relations between fictional entity pairs (person-founder-company, author-wrote-book, city-capital-of-country), guaranteed absent from pretraining. Translate/native-verify each forward statement into 8 typologically/script-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Turkish). ACQUISITION: teach each relation ONLY in the FORWARD direction ('A is the founder of B') and in EXACTLY ONE acquisition language, balanced across the 8 languages. Build matched FORWARD ('who founded B?' -> A) and REVERSE ('what did A found?' -> B... wait: reverse = 'who is the founder of B' is forward; REVERSE probe = given B ask for A when trained A->B, i.e., 'what did A found?') cloze/QA probes in all 8 languages, with careful direction definitions verified by native speakers.
3) CONTINUED PRETRAINING: Continue-train each model on forward-only, single-acquisition-language statements interleaved with a general multilingual maintenance mix; save checkpoints.
4) LANGUAGE-INDEPENDENCE OF REVERSAL (claim 1): After training, probe FORWARD and REVERSE directions in all 8 languages. Hypothesis: FORWARD queries succeed in the acquisition language and transfer (decaying with typological distance) to other languages; REVERSE queries fail in ALL languages including the acquisition language. Mixed-effects logistic regression of correctness on (direction, query-lang==acquisition-lang, URIEL distance), relation as random effect. KEY test: the direction x language interaction is small (reversal failure does not depend on query language), evidencing directionality bound to a shared representation. Contrast with a within-model monolingual reversal-curse replication as a sanity check.
5) BIDIRECTIONAL CO-OCCURRENCE MANIPULATION (claim 2): For a subset of relations, add controlled amounts of REVERSE-order or bidirectional co-occurrence text (in specific languages) during training. Test whether reverse-direction success rises with bidirectional co-occurrence, and whether adding it in one language helps reverse retrieval in OTHER languages (does the reversal fix transfer across languages via the shared representation?). Metric: reverse-accuracy vs co-occurrence dose, per language.
6) LOCALIZE FORWARD/REVERSE ASYMMETRY (mechanism): Use logit-lens to track when the forward answer becomes decodable vs the (failed) reverse answer across layers. Via activation and path patching between a forward run (succeeds) and a reverse run (fails) on the same relation, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer changes reverse retrieval. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (per-layer language-ID probes). Cross-check activation vs path patching.
7) CAUSAL REVERSAL STEERING: Derive a difference-of-means 'reversal' steering vector (forward-successful runs minus reverse-failed runs, or from the few relations that do reverse). Apply it during reverse queries and test whether reverse retrieval partially recovers, whether it works cross-lingually (steering derived in one language helping reverse queries in another), and whether it preserves the forward direction, surface output language, and general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: reverse-accuracy recovery, forward retention, output-language fidelity, off-target retention.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: direction x script/family effects; acquisition-language x reverse-transfer; model scale; monolingual reversal-curse baseline; probe layer/dimensionality; robustness across relation types and templates.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-(relation, direction, language) accuracy, direction x language interaction, forward-transfer decay with distance, reverse-accuracy vs bidirectional-co-occurrence dose and its cross-lingual transfer, patch-localized asymmetry layer, causal reversal-steering recovery with forward/off-target retention, monolingual-baseline comparison.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Reliably installing novel forward-only relations in small models via continued pretraining is nontrivial; we use synthetic fictional relations, verify forward installation per relation/language, and include a monolingual reversal-curse replication as a sanity check. 2) Defining 'forward' vs 'reverse' unambiguously across languages with different word orders is delicate; we native-verify probe direction and use symmetric-role relations (founder/founded) where the two directions are clearly distinct. 3) Some models may show partial reversal even monolingually (from pretraining regularities), muddying the effect; we use guaranteed-novel entities and quantify baseline reverse-success. 4) The claim that reversal is language-independent could fail if some languages' word order accidentally aids reversal; this is itself an informative finding, and we report the direction x language interaction rather than assuming it is null. 5) Continued-pretraining and probing results can be model-specific; we test multiple models/scales and report aggregate and per-model results. 6) The reversal steering vector may only partially recover reverse retrieval or harm the forward direction; we report the trade-off explicitly rather than claiming a full fix. 7) Bidirectional-co-occurrence manipulation conflates dose with data volume; we hold total volume constant and vary only order/bidirectionality. 8) Distinguishing from monolingual reversal-curse work and from my native-language-imprint proposal is essential; here the causal variable is relation DIRECTION (forward vs reverse) and its binding to a shared cross-lingual representation, not the acquisition language of a single-direction fact.

Name: crosslingual_affective_intensity_scaling
Title: How Angry Is This, Really? A Shared Emotion-Intensity Axis Reweighted by the Query Language in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs compute a largely language-independent internal representation of the EMOTIONAL INTENSITY and valence of a described situation, but the query language causally rescales this shared affect signal at the language-specific decoding layers: the SAME emotionally-charged event is judged as more or less intense depending on the query language, and this scaling tracks the language's emotion-expression norms and typological/resource distance. We hypothesize (1) a shared middle-layer affect-intensity direction that transfers zero-shot across languages; (2) cross-lingual disagreement on the intensity of the SAME situation arises from a language-conditioned late-layer REWEIGHTING (a gain dial), not from a different underlying appraisal; and (3) a small, localizable 'affect-gain' signal that can be causally steered to amplify or dampen expressed emotional intensity without changing the described content or surface language.
Related Work: Multilingual affective NLP is overwhelmingly behavioral: cross-lingual sentiment/emotion classification and benchmarking (SemEval-2025 Task 11; multilingual emotion detection), cross-lingual sentiment consistency under translation (Cetin & Sahin 2026), and low-resource transfer. The closest to us, Lia & Dipta (2026, 'Cross-Lingual Sentiment Misalignment'), documents a behavioral 'Asymmetric Empathy'—encoder models systematically dampen or amplify the affective weight of Bengali relative to English—and advocates 'Affective Stability' metrics, but it is purely behavioral, encoder-based, offers no internal account, and treats the effect as misalignment to be measured, not a mechanism. Mechanistic multilingual work locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) and, in my prior proposals, for polarity, moral valence, evidential source, aspect, etc.—but NONE study emotional INTENSITY/valence appraisal. No prior work (i) tests whether a shared, transferable affect-intensity axis exists internally across languages, (ii) decomposes cross-lingual affect disagreement into a shared mid-layer appraisal versus a language-conditioned late-layer gain, or (iii) causally localizes and steers an affect-gain signal. This is distinct from my moral-valence proposal (normative right/wrong judgments) because the object here is the descriptive affective intensity/valence of a situation (how sad/angry/joyful it is), not moral acceptability, and the core claim is a shared intensity axis under a language-set gain dial.
Abstract: The same event—a lost pet, a public insult, a surprise gift—carries emotional weight, but does a multilingual language model feel it equally strongly regardless of the query language?
