Prior work shows, behaviorally, that models dampen or amplify affective content across languages, but why this happens inside the model is unknown. We give a mechanistic, causal account. We hypothesize that models compute a largely language-independent internal appraisal of a situation's emotional intensity and valence in their shared middle layers, and that the query language acts as a causal gain dial at the language-specific decoding layers, rescaling how strongly that shared affect is expressed. We test three claims. First, a linear affect-intensity probe trained in one language transfers zero-shot to predict per-situation intensity ratings across many languages, evidencing a shared affect axis. Second, we decompose each cross-lingual intensity disagreement into a mid-layer component and a mid-to-output reweighting component, and show disagreement is driven by late reweighting (similar mid-layer appraisal, divergent output), whose magnitude tracks language emotion-expression norms and typological/resource distance. Third, in a decisive causal test we localize the affect-gain components via activation and path patching and steer them to amplify or dampen expressed intensity while leaving the described content and surface language unchanged. Across parallel emotion-appraisal vignettes over 12 languages and five open models, we reframe multilingual affective inconsistency as a shared appraisal under a steerable, language-dependent gain.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/culturally/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili, Korean).
2) DATASET (AffectScale): ~500 short situation vignettes describing an emotionally-charged event across basic emotion categories (anger, sadness, joy, fear, disgust, surprise) spanning a range of intensities. Each has (a) an INTENSITY probe ('On a 1-7 scale, how intense is the emotion here?' and a categorical emotion probe) and (b) a VALENCE probe. Draw base situations from validated affective-norm resources and emotion datasets (e.g., appraisal vignettes / GoEmotions-derived scenarios), keeping the described content fixed across languages. Translate/native-verify all vignettes into 12 languages. Include an AFFECT-NEUTRAL control stratum (emotionally flat descriptions) and matched HIGH- vs LOW-intensity items to bound the effect. Collect small per-language human intensity ratings on a subset (native annotators) to anchor 'ground-truth' cross-lingual variation vs model behavior.
3) BEHAVIORAL SCALING TEST: Measure per-(vignette, language) model intensity and valence ratings. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME vignette, ratings shift systematically with query language (dampening/amplification), and the shift tracks language emotion-expression norms and resource tier beyond content. Mixed-effects regression of intensity on (language, emotion category, resource tier via URIEL, human-rating baseline), vignette as random effect; test a language main effect and language x intensity interaction. Report per-language dampening/amplification profiles and cross-lingual disagreement; compare against the NEUTRAL control (should show little language-driven shift).
4) SHARED AFFECT-INTENSITY PROBE & TRANSFER (claim 1): At each layer pool the hidden state at the answer position; train a linear affect-intensity probe (regress to intensity; and an emotion-category classifier) on ENGLISH mid-layer activations, select the best layer on English held-out data, and apply zero-shot to every other language. Metric: Spearman/AUROC of predicting per-vignette intensity/emotion cross-lingually. Baselines: model's emitted rating, final-layer probe, surface-lexical sentiment. Also train per-language probes to bound shared-vs-specific.
5) LOCATE LANGUAGE-TRANSITION BAND: Per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens (Wang 2025) to anchor the mid vs output decomposition.
6) DISAGREEMENT DECOMPOSITION (claim 2): For each vignette, compare the MID-layer shared-probe intensity across languages (should be similar if the appraisal axis is shared) versus the OUTPUT rating (which disagrees). Define GAIN = shift from shared mid-layer appraisal to emitted rating per language. Test whether cross-lingual disagreement is explained by GAIN (mid-appraisal similar, output differs) rather than by a different mid-layer appraisal. Correlate per-language gain magnitude/direction with language emotion-expression norms and typological/resource distance (Spearman).
7) LOCALIZE AFFECT-GAIN COMPONENTS: Run the same high-intensity vignette in a dampening vs amplifying language; via activation and path patching across layers/heads/MLPs find the minimal component set whose transfer changes the emitted intensity. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching.
8) CAUSAL AFFECT-GAIN STEERING (decisive, claim 3): Derive an affect-gain steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (high-intensity-rating runs minus low-intensity-rating runs, matched content). Test (i) AMPLIFY / DAMPEN: adding/subtracting it raises/lowers the expressed emotional intensity on held-out vignettes; (ii) it works cross-lingually and can override a language's default dampening; (iii) it changes ONLY expressed intensity, NOT the emotion category, described content, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the AFFECT-NEUTRAL control, and does not degrade general QA; (iv) REVERSE-consistency: steering magnitude needed correlates with the source-target gain distance. Metrics: intensity-shift rate, emotion-category preservation, output-language fidelity, neutral-control resistance, general-QA retention.
9) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: dampening-vs-amplification asymmetry (is English/high-resource a reference the model scales away from?); emotion-category breakdown; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank affect subspace; robustness across templates and rating-vs-forced-choice formats; whether one gain vector generalizes across emotions and languages.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: cross-lingual affect-probe transfer Spearman/AUROC, per-language intensity/valence shift and its norm/distance regression, mid-appraisal-similarity vs output-disagreement (gain) decomposition, gain-vs-distance correlation, patch-localized gain layer, causal steering intensity-shift rate, emotion-category and content preservation, neutral-control resistance, general-QA retention, comparison to human per-language ratings.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Emotional-intensity 'ground truth' varies genuinely across cultures; we avoid claiming a single correct value and instead use human per-language ratings descriptively as norms, restrict scored items to vignettes with clear emotion categories, and use the neutral control to anchor. 2) Instruction-tuned models may hedge or compress ratings; we use both verbalized ratings and log-probability-based intensity scores and report scale-usage per language. 3) The shared mid-layer appraisal might itself differ by language for some items (no shared axis); this is an informative outcome and we quantify per-item how much disagreement is mid-appraisal vs gain rather than assuming the split. 4) Probe transfer could be confounded by latent English pivoting; we report per-language transfer, compare to per-language-trained probes, and include non-English source-language probes. 5) Effects could be driven by surface affective lexicon rather than a deep appraisal; matched-content parallel vignettes, the mid-appraisal-predicts-behavior link, and content-preserving steering guard against this. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Causal steering may harm fluency or shift the emotion category rather than only intensity; we report emotion-category and content preservation, output fidelity, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the reverse-consistency test to ensure a genuine gain dial. 8) A single affect-gain direction may be an oversimplification across emotions/valence; we test low-rank subspaces and per-emotion directions and report where a scalar dial is insufficient. 9) Distinguishing from my moral-valence proposal is essential; here the object is descriptive emotional intensity/valence of a situation, not normative moral acceptability, and from behavioral affective-stability work (Lia & Dipta 2026) by providing the internal, mechanistic, causal account they explicitly lack.

Name: crosslingual_homograph_concept_binding
Title: Same Spelling, Different World: Do Cross-Lingual Homographs Force Multilingual Models to Bind One Concept Across Two Languages, and Can the Wrong Binding Be Steered?
Short Hypothesis: Cross-lingual homographs—word forms that are identical in surface but denote unrelated concepts in two languages (e.g., 'gift' = present in English / poison in German, 'pan' = bread in Spanish / pot in Japanese romaji, 'brat' = child in Russian transliteration / sibling in English slang)—force a multilingual LLM to decide which language 'owns' the form for retrieving the associated concept, and by DEFAULT the model binds an out-of-context homograph to the DOMINANT (usually higher-resource) language's concept, causing a predictable, script-preserving cross-lingual sense-intrusion error. We hypothesize (1) an out-of-context homograph's internal representation is displaced toward the dominant language's concept even when the sentential context is unambiguously the other language, producing factual/inferential errors that track resource asymmetry between the two languages; (2) there exists a shared middle-layer 'context-language' signal that should gate which concept is retrieved, and homograph intrusion occurs when this gate is overridden by a stronger dominant-language lexical pull; and (3) a small, localizable 'binding-language' signal can be causally steered to force the context-correct concept, repairing intrusion errors without changing the surface language.
Related Work: False friends / cross-lingual homographs are studied in bilingual psycholinguistics (interlingual homograph recognition costs) and in NLP mainly as a translation-quality or word-sense-disambiguation nuisance (false-friend detection, code-switch disambiguation) — all behavioral and monolingual-decoder-agnostic. My prior 'codeswitch_concept_binding' proposal studies which language owns a concept when a word is EXPLICITLY switched into another language; here the word is NOT switched — it is a homograph whose surface form is identical across languages, so the model must resolve ownership from CONTEXT alone with no orthographic cue, a fundamentally harder and cleaner binding test. My 'colexification' proposal concerns two concepts fused into one word WITHIN a language; homographs are the cross-language mirror (one form, two languages, two unrelated concepts). Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies homograph binding, dominant-language intrusion, or its causal repair. No prior work (i) tests whether out-of-context homographs are silently bound to the dominant language's concept, (ii) ties intrusion magnitude to resource asymmetry, or (iii) causally localizes and steers the binding-language signal to repair sense intrusion.
Abstract: Some word forms are spelled identically across languages but mean entirely different things—English 'gift' is a present, German 'Gift' is poison; and across scripts, transliterated forms collide constantly. When a multilingual model reads such a cross-lingual homograph, it must decide which language owns the form to retrieve the right concept, using only the surrounding context because the surface form gives no clue. We ask whether models resolve this correctly, and if not, why. We hypothesize that models default to binding an out-of-context homograph to the DOMINANT (higher-resource) language's concept, causing a predictable cross-lingual sense-intrusion error whose size tracks the resource asymmetry between the two languages. We build HomographBind, a set of minimal-pair sentences across 8 languages in which a cross-lingual homograph appears in a context that is unambiguously one language, with a probe whose correct answer depends on selecting the context-language concept and an intrusion distractor reflecting the other-language concept. Behaviorally we measure intrusion rate and test its dependence on resource asymmetry and typological/script distance. We probe for a shared context-language gate that should select the concept, and via activation and path patching we localize a 'binding-language' signal and test whether intrusion occurs when a dominant-language lexical pull overrides the gate. In a decisive causal test we steer the binding-language signal to force the context-correct concept, repairing intrusion errors and, in reverse, inducing them, while leaving the surface language unchanged. We relate intrusion to resource asymmetry and script distance, reframing false-friend errors as a measurable, steerable property of concept binding.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages forming homograph pairs both within-script (English-German, Spanish-Italian, English-Dutch) and cross-script via standard transliteration/romanization (English-Russian, English-Hindi, English-Japanese romaji, English-Turkish, English-Indonesian). Code per-pair resource asymmetry from URIEL/resource tiers and script identity. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (HomographBind): Curate ~300 cross-lingual homograph forms with two unrelated concepts (one per language), verified via bilingual dictionaries and native speakers. For each, build minimal-pair sentences where the CONTEXT is unambiguously language L (grammar, surrounding words) and the homograph must be read as L's concept, with a probe (cloze/MC/QA) whose correct answer requires L's concept and an INTRUSION distractor reflecting the other language's concept. Render the identical target form in both languages' contexts (both directions of each pair). Include CONTROLS: (a) non-homograph words matched for frequency (should show no intrusion), (b) UNAMBIGUOUS-language items where only one concept is plausible, to bound the effect. Native-verify all items; answers scored via language-agnostic normalized matching.
3) BEHAVIORAL INTRUSION TEST: For each (item, context-language) measure whether the model selects the context-correct concept vs the intrusion concept. KEY hypothesis: out-of-context homographs are bound to the DOMINANT language's concept, so intrusion is higher when the context language is the LOWER-resource member of the pair (the dominant-language concept intrudes). Mixed-effects logistic regression of intrusion on (resource asymmetry between context vs other language, script distance, context-language), item as random effect; test that resource asymmetry predicts intrusion beyond overall accuracy; compare against non-homograph and unambiguous controls (should show minimal intrusion). Report per-pair intrusion profiles and directional asymmetry (dominant-into-nondominant vs reverse).
4) SHARED CONTEXT-LANGUAGE GATE PROBE: At each layer pool the hidden state at the homograph position; train a linear probe to decode the CONTEXT language (which language the sentence is in) and, separately, which CONCEPT (context-language vs other-language) the representation is aligned to. Test whether the context-language is cleanly decodable (a gate exists) yet the concept representation is displaced toward the dominant language on intrusion items — i.e., the gate is present but overridden. Correlate per-item concept-displacement with behavioral intrusion (link test). Use logit-lens to identify when the wrong (intruding) concept overtakes the correct one across depth.
5) LOCALIZE BINDING-LANGUAGE COMPONENTS: Via activation/path patching between a correctly-bound run (homograph read as context-language concept) and an intrusion run of the SAME item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose patching flips which concept is retrieved. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs path patching. Test patching the context-language gate/concept representation FROM an unambiguous or correctly-bound run INTO an intrusion run.
6) CAUSAL BINDING STEERING (decisive): Derive a binding-language steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (context-correct-concept runs minus intrusion runs). Test (i) REPAIR: adding it to intrusion-prone items (esp. lower-resource context language) increases correct context-concept selection toward control levels; (ii) INDUCE: subtracting it makes the model bind homographs to the dominant-language concept even in clear context; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where resource asymmetry is greatest; (iv) it does NOT change the surface output language or content (fidelity check), does not harm the non-homograph/unambiguous controls, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: intrusion-repair rate, intrusion-induction rate (reverse), output-language fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering should only change homograph binding, not unrelated answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
7) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress intrusion and steering efficacy on resource asymmetry, script distance (within-script vs cross-script homographs), and URIEL distance; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; token-pooling (homographs may split into different subwords across languages — report sensitivity); robustness across templates and MC-vs-cloze-vs-free formats; whether a single binding vector generalizes across homograph pairs and languages.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-pair per-direction intrusion rate, resource-asymmetry and script-distance regression coefficients, dominant-into-nondominant directional asymmetry, context-language gate probe accuracy and concept-displacement, displacement-vs-intrusion correlation, wrong-concept overtaking depth, patch-localized binding layer, cross-lingual binding transplant repair rate, causal steering repair and induction rates, output fidelity, control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Cross-script homographs depend on transliteration conventions; the 'same form' may tokenize very differently across languages, weakening the collision; we test both within-script (clean) and cross-script (via standard romanization) pairs, report token-pooling sensitivity, and treat within-script pairs as the cleanest test. 2) Some models may resolve homographs from context robustly (no intrusion) — this is itself an informative, publishable finding about the strength of context-gating, and we quantify how often intrusion occurs via probe displacement and behavior. 3) Homograph concept ownership can be graded (near-cognates, partial overlap); we use bilingual-dictionary + native verification, restrict to unrelated-concept pairs, and analyze partial-overlap items separately. 4) Intrusion could be driven by surface frequency rather than a genuine binding decision; the frequency-matched non-homograph control, the concept-displacement-predicts-behavior link, and the cross-lingual binding transplant guard against this, and resource asymmetry is measured separately from raw frequency. 5) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 6) Causal steering may trade fluency or control accuracy; we report output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the reverse (induction) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure steering manipulates homograph binding rather than generically boosting accuracy. 7) The binding signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants and report where a scalar direction is insufficient. 8) Distinguishing from my prior code-switch-binding and colexification proposals is essential; here there is NO orthographic switch cue (identical surface form) and the two concepts belong to two DIFFERENT languages (not fused within one), making this a distinct, cleaner test of context-driven cross-lingual concept binding.

Name: crosslingual_processing_load_capacity_gating
Title: Does the Query Language Set a Cheaper Working-Memory Budget? A Shared Difficulty Estimate Gated by a Language-Dependent Processing-Load Threshold
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs compute a largely language-independent internal estimate of a problem's PROCESSING LOAD (how many entities/dependencies must be simultaneously held), but the query language causally sets the effective WORKING-MEMORY BUDGET applied to that estimate: for the SAME structurally-demanding problem, the model 'gives up' (collapses to a shortcut/heuristic answer) at a lower load in some languages (usually lower-resource/high-fertility) than in others, producing a cross-lingual capacity gap that is separable from knowledge and tokenization and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable load-gating signal without changing the problem content or surface language.
Related Work: Prior multilingual work treats cross-lingual gaps as accuracy scalars (MGSM) or ties them to tokenization fertility ('token tax', Lundin 2025) and knowledge/calibration (Zhou 2025). Monolingual work shows transformers degrade with structural complexity (center-embedding, long dependencies, many entities) and build working-memory-like state, but is English-only and does not ask whether query LANGUAGE modulates the effective capacity budget. My prior proposals cover representational-feature leakage, step-level error localization, computational-DEPTH allocation, running-state tracking, and abstention thresholds; NONE frame cross-lingual failure as a shared processing-LOAD estimate gated by a language-dependent WORKING-MEMORY BUDGET, dissociate that budget from tokenization and knowledge, or causally shift a load-gating signal to equalize the point at which the model abandons full computation. This differs from my depth-allocation proposal (vertical layer-commitment) because the object here is the horizontal STRUCTURAL LOAD a problem imposes (entity/dependency count) and the language-set threshold at which the model switches from full computation to a shortcut, and from the running-state proposal because it targets the general capacity-gating decision rather than tally maintenance specifically.
Abstract: The same reasoning problem can require holding one fact in mind or juggling many interacting constraints. Humans and models both degrade as this processing load grows, but for multilingual models a sharper question arises: does the query language set how much load the model is willing to carry before it abandons full computation and falls back on a shortcut? We hypothesize that models compute a largely language-independent internal estimate of a problem's processing load—the number of entities and dependencies that must be simultaneously tracked—but apply a query-language-dependent working-memory budget to it, so the SAME structurally-demanding item is solved carefully in some languages and answered heuristically in others once its load exceeds a lower, language-set threshold. This predicts a cross-lingual capacity gap dissociable from knowledge and tokenization. We build LoadProbe, parallel reasoning items across 10 typologically diverse languages with a controlled, graded number of entities/dependencies (multi-constraint scheduling, nested relative clauses, multi-entity relational chains), each with a full-computation-correct answer and a shortcut/heuristic distractor. Behaviorally we locate each language's 'collapse load' (the load at which shortcut answers take over) and test whether it is lower for lower-resource languages beyond tokenization and knowledge. We train a linear probe for the shared processing-load estimate and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the collapse gap into a shared load estimate versus a language-set budget. In a decisive causal test we localize and shift a load-gating signal to raise the collapse load in low-budget languages—recovering full-computation accuracy—while leaving problem content and surface language unchanged. We reframe multilingual reasoning gaps as a shared load estimate under a steerable, language-dependent capacity budget.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource/fertility-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (LoadProbe): ~500 reasoning items in families whose PROCESSING LOAD is parametrically controllable: (a) MULTI-CONSTRAINT SATISFACTION (assign items under N constraints, N=1..6), (b) NESTED RELATIVE-CLAUSE / dependency-tracking comprehension (embedding depth 1..4), (c) MULTI-ENTITY RELATIONAL CHAINS (track M entities/relations, M=2..6). Each item has a FULL-COMPUTATION-CORRECT answer and a SHORTCUT/HEURISTIC distractor (the answer a load-limited solver would give, e.g., satisfying only the most recent constraint, resolving to the nearest antecedent, or a first-mentioned-entity bias). Vary load level within each family; hold content/knowledge requirements minimal so failures reflect load not ignorance. Translate/native-verify into all 10 languages; record per-item tokenization fertility (tokens/word) and a per-language single-load control (N=1) to establish baseline ability. Answers scored via language-agnostic normalized matching.
3) BEHAVIORAL COLLAPSE-LOAD TEST: For each (item, language) record full-computation-correct vs shortcut-distractor selection as a function of load level. Define per-language COLLAPSE LOAD = the load at which shortcut answers overtake correct ones. KEY hypothesis: collapse load is LOWER (capacity budget smaller) for lower-resource/high-fertility languages on the SAME items. Mixed-effects logistic regression of shortcut-selection on (load level, language, tokenization fertility, single-load baseline ability, resource tier via URIEL), item as random effect; test that query language shifts the collapse point beyond fertility and baseline ability. Report per-language accuracy-vs-load curves and cross-lingual collapse-load gaps.
4) SHARED PROCESSING-LOAD PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode the item's processing load (entity/dependency count) on ENGLISH data and apply zero-shot to other languages; report R^2/accuracy as evidence of a language-independent load estimate. Compare to per-language-trained probes. Also test whether the model internally represents load SIMILARLY across languages for the same item (cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the load representation).
5) BUDGET-vs-ESTIMATE DECOMPOSITION: For matched items, compare the shared mid-layer load estimate across languages (should be similar if the estimate is shared) versus the emitted full-vs-shortcut decision (which diverges at different loads). Fit per-language a decision boundary on the shared load estimate and test whether cross-lingual collapse differences are explained by a shifted BUDGET (boundary on a similar estimate) rather than a different estimate. Correlate per-language budget with resource tier, fertility, and typological distance (Spearman). Anchor the mid vs decision split with per-layer language-ID probes.
6) LOCALIZE THE LOAD-GATING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that still computes fully and one that has collapsed to the shortcut on the SAME high-load item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips shortcut->full-computation. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching. Test patching the load-gating components from a high-budget language into a collapsed low-budget run.
7) CAUSAL BUDGET STEERING (decisive): Derive a load-gating steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (full-computation runs minus shortcut runs at matched high load). Test (i) RAISE-BUDGET: adding it to collapsed low-budget-language items increases full-computation-correct answers toward high-budget levels; (ii) LOWER-BUDGET: subtracting it induces premature shortcut answers in high-budget languages even at moderate load; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where the budget gap was largest; (iv) it changes ONLY the compute-vs-shortcut decision, not the underlying answer when full computation succeeds, nor the surface language (fidelity check), does not harm the single-load control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: collapse-load-gap closure, full-computation-accuracy recovery, shortcut-induction rate (reverse), output-language fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering should shift the collapse load but not change single-load or knowledge-only answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: family breakdown (constraints vs nesting vs relational chains); which shortcut heuristics dominate per language; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single budget vector generalizes across families and languages; robustness across templates and MC-vs-free formats; explicit dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched load and by showing the internal (content-invariant) steering recovers accuracy without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language accuracy-vs-load curves and collapse load, collapse-load regression controlling for fertility/knowledge/resource, cross-lingual load-probe transfer R^2/accuracy and representation similarity, estimate-similarity vs decision-divergence (budget) decomposition, budget-vs-resource/fertility/typology correlation, patch-localized load-gating layer, cross-lingual gating transplant repair rate, causal budget-steering gap closure and shortcut-induction rates, answer/content fidelity, single-load-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Constructing items whose difficulty is purely processing LOAD (not knowledge or lexical difficulty) is delicate; we use synthetic constraint/nesting/relational templates with minimal world knowledge, native-verify, and use the single-load (N=1) control to separate baseline ability from load capacity. 2) Collapse could be driven by tokenization fertility rather than an internal budget; the design controls for fertility in regression, compares high- vs low-fertility languages at matched load, and—crucially—the causal steering does not change tokenization yet recovers accuracy, dissociating budget from the token tax. 3) Some models/languages may show no capacity gap (uniform budget); this is itself an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often a collapse gap exists. 4) The budget-vs-estimate split could be confounded if the load estimate itself differs by language; we test this directly by comparing shared-probe estimates across languages rather than assuming the split. 5) Identifying the shortcut distractor as the load-limited answer requires that the heuristic be well-defined; we design each family so the shortcut is a documented, predictable load-limited strategy (recency-only constraint satisfaction, nearest-antecedent attachment, first-entity bias) and validate that human/small-model load-limited solvers produce it. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Budget steering may trade fluency or induce errors on easy items; we report control retention, output fidelity, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the reverse (shortcut-induction) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure the intervention manipulates the capacity budget rather than generically boosting accuracy. 8) The load-gating signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 9) Distinguishing from my depth-allocation and running-state proposals is essential; here the object is the horizontal STRUCTURAL LOAD a problem imposes and the language-set threshold at which the model abandons full computation for a shortcut, not vertical layer-commitment depth or numeric tally maintenance.

Name: crosslingual_negotiation_concession_gating
Title: Who Blinks First? A Shared Bargaining-Value Estimate Gated by a Language-Dependent Concession Threshold in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM acts as an agent in a negotiation or bargaining interaction, it computes a largely language-independent internal estimate of the current deal's VALUE and of the other party's stance, but the query/interaction language causally sets the CONCESSION THRESHOLD applied to that estimate: for the SAME bargaining state, the model is willing to concede (accept a worse offer, drop demands, defer) at a lower threshold in some languages—often lower-resource or higher-'indirectness/collectivist'-norm languages—than in others, producing a cross-lingual concession asymmetry that is separable from the underlying deal-value estimate and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable concession-gating signal without changing the described deal or surface language.
Related Work: LLM negotiation/bargaining is an emerging behavioral area (NegotiationArena; multi-agent bargaining benchmarks; game-theoretic LLM-agent studies) but these are monolingual/English and measure outcomes (surplus split, agreement rate), never asking whether the interaction LANGUAGE modulates concession behavior or providing any internal mechanism. Cross-cultural negotiation is a classic topic in behavioral economics/cross-cultural psychology (Hofstede individualism/collectivism, high/low-context communication and its documented effect on concession-making), but has not been tested as a mechanistic property of multilingual LLM agents. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for interactive decision policies. My prior proposals frame cross-lingual gaps as a shared estimate under a language-set gate for calibration (know/don't-know), abstention (attempt/abstain), and processing-load (compute/shortcut); NONE address INTERACTIVE STRATEGIC behavior—the concede-vs-hold decision in a negotiation—its language-set concession threshold, or its causal steering. This is distinct because the object is an agentic strategic policy over a bargaining state (not a factual answer, an abstention, or an internal compute budget), with direct implications for fairness and safety when LLM agents negotiate on users' behalf across languages.
Abstract: As LLMs increasingly act as agents that negotiate, schedule, and bargain on users' behalf, a fairness-critical question arises: does the interaction language change how readily the agent gives ground? We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal estimate of a bargaining state—the current deal's value and the counterpart's firmness—but applies a query-language-dependent concession threshold to it, so that for the SAME state the agent concedes (accepts a worse offer, drops a demand, defers) at a lower threshold in some languages than others. This predicts a cross-lingual concession asymmetry dissociable from the underlying value estimate. We build ConcedeProbe, a set of parallel single-turn and multi-turn bargaining scenarios (price haggling, resource splits, scheduling, dispute resolution) rendered across 10 typologically and culturally diverse languages, each presenting a controlled deal state with a concede action and a hold action whose optimal choice is fixed by the state. Behaviorally we locate each language's concession threshold and test whether it shifts with the interaction language beyond deal value and resource level, and whether it tracks documented cultural communication norms. We train a linear probe for the shared deal-value estimate and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the concession gap into a shared value estimate versus a language-set threshold. In a decisive causal test we localize and shift a concession-gating signal to equalize the concede-vs-hold point across languages while leaving the described deal and surface language unchanged, and reverse-steer to induce over- or under-conceding. We reframe cross-lingual negotiation disparity as a shared valuation under a steerable, language-dependent concession gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/culturally/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili), coded for documented cultural communication norms (Hofstede individualism/collectivism, Hall high/low-context) plus URIEL typological/resource distance, treated as graded predictors.
2) DATASET (ConcedeProbe): ~500 bargaining scenarios in four families—(a) PRICE HAGGLING (a counter-offer is on the table; concede = accept, hold = counter/reject), (b) RESOURCE SPLIT (accept an uneven split vs insist on fair), (c) SCHEDULING (defer to the other party's slot vs hold your constraint), (d) DISPUTE RESOLUTION (drop a demand vs maintain). Each scenario fixes a controlled deal STATE (a scalar 'deal value' / reservation-price gap) so the value-optimal action is known, with a CONCEDE action and a HOLD action. Vary the state across a graded range so a concession threshold can be located per language. Include multi-turn variants where the counterpart escalates/softens. Keep the described numbers/facts identical across languages; the agent is instructed to bargain on the user's behalf for the user's benefit (so conceding when the state favors holding is a genuine loss). Translate/native-verify into all 10 languages; record tokenization fertility and a per-language single-clear-state control (state strongly favors holding) to establish baseline policy competence. Score actions via a language-agnostic concede/hold classifier validated against human labels.
3) BEHAVIORAL CONCESSION-ASYMMETRY TEST: For each (scenario, language) record concede vs hold as a function of deal state; define per-language CONCESSION THRESHOLD = the state at which the agent switches to conceding. KEY hypothesis: the threshold shifts with interaction language on the SAME state (some languages concede earlier), beyond deal value, fertility, and baseline competence. Mixed-effects logistic regression of concede on (deal state, language, tokenization fertility, single-clear-state baseline, resource tier via URIEL, cultural-norm codes), scenario as random effect; test the language effect and its correlation with cultural communication norms. Report per-language concede-vs-state curves and cross-lingual threshold gaps; compare against the clear-state control (should be language-flat).
4) SHARED DEAL-VALUE PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-decision position; train a linear probe to decode the deal state / value-to-the-user on ENGLISH data and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report R^2/AUROC as evidence of a language-independent value estimate. Compare to per-language-trained probes; measure cross-lingual representation similarity (CKA/cosine) of the value estimate for the same scenario.
5) THRESHOLD-vs-ESTIMATE DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer value estimate across languages (should be similar if shared) versus the emitted concede/hold decision (which switches at different states). Fit per-language a decision boundary on the shared estimate; test whether cross-lingual concession differences are explained by a shifted THRESHOLD rather than a different estimate. Correlate per-language threshold with cultural norms, resource tier, and typological distance (Spearman). Anchor the mid-vs-decision split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE CONCESSION-GATING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that holds and one that concedes on the SAME matched state, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips concede<->hold WITHOUT changing the decoded deal value. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching. Test patching the gating components from a firm (hold-prone) language into an over-conceding run.
7) CAUSAL THRESHOLD STEERING (decisive): Derive a concession-gating steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (hold runs minus concede runs at matched state). Test (i) RAISE-THRESHOLD (more firm): adding it to over-conceding languages makes the agent hold on states where holding is value-optimal, closing the gap toward a reference; (ii) LOWER-THRESHOLD (more conceding): subtracting it induces premature concession in firm languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where the gap was largest; (iv) it changes ONLY the concede/hold decision, not the decoded deal value or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the clear-state control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: threshold-gap closure, value-optimal-action recovery, over-concession-induction rate (reverse), output-language fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts the concession threshold but not deal-value readout or unrelated answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: family breakdown (price vs split vs scheduling vs dispute); single-turn vs multi-turn; whether the asymmetry tracks collectivism/high-context norms; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single gating vector generalizes across families and languages; robustness across templates and framings (agent-for-user vs neutral arbiter); explicit dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched state and by showing content-invariant steering recovers value-optimal behavior without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language concede-vs-state curves and concession threshold, threshold regression controlling for value/fertility/competence/resource with cultural-norm correlation, cross-lingual value-probe transfer R^2/AUROC and representation similarity, estimate-similarity vs decision-divergence (threshold) decomposition, threshold-vs-norm/resource/typology correlation, patch-localized gating layer, cross-lingual gating transplant repair rate, causal steering threshold-gap closure and over-concession-induction rates, value/content fidelity, clear-state-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Defining the value-optimal action requires a clean deal-state scalar; we use synthetic scenarios with explicit reservation-price gaps so the optimal concede/hold is unambiguous, and use the clear-state control to separate baseline policy competence from the language-set threshold. 2) Concession could be confounded by tokenization fertility or by genuine differences in how the scenario reads across languages; the design controls for fertility and holds numbers/facts fixed, compares high- vs low-fertility languages at matched state, and—crucially—the causal steering does not change tokenization yet recovers value-optimal behavior, dissociating the threshold from surface factors. 3) Some models/languages may show no concession asymmetry (uniform threshold); this is itself an informative, publishable fairness finding, and we quantify how often a gap exists. 4) The threshold-vs-estimate split could be confounded if the value estimate itself differs by language; we test this directly by comparing shared-probe estimates across languages rather than assuming the split. 5) Instruction-tuned models may refuse to 'bargain' or behave inconsistently; we use log-probability-based concede/hold scoring alongside generation, validate the action classifier against human labels, and report refusal rates. 6) Cultural-norm coding (Hofstede/Hall) is coarse and debated; we treat it as a graded predictor, report sensitivity to alternative codings, and note that a threshold effect is establishable even if its cultural correlate is weak. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Steering may trade firmness for cooperativeness or harm fluency; we report both directions (firmness recovery AND over-concession induction), value/content fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use reverse-consistency to ensure a genuine threshold dial. 9) The gating signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Misuse concern: concession steering could be abused to make agents exploitable or exploitative; we frame and use it strictly as an interpretability/fairness diagnostic on benign bargaining scenarios and report retention rather than deploying it. 11) Distinguishing from my calibration/abstention/processing-load proposals is essential; here the object is an INTERACTIVE STRATEGIC concede-vs-hold policy over a bargaining state, not a factual answer, an attempt/abstain gate, or an internal compute budget.

Name: crosslingual_numerical_precision_gating
Title: About Two Hundred or 203.4? A Shared Magnitude Estimate Gated by a Language-Dependent Numerical-Precision Threshold in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM produces a numerical answer, it computes a largely language-independent internal magnitude, but the query language causally sets the PRECISION/ROUNDING GRANULARITY at which that magnitude is reported: for the SAME quantity the model rounds more aggressively (reports coarser, more approximate numbers) in some languages—often lower-resource/high-fertility ones—than in others, producing a cross-lingual precision gap that is separable from the underlying magnitude and from arithmetic error, and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable precision-gating signal without changing the computed value or surface language. This matters most in safety-critical domains (clinical dosing, financial figures) where silent over-rounding is dangerous.
Related Work: Multilingual math is studied only behaviorally at the benchmark level (MGSM; MathMist 2025), reporting per-language accuracy and noting numerical-precision deficits in low-resource languages but never asking whether the GRANULARITY of a reported number is language-modulated, nor providing any mechanism. My prior number-naming proposal concerned the geometric distortion of a SINGLE spelled number's magnitude; the running-state proposal concerned dynamic tally maintenance; the measurement-units proposal concerned the assumed unit SYSTEM. NONE address numerical PRECISION/ROUNDING granularity—how many significant figures the model volunteers—as a language-set default, nor tie it to a shared magnitude estimate gated by a language-dependent precision threshold, nor causally localize/steer such a threshold, nor transfer it into safety-critical dosing. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but not for numerical precision. My calibration/abstention/processing-load proposals share the shared-estimate-plus-language-gate template but target confidence, attempt-vs-abstain, and compute budget respectively; the object here is a distinct behavior—the reported precision/rounding of a numeric answer—with distinct safety stakes.
Abstract: The same quantity can be reported as 'about 200' or as '203.4', and the difference matters: in a recipe it is trivial, in a drug dose it can be fatal. We ask whether a multilingual language model chooses this numerical precision independently of the query language, or whether the language silently sets how aggressively the model rounds. We hypothesize that models compute a largely language-independent internal magnitude but apply a query-language-dependent precision threshold, so that for the SAME quantity they report coarser, more approximate numbers in some languages than in others. This predicts a cross-lingual precision gap dissociable from the underlying magnitude and from arithmetic accuracy. We build PrecisionProbe, parallel numerical-answer items across 10 typologically and resource-diverse languages—arithmetic with non-round results, unit conversions, statistics, and a safety-critical clinical-dosing stratum—where a precise answer is available and the correct granularity is fixed by context. Behaviorally we measure per-language reported significant figures / rounding aggressiveness on identical quantities and test whether it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond arithmetic error. We train a linear probe for the shared magnitude estimate and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the precision gap into a shared magnitude versus a language-set granularity threshold. In a decisive causal test we localize and shift a precision-gating signal to equalize granularity across languages—making the model report the context-appropriate precision consistently—while leaving the computed value and surface language unchanged, and reverse-steer to induce over- or under-rounding. We reframe multilingual numerical inconsistency as a shared magnitude under a steerable, language-dependent precision gate, with direct safety implications.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource/fertility-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (PrecisionProbe): ~500 items in four strata whose EXACT answer is non-round so reported granularity is observable: (a) ARITHMETIC with non-round results (e.g., 1234/7, compound percentages), (b) UNIT CONVERSION producing many decimals (e.g., miles->km, lb->kg), (c) STATISTICS (mean/std of a small list), (d) SAFETY-CRITICAL CLINICAL DOSING (weight-based drug dose, e.g., 'mg = 12 mg/kg x 27.3 kg', where the exact value matters and over-rounding is dangerous). Each item has the exact value and a context-appropriate required precision; keep numbers/facts identical across languages. Translate/native-verify into all 10 languages; record tokenization fertility and a per-language exact-answer control (explicitly ask 'to N decimals') to establish that the model CAN produce the precise value when forced. Score reported precision via significant-figures / rounding-error metrics on the model's free-form answer.
3) BEHAVIORAL PRECISION-GAP TEST: For each (item, language) measure reported significant figures and rounding aggressiveness (deviation from the exact value attributable to rounding, not arithmetic error). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME quantity the model rounds more coarsely in lower-resource/high-fertility languages. Mixed-effects regression of reported-precision on (language, tokenization fertility, arithmetic-correctness indicator, resource tier via URIEL, stratum), item as random effect; test the language effect beyond fertility and arithmetic error; the forced-precision control should be language-flat. Report per-language precision profiles, cross-lingual disagreement on identical quantities, and dosing-stratum over-rounding rates.
4) SHARED MAGNITUDE PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the answer position; train a linear probe to decode the exact magnitude (regress to log-value) on ENGLISH data and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report R^2/MAE as evidence of a language-independent magnitude estimate, and cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the magnitude representation for the same item. Show the precise magnitude is internally present even when the emitted answer is coarsely rounded.
5) THRESHOLD-vs-ESTIMATE DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer magnitude estimate across languages (should be similar) versus the emitted precision (which diverges). Define GRANULARITY THRESHOLD per language; test whether cross-lingual precision differences are explained by a shifted threshold on a similar magnitude rather than a different magnitude. Correlate per-language threshold with resource tier, fertility, and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split via per-layer language-ID probes.
6) LOCALIZE THE PRECISION-GATING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a fine-precision language run and a coarse-rounding run on the SAME item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer changes reported precision WITHOUT changing the decoded magnitude. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gating components from a fine-precision language into a coarse run.
7) CAUSAL PRECISION STEERING (decisive): Derive a precision-gating steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (fine-precision runs minus coarse-rounding runs at matched magnitude). Test (i) SHARPEN: adding it to over-rounding languages (esp. on the dosing stratum) yields context-appropriate precise answers toward a reference; (ii) COARSEN: subtracting it induces over-rounding in fine-precision languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where the gap was largest; (iv) it changes ONLY reported precision, not the underlying value (fidelity: rounded and steered answers agree at the shared magnitude) nor the surface language, does not harm the forced-precision control, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: precision-gap closure, dosing over-rounding reduction, over-rounding-induction rate (reverse), value/output-language fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts granularity but not the computed magnitude or unrelated answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: stratum breakdown (arithmetic vs conversion vs stats vs dosing); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether one gating vector generalizes across strata and languages; robustness across templates and free-vs-forced formats; explicit dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched magnitude and by showing content-invariant steering restores precision without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language reported-precision and rounding-error, precision-gap regression controlling for fertility/arithmetic/resource, cross-lingual magnitude-probe transfer R^2/MAE and representation similarity, estimate-similarity vs output-precision-divergence (threshold) decomposition, threshold-vs-resource/fertility/typology correlation, patch-localized precision-gating layer, cross-lingual gating transplant repair rate, causal steering precision-gap closure and over-rounding-induction rates, value/output fidelity, forced-precision-control and general-QA retention, dosing-stratum safety metrics.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Distinguishing intentional rounding from arithmetic error is essential; we use non-round exact answers, score rounding-error separately from arithmetic-error (via the arithmetic-correctness indicator and the forced-precision control that confirms the model CAN produce the precise value), and analyze only items where the magnitude is internally present. 2) Reported precision could be confounded by tokenization fertility (more digits = more tokens in some languages); the design controls for fertility, compares high- vs low-fertility languages at matched magnitude, and—crucially—the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet restores precision, dissociating the threshold from surface factors. 3) Some models/languages may show no precision gap (uniform granularity); this is itself an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often a gap exists. 4) The threshold-vs-estimate split could be confounded if the magnitude estimate itself differs by language; we test this directly by comparing shared-probe magnitudes across languages rather than assuming the split. 5) What counts as 'context-appropriate precision' can be graded; we use strata with a clear required precision (especially dosing, where clinical standards fix it) and analyze ambiguous items separately. 6) Free-form precision detection is noisy; we validate the significant-figures/rounding scorer against human labels and report reliability. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Steering may trade fluency or induce spurious precision; we report value fidelity (the reported number must still equal the shared magnitude), control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the reverse (over-rounding-induction) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine precision dial. 9) The gating signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Safety framing: the dosing stratum is used strictly as an interpretability/safety diagnostic (does the model silently over-round doses in some languages?), not as clinical advice; we report over-rounding rates as a risk signal and do not deploy the steering. 11) Distinguishing from my number-naming, running-state, and units proposals is essential; here number words, tallies, and unit systems are held fixed and we manipulate only the reported PRECISION/ROUNDING granularity of a numeric answer.

Name: crosslingual_timeline_reconstruction
Title: Before the Flashback: Do Multilingual Models Build a Shared Chronological Timeline, and Does Tense/Connective Typology Govern How Robustly They Reorder Events?
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM reads a narrative whose events are presented in a non-chronological SURFACE order (flashbacks, 'before/after' clauses, tense/aspect cues), it reconstructs a largely language-independent internal CHRONOLOGICAL timeline that orders the events by their true time of occurrence rather than their order of mention; the ROBUSTNESS of this reordering is systematically modulated by the query language's temporal-marking typology (obligatory grammatical tense vs tenseless/aspect-based systems; explicit vs sparse temporal connectives), producing predictable cross-lingual disagreement about which of two events happened first for the SAME narrative. We hypothesize (1) a shared middle-layer 'chronological-order' representation whose pairwise before/after readout transfers zero-shot across languages; (2) reordering robustness and before/after accuracy track temporal-marking typology and typological distance, and degrade as surface order diverges more from chronological order; and (3) a small, localizable 'temporal-order' signal that can be causally steered to flip the model's inferred order of two events (making it treat a later event as earlier) without changing the narrative content or surface language.
Related Work: Temporal reasoning in LLMs is studied behaviorally and monolingually: event-ordering and timeline-extraction benchmarks (e.g., TempEval, MCTACO, TORQUE, TimeQA) and recent temporal-reasoning evaluations measure whether models order events, but almost entirely in English and without any internal account. Multilingual temporal work is sparse and behavioral (cross-lingual temporal tagging/normalization). My prior 'temporal_knowledge_asymmetry' proposal concerns per-language STALENESS of stored world facts, and 'grammatical_aspect_completion' concerns whether a SINGLE event is completed vs ongoing; NEITHER addresses reconstructing the CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER of MULTIPLE events from a non-linear surface narrative, nor whether that timeline is a shared cross-lingual representation, nor whether tense/connective typology governs reordering robustness. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies a running event-timeline. No prior work (i) tests whether an LLM builds a language-independent chronological-order representation distinct from surface mention order, (ii) ties reordering robustness to temporal-marking typology and surface-vs-chronological divergence, or (iii) causally localizes and steers a temporal-order signal to flip inferred event order. This makes it the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of narrative timeline reconstruction.
Abstract: Stories rarely unfold in order: a flashback, a 'the day before' clause, or a past-perfect verb signals that an event happened earlier than the sentence that mentions it. Understanding such narratives requires silently reconstructing the true chronological order from cues that contradict the surface order of mention. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal timeline that orders events by when they occurred rather than when they are stated, and whether a language's temporal-marking grammar governs how robustly it does so. We build TimelineProbe, parallel micro-narratives across 8 typologically diverse languages spanning obligatory-tense, aspect-based/tenseless, and connective-rich vs connective-sparse systems, in which two or more events are presented in a controlled surface order that diverges from their chronological order by cues (tense/aspect, temporal adverbials, 'before/after' connectives), each with a before/after probe whose correct answer follows chronology, not mention order. Behaviorally we measure before/after accuracy per language and test whether errors track temporal-marking typology and grow as surface order diverges more from chronology. We train a linear probe to decode the chronological relation between two events from hidden states and test whether it is shared and transfers zero-shot across languages, and whether the same narrative maps to the same internal order regardless of language. Via activation and path patching we localize a temporal-order signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to flip the model's inferred order of two events—making it treat a later event as earlier—while leaving the narrative and surface language unchanged. We relate reordering robustness to temporal-marking typology and typological distance, reframing timeline reconstruction as a measurable, steerable property of multilingual models.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 languages spanning temporal-marking typology: obligatory grammatical tense with rich connectives (English, Spanish, Russian, German), aspect-prominent/tense-reduced systems (Chinese [largely tenseless, aspect-marked], Japanese), and languages with distinct temporal-connective/relative-tense patterns (Turkish, Hindi). Code each language's temporal-marking profile (grammatical tense obligatoriness, aspect prominence, connective richness) from typological references (Comrie 'Tense'; WALS tense/aspect chapters) plus URIEL for typological distance; treat these as graded predictors. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (TimelineProbe): ~500 micro-narratives, each describing 2-4 events with a KNOWN ground-truth chronological order, rendered in a controlled SURFACE order that may match or diverge from chronology via cues: (a) tense/aspect (e.g., past-perfect 'had done' signals an earlier event mentioned later), (b) explicit temporal adverbials ('the day before', 'earlier that morning'), (c) 'before/after' connectives that invert mention order ('B happened, but only after A'). Vary the SURFACE-CHRONOLOGY DIVERGENCE (number of inversions / Kendall-tau distance between mention order and true order) as a graded factor. Probe: a before/after question ('Which happened first, A or B?') whose correct answer follows chronology, with a MENTION-ORDER distractor (the answer a surface-order heuristic gives). Include a CHRONOLOGICAL-CONTROL stratum where surface order equals true order (no reordering needed) to bound the effect. Translate/native-verify into all 8 languages, realizing temporal cues naturally with each language's tense/aspect/connective grammar; flag items where a cue has no natural equivalent. Answers scored via language-agnostic normalized matching.
3) BEHAVIORAL LEAKAGE TEST: For each (narrative, language) record whether the model gives the chronology-correct order vs the mention-order distractor. KEY hypothesis: aspect-prominent/tense-reduced and connective-sparse languages show more mention-order errors (weaker reordering) on the SAME narrative than obligatory-tense/connective-rich languages, and errors grow with surface-chronology divergence. Mixed-effects logistic regression of error on (temporal-marking typology, surface-chronology divergence, language, resource tier via URIEL), narrative as random effect; test typology and divergence coefficients beyond resource level; compare against the CHRONOLOGICAL-CONTROL (should be language-flat and near-ceiling). Report per-language accuracy-vs-divergence curves and cross-lingual disagreement on identical narratives.
4) SHARED CHRONOLOGICAL-ORDER REPRESENTATION & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-answer/event positions; train a linear probe to decode the CHRONOLOGICAL relation (A-before-B vs B-before-A) for an event pair on ENGLISH data and apply zero-shot to other languages; report AUROC/F1 transfer as evidence of a language-independent chronological-order representation that is distinct from surface mention order (control probe: decode MENTION order and show the two probes dissociate). Compare to per-language-trained probes to bound shared-vs-specific. CRITICAL invariance test: measure representational similarity (cosine/CKA) of the chronological-order state for the SAME narrative across languages; test whether invariance is higher for obligatory-tense languages.
5) DEPTH & TYPOLOGY ANALYSIS: Use logit-lens to identify when the chronological (vs mention-order) answer becomes decodable across depth (reorder-decision depth). Correlate reorder-decision depth and probe-decoded order with behavioral before/after accuracy within/across languages (link test), and correlate reordering robustness (probe confidence, cross-lingual invariance) with temporal-marking typology and URIEL distance (Spearman).
6) LOCALIZE TEMPORAL-ORDER COMPONENTS: Via activation/path patching between a run that answers chronologically and a run that answers by mention order on the SAME narrative (induced via different cue strengths or different languages), sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose patching flips the inferred order (read out by the chronological-order probe and the emitted answer). Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs path patching. Also test patching the chronological-order representation FROM an obligatory-tense language's run INTO a failing tense-reduced run to see if it repairs before/after accuracy.
7) CAUSAL TEMPORAL-ORDER STEERING (decisive): Derive a temporal-order steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (A-before-B runs minus B-before-A runs, matched content). Test (i) FLIP: adding/subtracting it makes the model treat a later event as earlier (and vice versa) on held-out narratives, as verified by the before/after answer; (ii) REPAIR: steering toward the correct chronological direction reduces mention-order errors in tense-reduced/connective-sparse languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually and can OVERRIDE the narrative's actual order cues; (iv) it changes ONLY the inferred event order, not the narrative content or surface output language (fidelity check), does not move the CHRONOLOGICAL-CONTROL answers, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: order-flip rate, mention-order-error reduction, output-language fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering should change before/after judgments but not content-only or single-event answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress reordering robustness and steering efficacy on temporal-marking typology, surface-chronology divergence, and URIEL distance; cue-type breakdown (tense/aspect vs adverbial vs connective); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; token-pooling; robustness across templates and MC-vs-cloze-vs-free formats; whether a single temporal-order vector generalizes across narratives and languages; whether the chronological-order representation is ordinal for 3-4 event chains (transitive consistency of decoded order).
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-(language) before/after accuracy and accuracy-vs-divergence curves, temporal-marking-typology and divergence regression coefficients, cross-lingual disagreement, shared chronological-order probe transfer AUROC/F1 and its dissociation from a mention-order probe, cross-lingual order-representation invariance (CKA/cosine), reorder-decision depth, internal-vs-behavior correlation, robustness-vs-typology correlation, patch-localized temporal-order layer, cross-lingual order transplant repair rate, causal steering order-flip and mention-order-error-reduction rates, output fidelity, chronological-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Realizing non-chronological narratives naturally and equivalently across languages is delicate, especially in tense-reduced languages (Chinese/Japanese) that rely on aspect/adverbials rather than grammatical tense; we native-verify naturalness, treat temporal-marking as a graded predictor, flag cues with no natural equivalent, and rely on the CHRONOLOGICAL-CONTROL and identical event content to isolate the reordering effect. 2) Some models may reconstruct chronology robustly in all languages (clean shared timeline) or default to mention order everywhere—either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often reordering fails via probe transfer and behavior. 3) Before/after answers can be genuinely ambiguous for simultaneous or ill-specified events; we restrict scored items to narratives with an unambiguous ground-truth order (native-verified) and analyze ambiguous ones separately. 4) The chronological-order probe could latch onto surface tense/adverbial tokens rather than an abstract timeline; the explicit dissociation from a mention-order probe, the cross-lingual invariance test, the internal-predicts-behavior link, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 5) Confound with training frequency of complex temporal constructions in lower-resource languages; we control with URIEL resource tiers and use the chronological-control (surface=true order) as a frequency-neutral within-item baseline. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Causal steering may trade fluency or control accuracy; we report output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the flip (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure steering manipulates event order rather than generically boosting accuracy. 8) The temporal-order signal may be low-rank or pairwise rather than a single global-timeline direction; we test low-rank subspace and per-pair variants, and probe transitive consistency for 3-4 event chains, reporting where a scalar direction is insufficient. 9) Distinguishing from my temporal-staleness and aspect-completion proposals is essential; here content is fixed and multiple events are present—we manipulate only the reconstructed CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER of events from a non-linear surface narrative, not stored factual recency or single-event completion.

Name: crosslingual_presupposition_accommodation_gating
Title: Taking It For Granted Across Languages: Whether Definiteness/Factivity Typology Governs How Silently Multilingual Models Accommodate (False) Presuppositions
Short Hypothesis: When a question or statement carries a PRESUPPOSITION (e.g., 'When did the king of France stop smoking?' presupposes a king of France exists and that he smoked), a multilingual LLM must decide whether to ACCOMMODATE it (silently accept it as background truth) or CHALLENGE it (flag the false presupposition). We hypothesize the model computes a largely language-independent internal representation of a claim's presupposed content, but the query language's presupposition-triggering grammar—how obligatorily and strongly it marks definiteness, factive verbs, and change-of-state—causally sets an ACCOMMODATION THRESHOLD: for the SAME presupposition, the model silently swallows a FALSE presupposition (answering as if it were true) more readily in languages with strong obligatory triggers and less readily in languages with weaker/optional marking, producing predictable cross-lingual disagreement on whether a false presupposition is challenged. We further hypothesize (1) a shared middle-layer 'presupposition-truth-commitment' signal that transfers zero-shot across languages; (2) accommodation rate tracks trigger-strength typology and typological distance; and (3) a small, localizable 'accommodation-gate' signal that can be causally steered to make the model challenge a false presupposition (or, in reverse, swallow a true-but-flagged one) without changing the surface answer or language.
Related Work: Presupposition and accommodation are core to formal semantics/pragmatics (Karttunen; Heim; von Fintel's 'Hey, wait a minute' test for false presuppositions) and vary sharply cross-linguistically in how presuppositions are TRIGGERED (obligatory definite articles vs bare nouns; factive-verb inventories; change-of-state morphology). In NLP, presupposition work is monolingual/English and behavioral: NOPE and IMPPRES-style datasets test whether models detect presuppositions or fail on questions with false premises, and recent work shows LLMs often answer loaded questions instead of challenging them—but none study this CROSS-LINGUALLY, tie accommodation to a language's presupposition-trigger typology, or give any mechanism. Cross-lingual factual-consistency work (Qi 2023; Wang 2025 'Lost in Multilinguality'; Ai 2025) shows facts live in a shared concept space with language-specific decoding and that consistency varies by language family/script, but concerns asserted facts, not PRESUPPOSED content or its accommodation. My prior proposals cover typological leakage into polarity/negation, aspect, evidential source, hypotheticality/irrealis, genericity, and gating templates for calibration/abstention/processing-load/concession/precision—but NONE address PRESUPPOSITION ACCOMMODATION, the silent acceptance of (false) presupposed content, or its modulation by definiteness/factivity trigger typology. This is distinct from my irrealis proposal (which concerns separating actual from hypothetical worlds) and my abstention proposal (attempt-vs-abstain on answerability): here the object is whether backgrounded, presupposed content is silently committed to as true, and how a language's trigger grammar sets that commitment—the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of presupposition accommodation, with direct hallucination-safety stakes (silently answering false-premise questions).
Abstract: Language quietly smuggles in assumptions: asking 'When did you stop cheating?' presupposes you were cheating, whether or not you were. Understanding such utterances requires deciding whether to accommodate the presupposition as background truth or to challenge it when it is false. Languages trigger presuppositions very differently—some obligatorily mark definiteness and factivity through articles, factive verbs, and change-of-state morphology, others leave these weak or optional. We ask whether a multilingual LLM represents presupposed content in a language-independent way, and whether a language's presupposition-triggering grammar governs how silently it accommodates (false) presuppositions, with direct implications for hallucination on loaded, false-premise questions. We build PresupProbe, parallel items across 8 typologically diverse languages, each pairing a statement or question carrying a presupposition—crossed with whether that presupposition is TRUE or FALSE—with a challenge-or-accommodate probe, spanning definiteness (existence), factive-verb (factivity), and change-of-state triggers. Behaviorally we measure how often the model silently accommodates a FALSE presupposition (answering as if true) versus challenging it, and test whether this tracks trigger-strength typology on the same underlying content. We train a linear probe to decode a claim's presupposed-truth commitment and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose cross-lingual accommodation differences into a shared commitment estimate versus a language-set accommodation threshold. Via activation and path patching we localize an accommodation-gate signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model challenge a false presupposition (or, in reverse, swallow a flagged one) while leaving the surface answer and language unchanged. We reframe multilingual over-accommodation of false presuppositions as a shared commitment under a steerable, language-dependent gate.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 languages spanning presupposition-trigger typology: strong obligatory definiteness/factivity marking (English, German, Spanish, Russian with rich definite/factive systems) versus weak/optional or article-less systems (Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Hindi—articleless or with different definiteness/factivity marking), coded for trigger strength (obligatory definite article presence, factive-verb inventory, change-of-state morphology) from typological references (WALS definite-article and related chapters; factivity literature) plus URIEL for typological distance; treat trigger strength as a graded per-trigger-type predictor. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (PresupProbe): ~500 items in three trigger strata—(A) DEFINITENESS/EXISTENCE ('the king of France', 'the CEO of <nonexistent company>'), (B) FACTIVE VERBS ('regret that X', 'know that X', which presuppose X), (C) CHANGE-OF-STATE ('stopped/continued doing X', presupposing prior X). Each base content is realized in a form carrying the presupposition, CROSSED with a TRUTH factor: the presupposition is either TRUE (verifiable, holds) or FALSE (the presupposed entity/fact does not hold), giving a 2x within-item design.
