Probes: (i) a CHALLENGE-OR-ANSWER probe (a loaded question whose felicitous response for a FALSE presupposition is to challenge it, e.g. 'When did the king of France stop smoking?' -> correct: 'there is no king of France'); (ii) a direct PRESUPPOSITION-TRUTH probe ('Does this sentence assume there is a king of France? Is that assumption true?'). Include a NO-PRESUPPOSITION control (matched content with the trigger removed / asserted openly) to bound the effect. Translate/native-verify all items into 8 languages, realizing each trigger naturally with each language's grammar (obligatory article/factive/change-of-state where required, closest natural equivalent elsewhere); flag items where a trigger has no natural equivalent. Score challenge-vs-accommodate via a validated classifier plus native checks; short scoreable answers where possible.
3) BEHAVIORAL LEAKAGE TEST: For FALSE-presupposition items, measure the ACCOMMODATION RATE = fraction where the model answers as if the presupposition were true instead of challenging it. KEY hypothesis: on the SAME false presupposition, strong-trigger languages accommodate (silently swallow) more than weak/optional-trigger languages, and trigger strength predicts accommodation beyond resource level. Mixed-effects logistic regression of accommodation on (trigger strength, trigger type, truth factor, language, resource tier via URIEL), item as random effect; test the trigger-strength coefficient and trigger x truth interaction; compare against the NO-PRESUPPOSITION control (open assertions should be challenged uniformly). Report per-language accommodation profiles, cross-lingual disagreement on identical false presuppositions, and per-trigger-type breakdown.
4) SHARED PRESUPPOSITION-COMMITMENT PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the answer/claim position; train a linear probe to decode (i) whether the sentence carries a presupposition and (ii) the presupposed-truth commitment (is the presupposed content being treated as true) on ENGLISH data, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC/F1 transfer as evidence of a language-independent presupposition-commitment representation. Compare to per-language-trained probes to bound shared-vs-specific. CRITICAL invariance test: measure representational similarity (cosine/CKA) of the presupposed-content state for the SAME presupposition across languages.
5) THRESHOLD-vs-ESTIMATE DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer commitment estimate across languages (should be similar if the representation is shared) versus the emitted challenge/accommodate decision (which diverges). Define an ACCOMMODATION THRESHOLD per language on the shared commitment axis; test whether cross-lingual accommodation differences are explained by a shifted threshold rather than a different estimate, and correlate the threshold with trigger strength, resource tier, and typological distance (Spearman). Use per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens to anchor where the shared estimate gives way to the language-specific decision.
6) LOCALIZE THE ACCOMMODATION-GATE: Via activation and path patching between a language that challenges and one that accommodates the SAME false presupposition, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips challenge<->accommodate WITHOUT changing the decoded presupposed content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching. Test patching the gate components from a challenging (weak-trigger) language into an accommodating run.
7) CAUSAL ACCOMMODATION STEERING (decisive): Derive an accommodation-gate steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (challenge runs minus accommodate runs on matched false-presupposition items). Test (i) CHALLENGE: adding it to over-accommodating (strong-trigger) languages makes the model flag false presuppositions toward a reference level (reducing false-premise hallucination); (ii) ACCOMMODATE: subtracting it makes weak-trigger languages silently swallow false presuppositions; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where accommodation was highest; (iv) it changes ONLY the challenge/accommodate behavior, not the decoded presupposed content or surface language (fidelity check), does not move the NO-PRESUPPOSITION control or the TRUE-presupposition items (which should still be accommodated correctly), and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: false-premise-accommodation reduction, accommodation-induction rate (reverse), true-presupposition retention, output-language fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering should change accommodation of presupposed content but not unrelated factual answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress accommodation and steering efficacy on trigger strength, trigger type, and URIEL distance; definiteness vs factive vs change-of-state breakdown; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; token-pooling; robustness across templates and MC-vs-free formats; whether a single accommodation-gate vector generalizes across trigger types and languages; whether accommodation on FALSE presuppositions predicts hallucination on standard false-premise QA benchmarks per language.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-(language,trigger,truth) accommodation/challenge rate, trigger-strength x truth interaction, cross-lingual disagreement, shared presupposition-commitment probe transfer AUROC/F1, cross-lingual commitment invariance (CKA/cosine), estimate-similarity vs decision-divergence (threshold) decomposition, threshold-vs-trigger/resource/typology correlation, patch-localized accommodation-gate layer, cross-lingual gate transplant repair rate, causal steering false-premise-challenge and accommodation-induction rates, true-presupposition and control retention, output fidelity, general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Realizing presupposition triggers naturally and equivalently across languages is delicate—articleless languages (Chinese/Japanese/Turkish) mark definiteness differently, and factive/change-of-state inventories differ; we native-verify naturalness, treat trigger strength as a graded per-type predictor, flag triggers with no natural equivalent, and rely on the NO-PRESUPPOSITION control and identical content to isolate the effect. 2) Some models may challenge false presuppositions robustly in all languages (no over-accommodation) or accommodate uniformly—either is an informative, publishable finding about presupposition-safety, and we quantify how often accommodation occurs via probe transfer and behavior. 3) Whether challenging a presupposition is 'correct' can be pragmatically graded (some false presuppositions are cooperatively repaired implicitly); we restrict scored items to clear false-existence/false-factive cases (drawing on validated presupposition stimuli) and analyze borderline ones separately, using von Fintel-style challenge as the felicity criterion. 4) Instruction-tuned models may refuse or hedge; we use both generation and log-probability-based challenge/accommodate scoring, validate the classifier against human labels, and report refusal rates. 5) The threshold-vs-estimate split could be confounded if the presupposition-commitment estimate itself differs by language; we test this directly by comparing shared-probe estimates across languages rather than assuming the split. 6) Accommodation could be driven by surface trigger tokens rather than a deep commitment representation; the cross-lingual invariance test, the internal-commitment-predicts-behavior link, and the cross-lingual gate transplant guard against this. 7) Confound with training frequency of trigger constructions in lower-resource languages; we control with URIEL resource tiers and use the no-presupposition control as a frequency-neutral within-content baseline. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) Causal steering may trade fluency, over-challenge true presuppositions, or harm general QA; we report true-presupposition retention, output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the reverse (accommodation-induction) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure the intervention manipulates the accommodation gate rather than generically boosting skepticism or accuracy. 10) The gate signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my irrealis (world-separation) and abstention (answerability) proposals is essential; here the object is whether BACKGROUNDED, PRESUPPOSED content is silently committed to as true and how definiteness/factivity trigger grammar sets that commitment, not separating hypothetical worlds or deciding attempt-vs-abstain on answerability.

Name: crosslingual_parse_reanalysis_gating
Title: Down the Garden Path in Many Languages: Whether Word-Order-Flexibility Typology Governs How Robustly Multilingual Models Revise a Committed Parse
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM incrementally reads a temporarily-ambiguous sentence, it commits to an initial syntactic parse and, upon hitting disambiguating material, must REANALYZE it; it computes a largely language-independent internal 'parse-commitment' representation, but the query language's word-order-flexibility typology causally sets how strongly it commits and thus how robustly it revises: rigid-word-order languages (English) induce strong garden-path commitment and costly/failed reanalysis, while flexible/free-word-order or morphologically-rich languages (Turkish, Russian, Japanese) induce weaker commitment and easier revision, producing predictable cross-lingual disagreement on the final interpretation of the SAME structurally-ambiguous sentence. We further hypothesize (1) a shared middle-layer parse-commitment/reanalysis signal that transfers zero-shot across languages; (2) reanalysis robustness tracks word-order-flexibility typology and typological distance; and (3) a small, localizable 'reanalysis' signal that can be causally steered to force revision of a garden-path parse (or to lock in the wrong one) without changing the sentence content or surface language.
Related Work: Garden-path reanalysis in LLMs is studied MONOLINGUALLY and behaviorally: Cao & Schuler (2025) find larger models are WORSE at resolving complement-clause vs relative-clause ambiguity after disambiguation; classic parallelism/competition accounts (Clifton & Staub) and Mandarin garden-path work (Yang 2025, showing subtler-than-Indo-European effects consistent with flexible parsing) are human-psycholinguistic. Cross-lingual disambiguation work (Thamburaj & Ramesh 2026) is a behavioral decision-support pipeline over ambiguity, with no internal account. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS, and my prior proposals cover typological leakage into polarity, aspect, evidentiality, genericity, temporal ordering, argument reconstruction, etc.—but NONE address INCREMENTAL SYNTACTIC PARSE COMMITMENT and structural REANALYSIS, whether a garden-path recovery signal is a shared cross-lingual representation, whether word-order-flexibility typology governs reanalysis robustness, or whether the reanalysis signal can be causally localized and steered. This is distinct from my temporal-ordering (event chronology) and argument-reconstruction (covert arguments) proposals: here the object is the model's committed SYNTACTIC STRUCTURE and its revision under disambiguation, grounded in word-order-flexibility typology and tested causally—turning the monolingual 'larger models are worse at reanalysis' finding into a cross-lingual, mechanistic, causal account.
Abstract: Readers routinely commit to a wrong syntactic analysis and must revise it: 'The horse raced past the barn fell' momentarily reads as a main clause before 'fell' forces reanalysis. Recovering from such garden paths is essential to comprehension, yet languages differ sharply in word-order rigidity—English fixes order and invites strong commitment, while morphologically rich, flexible-order languages (Turkish, Russian, Japanese) leave order underspecified and may commit more weakly. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent representation of its committed parse and of the reanalysis triggered by disambiguation, and whether a language's word-order-flexibility typology governs how robustly it revises. We build ReanalysisProbe, parallel temporarily-ambiguous sentences across 8 typologically diverse languages spanning rigid and flexible word order, covering main-clause/reduced-relative, complement/relative-clause, and attachment ambiguities, each with a comprehension probe whose correct answer requires successful reanalysis and a garden-path distractor reflecting the abandoned initial parse. Behaviorally we measure post-disambiguation comprehension per language and test whether reanalysis failure tracks word-order-flexibility typology on the same sentence. We train a linear probe to decode the committed parse from hidden states and test whether it is shared and transfers zero-shot across languages, and whether the same ambiguity maps to the same internal commitment. Via activation and path patching we localize a reanalysis signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to force revision of a garden-path parse (or lock in the abandoned one) while leaving the sentence and surface language unchanged. We relate reanalysis robustness to word-order flexibility and typological distance, reframing garden-path recovery as a measurable, steerable property of multilingual models.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 languages spanning word-order-flexibility typology: rigid (English, Chinese), moderately flexible (German, Spanish), and flexible/free-word-order or verb-final morphologically-rich (Russian, Turkish, Japanese, Hindi), coded for word-order flexibility and case/morphology richness from typological references (WALS word-order and morphology chapters) plus URIEL for typological distance; treat flexibility as a graded predictor. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (ReanalysisProbe): ~500 temporarily-ambiguous sentences in three families whose disambiguating region forces reanalysis: (A) MAIN-CLAUSE / REDUCED-RELATIVE ('The horse raced past the barn fell'), (B) COMPLEMENT-CLAUSE / RELATIVE-CLAUSE ambiguity (following Cao & Schuler), (C) ATTACHMENT ambiguity (PP/relative-clause high vs low attachment). Each item has a disambiguating continuation forcing the non-preferred parse, a comprehension probe whose correct answer requires the reanalyzed structure, and a GARDEN-PATH distractor reflecting the abandoned initial parse. Include an UNAMBIGUOUS control (same content, no garden path) to bound the effect. Adapt/translate each into all 8 languages with native verification, realizing the ambiguity and disambiguation naturally with each language's word order and morphology; flag items where no natural ambiguity exists in a language (for the transfer-limit analysis). Answers scored via language-agnostic normalized matching.
3) BEHAVIORAL LEAKAGE TEST: For each (sentence, language) record whether the model gives the reanalyzed-correct answer vs the garden-path distractor. KEY hypothesis: rigid-word-order languages show more reanalysis failures (more garden-path errors) on the SAME structural ambiguity than flexible-order languages, and word-order flexibility predicts reanalysis success beyond resource level. Mixed-effects logistic regression of reanalysis error on (word-order flexibility, ambiguity family, language, resource tier via URIEL), sentence as random effect; compare against the UNAMBIGUOUS control (should be language-flat, near-ceiling). Report per-language reanalysis-failure profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical ambiguities; also test the monolingual 'larger models worse at reanalysis' finding (Cao & Schuler) per language via model scale.
4) SHARED PARSE-COMMITMENT REPRESENTATION & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-disambiguation and post-disambiguation positions; train a linear probe to decode the CURRENTLY-COMMITTED parse (e.g., main-clause vs relative-clause reading) on ENGLISH data and apply zero-shot to other languages; report AUROC/F1 transfer as evidence of a language-independent parse-commitment representation. Compare to per-language-trained probes to bound shared-vs-specific. CRITICAL trajectory test: track the decoded parse ACROSS the disambiguating region to see whether/where the internal commitment flips from the initial to the reanalyzed parse (the reanalysis point), and whether this flip occurs more reliably in flexible-order languages. Measure cross-lingual similarity (CKA/cosine) of the commitment state for the SAME ambiguity.
5) DEPTH & TYPOLOGY ANALYSIS: Use logit-lens to identify the layer/token where the reanalyzed reading overtakes the initial reading (reanalysis depth). Correlate reanalysis depth and probe-decoded parse with behavioral comprehension within/across languages (link test), and correlate reanalysis robustness (whether the flip occurs, probe confidence) with word-order flexibility and URIEL distance (Spearman).
6) LOCALIZE REANALYSIS COMPONENTS: Via activation/path patching between a run that successfully reanalyzes and a run that stays garden-pathed on the SAME sentence (induced via different languages or ambiguity strengths), sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose patching flips the committed parse toward the reanalyzed reading. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs path patching. Test patching the reanalyzed-parse representation FROM a flexible-order language's run INTO a garden-pathed rigid-order run to see if it repairs comprehension.
7) CAUSAL REANALYSIS STEERING (decisive): Derive a reanalysis steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (successfully-reanalyzed runs minus garden-pathed runs, matched content). Test (i) FORCE REVISION: adding it to garden-pathed items (esp. rigid-order languages) increases correct reanalyzed answers toward flexible-order levels; (ii) LOCK-IN: subtracting it makes the model retain the abandoned initial parse even after disambiguation; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where reanalysis was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY the parse/interpretation, not the sentence content or surface output language (fidelity check), does not harm the UNAMBIGUOUS control, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: reanalysis-repair rate, garden-path-lock-in rate (reverse), output-language fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering should change garden-path comprehension but not unambiguous or content-only answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress reanalysis robustness and steering efficacy on word-order flexibility, morphology richness, and URIEL distance; ambiguity-family breakdown; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); model scale (test the larger-worse effect); probe layer/dimensionality; token-pooling; robustness across templates and MC-vs-cloze-vs-free formats; whether a single reanalysis vector generalizes across ambiguity families and languages.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-(language, family) reanalysis-correct vs garden-path rate, word-order-flexibility x family interaction, cross-lingual disagreement, shared parse-commitment probe transfer AUROC/F1, per-token parse trajectory and reanalysis flip point, cross-lingual commitment invariance (CKA/cosine), reanalysis depth, internal-vs-behavior correlation, robustness-vs-typology correlation, patch-localized reanalysis layer, cross-lingual parse transplant repair rate, causal steering reanalysis-repair and garden-path-lock-in rates, output fidelity, unambiguous-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Constructing temporarily-ambiguous sentences that are genuinely garden-pathing and equivalent across languages is delicate: reduced-relative and CC/RC ambiguities that exist in English may have no natural equivalent in a flexible-order or verb-final language; we native-verify, treat word-order flexibility as a graded predictor, flag items lacking a natural ambiguity (using them for transfer-limit analysis), and rely on the UNAMBIGUOUS control and matched content to isolate the reanalysis effect. 2) Some models may reanalyze robustly in all languages or fail uniformly—either is an informative, publishable finding (and the cross-lingual pattern of the Cao & Schuler larger-worse effect is itself of interest), and we quantify how often reanalysis fails via the parse trajectory and probe transfer. 3) Comprehension answers can be genuinely ambiguous for some attachment items; we restrict scored items to those with a clear disambiguation-forced correct reading (native-verified) and analyze truly ambiguous ones separately. 4) The parse-commitment probe could latch onto surface disambiguating tokens rather than an abstract structural representation; the per-token trajectory (flip during disambiguation), cross-lingual commitment invariance, the internal-predicts-behavior link, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 5) Confound with training frequency of complex constructions in lower-resource languages; we control with URIEL resource tiers and use the unambiguous control as a frequency-neutral within-content baseline. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Causal steering may trade fluency or control accuracy; we report output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the lock-in (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure steering manipulates parse revision rather than generically boosting accuracy. 8) The reanalysis signal may be low-rank or family-specific rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace and per-family variants and report where a scalar direction is insufficient. 9) Distinguishing from my temporal-ordering and argument-reconstruction proposals is essential; here the object is the committed SYNTACTIC STRUCTURE and its revision under disambiguation (garden-path recovery), not event chronology or covert-argument filling.

Name: crosslingual_default_referent_gating
Title: Whose World Is the Default? A Shared Underspecified-Referent Estimate Gated by a Language-Dependent Cultural-Default Threshold in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a prompt leaves a category referent UNDERSPECIFIED (e.g., 'the government', 'a typical wedding', 'the currency', 'a normal meal', 'a doctor'), a multilingual LLM must silently fill in a default instantiation, and it computes a largely language-independent internal 'underspecification' estimate (how ambiguous/open the referent is) but applies a query-language-dependent DEFAULT threshold: for the SAME underspecified referent, the model fills the slot with the query language community's culturally-typical instantiation in some languages while defaulting to a single dominant (usually US/English) instantiation in others, producing a cross-lingual default-referent gap that is separable from the underlying ambiguity estimate and from factual knowledge, and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable default-gating signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Cultural-bias benchmarks (FmLAMA, BLEnD, XNationQA, MSQA) document behaviorally that LLMs default to US/Western answers on culturally-variable questions and often do so regardless of query language, but they measure the bias as an outcome and offer no internal account. My prior contested_facts_language_switch proposal concerns questions with legitimately different stored ANSWERS (national dish) and whether language selects among them; crosslingual_persona_override concerns overriding an ASSIGNED persona. NEITHER addresses the silent default-FILLING of an UNDERSPECIFIED referent (no answer is asked for; the model must instantiate a category to proceed), nor frames it as a shared underspecification estimate gated by a language-set cultural-default threshold, nor causally localizes/steers that gate. My gating-template proposals (calibration know/don't-know, abstention attempt/abstain, processing-load compute/shortcut, concession, precision) target other decisions; the object here is the DEFAULT INSTANTIATION of an open category slot during ordinary comprehension/generation. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies default referent filling. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of how underspecified referents are silently defaulted and how query language sets that default.
Abstract: Much of language leaves the specifics unsaid: 'the currency', 'a typical breakfast', 'the government', 'a wedding', 'a doctor' each require the listener to silently fill in a default. We ask whether a multilingual LLM fills these underspecified referents with the query language community's culturally-typical instantiation, or silently defaults to a single dominant (usually US/English) instantiation regardless of language. We hypothesize that the model computes a largely language-independent estimate of HOW underspecified a referent is, but applies a query-language-dependent cultural-default threshold to it, so that for the SAME open slot it localizes the default in some languages and imports a dominant default in others. This predicts a cross-lingual default gap dissociable from the ambiguity estimate and from factual knowledge. We build DefaultProbe, parallel prompts across 12 languages that contain an underspecified culturally-variable referent and a continuation whose most natural completion reveals which instantiation the model assumed (e.g., the currency symbol it uses, the price range it treats as normal, the ceremony elements it mentions), each with a culture-localized and a dominant-default reading. Behaviorally we measure the default-localization rate per language and test whether it tracks resource level and typological/cultural distance. We train a linear probe for the shared underspecification estimate and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the gap into a shared estimate versus a language-set default threshold. In a decisive causal test we localize and shift a default-gating signal to make the model localize (or de-localize) the default consistently while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe multilingual cultural default bias as a shared underspecification estimate under a steerable, language-dependent gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/culturally/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili, Korean).
2) DATASET (DefaultProbe): ~500 prompts each containing an UNDERSPECIFIED culturally-variable referent (currency, typical meal/price, government structure, wedding/holiday customs, default sport, school system, address form, measurement in casual speech) followed by a continuation whose natural completion REVEALS the assumed instantiation (e.g., 'She paid for the coffee, about ___' reveals assumed currency/price; 'At the wedding, the ___ began' reveals assumed customs). For each item define a CULTURE-LOCALIZED instantiation set per language community and a DOMINANT-DEFAULT (US/English) instantiation, from native-sourced cultural references (BLEnD/FmLAMA/XNationQA-style plus native verification). Keep the propositional prompt fixed across languages; translate/native-verify. Include (a) an EXPLICIT-REFERENT control (the referent is specified, no defaulting needed; correct completion is language-flat) to bound the effect, and (b) a UNIVERSAL control (referent with a single cross-cultural instantiation) to check specificity.
3) BEHAVIORAL DEFAULT-GAP TEST: Per (item, language) classify the completion as culture-localized vs dominant-default (via a validated classifier + native checks; use short single-token-decodable slots where possible, e.g., currency symbol). KEY hypothesis: the default-localization rate shifts with query language, and lower-resource / greater-cultural-distance languages more often import the dominant default. Mixed-effects logistic regression of localization on (query language, resource tier via URIEL, cultural distance from dominant, referent category), item as random effect; test the language effect beyond factual knowledge (screen that the model KNOWS the localized instantiation when asked directly) and beyond the EXPLICIT-REFERENT control (should be language-flat). Report per-language localization profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical underspecified prompts.
4) SHARED UNDERSPECIFICATION PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the referent/pre-completion position; train a linear probe to decode HOW underspecified the referent is (a graded ambiguity/openness score, and a category-vs-specific classifier) on ENGLISH data and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report R^2/AUROC as evidence of a language-independent underspecification estimate, and cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the estimate for the same item. Also train a probe for WHICH instantiation is being filled (localized vs dominant) to read the default off the representation.
5) THRESHOLD-vs-ESTIMATE DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer underspecification estimate across languages (should be similar if shared) versus the emitted default (which diverges). Fit per-language a decision boundary/threshold on the shared estimate governing localize-vs-dominant; test whether cross-lingual default differences are explained by a shifted THRESHOLD on a similar estimate rather than a different estimate. Correlate per-language threshold with resource tier, cultural distance, and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE DEFAULT-GATING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a localizing language run and a dominant-default run on the SAME item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips localized<->dominant WITHOUT changing the decoded underspecification estimate. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gating components from a localizing language into a dominant-default run.
7) CAUSAL DEFAULT STEERING (decisive): Derive a default-gating steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (localized-default runs minus dominant-default runs). Test (i) LOCALIZE: adding it to dominant-defaulting languages makes the model fill the slot with the query community's typical instantiation toward a reference level; (ii) DE-LOCALIZE: subtracting it makes localizing languages import the dominant default; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where the gap was largest; (iv) it changes ONLY the default instantiation, not the decoded underspecification estimate, factual knowledge, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the EXPLICIT-REFERENT or UNIVERSAL controls, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: default-gap closure, localization-recovery rate, de-localization-induction rate (reverse), output-language fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts the default but not explicit-referent, universal-control, or unrelated answers, guarding against a generic lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: referent-category breakdown (currency vs customs vs government vs measurement); is English/US the imported dominant default the model de-localizes toward?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank default subspace; robustness across templates and completion formats; whether one gating vector generalizes across categories and languages.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language default-localization rate and its resource/cultural-distance regression, shared underspecification-probe transfer R^2/AUROC and representation similarity, estimate-similarity vs output-default-divergence (threshold) decomposition, threshold-vs-resource/culture/typology correlation, patch-localized default-gating layer, cross-lingual gating transplant repair rate, causal steering default-gap closure and de-localization-induction rates, underspecification-estimate/knowledge/output fidelity, explicit-referent and universal-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Culture-localized 'default' instantiations are fuzzy and value-laden; we use native-sourced instantiation SETS and score set membership (localized vs dominant) rather than single answers, restrict to referents with clear per-culture consensus, and analyze ambiguous ones separately. 2) The default gap could reflect a factual-knowledge gap (the model doesn't know the localized instantiation) rather than a defaulting threshold; we screen per-language that the model KNOWS the localized instantiation when asked directly and restrict the causal analysis to known items, so any residual defaulting is a gating effect. 3) Some models may be so US/English-biased that they never localize, giving little contested defaulting; this is itself an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often the default is even contested via probe transfer and behavioral variance. 4) The threshold-vs-estimate split could be confounded if the underspecification estimate itself differs by language; we test this directly by comparing shared-probe estimates across languages rather than assuming the split. 5) Reading the assumed default off a free continuation is noisy; we prefer short single-token-decodable slots (currency symbol, measurement unit), validate the completion classifier against human labels, and report reliability. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Causal steering may harm fluency or leak languages; we report underspecification-estimate fidelity, factual-knowledge retention, output-language fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the de-localization (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine default gate rather than a generic lever. 8) The default-gating signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 9) Distinguishing from my contested-facts and persona-override proposals is essential; here no answer is requested and no persona is assigned—the model must silently INSTANTIATE an underspecified category slot to continue, and the causal variable is the query-language-set default threshold on a shared underspecification estimate. 10) Misuse concern: default steering could be abused to homogenize or stereotype outputs; we frame and use it strictly as an interpretability/fairness diagnostic on benign cultural-default items and report retention rather than deploying it.

Name: crosslingual_overrefusal_caution_gating
Title: Too Cautious in Some Tongues: A Shared Sensitivity Estimate Gated by a Language-Dependent Over-Refusal Threshold in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: For BENIGN-but-sensitive-sounding requests (safe questions about medications, self-defense, historical violence, sexuality education, cybersecurity concepts), a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal estimate of a request's TOPIC SENSITIVITY, but the query language causally sets the CAUTION/OVER-REFUSAL threshold applied to that estimate: for the SAME benign request the model needlessly refuses (or hedges/deflects) at a lower threshold in some languages than others, producing a cross-lingual over-refusal asymmetry that is separable from genuine harm detection and from underlying knowledge, and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable caution-gating signal without changing the request or surface language. This is the mirror image of the well-studied under-refusal (harmful prompts slipping through low-resource languages): here safe prompts are wrongly blocked, unevenly, across languages.
Related Work: The multilingual safety literature is now large but almost entirely about UNDER-refusal: harmful prompts evading safeguards in low-resource languages (Illusion of Cross-Lingual Safety 2026; MSD 2026; cross-lingual jailbreaks) and the mechanism of the REFUSAL direction / safety neurons / safety pathways (Wang et al. 2025 'Refusal Direction is Universal'; Zhang et al. 2026 SS-Neurons; Miao et al. 2026 safety pathways; Kompella & Mahajan 2026 refusal circuit). Over-refusal/false-positive safety is studied only MONOLINGUALLY/behaviorally (XSTES/OR-Bench-style exaggerated-safety benchmarks) and BabelSteering (Stein et al. 2026) even notes English refusal steering INCREASES pseudo-harmful refusals cross-lingually as a side effect, but no work isolates over-refusal as its own cross-lingual phenomenon. Crucially, NO prior work (i) frames benign-request over-refusal as a shared TOPIC-SENSITIVITY estimate gated by a language-DEPENDENT caution threshold, (ii) dissociates this caution gate from genuine harm detection (the refusal direction) and from knowledge, or (iii) causally localizes and shifts a caution-gating signal to equalize over-refusal across languages while leaving genuine harm-refusal and content intact. This differs from my prior abstention proposal (attempt-vs-abstain on answerability/unanswerable questions) because the object here is needless SAFETY refusal of ANSWERABLE, benign requests and its language-set caution threshold, and from the refusal-direction literature because it targets FALSE-POSITIVE caution rather than true-harm detection.
Abstract: Multilingual safety research has focused on models being too permissive in some languages—letting harmful requests through. We study the opposite, under-examined failure: models being needlessly CAUTIOUS, refusing perfectly benign but sensitive-sounding requests, and doing so unevenly across languages. We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal estimate of a request's topic sensitivity, but applies a query-language-dependent caution threshold to it, so that the SAME safe request (how a medication works, lawful self-defense, sex education, a cybersecurity concept, historical atrocities) is answered in some languages and refused or deflected in others. This predicts a cross-lingual over-refusal asymmetry dissociable from genuine harm detection and from knowledge. We build BenignSensitive, parallel benign-but-sensitive requests plus matched genuinely-harmful controls across 12 languages, and measure per-language over-refusal (refusing safe items) alongside true-refusal (refusing harmful items). We train a linear probe for the shared sensitivity estimate and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the over-refusal gap into a shared sensitivity estimate versus a language-set caution threshold, and show this gate is distinct from the known refusal direction (which tracks genuine harm). In a decisive causal test we localize and shift the caution-gating signal to equalize over-refusal across languages—making the model answer safe requests consistently—while verifying that genuine harm-refusal, request content, and surface language are unchanged. We reframe multilingual exaggerated safety as a shared sensitivity estimate under a steerable, language-dependent caution gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili, Yoruba).
2) DATASET (BenignSensitive): ~500 BENIGN-BUT-SENSITIVE requests that a well-calibrated model should ANSWER (e.g., 'how does ibuprofen relieve pain?', 'what are lawful self-defense options?', 'explain what a SQL injection is so I can protect my site', age-appropriate sex education, historical accounts of violence, harm-reduction info), spanning topic domains (medical, legal/self-defense, sexuality, cybersecurity, historical violence, substances). Add ~300 matched GENUINELY-HARMFUL controls (adapted from AdvBench/HarmBench) that SHOULD be refused, sharing surface topic vocabulary with the benign items to force a genuine benign-vs-harmful distinction. Translate/native-verify all items into 12 languages; keep the request content fixed across languages. Include a NEUTRAL non-sensitive control (plainly safe, no sensitive vocabulary) to bound the effect. Screen that the model KNOWS/can answer the benign items (in at least one language) so over-refusal reflects caution, not ignorance.
3) RESPONSE LABELING: Classify each response as ANSWER vs REFUSE/DEFLECT (via a refusal-phrase detector validated against human labels, per language). Metrics per (item, language): over-refusal rate (refusing benign items), true-refusal rate (refusing harmful items), and refusal on the neutral control.
4) BEHAVIORAL OVER-REFUSAL ASYMMETRY TEST: KEY hypothesis: for the SAME benign request, over-refusal differs by query language, beyond knowledge and beyond genuine harm. Mixed-effects logistic regression of over-refusal on (query language, topic domain, resource tier via URIEL, knowledge indicator), item as random effect; test that query language shifts over-refusal beyond resource/knowledge. Report per-language over-refusal profiles, cross-lingual disagreement on identical benign items, and the SEPARATION from true-refusal: over-refusal and true-refusal should be dissociable (a language can over-refuse benign items while NOT better-refusing harmful ones), evidencing a caution shift rather than better harm detection.
5) SHARED SENSITIVITY PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-response/decision position; train a linear 'topic-sensitivity' probe (graded sensitivity, and a benign-vs-harmful axis) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report R^2/AUROC as evidence of a language-independent sensitivity estimate, and cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the estimate for the same item. Compare to per-language-trained probes.
6) GATE-vs-ESTIMATE DECOMPOSITION & DISTINCTNESS FROM THE REFUSAL DIRECTION: For each item, compare the shared mid-layer sensitivity estimate across languages (should be similar) versus the emitted answer/refuse decision (which diverges). Fit per-language a decision boundary on the shared estimate; test whether cross-lingual over-refusal differences are explained by a shifted CAUTION THRESHOLD rather than a different estimate. Correlate per-language threshold with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman). CRITICAL distinctness test: extract the known harm/refusal direction (Wang et al. 2025) and show the caution-gating axis governing over-refusal of BENIGN items is separable from it (low alignment; steering caution moves benign over-refusal without moving true-harm refusal). Anchor mid-vs-decision split with per-layer language-ID probes.
7) LOCALIZE THE CAUTION-GATING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that answers and one that over-refuses the SAME benign item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips over-refuse->answer WITHOUT changing the decoded sensitivity estimate or the true-harm refusal on control items. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gating components from a low-caution language into an over-refusing run.
8) CAUSAL CAUTION EQUALIZATION (decisive): Derive a caution-gating steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (answer runs minus over-refuse runs on matched benign items). Test (i) LOWER-CAUTION: adding it to over-refusing languages makes the model answer benign requests toward a reference level (closing the over-refusal gap); (ii) RAISE-CAUTION: subtracting it induces over-refusal in low-caution languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where over-refusal was worst; (iv) it changes ONLY over-refusal of BENIGN items, NOT true-refusal of genuinely-harmful controls (which must stay refused), the decoded sensitivity estimate, request content, or surface language (fidelity/safety checks), and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Baselines: per-language refusal-threshold tuning, prompt-based 'answer if safe' instruction, translate-to-English. Metrics: over-refusal-gap closure, benign-answer recovery, harmful-refusal retention (safety must not drop), over-caution-induction rate (reverse), content/output-language fidelity, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering should reduce benign over-refusal but NOT reduce harmful-refusal, guarding against a generic 'disable safety' lever.
9) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: topic-domain breakdown (which domains over-refuse most and where); is a dominant/high-resource language the low-caution reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank caution subspace; robustness across templates and generation-vs-forced-choice formats; whether one gating vector generalizes across domains and languages.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language over-refusal and true-refusal rates and their dissociation, over-refusal regression controlling for knowledge/resource, cross-lingual sensitivity-probe transfer R^2/AUROC and representation similarity, estimate-similarity vs decision-divergence (threshold) decomposition, distinctness of caution axis from the refusal direction, threshold-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized caution-gating layer, cross-lingual gating transplant repair rate, causal equalization over-refusal-gap closure with harmful-refusal retention, over-caution-induction rate, content/output fidelity, general-QA retention, comparison to threshold-tuning and translate-to-English baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Labeling a benign request as 'should be answered' can be contested; we restrict to items with clear native-consensus benignness (harm-reduction, education, lawful topics), native-verify, and analyze borderline items separately. 2) The most important safety guard: any caution-lowering intervention must NOT reduce genuine harm-refusal; we include matched harmful controls, report harmful-refusal retention as a primary metric, and use the reverse-consistency test to ensure the caution gate is distinct from and does not touch the true-harm refusal direction—if they are entangled, that is itself a publishable finding (over- and under-refusal share one dial). 3) Some models may over-refuse uniformly or not at all across languages, leaving little asymmetry; this is itself informative and we quantify how contested over-refusal is per language. 4) The gate-vs-estimate split could be confounded if the sensitivity estimate itself differs by language; we test this directly by comparing shared-probe estimates across languages rather than assuming the split. 5) Refusal-phrase detection is noisy across languages (deflection, hedging, partial answers); we validate the detector against human labels per language, report reliability, and use log-prob of an explicit refusal template as a complementary measure. 6) Over-refusal could reflect a knowledge gap rather than caution; we screen that the model can answer benign items and restrict causal analysis to known items. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Misuse concern: a caution-lowering steering vector could be abused to weaken safety; we frame and use it strictly as an interpretability/fairness diagnostic, evaluate only on benign over-refusal while explicitly verifying harmful-refusal is preserved, and report retention rather than releasing a jailbreak—distinguishing our benign-over-refusal target sharply from the jailbreak literature. 9) The caution signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my abstention proposal is essential; here items are answerable and benign, and the refusal is a needless SAFETY refusal governed by a language-set caution threshold, not an attempt-vs-abstain decision about answerability.

Name: crosslingual_deliberation_benefit_gating
Title: Should It Think, or Just Answer? Whether the Query Language Determines When Deliberate Reasoning Helps or Hurts in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Whether explicit deliberate reasoning (chain-of-thought / 'thinking mode') HELPS or HURTS accuracy is systematically query-language-dependent: for the SAME problem, forcing deliberation improves accuracy in some languages but causally DEGRADES it in others (often lower-resource or morphologically-distant ones), because deliberation induces a language-specific failure mode (drift to an unstable reasoning language, error compounding, or answer-format collapse) rather than a knowledge deficit. We hypothesize (1) a per-problem, per-language 'deliberation benefit' that is predictable from language typology/resource and problem type, and often NEGATIVE; (2) the harm arises from a localizable reasoning-drift/instability signal that fires more in harmed languages; and (3) a small, localizable 'deliberation-mode' signal can be causally steered per-language to enable deliberation where it helps and suppress it where it hurts, recovering accuracy without changing the surface answer language.
Related Work: Recent multilingual-reasoning work shows chain-of-thought helps globally when reasoning is forced into a shared/Latin script (Wang et al. 2025) and that ablating language boosts reasoning (Zhao et al. 2025), while cross-lingual reasoning suffers 'collapse'/language-drift mid-chain (Lim et al. 2026; Li et al. 2025). Critically, applied reports (Ayela & Sahni 2026, FinMMEval) document that enabling 'thinking mode' collapses Arabic accuracy to near-chance and CoT collapses Greek accuracy from 90.7% to 20.9%—a striking, unexplained sign-flip where deliberation is CATASTROPHIC in specific languages. All prior work treats CoT/deliberation as globally beneficial (to be steered toward a good reasoning language) or studies drift as a uniform degradation; NONE frame the HELP-vs-HURT sign of deliberation itself as a query-language-dependent, per-problem property, predict when deliberation is net-negative, attribute the harm to a localizable instability signal, or causally gate deliberation per-language. This is distinct from my prior reasoning-language-steering proposal (which language to think IN, assuming thinking helps) and my computational-depth proposal (vertical layer-commitment, no explicit CoT): here the object is whether to deliberate AT ALL and the causal sign of that choice by language.
Abstract: Chain-of-thought and 'thinking modes' are assumed to make language models smarter, and multilingual research has focused on which language a model should reason in. But a striking, unexplained observation cuts against the assumption: enabling deliberate reasoning can collapse accuracy to near-chance in specific languages (e.g., Arabic thinking mode, Greek CoT) while helping in others. We reframe this as a fundamental phenomenon: whether deliberate reasoning helps or hurts is query-language-dependent, and for many problem-language pairs its causal effect is NEGATIVE. We first quantify a per-problem, per-language 'deliberation benefit' (accuracy with forced deliberation minus direct answering) across typologically and resource-diverse languages and problem types, testing whether it is predictable from language typology/resource and whether it is systematically negative for certain languages—ruling out a mere knowledge deficit by showing direct answering succeeds where deliberation fails. We then diagnose the harm mechanistically: using per-layer language-ID probes and logit-lens we test whether deliberation in harmed languages triggers reasoning-language drift, error compounding, or answer-format collapse, and we train a linear 'reasoning-instability' probe that fires more where deliberation hurts. Finally, via activation and path patching we localize a 'deliberation-mode' signal and, in a decisive causal test, steer it per-language—suppressing deliberation where it hurts and enabling it where it helps—recovering accuracy while leaving the surface answer language unchanged. We reframe deliberate reasoning as a language-gated, sometimes-harmful, and steerable degree of freedom rather than a universal good.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Qwen3-14B (native thinking mode), Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Greek, Turkish), chosen to include the reported harm cases (Arabic, Greek).
2) DATA: Parallel problems where deliberation MIGHT help—MGSM (math word problems), multilingual MMLU subsets, multi-hop factual reasoning (Wikidata-derived), and multiple-choice exam-style items (FinMMEval-style) with short scoreable answers. Native-verified translations; record tokenization fertility and per-language direct-answer accuracy.
3) DELIBERATION-BENEFIT MEASUREMENT: For each (problem, language) run TWO conditions: DIRECT (answer immediately / no CoT / thinking-off) and DELIBERATE (forced CoT or thinking-on). Define deliberation benefit = DELIBERATE accuracy minus DIRECT accuracy, per problem and per language. KEY behavioral test: identify problem-language cells where benefit is significantly NEGATIVE (deliberation hurts), replicating and generalizing the Arabic/Greek collapse. Mixed-effects regression of benefit on (language typology/resource via URIEL, problem type, fertility), problem as random effect; test that the SIGN of benefit is predictable from language and that harm is not explained by knowledge (DIRECT succeeds where DELIBERATE fails).
4) HARM-MECHANISM DIAGNOSIS: In harmed cells, use per-layer language-ID probes and logit-lens on the deliberation trace to test three candidate failure modes: (a) REASONING-DRIFT (the CoT switches to an unstable/wrong reasoning language mid-chain), (b) ERROR-COMPOUNDING (early wrong steps propagate), (c) ANSWER-FORMAT COLLAPSE (the final answer fails to conform to the expected format after long reasoning). Quantify each mode's prevalence per language and correlate with negative benefit.
5) REASONING-INSTABILITY PROBE: Train a linear probe on hidden states during deliberation to predict whether the deliberation will end in a wrong answer; test whether it fires more strongly in harmed languages and transfers zero-shot across languages (a shared instability signal).
6) LOCALIZE THE DELIBERATION-MODE SIGNAL: Via activation/path patching between a DIRECT run and a DELIBERATE run on the same problem, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components that engage the deliberation trajectory; cross-check activation vs path patching. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band.
7) CAUSAL PER-LANGUAGE GATING (decisive): Derive a deliberation-mode steering vector (deliberate runs minus direct runs). Test (i) SUPPRESS: in harmed problem-language cells, steering toward the direct mode (or suppressing deliberation onset) recovers accuracy toward DIRECT levels; (ii) ENABLE: in helped cells, keeping deliberation preserves gains; (iii) build a per-problem GATE that predicts the sign of benefit from language/problem features and applies suppress/enable accordingly, and compare against always-deliberate, always-direct, best-fixed-policy, and force-English-CoT (Wang 2025) baselines; (iv) verify surface answer language unchanged and general QA unharmed. Metrics: accuracy of the gated policy vs baselines, harm-recovery rate in negative cells, retained gains in positive cells, output-language fidelity.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: which failure mode dominates per language; native thinking-mode (Qwen3) vs prompted CoT; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); problem-type breakdown (math vs factual vs MC); gate predictability (AUC for predicting benefit sign); robustness across templates.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-(problem,language) deliberation benefit and its sign-predictability, negative-benefit cell prevalence, failure-mode prevalence (drift/compounding/format-collapse), instability-probe AUC and cross-lingual transfer, patch-localized deliberation-mode layer, causal gating harm-recovery and retained-gain rates, gated-policy accuracy vs baselines, output-language fidelity, general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The DIRECT vs DELIBERATE contrast must be fair; we control prompt format, use both prompted-CoT and native thinking modes, and match answer-extraction so harm is not an artifact of parsing (though answer-format collapse is itself a hypothesized mechanism we measure explicitly). 2) Negative benefit could reflect a weak base rather than a genuine harm; we condition on DIRECT succeeding to show deliberation actively destroys correct answers. 3) Some models/languages may show uniformly positive benefit, leaving little harm to study—this is itself informative and we quantify how often the sign flips. 4) The instability probe may be noisy; we validate on English with gold labels and confirm findings causally via patching. 5) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test multiple models (including a native-thinking model where the collapse was reported) and cross-check activation vs path patching. 6) Per-language gating may trade some gains for harm-avoidance; we report the full trade-off (harm recovered vs gains retained) rather than claiming a free lunch. 7) Distinguishing from my reasoning-language-steering and computational-depth proposals is essential; here the object is the HELP-vs-HURT sign of engaging explicit deliberation at all, its language-dependence, and its causal per-language gating, not which language to reason in or vertical layer-commitment depth. 8) The deliberation-mode signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank variants.

Name: crosslingual_positional_bias_modulation
Title: Lost in the Middle, in Every Language? Whether Query/Context Language Reshapes Positional Attention Bias and Can Be Equalized at a Shared Positional Channel
Short Hypothesis: The 'lost-in-the-middle' positional attention bias is not language-invariant: for the SAME retrieval task, the shape of the positional accuracy curve (strength of primacy, recency, and the middle penalty) is systematically modulated by the language of the context/query, with lower-resource and higher-fertility languages suffering a deeper middle penalty and sharper recency reliance. We hypothesize this arises because a largely language-independent positional-attention mechanism (attention sinks / positional hidden-state channels) is applied with language-dependent gain, and that a single-channel/positional intervention derived in one language can be recalibrated to equalize the positional bias across languages, improving mid-context retrieval where it is worst.
Related Work: Positional bias / lost-in-the-middle is well-established but studied almost entirely MONOLINGUALLY (English): the U-shaped attention bias and its calibration (Hsieh et al. 2024 'Found-in-the-Middle'; Zehle & Assenmacher 2026 CALIOPE), its mechanistic locus in positional hidden-state channels (Yu et al. 2024/2025, mitigated by scaling a single channel), its RoPE/layer-scaling causes (Lv et al. 2026 LPES), its dependence on relative context-window fill (Veseli et al. 2025), and its emergence from retrieval demands during pretraining (Salvatore et al. 2025). NONE ask whether the positional bias is LANGUAGE-DEPENDENT: whether the U-curve's shape (middle penalty, primacy vs recency) shifts with context/query language, whether this tracks resource/typology beyond tokenization length, whether a shared positional mechanism is modulated by language, or whether the known single-channel/positional fix must be recalibrated per language to equalize retrieval. Multilingual RAG work documents behavioral cross-lingual retrieval gaps but attributes them to knowledge/translation, never to a language-modulated POSITIONAL attention bias with a mechanistic, causal fix. This is also distinct from all my prior proposals, which concerned semantic/typological leakage and decision-gating, never architectural positional/attention bias.
Abstract: Large language models notoriously lose information placed in the middle of a long context, an effect traced to a U-shaped positional attention bias, attention sinks, and specific positional hidden-state channels. This entire literature is monolingual. We ask a simple question with direct consequences for multilingual retrieval-augmented generation: is the lost-in-the-middle bias itself language-dependent? We hypothesize that a largely language-independent positional-attention mechanism is applied with a language-dependent gain, so that for the SAME needle-in-a-haystack task the shape of the positional accuracy curve—the depth of the middle penalty and the balance of primacy versus recency—shifts systematically with the language of the context and query, worst for lower-resource and higher-fertility languages, beyond what tokenization length explains. We test this with controlled multilingual needle-in-a-haystack and multi-document QA across typologically and resource-diverse languages, measuring per-language positional accuracy curves and per-language attention-bias profiles (attention-sink strength, U-curve shape). Mechanistically, we test whether the positional-hidden-state channel that carries the bias is shared across languages, and whether its magnitude is language-modulated. In a decisive causal test we recalibrate the single positional channel (extending Yu et al.) with a per-language gain to equalize the positional bias, and show it lifts mid-context retrieval most in the worst-hit languages while preserving accuracy where the bias was already mild. We reframe multilingual retrieval disparity as a language-modulated, mechanistically shared, and equalizable positional bias.
Experiments: 1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (long-context capable; inference + attention/hidden-state analysis on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource/fertility-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili). 2) DATA: (a) MULTILINGUAL NEEDLE-IN-A-HAYSTACK: a short factual 'needle' (a decodable key-value or fact) inserted at controlled RELATIVE positions (0%,10%,...,100%) within a distractor 'haystack', with needle, query, and haystack all in the same language; parallel across languages, with matched semantic content. (b) MULTILINGUAL MULTI-DOCUMENT QA (NaturalQuestions/MKQA-style translated) with the gold document placed at varied positions. Control context length by RELATIVE fill of each model's window (following Veseli et al.) and record per-language tokenization fertility (tokens/word) so positional effects can be separated from length. Native-verify translations; score via language-agnostic normalized matching. 3) PER-LANGUAGE POSITIONAL CURVE (behavioral): For each language, plot retrieval accuracy vs relative needle position; fit the U-curve and extract MIDDLE PENALTY (min-position accuracy vs boundary accuracy), PRIMACY and RECENCY strengths. KEY hypothesis: the middle penalty is deeper and recency reliance sharper in lower-resource/higher-fertility languages on the SAME task. Mixed-effects regression of accuracy on (relative position, language, tokenization fertility, resource tier via URIEL, relative context fill), item as random effect; test that language modulates curve shape BEYOND fertility and fill. Report per-language curve-shape parameters and cross-lingual disagreement at matched positions. 4) ATTENTION-BIAS PROFILE: For each language measure the U-shaped attention bias (attention mass to boundary vs middle positions, attention-sink strength at the first token) as a function of position, following Hsieh et al. Test whether the attention-bias profile is more skewed (stronger sink/boundary bias) in harmed languages and correlates per-language with the behavioral middle penalty (link test). 5) SHARED POSITIONAL CHANNEL & MODULATION (mechanism): Identify the positional-hidden-state channel(s) carrying position bias (Yu et al. 2024/2025 methodology) in English, and test whether the SAME channel carries positional information in other languages (probe position from that channel; measure cross-lingual transfer). Test whether the channel's MAGNITUDE / effective gain differs by language and predicts the per-language middle penalty—evidence that a shared positional mechanism is language-modulated rather than replaced. 6) CAUSAL EQUALIZATION (decisive): Extend the single-channel scaling intervention (Yu et al.) to a PER-LANGUAGE recalibration: scale the positional channel by a language-specific gain fit to flatten that language's positional bias. Test (i) mid-context retrieval accuracy rises most in the worst-hit languages, closing the cross-lingual positional gap toward the best language; (ii) boundary/already-mild languages are not harmed; (iii) surface output language and general QA (multilingual MMLU subset) are unchanged. Compare against (a) no calibration, (b) a single global (English-derived) channel scale applied uniformly, (c) Found-in-the-Middle attention calibration, (d) translate-context-to-English retrieval. Metrics: middle-penalty reduction, cross-lingual positional-gap closure, off-target/general retention, output fidelity. 7) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: primacy-vs-recency asymmetry by language; mixed-language conditions (query in language A, haystack in language B) to separate query-language from context-language effects; relative-fill dependence (does the language effect strengthen near the window limit, per Veseli et al.); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); channel/layer sensitivity; whether one recalibration generalizes across tasks (needle vs multi-doc QA). EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language U-curve parameters (middle penalty, primacy, recency) and their language regression controlling for fertility/fill, attention-bias profile vs behavior correlation, shared positional-channel transfer and language-modulated magnitude, causal per-language recalibration middle-penalty reduction and positional-gap closure, comparison to global-scale / attention-calibration / translate baselines, general-QA and output-fidelity retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Tokenization fertility confounds position with effective length (a needle at 50% relative position sits at different absolute token positions across languages); we control fertility in regression, use RELATIVE positions and relative context fill, and—crucially—the causal channel recalibration does not change tokenization yet should still equalize the bias, dissociating positional gain from length. 2) Some models may show a language-invariant U-curve (no modulation); this is itself an informative, publishable finding about the universality of positional bias, and we quantify how much curve shape varies by language. 3) The positional channel identified in English may not cleanly carry position in all languages; we test transfer explicitly and report per-language channel fidelity, using per-language recalibration only where a shared channel exists. 4) The behavioral middle penalty may be small in strong long-context models (as Tian et al. note some models are robust to lost-in-the-middle); we select tasks/fills where the penalty is measurable and report models where it is absent. 5) Per-language recalibration may trade boundary accuracy for middle accuracy; we report the full trade-off and off-target retention rather than claiming a free lunch. 6) Attention-bias measurement is architecture-specific (RoPE vs others); we test multiple RoPE models and report sensitivity. 7) Mixed-language query/context conditions may be unnatural; we treat them as a controlled dissociation, not a deployment setting. 8) Results may be model-specific; we test five models spanning English-centric and multilingual-centric pretraining and report aggregate and per-model results. 9) Distinguishing our contribution from the monolingual positional-bias literature (Hsieh 2024, Yu 2025, Veseli 2025) is essential; we include their methods/interventions as baselines and position the novelty as the language-modulation of positional bias, its shared-channel mechanism, and the per-language equalization, none of which they address.

Name: crosslingual_semantic_anticipation_signal
Title: Surprised in Silence: A Shared Cross-Lingual Semantic-Anticipation Signal Whose Expression Is Language-Gated
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs compute a largely language-independent internal 'semantic-anticipation' signal that registers whether an upcoming word is semantically congruent with its context (an N400-like prediction-error signal), but whether that anticipated incongruity is behaviorally EXPRESSED (a lowered probability for the anomalous word, a flagged anomaly, a corrected continuation) is gated by the query language: the SAME semantic anomaly is internally detected across languages yet surfaced far more weakly in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so a model can be internally 'surprised' while behaviorally 'silent'.
Related Work: Human psycholinguistics establishes the N400 as a graded, largely language-general prediction-error / semantic-congruity signal (Kutas & Federmeier). In NLP, monolingual work shows LLM surprisal correlates with N400 amplitude and that models predict upcoming words, but this is English-centric and behavioral. Cross-lingual work studies factual consistency (Qi 2023; Wang 2025) and locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS (Wang 2025; Lim 2025), and my prior proposals cover typological-feature leakage into semantics and various decision-gating templates. NONE ask whether a model computes a shared, language-independent SEMANTIC-ANTICIPATION / prediction-error signal for upcoming words, whether that internal signal is decoupled from its behavioral expression, whether the detect-vs-express gap tracks language resource level, or whether an anticipation signal can be causally localized and its expression steered. This reframes cross-lingual anomaly-blindness as an expression gate over a shared detection signal, distinct from prior facts-consistency and typological-leakage work.
Abstract: When a sentence takes an unexpected semantic turn ('He spread the warm bread with socks'), a fluent reader registers surprise before deciding what to do about it. In humans this is the N400, a largely language-general prediction-error signal. We ask whether a multilingual LLM computes an analogous shared, language-independent semantic-anticipation signal that detects an upcoming word's (in)congruity, and whether that internal detection is decoupled from how strongly the anomaly is behaviorally expressed across languages. We hypothesize that models internally 'notice' a semantic anomaly similarly across languages, but the query language gates whether that surprise is surfaced (a suppressed probability for the anomalous continuation, an explicit anomaly flag, a self-correction), so the same anomaly is detected internally yet acted on far less in lower-resource, typologically distant languages. We build AnomalyAnticipate, parallel high- and low-cloze sentence continuations across 10 languages, each with a congruent completion and a semantically anomalous one, plus a control-congruent stratum. Behaviorally we measure per-language expression (log-probability gap between congruent and anomalous continuations, explicit anomaly-detection accuracy) and test whether it collapses in some languages beyond tokenization and knowledge. We train a linear anticipation-error probe and test whether a single probe trained in one language transfers zero-shot across languages, evidencing a shared detection signal, then decompose the expression gap into a shared detection component versus a language-set expression gate. In a decisive causal test we localize and steer an expression-gating signal to make the model behaviorally surface an anomaly it internally detected, without changing the surface language. We reframe cross-lingual anomaly-blindness as a steerable gate over a shared anticipation signal.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (AnomalyAnticipate): ~500 sentence frames each with (a) a strongly-expected CONGRUENT completion and (b) a semantically ANOMALOUS completion (a real word that violates selectional/semantic expectations, N400-style), plus a CONTROL stratum where both completions are congruent (to bound the effect). Draw base frames from cloze-normed / N400 stimulus sets, extend and translate/native-verify into all 10 languages, keeping the anomaly type fixed across languages and the completion short and single-token-decodable where possible. Record per-language tokenization fertility and screen that the model KNOWS the relevant world/selectional fact (so expression failure is not ignorance).
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (frame, language) measure (i) the log-probability GAP between congruent and anomalous continuations (implicit expression), and (ii) explicit anomaly-detection accuracy ('Is this sentence sensible? yes/no' / 'which word is out of place?'). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME anomaly, expression (both the log-prob gap and explicit detection) is systematically weaker in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, beyond tokenization and knowledge. Mixed-effects regression of expression on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, knowledge indicator), frame as random effect; compare against the congruent control (should show no gap). Report per-language expression profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical anomalies.
4) SHARED ANTICIPATION-ERROR PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer, pool the hidden state at the pre-completion position; train a linear probe to decode CONGRUENT vs ANOMALOUS (semantic anticipation error) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot to every other language; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent detection signal. Compare to per-language-trained probes to bound shared-vs-specific, and measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the anticipation-error representation for the same frame.
5) DETECTION-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: For each frame, compare the shared mid-layer anticipation-error signal across languages (should be similar if detection is shared) versus the behavioral expression (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE = mapping from internal detection to surfaced behavior per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar detection signal rather than weaker detection. Correlate per-language gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor the mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE EXPRESSION-GATING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that surfaces the anomaly and one that stays silent on the SAME frame, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer makes the anomaly surface WITHOUT changing the decoded anticipation-error signal. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the anticipation-error representation FROM a high-expression language into a silent low-expression run.
7) CAUSAL EXPRESSION STEERING (decisive): Derive an expression-gating steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (surface-anomaly runs minus silent runs at matched detection). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to silent low-expression languages makes the model behaviorally flag / suppress the anomaly toward high-expression levels; (ii) SUPPRESS: subtracting it silences anomaly expression in high-expression languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where expression was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY anomaly expression, not the decoded anticipation signal or surface language (fidelity check), does not move the congruent control, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: expression-gap closure, explicit-detection recovery, suppression-induction rate (reverse), output-language fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering should change anomaly expression but not unrelated answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: anomaly-type breakdown (selectional-violation vs world-knowledge vs associative); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single expression-gating vector generalizes across frames and languages; robustness across templates and log-prob-vs-explicit formats; explicit dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched detection and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces the anomaly without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language congruent-vs-anomalous log-prob gap and explicit-detection accuracy, expression regression controlling for fertility/knowledge/resource, cross-lingual anticipation-error probe transfer AUROC and representation similarity, detection-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized expression-gating layer, cross-lingual anticipation transplant recovery rate, causal steering expression-gap closure and suppression-induction rates, anticipation-signal/output fidelity, congruent-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The detection-vs-expression split could be confounded if the anticipation signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by comparing shared-probe detection across languages rather than assuming the split, and report how much of the expression gap is detection vs gate. 2) Expression failure could reflect a knowledge gap rather than a gate;
