we screen that the model knows the relevant selectional/world fact and restrict causal analysis to known frames. 3) Tokenization fertility confounds the log-prob gap; we control for fertility, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched detection, and—crucially—the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet surfaces the anomaly, dissociating the gate from length. 4) Some models may detect and express anomalies uniformly across languages (no gap); this is itself an informative, publishable finding about the universality of anticipation, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 5) Constructing equivalent semantic anomalies across languages is delicate (selectional restrictions differ); we native-verify, keep anomaly type fixed, and use cloze-normed base stimuli where available, analyzing culture-specific anomalies separately. 6) The anticipation probe could latch onto surface cues rather than a genuine prediction-error signal; the cross-lingual invariance test, the detection-predicts-expression link, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Steering may harm fluency or leak languages; we report anticipation-signal fidelity, output-language fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the suppression (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine expression gate rather than a generic lever. 9) The gate signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my prior facts-consistency and typological-leakage proposals is essential; here the object is a next-word SEMANTIC-ANTICIPATION / prediction-error signal and the decoupling of its internal detection from its behavioral expression across languages, not stored factual consistency or feature leakage into a specific semantic dimension.

Name: crosslingual_incongruity_resolution_gating
Title: Getting the Joke, in Silence: A Shared Incongruity-Resolution Signal Whose Behavioral Expression Is Language-Gated in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM reads a two-stage humorous stimulus (a set-up plus a punchline that requires resolving an incongruity, e.g., a garden-path joke or pun-based twist), it computes a largely language-independent internal 'incongruity-resolution' signal that registers the surprise-then-reinterpretation of the set-up, but whether this resolution is behaviorally EXPRESSED (correctly identifying the intended second meaning, judging the item funny, selecting the resolving continuation) is gated by the query language: the SAME joke is internally resolved across languages yet surfaced far more weakly in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so the model can 'get it' internally while behaviorally 'missing it'.
Related Work: Humor is a canonical two-stage incongruity-resolution phenomenon in psycholinguistics (Suls; Attardo's General Theory of Verbal Humor). In NLP, humor detection/generation is studied mostly monolingually and behaviorally (SemEval humor tasks; pun detection), and recent LLM work shows models can rate/explain jokes in English but struggle to 'get' humor cross-lingually, treating the failure as a benchmark accuracy gap with no internal account. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS, and my prior proposals cover a literal-to-figurative transition for idioms/metaphor, a garden-path syntactic reanalysis signal, and a semantic-anticipation (N400-like) detection-vs-expression gate. This proposal is distinct: humor requires TWO-STAGE incongruity RESOLUTION (detect a semantic clash in the set-up AND reinterpret it via the punchline), not single-word anticipation (my anticipation proposal), single-clause figurative resolution (my metaphor proposal), or syntactic-only garden-path revision (my reanalysis proposal). No prior work asks whether an LLM computes a shared, language-independent incongruity-RESOLUTION signal for humor, whether its internal resolution is decoupled from its behavioral expression across languages, whether the get-it-vs-express-it gap tracks resource level, or whether the signal can be causally localized and its expression steered.
Abstract: A joke works in two beats: a set-up plants an expectation, and a punchline forces you to reinterpret it, resolving an incongruity. Getting the joke means detecting the clash and finding the alternative reading. We ask whether a multilingual LLM computes a shared, language-independent internal incongruity-resolution signal for such two-stage humor, and whether that internal 'getting it' is decoupled from how strongly the resolution is behaviorally expressed across languages. We hypothesize that models internally resolve the same joke similarly across languages, but the query language gates whether the resolution is surfaced (correctly naming the intended second meaning, judging funniness, choosing the resolving continuation), so the same joke is resolved internally yet acted on far less in lower-resource, typologically distant languages. We build JokeResolve, parallel two-stage humorous items across 8 languages, each with a resolving (funny) punchline, a non-resolving (incongruity-only, unfunny) foil, and a coherent (no-incongruity) control, plus a comprehension probe whose correct answer requires the reinterpreted meaning. Behaviorally we measure per-language expression (resolving-continuation preference, funniness judgment, intended-meaning accuracy) and test whether it collapses in some languages beyond tokenization and knowledge. We train a linear incongruity-resolution probe and test whether a single probe trained in one language transfers zero-shot across languages, evidencing a shared signal, then decompose the expression gap into a shared resolution component versus a language-set expression gate. In a decisive causal test we localize and steer an expression-gating signal to make the model surface a joke it internally resolved, without changing the surface language. We reframe cross-lingual humor-blindness as a steerable gate over a shared resolution signal.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Turkish).
2) DATASET (JokeResolve): ~450 two-stage humorous items, each a SET-UP plus three continuations: (a) a RESOLVING punchline that reinterprets the set-up (funny), (b) a NON-RESOLVING foil that introduces incongruity without resolution (unfunny), (c) a COHERENT control continuation (no incongruity, no humor). Use structure-based humor that survives translation (garden-path jokes, script-opposition twists, semantic-reinterpretation jokes) rather than untranslatable phonological puns; a separate PUN sub-stratum tests script-specific limits. Each item has a comprehension probe ('What is the second/intended meaning?' MC/cloze) whose correct answer requires the reinterpretation, and a funniness-rating probe. Translate/native-verify into all 8 languages; keep the humor mechanism fixed across languages; record tokenization fertility; screen that the model KNOWS the relevant world/lexical facts so expression failure is not ignorance.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (item, language) measure (i) log-probability preference for the RESOLVING vs NON-RESOLVING continuation, (ii) intended-meaning comprehension accuracy, (iii) funniness rating (resolving should exceed foil/control). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME joke, expression is systematically weaker in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond tokenization and knowledge. Mixed-effects regression of expression on (language, resource tier via URIEL, fertility, knowledge indicator), item as random effect; compare against the coherent control (no humor gap). Report per-language expression profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical jokes.
4) SHARED RESOLUTION PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the post-punchline position; train a linear probe to decode RESOLVED (funny reinterpretation) vs UNRESOLVED (foil) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, apply zero-shot to other languages; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent resolution signal. Compare to per-language-trained probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the resolution representation for the same item. Use logit-lens to track when the reinterpreted meaning overtakes the initial one (resolution depth).
5) RESOLUTION-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: For each item, compare the shared mid-layer resolution signal across languages (should be similar if resolution is shared) versus behavioral expression (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal resolution to surfaced behavior per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar resolution signal rather than weaker resolution. Correlate per-language gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes.
6) LOCALIZE THE EXPRESSION-GATING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that surfaces the joke and one that misses it on the SAME item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer makes the joke surface WITHOUT changing the decoded resolution signal. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the resolution representation FROM a high-expression language into a missing low-expression run.
7) CAUSAL EXPRESSION STEERING (decisive): Derive an expression-gating steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (surface-joke runs minus missed runs at matched resolution). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to low-expression languages makes the model prefer the resolving continuation / rate it funny / name the intended meaning toward high-expression levels; (ii) SUPPRESS: subtracting it silences humor expression in high-expression languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where expression was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY humor expression, not the decoded resolution signal or surface language (fidelity), does not move the coherent control, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: expression-gap closure, comprehension recovery, suppression-induction rate (reverse), output-language fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes humor expression but not unrelated answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: humor-mechanism breakdown (garden-path vs script-opposition vs pun sub-stratum); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single gating vector generalizes across items and languages; robustness across templates and log-prob-vs-explicit formats; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched resolution and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces the joke without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language resolving-preference/comprehension/funniness, expression regression controlling for fertility/knowledge/resource, cross-lingual resolution-probe transfer AUROC and representation similarity, resolution-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized gating layer, cross-lingual resolution transplant recovery rate, causal steering expression-gap closure and suppression-induction rates, resolution-signal/output fidelity, coherent-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The resolution-vs-expression split could be confounded if the resolution signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by comparing shared-probe resolution across languages rather than assuming the split, and report how much of the gap is resolution vs gate. 2) Expression failure could reflect a knowledge/lexical gap rather than a gate; we screen that the model knows the relevant facts and restrict causal analysis to known items. 3) Tokenization fertility confounds the log-prob preference; we control for fertility, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched resolution, and the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet surfaces the joke, dissociating the gate from length. 4) Some models may resolve and express humor uniformly (no gap) or fail to resolve at all; either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 5) Constructing translation-invariant two-stage jokes is hard, and funniness is subjective; we use structure-based humor (script-opposition, garden-path) that survives translation, native-verify, collect small per-language human funniness/comprehension ratings on a subset, restrict scored items to clear-consensus jokes, and analyze phonological puns separately as a known script-specific limit. 6) The resolution probe could latch onto surface cues rather than a genuine reinterpretation signal; the RESOLVING-vs-NON-RESOLVING foil contrast (both incongruous, only one resolves), cross-lingual invariance, the resolution-predicts-expression link, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Steering may harm fluency or leak languages; we report resolution-signal fidelity, output-language fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the suppression (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine expression gate rather than a generic accuracy lever. 9) The gate signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my prior semantic-anticipation (single-word N400 detection), metaphor (single-clause figurative), and garden-path-reanalysis (syntactic-only) proposals is essential; here the object is TWO-STAGE incongruity RESOLUTION for humor (semantic clash plus punchline reinterpretation) and the decoupling of its internal resolution from its behavioral expression across languages.

Name: crosslingual_analogy_mapping_gating
Title: Same Map, Different Roads: A Shared Relational-Analogy Representation Gated by a Language-Dependent Surface-Similarity Threshold in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When solving verbal analogies (A:B::C:?), a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of the RELATION between A and B, but the query language causally sets how much the model relies on that shared relational mapping versus SURFACE lexical/associative similarity: for the SAME analogy, the model completes it by correct relational mapping in some languages while defaulting to a surface-association distractor in others (usually lower-resource/typologically distant ones), producing predictable cross-lingual disagreement that is separable from vocabulary knowledge. We hypothesize (1) a shared middle-layer 'relation' direction that transfers zero-shot across languages; (2) the reliance on relational mapping vs surface similarity tracks resource level and typological distance; and (3) a small, localizable 'relational-mapping' signal that can be causally steered to force relational (vs associative) completion without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Analogical reasoning is a canonical relational-mapping task in cognitive science (Gentner's structure-mapping; Hummel & Holyoak's LISA). In NLP, word-analogy benchmarks (word2vec-style A:B::C:D) and recent LLM analogy work are overwhelmingly monolingual/English and behavioral, asking whether models solve analogies and whether they do so by memorized associations vs genuine relational mapping; recent probes (e.g., Mehmood et al. 2026) show LLMs default to high-probability training templates ('grounding gap', Einstellung effect) rather than abstract relations, but only in English. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for RELATIONAL analogy. My prior proposals cover typological-feature leakage into semantics, colexification of single concepts, and various decision-gating templates (calibration, abstention, processing-load, default-referent), but NONE address whether the RELATION in an analogy is a shared cross-lingual representation, whether reliance on relational mapping vs surface association is language-gated, or whether a relational-mapping signal is causally steerable. This differs from my colexification proposal (which concerns fusing two concepts within one word) because analogy requires MAPPING a relation across an entity pair (a second-order relational structure), and it is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of analogical relation-mapping vs surface-association reliance.
Abstract: Solving an analogy—'hand is to glove as foot is to ___'—requires abstracting the relation between the first pair and mapping it onto the second, rather than reaching for whatever word is most associated with 'foot'. Prior work shows English LLMs often default to surface association instead of genuine relational mapping, but whether this failure is language-dependent, and how it is implemented internally, is unknown. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent representation of an analogy's relation, and whether the query language governs how much it relies on that relational mapping versus surface lexical similarity. We build AnalogyMap, parallel four-term analogies (A:B::C:?) across 10 typologically diverse languages, each with a RELATIONALLY-CORRECT answer and a SURFACE-ASSOCIATION distractor (a word strongly associated with C but relationally wrong), spanning relation types (part-whole, function, antonym, category, causal). Behaviorally we measure per-language relational-mapping accuracy versus surface-association errors and test whether reliance on surface similarity tracks resource level and typological distance beyond vocabulary knowledge. We train a linear probe to decode the A–B relation from hidden states and test whether a single probe transfers zero-shot across languages, then decompose the cross-lingual gap into a shared relation estimate versus a language-set surface-similarity threshold. Via activation and path patching we localize a relational-mapping signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to force relational (over associative) completion—repairing surface-association errors, or in reverse inducing them—while leaving the surface language unchanged. We relate reliance on relational mapping to typological distance, reframing cross-lingual analogy gaps as a shared relational representation under a steerable, language-dependent surface-similarity gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (AnalogyMap): ~500 four-term analogies A:B::C:D spanning relation types (part-whole, function/tool, antonym, category-member, causal, agent-action). For each, provide the RELATIONALLY-CORRECT answer D and a SURFACE-ASSOCIATION distractor D' (a word strongly co-occurring/associated with C but relationally wrong, e.g., for 'foot' the associate 'shoe' when the relation demands a different mapping), verified via association norms + native speakers. Use content that translates cleanly; translate/native-verify into all 10 languages. Include a SURFACE-CONTROL stratum where the relationally-correct answer is ALSO the top associate (relation and association agree; no conflict) to bound the effect. Screen that the model KNOWS the relevant vocabulary in each language (so surface errors are not lexical ignorance). Answers as short single-token-decodable options where possible; use MC and cloze formats.
3) BEHAVIORAL LEAKAGE TEST: For each (analogy, language) record relationally-correct vs surface-association-distractor selection. KEY hypothesis: on the SAME analogy, lower-resource/typologically distant languages show more surface-association errors (weaker relational mapping), beyond vocabulary knowledge. Mixed-effects logistic regression of surface-error on (resource tier via URIEL, typological distance, relation type, language), analogy as random effect; compare against the SURFACE-CONTROL (should be language-flat, high accuracy). Report per-language relational-accuracy profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical analogies.
4) SHARED RELATION PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode the A–B RELATION TYPE (part-whole vs antonym vs function, etc.) on ENGLISH data and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report macro-F1/AUROC transfer as evidence of a language-independent relation representation. Compare to per-language-trained probes to bound shared-vs-specific. Measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the relation representation for the same analogy.
5) THRESHOLD-vs-ESTIMATE DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer relation estimate across languages (should be similar if shared) versus the emitted relational-vs-associative choice (which diverges). Define a per-language SURFACE-SIMILARITY THRESHOLD governing when the model abandons relational mapping for association; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a shifted threshold on a similar relation estimate rather than a different estimate. Correlate the threshold with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE RELATIONAL-MAPPING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that maps relationally and one that gives the surface-association answer on the SAME analogy, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips associative->relational WITHOUT changing the decoded relation estimate. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the relation representation FROM a relationally-mapping language into a surface-erroring run.
7) CAUSAL RELATIONAL STEERING (decisive): Derive a relational-mapping steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (relational-answer runs minus surface-association runs). Test (i) REPAIR: adding it to surface-erroring (lower-resource) languages increases relationally-correct completions toward a reference level; (ii) INDUCE: subtracting it makes relationally-mapping languages give surface-association answers; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where surface reliance was greatest; (iv) it changes ONLY relational-vs-associative selection, not the decoded relation estimate, vocabulary knowledge, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the SURFACE-CONTROL, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: relational-accuracy recovery, surface-association-induction rate (reverse), output-language fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering should change analogy completions but not unrelated answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: relation-type breakdown (which relations leak most); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single relational vector generalizes across relation types and languages; robustness across MC-vs-cloze formats and templates; dissociation from vocabulary knowledge by conditioning on known-word items.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language relational-accuracy and surface-error rate, surface-error regression controlling for vocabulary/resource/typology, cross-lingual relation-probe transfer F1/AUROC and representation similarity, estimate-similarity vs output-divergence (threshold) decomposition, threshold-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized relational-mapping layer, cross-lingual relation transplant repair rate, causal steering relational-repair and surface-induction rates, relation-estimate/output fidelity, surface-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Constructing analogies with a clean relational-vs-surface conflict that survives translation is delicate; we use association norms + native verification, restrict to relation types that translate cleanly, and use the SURFACE-CONTROL (relation and association agree) to bound the effect. 2) Surface errors could reflect vocabulary ignorance rather than a mapping gate; we screen per-language vocabulary knowledge and restrict causal analysis to known-word items, so residual surface reliance is a gating effect. 3) The threshold-vs-estimate split could be confounded if the relation estimate itself differs by language; we test this directly by comparing shared-probe relation estimates across languages rather than assuming the split. 4) Some models may map relationally in all languages (no gap) or default to association everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often the gap occurs via probe transfer and behavior. 5) The relation probe could latch onto surface cues rather than an abstract relation; the cross-lingual invariance test, the estimate-predicts-behavior link, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Causal steering may harm fluency or leak languages; we report relation-estimate fidelity, output-language fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the surface-induction (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine mapping gate rather than a generic accuracy lever. 8) The relational-mapping signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 9) Distinguishing from my colexification proposal is essential; here the object is second-order RELATIONAL mapping across an entity pair (analogy), not fusion of two concepts within one word, and the causal variable is the query-language-set reliance on relational mapping vs surface association.

Name: crosslingual_finetuned_skill_language_binding
Title: Does a Fine-Tuned Skill Speak Only Its Training Language? The Cross-Lingual Binding and Transfer of Newly-Learned Procedural Abilities
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM acquires a NEW procedural skill via fine-tuning (a novel task format/algorithm, not a fact) presented in a single training language, the skill is disproportionately bound to that language's execution path: it transfers to other languages far less reliably than the underlying task representation warrants, and this binding decomposes into a shared SKILL-ABSTRACTION component (the model learned the procedure language-independently) versus a language-specific EXECUTION-ACCESS component (the procedure is present internally but only invocable in the training language). We hypothesize (1) skill transfer to a new query language succeeds when the shared skill representation is correctly accessed, and fails otherwise; (2) the size and direction of transfer track typological/script distance from the training language; and (3) a small, localizable 'skill-access' signal can be causally steered (transplanted from the training language) to unlock the skill in a failing language without retraining, repairing execution-access failures but not abstraction failures.
Related Work: Cross-lingual transfer of fine-tuned abilities is studied behaviorally: zero-shot cross-lingual transfer after English fine-tuning (XTREME, BUFFET), and recent findings that instruction-tuning or task fine-tuning in one language partially transfers to others but unevenly. Blum et al. 2025 study whether FACTS transfer when representations unify (training dynamics), and my prior native_language_imprint proposal concerns which acquisition LANGUAGE a FACT is stored in. My crosslingual_task_vector_portability proposal concerns IN-CONTEXT (no-weight-update) task vectors and their portability. NONE address a WEIGHT-UPDATED, newly fine-tuned PROCEDURAL SKILL (an algorithm/task format learned via gradient updates), whether that skill is bound to its fine-tuning language, whether skill transfer decomposes into a shared skill-abstraction vs a language-specific execution-access component, or whether a skill-access signal can be causally transplanted to unlock the skill cross-lingually without retraining. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts, not for fine-tuned procedures. This is distinct: the object is a gradient-installed procedural ability and its cross-lingual accessibility, with a formation-tracing (checkpoint) + causal (transplant) account absent from all prior behavioral transfer work.
Abstract: When we teach a multilingual model a brand-new skill by fine-tuning it—say a novel puzzle format, a made-up arithmetic notation, or a specific reasoning procedure—in a single language, does the model learn the skill, or does it learn the skill-in-that-language? We ask whether a newly fine-tuned procedural ability is bound to its training language, and if transfer to other languages fails, whether the procedure was never abstracted or merely cannot be invoked outside the training language. Using LoRA fine-tuning, we install several novel procedural skills into open multilingual LLMs, each taught in exactly one training language, then evaluate execution in every language. Behaviorally we show these skills transfer across languages far worse than the underlying task representation warrants, with a gap that grows with typological and script distance from the training language. Mechanistically, we train a linear probe for the shared skill representation and test whether it is present in a failing language even when the model cannot execute the skill there—distinguishing SHARED-ABSTRACTION failures (the procedure is internally absent) from EXECUTION-ACCESS failures (present but not invocable). Tracking checkpoints, we trace when and how strongly the skill binds to its training language. In a decisive causal test we transplant the training language's skill-access representation into a failing language's run and show it unlocks the skill without retraining, repairing execution-access failures but not abstraction failures. Across five open models and eight typologically diverse languages, we reframe cross-lingual skill transfer as a decomposable, causally-repairable binding between a shared procedure and a language-specific access path.
Experiments:
1) MODELS: Open multilingual LLMs amenable to LoRA fine-tuning on an academic budget: Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B, Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Gemma-2-2B, BLOOM-1.7B (fine-tuning + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs).
2) NOVEL SKILL DATASET: Design ~6 NOVEL procedural skills that are genuinely new (not solvable zero-shot) and content-light so failures reflect procedure access, not knowledge: (a) a made-up arithmetic notation (e.g., a novel operator with defined rules), (b) a novel symbolic transformation (apply a taught rewrite system to a string), (c) a structured puzzle format (e.g., a small constraint-satisfaction template with a fixed solving procedure), (d) a novel multi-step reasoning schema, (e) a taught sorting/selection rule over lists, (f) a novel encoding/decoding cipher. Each skill has training examples and held-out test items, instantiated with language-native words but requiring no world knowledge, translated/native-verified into 8 typologically/script-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Turkish). Verify zero-shot baseline failure (skill is genuinely new).
3) SINGLE-LANGUAGE FINE-TUNING: For each skill, LoRA-fine-tune the model on examples in EXACTLY ONE training language, balanced across the 8 languages across skills; hold the number of training examples constant. Save checkpoints for formation tracing.
4) BEHAVIORAL TRANSFER TEST: Evaluate skill execution accuracy in all 8 languages. Hypothesis: accuracy is highest in the training language and decays with typological/script distance. Mixed-effects logistic regression of correctness on (query-lang==training-lang, URIEL distance, target-lang baseline ability), skill/item as random effects. Compare against a MULTI-LANGUAGE fine-tuning control (trained on all languages) to bound achievable transfer.
5) ABSTRACTION-vs-EXECUTION PROBE: Train a linear probe on the fine-tuned model's mid-layer hidden states (under the training language) to detect whether the skill's intermediate procedural state is represented; apply it to FAILING-language runs. Classify each cross-lingual failure as ABSTRACTION FAILURE (skill representation absent) vs EXECUTION-ACCESS FAILURE (present but skill not executed). Report the proportion per language and correlate with typological distance (predict execution-access failures dominate for close languages, abstraction failures for distant ones).
6) FORMATION TRACING: Across checkpoints, track (i) execution accuracy per language and (ii) probe accuracy for the shared skill representation, to see when the skill emerges internally vs when it becomes cross-lingually executable, and how strongly it binds to the training language over training.
7) CAUSAL SKILL-ACCESS TRANSPLANT (decisive): Derive a skill-access steering vector via difference-of-means over hidden states of successful training-language executions minus failed target-language executions (or transplant the training-language mid-layer skill-access representation via activation patching). Apply on held-out EXECUTION-ACCESS failures and test whether the skill is unlocked (correct execution) in the target language, while surface output language is preserved and general capability (multilingual MMLU subset) and unrelated skills are intact. Verify the transplant does NOT help ABSTRACTION failures (the procedure isn't there to invoke). Cross-check activation vs path patching.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: skill-type effects (symbolic vs arithmetic vs reasoning); training-language x script/family; model scale; probe layer/dimensionality; number of training examples; whether a single access-transplant vector generalizes across skills and languages; English-centric vs multilingual-centric pretraining.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-(skill, query-language) execution accuracy and training-language advantage, transfer decay with typological/script distance, proportion of abstraction vs execution-access failures with probe validation, checkpoint formation curves (skill-emergence vs cross-lingual-executability), causal transplant unlock rate on execution-access failures (and null effect on abstraction failures), output-language fidelity, general-capability and unrelated-skill retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Ensuring skills are truly novel and non-parametric is critical; we verify zero-shot failure per skill and use content-light symbolic/arithmetic tasks with no world knowledge. 2) LoRA fine-tuning may not install skills reliably in small models; we verify training-language installation per skill and include multiple model scales. 3) Distinguishing abstraction from execution-access failures depends on probe quality; we validate the probe on the training language (where ground truth is available), report AUROC, and confirm the split causally via transplant rather than relying on the probe alone. 4) Some skills may transfer robustly (no binding) or fail to abstract at all; either is informative, and we quantify how often each regime occurs rather than assuming binding. 5) The transplant may only partially unlock skills or harm fluency; we report unlock rate, output-language fidelity, and retention explicitly rather than claiming a free lunch. 6) Cross-lingual transfer could be confounded by tokenization fertility affecting effective training signal; we control token counts and report sensitivity. 7) Results may be model- and skill-specific; we test five models and six skills and report aggregate and per-condition results. 8) Distinguishing from my native_language_imprint (facts) and task_vector_portability (in-context) proposals is essential; here the object is a WEIGHT-UPDATED procedural SKILL and its cross-lingual execution-access binding, established via checkpoint formation tracing and causal transplant.

Name: crosslingual_cot_faithfulness_gap
Title: Does the Reasoning Show the Work, or Just Tell a Story? A Cross-Lingual Faithfulness Gap Between Chain-of-Thought and the Model's Internal Answer Computation
Short Hypothesis: The FAITHFULNESS of a chain-of-thought (CoT) to the model's actual internal answer computation is query-language-dependent: in some languages (typically high-resource) the visible reasoning trace causally drives the answer, while in others (typically lower-resource or typologically distant) the answer is committed internally BEFORE the trace and the trace is a post-hoc rationalization that does not change it. We hypothesize (1) the model reaches an internal answer commitment at an earlier point relative to the visible CoT in low-faithfulness languages, so intervening on the trace moves the answer less; (2) this faithfulness gap tracks resource level and typological distance and is separable from raw accuracy; and (3) the coupling between trace and answer is carried by a localizable signal whose strength is language-modulated, so faithfulness can be causally increased (making the trace matter) or decreased.
Related Work: Recent work shows open-weight models silently switch to English for internal reasoning even when the visible trace is in the target language (Hakimov et al. 2025), and that reasoning traces/summaries carry correctness signal unevenly (Algaba et al. 2026, observability ladder). Monolingual CoT-faithfulness work (Lanham et al. 2023; Turpin et al. 2023 'Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think'; Chua et al. 2024) measures whether English CoT reflects the true reason via perturbation/early-answering tests, but is English-only and offers no cross-lingual or mechanistic account. Multilingual reasoning work studies which language to reason in (Wang 2025), whether to deliberate, and reasoning-language drift (Lim 2026), but never asks whether the visible trace CAUSES the answer versus rationalizes it, nor whether that causal coupling varies by language. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but not for trace-answer coupling. This proposal is the first to (i) measure a cross-lingual CoT-faithfulness gap, (ii) decompose it into an early-commitment (trace-is-decorative) versus trace-drives-answer regime, and (iii) causally localize and steer the trace-answer coupling. It is distinct from my prior reasoning-language-steering (which language to think in), deliberation-gating (whether to think), and computational-depth (vertical layer-commitment) proposals: the object here is whether the emitted reasoning is causally load-bearing for the answer and how faithfulness is language-gated, with direct safety stakes for trace-based oversight.
Abstract: As models increasingly show their reasoning, we trust that trace to reveal how the answer was reached—and we use it to audit safety and correctness. But is the reasoning load-bearing, or is it a story told after the answer is already decided, and does this differ by language? We hypothesize a cross-lingual faithfulness gap: in some languages the visible chain-of-thought causally drives the answer, while in others the model commits internally before the trace, which then merely rationalizes a fixed answer—making trace-based oversight silently untrustworthy in exactly the languages where it is hardest to verify. We introduce CoTFaith, a battery of faithfulness tests applied cross-lingually across typologically and resource-diverse languages: perturbing/corrupting intermediate reasoning steps and measuring how much the final answer moves, forcing biased or mistaken steps and testing whether the answer follows, and early-answering probes that read the internal answer at successive points along the trace. Behaviorally we measure a per-language faithfulness score (how strongly answers track trace perturbations) and test whether it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond raw accuracy. Mechanistically, using logit-lens we locate the internal answer-commitment point relative to the visible trace per language, and train a probe reading the committed answer mid-trace; we then localize a 'trace-answer coupling' signal via activation and path patching and test whether its strength is language-modulated. In a decisive causal test we steer this coupling to make the trace causally matter in low-faithfulness languages (or make it decorative in high-faithfulness ones), without changing the surface language. We reframe multilingual CoT faithfulness as a measurable, localizable, steerable property with direct oversight implications.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Qwen3-14B (native thinking mode), Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATA: Parallel multi-step reasoning problems with verifiable answers and canonical step structure—MGSM (math word problems), multi-hop factual reasoning (Wikidata-derived, 2-3 hops), and symbolic/logic puzzles—native-verified translations, short scoreable answers, per-language tokenization fertility recorded.
3) BEHAVIORAL FAITHFULNESS TESTS (per language): For each solved problem, apply established CoT-faithfulness perturbations cross-lingually: (a) EARLY-ANSWERING: truncate the CoT at successive fractions and force an answer; faithfulness = how much the answer changes as more reasoning is revealed (a faithful trace should build to the answer). (b) STEP-CORRUPTION: inject an error into an intermediate step (e.g., alter a computed value / a factual hop) and measure whether the final answer follows the corrupted step. (c) BIASING-STEP: prepend a plausible-but-wrong suggested step and test whether the answer adopts it. Define a per-language FAITHFULNESS SCORE aggregating how strongly answers track trace content. KEY hypothesis: faithfulness is lower in lower-resource/typologically distant languages on the SAME problems. Mixed-effects regression of faithfulness on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, accuracy), problem as random effect; show the gap is separable from raw accuracy (condition on correct-in-both-languages items). Report per-language faithfulness profiles and cross-lingual disagreement.
4) INTERNAL ANSWER-COMMITMENT POINT: Using logit-lens/tuned-lens, at successive positions ALONG the generated trace, decode the model's current best answer and locate the COMMITMENT POINT (the trace fraction after which the internal top answer stops changing). Hypothesis: commitment occurs EARLIER (relative to the visible trace) in low-faithfulness languages—the answer is fixed before the reasoning is written—so the trace is decorative. Correlate commitment-point earliness with the behavioral faithfulness score within/across languages (link test).
5) MID-TRACE COMMITTED-ANSWER PROBE & TRANSFER: Train a linear probe on hidden states mid-trace to decode the eventual final answer on ENGLISH data and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; high early decodability in low-faithfulness languages evidences pre-committed answers. Compare to per-language probes.
6) LOCALIZE THE TRACE-ANSWER COUPLING: Via activation and path patching between a high-faithfulness run (trace drives answer) and a low-faithfulness run on matched problems, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer changes how much the trace influences the final answer. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs path patching. Test whether these coupling components are more strongly engaged in high-faithfulness languages.
7) CAUSAL COUPLING STEERING (decisive): Derive a trace-answer-coupling steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (high-faithfulness runs minus low-faithfulness runs). Test (i) INCREASE-FAITHFULNESS: adding it in low-faithfulness languages makes the answer track the (correct or corrupted) trace more—verified by re-running the step-corruption test and showing the answer now follows the trace, and by a later commitment point; (ii) DECREASE-FAITHFULNESS: subtracting it makes high-faithfulness languages' answers stop tracking the trace; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where the gap was largest; (iv) it changes ONLY trace-answer coupling, not the surface language or general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: faithfulness-gap closure, corrupted-step-following rate change, commitment-point shift, output-language fidelity, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering should change how much the trace matters, not unrelated answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: task-type breakdown (math vs factual vs logic); native thinking mode (Qwen3) vs prompted CoT; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched accuracy and by showing content-invariant steering changes faithfulness without changing tokenization; whether one coupling vector generalizes across tasks and languages.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language faithfulness score (early-answering, step-corruption, biasing-step) and its resource/typology regression controlling for accuracy/fertility, internal commitment-point earliness and its correlation with faithfulness, mid-trace committed-answer probe transfer AUROC, patch-localized coupling layer, causal steering faithfulness-gap closure and corrupted-step-following change with commitment-point shift, output-language fidelity, general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Faithfulness metrics are indirect proxies (perturbation-based); we use three complementary tests (early-answering, step-corruption, biasing-step) and require agreement, treating convergence as evidence rather than any single metric. 2) The faithfulness gap could reflect a knowledge/accuracy gap rather than a genuine rationalization difference; we condition on problems solved correctly in both the high- and low-faithfulness language, and the internal commitment-point analysis provides a mechanistic check independent of accuracy. 3) Tokenization fertility confounds trace length and perturbation granularity; we control for fertility, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched accuracy, and the content-invariant causal steering does not change tokenization yet shifts faithfulness, dissociating the two. 4) Some models/languages may be uniformly faithful or unfaithful, leaving little gap—this is itself an informative, publishable finding about the universality of CoT faithfulness, and we quantify how often a gap exists. 5) Logit-lens commitment-point estimates are noisy, especially for multi-token answers and low-resource languages; we prefer short single-token-decodable answers, validate lens fidelity per language, and cross-check tuned vs logit lens. 6) The coupling probe/steering could act as a generic accuracy lever rather than a faithfulness dial; the reverse (decrease-faithfulness) and reverse-consistency tests, plus verifying that increased faithfulness makes answers follow CORRUPTED (wrong) traces, guard against this—a genuine coupling increase should make the model follow the trace even into error. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models (including a native-thinking model), multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) The coupling signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 9) Safety framing: the decrease-faithfulness direction could be misused to make traces deceptive; we use it strictly as an interpretability diagnostic to demonstrate the coupling is causal, and emphasize the oversight risk that low-faithfulness languages already exhibit. 10) Distinguishing from my reasoning-language-steering, deliberation-gating, and computational-depth proposals is essential; here the object is whether the emitted reasoning trace is causally load-bearing for the answer and how that coupling is language-gated, not which language to reason in, whether to deliberate, or vertical layer-commitment depth.

Name: crosslingual_false_belief_tracking
Title: Believing What Isn't True, in Every Language: A Shared False-Belief Representation Whose Behavioral Expression Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When reading a false-belief (theory-of-mind) scenario, a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation that separates an agent's BELIEF from REALITY (tracking what the agent falsely thinks vs what is actually true), but whether that belief-tracking is behaviorally EXPRESSED (predicting the agent's action from their false belief rather than from reality) is gated by the query language: the SAME false-belief scenario is internally represented across languages yet answered correctly far less often in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so a model can internally 'know the agent's false belief' while behaviorally defaulting to reality.
Related Work: Theory-of-mind in LLMs is studied behaviorally and almost entirely monolingually: Kosinski-style false-belief (Sally-Anne / unexpected-contents) evaluations and multidimensional ToM benchmarks (e.g., Zhang 2026) measure whether models pass false-belief tasks in English, with no cross-lingual or mechanistic account. Cross-cultural/multilingual ToM work, where it exists, reports behavioral accuracy gaps without internal analysis. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for agent belief-states. My prior proposals cover typological-feature leakage into semantics and various decision-gating and detection-vs-expression templates (e.g., semantic anticipation, presupposition accommodation), but NONE address BELIEF TRACKING of another agent, the belief-vs-reality distinction, whether that representation is shared cross-lingually, whether its expression is language-gated, or whether it can be causally localized and steered. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of false-belief tracking: distinct from my irrealis (world-separation for hypotheticals, not agent beliefs) and evidentiality (information source, not another mind's false belief) proposals because the object is a SECOND agent's mental state and its divergence from reality.
Abstract: Understanding that someone can hold a false belief—Sally looks for her marble where she left it, not where it secretly moved—is a hallmark of theory of mind. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal representation that tracks an agent's belief separately from reality, and whether that internal belief-tracking is decoupled from how reliably it is behaviorally expressed across languages. We hypothesize that models internally represent the agent's false belief similarly across languages, but the query language gates whether that belief is surfaced in the answer, so the SAME false-belief scenario is tracked internally yet answered (predicting action from the false belief) far less often in lower-resource, typologically distant languages, where the model instead defaults to reality. We build BeliefTrack, parallel false-belief scenarios (Sally-Anne location-change and unexpected-contents) across 10 languages, each with a false-belief probe (where will the agent look? what does the agent think?) and a matched true-belief control where belief and reality coincide. Behaviorally we measure per-language false-belief accuracy and reality-default errors and test whether the gap tracks resource level and typological distance beyond knowledge. We train a linear 'belief-vs-reality' probe and test whether a single probe transfers zero-shot across languages, evidencing a shared belief representation, then decompose the expression gap into a shared belief-tracking component versus a language-set expression gate. Via activation and path patching we localize a belief-tracking signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model answer from the agent's false belief (or, in reverse, default to reality) while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual theory-of-mind gaps as a steerable gate over a shared belief representation.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (BeliefTrack): ~500 false-belief scenarios in two classic paradigms: (A) LOCATION-CHANGE (Sally-Anne: an object is moved while the agent is absent; probe: where will the agent look / where does the agent think it is); (B) UNEXPECTED-CONTENTS (a labeled container holds something unexpected; probe: what does an agent who hasn't looked inside think it contains). Each scenario has a FALSE-BELIEF probe whose correct answer follows the agent's (false) belief, a REALITY distractor (the true state), and a matched TRUE-BELIEF CONTROL where the agent witnessed the change so belief and reality coincide (bounds the effect and separates belief-tracking from basic comprehension). Include a NO-AGENT reality-only control. Keep scenario content fixed across languages; translate/native-verify. Use short single-token-decodable answers where possible. Screen that the model comprehends the base scenario (via the true-belief control) so false-belief failure is not mere reading failure.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (scenario, language) record false-belief-correct vs reality-default answers. KEY hypothesis: on the SAME scenario, false-belief accuracy is systematically lower (reality-default errors higher) in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond tokenization and comprehension. Mixed-effects logistic regression of reality-default error on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, true-belief-control accuracy), scenario as random effect; compare against the true-belief control (should be language-flatter, near-ceiling). Report per-language false-belief profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical scenarios.
4) SHARED BELIEF-vs-REALITY PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode the AGENT'S BELIEF STATE (belief-location / belief-contents, which diverges from reality in false-belief items) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent belief representation distinct from a reality probe (train a separate REALITY probe and show the two dissociate). Compare to per-language-trained probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the belief representation for the same scenario.
5) TRACKING-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: For each scenario, compare the shared mid-layer belief signal across languages (should be similar if belief-tracking is shared) versus the emitted answer (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal belief to surfaced answer per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar belief signal rather than weaker tracking. Correlate per-language gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens (identify the layer where the belief answer either overtakes or fails to overtake the reality answer).
6) LOCALIZE THE BELIEF-TRACKING / EXPRESSION SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that answers from the false belief and one that defaults to reality on the SAME scenario, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips reality-default -> false-belief WITHOUT changing the decoded reality state. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the belief representation FROM a high-expression language into a reality-defaulting run.
7) CAUSAL BELIEF STEERING (decisive): Derive a belief-tracking steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (false-belief-correct runs minus reality-default runs, matched content). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to reality-defaulting low-expression languages makes the model answer from the agent's false belief toward high-expression levels; (ii) SUPPRESS: subtracting it makes high-expression languages default to reality even on clear false-belief items; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where expression was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY belief-vs-reality answering, not the decoded reality state, scenario content, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the true-belief control, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: false-belief accuracy recovery, reality-default-induction rate (reverse), output-language fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering should change belief-vs-reality answers but not unrelated or reality-only-control answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: paradigm breakdown (location-change vs unexpected-contents); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single belief vector generalizes across paradigms and languages; robustness across templates and MC-vs-cloze-vs-free formats; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched belief-tracking and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces the false-belief answer without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language false-belief accuracy and reality-default error, expression regression controlling for fertility/comprehension/resource, cross-lingual belief-probe transfer AUROC and its dissociation from a reality probe, cross-lingual belief-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), tracking-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized belief-tracking layer, cross-lingual belief transplant recovery rate, causal steering false-belief-recovery and reality-default-induction rates, belief-signal/output fidelity, true-belief-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The tracking-vs-expression split could be confounded if the belief signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by comparing shared-probe belief decoding across languages rather than assuming the split, and report how much of the gap is tracking vs gate. 2) False-belief failure could reflect scenario-comprehension failure rather than a belief-expression gate; we use the matched true-belief control and comprehension screening so residual reality-default errors reflect belief tracking, not reading. 3) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy; we control for fertility, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched belief-tracking, and the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet surfaces the false-belief answer, dissociating the gate from length. 4) Some models may pass false-belief tasks uniformly across languages (no gap) or fail everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of ToM in LLMs, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 5) Kosinski-style false-belief tasks may be partly memorized/contaminated; we generate novel scenarios with fresh entities and settings and verify above-chance true-belief-control performance to ensure genuine comprehension. 6) The belief probe could latch onto surface cues rather than a genuine belief representation; the explicit dissociation from a reality probe, the cross-lingual invariance test, the tracking-predicts-behavior link, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Steering may harm fluency or leak languages; we report belief-signal fidelity, output-language fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the suppression (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine belief-expression gate rather than a generic accuracy lever. 9) The gate signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my irrealis (hypothetical-world separation) and evidentiality (information source) proposals is essential; here the object is a SECOND agent's belief state and its divergence from reality, the core of false-belief theory of mind.

Name: crosslingual_risk_attitude_reweighting
Title: Bolder in Some Tongues: A Shared Value/Probability Representation Reweighted by the Query Language in Multilingual LLMs' Decisions Under Risk
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs compute a largely language-independent internal representation of a gamble's outcomes and probabilities (an expected-value/prospect estimate), but the query language causally reweights this shared representation into a risk attitude at the language-specific decoding layers: for the SAME lottery, the model is systematically more risk-seeking/loss-averse or overweights small probabilities differently depending on the query language, tracking each language community's cultural risk norms and typological/resource distance. We hypothesize (1) a shared middle-layer value/probability representation that transfers zero-shot across languages; (2) cross-lingual disagreement in choices on identical gambles arises from a language-conditioned late-layer REWEIGHTING (a risk-attitude gain dial and a probability-distortion dial), not from a different underlying value estimate; and (3) a small, localizable 'risk-attitude' signal that can be causally steered to make the model more or less risk-seeking without changing the described gamble or surface language.
Related Work: Prospect-theory behavior in LLMs is now well-documented but ENTIRELY monolingual/English-centric: Jia et al. 2024 estimate risk preference, probability weighting, and loss aversion for commercial LLMs in a context-free setting; Payne 2025 shows prospect-theory framing effects emerge and are 'embedded within the language of the scenarios' (military vs civilian frames); Wang et al. 2025 ('Rethinking Prospect Theory for LLMs') show PT parameters are unstable under linguistic/epistemic uncertainty; Zhang et al. 2026 and Dhameja 2026 replicate/critique the fourfold pattern and persona effects. None examine whether the QUERY LANGUAGE itself modulates risk attitude or probability weighting, whether risk preference is a shared internal representation reweighted per language, or whether it can be causally localized and steered. Cross-cultural behavioral economics establishes that risk attitudes differ across cultures (e.g., cross-country prospect-theory replications), but this has not been tested as a mechanistic property of multilingual LLMs. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS, and my prior proposals cover moral valence, affect intensity, concession, and precision under the shared-estimate-plus-language-gate template. This proposal is distinct because the object is decision-making UNDER RISK—the nonlinear probability-weighting and loss-aversion machinery of prospect theory—not moral acceptability, descriptive affect, bargaining concession, or numeric rounding. It is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of language-modulated risk attitude and probability distortion, with direct stakes for LLM agents making financial/medical/insurance decisions across languages.
Abstract: Large language models increasingly make or advise on decisions under risk—investments, insurance, treatment trade-offs. A fairness- and safety-critical question is whether the query language changes how much risk the model is willing to take on identical gambles. Prior work shows LLMs exhibit prospect-theory patterns (risk aversion for gains, loss aversion, overweighting small probabilities), but entirely in English. We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of a gamble's outcomes and probabilities, but the query language causally reweights this shared representation into a risk attitude at the language-specific decoding layers, so the SAME lottery is chosen more or less boldly depending on the language, tracking cultural risk norms and typological distance. We build RiskWeigh, parallel lottery-choice and certainty-equivalent problems across 12 languages, spanning the classic prospect-theory design (gains/losses, small/large probabilities), with the numbers and options held fixed. Behaviorally we estimate per-language prospect-theory parameters (risk aversion, loss aversion, probability-weighting curvature) and test whether they shift with query language beyond the described gamble. We train a linear probe for the shared value/probability estimate and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose cross-lingual choice disagreement into a shared estimate versus a language-conditioned reweighting (a risk-attitude gain and a probability-distortion dial). Via activation and path patching we localize a risk-attitude signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model more or less risk-seeking—closing or opening cross-lingual choice gaps—while leaving the gamble and surface language unchanged. We reframe multilingual risk-preference inconsistency as a shared valuation under a steerable, language-dependent reweighting.
Experiments: 1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/culturally/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili, Korean). 2) DATASET (RiskWeigh): ~500 decision-under-risk items following the canonical prospect-theory paradigm: (a) BINARY CHOICE between a sure amount and a lottery, crossing GAIN vs LOSS domain and SMALL vs LARGE probability (the fourfold-pattern design); (b) CERTAINTY-EQUIVALENT elicitation (multiple-choice-list) to estimate value/weighting functions; (c) a matched RISK-NEUTRAL control where the expected-value-optimal choice is unambiguous (to bound the effect and separate risk attitude from arithmetic error). Keep all numbers, probabilities, and options identical across languages; translate/native-verify the surrounding wording. Record per-language tokenization fertility and per-language cultural risk-norm proxies (e.g., cross-country prospect-theory / uncertainty-avoidance indices) coded from published behavioral-economics references, treated as graded predictors. 3) BEHAVIORAL PARAMETER TEST: For each (item, language) record the choice / certainty equivalent. Estimate per-language prospect-theory parameters (risk-aversion / value-function curvature, loss aversion lambda, probability-weighting elevation & curvature) via the standard fitting workflow (as in Jia 2024). KEY hypothesis: parameters shift systematically with query language on identical gambles, and the shift tracks cultural risk norms and resource level beyond the described gamble. Mixed-effects models of choice on (language, domain [gain/loss], probability [small/large], numeric EV, cultural-norm code, resource tier via URIEL), item as random effect; test the language main effect and language x domain / language x probability interactions. Compare against the risk-neutral control (should be language-flat). Report per-language parameter profiles and cross-lingual choice-disagreement on identical lotteries. 4) SHARED VALUE/PROBABILITY PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-choice position; train linear probes to decode (i) the gamble's expected value / outcome magnitudes and (ii) the stated probability, on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report R^2/AUROC as evidence of a language-independent value/probability estimate, plus cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the estimate for the same item. Show the estimate is internally similar across languages even when the emitted choice differs. 5) LOCATE LANGUAGE-TRANSITION BAND: Per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens to anchor the mid vs output decomposition. 6) DISAGREEMENT DECOMPOSITION: For each item, compare the shared mid-layer value/probability estimate across languages (should be similar if shared) versus the emitted choice (which disagrees). Define REWEIGHTING = shift from the shared estimate to the choice per language, decomposed into a risk-attitude gain (value-function scaling) and a probability-distortion component (weighting-function shift). Test whether cross-lingual disagreement is explained by reweighting (similar estimate, divergent choice) rather than a different estimate. Correlate per-language reweighting magnitude/direction with cultural risk norms and typological/resource distance (Spearman). 7) LOCALIZE RISK-ATTITUDE COMPONENTS: Run the same gamble in a risk-averse vs risk-seeking language; via activation and path patching across layers/heads/MLPs find the minimal component set whose transfer flips the choice / shifts the certainty equivalent. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the risk-attitude components from a firm language into an over-risk-seeking run. 8) CAUSAL RISK-ATTITUDE STEERING (decisive): Derive a risk-attitude steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (risk-seeking-choice runs minus risk-averse-choice runs, matched gamble). Test (i) MORE / LESS RISK-SEEKING: adding/subtracting it shifts choices and certainty equivalents on held-out gambles in the predicted direction; (ii) it works cross-lingually and can override a language's default risk attitude, closing cross-lingual choice gaps toward a reference; (iii) it changes ONLY the risk attitude, not the decoded value/probability estimate, the described gamble, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the risk-neutral control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset); (iv) REVERSE-consistency: the steering magnitude needed correlates with the source-target risk-attitude distance, and (v) DOSE-RESPONSE: scaling the vector produces graded shifts in fitted prospect-theory parameters. Baselines: per-language temperature, prompt-based risk instructions, translate-to-English. Metrics: choice/CE shift, cross-lingual gap closure, value/probability-estimate fidelity, output-language fidelity, risk-neutral-control retention, general-QA retention. 9) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: gain-vs-loss and small-vs-large-probability breakdown (which prospect-theory component leaks most: value-function vs probability-weighting); is English/WEIRD the default the model reweights away from?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank risk subspace; robustness across templates and choice-vs-CE formats; whether one steering vector generalizes across gambles and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched estimate and showing content-invariant steering shifts risk attitude without changing tokenization. EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language prospect-theory parameters and their cultural-norm/resource regression, cross-lingual value/probability-probe transfer R^2/AUROC and representation similarity, estimate-similarity vs choice-divergence (reweighting) decomposition split into value-function vs probability-weighting components, reweighting-vs-cultural-distance correlation, patch-localized risk-attitude layer, cross-lingual risk-attitude transplant repair rate, causal steering choice/CE-shift with dose-response in fitted parameters, value/probability-estimate and output fidelity, risk-neutral-control and general-QA retention, comparison to temperature / prompt-instruction / translate-to-English baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Instruction-tuned models may refuse or give degenerate/always-safe choices; we use both choice and log-probability-based selection and certainty-equivalent elicitation, report refusal/degeneracy rates, and select model scales that exhibit measurable prospect-theory patterns (per Jia 2024). 2) Prospect-theory parameter estimates can be noisy and unstable (Wang 2025 shows sensitivity to linguistic uncertainty); we use the full multiple-choice-list CE paradigm, multiple items per cell, bootstrap confidence intervals, and treat instability itself as informative, focusing the causal claims on choice shifts and dose-response rather than only fitted parameters. 3) The estimate-vs-reweighting split could be confounded if the value/probability estimate itself differs by language; we test this directly by comparing shared-probe estimates across languages rather than assuming the split, and report how much disagreement is estimate vs reweighting. 4) Choice differences could be driven by arithmetic/expected-value miscomputation rather than risk attitude; the risk-neutral control (unambiguous EV-optimal choice), the value/probability-estimate fidelity checks under steering, and conditioning on items where the EV is correctly represented dissociate these. 5) Tokenization fertility confounds; we control for fertility, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched estimate, and the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts risk attitude, dissociating the two. 6) Cultural-risk-norm coding is coarse and debated; we treat it as a graded predictor, report sensitivity to alternative codings, and note that a language effect is establishable even if its cultural correlate is weak. 7) Some models/languages may show no cross-lingual risk shift (uniform attitude); this is itself an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often a shift exists. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) Causal steering may harm fluency or shift the value estimate rather than only the attitude; we report value/probability-estimate fidelity, output fidelity, control and general-QA retention, and use dose-response and reverse-consistency to ensure a genuine risk-attitude dial rather than a generic lever. 10) A single risk-attitude direction may be an oversimplification across the value-function and probability-weighting components; we test low-rank subspaces and separate value vs weighting directions and report where a scalar dial is insufficient. 11) Misuse concern: risk-attitude steering could be abused to make agents recklessly risk-seeking; we frame and use it strictly as an interpretability/fairness diagnostic on benign decision scenarios and report retention rather than deploying it. 12) Distinguishing from my moral-valence, affect-intensity, concession, and precision proposals is essential; here the object is decision-making UNDER RISK—nonlinear probability weighting and loss aversion—not normative moral judgment, descriptive emotion, bargaining concession, or numeric rounding.

Name: crosslingual_sound_symbolism_grounding
Title: Bouba or Kiki, in Every Language? Whether Text-Only Multilingual Models Recover a Shared Sound-Symbolic Mapping and How Ideophone Typology Gates Its Expression
Short Hypothesis: Despite reading only graphemes/subwords, multilingual LLMs recover a largely language-independent internal sound-symbolic mapping—the cross-linguistically universal iconic link between phoneme features and meaning dimensions (roundness/spikiness, bigness/smallness, brightness/darkness), as in the bouba/kiki effect—but whether this mapping is behaviorally EXPRESSED (matching a novel wordform to the iconically-congruent referent) is gated by the query language: the SAME nonce word is mapped congruently across languages internally yet surfaced far more reliably in languages with rich, grammaticalized ideophone/sound-symbolic systems (e.g., Japanese, Korean, many Bantu languages) and far more weakly in ideophone-sparse languages. We hypothesize (1) a shared middle-layer sound-symbolism direction that transfers zero-shot across languages; (2) expression strength tracks a language's ideophone-richness typology and typological/script distance; and (3) a small, localizable 'iconicity' signal that can be causally steered to force or suppress congruent mapping without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Sound symbolism (bouba/kiki; Kohler; Ramachandran & Hubbard; Sidhu & Pexman) and the maluma/takete size- and shape-symbolism effects are among the most robust cross-linguistic universals in psycholinguistics, and languages differ sharply in whether they grammaticalize iconicity through ideophone systems (Dingemanse; rich in Japanese/Korean/Bantu, sparse in e.g. English). In NLP, sound symbolism is barely studied: a few monolingual English probes ask whether embeddings capture bouba/kiki-style associations, and speech/phoneme-model work studies phonetic representation (Kim 2025; Goriely 2025) on spoken input—none on standard grapheme/subword text LLMs, none cross-lingual, and none mechanistic. My prior crosslingual_phonological_reasoning proposal concerns rhyme/homophone/pun (whether written words SOUND alike); this proposal is distinct: the object is sound-MEANING iconicity (whether a wordform's phonetic shape maps to a semantic dimension like size or roundness), a different psycholinguistic phenomenon grounded in ideophone typology rather than phonological form-similarity. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies iconicity. No prior work asks whether a text-only multilingual LLM recovers a shared sound-symbolic mapping, whether its internal iconicity is decoupled from behavioral expression, whether ideophone-richness typology gates that expression, or whether an iconicity signal can be causally localized and steered.
