Abstract: People robustly agree that 'bouba' names a round shape and 'kiki' a spiky one, that 'mil' is smaller than 'mal', and this sound-meaning iconicity is a near-universal of human language—yet languages differ enormously in how much they grammaticalize it, from ideophone-rich Japanese and Bantu languages to ideophone-sparse English. We ask whether a multilingual LLM, which reads only text and never hears sound, nonetheless recovers a shared, language-independent sound-symbolic mapping, and whether a language's ideophone typology governs how strongly that mapping is behaviorally expressed. We build IconProbe, a set of novel nonce wordforms paired with iconically-congruent and incongruent referents across three well-established dimensions (roundness/spikiness, bigness/smallness, brightness/darkness), with matched forced-choice and generation probes rendered in 8 typologically diverse languages. Behaviorally we measure per-language congruent-mapping accuracy and test whether it tracks ideophone-richness typology beyond tokenization. We train a linear sound-symbolism probe on hidden states and test whether a single probe transfers zero-shot across languages, evidencing a shared iconicity direction, then decompose the cross-lingual expression gap into a shared mapping component versus a language-set expression gate. Via activation and path patching we localize an iconicity signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to force congruent mapping in ideophone-sparse languages (or suppress it in rich ones) while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual iconicity as a measurable, steerable property of text-only multilingual models grounded in ideophone typology.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 languages spanning ideophone-richness typology: rich, grammaticalized ideophone/mimetic systems (Japanese, Korean, Swahili, Zulu), moderate (Turkish, Russian), and sparse (English, German), coded for ideophone richness from typological references (Dingemanse; ideophone surveys) plus URIEL for typological distance; treat ideophone-richness as a graded predictor. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (IconProbe): ~400 novel NONCE wordforms (guaranteed non-lexical, generated to vary phoneme features known to drive sound symbolism—rounded vs unrounded vowels, sonorant vs obstruent/stop consonants, voiced vs voiceless), each paired with a target semantic dimension: (A) ROUNDNESS/SPIKINESS (match to round vs spiky shape descriptions), (B) BIGNESS/SMALLNESS (match to a large vs small referent), (C) BRIGHTNESS/DARKNESS/VALENCE (match to bright/positive vs dark/negative referent). For each nonce form define the iconically-CONGRUENT referent (from the sound-symbolism literature) and an INCONGRUENT distractor. Probes: forced-choice ('Which is more likely a bouba/kiki-style match?'), generation ('Describe what <nonce> most likely refers to'), and a graded rating. Render each nonce form and probe naturally in all 8 languages/scripts (transliterating the nonce form into each script with native verification of pronunciation-equivalence); include a LEXICAL control (real words with known referents, where iconicity is irrelevant) to bound the effect. Record per-language tokenization fertility of the nonce forms.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (nonce form, language) measure congruent-mapping accuracy and the log-prob preference for congruent vs incongruent referent. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME nonce form, congruent mapping is expressed more strongly in ideophone-rich languages and weakly in sparse ones, beyond tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of congruent-mapping on (ideophone richness, dimension, language, tokenization fertility, resource tier via URIEL), nonce form as random effect; compare against the LEXICAL control (should show no ideophone-typology effect). Report per-language expression profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical nonce forms; also validate a baseline bouba/kiki replication in English against known human effects.
4) SHARED SOUND-SYMBOLISM PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the nonce-form position; train a linear probe to decode the iconic dimension value (round vs spiky / big vs small / bright vs dark implied by the form's phonetics) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot to other languages; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent sound-symbolism direction. Compare to per-language-trained probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the iconicity representation for the same transliterated nonce form across scripts.
5) MAPPING-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: For each nonce form, compare the shared mid-layer iconicity signal across languages (should be similar if the mapping is shared) versus behavioral expression (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal iconicity to surfaced behavior per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar mapping rather than weaker mapping. Correlate per-language gate strength with ideophone richness and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes.
6) LOCALIZE THE ICONICITY / EXPRESSION SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that expresses the congruent mapping and one that does not on the SAME nonce form, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer makes the congruent mapping surface WITHOUT changing the decoded iconicity signal. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the iconicity representation FROM an ideophone-rich language into a sparse-language run.
7) CAUSAL ICONICITY STEERING (decisive): Derive an iconicity steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (congruent-mapping runs minus incongruent runs at matched internal signal). Test (i) FORCE: adding it to ideophone-sparse languages increases congruent mapping toward rich-language levels; (ii) SUPPRESS: subtracting it silences congruent mapping in rich languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where expression was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY iconic mapping, not the decoded iconicity signal or surface language (fidelity), does not move the LEXICAL control, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: expression-gap closure, congruent-mapping recovery, suppression-induction rate (reverse), output-language fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes nonce-form mapping but not real-word or unrelated answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: dimension breakdown (shape vs size vs brightness); which phoneme features drive the effect internally; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; token-pooling (nonce forms split into varying subwords—report sensitivity); whether a single iconicity vector generalizes across dimensions and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal signal and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces the mapping without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language congruent-mapping accuracy and log-prob preference, expression regression controlling for fertility/resource with ideophone-richness effect, English bouba/kiki human-effect replication, cross-lingual sound-symbolism probe transfer AUROC and cross-script representation similarity, mapping-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-typology correlation, patch-localized iconicity layer, cross-lingual iconicity transplant recovery rate, causal steering expression-gap closure and suppression-induction rates, iconicity-signal/output fidelity, lexical-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Text-only models may lack any genuine sound-symbolic mapping since they never access phonetics directly (only orthography, which correlates imperfectly with sound); this is itself an informative, publishable finding about the limits of latent iconicity, and we quantify how often a mapping is present via probe transfer and the English bouba/kiki replication. 2) The mapping-vs-expression split could be confounded if the iconicity signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by comparing shared-probe iconicity across languages rather than assuming the split. 3) Tokenization fertility confounds nonce-form representation and the log-prob preference; we control for fertility, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal signal, and the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet surfaces the mapping, dissociating the gate from length. 4) Transliterating nonce forms across scripts may not preserve intended phonetics (e.g., vowel roundedness cues); we native-verify pronunciation-equivalence, treat script as a covariate, and analyze within-script effects separately. 5) Ideophone-richness coding is coarse and debated; we use documented typological surveys, treat richness as a graded predictor, and report sensitivity to alternative codings. 6) Congruent-referent ground truth relies on the sound-symbolism literature and may be graded; we restrict scored items to well-established form-meaning associations and analyze weaker ones separately, and collect small human ratings on a subset. 7) The iconicity probe could latch onto surface orthographic cues rather than a genuine phonetics-to-meaning mapping; the cross-script invariance test, the mapping-predicts-behavior link, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) Steering may harm fluency or leak languages; we report iconicity-signal fidelity, output-language fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the suppression (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine expression gate. 10) The gate signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my prior crosslingual_phonological_reasoning proposal is essential; here the object is sound-MEANING iconicity (form-to-semantic-dimension mapping) grounded in ideophone typology, not rhyme/homophone form-similarity.

Name: crosslingual_approximate_number_system
Title: Weber's Law in Every Language? A Shared Approximate-Number-System Signal Whose Expression Is Gated by the Query Language in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Text-only multilingual LLMs possess a largely language-independent internal Approximate Number System (ANS): a ratio-dependent magnitude representation whose comparison acuity obeys Weber's law (accuracy on 'which is more?' depends on the ratio of the two quantities, not their absolute difference). We hypothesize (1) a shared middle-layer numerical-magnitude direction that transfers zero-shot across languages and exhibits the signature ratio/distance effect; (2) the internal ANS acuity is similar across languages, but whether it is behaviorally EXPRESSED (correct approximate comparison) is gated by the query language, so the SAME comparison is answered correctly far less often in lower-resource / high-fertility languages despite an intact internal signal; and (3) a small, localizable 'magnitude-comparison' signal that can be causally steered to sharpen or blunt approximate-number acuity without changing the surface language.
Related Work: The Approximate Number System and its Weber-law ratio signature are among the most robust findings in numerical cognition (Dehaene; Feigenson, Dehaene & Spelke; Halberda). In NLP, numeracy probing shows monolingual LLMs place numbers on a roughly log-scaled subspace, and Montero et al. (2025) recently examine approximate-number-system biases and quantifier scales in MULTIMODAL LLMs cross-linguistically—but purely behaviorally, on image-grounded numerosity, with no internal/mechanistic account and no text-only analysis. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never for approximate numerical magnitude. My prior proposals concern spelled-number magnitude distortion (number naming), dynamic running tallies, assumed measurement units, and reported precision/rounding; NONE address the psychophysical ANS—the ratio-dependent approximate-comparison acuity governed by Weber's law—as a shared cross-lingual representation, whether its internal acuity is decoupled from behavioral expression across languages, or whether a magnitude-comparison signal is causally steerable. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of an ANS-like signal in text-only multilingual models, distinct from behavioral multimodal numerosity work and from exact-arithmetic numeracy probing.
Abstract: A hallmark of numerical cognition is the Approximate Number System: humans and animals compare quantities approximately, and their accuracy depends on the ratio of the two quantities (Weber's law)—80 vs 100 is harder than 20 vs 100. We ask whether a text-only multilingual LLM, reading only digits and number words, nonetheless builds a shared, language-independent approximate-number representation with this ratio signature, and whether that internal acuity is decoupled from how reliably it is behaviorally expressed across languages. We build ANSProbe, parallel approximate magnitude-comparison items ('which is more, X or Y?') across 10 typologically and resource-diverse languages, with the numeric ratio between the two quantities systematically varied to trace the Weber curve, plus an easy large-ratio control. Behaviorally we test whether comparison accuracy follows the ratio/distance effect in every language and whether the effect's steepness (an ANS-acuity proxy) tracks language resource level and typological distance beyond tokenization. We train a linear numerical-magnitude probe and test whether a single probe transfers zero-shot across languages and reproduces the ratio effect internally, then decompose the cross-lingual accuracy gap into a shared ANS-acuity component versus a language-set expression gate. Via activation and path patching we localize a magnitude-comparison signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to sharpen approximate-comparison accuracy in low-expression languages (or blunt it), while leaving the surface language and the compared numbers unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual number-sense gaps as a shared, Weber-law-obeying ANS signal under a steerable, language-dependent expression gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource/fertility-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (ANSProbe): ~600 approximate magnitude-comparison items 'Which is more, X or Y?' where X and Y are large quantities (in contexts discouraging exact computation, e.g., 'a jar with about X marbles vs about Y marbles', or bare numbers presented for rapid judgment). Systematically vary the RATIO r = larger/smaller across a graded range (e.g., 1.05, 1.1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 4) to trace the Weber curve, and vary absolute magnitude to test scale-invariance (ratio should matter, not absolute difference). Present numbers as DIGITS and, in a sub-stratum, as spelled NUMBER WORDS. Include an EASY control (large ratio, unambiguous) and an EXACT control (small numbers where exact comparison is trivial) to bound the effect. Translate/native-verify surrounding text; keep X and Y identical across languages. Record per-language tokenization fertility. Answers scored via language-agnostic normalized matching (which option).
3) BEHAVIORAL WEBER-CURVE TEST: For each language, plot comparison accuracy vs ratio r. KEY hypothesis: accuracy rises with r (ratio/distance effect) and is scale-invariant (depends on r, not absolute difference)—the ANS signature. Fit each language's psychometric curve and extract an ACUITY proxy (curve steepness / equivalent Weber fraction). Mixed-effects logistic regression of correctness on (log-ratio, absolute magnitude, language, tokenization fertility, resource tier via URIEL), item as random effect; confirm log-ratio dominates absolute magnitude (scale invariance) and test whether per-language acuity tracks resource/typological distance beyond fertility. Compare digits vs number-words. The EXACT control should show ceiling, language-flat accuracy.
4) SHARED MAGNITUDE PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the comparison/answer position; train a linear probe to decode the numerical magnitude (regress to log-value) and a comparison probe (which is larger) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report R^2/AUROC as evidence of a language-independent magnitude representation. CRITICAL: test whether the INTERNAL comparison signal itself shows the ratio effect (probe confidence / margin scales with r) and whether this internal acuity is SIMILAR across languages (cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the magnitude representation) even when behavioral accuracy differs.
5) ACUITY-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: For each item, compare the shared mid-layer internal comparison signal across languages (should be similar if ANS acuity is shared) versus the emitted answer (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal signal to surfaced answer per language; test whether cross-lingual accuracy differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar internal signal rather than weaker internal acuity. Correlate per-language gate strength with resource tier, fertility, and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE MAGNITUDE-COMPARISON SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that answers correctly and one that errs on the SAME hard-ratio item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips error->correct WITHOUT changing the decoded magnitudes. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the internal comparison representation FROM a high-expression language into an erroring low-expression run.
7) CAUSAL ACUITY STEERING (decisive): Derive a magnitude-comparison steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (correct-comparison runs minus errored runs at matched ratio). Test (i) SHARPEN: adding it to low-expression languages increases hard-ratio comparison accuracy toward high-expression levels (shifting the Weber curve); (ii) BLUNT: subtracting it degrades approximate-comparison accuracy in high-expression languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where expression was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY approximate-comparison accuracy, not the decoded magnitudes or surface language (fidelity), does not move the EXACT control, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: acuity-gap closure (Weber-curve shift), blunting-induction rate (reverse), output-language fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering should change approximate comparisons but not exact-control or unrelated answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: digits vs number-words; scale-invariance check; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single steering vector generalizes across ratios and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched ratio and by showing content-invariant steering shifts the Weber curve without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language Weber curves and acuity proxy, scale-invariance (log-ratio dominates absolute magnitude), acuity regression controlling for fertility/resource, cross-lingual magnitude-probe transfer R^2/AUROC and internal ratio effect, cross-lingual internal-acuity similarity (CKA/cosine), acuity-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized magnitude-comparison layer, cross-lingual signal transplant recovery rate, causal steering Weber-curve shift and blunting-induction rates, magnitude/output fidelity, exact-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Models might solve comparisons by exact computation rather than an approximate ANS, erasing the Weber signature; we discourage exact computation via 'about X' framing and rapid-judgment prompts, test scale-invariance (a genuine ANS depends on ratio not absolute difference), and treat the presence/absence of the ratio effect as an empirical question—its absence is itself informative. 2) The acuity-vs-expression split could be confounded if the internal signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by comparing shared-probe internal acuity across languages rather than assuming the split, and report how much of the gap is acuity vs gate. 3) Tokenization fertility confounds number representation and accuracy; we control for fertility, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched ratio, and the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts the Weber curve, dissociating the gate from length. 4) Some models may show a language-invariant Weber curve (no gap) or no ratio effect at all; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of an LLM ANS, and we quantify how often the gap and the ratio effect occur. 5) The magnitude probe could latch onto surface digit tokens rather than an abstract magnitude; the internal ratio effect, cross-lingual invariance, and cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report magnitude/output fidelity, exact-control and general-QA retention, and use the blunting (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine approximate-comparison signal rather than a generic boost. 8) The signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 9) Distinguishing from Montero et al. (multimodal, behavioral) and from my number-naming/units/precision proposals is essential; here the object is the text-only, ratio-dependent APPROXIMATE-NUMBER acuity (Weber's law) and the decoupling of its internal signal from behavioral expression across languages.

Name: crosslingual_belief_consistency_gating
Title: One Model, Many Minds: A Shared Truth-Commitment Representation Whose Consistency Is Broken by a Language-Dependent Contradiction-Tolerance Gate
Short Hypothesis: For factual claims that a multilingual LLM can verify, the model computes a largely language-independent internal 'truth-commitment' representation of whether a proposition is true, but the query language causally sets how tightly the model enforces logical consistency across mutually contradictory claims: when independently asked to affirm P and to affirm not-P (about the SAME fact) in different languages, the model holds internally incompatible commitments more readily in some languages (typically lower-resource / typologically distant) than others, producing a cross-lingual self-contradiction rate that is separable from underlying knowledge and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable contradiction-tolerance signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Cross-lingual factual consistency is documented behaviorally: models give different factual answers to the same question across languages (Qi et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2025 'Lost in Multilinguality'; Ai 2025), and knowledge-editing work shows facts are unevenly shared across languages (Ifergan et al. 2024). Monolingual work on logical/negation consistency shows models can simultaneously affirm P and not-P (belief inconsistency, LoNLI/self-contradiction studies) but is English-only. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts. NONE (i) frame per-language SELF-CONTRADICTION (holding P and not-P) as a shared truth-commitment representation gated by a language-dependent contradiction-tolerance threshold, (ii) dissociate this consistency-gate from underlying knowledge and from mere answer-variance across languages, or (iii) causally localize and steer a contradiction-tolerance signal to equalize logical consistency across languages. This differs from my prior calibration proposal (know/don't-know confidence on answered items) and from cross-lingual answer-variance work (which fact the model gives) because the object here is whether the model maintains a NON-CONTRADICTORY truth commitment across languages, a distinct logical-coherence property with a distinct mechanistic prediction (a shared truth axis under a language-set consistency gate).
Abstract: A single multilingual model should not believe both a claim and its negation, yet independently querying it in different languages can elicit exactly that. We ask whether this cross-lingual self-contradiction reflects a genuine per-language belief split or a shared truth judgment whose enforcement is language-gated. We hypothesize that the model computes a largely language-independent internal truth-commitment representation for verifiable propositions, but the query language causally sets a contradiction-tolerance threshold, so the model holds internally incompatible commitments more readily in some languages than others. We build ContradictProbe, parallel factual propositions across 12 typologically and resource-diverse languages, each posed as a true/false verification of both P and its negation not-P (about the same fact), plus a matched control where both queries are consistent. Behaviorally we measure per-language self-contradiction rate (affirming both P and not-P) and test whether it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond whether the model knows the fact. We train a linear truth-commitment probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the contradiction gap into a shared truth estimate versus a language-set consistency gate: high contradiction should coincide with a similar internal truth signal but weaker enforcement. Via activation and path patching we localize a contradiction-tolerance signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model enforce consistency (refusing to affirm not-P once it affirms P) in high-contradiction languages while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe multilingual belief inconsistency as a shared truth commitment under a steerable, language-dependent consistency gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili, Yoruba).
2) DATASET (ContradictProbe): ~500 verifiable factual propositions with clear truth values (from mLAMA/BMLAMA/Wikidata), each expressed as a proposition P and its negation not-P. Build TRUE/FALSE verification probes ('Is it true that X? yes/no') for both P and not-P; a logically consistent model affirms exactly one. Include a CONSISTENT control (two paraphrases of the same-polarity claim, which should both be affirmed) to bound the effect and separate contradiction from noise. Translate/native-verify all items into 12 languages; keep propositional content fixed. Per (fact, language) screen whether the model KNOWS the fact (correct on a direct query) so contradiction is measured on known items, isolating consistency from ignorance. Use short single-token yes/no answers.
3) BEHAVIORAL CONTRADICTION TEST: Per (fact, language) record whether the model affirms BOTH P and not-P (self-contradiction) vs exactly one (consistent). KEY hypothesis: on the SAME known fact, self-contradiction rate is higher in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond knowledge. Mixed-effects logistic regression of contradiction on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, knowledge indicator), fact as random effect; compare against the CONSISTENT control (should show low false-contradiction). Report per-language contradiction profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical facts.
4) SHARED TRUTH-COMMITMENT PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-answer position; train a linear truth-commitment probe (is the proposition being treated as true) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent truth axis. Compare to per-language-trained probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the truth representation for the same proposition. CRITICAL: on contradiction items, test whether the internal truth signal for P and for not-P is correctly OPPOSITE (the model internally knows they conflict) even when the emitted answers both say 'yes'.
5) GATE-vs-ESTIMATE DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer truth estimate across languages (should be similar / correctly opposite for P vs not-P if shared) versus the emitted answers (which contradict). Define a CONSISTENCY GATE mapping the internal truth signal to a coherent answer per language; test whether cross-lingual contradiction differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar (correct) internal truth signal rather than a genuinely confused truth estimate. Correlate per-language gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes.
6) LOCALIZE THE CONTRADICTION-TOLERANCE SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that stays consistent and one that self-contradicts on the SAME fact, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips contradict->consistent WITHOUT changing the decoded truth of P. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the consistency signal FROM a low-contradiction language into a self-contradicting run.
7) CAUSAL CONSISTENCY STEERING (decisive): Derive a contradiction-tolerance steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (consistent runs minus self-contradicting runs on matched items). Test (i) ENFORCE: adding it to high-contradiction languages makes the model give logically consistent P/not-P answers (affirming P and correctly denying not-P) toward a reference level; (ii) LOOSEN: subtracting it induces self-contradiction in low-contradiction languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where contradiction was worst; (iv) it changes ONLY logical consistency, not the decoded truth of P, factual knowledge, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not harm the CONSISTENT control, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: contradiction-rate reduction, consistency-loosening-induction rate (reverse), truth-of-P fidelity, output-language fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering should reduce P/not-P contradiction but not flip the underlying fact or unrelated answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: relation-type breakdown; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single consistency vector generalizes across facts and languages; robustness across templates and yes/no-vs-cloze formats; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched knowledge and by showing content-invariant steering enforces consistency without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language self-contradiction rate, contradiction regression controlling for knowledge/fertility/resource, cross-lingual truth-commitment probe transfer AUROC and correct-opposite P/not-P internal signal, cross-lingual truth-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), estimate-similarity vs answer-contradiction (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized contradiction-tolerance layer, cross-lingual consistency transplant repair rate, causal steering contradiction-reduction and loosening-induction rates, truth-of-P/output fidelity, consistent-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Self-contradiction could reflect a knowledge gap (the model doesn't know the fact) rather than a consistency gate; we screen per-language knowledge and measure contradiction only on known facts, so residual contradiction reflects enforcement failure. 2) The gate-vs-estimate split could be confounded if the internal truth signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by checking whether the P and not-P truth signals are correctly opposite internally across languages rather than assuming the split, and report how much of the gap is estimate vs gate. 3) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy on yes/no probes; we control for fertility, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched knowledge, and the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet enforces consistency, dissociating the gate from length. 4) Some models may be consistent across all languages (no gap) or contradict uniformly; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual belief coherence, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 5) Yes/no verification can be prompt-sensitive (acquiescence bias toward 'yes'); we counterbalance P/not-P order and phrasing, use log-prob-based yes/no scoring, and include the consistent control to estimate baseline false-contradiction. 6) Negation phrasing must be natural and truly negate P across languages; we native-verify negations and exclude ambiguous double-negation constructions. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report truth-of-P fidelity, output-language fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the loosening (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine consistency gate. 9) The gate signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my prior calibration proposal (confidence on answered items) and from cross-lingual answer-variance work (which fact is given) is essential; here the object is whether the model maintains a NON-CONTRADICTORY truth commitment (affirming P and not-P simultaneously) across languages, a distinct logical-coherence property.

Name: crosslingual_knowledge_curse_asymmetry
Title: Cursed in Every Language? A Shared Privileged-Knowledge Representation Whose Suppression for Perspective-Taking Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs suffer a 'curse of knowledge' when reasoning about a less-informed agent: they compute a largely language-independent internal representation of what THEY privately know (the answer/outcome), and correctly answering a perspective-taking question requires SUPPRESSING that privileged knowledge, but whether the suppression is behaviorally executed is gated by the query language—the SAME scenario is answered by wrongly leaking the model's own knowledge far more often in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so the model is internally 'cursed' equally but behaviorally leaks unevenly. The privileged-knowledge signal is causally localizable and its suppression is steerable, so leakage can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: The curse of knowledge / hindsight bias—the difficulty of setting aside privileged information when judging a less-informed agent—is a robust human finding (Birch & Bloom; Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber). In LLMs, related theory-of-mind and information-asymmetry evaluations exist mostly monolingually (Kosinski-style false belief; hindsight-neglect / 'curse of knowledge' probes in English), with no cross-lingual or mechanistic account. My prior crosslingual_false_belief_tracking proposal concerns tracking a SECOND agent's false belief (belief vs reality); the curse of knowledge is distinct—it is about suppressing the MODEL'S OWN privileged knowledge when adopting a less-informed perspective (a self-egocentricity / knowledge-leakage bias), not decoding another agent's mistaken belief-location. It also differs from my presupposition-accommodation and answerability-abstention gating proposals (which concern accepting presupposed content and deciding to attempt/abstain), and from cross-lingual factual-consistency work (which fact is retrieved). Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies privileged-knowledge suppression, perspective-taking, or its language-modulation. No prior work (i) tests whether the curse of knowledge is language-dependent in LLMs, (ii) decomposes it into a shared privileged-knowledge representation versus a language-set suppression gate, or (iii) causally localizes and steers the suppression.
Abstract: Once you know how a story ends, it is hard to judge what someone who doesn't know would think—the curse of knowledge. We ask whether multilingual LLMs suffer this bias when reasoning about a less-informed agent, and whether the bias is language-dependent. We hypothesize that the model computes a largely language-independent internal representation of its own privileged knowledge (the outcome/answer it can see), and that correct perspective-taking requires suppressing that knowledge; whether suppression is executed is gated by the query language, so the SAME scenario leaks the model's own knowledge into its judgment of the naive agent far more in lower-resource, typologically distant languages—the model is internally cursed equally, but behaviorally leaks unevenly. We build CurseProbe, parallel information-asymmetry scenarios across 10 languages: an agent lacks a piece of information the model is given, and a probe asks what the naive agent would believe, expect, or guess; the correct answer ignores the privileged information, while a curse distractor reflects the model's own knowledge. Behaviorally we measure per-language knowledge-leakage rate and test whether it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond comprehension. We train a linear probe for the shared privileged-knowledge signal and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the leakage gap into a shared knowledge representation versus a language-set suppression gate. Via activation and path patching we localize the suppression signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model correctly discount its own knowledge in high-leakage languages, while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe the cross-lingual curse of knowledge as a shared representation under a steerable, language-dependent suppression gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (CurseProbe): ~500 information-asymmetry scenarios in which the MODEL is given a piece of information (an outcome, a hidden answer, a solution) that an in-story AGENT does not have, plus a probe asking what the naive agent would believe/expect/guess/estimate. Families: (A) OUTCOME-KNOWLEDGE hindsight ('You know the experiment failed; before running it, how likely would a scientist unaware of the result think it would succeed?'), (B) HIDDEN-ANSWER estimation ('The answer is 7; how hard would someone who hasn't solved it find this puzzle / what would they guess?'), (C) TRANSPARENCY/illusory-obviousness ('You know the intended meaning; how obvious is this ambiguous message to a naive reader?'). Each item has a PERSPECTIVE-CORRECT answer (ignoring privileged info) and a CURSE distractor (the model's own knowledge leaked in). Include a matched NO-ASYMMETRY control where the agent shares the model's information (so leaking is actually correct) to bound the effect and separate the curse from comprehension. Keep scenario content fixed across languages; translate/native-verify. Screen base-scenario comprehension via the control. Use short scoreable / graded answers.
3) BEHAVIORAL LEAKAGE TEST: Per (scenario, language) record perspective-correct vs curse-distractor answers (and, for graded items, the magnitude of hindsight shift toward the model's knowledge). KEY hypothesis: on the SAME scenario, knowledge-leakage is systematically higher in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond comprehension and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic/linear regression of leakage on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, control-comprehension accuracy), scenario as random effect; compare against the NO-ASYMMETRY control (where 'leaking' is correct and should be language-flat). Report per-language leakage profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical scenarios; validate an English hindsight-bias replication against the human-bias direction.
4) SHARED PRIVILEGED-KNOWLEDGE PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode the PRIVILEGED information the model holds (e.g., the known outcome/answer) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent privileged-knowledge representation. Compare to per-language-trained probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the representation for the same scenario. Crucially, verify the privileged-knowledge signal is strongly present across ALL languages (the model is internally 'cursed' everywhere) even where behavioral leakage differs.
5) SUPPRESSION-vs-KNOWLEDGE DECOMPOSITION: For each scenario, compare the shared mid-layer privileged-knowledge signal across languages (should be similar—present everywhere) versus the behavioral leakage (which diverges). Define a SUPPRESSION GATE mapping internal privileged knowledge to whether it is discounted per language; test whether cross-lingual leakage differences are explained by a weaker suppression gate on a similarly-present knowledge signal rather than by differing knowledge. Correlate per-language gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE SUPPRESSION SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that correctly discounts and one that leaks on the SAME scenario, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips leak->correct WITHOUT changing the decoded privileged knowledge. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the suppression signal FROM a low-leakage language into a leaking run.
7) CAUSAL SUPPRESSION STEERING (decisive): Derive a suppression steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (correct-perspective runs minus curse-leak runs, matched content). Test (i) REPAIR: adding it to high-leakage languages makes the model discount its own knowledge and answer from the naive perspective toward low-leakage levels; (ii) INDUCE: subtracting it makes low-leakage languages leak privileged knowledge; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where leakage was worst; (iv) it changes ONLY the discount-vs-leak behavior, not the decoded privileged knowledge, scenario content, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the NO-ASYMMETRY control (where leaking is correct), and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: leakage reduction, curse-induction rate (reverse), knowledge-signal/output fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering should change perspective-taking but not unrelated or no-asymmetry-control answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: family breakdown (hindsight vs hidden-answer vs transparency); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single suppression vector generalizes across families and languages; robustness across templates and MC-vs-graded formats; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched knowledge-signal and by showing content-invariant steering repairs leakage without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language knowledge-leakage rate and hindsight-shift magnitude, leakage regression controlling for comprehension/fertility/resource, English hindsight replication, cross-lingual privileged-knowledge probe transfer AUROC and representation similarity (present everywhere), knowledge-similarity vs leakage-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized suppression layer, cross-lingual suppression transplant repair rate, causal steering leakage-reduction and curse-induction rates, knowledge-signal/output fidelity, no-asymmetry-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The suppression-vs-knowledge split could be confounded if the privileged-knowledge signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying the signal is present across all languages via probe transfer, rather than assuming, and report how much of the gap is knowledge vs gate. 2) Leakage could reflect a comprehension gap rather than a suppression-gate failure; we use the matched NO-ASYMMETRY control and comprehension screening so residual leakage reflects the curse, not reading failure. 3) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy; we control for fertility, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched knowledge-signal, and the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet repairs leakage, dissociating the gate from length. 4) Some models may be uniformly cursed (leak) or uniformly correct across languages (no gap); either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of the cross-lingual curse of knowledge, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 5) Hindsight/curse scenarios can be graded and prompt-sensitive; we use both forced-choice and graded-shift measures, restrict scored items to clear-consensus cases, validate against the known human-bias direction in English, and collect small human ratings on a subset. 6) The privileged-knowledge probe could latch onto surface cues rather than a genuine internal knowledge signal; the cross-lingual invariance test, the knowledge-present-everywhere check, the knowledge-predicts-leakage link, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Steering may harm fluency, act as a generic accuracy lever, or over-suppress on the no-asymmetry control; we report knowledge-signal/output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the curse-induction (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine suppression gate. 9) The gate signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my false-belief-tracking, presupposition-accommodation, and abstention proposals is essential; here the object is suppression of the MODEL'S OWN privileged knowledge when taking a less-informed perspective (curse of knowledge / self-egocentricity), not decoding another agent's false belief, accepting presupposed content, or deciding to attempt vs abstain.

Name: crosslingual_sequential_answer_anchoring
Title: Consistent for the Wrong Reason: Whether Cross-Lingual Consistency Is Genuine Shared Knowledge or Cheap Anchoring to the First-Answered Language
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM answers a question in language A and is then asked the SAME question in language B within a shared context, its language-B answer is causally ANCHORED to the already-committed language-A answer rather than being computed independently: much of the cross-lingual consistency that current metrics (and self-consistency RL objectives) reward is not genuine shared knowledge but a cheap first-answer anchoring effect. We hypothesize (1) the second-language answer flips toward the first-language answer far more than symmetric ordering would predict, producing an order-dependent consistency inflation that is largest exactly where the two languages independently DISAGREE; (2) this anchoring is carried by a localizable representation of the prior committed answer that gets read at the second query; and (3) causally removing/patching that prior-answer trace collapses the anchored consistency, revealing the model's true (lower) cross-lingual agreement, while amplifying it can raise or force anchoring.
Related Work: Cross-lingual self-consistency is studied behaviorally: Elhady et al. 2026 use it as an unsupervised RL reward (rewarding same-answer-across-languages), Moore et al. 2024 measure value consistency across translations, Lai et al. 2025 aggregate consistency across languages/paraphrases to improve reasoning, and Zhao et al. 2025 evaluate multilingual CoT consistency/faithfulness. All treat cross-lingual consistency as a GLOBAL, order-independent property to be measured or optimized, and none ask whether consistency observed within a single multi-turn context is genuine shared knowledge versus a sequential first-answer ANCHORING artifact, nor provide any mechanism. Sequential/anchoring and self-consistency-under-ambiguity effects (Bartsch et al. 2023) are monolingual and behavioral. My prior 'crosslingual_belief_consistency_gating' proposal concerns INDEPENDENT P/not-P queries in separate contexts (no ordering, no first-answer anchor); this proposal's causal variable is the FIRST committed answer and the ORDER of languages within one context, a fundamentally different dynamic. No prior work (i) isolates order-dependent consistency inflation, (ii) localizes a prior-committed-answer trace read at the second-language query, or (iii) causally shows that removing that trace collapses the (illusory) consistency to reveal true agreement. This directly bears on whether consistency-based metrics and RL rewards (Elhady 2026) measure knowledge or anchoring.
Abstract: Multilingual language models are increasingly praised, and even trained, for answering the same question consistently across languages. But within a single conversation, if a model has just answered a question in English, is its subsequent Spanish answer computed from what it knows, or does it simply anchor to the English answer it already gave? We argue much cross-lingual consistency observed in-context is the latter—a cheap first-answer anchoring artifact that inflates consistency metrics and rewards anchoring rather than knowledge. We introduce SeqAnchor, a framework that asks the same factual/opinion question in two languages within one context and manipulates the order. Behaviorally, we measure order-dependent consistency inflation: how much the second-language answer flips toward the first-language answer relative to a symmetric baseline, focusing on items where the two languages DISAGREE when asked independently. Mechanistically, we train a probe to detect the prior committed answer's representation at the second-language query and test whether its strength predicts anchoring. In a decisive causal test, we use activation patching to remove or suppress the prior-answer trace at the second query and show anchored consistency collapses toward the model's true, lower independent cross-lingual agreement, while amplifying the trace forces anchoring even against the model's independent answer. Across factual probing and opinion questions over 10 languages and five open models, we show that a large fraction of in-context cross-lingual consistency is anchoring, not shared knowledge, with direct implications for consistency-based evaluation and self-consistency RL objectives.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (SeqAnchor): (a) FACTUAL stratum: ~500 short-answer factual questions (mLAMA/BMLAMA/Wikidata) with decodable answers. (b) OPINION/UNDERSPECIFIED stratum: ~200 culturally-variable or value-laden questions (Moore-style) where cross-lingual answers legitimately vary. For each item, first establish INDEPENDENT per-language answers (each language asked alone, no other language in context). Identify DISAGREE items (languages give different independent answers) vs AGREE items (already same). Then build SEQUENTIAL contexts: ask the question in language A, get answer a, then ask the same question in language B in the same context; and the reversed order (B then A). Native-verify translations; short scoreable answers.
3) BEHAVIORAL ANCHORING TEST: For each ordered pair (A-then-B), measure whether the B-answer matches the A-answer (anchored) vs matches B's INDEPENDENT answer. KEY metric: ORDER-DEPENDENT CONSISTENCY INFLATION = in-context consistency minus independent consistency, and its asymmetry (does answering in A first pull B toward A more than vice versa?). Hypothesis: on DISAGREE items, the second answer flips toward the first far above a symmetric/null baseline, and this inflation is largest for lower-resource second languages (the model defers to the first-committed answer). Mixed-effects logistic regression of second-answer-flip on (order, first-language resource tier, second-language resource tier via URIEL, disagree-vs-agree, stratum), item as random effect. Report per-language-pair anchoring rates and the fraction of measured cross-lingual consistency attributable to order-dependent anchoring. Include a memory-control (a distractor turn between the two questions) to test anchoring persistence.
4) PRIOR-ANSWER TRACE PROBE: At the second-language query position, train a linear probe to decode the PRIOR COMMITTED ANSWER (the answer given in the first language) from hidden states. Test whether the prior-answer trace is strongly present, transfers across languages, and whether per-item trace strength predicts the behavioral anchoring flip (link test). Use logit-lens to see when the anchored (vs independent) answer becomes dominant across layers at the second query.
5) LOCALIZE THE ANCHORING MECHANISM: Via activation and path patching between an ANCHORED run (B pulled to A) and an INDEPENDENT run (B asked alone) on the SAME item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components carrying the prior-answer trace whose transfer flips the second answer. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs path patching. Attention analysis: test whether the second-query answer position attends to the first-answer tokens.
6) CAUSAL ANCHORING REMOVAL/INJECTION (decisive): (a) REMOVE: patch out / suppress the prior-answer trace components at the second-language query (or ablate attention to the first answer) and measure whether the in-context second answer reverts to B's INDEPENDENT answer—collapsing anchored consistency toward the model's true, lower cross-lingual agreement. (b) INJECT: derive a prior-answer steering vector (difference-of-means, anchored minus independent) and add a FALSE prior answer to test whether the model can be forced to anchor to an answer it would not independently give. Verify surface output language is unchanged and general QA (multilingual MMLU subset) is intact. Metrics: consistency-collapse magnitude (how much measured consistency was anchoring), forced-anchoring rate under injection, independent-answer-recovery rate, output-language fidelity, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: removal should reduce ONLY the anchored second answer, not first answers or unrelated items.
7) IMPLICATIONS FOR METRICS/RL: Recompute standard cross-lingual consistency metrics (and simulate an Elhady-style self-consistency reward) BEFORE vs AFTER anchoring removal, quantifying how much reported consistency (and reward signal) reflects anchoring rather than shared knowledge; test whether high-consistency items are disproportionately anchored.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: factual vs opinion stratum; first-language dominance (does English-first anchor more?); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); distractor-turn persistence; probe layer/dimensionality; robustness across templates and answer formats; whether anchoring strength tracks the resource GAP between the two languages (defer to the stronger language).
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: order-dependent consistency inflation and its asymmetry, per-language-pair anchoring rate, fraction of cross-lingual consistency attributable to anchoring, prior-answer probe accuracy and trace-strength vs anchoring correlation, attention-to-first-answer evidence, patch-localized anchoring layer, causal consistency-collapse under trace removal and forced-anchoring under injection, independent-answer-recovery, output/general-QA retention, before-vs-after metric/reward inflation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The 'anchoring vs genuine consistency' distinction hinges on trustworthy INDEPENDENT per-language answers; we establish these in isolated single-language contexts, restrict the sharp test to DISAGREE items, and treat AGREE items as a control where anchoring cannot inflate. 2) Some models may show little anchoring (compute each answer independently) or answer identically regardless of order—either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify anchoring magnitude rather than assuming it. 3) Anchoring could reflect legitimate in-context updating (the model reasonably reuses a just-derived answer) rather than a cheap artifact; we distinguish this by testing anchoring on DISAGREE items where reuse is unwarranted, and by the INJECTION test (forcing anchoring to a FALSE prior answer)—if the model anchors to an answer it would never independently give, the effect is artifactual, not principled updating. 4) Patching/probing results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching plus attention analysis. 5) The prior-answer trace may be low-rank or attention-mediated rather than a single direction; we test both attention-ablation and residual-stream patching and report which mechanism dominates. 6) Causal removal may harm fluency; we monitor output-language fidelity and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch. 7) Multi-token or open-ended answers complicate matching; we prefer short decodable answers and validate matching. 8) Distinguishing from behavioral cross-lingual consistency work (Elhady 2026, Moore 2024, Lai 2025) and from my belief-consistency-gating proposal is essential; here the causal variable is the FIRST committed answer and language ORDER within one context, and the core contribution is showing—mechanistically and causally—that a large fraction of in-context cross-lingual consistency (and the reward it generates) is anchoring rather than shared knowledge.

Name: crosslingual_grammaticality_illusion_gating
Title: Fooled by the Right Cue, in the Right Language: A Shared Agreement-Computation Signal Whose Susceptibility to Grammatical Illusions Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs compute a largely language-independent internal representation of the correct grammatical dependency (subject-verb number/gender agreement across an intervening attractor), but the query language causally sets how susceptible the model is to grammatical ILLUSIONS: for the SAME structural configuration, the model is misled by a local attractor (e.g., a plural noun between a singular subject and its verb, or 'grammaticality illusions' in doubly-nested negation) far more in some languages—typically morphologically-poorer or lower-resource ones—than in others, producing a cross-lingual illusion-susceptibility gap that is separable from underlying agreement knowledge and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable illusion-tolerance signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Agreement attraction and grammaticality illusions (the 'more is grammatical' illusion, e.g. Wagers/Phillips; comparative-illusion; NPI-illusion) are among the most robust findings in psycholinguistics, and languages differ sharply in how richly they mark agreement (morphology-rich Russian/Turkish vs morphology-poor English/Chinese). In NLP, monolingual English work uses attraction/agreement minimal pairs (Linzen et al.; BLiMP; targeted-syntactic evaluation) to probe whether models track long-distance agreement, and shows models are misled by attractors—but this is English-centric and behavioral. Multilingual grammaticality-judgment resources (CLiMP, multilingual acceptability) measure per-language accuracy without any account of ILLUSION susceptibility or its internal cause. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for the agreement-computation process or grammatical illusions. My prior code-switch-binding proposal studied which language drives agreement during an explicit lexical switch; this proposal is distinct because the object is susceptibility to a grammatical ILLUSION (a local attractor overriding the correct long-distance dependency) within a single language, whether that illusion-susceptibility is a shared-computation-plus-language-gate phenomenon, and whether it is causally steerable. No prior work (i) frames cross-lingual illusion susceptibility as a shared agreement signal gated by a language-set illusion-tolerance threshold, (ii) dissociates it from agreement knowledge and morphological richness, or (iii) causally localizes and steers an illusion-tolerance signal to equalize robustness across languages.
Abstract: Even fluent readers are fooled by grammatical illusions: a plural noun sitting between a singular subject and its verb ('The key to the cabinets ARE...') makes the ungrammatical verb feel acceptable. We ask whether multilingual LLMs suffer such illusions, and whether their susceptibility is language-dependent. We hypothesize that the model computes a largely language-independent internal representation of the correct grammatical dependency, but the query language causally sets how strongly a local attractor overrides it, so the SAME structural configuration is judged wrongly far more often in some languages—typically morphologically poorer or lower-resource ones—producing a cross-lingual illusion-susceptibility gap dissociable from underlying agreement knowledge. We build IllusionProbe, parallel agreement-attraction and grammaticality-illusion minimal pairs across 8 typologically diverse languages, each crossing structural grammaticality with the presence of a misleading local attractor, plus an attractor-free control. Behaviorally we measure per-language illusion susceptibility (how much an attractor shifts grammaticality judgments toward the wrong verb) and test whether it tracks morphological richness and resource level beyond agreement accuracy. We train a linear probe for the shared correct-agreement signal and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the illusion gap into a shared agreement computation versus a language-set illusion-tolerance gate: high susceptibility should coincide with a similar internal correct-agreement signal but weaker enforcement against the attractor. Via activation and path patching we localize an illusion-tolerance signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model resist the attractor in high-susceptibility languages (or induce illusions in robust ones) while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual syntactic fragility as a shared agreement computation under a steerable, language-dependent illusion gate.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 languages spanning agreement-morphology richness: rich (Russian, Turkish, Spanish, German), moderate (Hindi), and poor (English, Chinese, Indonesian), coded for agreement-morphology richness (number/gender/case marking on verbs and nouns) from typological references (WALS agreement chapters) plus URIEL for typological distance; treat morphological richness as a graded predictor. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (IllusionProbe): ~500 minimal-pair items in two families. (A) AGREEMENT ATTRACTION: a subject and its verb separated by an intervening 'attractor' noun of mismatched number/gender ('The key to the cabinets is/are...'), crossing GRAMMATICALITY (correct vs incorrect verb) x ATTRACTOR-MATCH (attractor matches vs mismatches the subject). The signature illusion: an ungrammatical verb is wrongly accepted more when the attractor matches it. (B) GRAMMATICALITY ILLUSION (nested-negation / comparative-illusion style where an ungrammatical structure is illusorily accepted). Each item has an ATTRACTOR-FREE control (no intervening mismatched noun) to establish baseline agreement accuracy and bound the effect. Probes: forced-choice acceptability ('Is this sentence grammatical? yes/no') and verb-form preference (log-prob of correct vs attractor-matched verb). Realize each construction naturally in all 8 languages with native verification, using each language's agreement morphology where present; flag constructions with no natural equivalent. Record per-language tokenization fertility.
3) BEHAVIORAL ILLUSION-SUSCEPTIBILITY TEST: For each (item, language) measure ILLUSION SUSCEPTIBILITY = the increase in accepting an ungrammatical verb (or the log-prob shift toward the attractor-matched verb) when the attractor matches vs mismatches, on the SAME structure. KEY hypothesis: susceptibility is higher in morphologically-poorer / lower-resource languages, beyond baseline agreement accuracy. Mixed-effects logistic regression of illusion-error on (morphological richness, attractor-match, grammaticality, language, tokenization fertility, resource tier via URIEL), item as random effect; test the morphological-richness x attractor-match interaction; compare against the ATTRACTOR-FREE control (should show high, language-flat agreement accuracy). Report per-language susceptibility profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical structures; validate an English attraction replication against the known human/model direction.
4) SHARED AGREEMENT-COMPUTATION PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the verb/agreement position; train a linear probe to decode the CORRECT agreement feature (the number/gender the verb SHOULD take, determined by the true subject, not the attractor) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent correct-agreement representation. Compare to per-language-trained probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the agreement representation for the same structure. CRITICAL: on illusion items, test whether the internal correct-agreement signal remains CORRECT (tracks the true subject) even when the emitted judgment is fooled by the attractor—evidence that the computation is right internally but not enforced.
5) GATE-vs-COMPUTATION DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer correct-agreement signal across languages (should be similar / correct if the computation is shared) versus the emitted illusion-susceptible judgment (which diverges). Define an ILLUSION-TOLERANCE GATE mapping the internal correct signal to a robust judgment per language; test whether cross-lingual susceptibility differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar (correct) internal signal rather than a genuinely wrong agreement computation. Correlate per-language gate strength with morphological richness, resource tier, and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens (identify where the attractor-matched verb overtakes the correct one).
6) LOCALIZE THE ILLUSION-TOLERANCE SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that resists the illusion and one that succumbs on the SAME item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips succumb->resist WITHOUT changing the decoded correct-agreement signal. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the illusion-tolerance signal FROM a robust (morphology-rich) language into a susceptible run. Attention analysis: test whether susceptible languages over-attend to the attractor noun.
7) CAUSAL ILLUSION-TOLERANCE STEERING (decisive): Derive an illusion-tolerance steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (illusion-resistant runs minus succumbing runs on matched items). Test (i) STRENGTHEN: adding it to high-susceptibility languages makes the model resist the attractor and judge agreement correctly toward a reference level; (ii) WEAKEN: subtracting it induces grammatical illusions in robust languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where susceptibility was worst; (iv) it changes ONLY illusion resistance, not the decoded correct-agreement signal, baseline agreement (attractor-free control), or surface language (fidelity checks), and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: susceptibility reduction, illusion-induction rate (reverse), agreement-signal/output fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering should change illusion susceptibility but not attractor-free-control or unrelated answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: family breakdown (attraction vs grammaticality-illusion); which agreement feature (number vs gender vs case) leaks most; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; attractor distance (adjacent vs far); whether a single tolerance vector generalizes across constructions and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched agreement-signal and by showing content-invariant steering reduces illusions without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language illusion susceptibility and attractor-free baseline accuracy, susceptibility regression controlling for agreement-knowledge/fertility/resource with morphological-richness interaction, English attraction replication, cross-lingual correct-agreement probe transfer AUROC and correct-internal-signal-under-illusion, cross-lingual agreement-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), computation-similarity vs judgment-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-morphology/resource/typology correlation, patch-localized illusion-tolerance layer and attention-to-attractor evidence, cross-lingual tolerance transplant repair rate, causal steering susceptibility-reduction and illusion-induction rates, agreement-signal/output fidelity, attractor-free-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Realizing agreement-attraction and grammaticality-illusion constructions naturally and equivalently across languages is delicate, especially in morphology-poor languages (Chinese/Indonesian) where verbal agreement is minimal or absent—we native-verify, treat morphological richness as a graded predictor, flag constructions with no natural equivalent (using them for transfer-limit analysis), and rely on the ATTRACTOR-FREE control and identical structure to isolate the illusion effect; where a language lacks the agreement dependency entirely we analyze the grammaticality-illusion family (which does not require rich agreement) separately. 2) Illusion susceptibility could reflect a baseline agreement-knowledge gap rather than a tolerance gate; we condition on the attractor-free control (baseline agreement accuracy) and measure susceptibility as the attractor-induced INCREMENT, so residual susceptibility reflects illusion, not ignorance. 3) The gate-vs-computation split could be confounded if the internal correct-agreement signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by checking whether the internal signal tracks the true subject across languages rather than assuming, and report how much of the gap is computation vs gate. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds; we control for fertility, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched agreement-signal, and the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet reduces illusions, dissociating the gate from length. 5) Some models may resist illusions uniformly (no gap) or succumb everywhere—either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual syntactic robustness, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 6) Acceptability judgments can be prompt-sensitive (acquiescence bias); we use both forced-choice and log-prob verb-preference measures, counterbalance grammaticality, and validate against the known attraction direction in English. 7) The correct-agreement probe could latch onto surface cues rather than a genuine computation; the correct-internal-signal-under-illusion test, cross-lingual invariance, and cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching plus attention analysis. 9) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report agreement-signal/output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the illusion-induction (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine illusion-tolerance gate. 10) The gate signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my prior code-switch-binding proposal is essential; here there is no lexical switch—the object is susceptibility to a grammatical ILLUSION (a local attractor overriding the correct long-distance dependency) within a single language and its language-set tolerance gate, not which language owns a switched concept's morphosyntax.

Name: crosslingual_sunk_cost_escalation_gating
Title: Throwing Good Money After Bad, in Some Tongues More Than Others: A Shared Prospective-Value Estimate Gated by a Language-Dependent Sunk-Cost Escalation Threshold
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM acts as a decision agent facing a sunk-cost / escalation-of-commitment scenario (a failing project with prior irrecoverable investment vs a fresh start), it computes a largely language-independent internal estimate of the PROSPECTIVE (forward-looking) value of continuing versus quitting, but the query language causally sets an ESCALATION THRESHOLD applied to that estimate: for the SAME scenario the model 'throws good money after bad' (irrationally honors sunk costs by continuing) at a lower threshold in some languages than others, tracking each language community's documented sunk-cost / loss-aversion norms and typological/resource distance. This escalation gap is separable from the prospective-value estimate and from arithmetic, and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable escalation-gating signal without changing the described scenario or surface language.
Related Work: Cognitive-bias detection in multilingual text is behavioral and corpus-based: CogDeBias (Shen et al. 2026) classifies sunk-cost/overconfidence/anchoring instances in corporate reports, and BiasLab (Guey et al. 2026) measures output-level bias across languages/framings, but neither studies whether the query language CAUSALLY modulates the strength of the sunk-cost fallacy, nor provides any internal representation or mechanism. Prospect-theory work on LLMs (Jia et al. 2024; Payne 2025) is monolingual/English and does not address sunk cost or its cross-lingual modulation. My prior crosslingual_risk_attitude_reweighting proposal targets nonlinear probability weighting and loss aversion over gambles; sunk-cost escalation is a distinct, temporally-extended irrationality (honoring irrecoverable past costs in a forward-looking choice), not a static lottery, and is measured by a normative benchmark: rational agents should ignore sunk costs entirely. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never for escalation-of-commitment decisions. My concession-gating proposal concerns interactive bargaining; here the object is a single-agent sunk-cost continue/quit decision. No prior work (i) frames sunk-cost escalation as a shared prospective-value estimate gated by a language-dependent escalation threshold, (ii) dissociates that gate from the forward-looking value estimate, or (iii) causally localizes and steers a sunk-cost-escalation signal to equalize the bias across languages.
Abstract: A rational agent ignores sunk costs: money already spent should not affect whether to continue a failing project. Humans notoriously fail this, and as multilingual LLMs increasingly advise on budgets, projects, and investments, a fairness-critical question arises: does the query language change how strongly the model honors sunk costs? We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal estimate of the PROSPECTIVE value of continuing versus quitting, but applies a query-language-dependent escalation threshold to it, so that for the SAME scenario—identical remaining costs and expected returns—the model irrationally continues a failing project (throwing good money after bad) at a lower threshold in some languages than others. This predicts a cross-lingual escalation gap dissociable from the forward-looking value estimate and from arithmetic. We build SunkProbe, parallel decision scenarios across 12 languages in which a prior irrecoverable investment is present or absent while the forward-looking economics are held fixed, with a continue-vs-quit choice whose rational answer ignores the sunk cost. Behaviorally we measure per-language sunk-cost susceptibility (the increase in continuing when a sunk cost is present) and test whether it tracks resource level and cultural norms beyond the prospective value. We train a linear probe for the shared prospective-value estimate, test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, and decompose the escalation gap into a shared estimate versus a language-set escalation threshold.
