Via activation and path patching we localize an escalation-gating signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model ignore sunk costs consistently across languages—or, in reverse, induce escalation—while leaving the scenario and surface language unchanged. We reframe multilingual sunk-cost bias as a shared valuation under a steerable, language-dependent escalation gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/culturally/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili, Korean).
2) DATASET (SunkProbe): ~500 escalation-of-commitment scenarios in families—(a) PROJECT COMPLETION (a project is failing; a prior large investment is already spent; continue [more cost, low expected return] vs abandon [start fresh / cut losses]); (b) INVESTMENT (hold a losing asset that has consumed resources vs reallocate); (c) TIME/EFFORT sunk cost (continue a task with heavy prior effort vs switch to a better option). Each scenario is built as a MINIMAL PAIR: a SUNK-COST version (prior irrecoverable investment stated) and a NO-SUNK-COST control (identical forward-looking economics—same remaining cost and expected return—but no prior investment), so that a rational agent should choose identically in both. The rational forward-looking choice is fixed and known; sunk-cost susceptibility = increased 'continue' rate when the sunk cost is present. Vary the magnitude of the sunk cost and the forward-looking value to trace a susceptibility curve. Keep all numbers/facts identical across languages; translate/native-verify surrounding wording. Record per-language tokenization fertility and per-language sunk-cost/loss-aversion cultural-norm proxies from behavioral-economics references (graded predictors). Score continue/quit via a validated classifier plus log-probability of the continue option.
3) BEHAVIORAL SUSCEPTIBILITY TEST: For each (scenario, language) compute sunk-cost susceptibility (continue-rate difference between SUNK-COST and NO-SUNK-COST minimal-pair versions). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME forward-looking economics, susceptibility differs by query language and tracks cultural norms/resource level beyond the prospective value. Mixed-effects logistic regression of continue on (sunk-cost present, language, sunk-cost magnitude, forward-looking value, tokenization fertility, cultural-norm code, resource tier via URIEL), scenario as random effect; test the sunk-cost x language interaction; the NO-SUNK-COST control should show language-flat rational choice. Report per-language susceptibility profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical scenarios.
4) SHARED PROSPECTIVE-VALUE PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-choice position; train a linear probe to decode the forward-looking value-of-continuing (from the remaining cost / expected return, ignoring sunk cost) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report R^2/AUROC as evidence of a language-independent prospective-value estimate, plus cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the estimate for the same scenario. Show the prospective value is internally similar across languages even when the emitted choice differs, and—crucially—test whether the sunk cost distorts this internal prospective estimate (it should not, for a rational computation) or only the downstream choice.
5) THRESHOLD-vs-ESTIMATE DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer prospective-value estimate across languages (should be similar if shared) versus the emitted continue/quit decision (which diverges under sunk cost). Fit per-language a decision boundary on the shared estimate; test whether cross-lingual escalation differences are explained by a shifted ESCALATION THRESHOLD rather than a different prospective estimate. Correlate the per-language threshold with cultural norms, resource tier, and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-decision split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE ESCALATION-GATING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that rationally quits and one that escalates on the SAME sunk-cost scenario, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips escalate->quit WITHOUT changing the decoded prospective value. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gating components from a low-escalation language into an escalating run.
7) CAUSAL ESCALATION STEERING (decisive): Derive an escalation-gating steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (rational-quit runs minus escalate runs on matched sunk-cost scenarios). Test (i) DE-ESCALATE: adding it to high-escalation languages makes the model ignore sunk costs and choose the forward-looking-optimal action toward a reference level; (ii) ESCALATE: subtracting it induces sunk-cost escalation in low-escalation languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where escalation was worst; (iv) it changes ONLY the continue/quit decision, not the decoded prospective value, the described scenario, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the NO-SUNK-COST control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Baselines: per-language temperature, prompt-based 'ignore sunk costs' instruction, translate-to-English. Metrics: escalation-gap closure, forward-looking-optimal-choice recovery, escalation-induction rate (reverse), prospective-value/output fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts sunk-cost susceptibility but not the prospective-value readout or unrelated answers, and dose-response: scaling the vector produces graded susceptibility shifts.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: family breakdown (project vs investment vs time/effort); is English/high-resource the low-escalation reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank escalation subspace; robustness across templates and choice-vs-rating formats; whether one gating vector generalizes across families and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched prospective value and by showing content-invariant steering shifts susceptibility without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language sunk-cost susceptibility and its cultural-norm/resource regression, cross-lingual prospective-value-probe transfer R^2/AUROC and representation similarity, estimate-similarity vs decision-divergence (threshold) decomposition, threshold-vs-norm/resource/typology correlation, patch-localized escalation-gating layer, cross-lingual gating transplant repair rate, causal steering escalation-gap closure with dose-response and escalation-induction rate, prospective-value/output fidelity, no-sunk-cost-control and general-QA retention, comparison to temperature/prompt-instruction/translate-to-English baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Instruction-tuned models may refuse or give degenerate always-cut-losses choices; we use both choice and log-probability-based selection, report degeneracy/refusal rates, and select model scales that exhibit measurable sunk-cost effects. 2) Escalation could reflect arithmetic error (miscomputing the forward-looking economics) rather than honoring sunk costs; the NO-SUNK-COST minimal-pair control (identical forward economics), conditioning on scenarios where the prospective value is correctly represented, and the prospective-value fidelity checks under steering dissociate these. 3) The threshold-vs-estimate split could be confounded if the prospective-value estimate itself differs by language, or if the sunk cost distorts the internal estimate; we test both directly by comparing shared-probe estimates across languages and across sunk-cost/no-sunk-cost versions rather than assuming the split. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched prospective value, and the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts susceptibility, dissociating the gate from length. 5) Cultural sunk-cost/loss-aversion norm coding is coarse and debated; we treat it as a graded predictor, report sensitivity to alternative codings, and note a language effect is establishable even if its cultural correlate is weak. 6) Some models/languages may show no cross-lingual escalation gap (uniform bias) or be uniformly rational; either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often a gap exists. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report prospective-value/output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the escalation-induction (reverse), reverse-consistency, and dose-response tests to ensure a genuine escalation-threshold dial. 9) The escalation signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Misuse concern: escalation steering could be abused to make agents irrationally persistent; we frame and use it strictly as an interpretability/fairness diagnostic on benign decision scenarios and report retention rather than deploying it. 11) Distinguishing from behavioral bias-detection work (CogDeBias, BiasLab) and from my risk-attitude and concession proposals is essential; here the object is the temporally-extended sunk-cost/escalation-of-commitment irrationality—honoring irrecoverable past costs in a forward-looking single-agent choice—with a clear normative benchmark (rational agents ignore sunk costs entirely), not nonlinear probability weighting over gambles or interactive bargaining concession.

Name: crosslingual_acquisition_order_alignment
Title: When Does a Model Learn a Fact in Each Language? Cross-Lingual Acquisition Order as a Trace of Representation Alignment Across Pretraining
Short Hypothesis: A concept/fact does not become accessible in all languages at once during pretraining: there is a systematic, largely fact-independent CROSS-LINGUAL ACQUISITION ORDER (the training step at which a fact becomes retrievable in each language), and this order is causally set by WHEN that language's representation of the fact aligns to the emerging shared concept space rather than merely by that language's raw token frequency. Concretely: (1) across pretraining checkpoints, facts become retrievable in a language exactly when the mid-layer representation of the fact in that language converges (crosses an alignment threshold) toward the dominant/anchor language's representation; (2) the per-language acquisition-onset step is predicted better by representation-alignment timing than by cumulative token exposure; and (3) the acquisition order is a stable staircase governed by typological/script distance to the anchor language, so a low-resource-but-typologically-close language can be acquired earlier than a high-resource-but-distant one.
Related Work: Prior multilingual mechanistic work is almost entirely INFERENCE-TIME: facts live in a shared concept space with language-specific decoding (Wang 2025; Lim 2025), and cross-lingual transfer/consistency is measured on fixed final models (Qi 2023; Ifergan 2024). Blum et al. 2025 ('Beyond the Rosetta Stone') show facts transfer only when representations UNIFY, but analyze unification as an end-state property of synthetic training, not the TEMPORAL ORDER in which real facts become accessible per language across checkpoints, and do not tie acquisition ONSET to an alignment threshold or contrast it with frequency. AdaXEval (Zhao 2025) studies knowledge-acquisition dynamics during domain adaptation but frames it via data recipes/frequency, without a per-fact per-language acquisition-onset measure or a representation-alignment mechanism. Curriculum/acquisition-order work (CLewR 2026; PROGRESS 2025) concerns training-efficiency ordering, not the emergent order in which concepts become cross-lingually accessible. My own prior 'native_language_imprint' proposal concerns which acquisition LANGUAGE a fact ends up bound to (an end-state imprint); this proposal instead traces the TEMPORAL SEQUENCE of cross-lingual acquisition across pretraining and its causal driver (alignment timing vs frequency). No prior work (i) measures a per-fact per-language acquisition-onset step across public multilingual checkpoints, (ii) tests whether onset coincides with a representation-alignment threshold, or (iii) shows the acquisition order is predicted by alignment timing beyond token frequency and tracks typological distance. This is a formation-tracing account absent from my entire backlog and from the literature.
Abstract: Multilingual language models can eventually answer the same question in many languages, but when, during training, does each language 'come online' for a given fact, and what governs that timing? We propose that cross-lingual knowledge is acquired in a systematic order across pretraining, and that a fact becomes retrievable in a language precisely when that language's internal representation of the fact aligns to the model's emerging shared concept space, rather than simply when the language has accumulated enough tokens. Using public multilingual models that release dozens of intermediate checkpoints (e.g., CroissantLLM, Salamandra), we probe a set of parallel factual items in multiple languages at every checkpoint to measure, per fact and per language, the ACQUISITION-ONSET step (the checkpoint after which the fact is reliably retrievable). We show these onsets form a stable staircase: within a fact, languages are acquired in a consistent order that tracks typological and script distance to the dominant/anchor language, so that a close low-resource language can precede a distant high-resource one. Mechanistically, at each checkpoint we measure the cross-lingual alignment of the fact's mid-layer representation to the anchor language and show that acquisition onset coincides with an alignment-threshold crossing, and that alignment timing predicts onset substantially better than cumulative token exposure. Finally, in a causal test, we accelerate a lagging language's acquisition by continued training that explicitly aligns its representation to the anchor manifold and show it advances the onset step. We reframe cross-lingual knowledge transfer as a temporally-ordered, alignment-gated acquisition process that is measurable, predictable, and steerable.
Experiments: 1) MODELS & CHECKPOINTS: Use open multilingual models that publicly release many intermediate pretraining checkpoints and (ideally) known data mixes: CroissantLLM (1.3B, dozens of checkpoints across steps, 1:1 English-French with a custom bilingual setup) and Salamandra (2B/7B, 35 European languages, checkpoints + released training scripts). Where a fully open checkpoint series is unavailable for some languages, supplement with a small controlled continued-pretraining run on an open base (Qwen2.5-1.5B / Llama-3.2-1B) that injects synthetic parallel facts with logged per-language exposure, giving ground-truth token counts (LoRA/light continued pretraining on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 2) PROBE SET: ~500 parallel factual items (mLAMA/BMLAMA/Wikidata) with short decodable answers, translated/native-verified into the languages covered by the checkpoint series (spanning multiple scripts/families where available; at minimum the model's supported set). Include a synthetic-novel-fact stratum (fictional entities absent from pretraining) for the controlled continued-pretraining runs so exposure is known exactly. 3) ACQUISITION-ONSET MEASUREMENT: At EVERY checkpoint, query each fact in each language; define per-(fact,language) ACQUISITION ONSET = the earliest step after which retrieval accuracy stays above a reliability threshold (with hysteresis to avoid noise). Produce per-language acquisition curves and per-fact onset vectors across languages. 4) ACQUISITION-ORDER STAIRCASE (behavioral): Test whether, within a fact, languages are acquired in a CONSISTENT order across facts (rank-correlation of per-language onset ranks across facts; Kendall's W). Test whether the order tracks URIEL typological/script distance to the anchor language and whether close-low-resource can precede distant-high-resource. Mixed-effects model of onset step on (typological distance to anchor, script identity, cumulative token exposure), fact as random effect. 5) ALIGNMENT-THRESHOLD MECHANISM: At each checkpoint, extract the fact's mid-layer representation in each language and measure cross-lingual ALIGNMENT to the anchor language (per-item cosine / CKA of the concept vector; also signed distance to the anchor's decoding manifold). Test whether acquisition onset coincides with an alignment-threshold crossing (per-fact-language, correlate onset step with alignment-crossing step; report lead/lag). 6) ALIGNMENT-vs-FREQUENCY PREDICTION (core test): Fit two predictors of per-(fact,language) onset step: (a) ALIGNMENT-TIMING (the step at which alignment crosses threshold) and (b) CUMULATIVE TOKEN EXPOSURE for that language up to onset (available exactly in the controlled runs; approximated via released data-mix proportions for the public models). Compare predictive power (incremental R^2, likelihood-ratio tests, cross-validated); hypothesis: alignment timing predicts onset better than exposure, and exposure adds little once alignment is controlled. 7) CAUSAL ACCELERATION (decisive): In the controlled continued-pretraining setting, for a LAGGING language take an intermediate checkpoint and continue training with an explicit representation-ALIGNMENT objective (a lightweight auxiliary loss pulling the lagging language's mid-layer fact representation toward the anchor manifold, or brief parallel-aligned exposure) while holding token count matched to a control condition of equal additional monolingual exposure. Test whether alignment-driven training ADVANCES the acquisition onset (facts become retrievable earlier) more than matched monolingual exposure, and whether the induced alignment-crossing precedes the retrieval gain. Verify no degradation of already-acquired languages or general capability (multilingual MMLU subset) and output-language fidelity. 8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: anchor-language identity (is the dominant/high-frequency language the anchor everyone aligns to, or a typological hub?); per-relation-type variation in acquisition order; probe layer/dimensionality; robustness of onset to reliability threshold and prompt templates; whether the staircase is steeper for script-distant languages; model scale (CroissantLLM vs Salamandra-2B/7B). EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-(fact,language) acquisition-onset steps, cross-fact order consistency (Kendall's W), onset-vs-typological-distance and onset-vs-frequency regressions with incremental R^2, alignment-crossing-vs-onset lead/lag correlation, alignment-timing vs exposure predictive comparison, causal acceleration onset-advance (alignment vs matched-exposure) with alignment-precedes-retrieval check, general-capability and language-fidelity retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Public checkpoint series may cover few languages or few steps, limiting resolution; we mitigate by combining public series (CroissantLLM/Salamandra) with controlled continued-pretraining runs that give exact per-language exposure and fine-grained checkpoints. 2) Onset is threshold-dependent and noisy for low-resource languages; we use hysteresis, multiple thresholds, and report sensitivity, and restrict analysis to facts reliably acquired in at least the anchor language. 3) Disentangling alignment timing from token exposure is the crux and is confounded in public models (exposure is only approximable from data-mix proportions); the controlled runs with logged exposure provide the clean test, and we treat public-model results as corroborative rather than definitive. 4) Some models may acquire all languages nearly simultaneously (no clear order) or acquire via early representation unification with no measurable staircase — either is an informative, publishable finding about when cross-lingual acquisition is/ isn't ordered, and we quantify order strength rather than assuming it. 5) The alignment-threshold coincidence could be correlational; the causal acceleration experiment (alignment objective vs matched monolingual exposure, with alignment-precedes-retrieval check) is designed to promote it to a causal claim, but the auxiliary-loss intervention has its own artifacts, which we control with the matched-exposure baseline and capability-retention checks. 6) Anchor-language choice may be model-specific; we test whether the anchor is the highest-frequency language or a typological hub and report per-model results. 7) Results may be model- and scale-specific; we test at least two public model families plus controlled runs and report aggregate and per-model findings. 8) Representation-alignment metrics (cosine/CKA/manifold distance) are imperfect proxies for a 'shared concept'; we triangulate across metrics and validate that high alignment predicts cross-lingual retrieval at the final checkpoint.

Name: crosslingual_causal_direction_asymmetry
Title: Which Way Does the Arrow Point? A Shared Cause-Effect Direction Representation Whose Expression Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When reasoning about a described situation, a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of the DIRECTED causal relation between two events (which is the cause and which is the effect, distinct from mere temporal order or associative co-occurrence), but whether that directed relation is behaviorally EXPRESSED (answering cause-vs-effect questions correctly rather than defaulting to salience or co-occurrence) is gated by the query language: the SAME causal scenario is directionally resolved internally across languages yet answered correctly far less often in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so the model can internally 'know which causes which' while behaviorally confusing cause and effect. The directed-causal signal is causally localizable and its expression is steerable, so cause/effect confusion can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: XCOPA (Ponti et al. 2020) shows causal commonsense (choosing a plausible cause vs effect) transfers poorly across languages, but it is purely behavioral, benchmark-level, and offers no internal representation or mechanism. Counterfactual/causal-statement detection work (Acar & Tekir 2024, Turkish; SemEval-2020 CFD) is a token-classification task, not a study of directed causal representation. My prior crosslingual_reversal_curse proposal concerns whether an ARBITRARY relation A->B reverses to B->A (relational directionality for facts), and my crosslingual_timeline_reconstruction proposal concerns CHRONOLOGICAL event order; NEITHER addresses CAUSAL direction (cause vs effect), which is semantically distinct from temporal precedence (a cause need not be the salient or first-mentioned event, and effects can precede causes in the surface text) and from arbitrary relation reversal (causation is an asymmetric dependency with its own directionality cues). Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for directed causal relations. No prior work asks whether an LLM computes a shared, language-independent cause->effect DIRECTION representation, whether its internal directionality is decoupled from behavioral expression across languages, whether cause/effect confusion tracks resource level, or whether the directed-causal signal can be causally localized and its expression steered. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of causal-direction representation.
Abstract: Understanding that fire causes smoke, not the reverse, requires representing causation as a directed relation, not just noticing that fire and smoke co-occur. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal representation of causal DIRECTION (which event is cause, which is effect), and whether that internal directionality is decoupled from how reliably it is behaviorally expressed across languages. We hypothesize that models internally resolve the cause->effect arrow similarly across languages, but the query language gates whether that direction is surfaced, so the SAME causal scenario is answered by confusing cause and effect (defaulting to salience or co-occurrence) far more in lower-resource, typologically distant languages. We build CausalDir, parallel two-event scenarios across 10 languages, each with a cause-identification and an effect-identification probe whose correct answer requires the directed relation, plus a reverse-direction distractor and a matched associative (non-causal co-occurrence) control. Behaviorally we measure per-language cause/effect confusion and test whether it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond comprehension. We train a linear cause-vs-effect probe and test whether a single probe transfers zero-shot across languages, evidencing a shared directed-causal signal, then decompose the expression gap into a shared direction component versus a language-set expression gate. Via activation and path patching we localize a directed-causal signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to flip the model's inferred causal direction (or repair confused cases) while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual causal-reasoning gaps as a steerable gate over a shared causal-direction representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili). MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (CausalDir): ~500 two-event scenarios with a KNOWN directed causal relation (drawn from/extending XCOPA and causal-commonsense resources, plus curated world-knowledge causal pairs, e.g. 'It rained heavily; the streets flooded'), controlling for surface order (present cause-first and effect-first variants) and salience so the correct cause/effect cannot be read off position or salience alone. Each item has (a) a CAUSE-identification probe ('Which event caused the other?'), (b) an EFFECT-identification probe, a REVERSE-direction distractor, and (c) an ASSOCIATIVE CONTROL (two co-occurring but non-causally-directed events, where no direction should be asserted) to bound the effect and separate causation from mere association. Translate/native-verify into all 10 languages; realize causal connectives naturally per language; record tokenization fertility; screen that the model knows the base causal fact (in >=1 language) so confusion is not ignorance. Short single-token-decodable answers where possible.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (scenario, language) record correct-direction vs reverse-distractor answers. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME scenario, cause/effect confusion is systematically higher in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond comprehension and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of confusion on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, surface-order, knowledge indicator), scenario as random effect; compare against the associative control. Report per-language confusion profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical scenarios; replicate an XCOPA-style baseline.
4) SHARED CAUSE-vs-EFFECT PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode which event is the CAUSE (directed relation, controlling for surface order) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent directed-causal representation, and show it dissociates from a TEMPORAL-order probe and a SALIENCE probe (the causal-direction signal is distinct from precedence/salience). Compare to per-language-trained probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the direction representation. Crucially, verify the correct causal direction is internally decodable across ALL languages even where behavioral accuracy differs.
5) DIRECTION-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: For each scenario, compare the shared mid-layer direction signal across languages (should be similar/correct if shared) versus behavioral answers (which diverge). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal direction to surfaced answer per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar (correct) internal signal rather than weaker direction resolution. Correlate per-language gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens (identify where the reverse-distributed answer overtakes or fails to overtake the correct one).
6) LOCALIZE THE DIRECTED-CAUSAL / EXPRESSION SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that answers the direction correctly and one that confuses cause/effect on the SAME scenario, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips confused->correct WITHOUT changing the decoded event identities. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the direction representation FROM a high-expression language into a confused low-expression run.
7) CAUSAL DIRECTION STEERING (decisive): Derive a causal-direction steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (correct-direction runs minus reversed runs, matched content). Test (i) REPAIR: adding it to confused low-expression languages increases correct cause/effect answers toward high-expression levels; (ii) FLIP: subtracting/adding it makes the model treat the effect as the cause (and vice versa) on well-resolved items; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where expression was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY causal-direction answering, not event identities, scenario content, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the associative control (where no direction should be asserted), and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: confusion reduction, direction-flip rate (reverse), direction-signal/output fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes cause/effect answers but not associative-control or unrelated answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: dissociation from temporal order and salience; surface-order (cause-first vs effect-first) effects; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single direction vector generalizes across scenarios and languages; robustness across templates and MC-vs-cloze-vs-free formats; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched direction-signal and showing content-invariant steering repairs confusion without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language cause/effect confusion rate, confusion regression controlling for comprehension/fertility/surface-order/resource, cross-lingual cause-vs-effect probe transfer AUROC and its dissociation from temporal/salience probes, cross-lingual direction-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), direction-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized directed-causal layer, cross-lingual direction transplant repair rate, causal steering confusion-repair and direction-flip rates, direction-signal/output fidelity, associative-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The direction-vs-expression split could be confounded if the direction signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying correct-direction decodability across all languages via probe transfer rather than assuming, and report how much of the gap is direction vs gate. 2) Cause/effect confusion could reflect scenario-comprehension failure or ignorance of the base causal fact rather than an expression gate; we use the associative control and knowledge screening so residual confusion reflects direction resolution, not reading or ignorance. 3) Distinguishing causal direction from temporal order and salience is essential and delicate; we control surface order (cause-first and effect-first variants), include items where the effect is mentioned first or is more salient, and explicitly show the causal-direction probe dissociates from temporal-order and salience probes. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched direction-signal, and the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet repairs confusion, dissociating the gate from length. 5) Some models may resolve causal direction uniformly across languages (no gap) or confuse it everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual causal reasoning, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 6) Causal ground truth can be graded for some commonsense pairs; we restrict scored items to clear-consensus directed causal relations (native-verified, drawing on XCOPA-style validated stimuli) and analyze ambiguous ones separately. 7) The direction probe could latch onto surface connective/order cues rather than a genuine directed-causal representation; the dissociation from temporal/salience probes, cross-lingual invariance, the direction-predicts-behavior link, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report direction-signal/output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the flip (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine causal-direction gate. 10) The gate/direction signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my reversal-curse (arbitrary relation A<->B) and timeline-reconstruction (chronological event order) proposals is essential; here the object is the directed CAUSAL dependency (cause vs effect), semantically distinct from arbitrary relational reversal and from temporal precedence.

Name: crosslingual_compositional_binding
Title: Primitives in One Tongue, Combinations in Another: Whether the Compositional Binding Operation Is Language-Independent and Its Expression Is Language-Gated
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM learns a set of primitives (e.g., a novel color-to-symbol mapping, a taught operator, an attribute vocabulary) in a training language and must interpret NOVEL COMBINATIONS of those primitives, the compositional binding operation that recombines them is largely language-independent, but whether a novel combination is correctly resolved is gated by the query language: the SAME novel combination is bound correctly internally across languages yet surfaced far less reliably in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so a model can internally 'compose' while behaviorally failing to generalize. We hypothesize (1) a shared middle-layer 'binding' representation that combines primitive slots and transfers zero-shot across languages; (2) cross-lingual compositional-generalization failures decompose into a shared BINDING-FAILURE (the combination is never internally formed) versus a language-specific EXPRESSION-GATE failure (the combination is bound internally but not surfaced in the query language); and (3) the binding signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated composition failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Compositional generalization is heavily studied but monolingually and behaviorally: SCAN/COGS/ReCOGS and CoFe (An et al. 2023, in-context composition), morphological composition (Ismayilzada et al. 2024, agglutinative languages), and math-composition trap problems (Zhao et al. 2024) show LLMs struggle to recombine known primitives, and the closest mechanistic work (Tang et al. 2025, 'An explainable transformer circuit for compositional generalization') identifies and ablates a compositional-induction circuit in a compact monolingual transformer. Multilingual factual-transfer work (Aggarwal et al. 2025 'Factuality Depends on the Language of Inquiry') shows knowledge fails to transfer across languages, and mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS. My prior crosslingual_task_vector_portability and crosslingual_finetuned_skill_language_binding proposals concern whole TASKS/SKILLS and their cross-lingual accessibility; NEITHER addresses the recombination of PRIMITIVES learned in one language into NOVEL COMBINATIONS queried in another, whether the binding operation is a shared cross-lingual representation, whether compositional-generalization failure decomposes into binding vs expression-gate components, or whether the binding signal is causally steerable across languages. No prior work asks whether compositional generalization—the systematic recombination of primitives—is language-bound, decoupled between internal binding and behavioral expression, or repairable via steering. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of the compositional binding operation itself.
Abstract: Human intelligence rests on composing known primitives into novel combinations, and much work shows LLMs do this imperfectly—but all of it is monolingual. We ask a new question: when a model learns primitives in one language, does it compose them in a language-independent way, and if cross-lingual compositional generalization fails, is it because the combination was never formed internally or because it was formed but not surfaced in the query language? We build CompBind, controlled primitive-and-combination suites—a taught color-to-symbol mapping, a novel operator applied to operands, and an attribute vocabulary—where primitives are presented in a training language and the model must interpret novel combinations of them, queried across 8 typologically diverse languages. Behaviorally we measure per-language compositional-generalization accuracy on held-out novel combinations and test whether failures track resource level and typological distance from the training language beyond primitive knowledge. We train a linear 'binding' probe that decodes the intended combination from hidden states and test whether a single probe transfers zero-shot across languages, evidencing a shared binding operation, then decompose each cross-lingual failure into a shared binding-failure (the combination is internally absent) versus a language-specific expression-gate failure (present internally but not surfaced). Via activation and path patching we localize a binding signal, and in a decisive causal test we transplant/steer it to make the model surface a combination it internally bound—repairing expression-gate failures but not binding failures—while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual compositional generalization as a decomposable, causally-repairable interplay of a shared binding operation and a language-specific expression gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs); plus small controlled continued/LoRA-fine-tuning runs on Qwen2.5-1.5B/Llama-3.2-1B where primitives must be taught by weight update. 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Turkish).
2) DATASET (CompBind): Three primitive-and-combination families designed so combinations are genuinely NOVEL (not solvable by memorized associations): (A) TAUGHT-MAPPING COMPOSITION—a novel color-to-symbol / word-to-label mapping is defined in-context (or via fine-tuning) and the model must apply it to novel multi-attribute objects (e.g., 'given blicket=X, dax=Y, describe a blicket dax object'); (B) NOVEL-OPERATOR COMPOSITION—a made-up operator with defined rules applied to novel operand combinations; (C) ATTRIBUTE-VOCABULARY COMPOSITION—primitives (shape, size, count) defined then combined into unseen conjunctions. Primitives are presented in a TRAINING LANGUAGE; held-out novel combinations are queried in all 8 languages. Content-light and world-knowledge-free so failures reflect composition, not knowledge; native-verify translations; record tokenization fertility; verify zero-shot baseline failure (combinations are genuinely new). Screen that the model KNOWS each primitive in each query language (via single-primitive probes) so compositional failure is not primitive ignorance.
3) BEHAVIORAL LEAKAGE TEST: Per (combination, query-language) record compositional-generalization accuracy on held-out novel combinations. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME novel combination with primitives taught in a fixed training language, accuracy is systematically lower in lower-resource/typologically distant query languages, beyond primitive knowledge and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of compositional error on (query-language resource tier via URIEL, typological distance from training language, family, primitive-knowledge indicator, tokenization fertility), combination as random effect; compare against a SINGLE-PRIMITIVE control (no composition needed; should be language-flatter). Report per-language compositional profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical combinations.
4) SHARED BINDING PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode the INTENDED COMBINATION (which primitives are bound together, e.g., the resolved attribute conjunction) on the TRAINING-LANGUAGE / ENGLISH data, select the best layer on held-out validation, and apply zero-shot to other query languages; report AUROC/F1 as evidence of a language-independent binding representation. Compare to per-language-trained probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the binding representation for the same combination. CRITICAL: verify the correct combination is internally decodable across languages even where behavioral accuracy differs.
5) BINDING-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: For each cross-lingual FAILURE, classify it via the binding probe as (A) BINDING FAILURE (the combination is NOT internally represented) vs (B) EXPRESSION-GATE FAILURE (present internally but the surface answer is wrong). Report the proportion of A vs B per language and correlate with typological distance (predict binding failures dominate for distant/low-resource, expression-gate failures for close languages). Anchor the internal-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens (identify when the correct combination becomes—or fails to become—dominant across depth).
6) LOCALIZE THE BINDING / EXPRESSION SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that composes correctly and one that fails on the SAME combination, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips failure->correct; report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching. Also test patching the binding representation FROM a successfully-composing language into a failing query-language run.
7) CAUSAL BINDING STEERING/TRANSPLANT (decisive): Derive a binding steering vector via difference-of-means (correct-combination runs minus failed runs) and/or transplant the successful-language binding representation. Test (i) REPAIR: applying it to EXPRESSION-GATE failures surfaces the correct combination in the failing language toward reference levels; (ii) NULL ON BINDING FAILURES: it does NOT help failures classified as binding failures (the combination isn't there to surface), validating the decomposition; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where the expression gap was largest; (iv) it changes ONLY compositional resolution, not the decoded primitives, combination content, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not harm the SINGLE-PRIMITIVE control, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: per-mode repair rate (expression-gate vs binding), output-language fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes novel-combination answers but not single-primitive or unrelated answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: family breakdown (mapping vs operator vs attribute); in-context-taught vs fine-tuning-taught primitives; training-language x query-language matrix (does composition transfer worse the farther the query language from where primitives were taught?); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single binding vector generalizes across combinations and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal binding and by showing content-invariant steering repairs composition without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language compositional-generalization accuracy and its resource/typology regression controlling for primitive-knowledge/fertility, cross-lingual binding-probe transfer AUROC/F1 and representation similarity (CKA/cosine), proportion of binding vs expression-gate failures with probe validation, patch-localized binding layer, cross-lingual binding transplant repair rate (and null effect on binding failures), causal steering per-mode repair rates, binding-signal/output fidelity, single-primitive-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Ensuring combinations are truly NOVEL and non-parametric is critical; we use taught arbitrary mappings, made-up operators, and world-knowledge-free attribute conjunctions, verify zero-shot baseline failure, and report per-combination whether the zero-composition baseline already succeeds. 2) Compositional failure could reflect primitive ignorance rather than a binding/expression issue; we screen per-language single-primitive knowledge and restrict compositional analysis to items where all primitives are known, so residual failure reflects composition. 3) The binding-vs-expression split depends on probe quality; we validate the probe on the training language (where ground truth is available), report AUROC, and confirm the split causally via the transplant test (repairs expression-gate but not binding failures) rather than relying on the probe alone. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal binding, and the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet repairs composition, dissociating the gate from length. 5) Some models may compose robustly across all languages (no gap) or fail to bind at all; either is an informative, publishable finding about the language-boundedness of compositional generalization, and we quantify how often each regime occurs. 6) The binding probe could latch onto surface cues rather than a genuine recombination representation; the cross-lingual invariance test, the internal-binding-predicts-behavior link, the SINGLE-PRIMITIVE control, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five inference models plus small fine-tuning runs, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report binding-signal/output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the reverse-consistency and null-on-binding-failures tests to ensure a genuine binding/expression mechanism. 9) The binding signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my task-vector-portability and fine-tuned-skill proposals is essential; here the object is the recombination of PRIMITIVES into NOVEL COMBINATIONS (compositional generalization / systematicity), not the portability of a whole task or the cross-lingual accessibility of a single learned skill, and from monolingual compositional-circuit work (Tang 2025) by providing the cross-lingual, decomposition, and causal-repair account it lacks.

Name: crosslingual_entrainment_accommodation_gating
Title: Speaking Your Style, in Some Tongues More Than Others: A Shared Interlocutor-Style Representation Whose Accommodation Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: In multi-turn dialogue, a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of the interlocutor's linguistic style (formality, verbosity, lexical/syntactic register), and it entrains toward that style (linguistic accommodation / convergence, a robust human dialogue phenomenon), but the DEGREE of behavioral accommodation is causally gated by the conversation language: for the SAME interlocutor style, the model matches it far more strongly in some languages (typically higher-resource / typologically closer to the model's dominant language) and far more weakly in others, producing a cross-lingual accommodation asymmetry that is separable from the model's ability to represent the style and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable accommodation-gating signal without changing the conversation language.
Related Work: Communication Accommodation Theory (Giles) establishes that speakers converge in linguistic style during dialogue, and human entrainment is well-studied (Savino 2016; prosodic/lexical entrainment). In LLMs, this is barely examined and only behaviorally: Chang & Wang (2025, AAAI Student Abstract) show LLM agents style-match users with ASYMMETRIC adaptation across national cultures and natural convergence over conversations, and Bhattacharya et al. (2026) analyze human-vs-model entrainment in code-switched speech, finding models rely on different features than humans—but both are purely behavioral, with no internal representation, no cross-lingual accommodation-gating account, and no causal intervention. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS, and my prior proposals cover typological-feature leakage into semantics, moral/affect/risk reweighting, and various detection-vs-expression and decision-gating templates. NONE address DIALOGUE-LEVEL linguistic accommodation: whether a multilingual model builds a shared, language-independent representation of the interlocutor's STYLE, whether its behavioral entrainment toward that style is decoupled from its internal representation of it, whether the accommodation degree is language-gated, or whether an accommodation signal can be causally localized and steered. This differs from my persona-override proposal (which concerns an ASSIGNED persona being overwritten by the query language) because here there is no assigned persona—the model must INFER and ADAPT to a live interlocutor's emergent style over turns, a dynamic conversational phenomenon; and from my honorific/status proposal (which concerns register keyed to relative social status) because accommodation is convergence toward whatever style the partner exhibits, independent of status. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of linguistic accommodation in multilingual LLMs.
Abstract: People unconsciously adjust their speaking style toward their conversation partner—becoming more formal with a formal speaker, more terse with a terse one. This linguistic accommodation is a hallmark of human dialogue, and early behavioral work shows LLM agents do it too, but unevenly across cultures. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal representation of an interlocutor's style, and whether its behavioral accommodation toward that style is decoupled from that representation and gated by the conversation language. We hypothesize that models internally register the partner's style similarly across languages, but the conversation language causally sets how strongly they entrain, so the SAME interlocutor style is matched strongly in some languages and weakly in others, independent of the model's ability to perceive the style. We build EntrainProbe, controlled multi-turn dialogues across 10 typologically and resource-diverse languages in which a simulated interlocutor exhibits a fixed style along measurable axes (formality, verbosity, lexical rarity, syntactic complexity), and we measure how far the model's replies shift toward that style over turns. Behaviorally we quantify per-language accommodation magnitude and test whether it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond the model's capacity to represent the style. We train a linear probe for the shared interlocutor-style representation and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the accommodation gap into a shared style-perception component versus a language-set accommodation gate. Via activation and path patching we localize an accommodation-gating signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model entrain in low-accommodation languages (or suppress entrainment in high ones) while leaving the conversation language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual accommodation asymmetry as a shared style perception under a steerable, language-dependent accommodation gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (EntrainProbe): Construct controlled multi-turn dialogues where a SIMULATED INTERLOCUTOR (scripted, held fixed across languages) exhibits a target style along measurable, automatically-scoreable axes: (a) FORMALITY (formal vs casual register), (b) VERBOSITY (terse vs elaborate turn length), (c) LEXICAL RARITY (common vs rare vocabulary), (d) SYNTACTIC COMPLEXITY (simple vs embedded clauses). Each dialogue seeds the model with a neutral opening; the interlocutor then speaks consistently in the target style over N turns; the model's replies are elicited turn-by-turn. Build ~400 dialogue seeds x 4 style axes, translated/native-verified into all 10 languages, keeping topic content fixed across languages. Define per-axis automatic style metrics that are language-robust (formality classifiers / formality lexicons per language; turn-length in tokens normalized by fertility; type-token/rare-word ratios from per-language frequency lists; dependency-depth via a multilingual parser). Include a NEUTRAL-INTERLOCUTOR control (no distinctive style) to bound baseline drift, and record per-language tokenization fertility.
3) BEHAVIORAL ACCOMMODATION TEST: For each (dialogue, language, axis) measure ACCOMMODATION = shift of the model's reply style toward the interlocutor's style over turns (slope of the model's style metric toward the target, relative to the neutral-interlocutor baseline). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME interlocutor style, accommodation magnitude is systematically larger in higher-resource / typologically closer languages and smaller in lower-resource / distant ones. Mixed-effects regression of accommodation on (language, resource tier via URIEL, typological distance, style axis, tokenization fertility), dialogue as random effect; compare against the neutral control (should show little drift). Report per-language accommodation profiles per axis and cross-lingual disagreement on identical interlocutor styles; replicate the Chang & Wang cross-cultural asymmetry as a sanity check.
4) SHARED INTERLOCUTOR-STYLE PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the model's pre-reply position; train a linear probe to decode the INTERLOCUTOR'S current style (formal vs casual, terse vs elaborate, etc.) from the model's hidden state on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent style-perception representation. Compare to per-language-trained probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the style representation for the same interlocutor style. CRITICAL: verify the interlocutor's style is decodable across ALL languages (the model PERCEIVES it) even where behavioral accommodation is weak.
5) PERCEPTION-vs-ACCOMMODATION DECOMPOSITION: For each dialogue, compare the shared mid-layer style-perception signal across languages (should be similar if perception is shared) versus behavioral accommodation (which diverges). Define an ACCOMMODATION GATE mapping perceived style to behavioral entrainment per language; test whether cross-lingual accommodation differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar perception signal rather than weaker perception. Correlate per-language gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE ACCOMMODATION-GATING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that entrains strongly and one that does not on the SAME interlocutor style, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer increases entrainment WITHOUT changing the decoded style-perception signal or the reply's semantic content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the perception representation FROM a high-accommodation language into a low-accommodation run (should not by itself induce accommodation if the gate, not perception, is the bottleneck).
7) CAUSAL ACCOMMODATION STEERING (decisive): Derive an accommodation-gating steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (high-entrainment replies minus low-entrainment replies at matched perceived style). Test (i) INCREASE: adding it in low-accommodation languages raises entrainment toward high-accommodation levels (verified by the style-shift metric); (ii) DECREASE: subtracting it suppresses entrainment in high-accommodation languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where accommodation was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY stylistic entrainment, not the reply's semantic content, decoded style-perception, or conversation language (fidelity checks), does not move the neutral-interlocutor control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: accommodation-gap closure, style-shift magnitude change, de-accommodation-induction rate (reverse), semantic-content and language fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering should change stylistic matching but not answer content or unrelated tasks, guarding against a generic lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: style-axis breakdown (which axis accommodates most/least across languages); does English/high-resource entrain most?; convergence dynamics (accommodation slope over turns) per language; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single accommodation vector generalizes across axes and languages; robustness across dialogue seeds and templates; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched perceived style and by showing content-invariant steering changes entrainment without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language per-axis accommodation magnitude and turn-wise convergence slope, accommodation regression controlling for style-perception/fertility/resource, cross-lingual style-perception probe transfer AUROC and representation similarity (present everywhere), perception-similarity vs accommodation-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized accommodation-gating layer, cross-lingual perception transplant (null-on-gate) test, causal steering accommodation-gap closure and de-accommodation-induction rates, semantic-content/language fidelity, neutral-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Cross-lingual style metrics (formality, complexity) are hard to make comparable across languages; we use per-language-calibrated metrics (formality classifiers/lexicons, fertility-normalized length, per-language frequency lists, multilingual dependency parsing), validate them against human style ratings on a subset, and analyze each axis separately rather than aggregating incomparable scales. 2) The perception-vs-accommodation split could be confounded if the style-perception signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying interlocutor-style decodability across all languages via probe transfer rather than assuming, and report how much of the gap is perception vs gate. 3) Weak accommodation could reflect a stylistic-generation deficit (the model cannot produce the target style in that language) rather than a gating choice; we screen per-language that the model CAN produce each style when explicitly instructed, so residual under-accommodation in natural dialogue reflects the gate, not incapacity. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds length-based style metrics; we normalize by fertility, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched perceived style, and the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts entrainment, dissociating the gate from length. 5) Some models may entrain uniformly across languages (no gap) or not entrain at all; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual accommodation, and we quantify how often the gap occurs, replicating the known cross-cultural asymmetry (Chang & Wang) as a baseline. 6) Simulated interlocutors may be less natural than real users; we use scripted, style-controlled turns for experimental control and validate that findings persist with a held-out set of naturalistic human-written stylized turns. 7) The style-perception probe could latch onto surface cues rather than a genuine style representation; the cross-lingual invariance test, the perception-predicts-accommodation link, and the perception-transplant (null-on-gate) test guard against this. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) Steering may harm fluency or alter semantic content rather than only style; we report semantic-content fidelity (reply meaning preserved), language fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the de-accommodation (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine accommodation gate rather than a generic lever. 10) The gate signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my persona-override (assigned persona overwritten) and honorific/status (register keyed to social status) proposals is essential; here the object is dynamic convergence toward a live interlocutor's emergent linguistic style over turns (communication accommodation), with no assigned persona and independent of relative status.

Name: crosslingual_tip_of_tongue_retrieval
Title: On the Tip of Which Tongue? A Shared Word-Retrieval State With Partial Lexical Access, Whose Resolution Into the Correct Wordform Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs enter a tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) state—a partial-retrieval condition in which the target CONCEPT and partial lexical features (first letter/sound, syllable count, semantic neighbors) are internally available but the exact wordform is not emitted—and this state is largely language-independent: the model computes a shared representation of 'which word is being sought' plus partial features, but whether that representation RESOLVES into the correct wordform is gated by the query language. The SAME hard-to-retrieve word is internally 'on the tip of the tongue' across languages yet correctly produced far less often in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so the model can internally 'know the word' (carry its partial features) while behaviorally failing to say it. We hypothesize (1) a shared middle-layer 'target-word' representation carrying partial lexical features that transfers zero-shot across languages; (2) retrieval-failure that decomposes into a shared RETRIEVAL failure (the target is never internally specified) versus a language-specific RESOLUTION-gate failure (target specified with partial features but not surfaced), tracking resource level and typological distance; and (3) a localizable 'lexical-resolution' signal that can be causally steered to surface a word the model was internally on the tip of the tongue about, without changing the surface language.
Related Work: The tip-of-the-tongue state is a classic psycholinguistic phenomenon (Brown & McNeill 1966; Schwartz & Metcalfe): people fail to retrieve a word yet reliably access partial features (first letter, syllable count, semantic and phonological neighbors), evidencing partial lexical activation. Bilingual TOT work shows TOT rates and partial access differ across a speaker's languages. In NLP, word-retrieval / lexical-access failure is barely studied and only as a monolingual generation/knowledge-gap issue; no work operationalizes an LLM TOT state, its partial-feature access, or its cross-lingual structure. My prior crosslingual_phonological_reasoning proposal concerns whether written words SOUND alike (rhyme/homophone); crosslingual_colexification concerns two concepts fused in one word; the native_language_imprint and reversal_curse proposals concern FACT storage/direction. NONE address a partially-retrieved LEXICAL TARGET—a word the model is trying and failing to produce despite carrying its concept and partial features—whether that TOT state is a shared cross-lingual representation, whether resolution into the correct wordform is language-gated, or whether the retrieval can be causally unblocked. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies lexical retrieval failure or partial-feature access. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of the tip-of-the-tongue state in language models, distinct from all prior facts/senses/phonology proposals because the object is the retrieval of a specific WORDFORM from a specified concept plus partial features.
Abstract: Everyone knows the frustration of a word on the tip of the tongue: you know exactly what you mean, you can feel its first letter and roughly its length, yet the word itself will not come. Decades of psycholinguistics show this reflects partial lexical activation—the concept and partial features are retrieved even when the wordform is not. We ask whether multilingual LLMs enter an analogous tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) state, whether that state is shared across languages, and whether the query language governs whether a word the model is internally reaching for is actually produced. We build TOTProbe, definition-to-word and description-to-word retrieval items for hard-to-retrieve target words, parallel across 8 languages, with metalinguistic partial-feature probes (first letter/sound, syllable/length, semantic neighbors) to diagnose partial access when the exact word is not produced. Behaviorally we measure per-language retrieval success and, on failures, whether partial features are still accessible (a TOT signature), testing whether retrieval failure tracks resource level and typological distance beyond the model simply not knowing the word. We train a linear probe to decode the intended target word (and its partial features) from hidden states and test whether a single probe transfers zero-shot across languages, then decompose retrieval failures into a shared retrieval failure (target internally absent) versus a language-specific resolution-gate failure (target present with partial features but unspoken). Via activation and path patching we localize a lexical-resolution signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to surface a word the model was internally on the tip of the tongue about, while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual word-retrieval gaps as a partly-shared TOT state under a steerable, language-dependent resolution gate.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Turkish). MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (TOTProbe): ~500 DEFINITION/DESCRIPTION-TO-WORD retrieval items targeting hard-to-retrieve words (low-frequency but real words, and rare-but-imageable concepts, chosen to induce retrieval difficulty), e.g. 'the fear of long words is called ___', 'a device for measuring atmospheric pressure is a ___'. Each has a unique target word. For each item build METALINGUISTIC PARTIAL-FEATURE probes to diagnose TOT-style partial access when the exact word is not produced: (a) FIRST-LETTER/SOUND ('what letter does the word start with?'), (b) LENGTH/SYLLABLE ('how many syllables/letters?'), (c) SEMANTIC-NEIGHBOR ('name a related word'), (d) RECOGNITION (multiple-choice: pick the target among distractors—partial access predicts above-chance recognition even when free recall fails). Translate/native-verify all items and target words into 8 languages, keeping the described concept fixed; the target word is the language-appropriate translation. Include (i) an EASY-RETRIEVAL control (high-frequency target the model reliably produces, to bound the effect and separate resolution from concept ignorance) and (ii) a KNOWLEDGE-SCREEN: verify per language that the model can RECOGNIZE the target (multiple-choice) so free-recall failure with intact recognition is a genuine TOT/resolution failure, not ignorance. Record tokenization fertility.
3) BEHAVIORAL TOT TEST: Per (item, language) record free-recall retrieval success. On FAILURES, measure partial-feature accuracy (first-letter, length, semantic-neighbor) and recognition accuracy—a TOT SIGNATURE is failed recall with above-chance partial-feature/recognition access. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME hard word, free-recall success is systematically lower in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, WHILE partial-feature/recognition access remains present—i.e. the model is internally 'on the tip of the tongue' but does not surface the word, more so in some languages. Mixed-effects logistic regression of recall-failure on (language, resource tier via URIEL, typological distance, tokenization fertility, recognition indicator), item as random effect; compare against the easy-retrieval control (language-flat). Report per-language recall vs partial-access profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical target concepts.
4) SHARED TARGET-WORD PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-output position; train a linear probe to decode the INTENDED TARGET WORD (over a closed per-item candidate set) and its PARTIAL FEATURES (first letter, length class) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC/accuracy as evidence of a language-independent target-word representation carrying partial features. Compare to per-language-trained probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the target-word representation for the same concept. CRITICAL: on recall-failure items, test whether the correct target (and its partial features) is internally decodable across ALL languages even when not emitted—the internal TOT signature.
5) RETRIEVAL-vs-RESOLUTION DECOMPOSITION: For each recall failure, classify it via the probe as (A) RETRIEVAL FAILURE (the target is NOT internally specified) vs (B) RESOLUTION-GATE FAILURE (target present with partial features but not surfaced). Report the proportion of A vs B per language and correlate with resource tier and typological distance (predict resolution-gate failures dominate for typologically close languages where the concept is shared but production is weak, retrieval failures for distant/low-resource ones). Anchor the internal-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens (identify when the correct word does—or fails to—become dominant across depth).
6) LOCALIZE THE LEXICAL-RESOLUTION SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that successfully retrieves and one that fails on the SAME target, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer surfaces the word WITHOUT changing the decoded concept. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the target-word representation FROM a successfully-retrieving language into a failing (TOT) run.
7) CAUSAL RESOLUTION STEERING (decisive): Derive a lexical-resolution steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (successful-retrieval runs minus TOT/failed runs at matched internal target). Test (i) UNBLOCK: adding it to TOT (resolution-gate) failures surfaces the correct word in the failing language toward successful-retrieval levels; (ii) NULL ON RETRIEVAL FAILURES: it does NOT help failures where the target was internally absent, validating the decomposition; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where the resolution gap was largest; (iv) it changes ONLY whether the target word is produced, not the decoded concept, the described meaning, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not harm the easy-retrieval control, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: per-mode unblock rate (resolution-gate vs retrieval), concept/output-language fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering surfaces the sought word but does not change unrelated or easy-control answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: which partial features are best preserved under failure per language; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; token-pooling (rare target words split into many subwords—report sensitivity); whether a single resolution vector generalizes across items and languages; robustness across definition-vs-description and free-recall-vs-recognition formats; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal target and by showing content-invariant steering unblocks retrieval without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language free-recall success and, on failures, partial-feature/recognition access (TOT signature), recall-failure regression controlling for recognition/fertility/resource/typology, cross-lingual target-word probe transfer AUROC/accuracy and internal-target-present-under-failure, cross-lingual target-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), proportion of retrieval vs resolution-gate failures with probe validation, patch-localized lexical-resolution layer, cross-lingual target transplant unblock rate (and null on retrieval failures), causal steering per-mode unblock rates, concept/output fidelity, easy-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Distinguishing a genuine TOT/resolution failure from simple ignorance is the crux; we use the recognition/knowledge-screen (intact recognition + preserved partial features under failed recall = TOT signature) and the internal-target-decodability test to establish partial access, and restrict the resolution-gate analysis to items where the target is internally present. 2) The retrieval-vs-resolution split depends on probe quality; we validate the probe on English (where ground truth is available), report AUROC, and confirm the split causally via the transplant/steering test (unblocks resolution-gate but not retrieval failures) rather than relying on the probe alone. 3) Some models may retrieve robustly across all languages (no TOT gap) or fail to specify the target at all (pure retrieval failure); either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual word retrieval, and we quantify how often each regime occurs. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds production of rare multi-subword target words; we control for fertility, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal target, use multiple token-pooling schemes, and show content-invariant steering unblocks retrieval without changing tokenization. 5) Partial-feature probes (first letter/syllable) are noisy for multi-subword words and non-alphabetic scripts (Chinese); we prefer alphabetic first-letter probes where meaningful, use script-appropriate features elsewhere (e.g. character count), and analyze scripts separately. 6) The target-word probe could latch onto surface cues rather than a genuine internal target representation; the internal-target-present-under-failure test, cross-lingual invariance, and cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report concept/output fidelity, easy-control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the null-on-retrieval-failures and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine lexical-resolution gate rather than a generic boost. 9) The resolution signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my phonological-reasoning, colexification, and fact-storage proposals is essential; here the object is a partially-retrieved LEXICAL TARGET (a specific wordform sought from a known concept plus partial features)—the tip-of-the-tongue state—not sound-similarity of written words, sense conflation, or factual knowledge storage.

Name: crosslingual_orthographic_composition_gating
Title: Spelling It Out in Every Script: A Shared Character-Composition Signal Whose Expression Is Gated by Writing-System Typology in Multilingual LLMs
