Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs reconstruct, in their intermediate layers, a largely writing-system-independent internal representation of a token's constituent orthographic sub-units (the characters that compose an alphabetic word, the letters+diacritics of an abjad word, the radicals/strokes of a logographic character, the aksharas of an abugida), but whether this composition is behaviorally EXPRESSED (correctly spelling out, counting, or identifying sub-components) is gated by the query language's writing-system type: the SAME token is internally decomposed across scripts yet surfaced far more weakly for logographic/abugida and lower-resource scripts than for alphabetic ones, so the model can internally 'know the spelling' while behaviorally failing. The composition signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so orthographic-composition failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Hiraoka & Inui (2025, 'Spelling-out is not Straightforward') show LLMs reconstruct character-level knowledge in intermediate/higher Transformer layers with a distinct 'breakthrough' during spelling-out (validated via probes, knowledge neurons, and attention), and note the embedding layer under-encodes characters beyond the first—but this is MONOLINGUAL (English tokens) and offers no cross-lingual or writing-system-typology account, no detection-vs-expression decomposition, and no causal steering. Character/byte-level and subword-composition work (ByT5, MrT5 [Kallini 2024], Char2Subword [Aguilar 2020], Vania 2020) studies robustness and morphology across languages but not whether the model internally recovers a token's orthographic sub-units as a shared cross-lingual representation. Reading-science work (Share 2025's Combinatorial Model; Chinese stroke/radical/logographeme units [Liang & Ng 2024]) establishes that writing systems combine a learnable set of sub-lexical units into words very differently across scripts (alphabet/abjad/abugida/logograph), but this is human reading, not LLM mechanism. My prior crosslingual_phonological_reasoning proposal concerns whether written words SOUND alike (rhyme/homophone) and intra_language_script_knowledge_fragmentation concerns knowledge access across scripts of ONE language; NEITHER addresses the internal DECOMPOSITION of a token into its constituent orthographic units, whether that composition is shared across writing systems, whether writing-system typology gates its expression, or whether it is causally steerable. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for orthographic composition. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual, writing-system-typology account of token-to-orthographic-unit composition, extending Hiraoka & Inui beyond English.
Abstract: Humans read by combining sub-lexical units—letters, diacritics, radicals, aksharas—into words, but writing systems do this very differently: alphabets map to phonemes, abjads omit vowels, abugidas bind consonant-vowel units, and logographs compose from radicals and strokes. Recent work shows English LLMs reconstruct a token's characters in their intermediate layers with a spelling 'breakthrough', but whether this orthographic composition is shared across writing systems, and whether a script's type governs whether the model can actually surface it, is unknown. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a largely writing-system-independent internal representation of a token's constituent orthographic units, and whether that internal composition is decoupled from its behavioral expression across scripts. We hypothesize that models internally decompose tokens similarly across writing systems, but the query language's writing-system type gates whether the composition is surfaced (spelling out, counting sub-units, identifying sub-components), so the SAME token is composed internally yet surfaced far more weakly for logographic/abugida and lower-resource scripts. We build OrthoProbe, parallel token-composition tasks across 8 languages spanning alphabet, abjad, abugida, and logographic scripts, each with spelling-out, sub-unit-count, and sub-component-identification probes and a matched control. Behaviorally we measure per-script expression and test whether it tracks writing-system type beyond tokenization. We train a linear composition probe and test whether a single probe transfers zero-shot across scripts, evidencing a shared signal, then decompose the expression gap into a shared composition component versus a language-set expression gate. Via activation and path patching we localize a composition signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to surface an orthographic decomposition the model internally computed, while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual orthographic-composition gaps as a steerable gate over a shared composition signal.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 languages spanning writing-system typology: ALPHABETIC (English, Spanish, Russian), ABJAD (Arabic, Hebrew), ABUGIDA (Hindi/Devanagari), LOGOGRAPHIC (Chinese), and a mixed/syllabic case (Japanese kana+kanji), coded for writing-system type and sub-unit grain (phoneme-letter vs consonant+diacritic vs akshara vs radical/stroke) from writing-systems references (Share 2025; Liang & Ng 2024) plus URIEL for typological distance; treat writing-system type as a categorical/graded predictor. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (OrthoProbe): ~500 tokens/words per language with known orthographic decompositions, each with three probe types: (A) SPELL-OUT ('write <token> one character/unit at a time'), (B) SUB-UNIT COUNT ('how many letters/aksharas/radicals/strokes?'), (C) SUB-COMPONENT IDENTIFICATION ('what is the 3rd character?' / 'which radical does this character contain?' / 'does this word contain the letter X?'). Define script-appropriate sub-units: letters (alphabet), letters+diacritics (abjad), aksharas/consonant-vowel units (abugida), radicals+strokes (logographic). Ground-truth decompositions from Unicode/orthographic references and native verification. Translate/parallelize across languages where meaning permits (or use frequency-matched native tokens per script); record per-token tokenization fertility (how many subword tokens the model's tokenizer assigns). Include a FIRST-CHARACTER control (which Hiraoka & Inui show is easy) to bound the effect. Screen recognition (can the model RECOGNIZE the correct decomposition in multiple-choice) so free-production failure with intact recognition indicates a genuine expression-gate, not ignorance.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (token, language, probe) measure composition accuracy. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME composition demand, expression is systematically weaker for logographic/abugida and lower-resource scripts than alphabetic ones, beyond tokenization fertility. Mixed-effects logistic regression of composition error on (writing-system type, probe type, language, tokenization fertility, resource tier via URIEL, recognition indicator), token as random effect; compare against the first-character control (should be script-flatter, high). Report per-script expression profiles and cross-script disagreement on matched composition demands; replicate the English spelling-out baseline (Hiraoka & Inui).
4) SHARED COMPOSITION PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the token position; train a linear probe to decode the token's sub-unit inventory / sub-component identity (e.g., presence of a given letter/radical, sub-unit count) on ENGLISH (alphabetic) data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot to other scripts; report AUROC/accuracy as evidence of a writing-system-independent composition representation. Compare to per-script-trained probes; measure cross-script CKA/cosine of the composition representation. Track across layers to locate the 'breakthrough' layer per script (extending Hiraoka & Inui cross-lingually) and test whether the composition signal is present in ALL scripts even where behavioral accuracy differs.
5) COMPOSITION-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: For each failure, classify via the probe as (A) COMPOSITION FAILURE (sub-units NOT internally represented) vs (B) EXPRESSION-GATE FAILURE (present internally but not surfaced). Report proportion of A vs B per script and correlate with writing-system type and resource tier (predict expression-gate failures dominate for logographic/abugida where composition is computed but production is weak). Anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE COMPOSITION / EXPRESSION SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching (and knowledge-neuron analysis following Hiraoka & Inui) between a script that surfaces the composition and one that fails on a matched token, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer surfaces the decomposition WITHOUT changing token identity. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band and the breakthrough layer; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the composition representation FROM a high-expression (alphabetic) script into a failing logographic/abugida run.
7) CAUSAL COMPOSITION STEERING (decisive): Derive a composition-expression steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (correct-composition runs minus failed runs at matched internal signal). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to low-expression scripts increases correct spelling/counting/identification toward alphabetic levels; (ii) NULL ON COMPOSITION FAILURES: it does not help failures where sub-units were internally absent, validating the decomposition; (iii) SUPPRESS: subtracting it degrades composition expression in alphabetic scripts; (iv) it changes ONLY composition expression, not token identity, meaning, or surface language (fidelity), does not move the first-character control, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: per-mode expression-gap closure, spelling/counting accuracy recovery, suppression-induction rate (reverse), token/output-language fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes composition tasks but not unrelated answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: writing-system-type breakdown (alphabet vs abjad vs abugida vs logographic) and sub-unit grain (letter vs radical vs akshara); probe-type breakdown (spell-out vs count vs identify); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality and breakthrough-layer location per script; token-pooling and tokenization-fertility dissociation (compare high- vs low-fertility tokens at matched internal composition, and show content-invariant steering repairs composition without changing tokenization); whether a single composition vector generalizes across scripts and sub-unit types.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-script composition accuracy (spell/count/identify) and first-character-control accuracy, expression regression controlling for fertility/recognition/resource with writing-system-type effect, English spelling replication, cross-script composition-probe transfer AUROC/accuracy and per-script breakthrough-layer, cross-script composition-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), composition-vs-expression-gate failure proportions with probe validation, patch-localized composition layer, cross-script composition transplant recovery rate (and null on composition failures), causal steering per-mode expression-gap closure and suppression-induction rates, token/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Tokenization is the central confound: logographic/abugida/abjad tokens split very differently into subwords, and the embedding layer under-encodes characters beyond the first (Hiraoka & Inui); we control for tokenization fertility in regression, compare high- vs low-fertility tokens at matched internal composition, use multiple token-pooling schemes, and—crucially—the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet repairs composition, dissociating the expression gate from tokenization. 2) The composition-vs-expression split depends on probe quality; we validate the probe on English (where ground truth and the breakthrough are known), report AUROC, and confirm the split causally via the transplant/steering test (surfaces expression-gate but not composition failures) rather than relying on the probe alone. 3) Sub-unit definitions differ across scripts and can be graded (radicals vs strokes vs logographemes; vowel diacritics often unwritten in abjads); we use script-appropriate, native-verified decompositions, treat sub-unit grain as a covariate, and analyze each writing-system type separately. 4) Some models may compose robustly across all scripts (no gap) or fail to compose at all for logographs (pure composition failure); either is an informative, publishable finding about the limits of cross-script orthographic composition, and we quantify how often each regime occurs. 5) Composition failure could reflect ignorance of the token's spelling rather than an expression gate; we use recognition screening (intact multiple-choice recognition + present internal composition signal = expression gate) and restrict the gate analysis to items where composition is internally present. 6) The composition probe could latch onto surface subword cues rather than a genuine orthographic-unit representation; the cross-script invariance test, the composition-predicts-behavior link, and the cross-script transplant guard against this. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching plus knowledge-neuron analysis. 8) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report token/output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the null-on-composition-failures and suppression (reverse) tests to ensure a genuine composition-expression gate. 9) The signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from Hiraoka & Inui (monolingual English) and from my phonological-reasoning (sound) and script-fragmentation (knowledge across scripts of one language) proposals is essential; here the object is the internal DECOMPOSITION of a token into its constituent ORTHOGRAPHIC units across WRITING SYSTEMS and the decoupling of that composition from its behavioral expression.

Name: crosslingual_vague_quantifier_scale_gating
Title: How Many Is 'A Few', in Every Language? A Shared Vague-Quantifier Scale Whose Calibration Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs map vague quantity/frequency/probability expressions ('a few', 'many', 'often', 'likely', 'sometimes') onto a largely language-independent internal numeric scale, but the query language causally recalibrates that mapping at the language-specific decoding layers: the SAME vague quantifier is grounded to a systematically different numeric value depending on the query language, tracking each language's translation-equivalent term conventions and typological/resource distance, and this cross-lingual scale drift is separable from the underlying shared magnitude representation and is causally steerable by shifting a localizable calibration signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Vague-quantifier interpretation is studied in psycholinguistics (the numeric values people assign to terms like 'a few'/'many'/'likely' vary systematically) and cross-linguistically (translation-equivalent quantifiers are not numerically equivalent across languages/cultures). In NLP, monolingual English work probes whether LLMs assign consistent numeric values to vague quantifiers and probability phrases, and multilingual factual-consistency work (Qi 2023; Wang 2025) shows answers differ across languages, but NONE examine whether a vague quantifier is grounded to the SAME internal numeric scale across languages, whether cross-lingual scale drift decomposes into a shared magnitude estimate versus a language-set calibration gate, or whether the calibration is causally localizable and steerable. My prior proposals cover exact number-naming distortion, dynamic tally maintenance, measurement units, reported precision, generic quantificational force, and the approximate-number-system Weber signature; NONE address the grounding of VAGUE quantity/frequency/probability terms onto a numeric scale, which is a distinct semantic phenomenon (mapping a lexical scalar to a magnitude, not composing, counting, converting units, rounding, or comparing). Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never for vague-quantifier scaling. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of vague-quantifier calibration.
Abstract: When someone says 'a few people came', how many is that—and does the answer change if the question is asked in Spanish, Arabic, or Chinese? Vague quantifiers ('a few', 'many', 'often', 'likely', 'sometimes') must be grounded onto a numeric scale to be used in reasoning, yet translation-equivalent terms carry different implied magnitudes across languages. We ask whether a multilingual LLM maps such terms onto a shared, language-independent internal scale, and whether the query language recalibrates that mapping. We hypothesize that the model computes a largely language-independent internal magnitude for a vague quantifier, but the query language causally shifts the numeric value it is grounded to at the decoding layers, so the SAME term implies a systematically different quantity across languages, tracking each language's term conventions and typological distance. We build QuantScale, parallel elicitation and reasoning items across 10 languages that ground quantity, frequency, and probability expressions to numeric values, with the surrounding content held fixed. Behaviorally we measure per-language grounded values and test whether cross-lingual scale drift tracks resource level and typological distance beyond translation. We train a linear probe for the shared vague-quantifier magnitude and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the drift into a shared magnitude estimate versus a language-set calibration gate. Via activation and path patching we localize a calibration signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to shift the grounded value of a quantifier (or equalize it across languages) while leaving the surface language and content unchanged. We reframe multilingual vague-quantifier inconsistency as a shared scale under a steerable, language-dependent calibration gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (QuantScale): ~500 items spanning three scalar families—(A) QUANTITY ('a few', 'several', 'many', 'a handful of', 'lots of'), (B) FREQUENCY ('rarely', 'sometimes', 'often', 'usually', 'always'), (C) PROBABILITY ('unlikely', 'possibly', 'probably', 'almost certainly'). Each item elicits a numeric grounding in a fixed context, via three probe types: (i) DIRECT ('If a report says "a few" people attended a 100-person meeting, about how many is that?' -> a number/percentage), (ii) FORCED-CHOICE between numeric ranges, (iii) DOWNSTREAM REASONING where the grounded value determines the answer. Keep the described scenario and the numeric anchor fixed across languages; the quantifier is the language-appropriate translation-equivalent (native-verified). Include a NUMERIC control (explicit numbers, no vague term; correct answer language-flat) to bound the effect. Record tokenization fertility. Optionally collect small per-language human grounding norms on a subset to anchor 'ground-truth' cross-lingual variation vs model behavior.
3) BEHAVIORAL SCALE-DRIFT TEST: For each (item, language) record the grounded numeric value. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME term-in-context, the grounded value shifts systematically with query language, and the drift tracks resource level and typological distance beyond translation. Mixed-effects regression of grounded value on (language, scalar family, term, tokenization fertility, resource tier via URIEL), item as random effect; test the language effect. Compare against the NUMERIC control (should be language-flat). Report per-language scale profiles, cross-lingual disagreement on identical terms, and whether the ORDERING of terms within a family is preserved across languages (a shared scale should preserve rank even if it stretches/shifts).
4) SHARED VAGUE-QUANTIFIER PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode the grounded magnitude (regress to the numeric value) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report R^2/rank-correlation as evidence of a language-independent scale representation, plus cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the magnitude representation for the same term-in-context. Show the shared magnitude is internally similar across languages even when the emitted grounded value differs.
5) GATE-vs-ESTIMATE DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer magnitude estimate across languages (should be similar if shared) versus the emitted grounded value (which drifts). Define a per-language CALIBRATION GATE (an affine shift/scale from the shared estimate to the emitted value); test whether cross-lingual drift is explained by a language-set calibration gate on a similar internal estimate rather than a different estimate. Correlate per-language gate parameters with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE CALIBRATION SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that grounds a term high and one that grounds it low on the SAME item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer shifts the grounded value WITHOUT changing the decoded shared magnitude estimate. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the calibration components from one language into another's run.
7) CAUSAL CALIBRATION STEERING (decisive): Derive a calibration steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (high-grounding runs minus low-grounding runs at matched shared estimate). Test (i) SHIFT: adding/subtracting it moves the grounded value of a quantifier up/down in a graded (dose-response) way on held-out items; (ii) EQUALIZE: apply per-language calibration to make the same term ground to the same value across languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually and can override a language's default calibration; (iv) it changes ONLY the grounded value, not the decoded shared magnitude estimate, the described content, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the NUMERIC control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: cross-lingual drift closure, dose-response of grounded value, content/output fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts vague-quantifier grounding but not explicit-number or unrelated answers, guarding against a generic lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: family breakdown (quantity vs frequency vs probability); rank-preservation across languages; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank calibration subspace; robustness across templates and direct-vs-forced-choice-vs-downstream formats; whether one calibration vector generalizes across terms and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched shared estimate and by showing content-invariant steering shifts grounding without changing tokenization; comparison of model drift against human grounding norms on the subset.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language grounded values and cross-lingual drift with resource/typology regression, within-family rank-preservation, cross-lingual vague-quantifier probe transfer R^2/rank-correlation and representation similarity, estimate-similarity vs output-drift (calibration gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized calibration layer, cross-lingual calibration transplant shift, causal steering drift closure with dose-response, content/output fidelity, numeric-control and general-QA retention, model-vs-human grounding comparison.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Vague-quantifier 'ground truth' is inherently fuzzy and culturally variable; we avoid claiming a single correct value, use human per-language norms descriptively where available, focus on relative cross-lingual drift and within-family rank-preservation, and use the numeric control to anchor. 2) The gate-vs-estimate split could be confounded if the shared magnitude estimate itself differs by language; we test this directly by comparing shared-probe estimates across languages rather than assuming, and report how much drift is estimate vs gate. 3) Scale drift could be a mere translation effect (the translated term genuinely means a different quantity) rather than an internal calibration gate; the shared-estimate-similarity finding, the internal-magnitude-predicts-grounding link, and the content-preserving steering (which shifts grounding without changing the term) dissociate a genuine internal calibration gate from lexical translation. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched shared estimate, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts grounding. 5) Instruction-tuned models may hedge or refuse to give numbers; we use both numeric generation and log-probability over numeric ranges, and report refusal rates. 6) Some models may ground quantifiers uniformly across languages (no drift) or fail to ground them at all; either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often drift occurs and whether a shared scale exists. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic lever; we report content/output fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention, and use dose-response and reverse-consistency to ensure a genuine calibration dial. 9) The calibration signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my number-naming, ANS (approximate comparison), generic-force, units, and precision proposals is essential; here the object is the grounding of VAGUE quantity/frequency/probability LEXICAL scalars onto a numeric scale and its language-set calibration, not exact-number distortion, ratio-based comparison, generic exception-tolerance, unit systems, or rounding.

Name: crosslingual_discourse_relation_inference_gating
Title: Reading Between the Sentences, in Every Language: A Shared Implicit-Discourse-Relation Signal Whose Expression Is Gated by Connective-Marking Typology
Short Hypothesis: When two clauses are juxtaposed WITHOUT an explicit connective (implicit discourse relation, e.g. cause, contrast, concession, elaboration), a multilingual LLM infers a largely language-independent internal representation of WHICH relation holds, but whether that inferred relation is behaviorally EXPRESSED (answering relation-dependent questions, choosing the coherent continuation, inserting the right connective) is gated by the query language's connective-marking typology: the SAME implicit relation is inferred internally across languages yet surfaced far more weakly in languages that habitually mark such relations explicitly (and in lower-resource / typologically distant languages), so the model can internally 'get the relation' while behaviorally missing it. The discourse-relation signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so implicit-relation failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Implicit discourse relation recognition (IDRR) is a long-standing task built on PDTB/RST-style corpora and cross-lingual resources (TED-MDB; Chinese/Turkish discourse treebanks), studied behaviorally as a classification problem; recent LLM work shows models struggle with implicit (vs explicit) relations and that performance varies across languages, but treats it as a benchmark accuracy gap with no internal representation, no detection-vs-expression decomposition, and no causal intervention. Cross-lingual discourse-marking typology (whether a language obligatorily or optionally signals coherence relations with connectives) is documented in linguistics (Asr & Demberg; discourse-connective inventories) but never tied to an internal LLM mechanism. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS, and my prior proposals cover typological-feature leakage into sentence-level semantics (polarity, aspect, evidentiality, genericity), a literal-to-figurative transition, temporal event ordering, causal direction, and various detection-vs-expression gating templates (semantic anticipation, false belief, humor). NONE address INTER-CLAUSAL discourse coherence: whether a multilingual model builds a shared, language-independent representation of the implicit relation BETWEEN two clauses, whether that internal inference is decoupled from behavioral expression across languages, whether connective-marking typology gates that expression, or whether a discourse-relation signal is causally localizable and steerable. This is distinct from my causal-direction proposal (which concerns cause-vs-effect direction of two EVENTS, not the discourse relation label—contrast/concession/elaboration—linking two CLAUSES) and from sentence-internal leakage proposals (the object here is a relation spanning two sentences). This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of implicit-discourse-relation inference.
Abstract: Coherent text depends on relations between clauses that are often left unstated: 'It was raining. The match was cancelled' implies a causal link no word marks. Recovering such implicit discourse relations is central to comprehension, and languages differ sharply in how habitually they signal these relations with explicit connectives. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal representation of the implicit relation between two clauses, and whether that internal inference is decoupled from how reliably it is behaviorally expressed across languages. We hypothesize that models infer the implicit relation similarly across languages, but the query language's connective-marking typology gates whether that relation is surfaced, so the SAME implicit relation is inferred internally yet answered (via relation-dependent questions, coherent-continuation choice, or connective insertion) far less often in some languages—especially those that usually mark such relations explicitly and lower-resource, typologically distant ones. We build DiscourseProbe, parallel clause pairs across 8 languages instantiating core relations (cause, contrast, concession, elaboration) in an IMPLICIT (no connective) and a matched EXPLICIT (connective present) form, with relation-identification, continuation-choice, and connective-insertion probes. Behaviorally we measure per-language implicit-relation expression and test whether it tracks connective-marking typology and resource level beyond comprehension. We train a linear relation probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the expression gap into a shared inference component versus a language-set expression gate. Via activation and path patching we localize a relation signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to surface a relation the model internally inferred (or flip it), while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual discourse-coherence gaps as a steerable gate over a shared relation representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages spanning connective-marking typology (English, German, Russian [explicit-marking-inclined], Spanish, Turkish, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese [more implicit/juxtaposition-tolerant]), coded for connective-marking richness/obligatoriness from discourse-typology references plus URIEL for typological distance; treat connective-marking as a graded predictor. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (DiscourseProbe): ~500 clause pairs instantiating four core discourse relations (CAUSE, CONTRAST, CONCESSION, ELABORATION), drawn from/extending PDTB/RST-style and cross-lingual discourse resources. Each pair appears in an IMPLICIT form (clauses juxtaposed, no connective) and a matched EXPLICIT form (correct connective inserted), holding propositional content fixed. Probes: (A) RELATION-IDENTIFICATION ('What is the relation between these two clauses?' MC over the relation set), (B) CONTINUATION-CHOICE (pick the coherent next clause, where the correct choice depends on the inferred relation), (C) CONNECTIVE-INSERTION (which connective best links them?). Include a matched EXPLICIT control (relation is overtly marked; should be language-flatter, near-ceiling) to bound the effect and separate relation inference from comprehension. Translate/native-verify into all 8 languages, keeping clause content fixed; record tokenization fertility; screen base-clause comprehension via the explicit form. Short scoreable answers where possible.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (pair, language) record correct-relation vs distractor answers on the IMPLICIT form. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME implicit relation, expression is systematically weaker in languages with richer explicit-connective habits and in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond comprehension and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of implicit-relation error on (connective-marking typology, relation type, language, tokenization fertility, explicit-form accuracy, resource tier via URIEL), pair as random effect; compare against the explicit control. Report per-language and per-relation expression profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical implicit pairs; replicate an English IDRR baseline.
4) SHARED RELATION PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the clause-boundary/pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode the discourse relation on ENGLISH implicit data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report macro-F1/AUROC as evidence of a language-independent relation representation. Compare to per-language-trained probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the relation representation for the same pair. CRITICAL: verify the correct relation is internally decodable across ALL languages on implicit pairs even where behavioral accuracy differs.
5) INFERENCE-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: For each implicit pair, compare the shared mid-layer relation signal across languages (should be similar if inference is shared) versus behavioral expression (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal relation to surfaced answer per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar inference signal rather than weaker inference. Correlate per-language gate strength with connective-marking typology, resource tier, and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE RELATION / EXPRESSION SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that surfaces the relation and one that fails on the SAME implicit pair, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer makes the correct relation surface WITHOUT changing the decoded clause content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the relation representation FROM a high-expression language into a failing low-expression run.
7) CAUSAL RELATION STEERING (decisive): Derive a relation steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (correct-relation runs minus failed/other-relation runs, matched content; also EXPLICIT-minus-IMPLICIT contrasts for the same relation). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to low-expression languages increases correct implicit-relation answers toward high-expression levels; (ii) FLIP: steering toward a different relation (e.g. contrast->cause) changes the model's relation-dependent answer on well-resolved items; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where expression was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY discourse-relation interpretation, not clause content or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the EXPLICIT control, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: expression-gap closure, relation-flip rate (reverse), relation-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes relation-dependent answers but not unrelated or explicit-control answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: relation-type breakdown (which relations leak most: concession/contrast vs cause/elaboration); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single relation vector generalizes across relation types and languages; robustness across templates and MC-vs-continuation-vs-connective formats; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal relation and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces the relation without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language per-relation implicit-relation accuracy and explicit-control accuracy, expression regression controlling for comprehension/fertility/resource with connective-marking effect, English IDRR replication, cross-lingual relation-probe transfer F1/AUROC and internal-relation-present-under-failure, cross-lingual relation-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), inference-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-typology correlation, patch-localized relation layer, cross-lingual relation transplant recovery rate, causal steering expression-gap closure and relation-flip rates, relation-signal/output fidelity, explicit-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The inference-vs-expression split could be confounded if the relation signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying correct-relation decodability across all languages via probe transfer rather than assuming, and report how much of the gap is inference vs gate. 2) Implicit-relation failure could reflect clause-comprehension failure rather than an expression gate; we use the matched EXPLICIT control and comprehension screening so residual failure reflects relation inference, not reading. 3) Discourse relations can be genuinely ambiguous (a pair may license multiple relations); we restrict scored items to clear-consensus single-relation pairs (native-verified, drawing on validated discourse-annotated stimuli) and analyze ambiguous ones separately. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal relation, and the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet surfaces the relation, dissociating the gate from length. 5) Some models may infer and express relations uniformly across languages (no gap) or fail everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual discourse coherence, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 6) Connective-marking typology coding is coarse and debated; we use documented discourse-typology sources, treat it as a graded predictor, and report sensitivity to alternative codings. 7) The relation probe could latch onto surface connective/lexical cues rather than a genuine inter-clausal relation representation; using IMPLICIT (connective-free) pairs, the cross-lingual invariance test, the internal-relation-predicts-behavior link, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report relation-signal/output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the flip (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine relation-expression gate. 10) The gate/relation signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my causal-direction (cause-vs-effect of two events) and sentence-internal leakage proposals is essential; here the object is the DISCOURSE RELATION (cause/contrast/concession/elaboration) linking two CLAUSES and the decoupling of its internal inference from behavioral expression across languages, gated by connective-marking typology.

Name: crosslingual_error_monitoring_gating
Title: Noticing the Mistake but Not Saying So: A Shared Error-Monitoring Signal Whose Behavioral Flagging and Correction Are Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs compute a largely language-independent internal 'error-monitoring' signal that registers when a reasoning step or a claim is wrong, but whether that detected error is behaviorally EXPRESSED (flagging it, refusing to endorse it, or correcting it) is gated by the query language: the SAME error is internally detected across languages yet surfaced far less often in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so a model can internally 'know it is wrong' while behaviorally under-flagging and failing to self-correct. The error-monitoring signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated under-flagging can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Self-correction work decomposes the ability into error detection, localization, and correction (Li 2025 'Accuracy-Correction Paradox'; Zhang 2024 'Learning to Check'), showing detection capability does not predict correction success and that intrinsic self-correction is often ineffective—all MONOLINGUAL (English) and behavioral. Multilingual error-detection is only benchmarked behaviorally: MedErrBench (Ma 2026) and pediatric/medical-error studies show large non-English performance gaps in detecting clinical errors, and M-GATE (Burkert 2026) finds models systematically UNDER-FLAG ungrammatical text with errors leaning toward accepting rather than raising alarms—but none provide an internal representation, a detection-vs-expression decomposition, or a causal intervention. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS, and my prior proposals include a CoT-faithfulness gap (whether the trace drives the answer), a semantic-anticipation (N400-like) detection-vs-expression gate for congruity of an UPCOMING word, and cross-lingual calibration (know/don't-know about the model's own knowledge). NONE address ERROR MONITORING—the internal detection that a given reasoning step or asserted claim is WRONG—whether that monitoring signal is shared across languages, whether its behavioral flagging/correction is language-gated, or whether it is causally localizable and steerable. This is distinct from my calibration proposal (confidence in the model's own answer) because the object here is detecting errors in a PRESENTED step/claim (self-monitoring of correctness), distinct from semantic-anticipation (congruity of a next word, not correctness of a reasoning step), and distinct from CoT-faithfulness (whether the trace causes the answer). This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of error monitoring, with direct safety stakes given documented multilingual under-flagging in medical and grammatical error detection.
Abstract: When a reasoning chain takes a wrong turn or a stated fact is false, a competent model should notice and flag it—yet benchmarks show multilingual models systematically under-flag errors, worst of all in non-English and clinical settings. We ask whether this under-flagging reflects a genuine failure to detect the error or a shared internal detection that simply is not surfaced, and whether that gap is language-dependent. We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal error-monitoring signal that registers when a presented step or claim is wrong, but the query language gates whether that detected error is behaviorally expressed (flagged, rejected, or corrected), so the SAME error is detected internally across languages yet acted on far less in lower-resource, typologically distant languages. We build ErrorMon, parallel items across 10 languages in which a reasoning step or factual claim is either correct or contains a planted error, with flag-detection, endorsement, and correction probes, plus an all-correct control. Behaviorally we measure per-language error-flagging and correction and test whether under-flagging tracks resource level and typological distance beyond the model's ability to detect the error. We train a linear error-monitoring probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the flagging gap into a shared detection component versus a language-set expression gate, verifying the error is internally detectable even where it is not flagged. Via activation and path patching we localize an error-monitoring signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model flag and correct an error it internally detected (or, in reverse, suppress flagging) while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual under-flagging as a steerable gate over a shared error-monitoring signal, with direct safety implications.
Experiments: 1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili). 2) DATASET (ErrorMon): ~500 items in three strata, each with a CORRECT version and a matched ERROR version (a single planted mistake): (A) REASONING-STEP items—a short multi-step solution (math/logic, from MGSM-style problems) where one step is altered to be wrong; probe: 'Is this reasoning correct? If not, which step is wrong?' (B) FACTUAL-CLAIM items—a stated claim that is true vs a plausible falsehood; probe: 'Is this statement correct?' (C) SAFETY-CRITICAL items—clinical/medical statements adapted from MedErrBench-style content where the error version contains a medication/diagnosis mistake; probe: 'Does this contain an error?'. Add a correction probe ('Give the corrected version') and an ENDORSEMENT probe (does the model continue as if the erroneous step were valid). Include an ALL-CORRECT control (no error present) to measure false-alarm/over-flagging and bound the effect. Translate/native-verify all items into 10 languages; keep the planted error and content fixed across languages; record tokenization fertility. Short scoreable answers where possible. 3) BEHAVIORAL UNDER-FLAGGING TEST: Per (item, language) record error-flag detection (correct on ERROR items), false-alarm on CORRECT items, localization accuracy (which step), and correction accuracy. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME planted error, flagging/correction is systematically lower in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond tokenization, and errors lean toward under-flagging (accepting the erroneous version). Mixed-effects logistic regression of flag-miss on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, stratum), item as random effect; compare against the all-correct control (false-alarm rate). Report per-language flagging/correction profiles, cross-lingual disagreement on identical errors, and replicate the M-GATE under-flagging asymmetry. 4) SHARED ERROR-MONITORING PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the post-step/claim position; train a linear probe to decode ERROR vs CORRECT (is the presented step/claim wrong) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent error-monitoring signal. Compare to per-language-trained probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the monitoring representation for the same item. CRITICAL: on flag-MISS items, test whether the error is still internally decodable (the monitor fired) across ALL languages even when not flagged. 5) DETECTION-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: For each flag-miss, classify via the probe as (A) DETECTION FAILURE (monitor did not fire) vs (B) EXPRESSION-GATE FAILURE (error internally detected but not surfaced). Report proportion of A vs B per language; correlate with resource tier and typological distance (predict expression-gate failures dominate for typologically close languages, detection failures for distant/low-resource). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping the internal monitoring signal to behavioral flagging; test whether cross-lingual under-flagging is explained by a weaker gate on a similar detection signal. Anchor mid-vs-output split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens. 6) LOCALIZE THE ERROR-MONITORING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that flags and one that misses on the SAME error item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer makes the error surface WITHOUT changing the decoded step/claim content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the monitoring representation FROM a high-flagging language into a missing low-flagging run. 7) CAUSAL EXPRESSION STEERING (decisive): Derive an error-monitoring expression steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (flag/correct runs minus miss runs at matched internal detection). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to low-flagging languages increases correct flagging and self-correction toward high-flagging levels; (ii) NULL ON DETECTION FAILURES: it does not help items where the monitor never fired, validating the decomposition; (iii) SUPPRESS: subtracting it makes high-flagging languages miss errors; (iv) it changes ONLY error flagging/correction, not the decoded content or surface language (fidelity), does not inflate false alarms on the ALL-CORRECT control, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: under-flagging-gap closure, correction-accuracy recovery, false-alarm change on control, suppression-induction rate (reverse), monitoring-signal/output fidelity, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes error handling but not unrelated or all-correct answers. 8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: stratum breakdown (reasoning-step vs factual vs safety-critical); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single expression vector generalizes across strata and languages; robustness across templates and detect-vs-correct formats; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal detection and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces errors without changing tokenization; safety-focused analysis of whether steering reduces dangerous medical under-flagging without raising false alarms. EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language error-flag/localization/correction accuracy and false-alarm rate, under-flagging regression controlling for detection/fertility/resource, M-GATE under-flagging replication, cross-lingual error-monitoring probe transfer AUROC and error-internally-detected-under-miss, cross-lingual monitoring-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), detection-vs-expression-gate failure proportions with probe validation, patch-localized error-monitoring layer, cross-lingual monitoring transplant recovery rate (and null on detection failures), causal steering under-flagging-gap closure and suppression-induction rates with false-alarm control, monitoring-signal/output fidelity, all-correct-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The detection-vs-expression split could be confounded if the monitoring signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying error decodability across all languages on flag-miss items via probe transfer rather than assuming, and report how much of the gap is detection vs gate. 2) Under-flagging could reflect a genuine detection deficit rather than an expression gate; the error-internally-detected-under-miss test and the null-on-detection-failures steering result dissociate these, and we restrict the gate analysis to items where the error is internally present. 3) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal detection, and the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet surfaces errors, dissociating the gate from length. 4) Some models may flag/correct uniformly across languages (no gap) or fail to detect errors at all; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual error monitoring, and we quantify how often each regime occurs. 5) Planted errors must be unambiguously wrong and equivalently rendered across languages; we native-verify, use clear-consensus errors (drawing on validated error-detection datasets like MedErrBench for the safety stratum), keep the error fixed across languages, and analyze ambiguous items separately. 6) Correction and localization scoring is noisy; we validate scorers against human labels, use the ALL-CORRECT control to measure false alarms, and report both detection and correction separately (per Li 2025, detection need not predict correction). 7) The monitoring probe could latch onto surface cues rather than a genuine error signal; the error-internally-detected-under-miss test, cross-lingual invariance, and cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) Steering may harm fluency, inflate false alarms, or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report false-alarm change on the all-correct control, monitoring-signal/output fidelity, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the null-on-detection-failures and suppression (reverse) tests to ensure a genuine error-monitoring expression gate. 10) The gate signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Safety framing: the medical stratum is used strictly as an interpretability/safety diagnostic (does the model silently accept dangerous errors in some languages?), not as clinical advice; the suppression direction is used only to demonstrate causality, not deployed. 12) Distinguishing from my calibration (confidence in the model's own answer), semantic-anticipation (congruity of an upcoming word), and CoT-faithfulness (whether the trace causes the answer) proposals is essential; here the object is the internal DETECTION that a presented reasoning step or claim is WRONG and the decoupling of that monitoring from its behavioral flagging/correction across languages.

Name: crosslingual_induction_head_language_gating
Title: Copy Me in Any Language? Whether In-Context Induction Is a Shared, Content-Level Mechanism Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs perform in-context induction/copying (completing an [A][B]...[A]->[B] pattern) via a largely language-independent, CONTENT-LEVEL mechanism that abstracts the pattern from surface tokens, but whether the completion is behaviorally EXPRESSED correctly is gated by the query language: the SAME abstract copy/induction pattern is internally computed across languages yet surfaced far less reliably when the pattern or query is in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, and—crucially—induction transfers cross-lingually at the CONCEPT level (an English demonstration completes a semantically-equivalent target in another language) more robustly than at the surface-token level. The induction signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated copy failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Induction heads are a foundational mechanistic finding (Olsson et al. 2022, 'In-context Learning and Induction Heads'; Elhage et al. 2021), but the entire literature is monolingual (English) and studies surface-token copying ([A][B]...[A]->[B]) with no cross-lingual or concept-level analysis. Function-vector / task-vector work (Todd et al. 2024; Hendel et al. 2023) shows in-context tasks are summarized by a mid-layer vector, and my prior crosslingual_task_vector_portability proposal studies whether whole TASK vectors port across languages; NEITHER studies the low-level induction/copying primitive itself—whether the induction mechanism is shared across languages, whether it operates on surface tokens vs abstract content, whether its expression is language-gated, or whether it copies at the CONCEPT level (translating the copied item). Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never studies induction heads or in-context copying. No prior work asks (i) whether induction is a language-independent content-level mechanism, (ii) whether cross-lingual copy failure decomposes into shared PATTERN-DETECTION vs a language-specific EXPRESSION gate, (iii) whether induction operates on a semantic/concept representation that enables cross-lingual (translating) copying, or (iv) whether the induction signal is causally steerable to repair language-gated failures. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of the induction/copying primitive.
Abstract: Induction heads—the circuit that, seeing a pattern [A][B]...[A], predicts [B]—are widely regarded as the engine of in-context learning, yet every study of them is monolingual. We ask three linked questions: is the induction/copying mechanism language-independent, does it operate on surface tokens or on abstract content, and does the query language gate whether an internally-detected pattern is actually completed? We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM detects and represents the abstract copy/induction pattern in a largely language-independent way, but the query language causally gates whether the completion is surfaced, so the SAME pattern is computed internally across languages yet completed far less reliably in lower-resource, typologically distant ones; and, strikingly, that induction operates partly at the CONCEPT level, so an English demonstration can complete a semantically-equivalent target in another language (a 'translating' copy). We build InductProbe, controlled in-context copying and induction sequences—within-language, cross-lingual surface (mixed scripts), and cross-lingual CONCEPT (the copied item must be translated)—across 8 typologically diverse languages, with a matched no-pattern control. Behaviorally we measure per-language and per-condition induction success. We train a linear probe to decode the to-be-copied item from hidden states and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose copy failures into a shared pattern-detection component versus a language-set expression gate, and test whether induction heads attend and copy at the concept level. Via activation and path patching we localize the induction signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to surface a copy the model internally detected (or to force/suppress copying) without changing the surface language. We reframe cross-lingual in-context learning as resting on a shared, content-level induction mechanism under a steerable, language-dependent expression gate.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Turkish). MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs. Also include a small model for a clean induction-head baseline if available.
2) DATASET (InductProbe): Controlled in-context sequences testing copying/induction in four conditions. (A) WITHIN-LANGUAGE: repeated [A][B]...[A]->[B] patterns using tokens/words of a single language (both random-token copying and meaningful word-pair induction). (B) CROSS-LINGUAL SURFACE: the demonstration pair is in language L1 and the query cue [A] reappears in L1 within an otherwise-L2 context (mixed-script), testing whether induction survives a language switch of surrounding context. (C) CROSS-LINGUAL CONCEPT (key novel condition): the demonstration establishes a semantic mapping (e.g. an English item paired with its continuation), and the query cue is the TRANSLATION of [A] into L2—correct completion requires copying the CONCEPT (producing the L2 translation of [B]), not the surface token. (D) NO-PATTERN control: matched sequences with no repeated/inducible structure (to bound false completion). Build ~500 items per condition, native-verified translations, short single-token-decodable targets where possible; record tokenization fertility.
3) BEHAVIORAL TEST: Per (item, language, condition) measure induction/copy success (does the model complete the pattern with the correct [B] / its translation). KEY hypotheses: (i) within-language induction success is systematically lower in lower-resource/typologically distant languages beyond tokenization; (ii) cross-lingual CONCEPT copying succeeds above surface-token baselines, evidencing content-level induction; (iii) both track resource level and typological distance. Mixed-effects logistic regression of success on (language, condition, tokenization fertility, resource tier via URIEL), item as random effect; compare against the no-pattern control. Report per-language/condition profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical patterns.
4) SHARED TO-BE-COPIED PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the query-cue position; train a linear probe to decode the to-be-copied item [B] (its identity, over a closed candidate set) on ENGLISH within-language data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot to other languages and conditions; report AUROC/accuracy as evidence of a language-independent copy-target representation. Compare to per-language-trained probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the copy-target representation. CRITICAL: on copy-FAILURE items, test whether the correct [B] is still internally decodable across languages (the pattern was detected) even when not emitted.
5) DETECTION-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: For each copy failure, classify via the probe as (A) DETECTION FAILURE (target not internally represented) vs (B) EXPRESSION-GATE FAILURE (target present but not surfaced). Report proportion of A vs B per language/condition and correlate with resource tier and typological distance (predict expression-gate failures dominate for close languages, detection failures for distant/low-resource). Anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE INDUCTION SIGNAL: Identify induction heads (via the standard prefix-matching / copying score on repeated random sequences) and test whether the SAME heads carry induction across languages and in the concept condition. Via activation and path patching between a run that copies correctly and one that fails on the SAME item, sweep layers/heads for the minimal components whose transfer surfaces the copy. Attention analysis: test whether the induction head attends to the semantically-matching prior token in the CONCEPT condition (concept-level attention) vs only surface-identical tokens. Report layer/head distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching.
7) CAUSAL INDUCTION STEERING (decisive): Derive an induction-expression steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (successful-copy runs minus failed runs at matched internal target). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to failing low-expression languages increases correct completion toward high-expression levels; (ii) NULL ON DETECTION FAILURES: it does not help items where the target was internally absent, validating the decomposition; (iii) SUPPRESS: subtracting it (or ablating induction heads) removes copying cross-lingually; (iv) it changes ONLY copy expression, not surface language or general QA (fidelity/retention). Metrics: per-mode success recovery, suppression/ablation effect, output-language fidelity, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes copy behavior but not no-pattern-control or unrelated answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: condition breakdown (within vs surface vs concept); random-token vs meaningful-word induction; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/head; token-pooling and tokenization-fertility dissociation (compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal target; show content-invariant steering repairs copying without changing tokenization); whether the same induction heads/steering vector generalize across languages and the concept condition.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language/condition induction success and cross-lingual-concept-vs-surface gap, success regression controlling for fertility/resource, cross-lingual copy-target probe transfer AUROC and target-present-under-failure, detection-vs-expression-gate failure proportions with probe validation, induction-head copying scores across languages and concept-level attention evidence, patch-localized induction layer/head, causal steering per-mode recovery and head-ablation suppression, output-language fidelity and general-QA retention, no-pattern-control retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The detection-vs-expression split could be confounded if the copy-target signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying target decodability across languages on failure items via probe transfer rather than assuming, and report how much of the gap is detection vs gate. 2) The cross-lingual CONCEPT condition conflates copying with translation ability; we screen that the model can translate [A]->[B] items outside the induction context and restrict concept-condition analysis to translatable items, so above-baseline concept copying reflects content-level induction rather than mere translation. 3) Tokenization fertility confounds copy success (multi-subword targets are harder to emit); we control for fertility, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal target, use multiple token-pooling schemes, and—crucially—the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet repairs copying, dissociating the gate from tokenization. 4) Some models may induct robustly across all languages/conditions (no gap) or fail to detect patterns at all; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality/content-level nature of induction, and we quantify how often each regime occurs. 5) Induction-head identification is model-specific and heads may be distributed; we use the standard copying-score methodology, test multiple models, and cross-check activation vs path patching plus attention analysis. 6) The copy-target probe could latch onto surface cues rather than a genuine copy representation; the target-present-under-failure test, cross-lingual invariance, concept-level attention evidence, and cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 7) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report output-language fidelity, no-pattern-control and general-QA retention, and use the null-on-detection-failures, suppression (head-ablation), and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine induction-expression mechanism. 8) The induction signal may be low-rank or head-mediated rather than a single residual-stream direction; we test both head-ablation and residual-stream steering and report which dominates. 9) Distinguishing from my task-vector-portability proposal is essential; here the object is the low-level INDUCTION/COPYING primitive (and its content-level, cross-lingual, gated nature), not the portability of a whole in-context TASK vector, and from monolingual induction-head work (Olsson 2022) by providing the cross-lingual, concept-level, decomposition, and causal-repair account it lacks.

Name: crosslingual_grammar_acquisition_ordering
Title: Does a Model Learn Grammar in the Same Order a Child Does? Cross-Lingual Recapitulation of Universal Acquisition Milestones Across Pretraining
Short Hypothesis: During pretraining, a multilingual LLM acquires grammatical phenomena in a systematic ORDER that recapitulates the universal human child-language acquisition sequence (e.g., word-order/basic agreement before complex embedding, morphological regulars before irregulars, simple negation before scope/concord), and this order is largely stable across typologically diverse languages and driven by the phenomenon's intrinsic learnability/complexity rather than merely its corpus frequency. We can measure a per-phenomenon per-language acquisition-onset checkpoint, show it matches the documented human developmental ordering above chance, and show that phenomena acquired early do so because a shared cross-lingual grammatical competence forms first, causally enabling later, harder phenomena.
Related Work: Human developmental psycholinguistics establishes robust, largely universal acquisition orderings (Brown's morpheme order; overregularization U-shaped curves; agreement/embedding difficulty hierarchies). In NLP, targeted-syntactic-evaluation suites (BLiMP, CLiMP, multilingual acceptability, BabyLM) measure grammatical competence at a fixed final checkpoint, and a few English-only studies track when specific constructions emerge over training or show U-shaped overregularization in single models. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS, and prior acquisition-order work (Blum 2025; AdaXEval 2025; my own crosslingual_acquisition_order_alignment) concerns FACT retrievability or curriculum efficiency, not GRAMMATICAL PHENOMENA. NONE (i) measure a per-phenomenon per-language grammatical acquisition-onset across public multilingual checkpoints, (ii) test whether the emergent order recapitulates the documented human developmental sequence CROSS-LINGUALLY, (iii) dissociate intrinsic phenomenon complexity from corpus frequency as the driver of ordering, or (iv) causally link early acquisition to the formation of a shared cross-lingual grammatical competence. This is a formation-tracing behavioral-discovery proposal grounded in a robust human-sciences finding, distinct from final-checkpoint benchmarking and from fact-acquisition studies.
Abstract: Children acquire grammar in a strikingly regular order: basic word order and simple agreement come before complex embedding, regular morphology before irregular exceptions, plain negation before scope-sensitive constructions. We ask whether a multilingual language model, trained only to predict text, silently recapitulates this human developmental sequence, and whether it does so across typologically diverse languages. Using open multilingual models that release many intermediate pretraining checkpoints, we probe a curated battery of grammatical phenomena, each with acceptability minimal pairs, in multiple languages at every checkpoint, and measure per-phenomenon per-language ACQUISITION-ONSET (the checkpoint after which the model reliably prefers the grammatical form). We test three claims. First, the emergent acquisition order matches the documented human developmental ordering above chance, and is largely stable across languages. Second, ordering is driven by the phenomenon's intrinsic complexity/learnability, not merely by corpus frequency: we estimate per-phenomenon frequency and show complexity predicts onset beyond it, including the signature U-shaped overregularization curve for irregular morphology. Third, early-acquired phenomena form a SHARED cross-lingual grammatical competence first: mid-layer probes for a phenomenon transfer zero-shot across languages exactly when it is acquired, and cross-lingual representation alignment for a phenomenon precedes its acquisition, causally scaffolding later phenomena. In a controlled continued-pretraining test we manipulate exposure to show complexity-driven ordering persists under matched frequency. We reframe grammatical competence as a developmentally-ordered, cross-lingually-shared, complexity-gated acquisition process that is measurable and partly steerable.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & CHECKPOINTS: Use open multilingual models that publicly release many intermediate pretraining checkpoints (CroissantLLM 1.3B, English-French with dense checkpoints; Salamandra 2B/7B, 35 European languages with released checkpoints). Supplement with a small controlled continued/LoRA-pretraining run on an open base (Qwen2.5-1.5B / Llama-3.2-1B) that injects grammatical constructions with logged per-phenomenon exposure for the frequency-dissociation test (1-2 A6000 GPUs).
2) PHENOMENON BATTERY: Curate ~20 grammatical phenomena with a documented human-developmental ordering and clear acceptability minimal pairs, spanning early (basic SVO/word order, simple subject-verb number agreement, plural marking), mid (embedded clauses, wh-questions, regular past-tense/case morphology), and late (long-distance/agreement-attraction, negative concord/scope, irregular morphology, filler-gap). Instantiate each in the languages covered by the checkpoint series (multiple scripts/families where available) using BLiMP/CLiMP/multilingual-acceptability templates, native-verified. For each (phenomenon, language) build grammatical-vs-ungrammatical minimal pairs scored by log-probability preference.
3) ACQUISITION-ONSET MEASUREMENT: At EVERY checkpoint, compute per-(phenomenon,language) acceptability accuracy (fraction of minimal pairs where the grammatical form is preferred); define ACQUISITION-ONSET = the earliest checkpoint after which accuracy stays above a reliability threshold (with hysteresis). Produce per-language acquisition curves and per-phenomenon onset vectors.
4) HUMAN-ORDER RECAPITULATION (claim 1): Rank phenomena by model onset and compare to the documented human developmental ordering (early/mid/late tiers and finer within-tier orderings) via rank correlation (Spearman/Kendall) against a null of random orderings. Test cross-lingual stability: rank-correlate per-language onset orders across languages (Kendall's W). Report which phenomena deviate from the human order and whether deviations track typological distance.
5) COMPLEXITY-vs-FREQUENCY (claim 2): Estimate per-(phenomenon,language) corpus frequency (from released data-mix proportions for public models; logged exactly in the controlled run) and a complexity/learnability score (dependency length, embedding depth, regular-vs-exception, scope-sensitivity, coded from linguistic references). Mixed-effects regression of onset on (complexity, frequency, typological distance), phenomenon as random effect; test that complexity predicts onset beyond frequency (incremental R^2, likelihood-ratio). Specifically track IRREGULAR MORPHOLOGY for a U-SHAPED overregularization curve (accuracy on irregulars rises, dips as the regular rule generalizes, then recovers) across checkpoints, per language.
6) SHARED-COMPETENCE FORMATION (claim 3): For each phenomenon, train a linear acceptability probe on mid-layer states in one language and measure zero-shot transfer to other languages at each checkpoint; test whether cross-lingual probe transfer (and cross-lingual representation alignment, CKA/cosine of the phenomenon representation) rises to threshold at or just before the phenomenon's acquisition onset. Test whether phenomena whose representations unify cross-lingually earlier are acquired earlier.
7) CONTROLLED FREQUENCY-MATCHED TEST (causal): In the continued-pretraining run, expose two phenomena of differing complexity with MATCHED exposure counts and test whether the lower-complexity one is still acquired first (complexity-driven ordering under equal frequency); and a frequency-varied ablation to bound how much frequency can reorder acquisition. Verify no degradation of already-acquired phenomena.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: onset reliability-threshold sensitivity; which phenomena drive cross-lingual instability; model scale (CroissantLLM vs Salamandra-2B/7B); probe layer/dimensionality; robustness across templates; whether high-resource anchor languages acquire earlier and scaffold others.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-(phenomenon,language) acquisition-onset checkpoints, rank correlation of model order vs human developmental order and its null comparison, cross-lingual order stability (Kendall's W), onset-vs-complexity and onset-vs-frequency regressions with incremental R^2, U-shaped overregularization curves for irregulars, cross-lingual probe-transfer/alignment onset vs acquisition-onset lead/lag, controlled frequency-matched ordering result.
