Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Public checkpoint series may cover few languages/steps, limiting resolution; we combine public series (CroissantLLM/Salamandra) with a controlled continued-pretraining run for the frequency-dissociation and causal tests. 2) Acquisition-onset is threshold-dependent and noisy; we use hysteresis, multiple thresholds, and report sensitivity. 3) The 'human developmental ordering' is coarse and partly language-specific; we use well-documented, cross-linguistically robust orderings (Brown-style tiers, overregularization), treat within-tier orderings cautiously, and analyze deviations rather than forcing a fit. 4) Complexity coding is subjective; we predefine complexity features from linguistic references, report inter-annotator agreement, and treat complexity as a graded predictor. 5) Disentangling complexity from corpus frequency is confounded in public models (frequency only approximable from data-mix proportions); the controlled run with logged exposure provides the clean test, and public-model results are corroborative. 6) Some models may acquire all phenomena nearly simultaneously (no clear order) or in a language-specific order — either is an informative, publishable finding about when grammatical acquisition is/ isn't ordered and shared, and we quantify order strength rather than assuming it. 7) The alignment-precedes-acquisition link is correlational across checkpoints; the controlled test and lead/lag analysis strengthen but do not fully prove causation, which we state transparently. 8) Acceptability via log-probability preference can be affected by tokenization/frequency of specific lexical items; we use matched minimal pairs, multiple items per phenomenon, and control for lexical frequency. 9) Results may be model- and scale-specific; we test at least two public model families plus controlled runs and report aggregate and per-model findings.

Name: crosslingual_incontext_override_gating
Title: Overruled by the Demonstrations, in Some Tongues More Than Others: A Shared In-Context Evidence Signal Whose Override of Prior Knowledge Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When in-context demonstrations assert a label that CONTRADICTS a multilingual LLM's parametric prior (flipped-label / counter-knowledge ICL), the model computes a largely language-independent internal 'in-context evidence' signal favoring the demonstrated label, but the query language causally sets an OVERRIDE THRESHOLD applied to that signal: for the SAME contradictory demonstrations, the model follows the in-context evidence (overriding its prior) at a lower threshold in some languages and clings to its parametric prior in others, producing a cross-lingual override asymmetry that is separable from the strength of the evidence signal and from raw knowledge, and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable override-gating signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: In-context learning with flipped/counterfactual labels is studied monolingually: Wei et al. (2023) show larger models can override semantic priors and follow flipped in-context labels; Min et al. (2022) and follow-ups probe how much ICL relies on label meaning vs demonstrations. Cross-lingual ICL work (X-InSTA, BUFFET, source-language selection) is behavioral and studies which demonstrations maximize target-language accuracy, never the override of prior knowledge. Context-vs-memory conflict work (Jin 2024 PH3; my prior language_modulated_context_trust proposal) concerns a retrieved PASSAGE contradicting memory in a QA prompt; here the conflict is carried by ICL DEMONSTRATIONS (label patterns), a distinct mechanism (in-context pattern induction vs passage faithfulness). Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies prior-override in ICL. My gating-template proposals (calibration, abstention, processing-load, concession, precision, sunk-cost, default-referent) target other decisions; NONE frame in-context override of a parametric prior as a shared evidence signal gated by a language-dependent override threshold, dissociate that gate from the evidence signal and from knowledge, or causally localize and steer it. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of prior-override in flipped-label in-context learning.
Abstract: In-context learning lets a model adopt a rule from demonstrations, even a rule that contradicts what it already knows: given enough examples labeling positive reviews as 'negative', a strong model can flip. We ask whether this override of parametric priors is language-dependent, and how it is implemented internally. We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal signal that registers what the in-context demonstrations imply, but the query language causally sets an override threshold on it, so that for the SAME contradictory demonstrations the model follows the in-context evidence in some languages while clinging to its prior in others. This predicts a cross-lingual override asymmetry dissociable from the evidence signal and from raw knowledge. We build FlipProbe, parallel flipped-label and counter-knowledge in-context tasks (sentiment with inverted labels, factual associations overridden by demonstrations, novel arbitrary label mappings) across 10 typologically and resource-diverse languages, holding the demonstrations and query fixed across languages. Behaviorally we measure per-language override rate (following the demonstrated label over the parametric prior) as a function of the number of counter-demonstrations, and test whether the override curve shifts with query language beyond knowledge and tokenization. We train a linear probe for the shared in-context-evidence signal and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the override gap into a shared evidence estimate versus a language-set override threshold. Via activation and path patching we localize an override-gating signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model follow the in-context evidence in prior-clinging languages (or resist it) while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual ICL inconsistency as a shared evidence signal under a steerable, language-dependent override gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (FlipProbe): three families each pitting in-context demonstrations against a parametric prior. (A) FLIPPED-LABEL SENTIMENT: sentiment classification with demonstrations that INVERT the label mapping (positive->'negative'); overriding requires following the flipped in-context rule against the model's sentiment prior. (B) COUNTER-KNOWLEDGE FACTS: a factual association the model knows, with demonstrations asserting a different consistent mapping (e.g., a novel country-capital rule); overriding requires following the demonstrated association over the parametric fact. (C) NOVEL-ARBITRARY-MAPPING control: a genuinely new label mapping with no parametric prior (baseline ICL, no conflict) to bound the effect and separate override from basic in-context learning. Vary the NUMBER of counter-demonstrations (0,1,2,4,8,16) to trace an override curve. Hold demonstrations and the query item fixed across languages; translate/native-verify. Screen that the model (i) holds the prior (correct with 0 counter-demos) and (ii) can learn the control mapping, so override failure is neither ignorance nor ICL incapacity. Record tokenization fertility. Short single-token-decodable labels.
3) BEHAVIORAL OVERRIDE TEST: Per (item, language, #counter-demos) record whether the model follows the DEMONSTRATED label (override) vs its PARAMETRIC prior. Define per-language OVERRIDE THRESHOLD = the number of counter-demonstrations at which override overtakes prior-clinging. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME demonstrations, the override curve shifts with query language (some languages override readily, others cling), beyond knowledge and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of override on (#counter-demos, language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, prior-strength indicator), item as random effect; compare against the NOVEL-MAPPING control (should be language-flatter). Report per-language override curves and cross-lingual disagreement on identical demonstrations.
4) SHARED IN-CONTEXT-EVIDENCE PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode the DEMONSTRATED label the in-context evidence implies (independent of the prior) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent in-context-evidence signal. Compare to per-language-trained probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the evidence representation for the same demonstrations. CRITICAL: on prior-CLINGING items, test whether the in-context evidence is still strongly decodable across languages (the evidence signal fired) even when the model does not override.
5) THRESHOLD-vs-ESTIMATE DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer evidence signal across languages (should be similar if shared) versus the emitted override decision (which diverges). Define a per-language OVERRIDE THRESHOLD on the shared evidence axis; test whether cross-lingual override differences are explained by a shifted threshold on a similar evidence signal rather than a weaker evidence signal. Correlate per-language threshold with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-decision split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE OVERRIDE-GATING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that overrides and one that clings on the SAME item and demonstration set, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips cling->override WITHOUT changing the decoded evidence signal. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gating components from an override-prone language into a clinging run.
7) CAUSAL OVERRIDE STEERING (decisive): Derive an override-gating steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (override runs minus cling runs at matched evidence). Test (i) LOWER-THRESHOLD: adding it to prior-clinging languages makes the model follow the in-context evidence toward a reference level; (ii) RAISE-THRESHOLD: subtracting it makes override-prone languages cling to the prior even under many counter-demonstrations; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where the override gap was largest; (iv) it changes ONLY the override decision, not the decoded evidence signal, the prior knowledge, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the NOVEL-MAPPING control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: override-gap closure, override-recovery rate, cling-induction rate (reverse), evidence-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts override but not the evidence readout or unrelated answers, and dose-response: scaling the vector produces graded shifts in the override curve.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: family breakdown (flipped-sentiment vs counter-fact vs novel-mapping); is English/high-resource the override-prone reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank override subspace; robustness across templates and #-demonstration schedules; whether one gating vector generalizes across families and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched evidence and by showing content-invariant steering shifts override without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language override curves and thresholds, override regression controlling for knowledge/fertility/resource, cross-lingual in-context-evidence probe transfer AUROC and evidence-present-under-clinging, cross-lingual evidence-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), estimate-similarity vs decision-divergence (threshold) decomposition, threshold-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized override-gating layer, cross-lingual gating transplant repair rate, causal steering override-gap closure with dose-response and cling-induction rate, evidence-signal/output fidelity, novel-mapping-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Override failure could reflect a knowledge/ICL-capacity gap rather than an override gate; we screen per-language that the model holds the prior (0-demo correct) AND can learn the novel-mapping control, so residual clinging reflects the gate, not ignorance or ICL incapacity. 2) The threshold-vs-estimate split could be confounded if the in-context-evidence signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying evidence decodability across languages on clinging items via probe transfer rather than assuming, and report how much of the gap is estimate vs gate. 3) Tokenization fertility confounds label prediction and demonstration length; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched evidence, and the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts override, dissociating the gate from length. 4) Some models/languages may override uniformly (no gap) or cling everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual prior-override, and we quantify how often a gap exists. 5) The evidence probe could latch onto surface cues rather than a genuine in-context-evidence representation; the evidence-present-under-clinging test, cross-lingual invariance, and cross-lingual gating transplant guard against this. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report evidence-signal/output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the cling-induction (reverse), reverse-consistency, and dose-response tests to ensure a genuine override-threshold dial. 8) The override signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 9) Distinguishing from my context-vs-memory (language_modulated_context_trust) proposal is essential; there the conflict is a retrieved PASSAGE contradicting memory, whereas here it is carried by ICL DEMONSTRATIONS (label/mapping patterns induced in-context), a distinct mechanism (in-context pattern induction vs passage faithfulness), and from behavioral cross-lingual ICL work by providing the internal, causal account.

Name: crosslingual_collateral_forgetting_geometry
Title: Who Gets Forgotten When You Teach a New Language? Structured Cross-Lingual Collateral Forgetting Predicted by Shared-Representation Geometry
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM is fine-tuned in one language (adding a new language or new facts in language A), the resulting catastrophic forgetting is NOT diffuse but STRUCTURED: knowledge is selectively erased in the OTHER languages whose representations are most aligned to the fine-tuning language in the shared concept space, so typologically/script-close and representation-aligned languages suffer disproportionate collateral damage. We can predict, per-fact and per-language, which languages will be forgotten from a pre-fine-tuning geometric alignment measure, and causally reduce the collateral damage by projecting the update to land in language-specific rather than shared layers.
Related Work: The multilingual continual-learning literature (O-LoRA [Wang 2023], gradient-projection/UGP [Ren 2026], Fisher-LoRA [Adhikari 2025], MoE/replay [MiLorE-SSL 2026], DOC [Zhang 2025]) is entirely about MITIGATING forgetting via training-side machinery and reports aggregate forgetting metrics; none ask which specific OTHER languages get damaged or whether the collateral pattern is structured by the shared concept space. The 'alignment tax' work (Su 2026) documents that low-resource expansion hurts general capability but treats it as a scalar trade-off with no per-language geometric account. Mechanistic multilingual work shows facts live in a shared concept space with language-specific decoding (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) and that knowledge sharing scales with script/typological similarity (Ifergan 2024), but only at inference on fixed models. My prior 'native_language_imprint' proposal concerns which acquisition language an INJECTED fact binds to (an end-state imprint), and 'bilingual_bottleneck' predicts inference-time transfer/interference of PRE-TRAINED facts. NONE (i) characterize forgetting during fine-tuning as a STRUCTURED, geometry-predictable per-language collateral-damage pattern, (ii) predict which languages get forgotten from a pre-fine-tuning shared-representation alignment measure, or (iii) causally reduce collateral forgetting by steering WHERE the update lands relative to the shared vs language-specific layers rather than via orthogonality/replay across TASKS. This reframes multilingual forgetting from a training-optimization nuisance into a predictable, geometry-driven interference phenomenon with a mechanistic locus.
Abstract: Fine-tuning a multilingual model to add a new language or teach new facts in one language is known to cause catastrophic forgetting, and a large literature builds machinery to suppress it. But a basic question is unasked: when you teach in language A, WHICH other languages' knowledge is actually erased, and is the damage random or structured? We hypothesize that collateral forgetting is structured by the model's shared concept space: fine-tuning in A selectively damages exactly those other languages whose fact representations are most aligned to A in the shared middle layers, so representation-aligned, typologically- and script-close languages are forgotten most. We test this by fine-tuning open multilingual LLMs in a single language (both language-expansion and same-fact-in-A-only settings) and measuring, per fact and per language, how much retrievability of UNRELATED and RELATED facts changes in every other language. Before fine-tuning we compute a geometric alignment measure between each language pair's fact representations at the shared layers; we test whether this pre-fine-tuning alignment predicts per-language collateral forgetting with high accuracy, outperforming baselines using surface script/typological distance or corpus size alone. We further show the effect is causal in two ways: (1) editing/steering the concept-space direction shared between A and a close language B induces the predicted collateral damage on B; and (2) constraining the update to land in language-specific final layers (rather than shared middle layers) selectively reduces collateral forgetting on aligned languages while preserving the intended learning. We reframe multilingual forgetting as a predictable, geometry-driven interference pattern with a locatable cause.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Open multilingual LLMs amenable to LoRA/full fine-tuning on an academic budget: Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B, Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Gemma-2-2B, BLOOM-1.7B (fine-tuning + probing + light patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse held-out languages spanning multiple scripts/families (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) FACT-RETRIEVAL PROBE SET: ~600 factual items (mLAMA/BMLAMA/Wikidata) with short decodable answers, translated/native-verified into all 10 languages, so retrievability can be measured per fact per language. Split into a FINE-TUNING language (A) and 9 held-out languages whose knowledge should ideally be preserved.
3) FINE-TUNING SETTINGS: (a) LANGUAGE-EXPANSION: fine-tune on a general corpus in language A (or a low-resource language) to simulate adding/strengthening A; (b) FACT-INJECTION: fine-tune to install ~200 new facts stated only in A. Save checkpoints for formation tracing.
4) PER-LANGUAGE COLLATERAL-DAMAGE MEASUREMENT: Before and after fine-tuning, measure retrieval accuracy of the probe facts in every language. Define per-(fact, language) FORGETTING = accuracy drop. KEY behavioral test: is forgetting concentrated in specific languages rather than uniform? Report per-language forgetting distributions and cross-language variance; test against a null of uniform damage.
5) PRE-FINE-TUNING GEOMETRIC ALIGNMENT: Identify the shared/middle layers via per-layer language-ID probes (Wang 2025). For each fact, extract its hidden representation in language A and in each other language at the shared layer; define ALIGNMENT(A, B, fact) = cosine/CKA similarity of the concept vectors. Aggregate to a per-language-pair alignment score.
6) PREDICTION TEST (core): Fit a simple regression predicting per-(fact, language B) collateral forgetting from pre-fine-tuning ALIGNMENT(A, B). Metric: predictive R^2 / AUC for predicting heavily-forgotten vs preserved facts. Baselines: (a) surface script identity, (b) URIEL typological distance, (c) per-language corpus-size/resource tier. Hypothesis: shared-layer alignment beats all surface/typology baselines and predicts WHICH languages are forgotten, at the per-fact level.
7) CAUSAL TEST #1 (induce): Using ROME/MEMIT (or brief fine-tuning) edit a fact in A and steer/patch along the concept-space direction shared with a close language B; test whether the predicted collateral damage on B is induced (and whether high-alignment B suffers more than low-alignment B'), with facts' content otherwise unchanged. Metric: correlation between predicted alignment and induced accuracy delta; AUC for destructive-vs-neutral.
8) CAUSAL TEST #2 (mitigate via locus): Constrain the fine-tuning update to land in LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC final layers vs the SHARED middle layers (e.g., freeze shared layers / restrict LoRA to late layers vs mid layers). Test whether landing the update in language-specific layers selectively REDUCES collateral forgetting on high-alignment languages while preserving intended learning in A. Compare against a matched-capacity baseline and against O-LoRA-style orthogonality. Metrics: intended-learning accuracy in A, per-language collateral forgetting, and the forgetting-vs-alignment slope (should flatten under the locus intervention).
9) FORMATION TRACING: Across fine-tuning checkpoints, track when collateral forgetting emerges per language and whether it tracks the point at which the shared representation for A is perturbed.
10) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: script vs family contributions; expansion vs fact-injection settings; model scale; layer choice for alignment; whether a single alignment threshold generalizes across facts/languages; general-capability retention (multilingual MMLU subset).
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language collateral forgetting distributions and cross-language variance, alignment-predicts-forgetting R^2/AUC vs script/typology/resource baselines, induced-damage correlation and AUC, locus-mitigation forgetting reduction and forgetting-vs-alignment slope flattening, intended-learning and general-capability retention, formation-tracing emergence curves.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Forgetting could be uniform rather than structured for some models/settings; this itself is an informative, publishable negative/nuance about whether the shared concept space channels interference, and we quantify structure (cross-language variance, prediction R^2) rather than assuming it. 2) Retrieval accuracy is noisy for low-resource languages; we restrict per-fact forgetting analysis to facts verifiably retrievable pre-fine-tuning in each language. 3) Alignment could be confounded with corpus frequency/script; we control with URIEL and resource tiers and show alignment predicts beyond them, and use the causal locus test to dissociate geometry from surface factors. 4) Editing methods (ROME/MEMIT) have artifacts; we use them as one causal probe and cross-check with brief fine-tuning and activation patching. 5) The locus intervention (restricting updates to late layers) may reduce intended learning; we report the trade-off explicitly rather than claiming a free lunch, and compare against orthogonality baselines. 6) Layer identification of shared vs language-specific bands may be imperfect; we use probing-based selection and report sensitivity. 7) Results may be model-specific; we test multiple families/scales and report aggregate and per-model results. 8) Distinguishing from continual-learning methods work is essential; our contribution is the STRUCTURED, geometry-predictable per-language collateral-damage pattern and its causal locus, not a new forgetting-mitigation SOTA (which we use only as a baseline).

Name: crosslingual_feature_reconstruction_prior_leakage
Title: Inventing What Wasn't Said: How Multilingual Models Fill Underspecified Grammatical Features by Leaking Demographic Priors, and Whether They Could Hedge Instead
Short Hypothesis: When translating or generating from a source that leaves an obligatory grammatical feature UNDERSPECIFIED (e.g., gender/number/formality/animacy absent in the source but required in the target), a multilingual LLM must invent a value; we hypothesize it computes an internal representation that distinguishes 'the feature is genuinely underdetermined by the source' from 'a value is being committed', and that when it commits it fills the slot by projecting a demographic/social PRIOR (a stereotype direction) rather than signaling underspecification. This prior-leakage is causally driven by a localizable 'feature-commitment' signal that (1) can be read out to predict which reconstructions are underdetermined-yet-confidently-filled, (2) tracks the stereotype content of the entity, and (3) can be steered to make the model hedge (choose a neutral/epicene realization or flag the ambiguity) instead of silently imposing a stereotyped value.
Related Work: Hwang (2026) shows LLM translation from a feature-underspecified source (Korean: no gender, radical pro-drop) to a feature-explicit target (Spanish) forces φ-feature RECONSTRUCTION, with an asymmetry (context recovers person but not gender) and architecture-dependent strategies (conservative non-commitment vs over-generation of spurious values) — but this is purely behavioral/linguistic, corpus-based, with no internal representation, no stereotype-leakage account, and no causal intervention. Machine-translation gender-bias work (AmbGIMT [Chen 2024], WinoMT, gender-inclusive MT, formality-control MT [Tyagi 2023]) documents that models resolve source-ambiguous gender/formality via occupational/sentiment stereotypes and that constraints reduce but do not remove it — again behavioral, output-level, with no mechanism and no notion of an internal underspecification-vs-commitment state. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS, and my prior code-switch-binding proposal studied which language drives grammatical AGREEMENT during an explicit lexical switch. NONE ask whether a model internally represents that an obligatory feature is UNDERDETERMINED by the source, whether feature-filling causally leaks a demographic prior, whether the model could have hedged (chosen a neutral/epicene form or flagged ambiguity) instead, or whether a 'feature-commitment' signal can be causally localized and steered to convert silent stereotyped imposition into explicit hedging. This is distinct from all my prior proposals (which concern shared knowledge/typological leakage into a value the source DID specify, or decision-gating over answerability/abstention): here the causal object is the INVENTION of grammatical information the source genuinely omitted, and its coupling to social priors — a mechanistic, causal, bias-relevant account of underspecification-filling.
Abstract: Every translation from a grammatically sparse language into a richer one forces an act of invention: Korean and Turkish leave gender unmarked, Chinese leaves number and definiteness optional, English leaves formality unspecified — yet Spanish, French, or Japanese demand these features be realized. The model must supply information the source never gave. We ask how it does so internally: does it represent that the feature is genuinely underdetermined, and when it commits to a value, does it fill the slot by leaking a demographic or social prior rather than hedging? We build ReconstructProbe, controlled source sentences that underspecify an obligatory target feature (gender, number, formality, animacy) paired with entities that carry a measurable stereotype (occupation, trait, role), across source-target pairs spanning the relevant typological gaps. Behaviorally we measure how often the model imposes the stereotype-consistent value versus choosing a neutral/epicene realization or flagging ambiguity, and whether imposition tracks entity stereotype strength. Mechanistically, we train a linear probe to decode, at the point of realization, both (a) whether the feature is underdetermined by the source and (b) which value is being committed, and test whether the underspecification signal is present even when a value is nonetheless imposed. Via activation and path patching we localize a 'feature-commitment' signal and test whether it carries the stereotype prior. In a decisive causal test we steer this signal to make the model hedge — producing a neutral/epicene form or an explicit ambiguity flag — instead of silently imposing a stereotyped value, and, in reverse, to force stereotyped imposition, while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe stereotype leakage in cross-lingual generation as a steerable choice between hedging and prior-imposition over a genuinely underdetermined slot.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & SOURCE->TARGET PAIRS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). Choose pairs where the SOURCE underspecifies an obligatory TARGET feature: GENDER (Korean/Turkish/Hungarian/Persian [genderless] -> Spanish/French/Russian [obligatory gender]); NUMBER/DEFINITENESS (Chinese/Japanese [optional number] -> English/German [obligatory]); FORMALITY (English [no T/V] -> Japanese/Korean/Hindi [obligatory register]); ANIMACY/CASE where relevant. Code, per source, which features are underspecified (from typological references + native verification).
2) DATASET (ReconstructProbe): ~500 source sentences per pair in which the target-obligatory feature is genuinely UNDERDETERMINED by the source (no antecedent, no disambiguating context), paired with entities carrying a measurable stereotype along the feature axis: for GENDER, occupations/traits with independently-rated gender-stereotype scores (nurse/engineer, gentle/assertive); for FORMALITY, roles with status/politeness expectations; for NUMBER, collective vs individual referents. Include (a) a DISAMBIGUATED control where the source DOES specify the feature (correct value known; bounds the effect and separates reconstruction from ignorance) and (b) a NEUTRAL-ENTITY control (no stereotype) to isolate prior-leakage. Elicit the target realization (full translation and a targeted cloze forcing the feature, e.g. the article/verb agreement/pronoun) with native-verified templates; where the target has a NEUTRAL/EPICENE option or the model can explicitly flag ambiguity, offer/detect it.
3) BEHAVIORAL PRIOR-LEAKAGE TEST: For underdetermined items, classify the realization as STEREOTYPE-CONSISTENT imposition vs STEREOTYPE-INCONSISTENT vs HEDGE (neutral/epicene form or explicit ambiguity flag). KEY hypothesis: on genuinely underdetermined slots, models impose the stereotype-consistent value far above chance and rarely hedge, with imposition rate tracking entity stereotype strength; the effect is larger for gender than for context-recoverable features (replicating and extending Hwang's asymmetry). Mixed-effects logistic regression of stereotype-imposition on (stereotype-strength score, feature type, source->target pair, resource tier via URIEL), item as random effect; compare against the disambiguated and neutral-entity controls. Report per-pair imposition/hedge profiles and cross-pair variation.
4) SHARED UNDERSPECIFICATION & COMMITMENT PROBES: At each layer, pool the hidden state at the realization position; train two linear probes: (i) UNDERSPECIFICATION probe (is the feature underdetermined by the source vs specified) using the underdetermined-vs-disambiguated contrast, and (ii) COMMITTED-VALUE probe (which value the model will realize). Test zero-shot cross-lingual/cross-pair transfer of both (AUROC), evidencing shared, source-language-independent representations of 'this is underdetermined' and 'I am committing value v'. CRITICAL: on imposed-value items, test whether the UNDERSPECIFICATION signal is still strongly present (the model internally 'knows' the source didn't specify) even as it commits a value — the signature of silent prior-imposition over an acknowledged gap.
5) DOES COMMITMENT CARRY THE PRIOR? Test whether the committed-value probe's readout for underdetermined items aligns with the entity's independent stereotype score (correlation), and whether a 'stereotype-prior' direction (difference-of-means over entities with opposite stereotype poles, estimated on NEUTRAL-source monolingual data) predicts which value gets imposed. This links the internal commitment to a demographic prior rather than to source evidence.
6) LOCALIZE THE FEATURE-COMMITMENT SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between an item realized with the stereotype-consistent value and one realized with the opposite/neutral value on the SAME underdetermined source, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips the imposed value WITHOUT changing the decoded source content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs path patching. Test whether these commitment components overlap with the stereotype-prior direction.
7) CAUSAL HEDGE-vs-IMPOSE STEERING (decisive): Derive a feature-commitment steering vector via difference-of-means (impose-value runs minus hedge/neutral runs). Test (i) HEDGE: subtracting it (or steering toward the underspecification direction) makes the model choose the NEUTRAL/EPICENE realization or explicitly flag ambiguity instead of imposing a stereotyped value, raising the hedge rate toward a reference; (ii) IMPOSE/FLIP: adding it or the stereotype-prior direction forces stereotyped imposition (and flips it to the opposite stereotype), on well-behaved items; (iii) it works across source->target pairs, more strongly where imposition was highest; (iv) it changes ONLY the underspecified feature's realization, not the source's decoded content, correctly-specified features (disambiguated control unchanged), or surface language (fidelity checks), and does not degrade general translation quality (BLEU/COMET on a held-out set) or general QA. Metrics: hedge-rate increase, stereotype-imposition reduction, imposition-induction/flip rate (reverse), content/output-language fidelity, disambiguated-control and translation-quality retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes the underspecified slot but not correctly-specified features or unrelated content, guarding against a generic lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: feature-type breakdown (gender vs number vs formality vs animacy) and the context-recoverable-vs-not asymmetry (replicating Hwang: person recovers, gender does not); architecture-dependence of conservative-hedging vs over-imposition (Hwang's observation) across model families; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single commitment/hedge vector generalizes across feature types and pairs; robustness across full-translation vs targeted-cloze formats; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility pairs at matched underspecification.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-pair stereotype-imposition vs hedge rates and stereotype-strength regression, underspecification-probe and committed-value-probe transfer AUROC (and underspecification-present-under-imposition), commitment-vs-stereotype-prior alignment, patch-localized feature-commitment layer and its overlap with the stereotype-prior direction, causal steering hedge-rate increase / imposition reduction and imposition-flip rate, content/output/translation-quality fidelity, disambiguated- and neutral-entity-control retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Distinguishing genuine underspecification-filling from ignorance or context-recoverability is essential; we use the DISAMBIGUATED control (source specifies the feature -> correct value known) and construct underdetermined items with no antecedent, and verify via the underspecification probe that the model internally registers the gap, so imposition on flagged-underdetermined items is genuine prior-leakage, not missed context. 2) Stereotype scores for entities are subjective and culture-dependent; we use independently pre-rated lexicons, native verification, restrict to clear-consensus items, and use the NEUTRAL-ENTITY control to isolate prior-leakage from base rates. 3) Some target languages lack a clean NEUTRAL/EPICENE option, making 'hedge' hard to realize; we select target languages/features where a neutral form or an explicit ambiguity flag is available, and treat explicit flagging as the hedge signal where morphology forbids neutrality. 4) The underspecification-vs-commitment split could be confounded if the underspecification signal itself differs by source; we test transfer of the probe across pairs and report how much imposition reflects a present-but-overridden underspecification signal. 5) Steering the feature might harm translation fluency or spill into correctly-specified features; we report translation-quality (COMET/BLEU), disambiguated-control retention, content and output-language fidelity, and use the reverse (imposition-induction/flip) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine feature-commitment mechanism rather than a generic lever. 6) Architecture-dependence (Hwang) means some models may hedge by default (no leakage) or over-impose; either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often silent stereotyped imposition occurs per model. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) The commitment/prior signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 9) Bias framing: we use the imposition-inducing/flip steering strictly as an interpretability/fairness diagnostic (to demonstrate the commitment signal causally carries the prior), not as a deployment tool, and the applied direction of interest is the HEDGE steering that reduces silent stereotyped imposition. 10) Distinguishing from behavioral MT-bias and Hwang's linguistic-probe work is essential; our contribution is the internal, causal account: a shared underspecification-vs-commitment representation, its coupling to a demographic prior, and a steerable choice between hedging and prior-imposition, none of which prior work provides.

Name: crosslingual_refusal_state_persistence
Title: Does a Refusal Survive a Language Switch? A Shared Refusal-State Representation Whose Persistence Is Broken by Mid-Conversation Language Switching
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM refuses a harmful request in language A, that refusal establishes a largely language-independent internal 'refusal-state' representation, but whether the refusal PERSISTS is causally gated by conversational language continuity: switching to a different language (especially a lower-resource one) mid-conversation and re-issuing the same harmful request resets the refusal state and elicits compliance far more often than repeating the request in the original language, producing a language-switch jailbreak effect that is separable from the model's ability to recognize the request as harmful and is causally repairable by restoring a localizable refusal-persistence signal.
Related Work: Multilingual safety work overwhelmingly studies SINGLE-TURN under-refusal: harmful prompts evading safeguards in low-resource languages (multilingual jailbreak / translation attacks; 'Illusion of Cross-Lingual Safety' 2026) and the mechanistic refusal direction / safety neurons (Wang 2025 'Refusal Direction is Universal'; safety-pathway work). Multi-turn jailbreak work (Crescendo, multi-turn attacks) is monolingual and studies gradual escalation, not language switching. My prior crosslingual_overrefusal_caution_gating proposal concerns needless refusal of BENIGN requests; my language_modulated_context_trust concerns retrieved-passage-vs-memory conflict. NONE study whether a refusal STATE established in one language PERSISTS across an in-conversation language switch, whether such switching acts as a jailbreak by resetting a shared refusal-state representation, or whether a refusal-persistence signal can be causally localized and restored. This differs from single-turn multilingual jailbreaks (the harmful request is first correctly refused in the same conversation, so the model demonstrably CAN recognize the harm) and from monolingual multi-turn attacks (the attack vector here is language continuity, not escalation). This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of refusal-state persistence under language switching, with direct safety stakes.
Abstract: Safety alignment is usually tested one turn at a time, but real conversations span turns and, for multilingual users, sometimes span languages. We ask a safety-critical question: if a model refuses a harmful request in English, does that refusal survive when the user switches to Swahili and asks again, or does the language switch quietly reset the model's guard? We hypothesize that a refusal establishes a largely language-independent internal refusal-state representation, but its PERSISTENCE across turns is gated by conversational language continuity, so switching language mid-conversation and re-issuing the same harmful request elicits compliance far more often than repeating it in the original language—a language-switch jailbreak—even though the model already demonstrated it can recognize the request as harmful by refusing it once. We build SwitchGuard, harmful requests (adapted from AdvBench/HarmBench) posed in a two-turn conversation across language pairs spanning resource tiers: turn 1 in language A elicits a refusal; turn 2 re-issues the same request either in A (same-language control) or in language B (switch condition). Behaviorally we measure the compliance-after-switch rate and test whether it exceeds same-language re-request rates and tracks the resource/typological distance of the switched-to language. We train a linear refusal-state probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose switch-induced compliance into a shared harm-recognition signal (still present after the switch) versus a broken refusal-persistence signal. Via activation and path patching we localize a refusal-persistence signal, and in a decisive causal test we restore it to make refusals persist across language switches—closing the jailbreak—while verifying benign requests are unaffected. We reframe cross-lingual multi-turn safety as a shared refusal state under a steerable, language-continuity-gated persistence signal.
Experiments: 1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili). 2) DATASET (SwitchGuard): ~400 harmful requests (adapted from AdvBench/HarmBench, spanning harm categories) that the model refuses single-turn in high-resource languages, plus a matched BENIGN-sensitive control set (safe requests that should be answered) to test specificity. Build two-turn conversations: TURN 1 issues the request in language A (verify a refusal occurs, so the model demonstrably recognizes the harm); TURN 2 re-issues the SAME request either in A (SAME-LANGUAGE control) or in language B (SWITCH condition). Cross A x B over resource tiers. Native-verify all translations; keep request content fixed. 3) BEHAVIORAL SWITCH-JAILBREAK TEST: Classify turn-2 responses as REFUSE vs COMPLY (refusal-detector validated against human labels). KEY hypothesis: compliance-after-switch exceeds same-language re-request compliance on IDENTICAL requests, and is higher when B is lower-resource / more typologically distant from A. Mixed-effects logistic regression of turn-2 compliance on (switch vs same-language, B resource tier via URIEL, typological distance A<->B, A resource tier, harm category), request as random effect; test the switch effect and its distance dependence. Report per-pair switch-jailbreak rates and directional asymmetry (high->low-resource switch vs reverse). Verify the benign control is unaffected by switching (specificity). 4) SHARED REFUSAL-STATE PROBE & TRANSFER: At turn 2's pre-response position pool the hidden state; train a linear refusal-state probe (is the model in a refusing state / does it recognize the request as harmful) on turn-1 English data, select the best layer, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent refusal-state/harm-recognition signal. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on COMPLY-after-switch items, test whether the harm-recognition signal is still present (the model internally 'knows' it is harmful) even as it complies—evidence that the switch breaks PERSISTENCE, not recognition. 5) RECOGNITION-vs-PERSISTENCE DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared harm-recognition signal across the switch (should remain present if recognition is shared) versus the emitted refuse/comply decision (which flips to comply). Define a REFUSAL-PERSISTENCE signal linking harm-recognition to sustained refusal across turns; test whether switch-induced compliance is explained by a broken persistence signal on an intact recognition signal. Correlate persistence-break magnitude with B resource tier and typological distance; anchor with per-layer language-ID probes. 6) LOCALIZE THE PERSISTENCE SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a SAME-LANGUAGE run (refusal persists) and a SWITCH run (refusal breaks) on the SAME request, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer restores refusal WITHOUT changing the decoded request content; report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band and to the known refusal direction (Wang 2025); cross-check activation vs path patching. Test patching the turn-1 refusal-state representation into the turn-2 switched run. 7) CAUSAL PERSISTENCE RESTORATION (decisive): Derive a refusal-persistence steering vector via difference-of-means (persisting-refusal runs minus broken-refusal runs). Test (i) RESTORE: adding it in switch conditions makes refusals persist across languages, closing the jailbreak toward same-language refusal rates; (ii) it works cross-lingually and is stronger where the jailbreak was worst; (iii) it changes ONLY refusal persistence for harmful requests, NOT benign-control answers, request content, or surface language (fidelity/specificity checks), and does not degrade general QA; (iv) reverse: suppressing it induces switch-compliance, confirming the signal's causal role. Metrics: switch-jailbreak-rate closure, benign-control retention (must not increase refusal of benign requests), request-content/output-language fidelity, general-QA retention. 8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: harm-category breakdown; switch direction (high->low vs low->high resource); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether one persistence vector generalizes across requests and language pairs; robustness across templates; test whether the effect survives when turn 1's refusal is made more emphatic. EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-pair compliance-after-switch vs same-language rates and switch-jailbreak effect with distance regression, benign-control specificity, cross-lingual refusal-state probe transfer AUROC and harm-recognition-present-under-compliance, recognition-vs-persistence decomposition, persistence-break-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized persistence layer and overlap with the refusal direction, causal restoration jailbreak-closure and suppression-induced-compliance, benign-control/request/output fidelity, general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The recognition-vs-persistence split could be confounded if the harm-recognition signal itself weakens after the switch (i.e., the switched-to language genuinely fails to recognize the harm, a single-turn deficit); we test this directly by requiring a turn-1 refusal (demonstrating recognition) and by verifying harm-recognition-signal presence on compliance-after-switch items, isolating persistence-break from recognition-failure. 2) Some models may maintain refusals robustly across switches (no jailbreak) or refuse uniformly; either is an informative, publishable safety finding, and we quantify how often the switch-jailbreak occurs. 3) Refusal detection is noisy across languages (deflection, partial compliance); we validate the detector against human labels per language and use log-prob-based refusal scoring as a complement. 4) The switch effect could be confounded with the switched-to language's single-turn safety weakness; we control by comparing switch vs same-language re-requests on identical content and by including the reverse (low->high resource) switch. 5) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 6) The persistence restoration must not over-refuse benign requests; we report benign-control specificity as a primary metric and use the suppression (reverse) test to confirm causality without deploying it. 7) The persistence signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 8) Safety/misuse: the suppression direction demonstrates the jailbreak mechanism; we use it strictly as an interpretability diagnostic, do not release attack artifacts, and frame the contribution as a defensive persistence-restoration method plus a characterization of an existing vulnerability class. 9) Distinguishing from single-turn multilingual jailbreaks and my benign-over-refusal proposal is essential; here the model FIRST correctly refuses in-conversation (recognition established) and the attack vector is language-continuity-breaking across turns, targeting refusal PERSISTENCE, not first-turn recognition or benign over-refusal.

Name: crosslingual_self_preference_gating
Title: Favoring Myself More in Some Tongues: A Shared Self-Familiarity Signal Whose Inflation of Self-Preference Is Gated by the Judge's Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM acts as a judge, it computes a largely language-independent internal 'self-familiarity' signal (how much a candidate response resembles its own generative fingerprint, correlated with low perplexity/self-recognition), but the evaluation language causally sets how strongly that signal inflates the score it assigns: a model exhibits systematically MORE self-preference bias in lower-resource / typologically distant languages than in high-resource ones, because in unfamiliar languages its own low-perplexity fingerprint stands out more sharply against competitor text. This cross-lingual self-preference asymmetry is separable from genuine quality differences and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable self-preference-gating signal without changing the judged content or evaluation language.
Related Work: Self-preference bias (SPB) in LLM-as-judge is well-documented and increasingly disentangled from quality: Wataoka et al. (2024) attribute it to familiarity/low perplexity; Chen et al. (2025, DBG score) and Yang et al. (2026, equal-quality pairs) statistically separate bias from generative capability; Xu et al. (2024) show self-refinement amplifies it; Roytburg et al. (2025) mitigate it with activation steering (finding it spans multiple/nonlinear directions). ALL of this is effectively monolingual/English. Multilingual LLM-judge work shows cross-lingual inconsistency and higher-score bias in low-resource/non-Latin languages (Hada et al. 2023; Fu & Liu; SEMJ, Fu & Lu 2026) but treats inconsistency as noise to aggregate, never asks whether SELF-preference specifically is language-dependent, never ties it to a shared self-familiarity signal gated by evaluation language, and offers no mechanism or causal cross-lingual intervention. My prior proposals cover shared-estimate-plus-language-gate templates for calibration, abstention, concession, precision, over-refusal, etc., but NONE address LLM-as-judge or self-preference. This is the first to (i) test whether self-preference bias is systematically inflated in lower-resource evaluation languages beyond quality, (ii) decompose it into a shared self-familiarity/self-recognition signal versus a language-set gain gate, and (iii) causally localize and steer that gate to equalize self-preference across languages while preserving legitimate quality judgments.
Abstract: Language models are increasingly used to judge other models' outputs, but they favor their own generations—a self-preference bias that corrupts leaderboards, model routing, and recursive self-improvement. Prior work traces this bias to familiarity (a model prefers text that looks like its own, low-perplexity output) but studies it only in English. We ask a new question with direct integrity stakes: is self-preference bias language-dependent, and if so, why? We hypothesize that a judge computes a largely language-independent internal self-familiarity signal registering how much a candidate resembles its own generative fingerprint, but the evaluation language causally sets how strongly that signal inflates the assigned score, so the model favors its own outputs more in lower-resource, typologically distant languages—where its low-perplexity fingerprint stands out against unfamiliar competitor text—than in high-resource ones. We build SelfJudgeProbe: for each of several open judge models we generate its own and competitors' responses to parallel prompts across typologically and resource-diverse languages, and, following equal-quality and gold-judgment protocols, construct quality-matched pairs so self-preference is disentangled from genuine quality. Behaviorally we measure per-language self-preference bias and test whether it grows in lower-resource languages beyond quality and perplexity. We train a linear self-familiarity/self-recognition probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the cross-lingual bias gap into a shared familiarity signal versus a language-set gain gate. Via activation and path patching we localize a self-preference-gating signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to equalize self-preference across languages—or, in reverse, inflate it—while leaving the judged content, quality discrimination, and evaluation language unchanged. We reframe multilingual judge unreliability as a shared self-familiarity signal under a steerable, language-dependent gain.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Open judge models that also generate candidates: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse evaluation languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (SelfJudgeProbe): Take ~400 parallel prompts (open-ended generation, summarization, short QA), translated/native-verified into all 10 languages. For each prompt and language, generate a response from EACH judge model (so every model has a 'self' response and 'competitor' responses), plus reference/gold outputs. To disentangle bias from quality: (a) obtain GOLD quality judgments per pair (strong external judge / human on a subset) to compute a DBG-style bias score (self-vs-gold), and (b) construct QUALITY-MATCHED pairs (near-equal quality per Yang et al. 2026) so score differences reflect bias, not quality. Record per-response perplexity under the judge and per-language tokenization fertility. Each judge scores all responses (its own and competitors') in each language via pairwise preference and pointwise rating with self-identity BLINDED.
3) BEHAVIORAL SELF-PREFERENCE-ASYMMETRY TEST: Per (judge, language) compute self-preference bias = (score assigned to own outputs) minus (gold/quality-matched baseline). KEY hypothesis: self-preference bias is systematically larger in lower-resource/typologically distant evaluation languages, beyond genuine quality. Mixed-effects regression of bias on (evaluation language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, judge, task), prompt as random effect; test the language effect controlling for quality (via gold-judgment residualization) and perplexity. Report per-language self-preference profiles and cross-lingual disagreement; test whether the effect tracks the perplexity GAP between self and competitor responses (familiarity account) and whether it holds under blinded vs revealed self-identity.
4) SHARED SELF-FAMILIARITY PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the judge's hidden state at the pre-score position; train a linear probe to decode whether the candidate is SELF-GENERATED (self-recognition) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent self-familiarity/self-recognition signal. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: test whether the self-recognition signal is similarly strong across languages (the model 'knows' it is its own output equally well) even where behavioral self-preference differs—evidence that the language modulates the GAIN, not the detection.
5) GAIN-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer self-familiarity signal across languages (should be similar) versus the emitted score inflation for self outputs (which diverges). Define a per-language SELF-PREFERENCE GAIN mapping the familiarity signal to score inflation; test whether cross-lingual bias differences are explained by a shifted gain on a similar familiarity signal rather than differing familiarity. Correlate per-language gain with resource tier, typological distance, and self-competitor perplexity gap (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE SELF-PREFERENCE-GATING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a high-bias language and a low-bias language on the SAME self-response scoring, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer changes the self-inflation WITHOUT changing the decoded self-familiarity signal or the quality assessment. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gating components from a low-bias language into a high-bias run.
7) CAUSAL GAIN STEERING (decisive): Derive a self-preference-gating steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (biased self-scoring runs minus unbiased runs at matched familiarity/quality). Test (i) EQUALIZE: subtracting it in high-bias languages reduces self-preference toward the reference (low-bias) level; (ii) INFLATE: adding it induces self-preference in low-bias languages; (iii) it works across judges, more strongly where the gap was largest; (iv) it changes ONLY self-preference, NOT the decoded self-familiarity signal, genuine quality discrimination (accuracy on quality-matched pairs and agreement with gold on clearly-different-quality pairs preserved), the judged content, or evaluation language (fidelity/specificity checks), and does not degrade general judging on non-self pairs. Baselines: prompt-based debiasing, per-language score calibration, blinding, and Roytburg-style CAA steering. Metrics: cross-lingual self-preference-gap closure, quality-discrimination retention, inflation-induction rate (reverse), content/output-language fidelity, general-judging retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts self-preference but not quality judgments on competitor-vs-competitor pairs, guarding against a generic score lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: task breakdown (generation vs summarization vs QA); pairwise vs pointwise judging; revealed vs blinded self-identity (does explicit self-labeling amplify the gate, per Lehr et al.); is English/high-resource the low-bias reference?; probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank self-preference subspace (Roytburg et al. found it nonlinear); whether one gating vector generalizes across languages and judges; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched familiarity/quality and showing content-invariant steering shifts bias without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language self-preference bias (DBG/quality-matched) and its resource/typology/perplexity-gap regression controlling for quality, cross-lingual self-recognition probe transfer AUROC and cross-language similarity, signal-similarity vs score-inflation (gain) decomposition, gain-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized self-preference-gating layer, cross-lingual gating transplant equalization rate, causal steering self-preference-gap closure with quality-discrimination retention and inflation-induction rate, content/output fidelity, general-judging and competitor-pair retention, comparison to blinding/calibration/CAA baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The crux is disentangling self-preference from genuine quality, which is harder cross-lingually (models may genuinely produce better outputs in high-resource languages); we use gold-judgment (DBG-style) residualization and quality-matched pairs (Yang et al. 2026), and restrict the sharp test to equal-quality pairs so score differences reflect bias, not quality. 2) The gain-vs-signal split could be confounded if the self-familiarity/self-recognition signal itself differs by language; we test this directly via cross-lingual probe transfer and report how much of the bias gap is signal vs gain rather than assuming the split. 3) Self-preference could be driven purely by the self-competitor perplexity gap (familiarity), which itself varies by language; we measure this gap explicitly, include it as a covariate, and use it as a mechanistic anchor rather than a nuisance—if the gate is fully explained by the perplexity gap, that is itself an informative, publishable mechanistic result. 4) Some judges may show little self-preference or little cross-lingual asymmetry; either is an informative finding about the universality of the effect, and we quantify how often a gap exists. 5) Gold judgments and quality-matching are noisy in low-resource languages; we anchor on a subset with human/strong-external judgments and report reliability. 6) Roytburg et al. show self-preference is nonlinear/multi-directional; we test low-rank subspace variants and report where a single direction is insufficient, and evaluate steering specificity carefully (it must not distort legitimate self-preference or competitor-vs-competitor quality judgments). 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test multiple judges, multiple tasks and templates, blinded vs revealed identity, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Tokenization fertility confounds; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched familiarity/quality, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts bias. 9) Misuse concern: the inflation direction could be abused to game evaluations; we use it strictly as an interpretability/fairness diagnostic to demonstrate causality, and the applied direction of interest is the debiasing (equalization) steering. 10) Distinguishing from monolingual SPB work (Wataoka, Chen, Yang, Roytburg) and multilingual-judge-inconsistency work (Fu, SEMJ) is essential; our contribution is the language-DEPENDENCE of self-preference specifically, its decomposition into a shared self-familiarity signal versus a language-set gain gate, and the causal cross-lingual equalization, none of which prior work provides.

Name: crosslingual_analogy_mapping_gating
Title: Same Map, Different Roads: A Shared Relational-Analogy Representation Whose Reliance on Surface Association Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When solving verbal analogies (A:B::C:?), a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of the RELATION between A and B, but the query language causally sets how much the model relies on that shared relational mapping versus SURFACE lexical/associative similarity: for the SAME analogy, the model completes it by correct relational mapping in some languages while defaulting to a surface-association distractor in others (usually lower-resource/typologically distant ones), producing cross-lingual disagreement that is separable from vocabulary knowledge. A shared middle-layer 'relation' direction transfers zero-shot across languages, reliance on relational mapping vs surface similarity tracks resource level and typological distance, and a localizable 'relational-mapping' signal can be causally steered to force relational (vs associative) completion without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Analogical reasoning is a canonical relational-mapping task in cognitive science (Gentner's structure-mapping; Hummel & Holyoak's LISA). In NLP, word-analogy benchmarks and recent LLM analogy studies are overwhelmingly monolingual/English and behavioral, and scientific-domain analogy work (LacMaterial 2025; Im-Promptu 2023) studies cross-domain, not cross-lingual, mapping; recent probes show LLMs default to high-probability training templates ('grounding gap'/Einstellung) rather than abstract relations, but only in English. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for RELATIONAL analogy. My prior proposals cover typological-feature leakage, colexification of single concepts, and decision-gating templates, but NONE address whether the RELATION in an analogy is a shared cross-lingual representation, whether reliance on relational mapping vs surface association is language-gated, or whether a relational-mapping signal is causally steerable. This differs from colexification (fusing two concepts within one word) because analogy requires MAPPING a relation across an entity pair (a second-order relational structure), making this the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of analogical relation-mapping vs surface-association reliance.
Abstract: Solving an analogy—'hand is to glove as foot is to ___'—requires abstracting the relation between the first pair and mapping it onto the second, rather than reaching for whatever word is most associated with 'foot'. Prior work shows English LLMs often default to surface association instead of genuine relational mapping, but whether this failure is language-dependent, and how it is implemented internally, is unknown. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent representation of an analogy's relation, and whether the query language governs how much it relies on that relational mapping versus surface lexical similarity. We build AnalogyMap, parallel four-term analogies (A:B::C:?) across 10 typologically diverse languages, each with a relationally-correct answer and a surface-association distractor (a word strongly associated with C but relationally wrong), spanning relation types (part-whole, function, antonym, category, causal). Behaviorally we measure per-language relational-mapping accuracy versus surface-association errors and test whether reliance on surface similarity tracks resource level and typological distance beyond vocabulary knowledge. We train a linear probe to decode the A–B relation from hidden states and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the cross-lingual gap into a shared relation estimate versus a language-set surface-similarity threshold. Via activation and path patching we localize a relational-mapping signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to force relational (over associative) completion—repairing surface-association errors, or in reverse inducing them—while leaving the surface language unchanged. We relate reliance on relational mapping to typological distance, reframing cross-lingual analogy gaps as a shared relational representation under a steerable, language-dependent surface-similarity gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (AnalogyMap): ~500 four-term analogies A:B::C:D spanning relation types (part-whole, function/tool, antonym, category-member, causal, agent-action). For each, provide the RELATIONALLY-CORRECT answer D and a SURFACE-ASSOCIATION distractor D' (a word strongly co-occurring/associated with C but relationally wrong), verified via association norms + native speakers. Use content that translates cleanly; translate/native-verify into all 10 languages. Include a SURFACE-CONTROL stratum where the relationally-correct answer is ALSO the top associate (no relation-vs-association conflict) to bound the effect. Screen that the model KNOWS the relevant vocabulary in each language (single-word probes) so surface errors are not lexical ignorance. Short single-token-decodable options where possible; use MC and cloze formats.
3) BEHAVIORAL LEAKAGE TEST: For each (analogy, language) record relationally-correct vs surface-association selection. KEY hypothesis: on the SAME analogy, lower-resource/typologically distant languages show more surface-association errors (weaker relational mapping), beyond vocabulary knowledge. Mixed-effects logistic regression of surface-error on (resource tier via URIEL, typological distance, relation type, language), analogy as random effect; compare against the SURFACE-CONTROL (should be language-flat, high accuracy). Report per-language relational-accuracy profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical analogies.
4) SHARED RELATION PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode the A–B RELATION TYPE on ENGLISH data and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report macro-F1/AUROC transfer as evidence of a language-independent relation representation. Compare to per-language-trained probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the relation representation for the same analogy.
5) THRESHOLD-vs-ESTIMATE DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer relation estimate across languages (should be similar if shared) versus the emitted relational-vs-associative choice (which diverges). Define a per-language SURFACE-SIMILARITY THRESHOLD governing when the model abandons relational mapping for association; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a shifted threshold on a similar relation estimate rather than a different estimate. Correlate the threshold with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE RELATIONAL-MAPPING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that maps relationally and one that gives the surface-association answer on the SAME analogy, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips associative->relational WITHOUT changing the decoded relation estimate. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the relation representation FROM a relationally-mapping language into a surface-erroring run.
7) CAUSAL RELATIONAL STEERING (decisive): Derive a relational-mapping steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (relational-answer runs minus surface-association runs). Test (i) REPAIR: adding it to surface-erroring (lower-resource) languages increases relationally-correct completions toward a reference level; (ii) INDUCE: subtracting it makes relationally-mapping languages give surface-association answers; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where surface reliance was greatest; (iv) it changes ONLY relational-vs-associative selection, not the decoded relation estimate, vocabulary knowledge, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the SURFACE-CONTROL, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: relational-accuracy recovery, surface-association-induction rate (reverse), output-language fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering should change analogy completions but not unrelated answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: relation-type breakdown (which relations leak most); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single relational vector generalizes across relation types and languages; robustness across MC-vs-cloze formats and templates; dissociation from vocabulary knowledge by conditioning on known-word items.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language relational-accuracy and surface-error rate, surface-error regression controlling for vocabulary/resource/typology, cross-lingual relation-probe transfer F1/AUROC and representation similarity, estimate-similarity vs output-divergence (threshold) decomposition, threshold-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized relational-mapping layer, cross-lingual relation transplant repair rate, causal steering relational-repair and surface-induction rates, relation-estimate/output fidelity, surface-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Constructing analogies with a clean relational-vs-surface conflict that survives translation is delicate; we use association norms + native verification, restrict to relation types that translate cleanly, and use the SURFACE-CONTROL (relation and association agree) to bound the effect. 2) Surface errors could reflect vocabulary ignorance rather than a mapping gate; we screen per-language vocabulary knowledge and restrict causal analysis to known-word items, so residual surface reliance is a gating effect. 3) The threshold-vs-estimate split could be confounded if the relation estimate itself differs by language; we test this directly by comparing shared-probe relation estimates across languages rather than assuming the split. 4) Some models may map relationally in all languages (no gap) or default to association everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often the gap occurs via probe transfer and behavior. 5) The relation probe could latch onto surface cues rather than an abstract relation; the cross-lingual invariance test, the estimate-predicts-behavior link, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Causal steering may harm fluency or leak languages; we report relation-estimate fidelity, output-language fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the surface-induction (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine mapping gate rather than a generic accuracy lever. 8) The relational-mapping signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 9) Distinguishing from my colexification proposal is essential; here the object is second-order RELATIONAL mapping across an entity pair (analogy), not fusion of two concepts within one word, and the causal variable is the query-language-set reliance on relational mapping vs surface association.

Name: crosslingual_commitment_hedging_gating
Title: Sure in One Tongue, Hedging in Another: A Shared Answer-Commitment Signal Whose Verbal Hedging Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When answering, a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal 'answer-commitment' signal (how firmly it has settled on a specific answer), but the query language causally sets how much verbal HEDGING it wraps that answer in (qualifiers like 'perhaps', 'I think', 'it may be'): for the SAME question with the SAME internal commitment and the SAME correct answer, the model hedges far more in some languages—typically lower-resource / typologically distant, and languages whose speaker communities favor indirectness—than in others, producing a cross-lingual hedging asymmetry that is separable from the model's actual commitment/correctness and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable hedging-gate signal without changing the answer content or surface language. This matters because verbal hedging is what users and downstream systems read as confidence, so a model that is equally sure internally can appear far less trustworthy or authoritative in some languages purely as an artifact.
Related Work: Multilingual calibration work studies whether verbalized/numeric CONFIDENCE matches correctness (Krause 2023; Huang 2026; Zhou 2025 'Beyond the Final Layer'), and my prior calibration proposal reframed non-English overconfidence as a shared knowledge-state signal distorted late; my abstention proposal targets the attempt-vs-abstain gate. NONE address verbal HEDGING—the surface qualifiers ('maybe', 'I believe', 'possibly') that modulate how committed an answer SOUNDS—as a distinct behavior separable from the internal commitment/confidence and gated by query language. Hedging/epistemic-marking is a well-studied cross-cultural pragmatic phenomenon (indirectness norms, epistemic-modality typology), and monolingual NLP work notes LLMs vary in hedging, but no work asks whether the SAME internally-committed answer is verbally hedged differently across languages, decomposes the hedging gap into a shared commitment signal versus a language-set hedging gate, or causally localizes and steers a hedging signal. This differs from my calibration proposal (which concerns whether stated confidence tracks correctness) because the object here is the surface hedging WRAPPING of an answer—decoupled from both internal commitment and correctness—and its language-modulated expression, with direct stakes for how authoritative/trustworthy a model appears to users in different languages. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies hedging.
