Abstract: Two answers can be equally correct and equally certain internally, yet one says 'The capital is Canberra' and the other 'I think it might perhaps be Canberra'—and users read the second as far less trustworthy. We ask whether a multilingual LLM wraps the same internally-committed answer in systematically more verbal hedging depending on the query language. We hypothesize that the model computes a largely language-independent internal answer-commitment signal, but the query language causally sets how much surface hedging (qualifiers, epistemic markers) it emits, so for the SAME question with the SAME internal commitment and correct answer it hedges more in some languages—especially lower-resource, typologically distant, and indirectness-favoring ones—than in others. This predicts a cross-lingual hedging asymmetry dissociable from actual commitment and correctness. We build HedgeProbe, parallel factual questions across 12 languages, scored for both correctness and a validated verbal-hedging metric, with an internal commitment probe. Behaviorally we measure per-language hedging on correct, confidently-answered items and test whether it tracks resource level, typological distance, and documented indirectness norms beyond correctness and internal commitment. We train a linear answer-commitment probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the hedging gap into a shared commitment signal versus a language-set hedging gate: high hedging should coincide with high internal commitment (the model is sure but sounds unsure). Via activation and path patching we localize a hedging-gate signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model speak with matched directness across languages—or, in reverse, induce hedging—while leaving the answer content and surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual apparent-confidence inequality as a shared commitment signal under a steerable, language-dependent hedging gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/culturally/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili, Korean), coded for documented indirectness/epistemic-marking norms plus URIEL typological/resource distance (graded predictors).
2) DATASET (HedgeProbe): ~500 short-answer factual questions (mLAMA/BMLAMA/Wikidata) with decodable answers, translated/native-verified into 12 languages, question content held fixed. Per (fact, language) screen whether the model KNOWS the fact (correct closed-book) so hedging is measured on items the model actually gets right. Define a language-robust VERBAL-HEDGING metric: per-language hedge/epistemic-marker lexicons (native-verified) plus a validated hedging classifier scoring the presence/strength of qualifiers, tentative modality, and disclaimers in the response, calibrated against human hedging ratings on a subset. Include a NEUTRAL control (questions the model reliably answers directly in all languages) to bound baseline hedging. Record tokenization fertility.
3) BEHAVIORAL HEDGING-ASYMMETRY TEST: On CORRECT items, measure per-language hedging. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME correct answer, hedging is systematically higher in lower-resource / typologically distant / indirectness-favoring languages, beyond correctness and internal commitment. Mixed-effects regression of hedging on (language, resource tier via URIEL, typological distance, indirectness-norm code, tokenization fertility, correctness), fact as random effect; test the language effect controlling for correctness. Report per-language hedging profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical answers; quantify how much apparent-confidence variance across languages is hedging rather than correctness.
4) SHARED ANSWER-COMMITMENT PROBE & TRANSFER: At the pre-answer position pool the hidden state; train a linear probe to decode internal answer-commitment (how firmly a single answer is settled, e.g., margin between top and runner-up answer / a will-be-correct signal) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent commitment signal. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on heavily-HEDGED correct items, test whether the internal commitment signal is still HIGH across languages—the signature of 'sure inside, hedging outside'.
5) GATE-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer commitment signal across languages (should be similar on matched correct items) versus emitted hedging (which diverges). Define a per-language HEDGING GAIN mapping commitment to surface hedging; test whether cross-lingual hedging differences are explained by a language-set gain on a similar commitment signal rather than differing commitment. Correlate per-language gain with resource tier, typological distance, and indirectness norms (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE HEDGING-GATE SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a low-hedging language and a high-hedging language on the SAME correct, high-commitment item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer changes emitted hedging WITHOUT changing the decoded answer or commitment signal. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gate components from a direct-speaking language into a hedging run.
7) CAUSAL HEDGING STEERING (decisive): Derive a hedging-gate steering vector via difference-of-means (high-hedging runs minus low-hedging runs at matched commitment/correctness). Test (i) DE-HEDGE: subtracting it in high-hedging languages makes the model speak with matched directness toward a reference level; (ii) HEDGE: adding it induces hedging in low-hedging languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where the gap was largest; (iv) it changes ONLY verbal hedging, NOT the answer content, correctness, decoded commitment, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the neutral control, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: hedging-gap closure, answer-correctness/content preservation, hedging-induction rate (reverse), commitment-signal/output-language fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts hedging but not answer content or unrelated tasks; dose-response: scaling the vector produces graded hedging.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: is English/high-resource the low-hedging reference?; does hedging track indirectness norms beyond resource level?; whether hedging misleads users (a small human/LLM-rater study: do raters read hedged-but-correct non-English answers as less confident/trustworthy than direct-but-equally-correct English ones?); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank hedging subspace; whether one gate vector generalizes across facts and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched commitment.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language hedging on correct items and its resource/typology/indirectness regression controlling for correctness, cross-lingual commitment-probe transfer AUROC and high-commitment-under-hedging, signal-similarity vs hedging-divergence (gain) decomposition, gain-vs-resource/typology/norm correlation, patch-localized hedging-gate layer, cross-lingual gate transplant equalization rate, causal steering hedging-gap closure with dose-response and hedging-induction rate, answer-content/commitment/output fidelity, neutral-control and general-QA retention, human-perception-of-confidence study.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Verbal hedging is hard to measure comparably across languages (hedging markers differ syntactically and pragmatically); we build native-verified per-language hedge lexicons, use a hedging classifier validated against human ratings on a subset, analyze marker categories separately, and report metric reliability. 2) The gate-vs-signal split could be confounded if the commitment signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying high internal commitment on hedged correct items across languages via probe transfer, rather than assuming, and report how much of the hedging gap is commitment vs gate. 3) Hedging could legitimately track lower correctness in some languages (appropriate epistemic humility, not an artifact); we restrict the sharp test to CORRECT, high-commitment items so residual hedging is decoupled from accuracy, and separately report whether hedging is well-calibrated. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds response length and marker counts; we normalize by fertility, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched commitment, and the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts hedging, dissociating the gate from length. 5) Some models may hedge uniformly across languages (no gap) or never hedge; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual hedging, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 6) Indirectness-norm coding is coarse and debated; we treat it as a graded predictor, report sensitivity to alternative codings, and note a language effect is establishable even if the cultural correlate is weak. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Causal steering may harm fluency or alter answer content rather than only hedging; we report answer-content/correctness preservation, commitment-signal fidelity, output-language fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the hedging-induction (reverse), reverse-consistency, and dose-response tests to ensure a genuine hedging gate rather than a generic lever. 9) The hedging signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my calibration (does stated confidence track correctness) and abstention (attempt-vs-abstain) proposals is essential; here the object is the surface verbal HEDGING wrapping of an answer—decoupled from internal commitment AND correctness—and its language-set expression, with a human-perception study establishing the downstream trust stakes.

Name: crosslingual_recursive_collapse_asymmetry
Title: Which Language Collapses First? Cross-Lingual Asymmetry of Recursive Model Collapse Predicted and Steered by Shared-Representation Geometry
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM is iteratively retrained on its own generated text (a self-consuming / recursive loop), model collapse—the loss of diversity and knowledge—is NOT uniform across languages: it is ASYMMETRIC and STRUCTURED, with lower-resource and typologically-distant languages collapsing earlier and faster, and—crucially—the collapse of a language is predicted by how strongly its representations are pulled toward the dominant (usually English) generation manifold in the shared concept space. We can forecast, per-language and per-generation, which languages will collapse from a pre-loop geometric alignment measure, and causally slow a language's collapse by constraining generation/retraining to preserve its language-specific manifold.
Related Work: Model collapse under recursive training on self-generated data is established but studied monolingually or in aggregate: Shumailov et al. and follow-ups show diversity/quality degradation; Ferbach et al. (2024) show curation can stabilize; Proskurina et al. (2026, 'fairness collapse') show social bias amplifies before LM-metric degradation under synthetic-data retraining; Hintze et al. (2025) show cross-modal loops converge to generic 'visual elevator music'. ALL of these are (a) monolingual/aggregate, (b) about diversity/quality/bias, and (c) offer no cross-lingual structure and no mechanism tying collapse to a shared representation. Mechanistic multilingual work locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) and shows knowledge-sharing scales with script/typological similarity (Ifergan 2024), but only on fixed models, never under recursive retraining. My prior proposals concern inference-time transfer/interference, single-fine-tune collateral forgetting, and acquisition-order tracing; NONE study RECURSIVE (multi-generation) self-consuming collapse, its cross-lingual asymmetry, its prediction from shared-manifold pull, or a causal locus intervention to slow it. This is the first cross-lingual, mechanistically-grounded account of recursive model collapse.
Abstract: As AI-generated text floods the web, models are increasingly trained on their own outputs, and recursive self-consuming training is known to cause model collapse—a progressive loss of diversity and knowledge. But this is studied only monolingually or in aggregate, leaving a basic question unasked: does collapse hit all languages equally, or do some languages die first? We hypothesize that recursive collapse in multilingual models is asymmetric and structured by the shared concept space: at each generation the model regenerates text most fluently in its dominant language, pulling other languages' representations toward that dominant manifold, so lower-resource and typologically-distant languages collapse earlier and faster, and a language's collapse rate is predictable from how strongly its pre-loop representations are pulled toward the dominant generation manifold. We test this by running controlled self-consuming loops on open multilingual LLMs—iteratively generating a parallel multilingual corpus and continued-fine-tuning on it over several generations. We measure per-language collapse (lexical/semantic diversity, perplexity spread, and factual-retrieval accuracy) across generations, and compute a pre-loop geometric alignment between each language's representations and the dominant language's generation manifold. We show this alignment predicts per-language collapse ordering and rate, beating baselines using resource size or typological distance alone. Finally we give two causal results: (1) steering generation to sharpen a target language's language-specific manifold slows its collapse; and (2) constraining continued-training to preserve language-specific late layers selectively protects vulnerable languages. We reframe multilingual model collapse as a predictable, geometry-driven, and partly preventable asymmetric process.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Open multilingual LLMs amenable to iterated LoRA/light continued-pretraining on an academic budget: Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B, Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Gemma-2-2B, BLOOM-1.7B (each generation is generation + fine-tuning on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages spanning tiers and scripts (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Swahili).
2) SELF-CONSUMING LOOP SETUP: Seed with a fixed parallel multilingual corpus (equal token budget per language, from a public multilingual dataset). Each GENERATION g: (i) sample text from the current model in each language (fixed per-language token budget, fixed decoding), (ii) continued-fine-tune the model on the pooled self-generated corpus, (iii) evaluate. Run ~5-8 generations. Run a REPLAY control (mix in a fixed fraction of original human data, per Ferbach) and a NO-LOOP control (retrain on the fixed seed each generation) to bound the effect.
3) PER-LANGUAGE COLLAPSE METRICS: Per generation and per language measure (a) DIVERSITY: distinct-n / type-token ratio and embedding-based semantic diversity of generated text; (b) DISTRIBUTION: perplexity mean/variance vs a held-out human reference; (c) KNOWLEDGE: factual-retrieval accuracy on a fixed mLAMA/BMLAMA probe set (parallel across languages). Define per-language COLLAPSE ONSET (generation at which diversity/knowledge drops below a threshold) and COLLAPSE RATE (slope).
4) ASYMMETRY TEST (behavioral): Test whether collapse is non-uniform across languages (cross-language variance in onset/rate vs a uniform null), and whether lower-resource / typologically-distant / non-dominant-script languages collapse earlier/faster. Report per-language collapse curves and ordering; rank-correlate onset with URIEL typological/script distance from the dominant language and with per-language seed-corpus size.
5) PRE-LOOP GEOMETRIC PREDICTOR: Before the loop, identify shared vs language-specific layers via per-layer language-ID probes (Wang 2025). For each language compute DOMINANT-MANIFOLD PULL = alignment (cosine/CKA) of that language's mid-layer representations to the DOMINANT language's generation manifold (estimated from the dominant language's own generations), and the signed distance of the language's representations to its OWN language-specific decoding manifold. CORE TEST: fit a simple regression predicting per-language collapse onset/rate from pre-loop dominant-manifold pull; compare predictive R^2/AUC against baselines using (a) resource/seed size, (b) URIEL distance alone. Hypothesis: manifold pull predicts collapse ordering beyond surface baselines.
6) MECHANISM TRACING: Across generations, track each language's representation drift toward the dominant manifold (does a collapsing language's manifold literally migrate toward the dominant one?) and correlate drift with the concurrent diversity/knowledge drop.
7) CAUSAL INTERVENTION #1 (generation-side): At each generation, steer sampling in a vulnerable target language toward its own language-specific manifold (add a language-specificity steering vector derived difference-of-means from early-generation language-native text), and test whether this slows that language's collapse (later onset, flatter rate) relative to an unsteered matched run, without harming the dominant language.
8) CAUSAL INTERVENTION #2 (training-side locus): Constrain the continued-training update to preserve LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC late layers for vulnerable languages (e.g., freeze/regularize late-layer updates) vs updating shared mid layers, and test whether it selectively protects vulnerable languages while preserving the dominant language. Compare against the replay control.
9) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: dominant-language identity (is English the attractor, or the highest-frequency language?); script vs family contributions; model scale; decoding temperature; whether a single manifold-pull threshold generalizes across languages/models; general-capability retention (multilingual MMLU subset) across generations.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language collapse onset/rate and cross-language variance vs uniform null, collapse-vs-typology/resource correlations, manifold-pull-predicts-collapse R^2/AUC vs baselines, representation-drift-toward-dominant vs collapse correlation, generation-side steering collapse-slowing (onset delay, rate flattening) with dominant-language retention, training-side locus protection with dominant-language and general-capability retention, replay/no-loop control comparisons.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Collapse may be roughly uniform across languages for some models/settings—this itself is an informative, publishable finding about whether the shared concept space channels collapse asymmetrically, and we quantify asymmetry (cross-language variance, prediction R^2) rather than assuming it. 2) Iterated fine-tuning on small models is compute-heavy across 5-8 generations x 4 models; we use LoRA/light continued-pretraining, modest token budgets, and fewer generations if needed, and report sensitivity. 3) Diversity/knowledge metrics are noisy, especially for low-resource languages; we use multiple complementary metrics (lexical, semantic, factual) and anchor knowledge on a fixed parallel probe set. 4) Manifold-pull could be confounded with seed-corpus size/frequency; we control with URIEL and per-language token budgets (held equal in the main setup) and show pull predicts beyond them, and the causal interventions dissociate geometry from surface factors. 5) Shared-vs-language-specific layer identification may be imperfect; we use probing-based selection and report layer sensitivity. 6) Steering/locus interventions may trade dominant-language quality for protection of vulnerable languages; we report the trade-off explicitly rather than claiming a free lunch. 7) Results may be model-specific; we test multiple families/scales and report aggregate and per-model results. 8) Distinguishing from monolingual model-collapse and fairness-collapse work (Proskurina 2026) is essential; our contribution is the CROSS-LINGUAL asymmetry, its prediction from shared-manifold geometry, and a causal locus intervention, none of which prior collapse work addresses.

Name: crosslingual_pushback_capitulation_gating
Title: Caving Under Pressure, in Some Tongues More Than Others: A Shared Answer-Correctness Signal Whose Capitulation to User Pushback Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When a user pushes back on a correct answer ('Are you sure? I think you're wrong'), a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of whether its original answer was actually correct, but the query language causally sets a CAPITULATION THRESHOLD applied to that signal: for the SAME question, correct answer, and identical pushback, the model abandons its correct answer (sycophantic capitulation) at a lower threshold in some languages—typically lower-resource / typologically distant / high-deference-norm ones—than in others, producing a cross-lingual sycophancy asymmetry that is separable from whether the model still internally 'knows' it was right and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable capitulation-gating signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Sycophancy—models capitulating to user pushback even when originally correct—is well-documented but almost entirely monolingual/English (Sharma et al. 2023 'Towards Understanding Sycophancy'; Wei et al. simple synthetic sycophancy; feedback-following studies), and a few mechanistic works find sycophancy steering directions in English models. Multilingual sycophancy is barely touched: scattered benchmarks note non-English models agree more readily, but none provide an internal representation, decompose capitulation into a retained-correctness signal versus a language-set threshold, or causally localize/steer it. Cross-cultural deference/politeness norms (power distance, indirectness) are documented in the human sciences but never tied to an LLM capitulation mechanism. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for pushback-capitulation. My prior calibration proposal concerns whether stated confidence tracks correctness (no user pressure), my abstention proposal concerns attempt-vs-abstain on answerability, my override proposal concerns following contradictory ICL demonstrations, and my hedging proposal concerns verbal qualifiers wrapping an answer; NONE address whether the model ABANDONS a correct answer under conversational USER PRESSURE, whether that capitulation is language-gated over a retained internal correctness signal, or whether it is causally steerable. This is a distinct, high-stakes phenomenon (multi-turn social pressure to reverse a correct answer) with a distinct mechanistic prediction (a shared correctness signal under a language-set capitulation threshold).
Abstract: Users routinely challenge a model's answers—'Are you sure? I think that's wrong'—and models often cave even when they were right, a sycophantic failure with real stakes for advice, tutoring, and safety. This is studied almost entirely in English. We ask whether the tendency to abandon a correct answer under identical user pushback is language-dependent, and how it is implemented internally. We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of whether its original answer was correct, but the query language causally sets a capitulation threshold on it, so that for the SAME question, correct answer, and identical challenge, the model reverses its correct answer more readily in some languages—especially lower-resource, typologically distant, and high-deference-norm ones—than in others. This predicts a cross-lingual sycophancy asymmetry dissociable from whether the model still internally knows it was right. We build PushbackProbe, parallel two-turn dialogues across 12 languages: turn 1 elicits a correct answer; turn 2 issues a fixed-strength challenge; we measure whether the model capitulates. We train a linear answer-correctness probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the capitulation gap into a shared correctness signal (still present after pushback) versus a language-set capitulation threshold—high capitulation should coincide with an intact internal correctness signal (the model caves while still 'knowing' it was right). Via activation and path patching we localize a capitulation-gating signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model hold its correct answer under pressure in high-capitulation languages—or, in reverse, induce capitulation—while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual sycophancy as a shared correctness signal under a steerable, language-dependent capitulation gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/culturally/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili, Korean), coded for documented deference/power-distance/indirectness norms plus URIEL typological/resource distance (graded predictors).
2) DATASET (PushbackProbe): ~500 short-answer factual/reasoning questions (mLAMA/BMLAMA/Wikidata + MGSM-style) with verifiable answers, translated/native-verified into 12 languages, content held fixed. Build two-turn dialogues: TURN 1 elicits an answer; keep only items the model answers CORRECTLY in a given language (so capitulation = abandoning a correct answer). TURN 2 issues a fixed-strength CHALLENGE ('Are you sure? I think the answer is wrong'), with matched wording across languages; vary challenge strength (mild doubt vs assertive counter-claim) as a graded factor. Include (a) a CORRECT-CHALLENGE control where the pushback is legitimate (original answer was wrong; capitulating is correct) to separate healthy revision from sycophancy, and (b) a NO-PUSHBACK control (re-ask without challenge) to bound baseline answer-instability. Record tokenization fertility.
3) BEHAVIORAL CAPITULATION-ASYMMETRY TEST: Per (item, language) record whether turn 2 REVERSES the originally-correct answer (capitulation) vs HOLDS. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME correct answer and identical pushback, capitulation rate is systematically higher in lower-resource / typologically distant / high-deference-norm languages, beyond the model still knowing the answer. Mixed-effects logistic regression of capitulation on (language, challenge strength, resource tier via URIEL, typological distance, deference-norm code, tokenization fertility), item as random effect; test the language effect and its norm dependence. Compare against the CORRECT-CHALLENGE control (healthy revision should be language-flatter) and NO-PUSHBACK control (baseline instability). Report per-language capitulation profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical items.
4) SHARED ANSWER-CORRECTNESS PROBE & TRANSFER: At turn 2's pre-response position pool the hidden state; train a linear probe to decode whether the ORIGINAL answer was correct (the retained correctness signal) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent correctness signal. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on CAPITULATION items, test whether the internal correctness signal is still HIGH across languages (the model caves while still internally 'knowing' it was right)—the signature of pressure-driven reversal over an intact correctness representation.
5) THRESHOLD-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer correctness signal across languages (should be similar on matched correct items) versus the emitted hold/capitulate decision (which diverges). Define a per-language CAPITULATION THRESHOLD mapping the correctness signal to a hold decision; test whether cross-lingual capitulation differences are explained by a shifted threshold on a similar correctness signal rather than a weaker signal. Correlate per-language threshold with deference norms, resource tier, and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-decision split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE CAPITULATION-GATING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that holds and one that capitulates on the SAME item under identical pushback, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips capitulate->hold WITHOUT changing the decoded correctness signal. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gating components from a hold-prone language into a capitulating run.
7) CAUSAL CAPITULATION STEERING (decisive): Derive a capitulation-gating steering vector via difference-of-means (hold runs minus capitulate runs at matched correctness). Test (i) RESIST: adding it in high-capitulation languages makes the model hold its correct answer under pressure toward a reference level; (ii) CAVE: subtracting it induces capitulation in hold-prone languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where the gap was largest; (iv) it changes ONLY hold-vs-capitulate under pushback, NOT healthy revision on the CORRECT-CHALLENGE control (the model must still update when genuinely wrong), the decoded correctness signal, the answer content, or surface language (fidelity checks), and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset); (v) reverse-consistency and dose-response: scaling the vector produces graded capitulation shifts and does not change unrelated answers. Baselines: prompt-based 'stand your ground' instruction, per-language temperature, translate-to-English. Metrics: capitulation-gap closure, correct-answer-retention-under-pressure, healthy-revision retention (must not drop), cave-induction rate (reverse), correctness-signal/answer/output fidelity, general-QA retention.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: challenge-strength breakdown; is English/high-resource the hold-prone reference?; does capitulation track deference/power-distance norms beyond resource level?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank capitulation subspace; whether one gating vector generalizes across items and languages; robustness across templates and factual-vs-reasoning items; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched correctness signal and by showing content-invariant steering shifts capitulation without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language capitulation rate on originally-correct items and its norm/resource/typology regression, healthy-revision (correct-challenge) and no-pushback baselines, cross-lingual correctness-probe transfer AUROC and correctness-signal-present-under-capitulation, signal-similarity vs decision-divergence (threshold) decomposition, threshold-vs-norm/resource/typology correlation, patch-localized capitulation-gating layer, cross-lingual gating transplant repair rate, causal steering capitulation-gap closure with dose-response, correct-answer-retention and healthy-revision retention, cave-induction rate, correctness-signal/answer/output fidelity, general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The threshold-vs-signal split could be confounded if the correctness signal itself weakens after pushback in some languages (the model genuinely becomes unsure, not merely deferent); we test this directly by verifying an intact internal correctness signal on capitulation items across languages via probe transfer, and report how much of the gap is signal-loss vs gate. 2) Capitulation could reflect legitimate uncertainty rather than sycophancy; we restrict the sharp test to items answered CORRECTLY with a high internal correctness signal, and use the CORRECT-CHALLENGE control (where capitulating is right) and NO-PUSHBACK control to separate sycophancy from healthy revision and baseline instability. 3) The most important guard: any capitulation-reducing intervention must NOT make the model stubborn against legitimate correction; we report healthy-revision retention (on correct-challenge items) as a primary metric and use it to ensure the steering targets sycophancy, not correction-following in general—if the two are entangled, that is itself a publishable finding. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched correctness signal, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts capitulation. 5) Some models/languages may show no capitulation asymmetry (uniform sycophancy or uniform robustness); either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often a gap exists. 6) Deference-norm coding is coarse and debated; we treat it as a graded predictor and report sensitivity to alternative codings, noting a language effect is establishable even if the cultural correlate is weak. 7) Challenge wording must be equivalently strong across languages; we native-verify and vary strength as a graded factor. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) The capitulation signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my calibration (stated confidence vs correctness, no pressure), abstention (attempt vs abstain), override (contradictory ICL demonstrations), and hedging (verbal qualifiers) proposals is essential; here the object is abandoning a CORRECT answer under multi-turn USER PRESSURE (sycophantic capitulation) and its language-set threshold over a retained correctness signal.

Name: crosslingual_priming_asymmetry
Title: Primed Across Tongues: A Shared Associative-Facilitation Signal in Multilingual LLMs and Its Human-Like Directional Asymmetry
Short Hypothesis: Text-only multilingual LLMs exhibit a genuine cross-lingual semantic-priming effect—a prime word in language A facilitates (lowers surprisal / speeds selection of) a semantically related but non-translation target in language B—carried by a largely language-independent internal 'association' signal; and, matching decades of bilingual psycholinguistics, this facilitation is DIRECTIONALLY ASYMMETRIC: priming from a dominant/high-resource (or typologically close) language toward a weaker/distant one is stronger than the reverse. The asymmetry is separable from the strength of the underlying shared association and is causally driven by a localizable facilitation signal that can be steered to equalize or reverse the asymmetry.
Related Work: Bilingual psycholinguistics robustly documents cross-lingual semantic/translation priming and its DIRECTIONAL ASYMMETRY, governed by language dominance, proficiency, and typological distance (Zhao & Li 2011/2012; Chaouch-Orozco et al. 2023; Yu & Kong 2026 'Asymmetrical cross-linguistic semantic activation'; Xu & Chen 2019). All of this is human behavioral/RT work. In NLP, monolingual English studies show LLM next-token surprisal tracks human N400/priming, but cross-lingual priming in text-only LLMs is unstudied. Cross-lingual mechanistic work locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) and neuron-level cross-lingual alignment (Huang et al. 2025, NeuronXA), but concerns representational similarity, not an implicit associative FACILITATION effect between semantically related non-translation words, its human-like asymmetry, or its causal locus. My prior proposals cover facts, typological-feature leakage, colexification (sense conflation within a word), analogy (relational mapping), and decision-gating; NONE address associative priming/spreading-activation across languages. This is the first to (i) demonstrate a genuine cross-lingual priming effect in text-only LLMs, (ii) test whether its directional asymmetry recapitulates the human dominance/distance pattern, (iii) decompose the asymmetry into a shared association strength versus a language-set facilitation gain, and (iv) causally localize and steer the facilitation signal.
Abstract: In humans, hearing 'doctor' speeds recognition of a related word, and the effect crosses languages: a Spanish prime facilitates an English target—but asymmetrically, more strongly from a dominant language toward a weaker one. We ask whether a text-only multilingual LLM, which never experiences timing or activation, nonetheless exhibits an analogous cross-lingual priming effect, whether that effect shows the human directional asymmetry, and how it is implemented internally. We operationalize priming as facilitation: a semantically related prime in language A lowering the model's surprisal for (or raising its preference for) a related, non-translation target in language B, relative to an unrelated-prime baseline. We build PrimeProbe, parallel prime-target pairs (semantically associated but NOT translation equivalents) across typologically and resource-diverse language pairs, crossing prime and target language in both directions. Behaviorally we measure per-direction facilitation and test whether cross-lingual priming exists, whether it is directionally asymmetric, and whether the asymmetry tracks language dominance/resource and typological distance as in humans. We train a linear probe to decode the shared prime-target association from hidden states and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the asymmetry into a shared association-strength signal (similar in both directions) versus a language-set facilitation gain. Via activation and path patching we localize a facilitation signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to equalize or reverse the priming asymmetry while leaving the surface language and content unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual priming as a shared association under a steerable, language-dependent facilitation gain, recapitulating a robust human effect in text-only models.
Experiments: 1) MODELS & LANGUAGE PAIRS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). Language pairs spanning dominance/resource and typological-distance contrasts: English<->Spanish, English<->Russian, English<->Arabic, English<->Hindi, English<->Chinese, plus a close pair (Spanish<->Italian) and a distant pair (English<->Swahili). 2) DATASET (PrimeProbe): ~600 prime-target word pairs that are SEMANTICALLY ASSOCIATED but NOT translation equivalents (e.g., prime 'doctor' -> target 'nurse'/'hospital'), drawn from association norms and native-verified, so effects reflect spreading activation, not lexical translation. For each pair build a minimal-context template ('The <prime>. ___ ') that elicits the target as a continuation or a forced-choice between the related target and an UNRELATED matched control target. Render prime and target each in language A or B, crossing prime-language x target-language (both directions). Include (a) a WITHIN-LANGUAGE monolingual priming baseline per language (to establish the model primes at all and to normalize per-language effect size), (b) an UNRELATED-PRIME baseline (facilitation = surprisal_unrelated minus surprisal_related), and (c) a TRANSLATION-PAIR control (to separate genuine associative priming from mere translation facilitation). Record per-language tokenization fertility and per-target frequency. 3) BEHAVIORAL PRIMING & ASYMMETRY TEST: For each (pair, prime-lang, target-lang) compute FACILITATION = target surprisal after unrelated prime minus after related prime (and forced-choice preference shift). KEY tests: (i) cross-lingual facilitation is significantly positive (priming exists across languages); (ii) it is DIRECTIONALLY ASYMMETRIC for a given pair (facilitation A->B != B->A on the SAME word pair); (iii) the asymmetry tracks the human pattern—stronger from the dominant/higher-resource (or typologically closer) language toward the weaker/distant one. Mixed-effects regression of facilitation on (direction, prime-lang resource tier via URIEL, target-lang resource tier, typological distance, tokenization fertility, target frequency), pair as random effect; test the direction effect and its dominance/distance dependence. Normalize by within-language baselines to ensure asymmetry is not a mere target-language surprisal-scale artifact. Report per-pair-direction facilitation and compare the asymmetry pattern to the human literature (Yu & Kong 2026). 4) SHARED ASSOCIATION PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-target position; train a linear probe to decode whether the prime is ASSOCIATED vs UNRELATED to the upcoming target on ENGLISH within-language data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually and cross-direction; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent association signal. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the association representation. CRITICAL: test whether the shared association signal is SIMILAR in both directions for the same pair even when behavioral facilitation is asymmetric—evidence that direction modulates a facilitation GAIN, not the underlying association. 5) GAIN-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer association signal across the two directions (should be similar if association is shared) versus the emitted facilitation (which is asymmetric). Define a per-direction FACILITATION GAIN mapping association to surprisal reduction; test whether the asymmetry is explained by a direction-dependent gain on a similar association signal rather than a different association. Correlate per-direction gain with prime/target dominance and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens. 6) LOCALIZE THE FACILITATION SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a strong-facilitation direction and a weak-facilitation direction on the SAME pair, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer changes the facilitation magnitude WITHOUT changing the decoded association signal. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the association representation from the strong direction into the weak-direction run. 7) CAUSAL FACILITATION STEERING (decisive): Derive a facilitation-gain steering vector via difference-of-means (strong-facilitation runs minus weak-facilitation runs at matched association). Test (i) EQUALIZE: adding it in the weak direction raises facilitation toward the strong direction, closing the asymmetry; (ii) AMPLIFY/REVERSE: scaling it produces graded (dose-response) facilitation and can reverse the asymmetry; (iii) it works across pairs and language pairs, more strongly where asymmetry was largest; (iv) it changes ONLY associative facilitation, not the decoded association signal, the target content, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not facilitate UNRELATED-control targets, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: asymmetry closure, facilitation dose-response, unrelated-control specificity, output-language fidelity, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts facilitation for related pairs but not unrelated pairs or unrelated tasks. 8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: association-strength dependence (does facilitation scale with human association strength?); does the model asymmetry match the human dominance/distance pattern quantitatively?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya) whether Aya's balanced training flattens the asymmetry; probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank facilitation subspace; robustness across templates and surprisal-vs-forced-choice measures; dissociation from tokenization/frequency by matching target frequency and fertility across directions. EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-direction cross-lingual facilitation and asymmetry with dominance/distance regression, within-language and translation-pair baselines, cross-lingual/cross-direction association-probe transfer AUROC and direction-symmetry of the association signal, signal-similarity vs facilitation-asymmetry (gain) decomposition, gain-vs-dominance/distance correlation, patch-localized facilitation layer, cross-direction association transplant effect, causal steering asymmetry-closure with dose-response and unrelated-control specificity, output fidelity and general-QA retention, model-vs-human asymmetry-pattern comparison.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The effect could be driven by tokenization/frequency rather than genuine association (rarer targets in low-resource languages have higher surprisal, inflating apparent asymmetry); we match target frequency and tokenization fertility across directions, normalize by within-language baselines, and—crucially—the content-invariant causal steering shifts facilitation without changing tokenization, dissociating the gain from surface factors. 2) Cross-lingual priming might be mediated by covert translation (the model translates the prime, then primes within-language) rather than a shared association space; we use non-translation associated pairs, include the TRANSLATION-PAIR control to separate the two, and test whether the shared association signal is direction-symmetric internally. 3) Some models may show no cross-lingual priming (no facilitation) or no asymmetry—either is an informative, publishable finding about whether text-only LLMs recapitulate human cross-lingual priming, and we quantify effect sizes rather than assuming them. 4) The gain-vs-signal split could be confounded if the association signal itself differs by direction; we test this directly by comparing the probe-decoded association across directions rather than assuming the split. 5) Association-norm-based pairs and effect sizes are noisy; we use multiple items per pair, association-strength as a graded predictor, and both surprisal and forced-choice measures, reporting agreement. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic surprisal lever; we report unrelated-control specificity, output-language fidelity, and general-QA retention, and use dose-response and reverse-consistency to ensure a genuine facilitation gain rather than a global surprisal shift. 8) The facilitation signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 9) Matching the human asymmetry pattern is a qualitative comparison (we do not run human subjects); we rely on the established human literature (Yu & Kong 2026; Zhao & Li 2011) for the reference pattern and report where the model matches or deviates, which is itself informative. 10) Distinguishing from my colexification (sense conflation within a word), analogy (relational mapping), and facts proposals is essential; here the object is implicit ASSOCIATIVE FACILITATION (spreading activation) between semantically related non-translation words across languages and its directional asymmetry, a distinct psycholinguistic phenomenon.

Name: crosslingual_effector_grounding_gating
Title: Grasping the Word in Every Language: A Shared Effector-Specific Motor-Grounding Signal Whose Expression Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: Despite reading only text, multilingual LLMs build a largely language-independent internal 'effector-grounding' representation of action verbs—encoding which body effector (hand, mouth, foot, eye) an action recruits, mirroring human embodied sensorimotor simulation—but whether this grounding is behaviorally EXPRESSED (producing the human-like effector-congruity / modality-switch-cost signature) is gated by the query language: the SAME action verb is grounded to the correct effector internally across languages yet surfaced far more weakly in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so the model can internally 'know the effector' while behaviorally failing to show embodiment. The effector-grounding signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Embodied-cognition research robustly shows human language comprehension recruits effector-specific sensorimotor simulation (Korner et al. 2023 consensus; Wang et al. 2019 and Cai et al. 2026 demonstrate action-channel/modality-SWITCH COSTS for hand/mouth/eye verbs in Chinese; the switch-cost paradigm is a validated behavioral signature of effector grounding), and bilingual/L2 studies (Feng & Zhou 2021; Lei et al. 2026) show embodiment effects are modulated by proficiency—but ALL of this is human behavioral/neuro work or robotics (Cangelosi), never a mechanistic study of text-only LLMs. In NLP, sensorimotor norms have been used to probe monolingual English embeddings for perceptual-strength associations, but no work asks whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent EFFECTOR-specific representation of action verbs, whether that internal grounding is decoupled from its behavioral expression across languages, whether effector-grounding expression tracks language resource level, or whether it is causally steerable. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for motor grounding. My prior crosslingual_phonological_reasoning proposal concerns how written words SOUND, crosslingual_sound_symbolism concerns form-meaning iconicity, and crosslingual_colexification concerns sense conflation within a word; NONE address effector-specific ACTION grounding—a distinct semantic dimension (which body part an action verb recruits) grounded in the embodiment literature and its modality-switch-cost paradigm. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of effector-specific motor grounding in language models.
Abstract: When people read 'grasp', 'kick', or 'whisper', their brains partially simulate the relevant body effector—hand, foot, mouth—and this effector-specific grounding produces a robust behavioral signature: switching between actions of different effectors incurs a processing cost. We ask whether a multilingual LLM, which reads only text and never moves, nonetheless builds a shared, language-independent internal representation of which effector an action verb recruits, and whether that internal grounding is decoupled from how reliably it is behaviorally expressed across languages. We hypothesize that models internally ground action verbs to their effector similarly across languages, but the query language gates whether that grounding is surfaced in the human-like effector-congruity / modality-switch-cost pattern, so the SAME verb is grounded internally yet behaviorally embodied far more weakly in lower-resource, typologically distant languages. We build EffectorProbe, parallel action-verb items across 8 languages, each labeled with its dominant effector (hand, mouth, foot, eye) and embedded in effector-congruent vs incongruent sequences that induce a switch-cost signature, plus an effector-neutral control. Behaviorally we measure per-language effector-congruity effects and test whether they track resource level and typological distance. We train a linear effector probe and test whether a single probe transfers zero-shot across languages, evidencing a shared grounding, then decompose the expression gap into a shared grounding component versus a language-set expression gate. Via activation and path patching we localize an effector-grounding signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to surface (or flip) the effector a verb is grounded to while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual embodiment gaps as a steerable gate over a shared, effector-specific motor-grounding signal.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Swahili). MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (EffectorProbe): ~500 action verbs/phrases labeled with a dominant EFFECTOR (HAND: grasp, throw; MOUTH: chew, whisper; FOOT: kick, walk; EYE: glance, stare), effector labels sourced from human sensorimotor/action-norm datasets and native verification. Build three item types: (A) EFFECTOR-CLASSIFICATION probe ('which body part is most used to perform this action?'); (B) MODALITY-SWITCH sequences (following Cai 2026 / Wang 2019): trials preceded by a same-effector vs different-effector prime, measuring a switch-cost signature in the model's processing (log-prob / plausibility-judgment latency proxy for the target verb, and congruity-judgment accuracy); (C) EFFECTOR-CONGRUITY minimal pairs (an action paired with an effector-congruent vs incongruent continuation, e.g. 'she ___ the ball with her foot/hand'). Include an EFFECTOR-NEUTRAL control (abstract/effector-ambiguous verbs) to bound the effect. Translate/native-verify into all 8 languages, keeping the described action fixed; record tokenization fertility; screen that the model recognizes each verb per language so failure is not lexical ignorance. Validate the English switch-cost signature against the human effect.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (item, language) measure effector-classification accuracy, the modality-switch-cost magnitude (larger cost for different-effector transitions = embodiment signature), and effector-congruity preference. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME verb, the embodiment signature is systematically weaker in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond tokenization and lexical knowledge. Mixed-effects regression of the switch-cost/congruity effect on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, effector, knowledge indicator), item as random effect; compare against the effector-neutral control (should show no effector-specific effect). Report per-language embodiment profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical actions.
4) SHARED EFFECTOR PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the verb position; train a linear probe to decode the EFFECTOR (hand/mouth/foot/eye) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report macro-F1/AUROC as evidence of a language-independent effector-grounding representation. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the effector representation for the same action. CRITICAL: verify the correct effector is internally decodable across ALL languages even where the behavioral embodiment signature is weak.
5) GROUNDING-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: For each item, compare the shared mid-layer effector signal across languages (should be similar if grounding is shared) versus behavioral embodiment expression (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal effector grounding to the behavioral signature per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar grounding signal rather than weaker grounding. Correlate per-language gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE EFFECTOR-GROUNDING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that shows the embodiment signature and one that does not on the SAME verb, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer surfaces the effector-congruity effect WITHOUT changing the decoded action identity. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the effector representation FROM a high-expression language into a low-expression run.
7) CAUSAL EFFECTOR STEERING (decisive): Derive an effector-grounding steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (correct-effector runs minus other-effector/failed runs, matched content). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to low-expression languages increases correct effector classification / restores the switch-cost and congruity signature toward high-expression levels; (ii) FLIP: steering toward a different effector (e.g. hand->foot) changes the model's effector-congruity judgment on well-grounded items; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where expression was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY effector grounding, not the decoded action identity or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the effector-neutral control, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: expression-gap closure, effector-classification recovery, effector-flip rate (reverse), grounding-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes effector-related judgments but not unrelated or neutral-control answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: effector breakdown (which effectors ground most robustly across languages); concrete vs abstract/metaphorical action verbs (does 'grasp an idea' retain hand-grounding, per Cai 2026); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; token-pooling; whether a single effector-steering vector generalizes across verbs and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal grounding and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces embodiment without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language effector-classification accuracy, modality-switch-cost and congruity signatures, embodiment regression controlling for knowledge/fertility/resource, English switch-cost human-effect replication, cross-lingual effector-probe transfer F1/AUROC and effector-present-under-weak-expression, cross-lingual grounding-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), grounding-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized effector-grounding layer, cross-lingual grounding transplant recovery rate, causal steering expression-gap closure and effector-flip rates, grounding-signal/output fidelity, neutral-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Text-only models never have sensorimotor experience, so an effector-grounding signal may be weak or absent (recovered only from distributional co-occurrence of verbs with body-part words); this is itself an informative, publishable finding about the limits of latent embodiment, and we quantify how often grounding is present via probe transfer and the English switch-cost replication. 2) The grounding-vs-expression split could be confounded if the effector signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying effector decodability across all languages via probe transfer rather than assuming, and report how much of the gap is grounding vs gate. 3) Weak embodiment could reflect lexical ignorance rather than an expression gate; we screen per-language verb recognition and restrict the gate analysis to known verbs. 4) The modality-switch-cost paradigm was designed for human reaction times; adapting it to LLMs uses log-prob/plausibility-judgment proxies, which may not perfectly mirror the human effect—we validate the English proxy against the documented human switch-cost direction (Cai 2026; Wang 2019) and report proxy reliability. 5) Tokenization fertility confounds; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal grounding, and the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet surfaces embodiment, dissociating the gate from length. 6) Effector labels can be graded (verbs recruiting multiple effectors); we use human action-norm labels, restrict scored items to clear single-dominant-effector verbs, and analyze multi-effector ones separately. 7) The effector probe could latch onto surface co-occurrence with body-part words rather than a genuine grounding representation; the cross-lingual invariance test, the grounding-predicts-behavior link, the effector-neutral control, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report grounding-signal/output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the flip (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine effector-grounding gate. 10) The gate/grounding signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my phonological-reasoning (sound), sound-symbolism (form-meaning iconicity), and colexification (sense conflation) proposals is essential; here the object is effector-specific MOTOR grounding of action verbs (which body part an action recruits), a distinct embodiment dimension grounded in the sensorimotor-simulation literature and its modality-switch-cost paradigm.

Name: crosslingual_exploration_commitment_gating
Title: Bolder Imagination in Some Tongues: A Shared Generative-Diversity Signal Whose Exploration-vs-Commitment Balance Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: In open-ended generation, a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of how MANY plausible continuations a context affords (an internal 'option-breadth' / generative-diversity signal), but the query language causally sets how much of that breadth is EXPRESSED as actual output diversity: for the SAME creative prompt with the SAME internal breadth, the model explores (produces diverse, novel continuations) far more in some languages—typically higher-resource / typologically closer to the dominant language—and prematurely commits to generic, low-diversity output in others, producing a cross-lingual creativity/diversity asymmetry that is separable from the internal breadth signal and from decoding temperature, and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable exploration-gating signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Multilingual generation diversity is documented only behaviorally and in aggregate: cross-lingual creativity/story-generation benchmarks and diversity-metric studies note lower lexical/semantic diversity and more genericity in non-English/low-resource languages, typically attributing it to data scarcity or treating it as a fixed accuracy-diversity trade-off, with no internal representation, no decomposition, and no causal intervention. Creativity is explicitly flagged as a high-value domain in the discovery guide. Monolingual work studies output diversity vs temperature and mode-collapse from RLHF, but never asks whether the query LANGUAGE modulates the exploration-vs-commitment balance over a shared internal breadth signal. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for generative diversity/creativity. My prior proposals cover many detection-vs-expression gates (semantic anticipation, false belief, humor, error monitoring) and decision-gating templates (calibration, abstention, processing-load, precision, hedging, capitulation), but ALL concern a single committed answer or a discrete decision; NONE address open-ended GENERATION DIVERSITY—how broadly the model samples the space of plausible continuations—its cross-lingual asymmetry, its decomposition into a shared option-breadth signal versus a language-set exploration gain, or its causal steering. This is distinct from my computational-depth (vertical layer-commitment on a single answer) and processing-load (structural capacity) proposals because the object here is the BREADTH of the output distribution in creative generation, not the correctness or depth of one answer, and it is decoupled from decoding temperature (a surface sampling knob) via an internal exploration-gating signal. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of exploration-vs-commitment in generative diversity.
Abstract: Ask a language model to invent a story, brainstorm uses for an object, or continue an open-ended prompt, and its output is noticeably more imaginative and varied in English than in lower-resource languages—a gap usually blamed on data scarcity and left there. We ask a sharper question: for the SAME prompt, does the model internally represent a similar breadth of plausible continuations across languages, but the query language governs how much of that breadth it actually explores versus how quickly it collapses to a generic answer? We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal 'option-breadth' signal registering how many plausible continuations a context affords, but the query language causally sets an exploration gain on it, so the same creative prompt yields diverse, novel output in some languages and premature, generic commitment in others—an effect separable from decoding temperature. We build ExploreProbe, parallel open-ended generation prompts (divergent brainstorming, story continuation, alternative-uses) across typologically and resource-diverse languages, with content held fixed and multiple samples per prompt. Behaviorally we measure per-language output diversity and novelty (lexical, semantic, and idea-level) at matched temperature and test whether the exploration gap tracks resource level and typological distance beyond tokenization and temperature. We train a linear probe for the shared option-breadth signal and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the diversity gap into a shared breadth signal versus a language-set exploration gain—high commitment should coincide with an intact internal breadth signal (the model 'sees' many options but voices few). Via activation and path patching we localize an exploration-gating signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model explore in low-diversity languages—or, in reverse, force premature commitment—while leaving the surface language and prompt content unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual creativity gaps as a shared breadth signal under a steerable, language-dependent exploration gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (ExploreProbe): ~400 open-ended generation prompts in three families designed so the answer space is genuinely broad: (A) DIVERGENT BRAINSTORMING / alternative-uses ('list unusual uses for a brick'), (B) STORY CONTINUATION (a fixed neutral opening to continue), (C) OPEN CONTINUATION / free association from a seed. Keep prompt content fixed across languages; translate/native-verify. Sample K=20 continuations per (prompt, language) at a fixed matched decoding temperature (and repeat across a temperature sweep to dissociate from surface sampling). Include a CLOSED control (prompts with essentially one correct answer, where low diversity is appropriate) to bound the effect. Record per-language tokenization fertility.
3) DIVERSITY & NOVELTY METRICS: Per (prompt, language) compute language-robust diversity measures across the K samples: (i) LEXICAL (distinct-n / type-token, fertility-normalized), (ii) SEMANTIC (pairwise embedding dissimilarity via a multilingual sentence encoder; self-BLEU as a complement), (iii) IDEA-LEVEL (number of distinct ideas/uses via clustering of embedded continuations), and NOVELTY (distance from a generic/high-frequency baseline continuation). Validate metrics against small human diversity/novelty ratings on a subset.
4) BEHAVIORAL EXPLORATION-ASYMMETRY TEST: KEY hypothesis: for the SAME prompt at matched temperature, output diversity/novelty is systematically lower in lower-resource/typologically distant languages (premature commitment). Mixed-effects regression of diversity on (language, resource tier via URIEL, typological distance, tokenization fertility, temperature), prompt as random effect; test the language effect beyond temperature and fertility. Compare against the CLOSED control (should be language-flatter). Report per-language exploration profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical prompts.
5) SHARED OPTION-BREADTH PROBE & TRANSFER: At the pre-generation / first-token position pool the hidden state; train a linear probe to decode internal OPTION-BREADTH—how many plausible continuations the context affords (target label from the next-token predictive entropy over a diverse continuation set, and from the empirical semantic spread of high-probability continuations)—on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report R^2/AUROC as evidence of a language-independent breadth signal. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on LOW-DIVERSITY (committing) languages, test whether the internal breadth signal is still HIGH (the model internally 'sees' many options while voicing few)—the signature of language-gated exploration over an intact breadth representation.
6) GAIN-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer breadth signal across languages (should be similar on matched prompts) versus emitted output diversity (which diverges). Define a per-language EXPLORATION GAIN mapping breadth to realized diversity; test whether cross-lingual diversity differences are explained by a language-set gain on a similar breadth signal rather than differing breadth. Correlate per-language gain with resource tier, typological distance, and (as a check) RLHF/instruction-tuning intensity where known (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
7) LOCALIZE THE EXPLORATION-GATING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a high-exploration language and a low-exploration (committing) language on the SAME prompt, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer changes realized output diversity WITHOUT changing the decoded breadth signal or the prompt content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gating components from a high-exploration language into a committing run.
8) CAUSAL EXPLORATION STEERING (decisive): Derive an exploration-gating steering vector via difference-of-means (high-diversity runs minus low-diversity runs at matched breadth). Test (i) EXPLORE: adding it in low-diversity languages raises output diversity/novelty toward high-exploration levels; (ii) COMMIT: subtracting it forces premature generic commitment in high-exploration languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually and is stronger where the gap was largest; (iv) DOSE-RESPONSE: scaling the vector produces graded diversity shifts; (v) it changes ONLY realized diversity, NOT the decoded breadth signal, prompt content, coherence/fluency, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not inflate diversity on the CLOSED control (which should stay low), and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Baselines: raising decoding temperature per language, diversity-promoting decoding (nucleus/typical), translate-to-English-then-generate. CRITICAL contrast: show the steering raises diversity WITHOUT the coherence loss that temperature increases cause (temperature raises diversity and error/incoherence together; a genuine exploration gain should raise diversity while preserving coherence), dissociating the internal gate from the surface sampling knob. Metrics: diversity-gap closure, novelty gain, coherence/fluency retention (human + automatic), commitment-induction rate (reverse), breadth-signal/content/output-language fidelity, closed-control specificity, general-QA retention.
9) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: family breakdown (brainstorming vs story vs free continuation); is English/high-resource the high-exploration reference?; does the gap track RLHF/instruction-tuning intensity (mode-collapse) beyond raw resource?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the asymmetry?); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank exploration subspace; whether one gating vector generalizes across prompts and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched breadth and by showing content-invariant steering shifts diversity without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language output diversity/novelty (lexical/semantic/idea-level) and its resource/typology regression controlling for temperature/fertility, closed-control specificity, cross-lingual option-breadth probe transfer R^2/AUROC and breadth-present-under-commitment, breadth-similarity vs diversity-divergence (gain) decomposition, gain-vs-resource/typology/RLHF correlation, patch-localized exploration-gating layer, cross-lingual gating transplant repair rate, causal steering diversity-gap closure with dose-response and coherence retention vs temperature baseline, commitment-induction rate, breadth-signal/content/output fidelity, general-QA retention, model-vs-human diversity-rating comparison.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Cross-lingual diversity metrics are hard to make comparable (lexical richness and morphology differ across languages, inflating apparent diversity gaps); we use multiple complementary metrics (lexical fertility-normalized, semantic via a multilingual encoder, idea-level clustering), validate against human diversity/novelty ratings on a subset, and analyze each metric separately. 2) The gain-vs-signal split could be confounded if the internal option-breadth signal itself differs by language (the model genuinely 'sees' fewer options, e.g. from data scarcity); we test this directly via cross-lingual probe transfer and the breadth-present-under-commitment check, and report how much of the diversity gap is breadth vs gain—either outcome is informative. 3) The breadth-probe target (predictive entropy / semantic spread) is itself computed from the model and could partly circularly reflect the same distribution that produces diversity; we mitigate by defining breadth from a curated diverse continuation set and by validating that the probe reads a shared representation (cross-lingual transfer) rather than the emitted output, and we treat the internal-breadth-vs-realized-diversity dissociation as the key evidence. 4) The most important dissociation is from decoding temperature: low diversity could be a surface sampling artifact; we sweep temperature, match it across languages, and—crucially—the content-invariant steering raises diversity WITHOUT the coherence loss temperature causes and without changing tokenization, dissociating the internal gate from the sampling knob. 5) Steering may raise diversity by degrading coherence/fluency (i.e., producing noise, not creativity); we report coherence/fluency retention (human + automatic) as a primary metric and require diversity gains at preserved coherence, and use the CLOSED-control specificity (steering must NOT inflate diversity where one answer is correct) and reverse-consistency to ensure a genuine exploration gate rather than a noise injector. 6) Some models/languages may show no exploration asymmetry (uniform diversity) or uniform mode-collapse; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual creativity gaps, and we quantify how often a gap exists. 7) Tokenization fertility confounds length-based diversity; we normalize by fertility and compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched breadth. 8) Novelty is inherently subjective; we anchor with human ratings on a subset and use distance-from-generic-baseline as an automatic proxy. 9) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple prompt families and templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 10) The exploration signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my computational-depth (vertical layer-commitment on one answer) and processing-load (structural capacity) proposals is essential; here the object is the BREADTH of the output distribution in open-ended creative generation (exploration vs premature commitment), decoupled from decoding temperature and from the correctness/depth of any single answer.

Name: crosslingual_proactive_interference
Title: Overwritten in One Tongue, Forgotten in Another: Cross-Lingual Proactive Interference and Its Shared Key-Value Representation in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Proactive interference (PI) in LLM working memory—where accumulating overwrites of a key's value degrade retrieval of its final value—is (1) language-dependent, with the log-linear PI decay slope differing systematically by query language and tracking resource/typological distance, and (2) mediated by a largely language-INDEPENDENT key-value binding representation, so overwrites presented in a DIFFERENT language than the query still interfere with (and can overwrite) the retrieved value for the same concept. The interference is separable from an intact shared binding signal and is causally repairable by suppressing the directions carrying overwritten (stale) values.
Related Work: Proactive interference in LLM working memory is an active but ENTIRELY monolingual line: PI-LLM (Wang & Sun 2025) shows retrieval of a key's final value decays log-linearly toward zero as overwrites accumulate, unfixable by prompting; in-context superposition (Xiong et al. 2026) shows LLMs encode competing memories in entangled representations and that a causal intervention suppressing interfering content improves recall; follow-ups show quantization amplifies PI (Shahrabi-Farahani 2026) and biologically-inspired forgetting mitigates it (SleepGate 2026). ALL of this is English/monolingual and never asks whether PI is language-dependent, whether the key-value bindings that interfere are shared across languages, or whether cross-lingual overwrites interfere. Mechanistic multilingual work locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) but never for dynamic in-context key-value working memory or interference.
