My prior 'running-state tracking' proposal concerns maintaining a numeric TALLY under number/classifier typology; PI is a distinct phenomenon (interference from OVERWRITTEN prior values of a key, a validated working-memory bottleneck), and no prior work of mine or others studies its cross-lingual structure, shared key-value representation, or causal repair. This is the first cross-lingual, mechanistic, causal account of proactive interference.
Abstract: Large language models suffer proactive interference: when a key's value is repeatedly overwritten in context and only the final value is queried, retrieval accuracy decays log-linearly as prior (stale) values accumulate—a working-memory bottleneck mirroring human cognition, robust across context lengths and resistant to prompting. This entire literature is monolingual. We ask whether proactive interference is language-dependent, and whether the key-value bindings that interfere live in a shared cross-lingual representation. We hypothesize that the PI decay slope differs systematically by query language and tracks resource/typological distance, and—more strikingly—that key-value bindings are largely language-independent, so a value written in one language interferes with, and can overwrite, retrieval of the same concept's value queried in another language. Adapting the PI-LLM paradigm cross-lingually, we stream semantically-related key-value updates (in a single language, or MIXED across languages) and query only the final value. Behaviorally we measure per-language PI slopes and cross-lingual overwriting rates. We train a linear probe to decode the currently-bound value from hidden states and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, showing the binding is shared; we then test whether intrusion errors correspond to stale-value directions that remain internally active. Via activation and path patching we localize the interference, and in a decisive causal test we suppress the directions carrying overwritten values and show it restores retrieval—closing the cross-lingual PI gap—while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual working-memory failure as interference over a shared, steerable key-value representation.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (XPI-LLM): Adapt the validated PI-LLM paradigm. A context streams key-value updates where a key (a concept, e.g. 'the meeting room') is assigned a value, then repeatedly OVERWRITTEN with new values; only the FINAL value is queried. Control the INTERFERENCE DEPTH (number of prior overwrites, 0..N). Build three conditions: (A) MONOLINGUAL: all updates and the query in one language, parallel across the 10 languages (same concepts/values, native-verified); (B) CROSS-LINGUAL OVERWRITE (key novel condition): the final (correct) value is written in language L, while some PRIOR (stale) overwrites of the same key are written in a DIFFERENT language L' (values are semantically-matched, non-identical), testing whether cross-language stale values still interfere; (C) NUMERIC CONTROL (from PI-LLM/Shahrabi-Farahani): numeric keys/values where interference is known to be weaker, to bound the semantic effect. Keep values short and single-token-decodable; record per-language tokenization fertility.
3) BEHAVIORAL PI-SLOPE TEST: Per language, plot final-value retrieval accuracy vs interference depth and fit the log-linear PI decay; extract a per-language PI SLOPE. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME task, PI slopes are steeper (faster forgetting) in lower-resource/typologically distant languages. Mixed-effects logistic regression of retrieval-error on (interference depth, language, tokenization fertility, resource tier via URIEL), item as random effect; test the depth x language interaction. Report per-language PI curves and cross-lingual disagreement; replicate the monolingual English log-linear decay as a sanity check.
4) INTRUSION-ERROR ANALYSIS: On errors, measure whether the model retrieves a PREVIOUSLY-OVERWRITTEN (stale) value (same-key intrusion) vs an unrelated value, per language, as in PI-LLM. Test whether stale-value intrusions dominate and whether their rate tracks the PI slope.
5) CROSS-LINGUAL OVERWRITING TEST (decisive behavioral): In condition B, measure whether stale values written in a DIFFERENT language than the query still interfere with (lower accuracy on / intrude for) the final value. KEY hypothesis: cross-language stale overwrites interfere substantially (interference is concept-level, not surface-string-level), and interference strength scales with the semantic relatedness of keys and DECREASES with typological/script distance between the overwrite language and query language (evidence of a partly-shared but distance-modulated key-value store). Mixed-effects regression of interference on (overwrite-language == query-language, typological distance between them, interference depth), item random effect.
6) SHARED KEY-VALUE PROBE & TRANSFER: At the pre-answer position pool the hidden state; train a linear probe to decode the CURRENTLY-BOUND (correct final) value for the queried key on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report accuracy as evidence of a language-independent key-value binding. Measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the binding representation. CRITICAL: on intrusion errors, probe whether the STALE (overwritten) value's direction is still strongly active (co-represented) alongside the correct value—the in-context-superposition signature (Xiong et al.) shown here to be cross-lingual.
7) LOCALIZE THE INTERFERENCE: Via activation and path patching between a low-interference run (correct retrieval) and a high-interference run (intrusion) on the SAME key, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the components whose transfer flips intrusion->correct. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs path patching. Attention analysis: does the query over-attend to stale-value tokens, more so in high-PI languages?
8) CAUSAL STALE-VALUE SUPPRESSION (decisive): Derive a stale-value-suppression steering vector via difference-of-means (correct-retrieval runs minus stale-intrusion runs), or directly project out the direction carrying the overwritten value (identified from the probe). Test (i) REPAIR: suppressing stale-value directions restores final-value retrieval under high interference, flattening the PI slope, more so in high-PI languages—closing the cross-lingual PI gap toward a reference; (ii) it works cross-lingually and in the cross-lingual-overwrite condition; (iii) REVERSE: amplifying the stale-value direction induces more intrusions; (iv) it changes ONLY which value is retrieved, not the surface language or general QA (fidelity/retention). Compare against prompting-to-ignore (shown ineffective by PI-LLM) and translate-to-English baselines. Metrics: PI-slope flattening, cross-lingual PI-gap closure, intrusion-rate reduction, output-language fidelity, general-QA (multilingual MMLU subset) retention. Reverse-consistency: suppression restores the correct value but does not corrupt low-interference or unrelated retrievals.
9) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: numeric vs semantic keys (PI should be weaker for numeric, per PI-LLM); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten PI asymmetry?); probe layer/dimensionality; interference depth range; whether a single suppression vector generalizes across keys and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched interference depth and by showing content-invariant suppression restores retrieval without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language PI decay slopes and cross-lingual PI-gap, PI-slope regression controlling for fertility/resource, stale-value intrusion rates, cross-lingual-overwrite interference and its distance dependence, cross-lingual key-value probe transfer accuracy and stale-value co-activation (superposition) evidence, patch-localized interference layer and attention-to-stale-value evidence, causal suppression PI-slope flattening / PI-gap closure and intrusion reduction (and reverse amplification), output-language fidelity and general-QA retention, comparison to prompt-to-ignore and translate-to-English baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Some models may show similar PI slopes across languages (no asymmetry); this is itself an informative, publishable finding about whether PI is a language-invariant working-memory constraint, and we quantify slope variance rather than assuming it. 2) Tokenization fertility confounds interference depth and retrieval (multi-token values are harder); we control for fertility in regression, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched interference depth, and—crucially—the content-invariant causal suppression restores retrieval without changing tokenization, dissociating the effect from length. 3) The cross-lingual-overwrite condition requires semantically-matched non-identical values across languages; we native-verify and use the numeric control to separate concept-level interference from surface-string collisions, and interpret the distance-modulation carefully. 4) The shared-key-value probe could latch onto surface value tokens rather than a genuine binding; the cross-lingual transfer, the stale-value co-activation (superposition) test, and the causal suppression guard against this. 5) Suppressing stale-value directions may harm low-interference or unrelated retrievals or fluency; we report reverse-consistency (must not corrupt correct low-interference retrievals), output-language fidelity, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the reverse (amplification->more intrusion) test to confirm the direction's causal role. 6) Patching/probing results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching plus attention analysis. 7) The stale-value signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 8) Prompting-to-ignore is a known-weak baseline (PI-LLM); we include it and translate-to-English to position our causal, representation-level repair as complementary. 9) Distinguishing from monolingual PI work (Wang & Sun 2025; Xiong et al. 2026) and from my running-state-tracking proposal is essential; our contribution is the cross-lingual structure of PI, the shared/ distance-modulated key-value store, cross-lingual overwriting, and the causal stale-value suppression across languages, none of which prior work addresses.

Name: crosslingual_tool_invocation_gating
Title: Reach for the Tool, or Just Answer? A Shared Tool-Need Estimate Gated by a Language-Dependent Invocation Threshold in Multilingual Agents
Short Hypothesis: When acting as a tool-using agent, a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal 'tool-need' estimate (whether a query requires an external tool vs. can be answered from parametric memory), but the query language causally sets an INVOCATION THRESHOLD applied to that estimate: for the SAME task the model calls a tool at a lower threshold in some languages and over-relies on its (often stale/unreliable) parametric memory in others (typically lower-resource / typologically distant), producing a cross-lingual tool-invocation asymmetry that is separable from the tool-need estimate and from raw knowledge, and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable invocation-gating signal without changing the surface language. A dissociable second gate governs Argument Language Mismatch (emitting tool arguments in the wrong language).
Related Work: Multilingual tool use is now studied behaviorally: Chauhan et al. (2026) name Argument Language Mismatch (right tool, wrong-language arguments) and mitigate it with SFT/RL; Mukherjee et al. (2026) show tool-using agents retain only ~71-73% of their action policy across 41 languages and break down below ~10B parameters; ITC (2026), PolyWorkBench (2026), and Arabic/Traditional-Chinese tool-calling work benchmark multilingual function calling and find large non-English gaps. ALL of these are behavioral/benchmark or training-side (data strategies, SFT/RL), with no internal representation of the tool-vs-memory decision, no decomposition into a shared tool-need estimate versus a language-set invocation threshold, and no causal inference-time intervention. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for agentic action selection. My prior gating-template proposals (calibration know/don't-know, abstention attempt/abstain, context-vs-memory trust, over-refusal, override) target other decisions; NONE address the agentic decision to INVOKE AN EXTERNAL TOOL versus answer from memory, its language-set invocation threshold, its dissociation from a shared tool-need signal, or its causal steering. This proposal is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of tool-invocation gating and of ALM as a dissociable language-realization gate, converting the behavioral observations of Chauhan and Mukherjee into an internal, steerable mechanism.
Abstract: As LLMs become tool-using agents acting on users' behalf, a reliability-critical question arises: does the query language change whether the agent reaches for an external tool or trusts its own memory? Behavioral studies show agents take systematically different actions across languages and generate tool arguments in the wrong language, but why this happens inside the model is unknown. We hypothesize that a multilingual agent computes a largely language-independent internal tool-need estimate—whether a task requires an external tool or can be answered from parametric memory—but applies a query-language-dependent invocation threshold to it, so that for the SAME task the model calls a tool in some languages while over-relying on stale memory in others. This predicts a cross-lingual tool-invocation asymmetry dissociable from the tool-need estimate and from knowledge, plus a second dissociable gate governing Argument Language Mismatch. We build ToolGateProbe, parallel agentic tasks across 12 languages, each labeled by whether a tool is genuinely needed (dynamic/current-info or precise-computation tasks) versus answerable from memory, with content held fixed. Behaviorally we measure per-language tool-invocation rate on tool-needed items and test whether under-invocation tracks resource level and typological distance beyond knowledge. We train a linear tool-need probe, test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, and decompose the invocation gap into a shared tool-need estimate versus a language-set invocation threshold. Via activation and path patching we localize an invocation-gating signal and a separate argument-language signal, and in decisive causal tests we steer them to equalize tool invocation and fix wrong-language arguments across languages—while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe multilingual agent unreliability as a shared tool-need estimate under a steerable, language-dependent invocation gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Open tool-using models Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, and a larger Qwen2.5-14B/Command-R-like model (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs; agents run in a controlled function-calling harness with stub tools). 12 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili, Yoruba).
2) DATASET (ToolGateProbe): ~500 agentic tasks, each presented with a fixed toolset (e.g., web-search/current-info, calculator, unit-converter, calendar). Two strata: (A) TOOL-NEEDED items whose correct answer requires an external tool (current/dynamic facts the model cannot know parametrically; precise multi-digit computation) so answering from memory is unreliable; (B) MEMORY-OK items answerable from stable parametric knowledge where a tool call is wasteful. Keep task content and available tools fixed across languages; translate/native-verify. For TOOL-NEEDED items, define the correct action = invoke the appropriate tool with correct arguments. Record per-language tokenization fertility; screen that the model KNOWS the relevant background so under-invocation is not ignorance-driven, and knows how to call the tool (can do it in >=1 language).
3) BEHAVIORAL INVOCATION-ASYMMETRY TEST: Per (task, language) record whether the model INVOKES the correct tool vs answers from memory, and for MEMORY-OK items over-invocation. KEY hypothesis: on TOOL-NEEDED items, tool-invocation rate is systematically lower in lower-resource/typologically distant languages (over-reliance on stale memory), beyond knowledge and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of under-invocation on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, background-knowledge indicator, stratum), task as random effect; test the language effect. Report per-language invocation profiles, cross-lingual disagreement on identical tasks, and replicate Mukherjee-style policy divergence at matched content.
4) SHARED TOOL-NEED PROBE & TRANSFER: At the pre-action position pool the hidden state; train a linear probe to decode TOOL-NEEDED vs MEMORY-OK on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent tool-need estimate. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on UNDER-INVOCATION (memory-answered but tool-needed) items, test whether the internal tool-need signal is still HIGH across languages—the model 'knows' a tool is needed but does not invoke it.
5) THRESHOLD-vs-ESTIMATE DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer tool-need estimate across languages (should be similar) versus the emitted invoke/answer decision (which diverges). Fit per-language a decision boundary/INVOCATION THRESHOLD on the shared estimate; test whether cross-lingual invocation differences are explained by a shifted threshold on a similar estimate rather than a different estimate. Correlate per-language threshold with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-decision split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE INVOCATION-GATING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that invokes and one that answers-from-memory on the SAME tool-needed task, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips answer->invoke WITHOUT changing the decoded tool-need estimate. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gating components from an invoke-prone language into an under-invoking run.
7) ARGUMENT-LANGUAGE (ALM) GATE (second, dissociable): On correctly-invoked tool calls, measure Argument Language Mismatch (arguments emitted in the wrong language). Train a probe for the intended argument-language and test whether ALM arises from a SEPARATE 'output-language for arguments' signal distinct from the invocation gate. Localize it via patching and show it is dissociable (steering it fixes argument language without changing whether a tool is invoked).
8) CAUSAL STEERING (decisive): (a) Derive an invocation-gating steering vector (invoke runs minus answer-from-memory runs at matched tool-need). Test that adding it in under-invoking languages raises correct tool invocation toward a reference (closing the gap), subtracting it induces memory over-reliance in invoke-prone languages, it works cross-lingually, and it changes ONLY the invoke/answer decision—not the decoded tool-need, background knowledge, or surface language—does not induce over-invocation on MEMORY-OK items (specificity), and does not degrade general QA. (b) Derive an argument-language steering vector and show it fixes ALM (arguments in the intended language) without changing invocation. Baselines: prompt-based 'use tools when needed', per-language decision-threshold tuning, translate-to-English, and SFT (Chauhan). Metrics: invocation-gap closure, correct-invocation recovery, over-invocation-induction rate (reverse), MEMORY-OK specificity, ALM reduction, argument/output-language fidelity, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency and dose-response for both gates.
9) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: tool-type breakdown (search vs calculator vs converter); is a high-resource language the invoke-prone reference?; model scale (does the effect vanish above ~10B, per Mukherjee?); English-centric vs multilingual-centric (Aya-style) pretraining; probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank gating subspace; whether one gating vector generalizes across tasks and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched tool-need.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language tool-invocation and over-invocation rates and their resource/typology regression controlling for knowledge/fertility, cross-lingual tool-need probe transfer AUROC and tool-need-present-under-under-invocation, estimate-similarity vs decision-divergence (threshold) decomposition, threshold-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized invocation-gating and argument-language layers with dissociation evidence, cross-lingual gating transplant repair rate, causal steering invocation-gap closure with dose-response and over-invocation-induction, ALM reduction, MEMORY-OK specificity, argument/output fidelity, general-QA retention, comparison to prompt/threshold-tuning/translate/SFT baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Under-invocation could reflect a background-knowledge gap or inability to call the tool rather than a gating choice; we screen per-language background knowledge and tool-calling ability, and restrict the sharp test to items where the model knows the background and can call the tool, so residual under-invocation reflects the gate. 2) The threshold-vs-estimate split could be confounded if the tool-need estimate itself differs by language; we test this directly via cross-lingual probe transfer and the tool-need-present-under-under-invocation check, reporting how much of the gap is estimate vs gate. 3) Tokenization fertility confounds action selection and argument generation; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched tool-need, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts invocation, dissociating the gate from length. 4) Some models (especially >10B, per Mukherjee) may show little invocation asymmetry; this is itself an informative, publishable scaling finding, and we quantify how often a gap exists across scales. 5) The invocation and argument-language gates could be entangled; we test their dissociation explicitly (steering one without moving the other) and report if they share a direction. 6) Defining 'tool genuinely needed' requires care; we use dynamic/current-info and precise-computation tasks where memory answers are demonstrably unreliable, and validate the labels. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and harness-specific; we test multiple models, tool formats, and templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Causal steering may harm fluency, cause over-invocation, or act as a generic lever; we report MEMORY-OK specificity, over-invocation-induction (reverse), argument/output fidelity, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use dose-response and reverse-consistency to ensure genuine threshold dials. 9) The gating signals may be low-rank rather than single directions; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from behavioral multilingual tool-use work (Chauhan 2026, Mukherjee 2026, ITC, PolyWorkBench) is essential; our contribution is the internal, causal account—a shared tool-need estimate under a language-set invocation threshold, plus a dissociable argument-language gate—and an inference-time steering repair, none of which those behavioral/training-side studies provide.

Name: crosslingual_figure_ground_asymmetry_gating
Title: The Bike Is Near the House, Not the House Near the Bike: A Shared Figure-Ground Spatial Signal Whose Expression Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When describing or interpreting a spatial relation between two objects, a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of the universal figure-ground asymmetry (the smaller/movable/salient object is the FIGURE located relative to the larger/stationary GROUND, e.g. 'the bike is near the house' not 'the house near the bike'), but whether that asymmetry is behaviorally EXPRESSED (choosing the canonical figure-ground ordering, judging reversed descriptions as odd, resolving underspecified relations with the correct reference object) is gated by the query language: the SAME spatial configuration is represented with the correct figure-ground roles internally across languages yet surfaced far more weakly in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so the model can internally 'know which is figure' while behaviorally producing or accepting the anomalous reversal. The figure-ground signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: The figure-ground (trajector-landmark) asymmetry is a robust cross-linguistic universal in cognitive linguistics: the entity to be located (figure) is smaller, more movable, and more salient, while the reference object (ground) is larger and more stationary, and reversing them yields anomaly ('?the house is near the bike') (Talmy; Langacker; Levinson). In NLP, spatial-language work in LLMs is behavioral and mostly multimodal: spatial-reasoning benchmarks and 3D visual grounding (SeeGround 2024), VSR, and frame-of-reference evaluations (COMFORT) test spatial relation understanding but never study figure-ground role assignment, its cross-lingual structure, or its internal mechanism. My prior crosslingual_spatial_frame_of_reference proposal concerns the COORDINATE SYSTEM (egocentric/intrinsic/absolute framing) a model reasons in; figure-ground is a distinct, more primitive asymmetry (which of two objects is the located figure vs the reference ground, independent of the coordinate frame), so this is not a re-run of that idea. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for spatial figure-ground roles. No prior work asks whether a text-only multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent figure-ground representation, whether its internal role assignment is decoupled from behavioral expression across languages, whether figure-ground expression tracks language resource level, or whether the signal is causally steerable. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of the figure-ground asymmetry in language models.
Abstract: We naturally say 'the bike is near the house', never 'the house is near the bike': the smaller, movable object is the figure we locate relative to the larger, stationary ground, and reversing the two feels wrong. This figure-ground asymmetry is a cross-linguistic universal, yet whether multilingual LLMs honor it, whether they do so equally across languages, and how it is implemented internally are unknown. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal representation of which object is figure and which is ground, and whether that internal assignment is decoupled from how reliably it is behaviorally expressed across languages. We hypothesize that models internally assign figure-ground roles similarly across languages, but the query language gates whether that assignment is surfaced (producing the canonical ordering, judging reversals as anomalous, resolving underspecified relations with the correct reference object), so the SAME configuration is represented correctly internally yet surfaced far more weakly in lower-resource, typologically distant languages. We build FigGroundProbe, parallel object-pair spatial descriptions across 8 languages, each with a canonical figure-ground form and an anomalous reversed form, plus a symmetric-pair control (two objects of equal size/movability where either ordering is acceptable), with production-choice, anomaly-judgment, and underspecified-resolution probes. Behaviorally we measure per-language figure-ground expression and test whether it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond object knowledge. We train a linear figure-ground probe and test whether a single probe transfers zero-shot across languages, evidencing a shared assignment, then decompose the expression gap into a shared assignment component versus a language-set expression gate. Via activation and path patching we localize a figure-ground signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to surface (or flip) the figure-ground roles while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual spatial-description gaps as a steerable gate over a shared figure-ground representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Swahili). MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (FigGroundProbe): ~500 object pairs with a clear figure-ground asymmetry (smaller/movable vs larger/stationary: bike/house, cup/table, cat/car, boat/lake), figure-ground roles labeled from size/movability norms and native verification. Three item types: (A) PRODUCTION-CHOICE ('Which description is more natural?' canonical 'the bike is near the house' vs reversed 'the house is near the bike'); (B) ANOMALY-JUDGMENT (rate/accept-reject the reversed form as odd); (C) UNDERSPECIFIED-RESOLUTION (a context requiring the model to pick which object is located relative to which). Include a SYMMETRIC-PAIR control (two objects of comparable size/movability, e.g. two chairs, where either ordering is acceptable) to bound the effect, and screen that the model knows the objects' relative size/movability per language (so failure is not object ignorance). Translate/native-verify into all 8 languages, keeping the object pair fixed; render spatial prepositions naturally per language; record tokenization fertility. Validate an English figure-ground preference against the documented human asymmetry.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (pair, language) record canonical-vs-reversed selection and reversed-anomaly acceptance. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME asymmetric pair, figure-ground expression (preferring canonical, rejecting reversed) is systematically weaker in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond object knowledge and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of figure-ground error on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, knowledge indicator), pair as random effect; compare against the symmetric-pair control (should show no asymmetry). Report per-language expression profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical pairs.
4) SHARED FIGURE-GROUND PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the relation position; train a linear probe to decode which object is FIGURE vs GROUND on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent figure-ground representation. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the figure-ground representation for the same pair. CRITICAL: verify the correct figure-ground assignment is internally decodable across ALL languages even where behavioral expression is weak.
5) ASSIGNMENT-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: For each pair, compare the shared mid-layer figure-ground signal across languages (should be similar if assignment is shared) versus behavioral expression (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal assignment to surfaced behavior per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar assignment signal rather than weaker assignment. Correlate per-language gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE FIGURE-GROUND SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that surfaces the asymmetry and one that fails on the SAME pair, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer surfaces the canonical figure-ground ordering WITHOUT changing the decoded object identities. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the figure-ground representation FROM a high-expression language into a low-expression run.
7) CAUSAL FIGURE-GROUND STEERING (decisive): Derive a figure-ground steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (canonical-role runs minus reversed/failed runs, matched content). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to low-expression languages increases canonical figure-ground preference / reversed-anomaly rejection toward high-expression levels; (ii) FLIP: subtracting/reversing it makes the model treat the ground as figure (accept 'the house is near the bike') on well-assigned items; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where expression was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY figure-ground role assignment, not the decoded object identities or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the symmetric-pair control, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: expression-gap closure, canonical-preference recovery, role-flip rate (reverse), assignment-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes figure-ground judgments but not symmetric-control or unrelated answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: object-property breakdown (size vs movability vs salience as the figure-ground driver); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single figure-ground vector generalizes across pairs and languages; robustness across production-vs-judgment-vs-resolution formats; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal assignment and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces the asymmetry without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language figure-ground expression (canonical-preference, reversed-anomaly rejection, underspecified-resolution accuracy), expression regression controlling for knowledge/fertility/resource, English figure-ground human-asymmetry replication, cross-lingual figure-ground probe transfer AUROC and assignment-present-under-weak-expression, cross-lingual assignment-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), assignment-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized figure-ground layer, cross-lingual assignment transplant recovery rate, causal steering expression-gap closure and role-flip rates, assignment-signal/output fidelity, symmetric-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The assignment-vs-expression split could be confounded if the figure-ground signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying correct-assignment decodability across all languages via probe transfer rather than assuming, and report how much of the gap is assignment vs gate. 2) Weak expression could reflect object-knowledge ignorance (the model doesn't know relative size/movability in that language) rather than an expression gate; we screen per-language object-property knowledge and restrict the gate analysis to known items. 3) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal assignment, and the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet surfaces the asymmetry, dissociating the gate from length. 4) Some models may honor figure-ground uniformly across languages (no gap) or fail everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of the asymmetry in LLMs, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 5) Figure-ground preference can be graded (some pairs are near-symmetric); we use clear-asymmetry pairs (native-verified size/movability norms), include the symmetric-pair control, and analyze borderline pairs separately. 6) The figure-ground probe could latch onto surface preposition/order cues rather than a genuine role representation; the cross-lingual invariance test, the assignment-predicts-behavior link, the symmetric-pair control, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report assignment-signal/output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the flip (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine figure-ground gate. 9) The gate/assignment signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my crosslingual_spatial_frame_of_reference proposal is essential; there the object is the COORDINATE SYSTEM (relative/intrinsic/absolute), whereas here it is the more primitive FIGURE-GROUND role assignment (which object is located relative to which), independent of coordinate frame.

Name: crosslingual_leading_question_framing_gating
Title: Led by the Question, in Some Tongues More Than Others: A Shared Unbiased-Answer Signal Whose Susceptibility to Leading-Question Framing Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When a question is posed with SUGGESTIVE (leading) framing that hints at a particular answer (e.g., 'Isn't it true that X?', 'Most experts agree X, right?', 'How much better is X than Y?'), a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of the unbiased correct answer, but the query language causally sets how strongly the leading framing pulls the emitted answer away from it: for the SAME question and framing, the model is swayed by the suggestion at a lower threshold in some languages—typically lower-resource / typologically distant / higher-deference-norm ones—than in others, producing a cross-lingual framing-susceptibility asymmetry that is separable from the model's internal unbiased answer and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable framing-gate signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Question-framing / leading-question and acquiescence effects are robust in survey methodology and psycholinguistics (loaded questions bias responses), and monolingual English NLP work notes LLMs are swayed by suggestive phrasing, but this is behavioral and English-only. My prior proposals cover a shared-signal-plus-language-gate template for calibration (know/don't-know), abstention (attempt/abstain), presupposition accommodation (accepting backgrounded content), sycophantic capitulation (reversing under USER PUSHBACK), verbal hedging (qualifiers wrapping an answer), and ICL override (following contradictory demonstrations). This proposal is distinct: the causal variable is the SUGGESTIVE FRAMING of the FIRST, single-turn question itself (a loaded phrasing that hints at an answer), not backgrounded presupposed content (presupposition), not multi-turn user pushback after an answer (capitulation), not in-context demonstrations (override), and not the surface qualifiers of an answer (hedging). Recent multilingual work (FinMMEval 2026) documents dramatic language-asymmetric answer shifts under prompt changes, and Bernardelle et al. (2026) show a task signal can be internally encoded yet under-expressed in output and only partially transfer across languages—both support decomposing behavior into a shared internal signal versus a language-set expression/susceptibility gate. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies framing susceptibility. No prior work (i) tests whether leading-question susceptibility is language-dependent, (ii) decomposes it into a shared unbiased-answer signal versus a language-set framing gate, or (iii) causally localizes and steers a framing-susceptibility signal.
Abstract: The way a question is phrased can quietly steer the answer: 'Isn't Product A clearly better?' invites agreement in a way 'Compare A and B' does not. As LLMs advise users worldwide, a fairness- and safety-critical question arises: does the query language change how easily the model is led by such suggestive framing? We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of the unbiased correct answer, but the query language causally sets how strongly a leading framing pulls the emitted answer away from it, so the same loaded question sways the model more in some languages—especially lower-resource, typologically distant, and higher-deference-norm ones—than in others. This predicts a cross-lingual framing-susceptibility asymmetry dissociable from the model's internal unbiased answer. We build FrameLeadProbe: parallel factual and evaluative questions across 12 languages, each posed in a NEUTRAL and a matched LEADING form that suggests a specific (often wrong) answer, with the question content held fixed. Behaviorally we measure per-language framing susceptibility (the shift from the neutral answer toward the suggested one) and test whether it tracks resource level, typological distance, and documented deference norms beyond the model's underlying knowledge. We train a linear unbiased-answer probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the susceptibility gap into a shared unbiased-answer signal (still present under leading framing) versus a language-set framing gate—high susceptibility should coincide with an intact internal unbiased answer (the model is led while still 'knowing' the right answer). Via activation and path patching we localize a framing-gate signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model resist leading framing across languages—or, in reverse, induce susceptibility—while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual framing bias as a shared unbiased-answer signal under a steerable, language-dependent framing gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/culturally/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili, Korean), coded for documented deference/acquiescence/indirectness norms plus URIEL typological/resource distance (graded predictors).
2) DATASET (FrameLeadProbe): ~500 questions with a verifiable or clearly-preferable correct answer, in two strata: (A) FACTUAL (mLAMA/BMLAMA/Wikidata short-answer) and (B) EVALUATIVE (comparisons/recommendations with a defensible correct choice). For each item build a NEUTRAL form ('What is the capital of X?' / 'Compare A and B') and a matched LEADING form that suggests a specific, often INCORRECT answer via loaded phrasing ('Isn't the capital of X actually Y?', 'Most people say A is worse than B, don't they?', presupposition-free but suggestive). Vary leading strength (mild hint vs strong assertion) as a graded factor. Keep content fixed across languages; translate/native-verify, ensuring the leading device is natural per language. Screen that the model gives the CORRECT answer under the NEUTRAL form (so susceptibility = being led away from a correct answer it holds). Include a NEUTRAL-only control and a CORRECTLY-LEADING control (the suggestion happens to be right; following it is fine) to bound the effect and separate genuine framing-bias from healthy agreement. Record tokenization fertility.
3) BEHAVIORAL SUSCEPTIBILITY TEST: Per (item, language) measure FRAMING SUSCEPTIBILITY = shift from the neutral-form answer toward the suggested (wrong) answer under the leading form. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME question and leading framing, susceptibility is systematically higher in lower-resource / typologically distant / higher-deference-norm languages, beyond the model's underlying knowledge. Mixed-effects logistic regression of leading-induced error on (language, leading strength, resource tier via URIEL, typological distance, deference-norm code, tokenization fertility, neutral-form correctness), item as random effect; test the language effect. Compare against the NEUTRAL-only and CORRECTLY-LEADING controls (healthy agreement should be language-flatter). Report per-language susceptibility profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical loaded questions.
4) SHARED UNBIASED-ANSWER PROBE & TRANSFER: At the pre-answer position (under the LEADING form) pool the hidden state; train a linear probe to decode the UNBIASED correct answer on ENGLISH data (using neutral-form labels), select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent unbiased-answer signal. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on LED (susceptible) items, test whether the internal unbiased-answer signal is still strong across languages—the signature of 'led on the surface, correct inside'.
5) THRESHOLD-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer unbiased-answer signal across languages (should be similar on matched items) versus the emitted led/resist decision (which diverges). Define a per-language FRAMING GATE mapping the unbiased signal to the emitted answer under leading framing; test whether cross-lingual susceptibility differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar unbiased signal rather than a weaker unbiased signal. Correlate per-language gate strength with deference norms, resource tier, and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE FRAMING-GATE SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that resists and one that is led on the SAME loaded question, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips led->resist WITHOUT changing the decoded unbiased-answer signal. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gate components from a resist-prone language into a led run. Attention analysis: does the led response over-attend to the suggestive phrasing tokens, more so in high-susceptibility languages?
7) CAUSAL FRAMING STEERING (decisive): Derive a framing-gate steering vector via difference-of-means (resist runs minus led runs at matched unbiased signal). Test (i) RESIST: adding it in high-susceptibility languages makes the model hold its unbiased answer under leading framing toward a reference level; (ii) LEAD: subtracting it induces susceptibility in resist-prone languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where the gap was largest; (iv) it changes ONLY resist-vs-led behavior under suggestive framing, NOT healthy agreement on the CORRECTLY-LEADING control (the model must still adopt a correct suggestion), the decoded unbiased-answer signal, the answer content on neutral items, or surface language (fidelity checks), and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset); (v) reverse-consistency and dose-response: scaling the vector produces graded susceptibility shifts and does not change unrelated answers. Baselines: prompt-based 'ignore any suggestion', per-language temperature, translate-to-English. Metrics: susceptibility-gap closure, unbiased-answer-retention-under-framing, healthy-agreement retention (correctly-leading control), lead-induction rate (reverse), unbiased-signal/answer/output fidelity, general-QA retention.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: leading-strength breakdown; factual vs evaluative strata; is English/high-resource the resist-prone reference?; does susceptibility track deference/acquiescence norms beyond resource level?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank framing subspace; whether one gate vector generalizes across items and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched unbiased signal and by showing content-invariant steering shifts susceptibility without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language framing susceptibility and its norm/resource/typology regression controlling for underlying knowledge, neutral-only and correctly-leading baselines, cross-lingual unbiased-answer probe transfer AUROC and unbiased-signal-present-under-being-led, signal-similarity vs decision-divergence (framing-gate) decomposition, gate-vs-norm/resource/typology correlation, patch-localized framing-gate layer and attention-to-suggestion evidence, cross-lingual gate transplant repair rate, causal steering susceptibility-gap closure with dose-response and lead-induction rate, unbiased-answer-retention and healthy-agreement retention, unbiased-signal/answer/output fidelity, general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The threshold-vs-signal split could be confounded if the unbiased-answer signal itself weakens under leading framing in some languages (the model genuinely becomes unsure, not merely deferent); we test this directly by verifying an intact internal unbiased-answer signal on led items across languages via probe transfer, and report how much of the gap is signal-loss vs gate. 2) Being led could reflect a knowledge gap rather than a framing gate; we screen that the model answers correctly under the NEUTRAL form (holds the unbiased answer) and restrict the sharp test to such items, so residual leading-induced error reflects the gate. 3) The key guard: any susceptibility-reducing intervention must NOT make the model ignore legitimately-correct suggestions; we include the CORRECTLY-LEADING control and report healthy-agreement retention as a primary metric, using it to ensure the steering targets undue susceptibility, not suggestion-following in general—if the two are entangled, that is itself a publishable finding. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched unbiased signal, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts susceptibility. 5) Some models/languages may show no framing-susceptibility asymmetry (uniform robustness or uniform gullibility); either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual framing bias, and we quantify how often a gap exists. 6) Constructing equivalently-strong leading framings across languages is delicate; we native-verify, vary leading strength as a graded factor, and report sensitivity. 7) Deference/acquiescence-norm coding is coarse and debated; we treat it as a graded predictor and report sensitivity to alternative codings, noting a language effect is establishable even if the cultural correlate is weak. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching plus attention analysis. 9) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report unbiased-signal/answer/output fidelity, healthy-agreement and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the lead-induction (reverse), reverse-consistency, and dose-response tests to ensure a genuine framing-gate dial. 10) The framing signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my presupposition-accommodation (backgrounded content), capitulation (multi-turn user pushback), hedging (surface qualifiers), and override (ICL demonstrations) proposals is essential; here the causal object is the SUGGESTIVE FRAMING of the single-turn question itself and its language-set susceptibility gate over a retained unbiased-answer signal.

Name: crosslingual_event_duration_reweighting
Title: How Long Did It Take, in Every Language? A Shared Event-Duration Representation Reweighted by the Query Language in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Text-only multilingual LLMs place described events on a largely language-independent internal duration scale (a 'mental timeline' encoding roughly log-scaled event lengths from seconds to years), but the query language causally reweights how that shared magnitude is expressed as an estimated duration: for the SAME event, the model's estimated duration is systematically compressed or dilated depending on the query language, tracking each language community's time-expression conventions and typological/resource distance. This cross-lingual duration bias is separable from the shared magnitude representation and is causally steerable by a localizable duration-reweighting signal without changing the event content or surface language.
Related Work: Human time-perception research robustly documents systematic duration-estimation biases (short intervals overestimated, long ones underestimated; a modifiable 'central pacemaker'; Weber-law scaling) and cross-cultural variation in temporal cognition (Jaffe et al. 2012; Requena-Komuro et al. 2025; time-perception reviews). In NLP, temporal work is either speech-timing/duration-modeling (van Santen 1997; multilingual TTS) or event-ordering/temporal-tagging benchmarks; monolingual work shows LLMs encode rough event durations, but NO work asks whether a TEXT-ONLY multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent EVENT-DURATION magnitude scale, whether the query language distorts the estimated duration of the same event, whether that distortion tracks time-expression typology, or whether it is causally localizable and steerable. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for event duration. My prior temporal proposals concern per-language STALENESS of stored facts, aspectual COMPLETION (finished vs ongoing) of a single event, and CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER of multiple events; NONE address the estimated DURATION/length of an event on a magnitude scale, which is a distinct psychophysical dimension. My number-naming and approximate-number proposals concern abstract numeric magnitude, not the semantic duration attached to real-world events. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of event-duration perception in language models.
Abstract: How long does 'brewing a cup of tea' take, versus 'building a bridge'? Humans place events on a mental timeline spanning seconds to years, with systematic estimation biases and cross-cultural variation. We ask whether a text-only multilingual LLM, which never experiences time, nonetheless builds a shared, language-independent internal representation of event duration, and whether the query language distorts the duration it estimates for the same event. We hypothesize that the model computes a largely language-independent internal duration magnitude but the query language causally reweights it at the decoding layers, so the SAME event is judged to take systematically longer or shorter depending on the language, tracking time-expression conventions and typological distance. We build DurationProbe, parallel event descriptions across 10 languages spanning durations from seconds to years, with the event content held fixed, eliciting numeric duration estimates and duration comparisons. Behaviorally we measure per-language duration estimates and test whether cross-lingual distortion tracks resource level and typological distance beyond translation, and whether the model reproduces the human short-overestimate/long-underestimate bias. We train a linear probe for the shared duration magnitude and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the distortion into a shared magnitude signal versus a language-set reweighting gain. Via activation and path patching we localize a duration-reweighting signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to shift the estimated duration of an event (or equalize it across languages) while leaving the event content and surface language unchanged. We reframe multilingual duration inconsistency as a shared timeline under a steerable, language-dependent reweighting.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (DurationProbe): ~500 described events with a documented typical duration spanning ~8 orders of magnitude (seconds: 'snapping fingers'; minutes: 'boiling an egg'; hours: 'a movie'; days: 'a conference'; months/years: 'building a house', 'a university degree'), each with a consensus reference duration (from human-annotated event-duration datasets / native verification). Probes: (A) DIRECT ESTIMATION ('About how long does this take?' -> a numeric duration + unit), (B) DURATION COMPARISON (forced choice: which of two events takes longer, where the ratio is varied to trace a Weber-style curve), (C) BUCKET CLASSIFICATION (seconds/minutes/hours/days/months/years). Keep the event fixed across languages; translate/native-verify. Include an EXPLICIT control where the duration is stated (answer language-flat) to bound the effect. Record per-language tokenization fertility.
3) BEHAVIORAL DISTORTION TEST: Per (event, language) record the log-duration estimate. KEY hypotheses: (i) cross-lingual DISTORTION exists—the same event is estimated to take systematically longer/shorter across languages; (ii) it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond translation; (iii) the model reproduces the human short-overestimate/long-underestimate bias, and its magnitude varies by language. Mixed-effects regression of log-estimate on (language, reference log-duration, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility), event as random effect; test the language main effect and language x reference-duration interaction (differential compression/dilation). Confirm ordering is preserved across languages (a shared scale should keep rank even if it shifts/stretches). Compare against the EXPLICIT control (language-flat).
4) SHARED DURATION-MAGNITUDE PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-answer position; train a linear probe to regress the reference log-duration on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report R^2/rank-correlation as evidence of a language-independent duration scale, plus cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the magnitude representation for the same event. Show the shared magnitude is internally similar across languages even when emitted estimates differ.
5) GAIN-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer duration magnitude across languages (should be similar if shared) versus the emitted estimate (which diverges). Define a per-language REWEIGHTING GAIN (an affine shift/scale from the shared magnitude to the emitted log-duration); test whether cross-lingual distortion is explained by a language-set gain on a similar magnitude rather than a different magnitude. Correlate per-language gain with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE DURATION-REWEIGHTING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that estimates an event long and one that estimates it short on the SAME event, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer shifts the emitted duration WITHOUT changing the decoded shared magnitude. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the reweighting components from one language into another's run.
7) CAUSAL DURATION STEERING (decisive): Derive a duration-reweighting steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (long-estimate runs minus short-estimate runs at matched shared magnitude). Test (i) SHIFT: adding/subtracting it moves the estimated duration up/down in a graded (dose-response) way on held-out events; (ii) EQUALIZE: per-language reweighting makes the same event estimated to take the same duration across languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually and can override a language's default; (iv) it changes ONLY the estimated duration, not the decoded magnitude, the event content, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the EXPLICIT control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: cross-lingual distortion closure, dose-response of estimated duration, magnitude/content/output fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts duration but not unrelated numeric or factual answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: duration-bucket breakdown (do short vs long events reweight differently by language?); is English/high-resource the reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank reweighting subspace; robustness across estimation-vs-comparison-vs-bucket formats and templates; whether one reweighting vector generalizes across events and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched shared magnitude and by showing content-invariant steering shifts duration without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language duration estimates and cross-lingual distortion with resource/typology regression, short-overestimate/long-underestimate bias replication, rank-preservation across languages, cross-lingual duration-probe transfer R^2/rank-correlation and representation similarity, magnitude-similarity vs estimate-divergence (gain) decomposition, gain-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized reweighting layer, cross-lingual reweighting transplant shift, causal steering distortion closure with dose-response, magnitude/content/output fidelity, explicit-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Event 'ground-truth' durations are inherently variable and culturally dependent; we use consensus reference durations from human-annotated event-duration datasets, native verification, restrict to events with clear typical durations, and analyze culturally-variable events separately; the analysis focuses on relative cross-lingual distortion and rank-preservation rather than absolute correctness. 2) The gain-vs-signal split could be confounded if the shared magnitude itself differs by language; we test this directly by comparing shared-probe magnitudes across languages rather than assuming, and report how much distortion is magnitude vs gain. 3) Distortion could be a mere translation effect (the translated event phrase genuinely implies a different duration); we hold event content fixed via native-verified parallel descriptions, and the internal-magnitude-predicts-estimate link plus content-preserving steering (which shifts the estimate without changing the event) dissociate a genuine internal reweighting from lexical translation. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds numeric output; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched shared magnitude, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts estimates. 5) Instruction-tuned models may refuse or give ranges; we use both numeric generation and log-probability over duration buckets, and report refusal/range rates. 6) Some models may estimate durations uniformly across languages (no distortion) or lack a coherent duration scale; either is an informative, publishable finding about whether text-only LLMs build a mental timeline, and we quantify how often distortion occurs and whether a shared scale exists. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic numeric lever; we report magnitude/content/output fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention, and use dose-response and reverse-consistency to ensure a genuine duration-reweighting dial rather than a global numeric shift. 9) The reweighting signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my temporal-staleness (per-language recency of stored facts), aspect-completion (finished vs ongoing single event), and chronological-ordering (order of multiple events) proposals is essential; here the object is the estimated DURATION/length of an event on a magnitude scale, a distinct psychophysical dimension grounded in human time-perception research.

Name: crosslingual_serial_position_asymmetry
Title: Primacy in the Weaker Tongue: Do Multilingual Models Recapitulate the Human Bilingual Serial-Position Asymmetry, and Is Recency a Shared Language-Invariant Buffer?
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM must freely recall a just-presented list of items, its serial-position curve is language-dependent in a specific, human-mirroring way: RECENCY (recall of the last items) is largely language-invariant—carried by a shared, position-based recency buffer—while PRIMACY (recall of the first items), which depends on rehearsal/encoding, is systematically weaker in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, exactly the asymmetry found in human bilinguals (stronger primacy in L1 than L2, equivalent recency). The recency buffer is a shared, language-independent representation, whereas primacy recall is gated by the query language.
Related Work: Serial-position effects (U-shaped free-recall curve: primacy + recency) are among the most robust findings in human memory, with primacy tied to rehearsal/long-term encoding and recency to a short-term buffer (Phillips 1967; Kamp 2012). Bilingual psycholinguistics finds a specific ASYMMETRY: Yoo & Kaushanskaya (2015) show stronger primacy/pre-recency in bilinguals' L1 than L2 but EQUIVALENT recency, and clinical work (Mizrahi 2023) confirms language-sensitive primacy. In LLMs, position bias / 'lost-in-the-middle' is documented for single-item retrieval and essay scoring (Çelik 2026), and my prior positional-attention proposal studied needle-by-position retrieval driven by attention sinks. NONE study multi-item FREE-RECALL serial-position CURVES in multilingual LLMs, whether the primacy-vs-recency asymmetry recapitulates the human bilingual pattern (language-invariant recency, language-gated primacy), whether recency is a shared cross-lingual buffer, or whether the effect is causally localizable. This is a clean human-sciences transfer distinct from my positional-attention proposal: the object here is completeness and the SHAPE of the recall curve over a memorized list and the primacy/recency dissociation, not retrieval of one item by absolute position, and the central, falsifiable prediction (recency shared/invariant, primacy language-gated) comes directly from the human bilingual literature.
Abstract: Humans recall the first and last items of a list best—the U-shaped serial-position curve—and decades of work tie primacy to rehearsal-based encoding and recency to a short-term buffer. Strikingly, bilinguals show an asymmetry: primacy is stronger in their dominant language while recency is equivalent across languages. We ask whether a multilingual LLM, prompted to memorize and then freely recall a list, reproduces this signature, and whether it reflects a shared, language-invariant recency buffer plus a language-gated primacy process. We present lists of items in each of several typologically and resource-diverse languages, ask the model to recall them, and score recall accuracy by serial position to reconstruct per-language primacy, middle, and recency components. We test three claims: (1) recency recall is largely language-invariant while primacy recall is systematically weaker in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, mirroring the human bilingual asymmetry; (2) a linear probe for 'which items are still held in the recency buffer' trained in one language transfers zero-shot across languages, evidencing a shared position-based buffer, whereas a primacy/encoding probe transfers less; and (3) the effect is separable from tokenization and item knowledge and is causally traceable—ablating the shared recency signal degrades last-item recall across languages, while the primacy deficit tracks a distinct, language-modulated encoding signal. We reframe multilingual recall gaps as a dissociation between a shared recency buffer and a language-gated primacy process, recapitulating a robust human memory phenomenon.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + light patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) TASK & DATA (SerialRecallProbe): Present a list of N items (vary N=8,12,16) then prompt free recall ('list the items you just saw, in any order'). Use several item types to dissociate memory from knowledge: (A) common concrete NOUNS (translated/native-verified parallel lists), (B) NOVEL pseudo-words / arbitrary symbol strings (language-agnostic, removing lexical-frequency confounds), (C) DIGITS/number lists. Keep the SAME underlying item sequence across languages (parallel translations for nouns; identical tokens for pseudo-words/digits). Randomize item order across trials so serial position is decorrelated from item identity. Record per-language tokenization fertility.
3) BEHAVIORAL SERIAL-POSITION CURVE: For each (language, N, item-type), score recall accuracy per serial position and average across trials to get primacy (first ~3), middle, and recency (last ~3) components. KEY hypothesis: RECENCY is roughly language-invariant while PRIMACY is systematically lower in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, mirroring Yoo & Kaushanskaya. Mixed-effects regression of per-position recall on (serial-position region [primacy/middle/recency], language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, item-type, N), item-sequence as random effect; test the region x language interaction (predicted significant for primacy, null for recency). Report per-language U-curves and cross-lingual disagreement, and replicate the English U-shape as a sanity check.
4) DISSOCIATION FROM CONFOUNDS: (i) Pseudo-word lists remove lexical-frequency/knowledge confounds—test whether the primacy asymmetry persists (a genuine memory effect) or vanishes (a knowledge effect). (ii) Control tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched N and via digit/pseudo-word items. (iii) Test whether the recency-invariance / primacy-gating pattern holds within pseudo-words, the cleanest condition.
5) SHARED RECENCY-BUFFER PROBE & TRANSFER: At the pre-recall position, pool hidden states and train a linear probe to decode whether a given list item is in the RECENCY window (among the last k presented) on ENGLISH data; apply zero-shot cross-lingually and report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent position-based recency buffer. Separately train a PRIMACY/encoding probe (is the item among the first, well-encoded items). Hypothesis: the recency probe transfers well across languages (shared buffer) while the primacy probe transfers less and its per-language strength tracks the behavioral primacy deficit. Measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the recency vs primacy representations.
6) CAUSAL CHECK (light): Via activation patching / ablation, suppress the shared recency signal and test whether last-item recall drops across languages (confirming the shared buffer's causal role), while patching the primacy/encoding signal selectively affects first-item recall; test whether transplanting a high-primacy language's encoding representation into a low-primacy run improves first-item recall. Report specificity (recency ablation should not hurt primacy and vice versa) and output-language fidelity.
7) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: item-type breakdown (nouns vs pseudo-words vs digits); list length N effects on the curve shape per language; is English/high-resource the strong-primacy reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the primacy asymmetry, mirroring proficiency effects in humans?); probe layer/dimensionality; robustness across recall prompts and trial orderings.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language primacy/middle/recency recall and U-curve shape, region x language interaction (primacy language-gated, recency invariant), pseudo-word control result, tokenization-controlled regression, cross-lingual recency-probe vs primacy-probe transfer AUROC and representation similarity, primacy-probe-strength vs behavioral-primacy correlation, causal recency-ablation last-item drop and primacy-transplant first-item gain with specificity, English U-shape and human-asymmetry replication.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) LLM free recall from a prompt is a within-context (in-context) memory task, not the human short-term-store paradigm; the mapping to human primacy/recency is analogical—we treat the human bilingual asymmetry as a predicted PATTERN to test, validate the English U-shape as a sanity check, and interpret cautiously. 2) The primacy asymmetry could be a lexical-frequency/knowledge effect rather than a memory-encoding effect; the pseudo-word and digit conditions dissociate these, and finding the asymmetry in pseudo-words would be strong evidence for a genuine encoding effect. 3) Tokenization fertility confounds recall of longer non-English items; we control via matched-N, digit/pseudo-word items, fertility regression, and by testing whether the recency-invariance holds within tokenization-matched conditions. 4) Some models may show no U-shape, no asymmetry, or uniform curves across languages—any of these is an informative, publishable finding about whether LLMs recapitulate human serial-position memory, and we quantify curve shape and the region x language interaction rather than assuming them. 5) Free-recall scoring (matching recalled items to the list, order-independent) is noisy, especially cross-lingually; we use normalized/translation-aware matching validated against human labels on a subset, and prefer digit/pseudo-word items where matching is unambiguous. 6) The recency/primacy probes could latch onto surface recency of tokens rather than a genuine buffer; the cross-lingual transfer, the recency-vs-primacy dissociation, and the causal ablation/transplant guard against this. 7) Causal patching results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check ablation vs patching, and report where effects are absent. 8) Distinguishing from my prior positional-attention ('lost-in-the-middle') proposal is essential; there the object was retrieval of a single needle by absolute position driven by attention sinks, whereas here it is multi-item free-recall completeness, the SHAPE of the primacy/recency curve, and specifically the human-mirroring prediction that recency is a shared language-invariant buffer while primacy is language-gated.

Name: crosslingual_quotation_firewall_gating
Title: Whose Claim Is It? A Shared Quotation-Firewall Representation That Quarantines Reported Content From the Model's Own Belief, Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When a text embeds a claim that belongs to another source (direct/indirect quotation, reported speech, 'according to X'), a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal 'quotation-firewall' representation that tags the claim as SOMEONE ELSE'S (quarantined from the model's own commitment), but whether that firewall is behaviorally ENFORCED—correctly attributing the claim to its source and NOT endorsing it as the model's own belief—is gated by the query language: the SAME quoted claim is internally quarantined across languages yet leaks into the model's own asserted belief (or is mis-attributed) far more often in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so the model can internally 'know it was only reported' while behaviorally endorsing a false quoted claim or attributing it to the wrong party. The firewall signal is causally localizable and its enforcement steerable, so language-gated attribution leakage can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Attribution/faithfulness in generation is studied behaviorally and largely monolingually: quote-attribution and reported-speech datasets (PARC/PDNC-style quote attribution), source-attribution and citation-faithfulness work, and 'according-to' prompting to ground answers in sources—none study whether a model internally quarantines quoted content from its own belief, whether that quarantine is language-dependent, or its mechanism. My prior crosslingual_evidentiality proposal concerns GRAMMATICAL information source (witnessed/inferred/hearsay marking of a single assertion), crosslingual_presupposition_accommodation concerns silently accepting BACKGROUNDED presupposed content, and language_modulated_context_trust concerns trusting a retrieved PASSAGE vs parametric memory. This proposal is distinct: the object is the ATTRIBUTION firewall between a source's REPORTED claim and the model's OWN asserted belief (whose claim is it, and does the model endorse it), a stance-attribution/quarantine phenomenon rather than grammatical evidentiality, presupposition, or passage-faithfulness. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for quotation/stance quarantine. No prior work asks whether an LLM builds a shared, language-independent quotation-firewall representation, whether its internal quarantine is decoupled from behavioral attribution/endorsement across languages, whether firewall enforcement tracks resource level, or whether it is causally steerable—with direct hallucination-safety stakes (endorsing a source's false claim as fact, or misattributing claims).
Abstract: Text constantly carries claims that are not the author's own: 'The minister said the economy grew 8%', 'According to the rumor, the drug cures cancer.' Understanding such text requires keeping the reported claim quarantined from one's own belief and attributing it to its source—otherwise a model may endorse a false quoted claim as fact or blame the wrong party.
