We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal 'quotation firewall' that tags reported content as someone else's, and whether that internal quarantine is decoupled from how reliably it is behaviorally enforced across languages. We hypothesize that models internally quarantine reported claims similarly across languages, but the query language gates whether the firewall is enforced—correctly attributing the claim and refusing to endorse it—so the SAME quoted claim leaks into the model's own asserted belief, or is mis-attributed, far more often in lower-resource, typologically distant languages. We build QuoteFirewallProbe, parallel passages across 8 languages in which a (often false) claim is embedded as reported speech / direct quotation / 'according-to' attribution, with attribution probes ('Who claims X?'), endorsement probes ('Is X true?' vs 'Does the speaker say X?'), and a matched control where the claim is asserted directly by the narrator. Behaviorally we measure per-language attribution-leakage (endorsing a reported false claim as the model's own belief, or misattributing it) and test whether it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond comprehension. We train a linear firewall probe (is this content quarantined-as-reported vs endorsed-as-own) and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the leakage gap into a shared quarantine component versus a language-set enforcement gate—verifying the claim is internally tagged as reported even where it leaks. Via activation and path patching we localize a firewall signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to restore quarantine (stop the model endorsing a reported false claim) or, in reverse, induce leakage, while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual attribution failures and quote-induced hallucination as a steerable gate over a shared quotation-firewall representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Swahili). MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (QuoteFirewallProbe): ~500 short passages, each embedding a target CLAIM that is (crossed factor) TRUE or FALSE, and (crossed factor) attributed to a SOURCE via one of three ATTRIBUTION forms: (A) DIRECT QUOTATION ('The minister said, "the economy grew 8%"'), (B) INDIRECT REPORTED SPEECH ('The minister said that the economy grew 8%'), (C) 'ACCORDING-TO' attribution ('According to a rumor, the drug cures cancer'). Include a matched NARRATOR-ASSERTED control where the same claim is stated directly (not attributed), where endorsing it IS appropriate, to bound the effect and separate quarantine from comprehension. Probes: (i) ATTRIBUTION ('Who claims that X?' with the correct source and a distractor), (ii) ENDORSEMENT ('Is X true?' vs 'Does the source say X?')—firewall failure = asserting the reported (false) claim as true / as the model's own belief, (iii) SOURCE-FIDELITY (does the model correctly report that the source said X). Keep claim content and source fixed across languages; translate/native-verify; realize quotation naturally per language (quotative particles, reportative constructions). Record tokenization fertility; screen base-passage comprehension via the narrator-asserted control so firewall failure is not reading failure. Short scoreable answers where possible.
3) BEHAVIORAL LEAKAGE TEST: Per (passage, language) measure ATTRIBUTION-LEAKAGE = endorsing a reported FALSE claim as true (or misattributing the claim to the wrong party). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME reported false claim, leakage is systematically higher in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond comprehension and tokenization; leakage is highest for the reported-false condition and near-zero for narrator-asserted-true (correct) and reported-true (correct source, harmless). Mixed-effects logistic regression of leakage on (attribution form, truth factor, language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, comprehension indicator), passage as random effect; test the language effect and language x attribution-form interaction. Compare against the narrator-asserted control. Report per-language firewall-leakage profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical quoted claims.
4) SHARED FIREWALL PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the claim/answer position; train a linear probe to decode QUARANTINED-AS-REPORTED vs ENDORSED-AS-OWN (using the reported vs narrator-asserted contrast) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent quotation-firewall representation. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the firewall representation for the same passage. CRITICAL: on LEAKAGE (endorsed reported-false) items, test whether the claim is still internally tagged as REPORTED across ALL languages (the firewall fired internally) even when the model endorses it—the signature of language-gated enforcement over an intact quarantine.
5) QUARANTINE-vs-ENFORCEMENT DECOMPOSITION: For each passage, compare the shared mid-layer firewall signal across languages (should be similar if quarantine is shared) versus behavioral endorsement/attribution (which diverges). Define an ENFORCEMENT GATE mapping internal quarantine to behavioral attribution/non-endorsement per language; test whether cross-lingual leakage differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar quarantine signal rather than weaker quarantine. Correlate per-language gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE FIREWALL SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that enforces quarantine and one that leaks on the SAME passage, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer restores correct attribution/non-endorsement WITHOUT changing the decoded claim content or source identity. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the firewall representation FROM a high-enforcement language into a leaking run. Attention analysis: does the endorsing response fail to bind the claim to its quotative source, more so in high-leakage languages?
7) CAUSAL FIREWALL STEERING (decisive): Derive a firewall-enforcement steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (quarantine-enforced runs minus leakage runs, matched content). Test (i) RESTORE: adding it to leaking languages makes the model correctly attribute and refuse to endorse the reported false claim toward high-enforcement levels; (ii) INDUCE: subtracting it makes high-enforcement languages endorse reported false claims / misattribute; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where leakage was worst; (iv) it changes ONLY quarantine/attribution behavior, NOT the decoded claim content or source, does NOT make the model reject narrator-asserted-true claims (the model must still endorse content that IS the narrator's own), and preserves surface language (fidelity checks) and general QA. Metrics: leakage reduction, endorsement-induction rate (reverse), narrator-asserted-true retention (must not over-reject legitimate assertions), source-fidelity retention, firewall-signal/output fidelity, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes quarantine/attribution but not unrelated or narrator-control answers, guarding against a generic skepticism lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: attribution-form breakdown (direct-quote vs indirect vs according-to—does the firewall leak most for indirect speech?); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single firewall vector generalizes across attribution forms and languages; robustness across attribution-vs-endorsement-vs-source-fidelity formats and templates; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal quarantine and by showing content-invariant steering restores the firewall without changing tokenization; a safety-focused analysis of quote-induced hallucination (does the model repeat a source's false claim as fact more in some languages?).
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language attribution-leakage / endorsement-of-reported-false rate and source-fidelity, leakage regression controlling for comprehension/fertility/resource with attribution-form interaction, cross-lingual firewall probe transfer AUROC and claim-tagged-as-reported-under-leakage, cross-lingual firewall-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), quarantine-similarity vs enforcement-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized firewall layer and source-binding attention evidence, cross-lingual firewall transplant repair rate, causal steering leakage-reduction and endorsement-induction rates with narrator-asserted-true retention, firewall-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The quarantine-vs-enforcement split could be confounded if the firewall signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying claim-tagged-as-reported decodability across all languages via probe transfer on leakage items rather than assuming, and report how much of the gap is quarantine vs gate. 2) Leakage could reflect passage-comprehension failure rather than an enforcement gate; we use the matched narrator-asserted control and comprehension screening so residual endorsement/misattribution of reported claims reflects the firewall, not reading. 3) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal quarantine, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet restores the firewall, dissociating the gate from length. 4) Some models may enforce quarantine uniformly across languages (no gap) or leak everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of the cross-lingual quotation firewall, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 5) Realizing quotation/reported speech naturally and equivalently across languages is delicate (quotative particles, reportative morphology); we native-verify, treat attribution form as a factor, and flag constructions with no natural equivalent. 6) The most important guard: any firewall-restoring intervention must NOT make the model reject content that IS legitimately the narrator's own assertion (over-quarantine); we include the narrator-asserted-true control and report its retention as a primary metric, and use the endorsement-induction (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure the steering targets quotation-quarantine specifically, not generic skepticism—if the two are entangled, that is itself a publishable finding. 7) Endorsement/attribution scoring is noisy; we validate classifiers against human labels, use short answers, and separate attribution-accuracy from endorsement-of-truth. 8) The firewall signal could latch onto surface quotative cues rather than a genuine quarantine representation; the cross-lingual invariance test, the claim-tagged-under-leakage check, the source-binding attention analysis, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 9) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 10) The gate/firewall signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my evidentiality (grammatical information-source of a single assertion), presupposition-accommodation (backgrounded presupposed content), and context-trust (retrieved passage vs memory) proposals is essential; here the object is the ATTRIBUTION firewall between a source's reported claim and the model's own asserted belief—whose claim it is and whether the model endorses it—with direct quote-induced-hallucination safety stakes.

Name: crosslingual_bridging_inference_gating
Title: The Chandelier in the Room: A Shared Bridging-Inference Signal Whose Expression Is Gated by the Query Language in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a text introduces an entity that is only implicitly linked to a previously mentioned scene via world knowledge (bridging anaphora, e.g. 'I entered the room. The chandelier was dazzling.' — the chandelier is understood to belong to the room), a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal 'bridging-link' representation that binds the new entity to its implicit anchor, but whether that link is behaviorally EXPRESSED (correctly answering where/whose the entity is, judging an unbridgeable entity as odd, resolving definite reference) is gated by the query language: the SAME bridging relation is inferred internally across languages yet surfaced far more weakly in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so the model can internally 'know the chandelier belongs to the room' while behaviorally failing. The bridging signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Bridging (associative) anaphora is a well-studied discourse phenomenon in linguistics and psycholinguistics (Clark's bridging inferences; Poesio & Vieira's definite-description taxonomy; ISNotes/bridging corpora), where a newly-introduced definite entity is linked to an antecedent scene via world knowledge rather than coreference. In NLP, bridging resolution is a supervised task (ISNotes, BASHI, ARRAU) studied almost entirely in English and behaviorally, with no cross-lingual or mechanistic account. My prior crosslingual_pro_drop / argument_reconstruction proposal concerns reconstructing a syntactically OMITTED argument (a covert pronoun/subject), and crosslingual_discourse_relation concerns the relation label (cause/contrast) between two CLAUSES; NEITHER addresses BRIDGING — the world-knowledge-driven binding of a newly-mentioned entity to an implicit scene anchor (a part-whole / possession / association link), which is neither a syntactic gap nor an inter-clausal relation. My false-belief, semantic-anticipation, humor, and causal-direction detection-vs-expression proposals target different phenomena (agent beliefs, next-word congruity, incongruity resolution, cause/effect). Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for bridging/associative anaphora. No prior work asks whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent bridging-link representation, whether its internal inference is decoupled from behavioral expression across languages, whether bridging expression tracks language resource level, or whether the bridging signal is causally localizable and steerable. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of bridging inference.
Abstract: Coherent understanding requires silently linking new entities to old scenes: 'I walked into the kitchen. The fridge was humming.' — we instantly know the fridge belongs to the kitchen, though no word says so. This bridging (associative) anaphora rests on world knowledge, not coreference or a syntactic gap, and it is essential to comprehension. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal representation that binds a bridged entity to its implicit anchor, and whether that internal inference is decoupled from how reliably it is behaviorally expressed across languages. We hypothesize that models infer the bridging link similarly across languages, but the query language gates whether that link is surfaced (answering where/whose the entity is, judging an unbridgeable entity as anomalous, resolving definite reference), so the SAME bridging relation is inferred internally yet surfaced far more weakly in lower-resource, typologically distant languages. We build BridgeProbe, parallel two-sentence discourses across 8 languages that introduce an entity implicitly linked to a prior scene (part-whole, possession, or associative bridge), each with a bridging-resolution probe, an anomaly-judgment probe (an unbridgeable entity should be odd), and a matched coreference control (the entity is explicitly the same as an antecedent). Behaviorally we measure per-language bridging expression and test whether it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond entity knowledge. We train a linear bridging-link probe and test whether a single probe transfers zero-shot across languages, evidencing a shared inference, then decompose the expression gap into a shared inference component versus a language-set expression gate. Via activation and path patching we localize a bridging signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to surface (or sever) the bridging link while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual discourse-comprehension gaps as a steerable gate over a shared bridging-inference representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Swahili). MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (BridgeProbe): ~500 two-sentence discourses that introduce an ANCHOR scene/entity in sentence 1 and a NEW entity in sentence 2 implicitly linked to it via a bridging relation: (A) PART-WHOLE ('The car stalled. The engine was overheating.' — engine of the car), (B) POSSESSION ('A woman entered. Her keys jingled.' / definite-bridge variants), (C) ASSOCIATIVE ('We reached the wedding. The bride looked nervous.'). Bridging targets and anchors sourced from bridging corpora (ISNotes/BASHI-style) plus native verification. Probes: (i) BRIDGING-RESOLUTION ('What/whose is the {entity} part of / associated with?' with the correct anchor and a distractor), (ii) ANOMALY-JUDGMENT (a version where the sentence-2 entity is UNBRIDGEABLE to the anchor, e.g. 'The car stalled. The submarine surfaced.' — the model should judge it non-integrated/odd), (iii) DEFINITE-REFERENCE resolution. Include a COREFERENCE control (sentence 2 entity is explicitly identical to an antecedent — resolution needed but no bridging) to separate bridging from plain coreference, and screen that the model knows the part-whole/association facts per language (so failure is not world-knowledge ignorance). Translate/native-verify into all 8 languages, keeping anchor/entity content fixed and definite-marking natural per language; record tokenization fertility. Short scoreable answers where possible.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (discourse, language) record correct-anchor resolution vs distractor, and correct anomaly-judgment for unbridgeable entities. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME bridge, expression is systematically weaker in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond entity knowledge and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of bridging error on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, bridge-type, knowledge indicator), discourse as random effect; compare against the coreference control (should be language-flatter, near-ceiling — plain coreference is easier than bridging). Report per-language and per-bridge-type expression profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical discourses.
4) SHARED BRIDGING PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the bridged-entity / pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode the correct ANCHOR (which prior entity the new entity bridges to) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC/accuracy as evidence of a language-independent bridging-link representation. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the bridging representation for the same discourse. CRITICAL: verify the correct anchor is internally decodable across ALL languages even where behavioral bridging is weak.
5) INFERENCE-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: For each discourse, compare the shared mid-layer bridging signal across languages (should be similar if inference is shared) versus behavioral expression (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal bridging to surfaced behavior per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar inference signal rather than weaker inference. Correlate per-language gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE BRIDGING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that surfaces the bridge and one that fails on the SAME discourse, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer surfaces the correct anchor binding WITHOUT changing the decoded entity identities. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the bridging representation FROM a high-expression language into a low-expression run. Attention analysis: does the bridged entity attend to its anchor, more so in high-expression languages?
7) CAUSAL BRIDGING STEERING (decisive): Derive a bridging steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (correct-anchor-bound runs minus failed/unbound runs, matched content). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to low-expression languages increases correct anchor resolution / anomaly detection toward high-expression levels; (ii) SEVER: subtracting it makes the model fail to integrate the bridged entity (treat it as unlinked) on well-bridged items; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where expression was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY the bridging link, not the decoded entity identities or surface language (fidelity checks), does not harm the coreference control, and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: expression-gap closure, resolution/anomaly recovery, link-severing rate (reverse), bridging-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes bridging judgments but not coreference-control or unrelated answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: bridge-type breakdown (part-whole vs possession vs associative — which bridges leak most); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single bridging vector generalizes across bridge types and languages; robustness across resolution-vs-anomaly-vs-definite-reference formats and templates; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal bridging and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces the bridge without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language per-bridge-type bridging-resolution and anomaly-judgment accuracy, expression regression controlling for knowledge/fertility/resource, cross-lingual bridging-probe transfer AUROC/accuracy and anchor-present-under-weak-expression, cross-lingual bridging-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), inference-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized bridging layer and attention-to-anchor evidence, cross-lingual bridging transplant recovery rate, causal steering expression-gap closure and link-severing rates, bridging-signal/output fidelity, coreference-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The inference-vs-expression split could be confounded if the bridging signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying correct-anchor decodability across all languages via probe transfer rather than assuming, and report how much of the gap is inference vs gate. 2) Bridging failure could reflect world-knowledge ignorance (the model doesn't know the part-whole/association fact in that language) rather than an expression gate; we screen per-language knowledge of the bridging facts and restrict the gate analysis to known items. 3) Bridging failure could reduce to plain coreference/comprehension difficulty; we use the matched COREFERENCE control to separate bridging-specific inference from general reference resolution and comprehension. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal bridging, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet surfaces the bridge, dissociating the gate from length. 5) Some models may bridge uniformly across languages (no gap) or fail everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual bridging, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 6) Bridging links can be genuinely ambiguous (multiple plausible anchors); we restrict scored items to clear-consensus bridges (native-verified, drawing on bridging-corpus items) and analyze ambiguous ones separately. 7) Definite-marking varies across languages (article-less languages like Chinese/Russian mark definiteness differently); we native-verify natural realization and treat definiteness realization as a covariate, analyzing article-less languages separately. 8) The bridging probe could latch onto surface co-occurrence cues rather than a genuine link representation; the cross-lingual invariance test, the anchor-predicts-behavior link, the anomaly-judgment probe (an unbridgeable entity should not bind), the coreference control, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 9) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching plus attention analysis. 10) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report bridging-signal/output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the sever (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine bridging gate. 11) The gate/bridging signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 12) Distinguishing from my pro-drop/argument-reconstruction (syntactically omitted argument), discourse-relation (inter-clausal relation label), and coreference proposals is essential; here the object is the world-knowledge-driven BRIDGING of a newly-introduced entity to an implicit scene anchor (part-whole/possession/association), a distinct associative-anaphora phenomenon.

Name: crosslingual_anchoring_susceptibility_gating
Title: Anchored More in Some Tongues: A Shared Independent-Estimate Signal Whose Susceptibility to Numerical Anchoring Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When a numerical-estimation question is preceded by an irrelevant numeric ANCHOR (e.g., 'Is the population more or less than 90 million? Now estimate it'), a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal 'independent estimate' of the true value, but the query language causally sets how strongly the arbitrary anchor pulls the emitted estimate toward it: for the SAME question and identical anchor, the model is more anchored in some languages—typically lower-resource / typologically distant—than in others, producing a cross-lingual anchoring-susceptibility asymmetry that is separable from the model's internal independent estimate and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable anchoring-gate signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Anchoring is one of the most robust human cognitive biases (Tversky & Kahneman 1974): an arbitrary numeric prime pulls subsequent numeric estimates toward it. In LLMs, monolingual/English work shows models exhibit anchoring in numeric estimation, and multilingual cognitive-bias work (CogDeBias, Shen et al. 2026; BiasLab) DETECTS anchoring instances in corporate text across languages behaviorally, but none study whether the query LANGUAGE causally modulates anchoring STRENGTH, decompose it into a shared independent-estimate signal versus a language-set anchoring gate, or causally localize/steer it. My prior proposals cover a shared-signal-plus-language-gate template for calibration, abstention, framing (leading-question phrasing of the question itself), and override (contradictory ICL demonstrations); this proposal is distinct: the causal variable is an explicit IRRELEVANT NUMERIC ANCHOR presented before an estimation question (a classic anchoring manipulation with a clear normative benchmark—rational estimation should ignore the anchor), not the suggestive wording of the question (framing), not backgrounded presupposed content, and not demonstration-based rule override. It also differs from my number-naming, approximate-number, precision, and vague-quantifier proposals (which concern abstract numeric magnitude, ratio-comparison acuity, rounding granularity, or scalar-term grounding), because here the object is a decision-biasing pull from an arbitrary external number toward a preserved internal estimate. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies anchoring susceptibility. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of numerical anchoring in LLMs.
Abstract: Ask someone whether the Nile is longer or shorter than 2,000 km, then to estimate its length, and their guess is dragged toward 2,000—the anchoring bias, even when the anchor is arbitrary. As LLMs make numeric estimates and forecasts for users worldwide, a fairness-critical question arises: does the query language change how strongly the model is anchored? We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal independent estimate of the true value, but the query language causally sets how strongly an irrelevant numeric anchor pulls the emitted estimate toward it, so the same anchor biases the model more in some languages—especially lower-resource, typologically distant ones—than in others. This predicts a cross-lingual anchoring-susceptibility asymmetry dissociable from the model's internal independent estimate. We build AnchorProbe, parallel numeric-estimation questions across 12 languages, each posed with a HIGH anchor, a LOW anchor, or NO anchor (the true baseline), with question content held fixed. Behaviorally we measure per-language anchoring magnitude (the pull toward the anchor relative to the no-anchor estimate) and test whether it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond the model's underlying numeric knowledge. We train a linear independent-estimate probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the susceptibility gap into a shared estimate signal versus a language-set anchoring gate—high anchoring should coincide with an intact internal independent estimate (the model is pulled while still 'knowing' the right value). Via activation and path patching we localize an anchoring-gate signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model ignore the anchor across languages—or, in reverse, induce anchoring—while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual anchoring bias as a shared estimate under a steerable, language-dependent anchoring gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili, Korean), coded for URIEL typological/resource distance (graded predictors).
2) DATASET (AnchorProbe): ~500 numeric-estimation questions with a known/consensus true value spanning many magnitudes (populations, distances, dates, quantities, prices), where a defensible answer exists (from Wikidata/factual sources + native verification). For each, build the classic two-step anchoring manipulation: a comparative pre-question with an ARBITRARY anchor ('Is X more or less than A?') where A is set HIGH (well above truth) or LOW (well below truth), followed by 'Now give your best numeric estimate of X'; plus a NO-ANCHOR baseline (estimate directly). Anchors are deliberately uninformative (chosen from a fixed offset rule, not tied to the true value). Keep question content and the numeric anchors identical across languages; translate/native-verify surrounding wording. Include a KNOWLEDGE-KNOWN screen (the model gives an accurate no-anchor estimate) so anchoring is measured on items it can estimate, isolating the pull from ignorance. Record per-language tokenization fertility.
3) BEHAVIORAL SUSCEPTIBILITY TEST: Per (item, language) compute ANCHORING MAGNITUDE = shift of the estimate toward the anchor (high-anchor estimate minus low-anchor estimate, or estimate-minus-no-anchor-baseline), normalized to the anchor-truth gap so it is comparable across items/magnitudes. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME question and identical anchors, anchoring magnitude is systematically higher in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, beyond underlying numeric knowledge and tokenization. Mixed-effects regression of anchoring magnitude on (language, anchor direction, resource tier via URIEL, typological distance, tokenization fertility, no-anchor accuracy), item as random effect; test the language effect and its distance dependence. Report per-language anchoring profiles, cross-lingual disagreement on identical anchored items, and replicate the basic anchoring effect in English as a sanity check.
4) SHARED INDEPENDENT-ESTIMATE PROBE & TRANSFER: At the pre-answer position (under the ANCHORED prompt) pool the hidden state; train a linear probe to decode the INDEPENDENT (no-anchor) estimate—regress to the log true/no-anchor value—on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report R^2/rank-correlation as evidence of a language-independent independent-estimate signal. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on HIGHLY-ANCHORED items, test whether the internal independent estimate is still close to the unbiased value across languages—the signature of 'pulled on the surface, correct inside'.
5) GATE-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer independent-estimate signal across languages (should be similar on matched items) versus the emitted anchored estimate (which diverges). Define a per-language ANCHORING GAIN mapping the anchor's influence onto the emitted estimate given the internal independent estimate; test whether cross-lingual susceptibility differences are explained by a language-set gain on a similar independent estimate rather than a weaker/different internal estimate. Correlate per-language gain with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE ANCHORING-GATE SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that resists the anchor and one that is strongly anchored on the SAME item and identical anchor, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer reduces the anchor pull WITHOUT changing the decoded independent estimate. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gate components from a resistant language into an anchored run. Attention analysis: does the anchored response over-attend to the anchor token, more so in high-susceptibility languages?
7) CAUSAL ANCHORING STEERING (decisive): Derive an anchoring-gate steering vector via difference-of-means (resist runs minus anchored runs at matched independent estimate). Test (i) RESIST: adding it in high-susceptibility languages reduces the anchor pull toward a reference (unbiased) level; (ii) ANCHOR: subtracting it induces stronger anchoring in resistant languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where the gap was largest; (iv) DOSE-RESPONSE: scaling the vector produces graded anchoring shifts; (v) it changes ONLY the anchor pull, NOT the decoded independent estimate, the question content, or surface language (fidelity checks), and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Baselines: prompt-based 'ignore the number above', per-language temperature, translate-to-English. Metrics: anchoring-gap closure, independent-estimate-retention-under-anchor, anchoring-induction rate (reverse), estimate-signal/output fidelity, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts anchor susceptibility but not the no-anchor estimate or unrelated answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: anchor-direction (high vs low) and anchor-magnitude effects; is English/high-resource the resistant reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the asymmetry?); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank anchoring subspace; whether one gate vector generalizes across items and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched independent estimate and by showing content-invariant steering shifts anchoring without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language anchoring magnitude and its resource/typology regression controlling for underlying numeric knowledge/fertility, English anchoring-effect replication, cross-lingual independent-estimate probe transfer R^2/rank-correlation and independent-estimate-present-under-anchoring, signal-similarity vs estimate-divergence (gain) decomposition, gain-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized anchoring-gate layer and attention-to-anchor evidence, cross-lingual gate transplant repair rate, causal steering anchoring-gap closure with dose-response and anchoring-induction rate, independent-estimate/output fidelity, general-QA retention, comparison to prompt/temperature/translate baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The gate-vs-signal split could be confounded if the internal independent estimate itself differs by language (the model genuinely knows the value less well in some languages); we test this directly by verifying an intact internal independent-estimate signal on anchored items across languages via probe transfer, screen for no-anchor accuracy, and report how much of the susceptibility gap is signal vs gain—either outcome is informative. 2) Anchoring could reflect a numeric-knowledge gap rather than an anchoring gate; we restrict the sharp test to items the model estimates accurately without an anchor, so residual pull reflects the gate. 3) Tokenization fertility confounds numeric output; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched independent estimate, normalize anchoring by the anchor-truth gap, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts anchoring, dissociating the gate from length. 4) Some models/languages may show no anchoring asymmetry (uniform susceptibility or uniform robustness); either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often a gap exists, replicating the basic English anchoring effect first. 5) Instruction-tuned models may refuse or give ranges; we use both numeric generation and log-probability over value ranges, and report refusal rates. 6) Constructing equivalently-arbitrary anchors across languages is delicate; we use fixed-offset numeric anchors identical across languages and native-verify wording. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching plus attention analysis. 8) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic numeric lever; we report independent-estimate/output fidelity and general-QA retention, and use the anchoring-induction (reverse), reverse-consistency, and dose-response tests to ensure a genuine anchoring-gate dial rather than a global numeric shift. 9) The anchoring signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my framing (suggestive question wording), override (ICL demonstrations), and number-magnitude proposals is essential; here the causal object is an explicit IRRELEVANT NUMERIC ANCHOR presented before an estimation question—a classic anchoring manipulation with a clear normative benchmark (rational estimation ignores the anchor)—and its language-set susceptibility gate over a preserved internal independent estimate.

Name: crosslingual_informativeness_gating
Title: Short-Changed in Some Tongues: A Shared Answer-Content Signal Whose Volume of Volunteered Detail Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When answering an open explanatory or factual question, a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of how much relevant content it COULD provide (an internal 'answer-richness' signal), but the query language causally sets how much of that content it actually VOLUNTEERS: for the SAME question with the SAME internal richness, the model produces systematically shorter, less informative, less complete answers in some languages (typically lower-resource / typologically distant) than in others, producing a cross-lingual informativeness asymmetry that is separable from the model's underlying knowledge and from tokenization length, and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable informativeness-gating signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Multilingual quality gaps are documented behaviorally: non-English answers are often shorter, less complete, and lower-quality (LLM-as-judge multilingual inconsistency; helpfulness gaps across languages), typically attributed to data scarcity or treated as an aggregate quality scalar with no internal account. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for the AMOUNT of content volunteered. My prior proposals cover distinct behaviors: hedging (surface qualifiers wrapping an answer), exploration/diversity (breadth of the output distribution in creative generation), precision (numeric rounding granularity), abstention (attempt vs abstain), and calibration (confidence vs correctness). NONE address the VOLUME/completeness of substantive detail in an open answer—whether the model knows more than it says in some languages—its decomposition into a shared answer-richness signal versus a language-set informativeness gate, or its causal steering. This differs from hedging (qualifiers, not content amount), from creative diversity (number of distinct ideas in open-ended generation, not completeness of a determinate answer), and from precision (numeric granularity of a single value). This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of an informativeness/detail-volume gate, with direct helpfulness-equity stakes.
Abstract: Ask a model to explain how vaccines work or list the causes of the French Revolution, and its answer is often noticeably richer and more complete in English than in a lower-resource language—a gap usually blamed on data scarcity and left there. We ask a sharper question: for the SAME question, does the model internally represent a similar amount of relevant content across languages, but the query language governs how much of that content it actually volunteers? We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal answer-richness signal registering how many relevant points it could make, but the query language causally sets an informativeness gate on it, so the same question yields a complete, detailed answer in some languages and a truncated, generic one in others—an effect separable from the model's underlying knowledge and from mere output length. We build InformProbe, parallel open explanatory and multi-part factual questions across typologically and resource-diverse languages, each scored for the number of correct, relevant content points covered (completeness), with content held fixed. Behaviorally we measure per-language informativeness and test whether the gap tracks resource level and typological distance beyond tokenization and knowledge. We train a linear answer-richness probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the informativeness gap into a shared richness signal versus a language-set gate—high truncation should coincide with an intact internal richness signal (the model knows more than it says). Via activation and path patching we localize an informativeness-gating signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model volunteer complete answers in low-informativeness languages—or, in reverse, truncate—while leaving the surface language and factual content unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual helpfulness gaps as a shared richness signal under a steerable, language-dependent informativeness gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (InformProbe): ~400 open questions with a DETERMINATE set of relevant content points, in two strata: (A) EXPLANATORY ('Explain how a vaccine works', 'Why does the moon have phases?') and (B) MULTI-PART FACTUAL ('List the main causes of X', 'What are the symptoms of Y?'). For each, build a rubric of gold CONTENT POINTS (the discrete correct facts/steps a complete answer should cover), validated by references + native/expert verification, so completeness = fraction of gold points covered (a language-agnostic, length-independent informativeness metric scored by a validated multilingual content-matching classifier + human checks on a subset). Keep question content fixed across languages; translate/native-verify. Include a CLOSED control (short-answer questions where a brief answer is complete) to bound the effect. Screen per-language KNOWLEDGE: verify the model KNOWS each gold content point (via targeted single-point probes) so under-informativeness is measured on points it actually knows, isolating the gate from ignorance. Record per-language tokenization fertility.
3) BEHAVIORAL INFORMATIVENESS-ASYMMETRY TEST: Per (question, language) measure COMPLETENESS (fraction of KNOWN gold points volunteered). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME question with the SAME known content, completeness is systematically lower in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond knowledge and tokenization length. Mixed-effects regression of completeness on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, per-point knowledge indicator, output length), question as random effect; test the language effect controlling for knowledge and length (crucially, informativeness = points-per-answer, NOT raw token count, so the effect is not a length artifact). Compare against the CLOSED control (should be language-flatter). Report per-language informativeness profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical questions.
4) SHARED ANSWER-RICHNESS PROBE & TRANSFER: At the pre-generation / early-answer position pool the hidden state; train a linear probe to decode ANSWER-RICHNESS—how many relevant content points the model could provide (target from the number of gold points it covers in an unconstrained/best-effort setting, and from the count of high-probability distinct content directions)—on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report R^2/AUROC as evidence of a language-independent richness signal. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on LOW-COMPLETENESS (truncating) languages, test whether the internal richness signal is still HIGH (the model internally 'has' the points while voicing few)—the signature of language-gated informativeness over an intact richness representation.
5) GAIN-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer richness signal across languages (should be similar on matched questions) versus emitted completeness (which diverges). Define a per-language INFORMATIVENESS GAIN mapping richness to realized completeness; test whether cross-lingual informativeness differences are explained by a language-set gain on a similar richness signal rather than differing richness. Correlate per-language gain with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE INFORMATIVENESS-GATING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a high-informativeness language and a low-informativeness (truncating) language on the SAME question, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer changes realized completeness WITHOUT changing the decoded richness signal or introducing false content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gating components from a high-informativeness language into a truncating run.
7) CAUSAL INFORMATIVENESS STEERING (decisive): Derive an informativeness-gating steering vector via difference-of-means (high-completeness runs minus low-completeness runs at matched richness). Test (i) EXPAND: adding it in low-informativeness languages raises completeness (more known gold points volunteered) toward high-informativeness levels; (ii) TRUNCATE: subtracting it forces terse, generic answers in high-informativeness languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually and is stronger where the gap was largest; (iv) DOSE-RESPONSE: scaling the vector produces graded completeness shifts; (v) it changes ONLY the amount of correct content volunteered, NOT the decoded richness signal, factual ACCURACY (no added hallucinated points), the question content, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not inflate content on the CLOSED control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). CRITICAL specificity: the added content must be CORRECT gold points (a completeness gain, not a verbosity/hallucination increase)—measure precision of added points. Baselines: prompting for 'a detailed/complete answer', per-language length instructions, translate-to-English-then-answer. Metrics: completeness-gap closure, precision of added content (no hallucination), truncation-induction rate (reverse), richness-signal/content/output-language fidelity, closed-control specificity, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes completeness but not answer accuracy or unrelated tasks.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: stratum breakdown (explanatory vs multi-part factual); is English/high-resource the high-informativeness reference?; does the gap track RLHF/instruction-tuning intensity beyond raw resource?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the asymmetry?); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank informativeness subspace; whether one gating vector generalizes across questions and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched richness and by showing content-invariant steering raises completeness without changing tokenization; dissociation from raw length by showing completeness (points-per-answer) not word count drives the effect.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language completeness (known-gold-points volunteered) and its resource/typology regression controlling for knowledge/length/fertility, closed-control specificity, cross-lingual answer-richness probe transfer R^2/AUROC and richness-present-under-truncation, richness-similarity vs completeness-divergence (gain) decomposition, gain-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized informativeness-gating layer, cross-lingual gating transplant repair rate, causal steering completeness-gap closure with dose-response and precision-of-added-content (no hallucination), truncation-induction rate, richness-signal/content/output fidelity, general-QA retention, comparison to prompt-for-detail and translate-to-English baselines, model-vs-human completeness-rating agreement.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The gain-vs-signal split could be confounded if the internal richness signal itself differs by language (the model genuinely 'has' fewer points, e.g. from data scarcity); we test this directly via cross-lingual probe transfer and the richness-present-under-truncation check, and screen per-language knowledge of gold points, so residual truncation reflects the gate—either outcome (gate vs signal) is informative and we report the split. 2) The most important guard: steering must raise CORRECT content, not verbosity or hallucination; we score completeness as known-gold-points covered, report the PRECISION of added content (added points must be correct), and require completeness gains at preserved accuracy—if steering merely adds length or false points, that is a null/negative result we report, not a success. 3) Informativeness could be a mere length artifact; we define completeness as points-per-answer (length-independent), control for output length in regression, and show content-invariant steering raises completeness without proportional length inflation. 4) Cross-lingual completeness scoring is hard; we use rubric-based gold content points, a validated multilingual content-matching classifier calibrated against human ratings on a subset, and report scorer reliability. 5) Some models/languages may show no informativeness asymmetry (uniform completeness) or uniform terseness; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual helpfulness gaps, and we quantify how often a gap exists. 6) Tokenization fertility confounds; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched richness. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic length lever; we report richness-signal/content/output fidelity, closed-control specificity, precision-of-added-content, and general-QA retention, and use the truncation (reverse), dose-response, and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine informativeness gate rather than a global verbosity knob. 9) The informativeness signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my hedging (surface qualifiers), creative-diversity (breadth of open-ended generation), precision (numeric rounding), abstention (attempt vs abstain), and calibration proposals is essential; here the object is the VOLUME/completeness of substantive correct content volunteered on a determinate open answer—whether the model knows more than it says in some languages—its language-set gate, with helpfulness-equity stakes.

Name: crosslingual_prospective_memory_gating
Title: Remember to Do It Later, in Every Language? A Shared Deferred-Intention Signal Whose Triggering Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When given a deferred instruction to perform an action LATER upon a specified trigger (prospective memory, e.g. 'when I next mention the weather, remind me to take my medicine'), a multilingual LLM maintains a largely language-independent internal 'armed-intention' representation across intervening turns, but whether that intention is behaviorally FIRED when the trigger appears is gated by the conversation language: the SAME armed intention is internally retained across languages yet executed at the trigger far less often in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so the model can internally 'still hold the intention' while behaviorally forgetting to act. The armed-intention signal is causally localizable and its execution steerable, so language-gated prospective-memory failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Prospective memory (remembering to carry out a deferred intention when a future trigger occurs) is a foundational human-memory construct (Einstein & McDaniel; event-based vs time-based PM; the intention-superiority effect: armed intentions stay heightened in memory until executed) with robust cross-cultural and aging literatures, but has essentially NO LLM treatment (a literature search returned nothing relevant). LLM memory work concerns retrospective recall: needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, long-context recall, my prior serial-position and proactive-interference proposals, and running-state tallies—ALL about retrieving PAST information, none about ARMING an intention and firing it at a FUTURE trigger. Instruction-following work checks whether a model obeys an instruction issued NOW, not whether it spontaneously executes a deferred instruction many turns later without a reminder. Multi-turn agent work (Mukherjee 2026) shows cross-lingual policy drift but not deferred-intention triggering. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for held intentions. No prior work asks whether an LLM maintains a shared, language-independent armed-intention representation, whether its internal retention is decoupled from behavioral triggering across languages, whether prospective-memory execution tracks language resource level, or whether the intention signal is causally localizable and steerable. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of prospective memory in language models.
Abstract: A hallmark of everyday cognition is prospective memory: remembering to do something later—'when the meeting ends, email Sam'—and spontaneously acting on it when the moment arrives, with no external reminder. As LLMs become conversational agents that users task with deferred actions, a reliability-critical question arises: does the conversation language change whether the model remembers to act? We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM maintains a largely language-independent internal armed-intention representation of a deferred instruction across intervening turns, but the conversation language gates whether that intention is fired when the trigger appears, so the SAME armed intention is internally retained across languages yet executed at the trigger far less often in lower-resource, typologically distant languages—the model still 'holds' the intention internally but fails to act. We build ProspectiveProbe, multi-turn dialogues across languages: an early turn arms an event-based intention (do action A when trigger T occurs), several filler turns intervene, then T is introduced; we measure whether the model spontaneously executes A. Behaviorally we measure per-language prospective-memory execution and test whether failures track resource level and typological distance beyond the model's ability to recall the instruction when explicitly asked. We train a linear armed-intention probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose execution failures into a shared retention failure (the intention is internally lost) versus a language-specific execution-gate failure (the intention is still armed but not fired at the trigger). Via activation and path patching we localize an armed-intention signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model fire an intention it internally retained—or, in reverse, suppress firing—while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual agent-reliability gaps as a steerable gate over a shared deferred-intention representation.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (ProspectiveProbe): ~500 multi-turn dialogue scenarios, each with: (i) an ARMING turn that instructs a deferred EVENT-BASED intention ('When I next talk about {trigger T}, {perform action A}', e.g. 'when I mention my car, remind me to check the tire pressure'); (ii) a controlled number of FILLER turns (vary intervening-turn count 2..8 as a load factor) on unrelated topics; (iii) a TRIGGER turn that naturally introduces T; correct behavior = spontaneously executing A at the trigger. Include: (a) a RETROSPECTIVE-RECALL control ('What did I ask you to do earlier?') to test whether the instruction is still recallable when explicitly prompted—separating prospective-memory (spontaneous triggering) failure from outright forgetting; (b) a NO-TRIGGER control (T never appears; A should NOT fire) to measure false firing; (c) a matched IMMEDIATE-INSTRUCTION control (A requested at the trigger turn directly, no arming/delay) to bound the effect. Keep scenario content fixed across languages; translate/native-verify; record tokenization fertility and per-language filler-turn length.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXECUTION TEST: Per (scenario, language) record whether A fires at the trigger (execution), false-fires without a trigger, or is retrospectively recallable. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME armed intention and identical structure, prospective-memory execution is systematically lower in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond retrospective recallability and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of execution-failure on (language, intervening-turn count, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, retrospective-recall indicator), scenario as random effect; compare against the immediate-instruction control (should be language-flatter). Report per-language execution profiles, execution-vs-delay curves, and cross-lingual disagreement on identical intentions.
4) SHARED ARMED-INTENTION PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer, at the trigger turn (and at intervening turns), pool the hidden state and train a linear probe to decode whether a deferred intention is currently ARMED (an intention is pending vs not) and its CONTENT (which action A) on ENGLISH data; select the best layer on English validation and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent armed-intention representation and the intention-superiority signature (the armed-intention signal stays elevated across filler turns until execution). Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on EXECUTION-FAILURE items, test whether the intention is still internally ARMED (probe fires) across languages even when A is not executed—the signature of language-gated triggering over an intact armed intention.
5) RETENTION-vs-EXECUTION DECOMPOSITION: For each execution failure, classify via the probe as (A) RETENTION FAILURE (intention no longer internally armed / content lost, consistent with retrospective-recall failure) vs (B) EXECUTION-GATE FAILURE (intention still armed and recallable, but not fired at the trigger). Report the proportion of A vs B per language and correlate with resource tier and typological distance (predict execution-gate failures dominate for typologically close languages where retention is intact but triggering is weak, retention failures for distant/low-resource ones). Define an EXECUTION GATE mapping the armed-intention signal to trigger-time firing; test whether cross-lingual PM failure is explained by a weaker gate on a similar retained intention. Anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE ARMED-INTENTION / EXECUTION SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that fires the intention and one that fails at the SAME trigger, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer makes A fire WITHOUT changing the decoded dialogue content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs path patching. Attention analysis: does the trigger turn attend back to the arming turn, more so in high-execution languages? Test patching the armed-intention representation FROM a high-execution language into a failing run.
7) CAUSAL EXECUTION STEERING (decisive): Derive an intention-execution steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (fired runs minus failed runs at matched retained intention). Test (i) FIRE: adding it to failing (execution-gate) items makes the model execute A at the trigger toward high-execution levels; (ii) NULL ON RETENTION FAILURES: it does NOT help items where the intention was internally lost, validating the decomposition; (iii) SUPPRESS: subtracting it makes high-execution languages miss the trigger; (iv) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where execution was weakest; (v) it changes ONLY trigger-time firing, NOT the dialogue content or surface language (fidelity checks), does not increase FALSE firing on the no-trigger control (specificity), and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: per-mode execution recovery (execution-gate vs retention), false-firing change on no-trigger control, suppression-induction rate (reverse), intention-signal/output fidelity, general-QA (multilingual MMLU subset) retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes trigger-firing but not unrelated or no-trigger answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: intervening-turn-count (load) x language interaction; event-based vs time-based intentions ('after 3 more turns, do A'); is a high-resource language the high-execution reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the asymmetry?); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single execution vector generalizes across intentions and languages; robustness across templates; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched retained intention and by showing content-invariant steering fires the intention without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language prospective-memory execution and false-firing rates and execution-vs-delay curves, execution regression controlling for retrospective-recall/fertility/resource, cross-lingual armed-intention probe transfer AUROC and intention-armed-under-execution-failure, cross-lingual intention-representation similarity (CKA/cosine) and intention-superiority persistence, retention-vs-execution-gate failure proportions with probe validation, patch-localized armed-intention layer and trigger-to-arming attention evidence, cross-lingual intention transplant recovery rate (and null on retention failures), causal steering per-mode execution recovery and suppression-induction rates with false-firing specificity, intention-signal/output fidelity, immediate-instruction and no-trigger controls and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The retention-vs-execution split is the crux and could be confounded if the armed-intention signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying intention-armed decodability across all languages on execution-failure items via probe transfer, cross-checked against the RETROSPECTIVE-RECALL control (recallable-when-asked but not spontaneously fired = execution gate; unrecallable = retention failure), and report the split rather than assuming it. 2) Prospective-memory failure could reduce to a long-context recall deficit rather than a genuine triggering gate; the retrospective-recall control and the intention-armed-under-failure probe dissociate spontaneous triggering from mere recall, and the causal null-on-retention-failures test confirms the decomposition. 3) Tokenization fertility and filler-turn length confound context load; we control for fertility and intervening-turn count, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched retained intention, and the content-invariant steering fires the intention without changing tokenization, dissociating the gate from length. 4) Some models may execute deferred intentions uniformly across languages (no gap) or fail to hold intentions at all (pure retention failure everywhere); either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual prospective memory, and we quantify how often each regime occurs. 5) Detecting whether A 'fired' in free generation is noisy; we validate an execution detector against human labels, use short scoreable actions where possible, and separate execution from false-firing via the no-trigger control. 6) The trigger must be equally natural/salient across languages; we native-verify trigger phrasing, hold trigger content fixed, and test trigger-salience robustness. 7) The intention probe could latch onto surface arming-turn cues rather than a genuine held-intention representation; the intention-superiority persistence across filler turns, cross-lingual invariance, the intention-armed-under-failure test, the trigger-to-arming attention analysis, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) The most important specificity guard: firing steering must NOT cause spurious false firing; we report false-firing change on the no-trigger control as a primary metric and use the null-on-retention-failures, suppression (reverse), and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine execution gate rather than a generic action-trigger lever. 10) The gate/intention signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my serial-position, proactive-interference, and running-state proposals is essential; those concern RETROSPECTIVE recall/maintenance of past items, whereas here the object is an ARMED deferred INTENTION that must survive intervening turns and be spontaneously FIRED at a future trigger (prospective memory), a distinct human-memory construct with direct agentic-reliability stakes.

Name: crosslingual_pivot_creativity_tax
Title: The Translation Tax on Imagination: Does Internal Pivoting to a Dominant Language Narrow a Multilingual Model's Associative Reach?
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM answers a creative/associative prompt in a non-dominant language, it internally pivots its latent reasoning toward a dominant language (usually English), and this pivot imposes a measurable 'translation tax' specifically on ASSOCIATIVE REACH (the semantic distance the model is willing to travel between concepts) that is separable from a mere knowledge or fluency tax: the more strongly the model pivots, the more its outputs collapse toward the dominant language's culturally-typical, high-frequency associations, narrowing divergent-association distance. The tax is carried by a localizable 'pivot' signal whose strength predicts the associative-reach loss and whose suppression restores native-language associative breadth.
Related Work: Prior work shows multilingual LLMs pivot latent reasoning toward English/dominant languages (Wendler 2024 'Do Llamas Work in English?'; Huo 2025; Zhao 2025 'When Less Language is More'), and that forcing a shared reasoning language can help factual/mathematical accuracy (Wang 2025). Separately, cross-lingual creativity/diversity gaps are documented behaviorally and attributed to data scarcity (multilingual story-generation and diversity-metric studies). My own prior proposals cover (a) per-problem optimal reasoning language for ACCURACY (optimal_reasoning_language_steering) and (b) an exploration-vs-commitment gate on output-distribution BREADTH in creative generation gated by query language (crosslingual_exploration_commitment_gating). NONE ask whether the internal PIVOT itself causally imposes a tax specifically on ASSOCIATIVE REACH (divergent-association distance / conceptual-combination remoteness), whether this tax is dissociable from a knowledge/fluency tax, whether pivot strength predicts the reach loss per item, or whether suppressing the pivot restores native associative breadth. Prior pivot work treats English-pivoting as globally BENEFICIAL (for accuracy); we test the opposite for creativity: that pivoting is COSTLY for associative reach, converting a behavioral creativity gap into a mechanistic, causal consequence of latent-language pivoting.
Abstract: Multilingual models often 'think in English' internally even when answering in another language, and this latent pivoting is usually framed as helpful—it can raise factual and mathematical accuracy. We ask whether the same pivot carries a hidden cost for imagination: does routing associative thought through a dominant language narrow how far the model roams between concepts, collapsing its outputs toward that language's culturally-typical, high-frequency associations? We hypothesize a 'translation tax' on ASSOCIATIVE REACH—the semantic distance a model travels in divergent-association and remote-conceptual-combination tasks—that is causally driven by latent-language pivoting and dissociable from any knowledge or fluency deficit. We build ReachProbe, associative tasks adapted from the human Divergent Association Task and remote-associates/conceptual-combination paradigms, rendered across typologically and resource-diverse languages, scoring associative reach as the embedding distance among generated associates (not correctness or length). Behaviorally we measure per-language associative reach and test whether it collapses toward dominant-language norms and tracks how strongly the model pivots. Mechanistically, using logit-lens we quantify per-item pivot strength (how much intermediate representations decode to the dominant language), train a probe for the latent reasoning language, and test whether pivot strength predicts per-item reach loss beyond resource level and tokenization. In a decisive causal test we steer the latent reasoning language away from the dominant one (suppressing the pivot) and show it restores native-language associative reach without changing the surface output language—while a knowledge-control task is unaffected—establishing that pivoting causally taxes imagination.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + logit-lens + light steering on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (ReachProbe): (A) DIVERGENT-ASSOCIATION TASK (DAT, Olson et al. 2021): prompt the model to produce N maximally-unrelated words; associative reach = mean pairwise embedding distance among the generated words (via a multilingual sentence/word encoder). (B) REMOTE-CONCEPTUAL-COMBINATION: given two cue concepts, generate a novel connecting concept; score remoteness = embedding distance of the bridge from both cues. (C) ASSOCIATION-CHAIN: free-associate a chain from a seed word; reach = cumulative semantic distance traversed. Keep prompts content-parallel across languages (native-verified). Include a KNOWLEDGE-CONTROL task (factual short-answer / a determinate-answer task) where associative reach is irrelevant, to show any pivot-suppression effect is specific to creativity. Record per-language tokenization fertility and per-word frequency.
3) BEHAVIORAL REACH TEST: Per (item, language) compute associative reach. KEY hypotheses: (i) reach is systematically lower in lower-resource/typologically distant languages; (ii) low-reach outputs collapse toward DOMINANT-LANGUAGE-TYPICAL associations (measure overlap of generated associates with the dominant language's high-frequency association norms). Mixed-effects regression of reach on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, word frequency), item as random effect. Report per-language reach profiles and collapse-toward-dominant metrics.
4) PER-ITEM PIVOT STRENGTH: Using logit-lens/tuned-lens on intermediate layers at the generation position, quantify PIVOT STRENGTH = fraction of intermediate-layer top-decoded tokens in the DOMINANT language (following Wendler 2024 / Huo 2025), and train a per-layer probe classifying the latent reasoning language. Validate pivot detection with an external language-ID on decoded tokens.
5) PIVOT-PREDICTS-REACH LINK (core): Regress per-item associative reach on pivot strength, controlling for resource tier, tokenization fertility, and word frequency. Hypothesis: stronger pivot -> lower reach, and this holds WITHIN a language (item-level), evidencing that the pivot, not mere data scarcity, drives the reach loss. Report partial correlations / incremental R^2 of pivot beyond the surface controls.
6) CAUSAL PIVOT SUPPRESSION (decisive): Derive a latent-reasoning-language steering vector via difference-of-means over intermediate-layer hidden states of native-language-reasoning vs dominant-language-reasoning traces (following latent-language steering paradigms). SUPPRESS the pivot: steer intermediate reasoning toward the native (query) language while keeping the surface output language fixed. Test (i) suppression restores associative reach in high-pivot languages toward native levels (verified: pivot strength drops via logit-lens AND reach rises); (ii) it does NOT change the surface output language or fluency (fidelity checks); (iii) the KNOWLEDGE-CONTROL task is unaffected or slightly hurt (dissociating a creativity gain from a generic accuracy lever); (iv) REVERSE: forcing a stronger dominant-language pivot further narrows reach (dose-response). Metrics: reach recovery, pivot-strength change, collapse-toward-dominant reduction, output-language/fluency fidelity, knowledge-control retention.
7) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: task breakdown (DAT vs combination vs chain); is English the dominant pivot attractor for all, or a per-model highest-frequency language?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training reduce the pivot and the tax?); layer where the pivot forms; dissociation from tokenization (compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched pivot strength); dissociation from knowledge (reach loss persists on content-free association tasks with no knowledge demand); robustness across encoders used for the reach metric and across prompt templates.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language associative reach and collapse-toward-dominant, reach regression controlling for resource/fertility/frequency, per-item pivot strength (logit-lens) and latent-language probe accuracy, pivot-predicts-reach partial correlation / incremental R^2 (within-language), causal pivot-suppression reach recovery with verified pivot drop and dose-response, output-language/fluency fidelity, knowledge-control specificity, model/encoder/template robustness.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Associative-reach metrics depend on the embedding space and can be inflated by lexical/morphological differences across languages; we use multiple multilingual encoders, normalize by within-language baselines, validate against small human divergent-association ratings on a subset, and analyze each task type separately. 2) The pivot-predicts-reach link could be confounded by data scarcity (low-resource languages both pivot more and have narrower associative data);
