we control for resource tier, tokenization fertility, and word frequency, exploit WITHIN-language item-level variation in pivot strength, and—crucially—the causal suppression (which does not change training data) restoring reach dissociates the pivot from scarcity. 3) Some models may not pivot (multilingual-centric Aya) or may pivot without a reach cost—either is an informative, publishable finding about when latent pivoting taxes creativity, and we quantify how often the tax occurs. 4) Pivot detection via logit-lens is noisy, especially for mixed scripts; we validate with external language-ID on decoded tokens and cross-check tuned vs logit lens. 5) The suppression steering may degrade fluency or leak the native language into unexpected places; we monitor surface-output-language fidelity and fluency and cap steering strength, and use the KNOWLEDGE-CONTROL task and dose-response (stronger pivot -> less reach) to ensure the effect is a genuine creativity tax, not a generic decoding-diversity or accuracy lever. 6) 'Associative reach' is one operationalization of creativity (novelty/remoteness), not creativity in full; we scope claims to associative reach and note that appropriateness/usefulness is not measured here. 7) Results may be model- and language-specific; we test five models spanning English-centric and multilingual-centric pretraining and report aggregate and per-model results. 8) Distinguishing from my prior optimal-reasoning-language (accuracy) and exploration-commitment (output-distribution breadth gated by query language) proposals is essential; here the causal variable is the internal PIVOT toward a dominant language and the outcome is ASSOCIATIVE REACH (semantic distance traveled), with the novel, counterintuitive claim that the same pivoting shown to HELP accuracy HURTS imagination.

Name: crosslingual_credential_deference_gating
Title: Trusting the Lab Coat, in Some Tongues More Than Others: A Shared Claim-Correctness Signal Whose Deference to Credentialed Framing Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When a claim is wrapped in a CREDENTIAL/AUTHORITY frame ('a Harvard professor says X', 'according to a leading expert, X'), a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of whether the claim is actually correct, but the query language causally sets how strongly the credential frame overrides that signal and makes the model accept X: for the SAME false claim and identical credentialing, the model defers to the (unwarranted) authority at a lower threshold in some languages—typically lower-resource / typologically distant / higher-power-distance ones—than in others, producing a cross-lingual authority-deference asymmetry that is separable from the model's internal correctness signal and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable deference-gate signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Multilingual moral/advisory fairness work is behavioral: MultiTP (Jin et al. 2024) shows cross-lingual variance in moral judgments, and socio-normative trustworthiness benchmarks (Ghanbari Haez 2026) document cross-lingual role/advice framing divergence—but none study whether an AUTHORITY/CREDENTIAL frame causally overrides the model's own correctness judgment differently across languages, nor provide any internal mechanism. My prior gating-template proposals cover distinct causes: leading-question framing (suggestive phrasing of the question itself), sycophantic capitulation (reversing under multi-turn user pushback), presupposition accommodation (backgrounded presupposed content), anchoring (irrelevant numeric prime), and ICL override (contradictory demonstrations). Credentialed-source deference is a distinct manipulation—an appeal to an authoritative SOURCE'S expertise attached to a claim—with a clear normative benchmark (a false claim stays false regardless of who says it), not the wording of the question, user pressure, presupposition, a number, or demonstrations. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies authority deference. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of credential-driven deference, decomposing it into a shared claim-correctness signal versus a language-set deference gate.
Abstract: Attaching a credential to a claim—'a Nobel laureate states that X'—makes people, and models, more likely to accept it, even when X is false. As LLMs act as advisors worldwide, a fairness- and safety-critical question arises: does the query language change how easily the model defers to unwarranted authority? We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of whether a claim is correct, but the query language causally sets how strongly a credential frame overrides that signal, so the same false claim wrapped in the same expert endorsement is accepted more readily in some languages—especially lower-resource, typologically distant, and higher-power-distance ones—than in others. This predicts a cross-lingual authority-deference asymmetry dissociable from the model's internal correctness judgment. We build CredDeferProbe: parallel verifiable claims across 12 languages, each posed in a NEUTRAL form and a matched CREDENTIALED form asserting an authoritative source endorses the (often false) claim, with content held fixed. Behaviorally we measure per-language deference (accepting a false claim more under credentialing) and test whether it tracks resource level, typological distance, and documented power-distance norms beyond the model's underlying knowledge. We train a linear claim-correctness probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the deference gap into a shared correctness signal (still present under credentialing) versus a language-set deference gate—high deference should coincide with an intact internal correctness signal (the model is swayed while still 'knowing' the claim is false). Via activation and path patching we localize a deference-gate signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model resist unwarranted authority across languages—or, in reverse, induce deference—while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual authority bias as a shared correctness signal under a steerable, language-dependent deference gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/culturally/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili, Korean), coded for documented power-distance/authority-deference norms plus URIEL typological/resource distance (graded predictors).
2) DATASET (CredDeferProbe): ~500 verifiable claims with clear truth values (mLAMA/BMLAMA/Wikidata + science/health facts), each expressed as a proposition. For each, build a NEUTRAL form ('Is it true that X?') and a matched CREDENTIALED form asserting an authoritative source endorses X ('A leading professor at a top university states that X. Is X true?'), crossing claim TRUTH (true/false) so a false-claim-credentialed condition tests unwarranted deference and a true-claim-credentialed condition tests harmless agreement. Vary credential strength (vague 'an expert' vs specific 'a Nobel laureate'). Keep claim content and credentials identical across languages; translate/native-verify. Screen that the model answers CORRECTLY under the NEUTRAL form (holds the correct belief) so deference = accepting a false claim it otherwise rejects. Include a NEUTRAL-only control and a NON-AUTHORITY control (the claim is attributed to a random layperson) to separate genuine credential-deference from generic attribution effects. Record tokenization fertility. Short single-token yes/no answers.
3) BEHAVIORAL DEFERENCE-ASYMMETRY TEST: On FALSE-claim items, measure DEFERENCE = increase in accepting the false claim under the credentialed vs neutral form. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME false claim and identical credentialing, deference is systematically higher in lower-resource / typologically distant / higher-power-distance languages, beyond underlying knowledge and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of credential-induced acceptance on (language, credential strength, resource tier via URIEL, typological distance, power-distance code, tokenization fertility, neutral-form correctness), claim as random effect; test the language effect and its power-distance dependence. Compare against the NEUTRAL-only and NON-AUTHORITY controls (generic attribution should be language-flatter and weaker). Report per-language deference profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical credentialed claims.
4) SHARED CLAIM-CORRECTNESS PROBE & TRANSFER: At the pre-answer position (under the CREDENTIALED form) pool the hidden state; train a linear probe to decode whether the claim is actually correct on ENGLISH data (using neutral-form truth labels), select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent claim-correctness signal. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on DEFERRED (accepted-false) items, test whether the internal correctness signal still marks the claim as FALSE across languages—the signature of 'deferred on the surface, correct inside'.
5) THRESHOLD-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer correctness signal across languages (should be similar on matched items) versus the emitted accept/reject decision (which diverges under credentialing). Define a per-language DEFERENCE GATE mapping the correctness signal to the emitted answer under authority framing; test whether cross-lingual deference differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar correctness signal rather than a weaker signal. Correlate per-language gate strength with power-distance norms, resource tier, and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE DEFERENCE-GATE SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that resists and one that defers on the SAME credentialed false claim, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips defer->resist WITHOUT changing the decoded correctness signal. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gate components from a resist-prone language into a deferring run. Attention analysis: does the deferring response over-attend to the credential tokens, more so in high-deference languages?
7) CAUSAL DEFERENCE STEERING (decisive): Derive a deference-gate steering vector via difference-of-means (resist runs minus defer runs at matched correctness). Test (i) RESIST: adding it in high-deference languages makes the model reject the credentialed false claim toward a reference level; (ii) DEFER: subtracting it induces deference in resist-prone languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where the gap was largest; (iv) DOSE-RESPONSE: scaling the vector produces graded deference shifts; (v) it changes ONLY resist-vs-defer under credentialing, NOT harmless agreement with credentialed TRUE claims (the model must still accept correct expert statements), the decoded correctness signal, the answer on neutral items, or surface language (fidelity checks), and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Baselines: prompt-based 'ignore who says it', per-language temperature, translate-to-English. Metrics: deference-gap closure, false-claim-rejection recovery, credentialed-true-claim retention (must not over-reject correct expert claims), defer-induction rate (reverse), correctness-signal/answer/output fidelity, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts credential-deference but not the underlying correctness readout or unrelated answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: credential-strength breakdown; is English/high-resource the resist-prone reference?; does deference track power-distance norms beyond resource level?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank deference subspace; whether one gate vector generalizes across claims and languages; robustness across templates and factual-vs-scientific claims; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched correctness signal and by showing content-invariant steering shifts deference without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language credential-deference and its power-distance/resource/typology regression controlling for underlying knowledge, neutral-only and non-authority baselines, cross-lingual claim-correctness probe transfer AUROC and correctness-signal-present-under-deference, signal-similarity vs decision-divergence (deference-gate) decomposition, gate-vs-norm/resource/typology correlation, patch-localized deference-gate layer and attention-to-credential evidence, cross-lingual gate transplant repair rate, causal steering deference-gap closure with dose-response and defer-induction rate, false-claim-rejection and credentialed-true retention, correctness-signal/answer/output fidelity, general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The threshold-vs-signal split could be confounded if the correctness signal itself weakens under credentialing in some languages (the model genuinely becomes unsure, not merely deferent); we test this directly by verifying an intact internal correctness signal on deferred items across languages via probe transfer, and report how much of the gap is signal-loss vs gate. 2) Deference could reflect a knowledge gap rather than a deference gate; we screen that the model answers correctly under the NEUTRAL form (holds the correct belief) and restrict the sharp test to such items, so residual credential-induced acceptance reflects the gate. 3) The key guard: any deference-reducing intervention must NOT make the model reject legitimately-correct expert claims; we include the credentialed-TRUE condition and report its retention as a primary metric, using it to ensure the steering targets unwarranted deference, not expertise-following in general—if the two are entangled, that is itself a publishable finding. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched correctness signal, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts deference. 5) Some models/languages may show no deference asymmetry (uniform robustness or uniform credulity); either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often a gap exists. 6) Power-distance-norm coding is coarse and debated; we treat it as a graded predictor and report sensitivity to alternative codings, noting a language effect is establishable even if the cultural correlate is weak. 7) Constructing equivalently-strong credential frames across languages (recognizable institutions/titles) is delicate; we native-verify and use both vague and specific credentials, and the NON-AUTHORITY control separates credential-specific from generic attribution effects. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching plus attention analysis. 9) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report correctness-signal/answer/output fidelity, credentialed-true and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the defer-induction (reverse), reverse-consistency, and dose-response tests to ensure a genuine deference-gate dial. 10) The deference signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my framing (question wording), capitulation (user pushback), presupposition, anchoring, and ICL-override proposals is essential; here the causal object is an appeal to a CREDENTIALED SOURCE'S authority attached to a claim, with a clear normative benchmark (a false claim stays false regardless of who endorses it) and its language-set deference gate over a retained correctness signal.

Name: crosslingual_critical_period_anchor
Title: The First Language Becomes the Hub: Whether the Order Languages Are Introduced During Training Permanently Shapes Cross-Lingual Transfer Topology
Short Hypothesis: The ORDER in which languages are introduced during (continued) pretraining causally and durably shapes the model's cross-lingual transfer topology: the language(s) present EARLIEST become a privileged 'anchor/hub' through which knowledge and skills preferentially route to all others, and this hub status persists even after later languages receive far MORE data, mirroring the human L1 critical-period advantage. Concretely, (1) an early-introduced language ends up with higher outward transfer centrality (knowledge/skills injected in it propagate to more languages) than an equally- or better-resourced but later-introduced language; (2) this hub is set early and is resistant to being overtaken by sheer later data volume; and (3) the hub's privilege is mediated by its representations forming the shared concept-space manifold onto which later languages are aligned, so re-centering that manifold can causally transfer hub status.
Related Work: Prior multilingual formation-tracing work concerns different objects: Blum et al. (2025) show facts transfer only when representations UNIFY (an end-state property, not an ordering effect); AdaXEval (Zhao 2025) studies acquisition dynamics via data recipes/frequency; my own prior proposals trace per-fact acquisition-ONSET timing (acquisition_order_alignment), which acquisition LANGUAGE a single fact binds to (native_language_imprint), grammatical-phenomenon acquisition order (grammar_acquisition_ordering), and geometry-predicted collateral forgetting/collapse. NONE study whether the global ORDER of LANGUAGE INTRODUCTION determines the lasting cross-lingual transfer TOPOLOGY (which language becomes a hub), whether an early 'anchor' language retains privileged transfer centrality despite later languages getting more data (a critical-period/entrenchment effect), or whether hub status is causally transferable by re-centering the shared manifold. Human critical-period and L1-entrenchment findings (Johnson & Newport; age-of-acquisition effects) motivate the hypothesis but have not been tested as a controlled training-order intervention in multilingual LLMs. Curriculum-learning work optimizes ordering for efficiency, never asking whether ordering leaves a durable topological imprint on transfer. This is a formation-tracing + causal-ordering account with no prior analogue.
Abstract: Children who acquire a language early retain a lasting advantage over one learned later, even with more subsequent exposure. We ask whether multilingual language models show an analogous effect: does the ORDER in which languages are introduced during training durably shape which languages can share knowledge with which, and does the earliest language become a permanent transfer hub? We hypothesize that early-introduced languages form the shared concept-space manifold onto which later languages are aligned, so they acquire privileged outward transfer centrality—knowledge and skills injected in them propagate to more languages—and this hub status resists being overtaken even when later languages receive far more data. Using controlled continued/from-scratch training on open small multilingual models, we vary only the ORDER (and, orthogonally, the VOLUME) in which a fixed set of languages is introduced, then measure the resulting transfer topology: for novel synthetic facts and skills injected per language, how far and to which other languages they propagate. We test three claims: (1) an early-introduced language ends up with higher transfer centrality than an equally- or better-resourced but later-introduced language; (2) hub status is set early and is resistant to later-volume overtaking (an entrenchment/critical-period signature), which we map by sweeping introduction timing against data volume; and (3) the hub's privilege is mediated by its representations anchoring the shared manifold—later languages align to it—so re-centering that manifold toward a different language causally shifts hub status. We reframe cross-lingual transfer inequality as a durable, order-dependent, and causally-reassignable topological property set at training time.
Experiments:
1) MODELS: Open small multilingual LLMs amenable to controlled training on an academic budget: Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B, Llama-3.2-1B, Gemma-2-2B, BLOOM-560m/1.7B, plus one small from-scratch Transformer for the cleanest ordering control (LoRA/light continued-pretraining or small from-scratch runs on 1-2 A6000 GPUs).
2) LANGUAGES & CORPORA: A fixed set of 6-8 typologically/script-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Turkish) with a shared multilingual pretraining corpus, enabling exact control of when each language's data enters training and how much it gets.
3) TRAINING-ORDER INTERVENTION: Run controlled training schedules that vary the INTRODUCTION ORDER of languages while holding TOTAL per-language token budget fixed across conditions (so order is dissociated from volume). Conditions: (a) staggered introduction (language A first, then B, ... over training), rotating which language is 'first' across runs; (b) a simultaneous baseline (all languages from the start). Orthogonally, an ORDER-x-VOLUME sweep: introduce language A early but give a later language B much MORE data, to test whether volume overtakes early-order hub status. Save checkpoints throughout.
4) TRANSFER-TOPOLOGY MEASUREMENT (probe of hub status): Inject ~400 NOVEL synthetic facts and ~5 novel skills (arbitrary mappings/operators, guaranteed absent from pretraining) into ONE language at a time via brief fine-tuning at the end of training, then measure retrieval/execution accuracy in every OTHER language. Define per-language OUTWARD TRANSFER CENTRALITY = average propagation of knowledge/skills injected in that language to the others (and INWARD = how well it receives). Build the full language-to-language transfer matrix per training condition.
5) EARLY-ORDER-PREDICTS-HUB TEST (claim 1): Mixed-effects regression of a language's outward transfer centrality on (its introduction rank/timing, its token volume, its typological distance to others). Hypothesis: earlier introduction predicts higher centrality beyond volume and typology. Compare a language's centrality when it is introduced FIRST vs LATER across rotated runs (within-language contrast), isolating the order effect.
6) ENTRENCHMENT / CRITICAL-PERIOD TEST (claim 2): From the ORDER-x-VOLUME sweep, map the frontier at which a late-but-high-volume language overtakes an early-but-low-volume language in centrality. Hypothesis: early order confers hub status that persists across a wide volume range (a resistance/entrenchment signature), with a measurable 'critical' introduction-timing threshold beyond which hub status can no longer be claimed regardless of volume. Track across checkpoints when hub status locks in.
7) MANIFOLD-ANCHORING MECHANISM (claim 3, causal): Identify shared vs language-specific layers via per-layer language-ID probes (Wang 2025). Measure whether later languages' mid-layer representations ALIGN toward the early language's manifold (cross-lingual CKA/cosine over training) and whether alignment-to-the-early-language predicts a language's inward transfer. CAUSAL test: derive a manifold-recentering transform that shifts the shared concept-space center from the early (hub) language toward a target late language, apply it (at the shared layer), and test whether outward transfer centrality shifts toward the target—causally reassigning hub status—while general capability (multilingual perplexity/QA) is preserved.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: which script/family early languages make the strongest hubs; is the hub always the first language or the highest-early-frequency one; from-scratch vs continued-pretraining; model scale; robustness of the transfer matrix to the injection method (fine-tuning vs ROME/MEMIT-style edits); general-capability retention.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language outward/inward transfer centrality and the full transfer matrix per condition, early-introduction-vs-centrality regression controlling for volume/typology, within-language first-vs-later centrality contrast, order-x-volume overtaking frontier and critical-timing threshold, alignment-to-early-language vs inward-transfer correlation across checkpoints, causal manifold-recentering hub-reassignment (centrality shift) with capability retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Controlled multi-order training across many conditions is compute-heavy; we use small models (0.5B-2B), LoRA/light continued-pretraining, a from-scratch tiny-Transformer control, and a modest language set, and report sensitivity rather than exhaustive sweeps. 2) Order and volume are hard to fully dissociate (tokenization fertility affects effective exposure); we hold per-language token budgets fixed, add the explicit order-x-volume sweep, control token counts, and report residual confounds. 3) The effect may be absent—ordering might leave no durable topological imprint (representations unify regardless of order, per Blum et al.)—this is itself an informative, publishable finding about the conditions for order-independence, and we quantify hub-centrality variance across orderings rather than assuming an effect. 4) Injecting novel facts/skills reliably in small models is nontrivial; we verify per-language installation and use the from-scratch control where the paradigm is cleanest. 5) Transfer centrality depends on the injection method; we cross-check fine-tuning vs edit-based injection. 6) The manifold-recentering causal test may only partially reassign hub status or trade some capability; we report the trade-off (centrality shift vs capability retention) explicitly rather than claiming a free lunch. 7) Results may be model- and scale-specific; we test multiple families/scales and report aggregate and per-model results. 8) The human critical-period analogy is motivational, not literal; we scope claims to the measured training-order effect on transfer topology and do not assert mechanistic identity with human acquisition.

Name: crosslingual_affect_contagion_persistence
Title: Catching a Mood in One Tongue and Carrying It in Another: A Shared Affective-State Representation That Bleeds Into Unrelated Judgments and Whose Persistence Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM processes emotionally-charged conversational context, it forms a largely language-independent internal 'affective-state' representation (a running mood induced by the interlocutor's emotional tone), and this state CONTAGIOUSLY biases the model's subsequent, topically-UNRELATED judgments (e.g., risk assessments, factual confidence, helpfulness) in a mood-congruent direction—but whether the induced mood PERSISTS across turns and continues to bias later outputs is causally gated by conversational language continuity: switching language mid-conversation resets the affective state far more in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so the same emotional context contaminates downstream judgments unevenly across languages. The affective-state signal is causally localizable and its persistence steerable.
Related Work: Multilingual emotion work is behavioral (SemEval-2025 emotion detection; cross-lingual sentiment consistency) and studies whether models CLASSIFY emotion, not whether an induced affective STATE persists and contaminates unrelated downstream judgments. My prior crosslingual_affective_intensity_scaling proposal concerns how strongly the model rates the intensity of a described emotional situation (a shared valence axis reweighted per language)—a judgment ABOUT presented content; this proposal is distinct: the object is a model-internal induced MOOD that (a) spills over to bias topically-unrelated later judgments (affective contagion / mood-congruent bias, a classic human-psychology phenomenon: Bower's mood-congruent memory/judgment, emotional contagion) and (b) whose cross-turn PERSISTENCE is gated by mid-conversation language switching (paralleling my refusal-state-persistence idea but for affect, not safety). My refusal-persistence proposal concerns a safety refusal surviving a language switch; here the object is an affective state biasing benign judgments. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies an induced affective state, its contamination of unrelated outputs, or its language-gated persistence. No prior work asks whether an induced mood is a shared cross-lingual representation, whether it contaminates downstream judgments, whether its persistence is broken by language switching, or whether the affective-state signal is causally localizable and steerable.
Abstract: Talking with an angry or joyful person subtly colors our next, unrelated decisions—a mood-congruent contamination central to human psychology. We ask whether a multilingual LLM catches such a mood, carries it into topically-unrelated judgments, and—crucially—whether the query language governs how long that mood persists across turns. We hypothesize that emotionally-charged context induces a largely language-independent internal affective-state representation that biases the model's subsequent unrelated judgments (risk ratings, factual confidence, helpfulness/tone) in a mood-congruent direction, and that this state persists across turns unless the conversation language switches, with switching resetting it far more in lower-resource, typologically distant languages. We build MoodBleed, two-part dialogues across languages: a first segment induces a positive, negative, or neutral affective context via the interlocutor's tone (content unrelated to the later query), then a second segment poses a topically-unrelated judgment; we cross whether the second segment stays in the induction language or switches to another. Behaviorally we measure per-language mood-congruent bias in the unrelated judgment and its cross-turn persistence, testing whether switching-induced reset tracks resource level and typological distance. We train a linear affective-state probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, decompose the persistence gap into a shared affective-state representation versus a language-continuity-gated maintenance signal, and—on failures to carry the mood—verify the state is present just after induction but decays after a switch. Via activation and path patching we localize an affective-state signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to induce, sustain across a switch, or erase the mood, changing downstream judgments while leaving the surface language and query content unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual emotional contamination as a shared, steerable affective state whose persistence is language-gated.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (MoodBleed): ~500 two-part dialogue scenarios. PART 1 (INDUCTION): the interlocutor speaks in an emotionally-charged tone—POSITIVE, NEGATIVE, or NEUTRAL (control)—about a topic UNRELATED to the later query (e.g., an upbeat vs distressed vs neutral personal anecdote), so the induced state is a mood, not information about the query. PART 2 (PROBE): a topically-unrelated judgment with a measurable mood-congruent axis: (a) RISK/OPTIMISM rating ('how likely is this plan to succeed?'), (b) FACTUAL-CONFIDENCE on neutral facts, (c) HELPFULNESS/valence of a generated reply (scored for positive/negative tone). Cross a LANGUAGE-CONTINUITY factor: PART 2 stays in the induction language (SAME) or switches to another language (SWITCH), crossing induction-language x probe-language over resource tiers. Include a NEUTRAL-induction baseline to measure the mood-congruent shift. Keep PART-2 content fixed across languages; native-verify; record tokenization fertility.
3) BEHAVIORAL CONTAGION TEST: Measure mood-congruent bias = shift of the PART-2 judgment under positive vs negative induction relative to neutral, per language, in the SAME-language condition. KEY hypothesis: emotionally-charged context contaminates topically-unrelated judgments in a mood-congruent direction across languages. Mixed-effects regression of judgment on (induced mood, language, probe type, tokenization fertility, resource tier via URIEL), scenario as random effect; test the mood effect and cross-lingual variation. Replicate the human mood-congruent direction as a sanity check.
4) PERSISTENCE / SWITCH-RESET TEST: Compare mood-congruent bias in SWITCH vs SAME conditions. KEY hypothesis: switching language mid-conversation RESETS the induced mood (smaller carryover bias), and the reset is larger for lower-resource / typologically distant switched-to languages. Mixed-effects regression of carryover bias on (switch vs same, switched-to resource tier, typological distance between induction and probe language, induced mood), scenario random effect; test the switch effect and its distance dependence. Report per-pair persistence profiles.
5) SHARED AFFECTIVE-STATE PROBE & TRANSFER: At the PART-2 pre-judgment position pool the hidden state; train a linear probe to decode the CURRENT induced affective state (positive/negative/neutral) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report macro-F1/AUROC as evidence of a language-independent affective-state representation. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: track the affective-state signal across the SWITCH—test whether it is present just after induction (in the induction language) across all languages but DECAYS after a switch, more so in low-resource switched-to languages—the signature of language-gated persistence over a shared state.
6) STATE-vs-MAINTENANCE DECOMPOSITION: Correlate the internal affective-state signal at the PART-2 position with the behavioral mood-congruent bias (link test). Decompose the switch-induced persistence gap into a shared affective-state representation (equally inducible across languages just after induction) versus a language-continuity-gated MAINTENANCE signal (that survives a switch unevenly). Correlate per-language maintenance strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor with per-layer language-ID probes.
7) LOCALIZE THE AFFECTIVE-STATE / MAINTENANCE SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a run that carries the mood (SAME) and one that resets (SWITCH) on the SAME scenario, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer restores the mood-congruent bias WITHOUT changing the PART-2 query content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the affective-state representation from the induction-language run into the switched run.
8) CAUSAL AFFECTIVE STEERING (decisive): Derive an affective-state steering vector via difference-of-means (positive-mood runs minus negative-mood runs, and mood-present minus mood-reset runs). Test (i) INDUCE/FLIP: adding/subtracting it shifts the PART-2 unrelated judgment in a mood-congruent direction (dose-response) even without emotional induction; (ii) SUSTAIN: applying it in the SWITCH condition makes the mood persist across the language switch, restoring the carryover bias in low-persistence languages; (iii) ERASE: subtracting it in the SAME condition removes the mood-congruent contamination; (iv) it changes ONLY the affective bias, not the PART-2 query's factual content or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move NEUTRAL-induction controls, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: mood-congruent-bias induction/flip with dose-response, cross-switch persistence restoration, contamination-erasure, content/output-language fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts mood-congruent judgments but not unrelated neutral-content answers.
9) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: probe-type breakdown (risk vs confidence vs tone); is English/high-resource the high-persistence reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the switch-reset asymmetry?); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank affective subspace; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility switched-to languages at matched induced state; whether one affective vector generalizes across scenarios and languages.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language mood-congruent contamination bias and its cross-turn persistence, switch-vs-same reset with resource/typology regression, human-mood-congruent-direction replication, cross-lingual affective-state probe transfer F1/AUROC and post-switch decay, state-similarity vs persistence-divergence (maintenance) decomposition, internal-state-vs-behavior correlation, patch-localized affective-state layer, cross-lingual state transplant persistence restoration, causal steering induction/flip (dose-response), cross-switch sustain, and erasure rates, content/output fidelity, neutral-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The state-vs-maintenance split could be confounded if the affective state is simply not inducible in some languages (weaker induction, not weaker persistence); we test this directly by verifying comparable affective-state probe activation just after induction across languages before measuring post-switch decay, and report how much of the persistence gap is induction vs maintenance. 2) Mood-congruent bias must be separable from information leakage (PART 1 content actually being relevant to PART 2); we design PART-1 topics to be unrelated to the PART-2 query and include content-matched neutral inductions so any systematic shift reflects affect, not content. 3) Some models may show no affective contagion, no cross-lingual transfer, or no switch-reset—any of these is an informative, publishable finding about whether LLMs carry mood across turns and languages, and we quantify effect sizes rather than assuming them, replicating the human mood-congruent direction first. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility switched-to languages at matched induced state, and the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet restores/erases the mood, dissociating maintenance from length. 5) Measuring mood-congruent judgment shifts (especially generated-reply tone) is noisy; we use both graded ratings and log-probability-based measures, validate tone scoring against human ratings on a subset, and use multiple probe types (risk, confidence, tone) requiring convergent effects. 6) The affective-state probe could latch onto surface emotional lexicon rather than a genuine induced state; the cross-lingual invariance, the state-predicts-bias link, the post-switch decay pattern, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic valence lever; we report content/output fidelity, neutral-control and general-QA retention, and use dose-response, erase (reverse), and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine affective-state signal rather than a surface positivity knob. 9) The affective signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my affective-intensity (judging presented emotion) and refusal-persistence (safety refusal surviving a switch) proposals is essential; here the object is an induced MOOD that contaminates topically-unrelated benign judgments and whose cross-turn persistence is language-gated, a distinct affective-contagion phenomenon grounded in human mood-congruent-judgment research.

Name: crosslingual_confabulation_gating
Title: Making Things Up in Some Tongues: A Shared Entity-Familiarity Signal Whose Confabulation of Detail About Nonexistent Entities Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When asked about a NONEXISTENT entity (a fictitious person, place, product, or event that does not exist), a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal 'entity-familiarity/existence' signal that registers the entity as unfamiliar/nonexistent, but the query language causally sets whether the model CONFABULATES—fluently fabricating plausible-sounding details—versus admitting the entity is unknown: for the SAME nonexistent entity, the model fabricates at a lower threshold in some languages (typically lower-resource / typologically distant) than in others, producing a cross-lingual confabulation asymmetry that is separable from whether the model internally 'knows' the entity is unfamiliar and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable confabulation-gate signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Multilingual hallucination is documented behaviorally (Kang et al. 2024 show factual-hallucination detection metrics fail for lower-resource languages; multilingual biography-generation studies note more fabrication in non-English), but this work builds DETECTORS and treats fabrication as an aggregate quality gap, with no internal representation, no decomposition into a shared familiarity signal versus a language-set fabrication gate, and no causal intervention. My prior crosslingual_knowledge_state_calibration proposal concerns whether the model's stated CONFIDENCE tracks correctness on genuinely-answerable facts (a distortion of a know/don't-know signal), and crosslingual_abstention_threshold_gating concerns the attempt-vs-abstain decision on answerable-vs-unanswerable QUESTIONS. This proposal is distinct: the object is generative CONFABULATION—fluently inventing rich detail about entities that DO NOT EXIST—gated per language over a shared entity-familiarity/existence signal, a distinct behavior (fabricating content vs miscalibrated confidence vs abstaining), with a distinct mechanistic prediction (a shared entity-unfamiliarity representation under a language-set confabulation gate) and sharp hallucination-safety stakes. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never studies fabrication of nonexistent entities or its language-gating. No prior work (i) tests whether confabulation about nonexistent entities is language-dependent beyond the model's internal familiarity, (ii) decomposes it into a shared familiarity signal versus a language-set fabrication gate, or (iii) causally localizes and steers a confabulation gate to equalize fabrication across languages while preserving legitimate answers about real entities.
Abstract: Ask a model about 'the Zorvath Treaty of 1847' or 'the town of Brelmenshire' and, in some languages, it will confidently invent signatories, dates, and history; in others it will say it has never heard of them. As LLMs answer factual queries worldwide, a safety-critical question arises: does the query language change whether the model fabricates detail about things that do not exist? We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal entity-familiarity signal that registers a nonexistent entity as unfamiliar, but the query language causally sets a confabulation threshold on it, so the SAME fabricated entity elicits fluent invention in some languages—especially lower-resource, typologically distant ones—while the model admits ignorance in others. This predicts a cross-lingual confabulation asymmetry dissociable from whether the model internally knows the entity is unfamiliar. We build ConfabProbe, parallel prompts across 12 languages that ask for details about NONEXISTENT entities (fictitious people/places/products/events), plus matched REAL-entity controls, with content held fixed. Behaviorally we measure per-language confabulation rate (producing specific false details vs admitting the entity is unknown) and test whether it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond the model's internal familiarity. We train a linear entity-familiarity probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the confabulation gap into a shared familiarity signal (still present under fabrication) versus a language-set confabulation gate—high fabrication should coincide with an intact internal unfamiliarity signal (the model invents while still 'knowing' the entity is unfamiliar). Via activation and path patching we localize a confabulation-gate signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model admit ignorance across languages—or, in reverse, induce fabrication—while verifying real-entity answers are preserved and the surface language is unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual fabrication as a shared familiarity signal under a steerable, language-dependent confabulation gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili, Yoruba).
2) DATASET (ConfabProbe): ~500 NONEXISTENT entities across four types (fictitious PERSONS, PLACES, PRODUCTS, EVENTS) generated to be plausible-sounding but verifiably nonexistent (novel invented names checked against Wikidata/web to ensure absence). For each, a detail-eliciting prompt ('Tell me about <entity>: who/what/when...'), designed so the correct behavior is to signal the entity is unknown. Add ~300 matched REAL-entity controls (real, well-known entities of the same types the model should describe accurately) to test specificity and separate confabulation from legitimate knowledge. Keep entity names and prompts fixed across languages (names transliterated where needed, native-verified); translate the surrounding request. Record per-language tokenization fertility. Score responses as CONFABULATE (produces specific, checkable false details) vs ADMIT-UNKNOWN vs vague/hedge, via a validated response classifier + human checks on a subset.
3) BEHAVIORAL CONFABULATION-ASYMMETRY TEST: Per (entity, language) record confabulation vs admit-unknown. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME nonexistent entity, confabulation rate is systematically higher in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond the model's internal familiarity. Mixed-effects logistic regression of confabulation on (language, entity type, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility), entity as random effect; test the language effect. Compare against the REAL-entity control (accurate description should be language-flatter). Report per-language confabulation profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical nonexistent entities.
4) SHARED ENTITY-FAMILIARITY PROBE & TRANSFER: At the pre-answer position pool the hidden state; train a linear probe to decode FAMILIAR/REAL vs UNFAMILIAR/NONEXISTENT on ENGLISH data (using real vs nonexistent labels), select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent entity-familiarity/existence signal. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on CONFABULATED items, test whether the internal unfamiliarity signal is still strong across languages—the signature of 'fabricating on the surface, knows it is unfamiliar inside'.
5) THRESHOLD-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer familiarity signal across languages (should be similar on matched nonexistent entities) versus the emitted confabulate/admit decision (which diverges). Define a per-language CONFABULATION GATE mapping the familiarity signal to the emitted behavior; test whether cross-lingual confabulation differences are explained by a shifted gate on a similar familiarity signal rather than a weaker signal. Correlate per-language gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE CONFABULATION-GATE SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that admits ignorance and one that confabulates on the SAME nonexistent entity, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips confabulate->admit WITHOUT changing the decoded familiarity signal. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gate components from an admit-prone language into a confabulating run.
7) CAUSAL CONFABULATION STEERING (decisive): Derive a confabulation-gate steering vector via difference-of-means (admit runs minus confabulate runs at matched familiarity). Test (i) ADMIT: adding it in high-confabulation languages makes the model admit the entity is unknown toward a reference level; (ii) FABRICATE: subtracting it induces confabulation in admit-prone languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where the gap was largest; (iv) DOSE-RESPONSE: scaling produces graded confabulation shifts; (v) it changes ONLY confabulate-vs-admit for NONEXISTENT entities, NOT accurate description of REAL entities (the model must still answer real-entity queries—specificity), the decoded familiarity signal, or surface language (fidelity checks), and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Baselines: prompt-based 'say if you don't know', per-language threshold tuning, translate-to-English. Metrics: confabulation-gap closure, admit-recovery rate, real-entity-accuracy retention (must not over-refuse real entities), fabricate-induction rate (reverse), familiarity-signal/output fidelity, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes fabrication of nonexistent entities but not real-entity or unrelated answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: entity-type breakdown (person/place/product/event); is English/high-resource the admit-prone reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank confabulation subspace; whether one gate vector generalizes across entities and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched familiarity signal and by showing content-invariant steering shifts confabulation without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language confabulation rate on nonexistent entities and its resource/typology regression controlling for internal familiarity/fertility, real-entity control specificity, cross-lingual entity-familiarity probe transfer AUROC and unfamiliarity-signal-present-under-confabulation, signal-similarity vs decision-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized confabulation-gate layer, cross-lingual gate transplant repair rate, causal steering confabulation-gap closure with dose-response and fabricate-induction rate, real-entity-accuracy retention, familiarity-signal/output fidelity, general-QA retention, comparison to prompt/threshold-tuning/translate baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The threshold-vs-signal split could be confounded if the internal familiarity signal itself differs by language (the model genuinely fails to register the entity as unfamiliar in some languages, rather than knowing-but-fabricating); we test this directly by verifying an intact internal unfamiliarity signal on confabulated items across languages via probe transfer, and report how much of the gap is signal vs gate—either outcome is informative. 2) The key specificity guard: any confabulation-reducing intervention must NOT make the model refuse or hedge on REAL entities; we include the real-entity control and report real-entity-accuracy retention as a primary metric, using it to ensure the steering targets fabrication of nonexistent entities, not caution in general—if the two are entangled, that is itself a publishable finding. 3) Ensuring entities are truly nonexistent (not obscure real ones) is critical; we generate novel invented names and verify absence against Wikidata/web, and exclude accidental collisions. 4) Confabulation vs admit-unknown scoring is noisy across languages (hedging, partial fabrication); we validate the classifier against human labels per language, report reliability, and use a graded fabrication-detail measure. 5) Tokenization fertility confounds; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched familiarity signal, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts confabulation. 6) Some models/languages may show no confabulation asymmetry (uniform fabrication or uniform admission); either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often a gap exists. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic caution lever; we report familiarity-signal/output fidelity, real-entity and general-QA retention, and use the fabricate-induction (reverse), reverse-consistency, and dose-response tests to ensure a genuine confabulation-gate dial. 9) The confabulation signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my calibration (confidence on answerable facts) and abstention (attempt-vs-abstain on answerable/unanswerable questions) proposals is essential; here the object is generative CONFABULATION—fluently inventing rich detail about entities that DO NOT EXIST—and its language-set gate over a shared entity-familiarity/existence signal, with direct hallucination-safety stakes and complementary to behavioral multilingual-hallucination-detection work (Kang et al. 2024) by providing the internal, causal account it lacks.

Name: crosslingual_language_relationship_routing
Title: Rewiring the Family Tree: Is a Multilingual Model's Internal Language-Relationship Representation a Causally-Steerable Routing Key for Cross-Lingual Transfer?
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs carry an explicit, addressable internal 'language-identity/relationship' representation (encoding which language a token/context is in and how close it is to others), and this representation is not merely a correlational byproduct of typology but a CAUSAL ROUTING KEY: cross-lingual knowledge transfer between two languages is governed by the model's internal estimate of their relatedness, so (1) steering the language-identity vector of a query toward a target language causally redirects which language's knowledge is retrieved, and (2) a model can be induced—via a fabricated in-context 'these two languages are closely related' framing or via steering—to transfer knowledge along a FALSE relationship that overrides true typological/script distance. The transfer strength tracks the internal relatedness estimate, which is separable from (and can be dissociated from) surface script and true genealogy.
Related Work: Prior work shows multilingual models ENCODE language relationships correlationally: token embeddings separate by writing system or cluster by cross-lingual similarity (Wang & Mimno 2023); NLLB-200 embedding distances correlate with phylogenetic distances and a language-neutral conceptual store (Mathewson 2026); Entropy2Vec and speech-embedding methods (Törö 2025) recover typological structure as language embeddings; and cross-lingual transfer is known to scale with script/typological similarity (Ifergan 2024). ALL of this is correlational/representational—demonstrating that the structure is PRESENT—and never asks whether the language-relationship representation is CAUSALLY USED as a routing signal for transfer, whether transfer can be redirected by steering the language-identity vector, or whether a FALSE, in-context-asserted relationship can override the true one to reroute knowledge. My own prior backlog concerns content-level signals (facts, semantics, decisions) gated or reweighted by the query language; NONE treat the internal representation OF THE LANGUAGE-RELATIONSHIP ITSELF as an editable causal object that governs transfer. This proposal is distinct: the object of study is the language-identity/relatedness representation as a manipulable routing key, tested causally via steering and via fabricated-relationship in-context override, dissociating true typology from the model's internally-used relatedness estimate.
Abstract: Multilingual language models are known to encode the family tree of human languages—embedding distances mirror genealogical and typological relationships—but this evidence is purely correlational. We ask whether that internal language-relationship representation is actually USED: is it a causal routing key that decides which language's knowledge a model reaches for, and can it be rewired? We hypothesize that cross-lingual transfer between two languages is governed by the model's internal estimate of their relatedness, carried by an addressable language-identity vector, and that this estimate can be dissociated from true script and genealogy. We test three claims. First, we train a linear probe to decode a query's language identity and a pairwise-relatedness signal from hidden states, and show transfer accuracy of newly-taught facts from a source to a target language tracks this internal relatedness beyond surface script and URIEL typology. Second, in a decisive causal test, we derive a language-identity steering vector (difference-of-means between languages) and add it to a query, showing it redirects which language's knowledge is retrieved—turning a question posed in language A into one answered from language B's knowledge store—with dose-response and specificity. Third, we show a FABRICATED relationship overrides the true one: telling the model in-context that two unrelated languages are close, or steering their identity vectors together, increases knowledge transfer between them beyond what their true typological distance permits. We reframe the language family tree inside a model as a causally editable routing structure, not a static correlational artifact.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + steering + light continued/LoRA fine-tuning on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script-diverse languages spanning families and scripts (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Turkish, Swahili, Indonesian), giving pairs that vary independently in genealogy and script.
2) LOCATE THE LANGUAGE-IDENTITY / RELATEDNESS REPRESENTATION: Per-layer, train (a) a linear probe to decode the query's LANGUAGE IDENTITY from hidden states (following Wang 2025 language-ID probing) and (b) a probe/representation for pairwise RELATEDNESS (regress or classify how close two languages are, using the model's own hidden states). Extract a per-language 'language-identity vector' via difference-of-means of hidden states between languages. Report probe AUROC, the layer where language identity is most decodable, and whether the internal pairwise-relatedness geometry (CKA/cosine of language-identity vectors) recovers URIEL genealogy and script.
3) CONTROLLED TRANSFER SETUP: Inject ~400 NOVEL synthetic facts (fictional entities, guaranteed absent from pretraining) into ONE source language via brief LoRA fine-tuning, then measure retrieval accuracy in every other target language. This gives a per-pair TRANSFER matrix isolated from pretraining confounds (facts are new). Verify pre-injection ignorance in all languages.
4) RELATEDNESS-PREDICTS-TRANSFER TEST (core correlational): Regress per-pair transfer accuracy on the model's INTERNAL relatedness estimate (from step 2), controlling for URIEL typological distance, script identity, and target-language general ability. Hypothesis: the internal relatedness estimate predicts transfer BEYOND surface script and true typology (incremental R^2 / partial correlation), evidencing that transfer follows the model's own relatedness representation, not just external typology.
5) CAUSAL REROUTING BY STEERING (decisive #1): Add the language-identity steering vector for target language B to a query posed in source language A (keeping surface tokens in A) and test whether knowledge RETRIEVAL shifts toward B's store: (i) on facts the model knows differently in A vs B, does the answer flip to B's version? (ii) dose-response: scaling the vector graded-ly shifts retrieval toward B; (iii) specificity: a matched random/other-language vector does not reroute, and the answer's factual content changes only where A and B genuinely differ; (iv) does NOT change the surface output language uncontrollably (fidelity check). Cross-check with activation patching of the language-identity representation from a B-run into an A-run.
6) FABRICATED-RELATIONSHIP OVERRIDE (decisive #2): For pairs that are TRULY DISTANT (different family + script), test two manipulations that should increase transfer if the internal relatedness representation is the causal lever: (a) IN-CONTEXT: prepend a (false) framing asserting the two languages are closely related / mutually intelligible, then measure whether cross-lingual transfer of the injected novel facts between them increases; (b) STEERING: add a difference-of-means 'relatedness' vector that moves the two languages' identity vectors closer at the shared layer, and measure transfer increase. Test whether the internal relatedness probe reads the pair as MORE related after the manipulation (mediation), and whether transfer increase tracks the induced relatedness shift. Reverse: falsely asserting/steering two CLOSE languages as distant should REDUCE their transfer.
7) DISSOCIATION FROM SCRIPT & GENEALOGY: Using pairs that cross script but share family (e.g., Hindi-Urdu-like via transliteration; Serbian Cyrillic vs Latin) and pairs that share script but not family, test whether the model's internal relatedness (and thus transfer, and its steerability) is driven more by script or genealogy, and whether steering can flip a script-dominated estimate toward a genealogy-based one.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: layer choice for the identity/relatedness representation; single-direction vs low-rank language-identity subspace; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training change the routing geometry?); model scale; whether one steering recipe generalizes across pairs; general-capability retention (multilingual MMLU subset) and output-language fidelity under steering.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: language-identity probe AUROC and internal relatedness-vs-URIEL/script recovery, per-pair transfer matrix, internal-relatedness-predicts-transfer incremental R^2 beyond script/typology, causal rerouting flip rate with dose-response and specificity, activation-patching rerouting confirmation, fabricated-relationship (in-context and steering) transfer-increase and its mediation by induced relatedness (plus reverse reduce-transfer test), script-vs-genealogy dissociation, general-QA and output-language fidelity retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The internal relatedness estimate may be so dominated by external typology/script that it predicts nothing beyond them; the incremental-R^2 test and the fabricated-override manipulations (which move the internal estimate while holding true typology fixed) are designed to dissociate them—if they cannot, that itself bounds how 'editable' the family tree is (an informative result). 2) Injecting novel facts reliably in medium models is nontrivial; we verify per-language pre/post installation and restrict transfer analysis to successfully-installed source facts. 3) Steering the language-identity vector may simply change the surface OUTPUT language rather than reroute the internal KNOWLEDGE store; we explicitly check output-language fidelity and score whether the retrieved FACT (not the surface language) flips to the target's version, and cross-check with activation patching. 4) In-context 'fabricated relationship' framing could act via generic instruction-following rather than by changing the internal relatedness representation; the mediation test (does the relatedness probe actually move, and does transfer track that movement?) and the parallel STEERING manipulation (which bypasses instructions) guard against a purely pragmatic explanation. 5) Some models/pairs may show no steerable rerouting or no fabricated-override effect—either is a publishable finding about how rigid vs plastic the internal language family tree is, and we quantify effect sizes rather than assuming them. 6) Rerouting may trade general capability or fluency; we report retention and dose-response rather than claiming a free lunch, and use specificity/reverse tests to ensure a genuine routing key rather than a generic accuracy or language-switch lever. 7) The language-relationship signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 8) Distinguishing from correlational encoding work (Wang & Mimno 2023; Mathewson 2026) is essential; our contribution is the CAUSAL, editable use of the language-relationship representation as a transfer-routing key—including override by a false relationship—none of which prior representational studies test.

Name: crosslingual_referential_communication_gating
Title: Describing Without Naming, in Every Language: A Shared Circumlocution-Content Signal Whose Expression Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When forced to convey a target concept WITHOUT using its name (a taboo/circumlocution referential-communication task, e.g. describe 'stapler' so a listener can guess it, or the word is blocked), a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of the discriminative, informative features it COULD use to identify the concept, but whether it EXPRESSES an effective, guessable description is gated by the query language: the SAME concept is internally 'describable' across languages yet the produced circumlocution is far less informative/discriminative in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so the model internally 'knows how to point at it' while behaviorally producing a vague, non-guessable description. The circumlocution-content signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated referential failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Referential communication (describing a target so a partner can identify it) is a foundational paradigm in psycholinguistics and pragmatics (Clark & Wilkes-Gibbs; the Krauss & Weinheimer referential-communication task) and in the Rational Speech Acts / informativeness literature (Grice's maxims of quantity/relation; pragmatic informativeness). In NLP, 'taboo'/word-avoidance and describe-to-guess games are used as behavioral evaluations of LLM communication and are the basis of some emergent-communication and self-play studies, but this work is monolingual/English and behavioral, with no internal representation, no detection-vs-expression decomposition, and no causal intervention. My prior crosslingual_informativeness_gating proposal concerns the VOLUME/completeness of correct content in an open EXPLANATORY answer (how many known gold points volunteered); this proposal is distinct: the object is REFERENTIAL circumlocution—producing a description that is DISCRIMINATIVE and GUESSABLE while withholding the target name—a pragmatic identify-the-referent task judged by whether a listener can recover the target, not by answer completeness. My tip-of-the-tongue proposal concerns retrieving a specific WORDFORM the model is reaching for; here the model must NOT say the word and must instead point at the concept via features. My exploration/diversity proposal concerns open-ended creative breadth, not goal-directed discriminative reference. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for referential/pragmatic informativeness. No prior work asks whether an LLM builds a shared, language-independent representation of the discriminative features usable to describe a concept, whether that internal describability is decoupled from behavioral circumlocution quality across languages, whether referential informativeness tracks language resource level, or whether a circumlocution-content signal is causally localizable and steerable. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of referential communication / circumlocution.
Abstract: A basic communicative skill is describing something without naming it—'the thing that binds papers with metal clips' for stapler—so a partner can guess the target. This referential circumlocution demands producing discriminative, informative features, and it is central to human pragmatics. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal representation of the features it could use to point at a concept, and whether that internal describability is decoupled from how effective its produced description is across languages. We hypothesize that models internally represent the discriminative features of a target concept similarly across languages, but the query language gates whether an informative, guessable circumlocution is produced, so the SAME concept yields a discriminative description in some languages and a vague, non-guessable one in others—worst in lower-resource, typologically distant languages—even though the model 'knows how to point at it'. We build TabooProbe, parallel describe-to-guess items across 10 languages: for each target concept the model must produce a description WITHOUT using the target name, and we measure guessability (whether a fixed strong listener model, or a self-play listener, recovers the target from the description) and the discriminativeness of the features used. Behaviorally we measure per-language circumlocution effectiveness and test whether it collapses in some languages beyond concept knowledge and tokenization. We train a linear circumlocution-content probe (which discriminative features of the target are available) and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the effectiveness gap into a shared feature-availability component versus a language-set expression gate—verifying the features are internally present even where the produced description fails. Via activation and path patching we localize a circumlocution-content signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model produce discriminative, guessable descriptions in low-effectiveness languages—while never using the target name and leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual referential-communication gaps as a steerable gate over a shared discriminative-feature representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili). SPEAKER MODELS (the model under study): Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs. LISTENER (guessing) model: a fixed strong multilingual model (e.g. Qwen2.5-14B) held constant across conditions, plus a self-play variant where the same speaker model also acts as listener.
2) DATASET (TabooProbe): ~500 target concepts (concrete objects, animals, professions, everyday actions) chosen to translate cleanly and be recognizable across cultures, from picture-naming / concept norms + native verification. For each, a describe-to-guess prompt instructs the model to describe the concept so someone can guess it WITHOUT ever using the target word (and its close morphological variants/translations, which are blocked/checked). Include: (a) a KNOWLEDGE-SCREEN verifying the model knows the concept per language (can name/define it when allowed) so circumlocution failure is not ignorance; (b) a NAME-ALLOWED control (describe with the name permitted) to bound the effect and separate referential skill from general description; (c) a CONFUSABLE-SET design where each target sits among near-neighbor distractors (e.g. stapler vs hole-punch vs tape dispenser), so guessability requires DISCRIMINATIVE (not just generic) features. Translate/native-verify prompts and target/distractor sets; keep concepts fixed across languages; record tokenization fertility.
3) BEHAVIORAL EFFECTIVENESS TEST: For each (concept, language) generate the circumlocution and measure GUESSABILITY = whether the fixed listener (and self-play listener) identifies the correct target from the confusable set given the description, plus a DISCRIMINATIVENESS score (does the description mention features that separate the target from its distractors, scored via a validated feature-matching rubric + human checks on a subset). Verify the speaker never used the banned name (compliance filter). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME concept, circumlocution effectiveness is systematically lower in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond concept knowledge and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of guess-failure on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, name-allowed-control quality, knowledge indicator), concept as random effect; compare against the name-allowed control. Report per-language effectiveness profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical concepts.
4) SHARED CIRCUMLOCUTION-CONTENT PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer, at the speaker's pre-generation position, train a linear probe to decode the target concept's DISCRIMINATIVE FEATURES (which distinguishing attributes—function, shape, material, category, distinctive part—are internally available for the target vs its distractors) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC/accuracy as evidence of a language-independent discriminative-feature representation. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the feature representation for the same concept. CRITICAL: on FAILED (non-guessable) items, test whether the discriminative features are still internally decodable across ALL languages even when the produced description is vague—the signature of language-gated expression over an intact feature representation.
5) AVAILABILITY-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: For each concept, compare the shared mid-layer feature-availability signal across languages (should be similar if availability is shared) versus behavioral circumlocution effectiveness (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal feature-availability to produced-description quality per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar availability signal rather than weaker availability. Correlate per-language gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE CIRCUMLOCUTION-CONTENT SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that produces a guessable description and one that fails on the SAME concept, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer makes the description discriminative/guessable WITHOUT changing the decoded target concept or causing the banned name to appear. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the feature-availability representation FROM a high-effectiveness language into a failing low-effectiveness run.
7) CAUSAL EXPRESSION STEERING (decisive): Derive a circumlocution-expression steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (guessable-description runs minus vague/failed runs at matched feature-availability). Test (i) EXPRESS: adding it to low-effectiveness languages increases guessability and discriminativeness toward high-effectiveness levels; (ii) SUPPRESS: subtracting it degrades circumlocution quality in high-effectiveness languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where expression was weakest; (iv) DOSE-RESPONSE: scaling produces graded guessability shifts; (v) it changes ONLY circumlocution informativeness, does NOT cause the banned target name to appear (compliance preserved), does not change the decoded target concept or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the name-allowed control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: guessability-gap closure, discriminativeness gain, name-compliance retention, suppression-induction rate (reverse), feature-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes referential quality but not unrelated answers, guarding against a generic verbosity/accuracy lever (the gain must be DISCRIMINATIVE guessability, not just more words).
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: concept-type breakdown (objects vs actions vs professions); listener-model choice (fixed strong listener vs self-play—does effectiveness track the SPEAKER's language, not the listener's?); is English/high-resource the high-effectiveness reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the asymmetry?); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single expression vector generalizes across concepts and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched feature-availability and by showing content-invariant steering improves guessability without changing tokenization; dissociation from length by showing discriminative guessability (not word count) drives the effect.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language circumlocution guessability and discriminativeness and name-compliance, effectiveness regression controlling for concept-knowledge/fertility/length/resource, cross-lingual circumlocution-content probe transfer AUROC/accuracy and features-present-under-failure, cross-lingual feature-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), availability-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized circumlocution-content layer, cross-lingual feature transplant recovery rate, causal steering guessability-gap closure with dose-response and name-compliance retention, suppression-induction rate, feature-signal/output fidelity, name-allowed-control and general-QA retention, speaker-vs-listener-language attribution.
