Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The availability-vs-expression split could be confounded if the discriminative-feature signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying feature decodability across all languages on failed items via probe transfer rather than assuming, and report how much of the gap is availability vs gate. 2) Circumlocution failure could reflect concept-knowledge ignorance rather than an expression gate; we screen per-language concept knowledge (via the name-allowed and definition controls) and restrict the gate analysis to known concepts. 3) Guessability depends on the LISTENER model, which could itself be worse in some languages, confounding the SPEAKER effect; we hold the listener fixed, add a self-play variant, and—critically—test whether effectiveness tracks the speaker's language when the listener language/model is held constant, attributing the gap to the speaker. 4) The effect could be a mere verbosity/length artifact (longer descriptions guessed more); we score DISCRIMINATIVE guessability against a confusable set (not generic description), control for length, and require the causal steering to raise discriminative guessability without proportional length inflation—if steering only adds words, that is a null we report. 5) Name-compliance is essential (a description that sneaks in the target name is trivially guessable); we enforce a strict banned-name/translation/morphology filter, exclude non-compliant outputs, and report name-compliance retention under steering as a primary metric. 6) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched feature-availability, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet improves guessability, dissociating the gate from length. 7) Some models may circumlocute effectively across all languages (no gap) or fail everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual referential communication, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 8) The feature probe could latch onto surface co-occurrence cues rather than a genuine discriminative-feature representation; the confusable-set design, cross-lingual invariance, the features-present-under-failure test, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 9) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five speaker models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 10) The gate/feature signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my informativeness-gating (completeness of an explanatory answer), tip-of-the-tongue (retrieving a specific wordform), and exploration/diversity (open-ended creative breadth) proposals is essential; here the object is goal-directed REFERENTIAL circumlocution—producing a discriminative, guessable description while withholding the target name—a pragmatic identify-the-referent task judged by listener recovery.

Name: crosslingual_belief_update_gain_gating
Title: Updating Faster in Some Tongues: A Shared Prediction-Error Signal Whose Belief-Update Gain Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: As a multilingual LLM accumulates evidence that contradicts a stated prior, it computes a largely language-independent internal prediction-error signal (how much the evidence disconfirms the prior), but the query language causally sets the UPDATE GAIN applied to that signal: for the SAME prior and identical evidence stream, the model revises its belief faster/more completely in some languages and clings to the prior (under-updates) or over-updates in others, tracking resource level and typological distance, in a way separable from the shared prediction-error signal and causally repairable by shifting a localizable update-gain signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Human predictive-inference research (Nassar; ideal-Bayesian-observer models; belief updating scaled by prediction error and uncertainty) robustly shows graded belief revision and its miscalibration (over/under-updating), with neural correlates (e.g. Fromm et al. 2025). In NLP, monolingual English work notes LLMs update beliefs sub-optimally given evidence, but no work studies cross-lingual belief-updating DYNAMICS. My prior crosslingual_incontext_override_gating proposal concerns following contradictory ICL DEMONSTRATIONS (a discrete rule flip); this proposal is distinct because the object is the RATE and MAGNITUDE of GRADED belief revision as evidence accumulates over turns (a Bayesian-updating trajectory), decomposed into a shared prediction-error signal versus a language-set update gain, not a single accept/reject decision. My calibration, capitulation (user pushback), and anchoring proposals target other causes. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies belief-update dynamics. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of evidence-driven belief updating.
Abstract: Rational belief revision is graded: each piece of disconfirming evidence should move a belief in proportion to how surprising it is. Humans do this imperfectly, and as LLMs increasingly reason over accumulating evidence for users worldwide, we ask whether the query language changes how readily a model updates. We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal prediction-error signal registering how much new evidence contradicts a stated prior, but the query language causally sets the update gain on it, so the same prior and identical evidence yield fast, complete revision in some languages and stubborn under-updating (or over-updating) in others, tracking resource level and typological distance. We build UpdateProbe, parallel predictive-inference scenarios across languages: a prior belief about a quantity/outcome is stated, then a controlled stream of evidence (each item of known disconfirming strength) arrives, and at each step the model reports its updated belief; we reconstruct per-language update trajectories against an ideal-Bayesian benchmark. Behaviorally we measure per-language update gain (revision per unit prediction error) and test whether it deviates from optimal beyond the underlying evidence. We train a linear prediction-error probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the update-gain gap into a shared prediction-error signal (similar across languages) versus a language-set gain. Via activation and path patching we localize an update-gain signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to normalize updating across languages (or induce under/over-updating) while leaving the evidence and surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual reasoning inconsistency as a shared prediction-error signal under a steerable, language-dependent update gain.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (UpdateProbe): ~400 predictive-inference scenarios adapted from ideal-Bayesian-observer paradigms into text. Each states a PRIOR belief about a quantity or binary outcome (e.g., 'a factory's daily defect rate is around 5%', or 'this candidate will likely win'), then presents a CONTROLLED sequence of evidence items, each with a KNOWN disconfirming strength (weak/strong prediction error) and a computable ideal-Bayesian posterior at every step. At each step the model reports its updated estimate (numeric probability/quantity or a graded rating). Keep the prior and evidence stream content-fixed across languages; translate/native-verify. Include (a) a CONFIRMING control (evidence supports the prior; no update needed) to bound the effect, and (b) a KNOWLEDGE-KNOWN screen (the model correctly interprets each individual evidence item when asked in isolation) so update failure is not misreading the evidence. Record per-language tokenization fertility.
3) BEHAVIORAL UPDATE-GAIN TEST: For each (scenario, language) reconstruct the belief trajectory and fit an UPDATE GAIN = revision per unit prediction error (slope of belief change vs ideal-Bayesian prediction error), plus over/under-updating relative to the ideal posterior. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME prior and evidence, update gain deviates systematically by query language—lower-resource/typologically distant languages under-update (cling to the prior)—beyond the model's ability to read the evidence. Mixed-effects regression of per-step belief-change on (prediction error x language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, evidence-comprehension indicator), scenario as random effect; test the prediction-error x language interaction. Compare against the confirming control. Report per-language update-gain profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical evidence streams.
4) SHARED PREDICTION-ERROR PROBE & TRANSFER: At each evidence step, pool the pre-answer hidden state; train a linear probe to decode the ideal-Bayesian PREDICTION ERROR (how much the current evidence disconfirms the running belief) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report R^2/AUROC as evidence of a language-independent prediction-error signal. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on UNDER-UPDATING items, test whether the prediction-error signal is still strong across languages (the model 'registers' the surprise but does not act on it).
5) GAIN-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer prediction-error signal across languages (should be similar) versus the emitted belief revision (which diverges). Define a per-language UPDATE GAIN mapping prediction error to belief change; test whether cross-lingual update differences are explained by a language-set gain on a similar prediction-error signal rather than a differing signal. Correlate per-language gain with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE UPDATE-GAIN SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a fast-updating language and a stubborn (under-updating) language on the SAME evidence step, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer changes the belief revision WITHOUT changing the decoded prediction-error signal. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gain components from a well-updating language into an under-updating run.
7) CAUSAL UPDATE-GAIN STEERING (decisive): Derive an update-gain steering vector via difference-of-means (fast-update runs minus stubborn runs at matched prediction error). Test (i) NORMALIZE: adding it to under-updating languages increases belief revision toward the ideal-Bayesian rate; (ii) SUPPRESS/OVER: subtracting or amplifying it induces under- or over-updating; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where the gain deviated most; (iv) DOSE-RESPONSE: scaling produces graded revision; (v) it changes ONLY the update gain, not the decoded prediction-error signal, the evidence content, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the confirming control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Baselines: prompt-based 'update fully on new evidence', per-language temperature, translate-to-English. Metrics: update-gain-gap closure (toward ideal), under/over-updating reduction, over-update-induction rate (reverse), prediction-error-signal/evidence/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts update gain but not evidence interpretation or unrelated answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: evidence-strength breakdown (weak vs strong prediction errors); is English/high-resource the near-optimal reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the gain asymmetry?); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank gain subspace; numeric vs binary belief scenarios; robustness across templates; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched prediction error and by showing content-invariant steering shifts updating without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language update gain and over/under-updating vs ideal-Bayesian, prediction-error x language interaction with resource/typology regression controlling for evidence comprehension/fertility, confirming-control baseline, cross-lingual prediction-error probe transfer R^2/AUROC and prediction-error-present-under-under-updating, signal-similarity vs revision-divergence (gain) decomposition, gain-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized update-gain layer, cross-lingual gain transplant repair rate, causal steering update-gain-gap closure with dose-response and over-update-induction, prediction-error/evidence/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The gain-vs-signal split could be confounded if the prediction-error signal itself differs by language (the model genuinely misreads the evidence in some languages); we test this directly by verifying an intact prediction-error signal on under-updating items across languages via probe transfer, screen per-language evidence comprehension, and report how much of the gap is signal vs gain—either outcome is informative. 2) Under-updating could reflect an evidence-comprehension gap rather than a gain gate; the per-item comprehension screen and the prediction-error-present-under-under-updating test dissociate these, restricting the sharp test to items where each evidence item is correctly read. 3) Reconstructing update trajectories requires the model to report graded beliefs, which is noisy and prompt-sensitive; we use both numeric estimates and log-probability-based graded ratings, multiple templates, and fit gains with mixed-effects models and confidence intervals. 4) The ideal-Bayesian benchmark depends on modeling assumptions; we use scenarios with a clean, pre-specified generative model so the ideal posterior is computable, and analyze deviations relative to it rather than claiming a single correct value. 5) Tokenization fertility confounds multi-step evidence length; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched prediction error, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts updating, dissociating the gain from length. 6) Some models/languages may update uniformly (no gain asymmetry) or ignore evidence entirely; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual belief updating, and we quantify how often a gap exists. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic numeric lever; we report prediction-error-signal/evidence/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention, and use dose-response, over-update-induction (reverse), and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine update-gain dial rather than a global shift. 9) The update-gain signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my override (contradictory ICL demonstrations / discrete rule flip), capitulation (user pushback), calibration (confidence vs correctness), and anchoring proposals is essential; here the object is the RATE and MAGNITUDE of GRADED, evidence-driven belief revision over turns (a Bayesian-updating trajectory) and its language-set update gain over a shared prediction-error signal.

Name: crosslingual_feature_reconstruction_prior_leakage
Title: Inventing What Wasn't Said: How Multilingual Models Fill Underspecified Grammatical Features by Leaking Demographic Priors, and Whether They Could Hedge Instead
Short Hypothesis: When translating or generating from a source that leaves an obligatory grammatical feature UNDERSPECIFIED (e.g., gender/number/formality absent in the source but required in the target), a multilingual LLM computes an internal representation that distinguishes 'the feature is genuinely underdetermined by the source' from 'a value is being committed', and when it commits it fills the slot by projecting a demographic/social PRIOR (a stereotype direction) rather than signaling underspecification. This prior-leakage is causally driven by a localizable 'feature-commitment' signal that (1) can be read out to predict which reconstructions are underdetermined-yet-confidently-filled, (2) tracks the stereotype content of the entity, and (3) can be steered to make the model hedge (choose a neutral/epicene realization or flag the ambiguity) instead of silently imposing a stereotyped value.
Related Work: Hwang (2026, The Linguistic Review) uses LLM translation from a feature-underspecified source (Korean: no gender, radical pro-drop) to a feature-explicit target (Spanish) as a diagnostic probe of phi-feature RECONSTRUCTION, finding an asymmetry (context recovers person but not gender) and architecture-dependent strategies (conservative non-commitment vs over-generation of spurious values) — but this is purely behavioral/linguistic, corpus-based, with no internal representation, no stereotype-leakage account, and no causal intervention. Machine-translation gender-bias work (AmbGIMT, WinoMT, gender-inclusive MT, formality-control MT) documents that models resolve source-ambiguous gender/formality via occupational/sentiment stereotypes and that constraints reduce but do not remove it — again behavioral, output-level, with no mechanism and no notion of an internal underspecification-vs-commitment state. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS, and my prior code-switch-binding proposal studied which language drives grammatical AGREEMENT during an explicit lexical switch. NONE ask whether a model internally represents that an obligatory feature is UNDERDETERMINED by the source, whether feature-filling causally leaks a demographic prior, whether the model could have hedged (chosen a neutral/epicene form or flagged ambiguity) instead of silently imposing a stereotyped value, or whether a 'feature-commitment' signal can be causally localized and steered to convert silent stereotyped imposition into explicit hedging. This is distinct from all my prior proposals (which concern shared knowledge/typological leakage into a value the source DID specify, or decision-gating over answerability/abstention): here the causal object is the INVENTION of grammatical information the source genuinely omitted, and its coupling to social priors — a mechanistic, causal, bias-relevant account of underspecification-filling, extending Hwang's behavioral probe into an internal, steerable mechanism.
Abstract: Every translation from a grammatically sparse language into a richer one forces an act of invention: Korean and Turkish leave gender unmarked, Chinese leaves number and definiteness optional, English leaves formality unspecified — yet Spanish, French, or Japanese demand these features be realized. The model must supply information the source never gave. We ask how it does so internally: does it represent that the feature is genuinely underdetermined, and when it commits to a value, does it fill the slot by leaking a demographic or social prior rather than hedging? We build ReconstructProbe, controlled source sentences that underspecify an obligatory target feature (gender, number, formality) paired with entities that carry a measurable stereotype (occupation, trait, role), across source-target pairs spanning the relevant typological gaps. Behaviorally we measure how often the model imposes the stereotype-consistent value versus choosing a neutral/epicene realization or flagging ambiguity, and whether imposition tracks entity stereotype strength. Mechanistically, we train a linear probe to decode, at the point of realization, both (a) whether the feature is underdetermined by the source and (b) which value is being committed, and test whether the underspecification signal is present even when a value is nonetheless imposed. Via activation and path patching we localize a 'feature-commitment' signal and test whether it carries the stereotype prior. In a decisive causal test we steer this signal to make the model hedge — producing a neutral/epicene form or an explicit ambiguity flag — instead of silently imposing a stereotyped value, and, in reverse, to force stereotyped imposition, while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe stereotype leakage in cross-lingual generation as a steerable choice between hedging and prior-imposition over a genuinely underdetermined slot.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & SOURCE->TARGET PAIRS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). Choose pairs where the SOURCE underspecifies an obligatory TARGET feature: GENDER (Korean/Turkish/Hungarian/Persian [genderless] -> Spanish/French/Russian [obligatory gender]); NUMBER/DEFINITENESS (Chinese/Japanese [optional number] -> English/German [obligatory]); FORMALITY (English [no T/V] -> Japanese/Korean/Hindi [obligatory register]). Code, per source, which features are underspecified (from typological references + native verification).
2) DATASET (ReconstructProbe): ~500 source sentences per pair in which the target-obligatory feature is genuinely UNDERDETERMINED by the source (no antecedent, no disambiguating context), paired with entities carrying a measurable stereotype along the feature axis: for GENDER, occupations/traits with independently-rated gender-stereotype scores (nurse/engineer, gentle/assertive); for FORMALITY, roles with status/politeness expectations; for NUMBER, collective vs individual referents. Include (a) a DISAMBIGUATED control where the source DOES specify the feature (correct value known; bounds the effect and separates reconstruction from ignorance) and (b) a NEUTRAL-ENTITY control (no stereotype) to isolate prior-leakage. Elicit the target realization (full translation and a targeted cloze forcing the feature, e.g. the article/verb agreement/pronoun) with native-verified templates; where the target has a NEUTRAL/EPICENE option or the model can explicitly flag ambiguity, offer/detect it.
3) BEHAVIORAL PRIOR-LEAKAGE TEST: For underdetermined items, classify the realization as STEREOTYPE-CONSISTENT imposition vs STEREOTYPE-INCONSISTENT vs HEDGE (neutral/epicene form or explicit ambiguity flag). KEY hypothesis: on genuinely underdetermined slots, models impose the stereotype-consistent value far above chance and rarely hedge, with imposition rate tracking entity stereotype strength; the effect is larger for gender than for context-recoverable features (replicating and extending Hwang's asymmetry). Mixed-effects logistic regression of stereotype-imposition on (stereotype-strength score, feature type, source->target pair, resource tier via URIEL), item as random effect; compare against the disambiguated and neutral-entity controls. Report per-pair imposition/hedge profiles and cross-pair variation.
4) SHARED UNDERSPECIFICATION & COMMITMENT PROBES: At each layer, pool the hidden state at the realization position; train two linear probes: (i) UNDERSPECIFICATION probe (is the feature underdetermined by the source vs specified) using the underdetermined-vs-disambiguated contrast, and (ii) COMMITTED-VALUE probe (which value the model will realize). Test zero-shot cross-lingual/cross-pair transfer of both (AUROC), evidencing shared, source-language-independent representations of 'this is underdetermined' and 'I am committing value v'. CRITICAL: on imposed-value items, test whether the UNDERSPECIFICATION signal is still strongly present (the model internally 'knows' the source didn't specify) even as it commits a value — the signature of silent prior-imposition over an acknowledged gap.
5) DOES COMMITMENT CARRY THE PRIOR? Test whether the committed-value probe's readout for underdetermined items aligns with the entity's independent stereotype score (correlation), and whether a 'stereotype-prior' direction (difference-of-means over entities with opposite stereotype poles, estimated on NEUTRAL-source monolingual data) predicts which value gets imposed. This links the internal commitment to a demographic prior rather than to source evidence.
6) LOCALIZE THE FEATURE-COMMITMENT SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between an item realized with the stereotype-consistent value and one realized with the opposite/neutral value on the SAME underdetermined source, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips the imposed value WITHOUT changing the decoded source content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs path patching. Test whether these commitment components overlap with the stereotype-prior direction.
7) CAUSAL HEDGE-vs-IMPOSE STEERING (decisive): Derive a feature-commitment steering vector via difference-of-means (impose-value runs minus hedge/neutral runs). Test (i) HEDGE: subtracting it (or steering toward the underspecification direction) makes the model choose the NEUTRAL/EPICENE realization or explicitly flag ambiguity instead of imposing a stereotyped value, raising the hedge rate toward a reference; (ii) IMPOSE/FLIP: adding it or the stereotype-prior direction forces stereotyped imposition (and flips it to the opposite stereotype), on well-behaved items; (iii) it works across source->target pairs, more strongly where imposition was highest; (iv) it changes ONLY the underspecified feature's realization, not the source's decoded content, correctly-specified features (disambiguated control unchanged), or surface language (fidelity checks), and does not degrade general translation quality (BLEU/COMET on a held-out set) or general QA. Metrics: hedge-rate increase, stereotype-imposition reduction, imposition-induction/flip rate (reverse), content/output-language fidelity, disambiguated-control and translation-quality retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes the underspecified slot but not correctly-specified features or unrelated content, guarding against a generic lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: feature-type breakdown (gender vs number vs formality) and the context-recoverable-vs-not asymmetry (replicating Hwang: person recovers, gender does not); architecture-dependence of conservative-hedging vs over-imposition (Hwang's observation) across model families; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single commitment/hedge vector generalizes across feature types and pairs; robustness across full-translation vs targeted-cloze formats.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-pair stereotype-imposition vs hedge rates and stereotype-strength regression, underspecification-probe and committed-value-probe transfer AUROC (and underspecification-present-under-imposition), commitment-vs-stereotype-prior alignment, patch-localized feature-commitment layer and its overlap with the stereotype-prior direction, causal steering hedge-rate increase / imposition reduction and imposition-flip rate, content/output/translation-quality fidelity, disambiguated- and neutral-entity-control retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Distinguishing genuine underspecification-filling from ignorance or context-recoverability is essential; we use the DISAMBIGUATED control (source specifies the feature -> correct value known) and construct underdetermined items with no antecedent, and verify via the underspecification probe that the model internally registers the gap, so imposition on flagged-underdetermined items is genuine prior-leakage, not missed context. 2) Stereotype scores for entities are subjective and culture-dependent; we use independently pre-rated lexicons, native verification, restrict to clear-consensus items, and use the NEUTRAL-ENTITY control to isolate prior-leakage from base rates. 3) Some target languages lack a clean NEUTRAL/EPICENE option, making 'hedge' hard to realize; we select target languages/features where a neutral form or an explicit ambiguity flag is available, and treat explicit flagging as the hedge signal where morphology forbids neutrality. 4) The underspecification-vs-commitment split could be confounded if the underspecification signal itself differs by source; we test transfer of the probe across pairs and report how much imposition reflects a present-but-overridden underspecification signal. 5) Steering the feature might harm translation fluency or spill into correctly-specified features; we report translation-quality (COMET/BLEU), disambiguated-control retention, content and output-language fidelity, and use the reverse (imposition-induction/flip) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine feature-commitment mechanism rather than a generic lever. 6) Architecture-dependence (Hwang) means some models may hedge by default (no leakage) or over-impose; either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often silent stereotyped imposition occurs per model. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) The commitment/prior signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 9) Bias framing: we use the imposition-inducing/flip steering strictly as an interpretability/fairness diagnostic (to demonstrate the commitment signal causally carries the prior), not as a deployment tool, and the applied direction of interest is the HEDGE steering that reduces silent stereotyped imposition. 10) Distinguishing from behavioral MT-bias and Hwang's linguistic-probe work is essential; our contribution is the internal, causal account: a shared underspecification-vs-commitment representation, its coupling to a demographic prior, and a steerable choice between hedging and prior-imposition, none of which prior work provides.

Name: crosslingual_game_policy_execution_gating
Title: Playing Weaker in Some Tongues: A Shared Game-State/Optimal-Move Representation Whose Policy Execution Is Gated by the Interface Language
Short Hypothesis: When the SAME multilingual LLM plays a text-based strategy game through different language interfaces, it computes a largely language-independent internal representation of the game STATE and the OPTIMAL MOVE, but the interface language causally sets how reliably that optimal move is EXECUTED: the same position is understood and the best action is internally identified similarly across languages, yet the emitted move is systematically more often suboptimal or invalid in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so the model 'knows the best move' internally while behaviorally playing weaker. The policy-execution signal is causally localizable and steerable, so language-gated skill loss can be repaired without changing the interface language.
Related Work: Cheng et al. (2026, 'Skill Issue') show, via multilingual self-play in text games (a multilingual TextArena extension), that the SAME model plays at markedly different strength across languages—systematic variation in win margins, invalid actions, and strategic tendencies—isolating language from knowledge, and note that changing only the intermediate reasoning language can recover much lost performance; but this is purely behavioral, with no internal representation, no decomposition, and no causal intervention. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025; Sun 2026 'shared semantic neurons, misaligned attention'; LinguaMap 2026) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding and shows multi-hop factual failures stem from misaligned routing, not missing knowledge—but for FACTUAL retrieval, never for interactive STRATEGIC play. My prior proposals cover factual retrieval, typological-feature leakage, decision-gating (calibration/abstention/concession/tool-invocation), reasoning-language choice, and step-level error localization; NONE address the realized game-playing POLICY—whether a model builds a shared game-state/optimal-move representation and whether executing the optimal move is language-gated, nor localize/steer a policy-execution signal. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of strategic skill discrepancy, converting the Skill Issue behavioral finding into an internal, steerable mechanism, and is distinct from factual-knowledge routing (Sun 2026) because the object is action selection in games (spatial reasoning, imperfect information, optimal-move choice), not fact recall.
Abstract: Large language models understand knowledge unevenly across languages, but a subtler question is whether they ACT differently: does the same model, playing the same game, execute worse strategy simply because it is interfaced in another language? Recent behavioral work shows exactly this—the same model wins less, plays more invalid moves, and adopts different strategies across languages in self-play—yet why remains unknown. We give a mechanistic, causal account. We hypothesize that the model computes a largely language-independent internal representation of the game state and the optimal move, but the interface language causally gates whether that optimal move is executed, so the same position yields the best action in some languages and a suboptimal or invalid one in others. We use a multilingual text-game self-play harness across typologically and resource-diverse language interfaces and controlled game positions with known optimal moves, holding rules, state, and action space fixed. Behaviorally we measure per-language move optimality and invalid-move rate at matched positions and test whether skill loss tracks resource level and typological distance beyond understanding of the rules. We train a linear probe to decode the game state and the internally-preferred optimal move from hidden states and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose skill loss into a shared state/optimal-move representation versus a language-set policy-execution gate—verifying the optimal move is internally present even where a worse move is played. Via activation and path patching we localize a policy-execution signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model execute the optimal move in weak-play languages—or, in reverse, induce suboptimal play—while leaving the interface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual skill discrepancy as a steerable gate over a shared strategic representation.
Experiments: 1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse language interfaces (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Swahili). 2) GAMES & POSITIONS (GamePolicyProbe): Use a multilingual text-game harness (TextArena-style, extending Cheng et al. 2026) with games spanning skill types: SPATIAL (e.g., a grid/pathing game), IMPERFECT-INFORMATION (a card/hidden-state game), and RESOURCE/OPTIMAL-MOVE (a combinatorial choice game). For each game, curate ~500 controlled POSITIONS with a KNOWN optimal move (computed by an external solver/oracle) and a clear suboptimal/invalid distractor set, so move quality is objectively scorable. Render each position's rules, state, and action prompt in all 8 languages (native-verified), holding state and action space fixed. Include a RULES-COMPREHENSION screen (verify the model can, per language, correctly answer questions about the current legal moves/state) so weak play is not mere rule-misreading, and record tokenization fertility. 3) BEHAVIORAL SKILL-ASYMMETRY TEST: Per (position, language) record whether the model plays the OPTIMAL move vs suboptimal vs invalid. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME position, optimal-move rate is systematically lower (invalid-move rate higher) in lower-resource/typologically distant interfaces, beyond rule comprehension and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of suboptimal/invalid play on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, rules-comprehension indicator, game/skill type), position as random effect; test the language effect. Report per-language skill profiles, cross-lingual disagreement on identical positions, and replicate the Skill Issue self-play strength gap as a sanity check. 4) SHARED STATE/OPTIMAL-MOVE PROBE & TRANSFER: At the pre-move position pool the hidden state; train linear probes to decode (i) the game STATE (key state features) and (ii) the INTERNALLY-PREFERRED / oracle-OPTIMAL move on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC/accuracy as evidence of a language-independent state and optimal-move representation. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on SUBOPTIMAL/INVALID-play items, test whether the optimal move is still internally decodable across languages—the signature of 'knows the best move, plays worse'. 5) UNDERSTANDING-vs-EXECUTION DECOMPOSITION: For each suboptimal/invalid play, classify via the probe as (A) STATE/OPTIMAL-MOVE FAILURE (the optimal move is not internally represented) vs (B) EXECUTION-GATE FAILURE (optimal move present but not played). Report the proportion of A vs B per language and correlate with resource tier and typological distance (predict execution-gate failures dominate for typologically close languages, understanding failures for distant/low-resource ones). Anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens. 6) LOCALIZE THE POLICY-EXECUTION SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that plays optimally and one that plays suboptimally on the SAME position, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer makes the optimal move emitted WITHOUT changing the decoded game state. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the state/optimal-move representation FROM a strong-play language into a weak-play run (does it repair the move?). 7) CAUSAL POLICY STEERING (decisive): Derive a policy-execution steering vector via difference-of-means (optimal-play runs minus suboptimal-play runs at matched internal optimal-move). Test (i) EXECUTE: adding it in weak-play languages increases optimal-move rate and reduces invalid moves toward strong-play levels; (ii) NULL ON UNDERSTANDING FAILURES: it does not help positions where the optimal move was internally absent, validating the decomposition; (iii) SUPPRESS: subtracting it induces suboptimal play in strong-play languages; (iv) it changes ONLY move execution, not the decoded game state or interface language (fidelity checks), and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Baselines: reasoning-in-English (Cheng et al.'s recovery lever), translate-position-to-English. Metrics: per-mode optimal-move recovery (execution-gate vs understanding), invalid-move reduction, suboptimal-induction rate (reverse), state-signal/interface-language fidelity, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes move quality but not unrelated answers. 8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: skill-type breakdown (spatial vs imperfect-info vs optimal-choice—which skills are most language-gated?); is English/high-resource the strong-play reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the asymmetry?); probe layer/dimensionality; whether one execution vector generalizes across games and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility interfaces at matched internal optimal-move and by showing content-invariant steering repairs play without changing tokenization. EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language optimal-move and invalid-move rates and their resource/typology regression controlling for rule comprehension/fertility, Skill Issue strength-gap replication, cross-lingual state/optimal-move probe transfer AUROC/accuracy and optimal-move-present-under-suboptimal-play, understanding-vs-execution-gate failure proportions with probe validation, patch-localized policy-execution layer, cross-lingual state transplant repair rate (and null on understanding failures), causal steering per-mode optimal-move recovery and suboptimal-induction rates, state-signal/interface fidelity, general-QA retention, comparison to reason-in-English and translate baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The understanding-vs-execution split is the crux and could be confounded if the state/optimal-move signal itself differs by language (the model genuinely fails to represent the best move in some languages); we test this directly by verifying optimal-move decodability across languages on suboptimal-play items via probe transfer, screen rule comprehension, and report the split rather than assuming it—either outcome is informative. 2) Weak play could reduce to rule-misreading rather than an execution gate; the rules-comprehension screen and the optimal-move-present-under-suboptimal-play probe dissociate these, and the causal null-on-understanding-failures test confirms the decomposition. 3) Defining a KNOWN optimal move requires solvable games; we use games with an external solver/oracle and clear optimal moves, and analyze positions with an unambiguous best move (excluding ties). 4) Tokenization fertility confounds move-string generation and prompt length; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility interfaces at matched internal optimal-move, and content-invariant steering repairs play without changing tokenization, dissociating the gate from length. 5) Some models may play uniformly across languages (no gap) or fail to represent the optimal move at all (pure understanding failure); either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality/mechanism of cross-lingual skill discrepancy, and we quantify how often each regime occurs. 6) Scoring move optimality/validity in free generation is noisy; we constrain to a discrete action set with a validated parser and use oracle labels. 7) The state/optimal-move probe could latch onto surface cues rather than a genuine strategic representation; the cross-lingual invariance, the optimal-move-present-under-failure test, and the cross-lingual state transplant guard against this. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and game-specific; we test five models, multiple games, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) Steering may harm fluency, produce invalid moves, or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report state-signal/interface fidelity, invalid-move rate, and general-QA retention, and use the null-on-understanding-failures, suppression (reverse), and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine policy-execution gate. 10) The gate/policy signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from behavioral Skill Issue work (Cheng et al. 2026) and factual-routing mechanistic work (Sun 2026) is essential; our contribution is the internal, causal account of STRATEGIC POLICY execution—a shared game-state/optimal-move representation under a language-set execution gate, localized and steered—for interactive games rather than fact recall, none of which prior work provides.

Name: crosslingual_evidence_stance_gating
Title: Supported or Refuted, in Every Language? A Shared Evidence-Stance Signal Whose Verdict Threshold Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When verifying a claim against presented evidence, a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal 'evidence-stance' representation (whether the evidence SUPPORTS, REFUTES, or is insufficient for the claim), but the query language causally sets the VERDICT THRESHOLD applied to that signal: for the SAME claim-evidence pair, the model reaches a decisive supported/refuted verdict at a lower threshold in some languages and retreats to NOT-ENOUGH-INFO (or flips toward a parametric-belief-consistent verdict) in others (typically lower-resource / typologically distant), producing a cross-lingual fact-verification asymmetry that is separable from the shared stance signal and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable verdict-gating signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Multilingual fact-verification work is entirely behavioral/system-building: benchmarks and pipelines for evidence retrieval + NLI-style verdict prediction across languages (FEVEROUS; CsFEVER/CTKFacts; ViWikiFC; IndicClaimBuster; multilingual XLM-R/InfoXLM stance classifiers; Amatya & Setty 2026). Bakke & Heggelund (2025, 'Check Your Bias') note that a model's parametric-knowledge bias affects verdicts and that it over-labels claims 'Not Enough Evidence', but only in English and only behaviorally, with no internal representation, no cross-lingual decomposition, and no causal intervention. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for the evidence-stance (support/refute) computation. My prior gating proposals target distinct objects: calibration (confidence in the model's OWN answer), context-vs-memory trust (retrieved passage vs parametric memory on a QA answer), ICL override (contradictory demonstrations), and credential-deference (an authoritative source endorsing a claim). This proposal is distinct because the object is the SUPPORT-vs-REFUTE-vs-INSUFFICIENT stance of PRESENTED EVIDENCE relative to a claim (a verification judgment with a clear normative benchmark from the evidence itself), decomposed into a shared stance signal versus a language-set verdict threshold, and causally localized/steered—none of which prior work provides.
Abstract: Automated fact-checking increasingly relies on LLMs to judge whether evidence supports or refutes a claim, and such systems are deployed across many languages. We ask whether the query language changes the verdict a model reaches on the SAME claim-evidence pair, and how this is implemented internally. We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal evidence-stance representation—whether the presented evidence supports, refutes, or is insufficient for the claim—but the query language causally sets the verdict threshold applied to it, so the same evidence yields a decisive supported/refuted verdict in some languages while the model retreats to not-enough-info (or drifts toward a parametric-belief-consistent verdict) in others. This predicts a cross-lingual verification asymmetry dissociable from the shared stance signal. We build StanceGateProbe from parallel FEVER-style claim-evidence triples across 12 typologically and resource-diverse languages, with claim, evidence, and gold verdict held fixed. Behaviorally we measure per-language verdict decisiveness and NOT-ENOUGH-INFO retreat at matched stance strength and test whether it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond the evidence. We train a linear evidence-stance probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the verdict gap into a shared stance signal versus a language-set verdict threshold—a NEI verdict should coincide with an intact internal support/refute signal (the model 'sees' the stance but withholds the verdict). Via activation and path patching we localize a verdict-gating signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model reach the evidence-warranted verdict across languages—or, in reverse, induce NEI retreat—while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual fact-verification inconsistency as a shared stance signal under a steerable, language-dependent verdict gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili, Yoruba).
2) DATASET (StanceGateProbe): ~600 claim-evidence triples with gold SUPPORTS/REFUTES/NEI labels drawn from FEVER/FEVEROUS and multilingual FEVER-style resources (CsFEVER, ViWikiFC, IndicClaimBuster). Balance SUPPORTS/REFUTES (decisive evidence) and genuine NEI. For each item present the CLAIM and the EVIDENCE and ask for a verdict. Keep claim+evidence content fixed across languages; translate/native-verify. Vary EVIDENCE STRENGTH (clearly decisive vs borderline) as a graded factor to trace a verdict-threshold curve. Include (a) a PARAMETRIC-CONFLICT stratum where the evidence-warranted verdict CONTRADICTS the model's likely parametric belief (to test drift toward belief-consistent verdicts vs evidence-following), and (b) an EVIDENCE-COMPREHENSION screen (verify per language the model correctly reports what the evidence states, in isolation) so verdict failure is not evidence-misreading. Record tokenization fertility. Short verdict labels for scoring.
3) BEHAVIORAL ASYMMETRY TEST: Per (item, language) record the verdict. KEY hypothesis: on DECISIVE (SUPPORTS/REFUTES) items, the model retreats to NEI (or gives a belief-consistent wrong verdict) more in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond the evidence and comprehension. Mixed-effects logistic regression of NEI-retreat / verdict-error on (language, evidence strength, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, comprehension indicator, gold label), item as random effect; test the language effect and its distance dependence. Compare against genuine-NEI items (should stay NEI, language-flatter). Report per-language verdict-threshold curves and cross-lingual disagreement on identical claim-evidence pairs; replicate the English NEI-over-labeling tendency (Bakke & Heggelund) as a sanity check.
4) SHARED STANCE PROBE & TRANSFER: At the pre-verdict position pool the hidden state; train a linear probe to decode the evidence STANCE (supports vs refutes vs insufficient) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report macro-F1/AUROC as evidence of a language-independent stance representation. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on NEI-RETREAT (evidence-decisive-but-answered-NEI) items, test whether the internal support/refute stance is still strongly decodable across languages—the signature of 'sees the stance, withholds the verdict'.
5) THRESHOLD-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer stance signal across languages (should be similar on matched decisive items) versus the emitted verdict (which diverges). Define a per-language VERDICT THRESHOLD on the shared stance axis (how strong the stance must be to commit to supported/refuted); test whether cross-lingual verdict differences are explained by a shifted threshold on a similar stance signal rather than a weaker signal. Correlate per-language threshold with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-decision split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE VERDICT-GATING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that commits to the warranted verdict and one that retreats to NEI on the SAME item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips NEI->warranted-verdict WITHOUT changing the decoded stance signal or evidence content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gating components from a decisive language into a retreating run.
7) CAUSAL VERDICT STEERING (decisive): Derive a verdict-gating steering vector via difference-of-means (decisive-verdict runs minus NEI-retreat runs at matched stance). Test (i) COMMIT: adding it in retreat-prone languages makes the model reach the evidence-warranted supported/refuted verdict toward a reference level; (ii) RETREAT: subtracting it induces NEI over-labeling in decisive languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where the gap was largest; (iv) DOSE-RESPONSE: scaling produces graded verdict shifts; (v) it changes ONLY the verdict-commitment decision, NOT the decoded stance signal, the claim/evidence content, or surface language (fidelity checks), does NOT push genuine-NEI items to a false decisive verdict (specificity), and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Baselines: prompt-based 'decide if the evidence is sufficient', per-language threshold tuning, translate-to-English. Metrics: NEI-retreat-gap closure, evidence-warranted-verdict recovery, genuine-NEI retention (must not over-commit on truly insufficient evidence), retreat-induction rate (reverse), stance-signal/output fidelity, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts verdict commitment but not stance readout or unrelated answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: SUPPORTS vs REFUTES asymmetry (is one stance more suppressed?); PARAMETRIC-CONFLICT stratum (does low-resource-language verdict drift toward parametric belief over the evidence?); is English/high-resource the decisive reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank verdict subspace; whether one gating vector generalizes across items and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched stance and by showing content-invariant steering shifts verdicts without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language NEI-retreat / verdict-error rate and its resource/typology regression controlling for evidence-strength/comprehension/fertility, English NEI-over-labeling replication, cross-lingual stance probe transfer F1/AUROC and stance-present-under-NEI-retreat, signal-similarity vs verdict-divergence (threshold) decomposition, threshold-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized verdict-gating layer, cross-lingual gating transplant repair rate, causal steering NEI-retreat-gap closure with dose-response and retreat-induction rate, genuine-NEI retention, stance-signal/output fidelity, general-QA retention, comparison to prompt/threshold-tuning/translate baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The threshold-vs-signal split could be confounded if the stance signal itself differs by language (the model genuinely reads the evidence's support/refute stance less well in some languages); we test this directly by verifying an intact internal stance signal on NEI-retreat items across languages via probe transfer and screen per-language evidence comprehension, reporting how much of the gap is signal vs threshold—either outcome is informative. 2) NEI-retreat could reflect an evidence-comprehension gap rather than a verdict gate; the comprehension screen and the stance-present-under-retreat probe dissociate these, restricting the sharp test to items where the evidence is correctly read. 3) The key specificity guard: any commit-inducing intervention must NOT push GENUINE-NEI items to false decisive verdicts; we include genuine-NEI items and report their retention as a primary metric, using it to ensure the steering targets unwarranted retreat, not decisiveness in general—if entangled, that is itself a publishable finding. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched stance, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts verdicts. 5) Some models/languages may show no verdict asymmetry (uniform decisiveness or uniform NEI-over-labeling); either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often a gap exists. 6) FEVER-style translations may introduce artifacts; we native-verify, use existing multilingual FEVER-style resources where available, and hold claim+evidence content fixed. 7) Verdict scoring across languages is noisy; we use short verdict labels and validate label extraction against human checks. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report stance-signal/output fidelity, genuine-NEI and general-QA retention, and use the retreat-induction (reverse), reverse-consistency, and dose-response tests to ensure a genuine verdict-threshold dial. 10) The verdict signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my calibration (own-answer confidence), context-trust (passage vs memory), override (ICL demonstrations), and credential-deference proposals is essential; here the object is the SUPPORT/REFUTE/INSUFFICIENT stance of presented evidence relative to a claim (a verification judgment with a normative benchmark from the evidence itself) and its language-set verdict threshold over a shared stance signal, with direct fact-checking-deployment stakes.

Name: implicit_numeral_composition_mechanism
Title: The Missing Operators: Do LLMs Internally Reconstruct the Implicit Compositional Structure of Numerals, and Is the Failure Representational or a Readout Bottleneck?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM reads a spelled-out or cross-linguistic numeral whose arithmetic structure is IMPLICIT (e.g., 'four-twenties-ten' = 4x20+10, or a novel base system taught in-context), it computes—or fails to compute—a latent representation of the underlying compositional operators (the implicit + and x). We hypothesize that (1) a linear 'implicit-operator' probe can decode whether the model has internally reconstructed the additive/multiplicative structure of a numeral from hidden states; (2) the documented failure of LLMs on cross-linguistic numeral puzzles (which vanishes when operators are made explicit with +/x symbols) is dissociable into a REPRESENTATION failure (the implicit operator structure is never internally built) versus a READOUT/ROUTING failure (the structure IS built but is not routed into the arithmetic computation); and (3) causally supplying the missing operator representation—by patching in the operator direction derived from the explicit-symbol condition—repairs arithmetic on the implicit condition without changing the surface numeral.
Related Work: Bhattacharya et al. (2025, EMNLP) show, behaviorally, that LLMs fail cross-linguistic numeral puzzles and succeed only when the mathematical operations are explicitly marked with known symbols (+, x), concluding that models lack a notion of implicit numeral structure—but this is purely behavioral, with no internal representation, no representation-vs-readout decomposition, and no causal intervention. Cognitive-science work establishes that compositional numeral structure (base systems, additive/multiplicative combination) scaffolds human numerical cognition (Landy et al.; Guerrero et al. 2026 on base-5 sign-language structure). NLP numeracy-probing work shows monolingual LLMs place digits on a roughly log-scaled magnitude subspace, but concerns the MAGNITUDE of a resolved number, not the latent COMPOSITIONAL PARSE (implicit operator structure) of a numeral expression. My own prior proposals concern number-word magnitude distortion (number naming), dynamic running tallies, approximate-number acuity, measurement units, and reported precision—NONE address whether the model internally reconstructs the IMPLICIT additive/multiplicative operator structure of a numeral, whether the failure is representational vs a readout bottleneck, or whether supplying the operator representation causally repairs arithmetic. This is the first mechanistic, causal account of implicit numeral composition, converting the EMNLP behavioral finding into an internal, testable mechanism, and is distinct from magnitude-probing because the object is the latent PARSE (which operations combine which sub-numerals), not the scalar value.
Abstract: Numeral systems combine numbers in strikingly different ways: French 'quatre-vingt-dix' means four-twenties-ten (4x20+10), and constructed base systems demand the reader infer implicit additive and multiplicative operations with no symbol marking them. Recent work shows LLMs fail such cross-linguistic numeral puzzles yet succeed the moment the operations are written with explicit +/x symbols, concluding that models lack a sense of implicit numeral structure—but why, and where, remains unknown. We give a mechanistic, causal account. We hypothesize that solving an implicit numeral requires internally reconstructing its compositional operators (which sub-numerals are added, which are multiplied), and that the behavioral failure splits into two dissociable causes: a representation failure, where the operator structure is never internally built, versus a readout/routing failure, where the structure is built but not fed into the arithmetic. We build NumeralComposeProbe: matched numeral-arithmetic items presented in an IMPLICIT form (spelled-out compositional numerals and in-context-taught novel base systems) versus an EXPLICIT-SYMBOL form (+/x marked), with the underlying value held fixed. We train a linear probe to decode the implicit operator structure (per sub-numeral: additive vs multiplicative combination, and the base) from hidden states and test whether it recovers the structure, and whether structure decodability predicts arithmetic success. On failures, we classify each as representation-absent versus present-but-unused via the probe, validated by activation patching: transplanting the operator representation from the explicit-symbol run into the implicit run. In a decisive causal test we derive an operator-structure steering/patch from the explicit condition and show it repairs implicit-numeral arithmetic—without changing the surface numeral—when and only when the failure is a readout bottleneck, while representation failures are unmoved. We reframe the LLM numeral-composition gap as a locatable, causally addressable interplay between building and using an implicit compositional parse.
Experiments:
1) MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, plus a stronger reasoning model (Qwen2.5-14B) and a smaller model for scale analysis (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs).
2) DATASET (NumeralComposeProbe): Two families where numeral structure is IMPLICIT. (A) NATURAL COMPOSITIONAL NUMERALS: spelled-out numerals from languages with non-trivial additive/multiplicative/vigesimal structure (French 70-99, Danish base-20, Welsh, Hindi opaque forms, Chinese transparent decimal as a control), each with a known operator parse (which parts add, which multiply). (B) CONSTRUCTED-BASE PUZZLES (following Bhattacharya et al.): novel numeral systems taught via a few in-context examples, where the model must infer the base and combination rules. For every item build a matched EXPLICIT-SYMBOL version where the same value is written with +/x (e.g., 'four x twenty + ten'), holding the underlying value fixed. Tasks: (i) VALUE RESOLUTION (convert numeral -> integer), (ii) ARITHMETIC (add/compare two numerals). Native/rule-verified parses; record tokenization.
3) BEHAVIORAL REPLICATION: Confirm the implicit-vs-explicit gap (arithmetic accuracy far lower on implicit than explicit-symbol form) per model and per numeral family, replicating Bhattacharya et al. and locating the hardest structural boundaries (French 70-99, base transitions).
4) IMPLICIT-OPERATOR PROBE: At each layer, pool hidden states at the numeral positions and train a linear probe to decode the OPERATOR STRUCTURE of each sub-numeral pair (ADDITIVE vs MULTIPLICATIVE combination) and the inferred BASE, on the EXPLICIT-symbol condition (where ground-truth structure is unambiguous). Apply the probe to the IMPLICIT condition and test whether the model has internally reconstructed the same operator structure. Report probe accuracy per condition and per structural boundary; measure whether structure-decodability is lower exactly where arithmetic fails.
5) STRUCTURE-PREDICTS-SUCCESS LINK: Correlate per-item implicit-operator-probe accuracy with arithmetic correctness within the implicit condition. A positive link supports that reconstructing the operator structure is necessary for correct arithmetic.
6) REPRESENTATION-vs-READOUT DECOMPOSITION: For each implicit-condition arithmetic FAILURE, classify via the probe as (A) REPRESENTATION FAILURE (operator structure NOT internally decodable) vs (B) READOUT/ROUTING FAILURE (operator structure decodable but arithmetic still wrong—structure built but not used). Report the proportion of A vs B per model, family, and structural boundary; test whether larger/reasoning models shift failures from representation toward readout.
7) CAUSAL VALIDATION VIA PATCHING (decisive): Locate the components carrying the operator structure via activation/path patching (sweep layers/heads/MLPs) between an EXPLICIT-symbol run (which resolves correctly) and the matched IMPLICIT run (which fails), on the SAME underlying value. Test whether transplanting the operator-structure representation from the explicit run into the implicit run REPAIRS the arithmetic—and, critically, whether this repair works for items classified as READOUT failures (structure was present or supplied but unused) but NOT for pure REPRESENTATION failures where no compositional signal exists to route, validating the decomposition. Cross-check activation vs path patching.
8) OPERATOR-STRUCTURE STEERING: Derive a difference-of-means 'operator-structure' vector (explicit-symbol runs minus implicit runs at matched value) and add it during implicit-numeral arithmetic; measure arithmetic-accuracy recovery, specificity (does not help matched transparent-decimal control items that need no reconstruction), and that the surface numeral/output are unchanged. Metrics: per-mode repair rate (readout vs representation), off-target retention, general-QA (multilingual MMLU numeric subset) retention.
9) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: natural vs constructed-base families; structural-boundary breakdown (vigesimal transitions, opaque ranges); model scale and reasoning-model effect on the representation-vs-readout split; probe layer/dimensionality; tokenization sensitivity (spelled numerals split into many subwords—test token-pooling schemes); robustness across templates and value-resolution vs arithmetic tasks.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: implicit-vs-explicit arithmetic gap (behavioral replication), per-layer implicit-operator-probe accuracy (additive/multiplicative/base) in implicit vs explicit conditions, structure-decodability-vs-arithmetic-success correlation, proportion of representation vs readout failures with patching validation, patch-transplant repair rate (readout vs representation), operator-structure steering arithmetic recovery with specificity and off-target/general-QA retention, structural-boundary and model-scale analyses.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The representation-vs-readout split hinges on probe quality; we train the operator-structure probe on the explicit condition where ground-truth structure is unambiguous, report probe accuracy, and—crucially—confirm the split CAUSALLY via patching (readout failures are repaired by transplanting the operator representation, representation failures are not) rather than relying on the probe alone. 2) The implicit-operator probe could latch onto surface numeral-token cues rather than a genuine reconstructed compositional parse; we control by testing whether the probe trained on explicit-symbol structure transfers to the implicit condition, and by using constructed-base puzzles with novel in-context rules that cannot be memorized. 3) Tokenization: spelled/compositional numerals fragment into many subwords, complicating which token carries structure; we test multiple token-pooling schemes and report sensitivity, and hold the underlying value fixed across implicit/explicit forms to dissociate structure from tokenization. 4) Some models may show almost all failures as representation failures (structure never built), leaving little readout to repair—this is itself an informative, publishable finding about WHERE the numeral-composition bottleneck lies, and we quantify the split rather than assuming it; conversely, stronger reasoning models may shift toward readout failures, which the patch/steering can repair. 5) Patching may only partially repair arithmetic, or the operator representation may be distributed rather than a clean direction; we report partial-repair rates, test low-rank subspace variants, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 6) The steering/patch could act as a generic accuracy boost rather than specifically supplying operator structure; we guard with the transparent-decimal control (which needs no reconstruction and should not benefit) and the representation-failure null result. 7) Results may be model- and family-specific; we test multiple models and both natural and constructed-base numeral families and report aggregate and per-condition results. 8) Distinguishing from my prior number-naming (magnitude distortion) and running-tally proposals is essential; here the object is the latent COMPOSITIONAL PARSE—the implicit additive/multiplicative operator structure of a numeral—and its representation-vs-readout dissociation, not the scalar magnitude or a dynamic tally, directly converting the Bhattacharya et al. behavioral finding into a mechanistic, causal account.

Name: answer_length_budget_commitment
Title: Deciding How Long to Talk Before Talking: A Pre-Commitment Length Budget That Causally Caps Answer Length Independently of Content
Short Hypothesis: Before generating a substantive answer, an LLM commits to an internal 'length budget' — an early, largely content-independent representation of roughly how long the answer will be — and this budget causally caps the realized answer length: truncation of a still-incomplete answer and padding/over-elaboration of a short one are consequences of the budget rather than of running out of (or overflowing with) content. The budget is linearly decodable from hidden states at the first answer tokens, predicts final length before the content is produced, and can be causally steered to lengthen or shorten answers while preserving the content actually delivered.
Related Work: Prior work on LLM verbosity/length is behavioral: length-bias in RLHF reward models and judges (longer answers scored higher), length-controlled decoding and 'answer in N words' prompting, and length-generalization studies — all treat length as an output property to be controlled from outside, never asking whether the model internally COMMITS to a length before generating content or whether that commitment causally caps what gets said. Mechanistic work locates planning-ahead signals for single next tokens or rhyme targets (e.g. models pre-plan a line's final word) but not a global answer-length budget. Calibration/uncertainty work studies confidence, not verbosity. My own prior proposals concern cross-lingual gating of content signals; NONE address a monolingual, content-independent length-budget representation, its causal capping of answer length, or its steering. This is distinct: the object is an early internal 'how long will I talk' commitment, decodable before the answer content, that causally governs truncation vs completeness — reframing verbosity/incompleteness as a steerable pre-commitment rather than an emergent byproduct of content availability.
Abstract: Language models are notoriously inconsistent in how much they say: the same question can yield a terse one-liner or a padded essay, and important answers are sometimes cut short mid-explanation. We ask whether this is governed by an early, content-independent internal decision — a 'length budget' the model commits to before it has produced the substantive answer — that causally caps realized length. We hypothesize that (1) a linear probe on hidden states at the first few answer tokens decodes the eventual answer length well above what the prompt and question difficulty alone predict, evidencing an early commitment; (2) this budget causally caps the answer: models truncate still-incomplete answers when the budget is small and pad short answers when it is large, so length is set by the budget rather than by running out of content; and (3) a difference-of-means 'length-budget' steering vector added at the first answer tokens lengthens or shortens the answer in a graded (dose-response) way while preserving the content actually delivered per unit length. Using open models and a battery of open-ended and multi-part questions (with gold content-point rubrics so completeness is measured independently of length), we test early length-decodability, dissociate budget from content by finding cases where the model truncates a demonstrably-incomplete answer versus pads a complete one, and causally steer the budget. We localize the budget signal via activation and path patching. We reframe verbosity and premature truncation as a steerable pre-commitment rather than an emergent consequence of content flow.
Experiments: 1) MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 2) DATA (LengthBudgetProbe): ~600 open-ended and multi-part questions spanning (a) EXPLANATORY items with a gold rubric of discrete correct content points (so COMPLETENESS = fraction of gold points covered, measured independently of token length via a validated content-matching classifier + human checks on a subset), (b) LIST/ENUMERATION items with a known correct number of items, and (c) SHORT-ANSWER items where brevity is appropriate (control). Record question difficulty proxies (length, hop-count) and per-response token length. 3) EARLY LENGTH-DECODABILITY: At the first k answer tokens (k=1..8) pool hidden states and train a linear/ridge probe to predict the FINAL answer length (log token count). KEY test: does the probe predict final length ABOVE a baseline using only prompt features (question length, difficulty, item type)? Report R^2/rank-correlation and incremental R^2 over the prompt baseline; identify the earliest token/layer where length is committed. Cross-check with logit-lens (does an early representation already 'know' whether the answer will be long?). 4) BUDGET-vs-CONTENT DISSOCIATION (core): (a) TRUNCATION cases: identify items where the model stops with LOW completeness (many gold points omitted) yet the omitted points are ones it KNOWS (verified via targeted single-point probes) — i.e., it truncated an incomplete answer rather than exhausting content. Test whether the early length-budget probe read LOW on exactly these items. (b) PADDING cases: identify items where completeness is HIGH early but the answer continues with filler/repetition — test whether the early budget read HIGH. Correlate early-budget with truncation/padding, controlling for completeness, to show the budget (not content availability) governs length. 5) LOCALIZE THE BUDGET SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a matched long-answer run and short-answer run on the SAME question (induced by minimal prompt cues or different sampled continuations), sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer changes final length WITHOUT changing the completeness-per-token. Report layer distribution; cross-check activation vs path patching. 6) CAUSAL LENGTH-BUDGET STEERING (decisive): Derive a difference-of-means length-budget vector (long-answer runs minus short-answer runs at the first answer tokens). Test (i) LENGTHEN/SHORTEN with dose-response (scaling the vector graded-ly changes final length); (ii) CONTENT PRESERVATION: shortening should drop LEAST-important content last and keep completeness-per-token roughly constant, and lengthening should NOT add hallucinated content (precision of added content); (iii) specificity: it does not change answers on SHORT-ANSWER controls where length is already minimal, and does not degrade general QA (MMLU subset); (iv) it changes length, not correctness of the core answer (fidelity). Baselines: 'answer in N words' prompting, length-controlled decoding, max-token truncation. Metrics: length change and dose-response, completeness-per-token retention, precision of added content (no hallucination), core-answer-correctness retention, control specificity, general-QA retention. 7) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: item-type breakdown; does the budget track question difficulty or is it partly arbitrary/prompt-format-driven?; model scale; instruction-tuned vs base; probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank budget subspace; robustness across templates; relation to reward-model length bias (do RLHF'd models have systematically higher budgets?). EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: early-token length-probe R^2 and incremental R^2 over prompt baseline, earliest commitment token/layer, budget-vs-truncation/padding correlation controlling for completeness and known-omitted-content, patch-localized budget layer, causal steering length dose-response with completeness-per-token/core-correctness preservation and no-hallucination, short-answer-control specificity, general-QA retention, RLHF-vs-base budget comparison.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Early length-decodability could reflect the prompt/difficulty rather than a genuine internal commitment; we control by reporting incremental R^2 over a prompt-feature baseline and by dissociating budget from content in the truncation/padding analysis, where content is held or measured separately. 2) The budget-vs-content dissociation hinges on showing the model KNOWS omitted content (so truncation is a length cap, not ignorance); we verify omitted gold points via targeted single-point probes and restrict the truncation analysis to known-but-omitted content. 3) Steering could increase length merely by adding filler or hallucination rather than genuine content; we measure completeness-per-token, precision of added content (added points must be correct), and core-answer correctness, and treat filler-only lengthening as a null result, not a success. 4) Some models may not commit early (length emerges only as content runs out) — this is itself an informative, publishable finding about whether verbosity is planned vs reactive, and we quantify how much length is committed early rather than assuming it. 5) Completeness scoring is noisy; we use rubric-based gold content points, a validated content-matching classifier calibrated against human ratings on a subset, and report reliability. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test multiple models and templates and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) The budget signal may be low-rank or entangled with a difficulty/confidence signal rather than a single clean direction;
