we test low-rank subspace variants and check whether the budget dissociates from a difficulty probe. 8) Distinguishing from external length-control (prompting/decoding) is essential; our contribution is the INTERNAL, pre-content length-budget representation and its causal capping of answer length, established via early-token decoding, budget-vs-content dissociation, and content-preserving steering — none of which external length-control methods provide.

Name: crosslingual_temporal_deixis_anchor_gating
Title: Now, Here, in Whose Frame? A Shared Deictic-Anchor Representation for 'Now/Today/Recently' Whose Temporal Resolution Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When a text uses a TEMPORAL DEICTIC expression whose reference depends on an unstated 'now' anchor (e.g. 'the recent election', 'the current president', 'last year', 'nowadays'), a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal 'deictic-anchor' representation binding the expression to an implicit reference time, but whether that anchor is behaviorally EXPRESSED correctly — resolving 'recent/current/last year' to the appropriate time and NOT defaulting to the model's training-cutoff/English-centric 'now' — is gated by the query language: the SAME deictic expression is anchored consistently internally across languages yet resolved to a systematically different (often stale or dominant-language-typical) reference time in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so the model can internally 'know which now it means' while behaviorally mis-anchoring. The deictic-anchor signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated deixis-resolution failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Temporal deixis (the anchoring of 'now/today/recently/current' to an implicit reference time) is a core phenomenon in linguistics and pragmatics (Fillmore's deixis; Levinson), distinct from tense (grammatical time-marking), aspect (completion), chronological ordering (event sequence), and factual staleness (recency of stored facts). In NLP, temporal reasoning benchmarks (TempEval, MCTACO, TimeQA) and time-sensitive-QA work are behavioral and largely English, and my prior temporal proposals concern per-language STALENESS of stored facts (temporal_knowledge_asymmetry), aspectual COMPLETION (grammatical_aspect_completion), CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER of multiple events (crosslingual_timeline_reconstruction), and estimated event DURATION (crosslingual_event_duration_reweighting); NONE address the resolution of DEICTIC temporal expressions to an implicit 'now' anchor, whether that anchor is a shared cross-lingual representation, whether its behavioral resolution is language-gated (e.g. defaulting to a dominant-language/training-cutoff 'now'), or whether the anchor signal is causally localizable and steerable. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for deictic anchoring. My detection-vs-expression and threshold-gating templates target other objects (false belief, bridging, evidence stance, confabulation). This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of temporal-deixis anchoring, with direct stakes for time-sensitive answers that silently assume the wrong 'now' in some languages.
Abstract: Words like 'now', 'today', 'the current president', or 'the recent crisis' mean nothing without an anchor — an implicit reference time that fixes which 'now' is intended. Deciding that anchor is essential to answering time-sensitive questions, yet the anchor is never stated. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal representation that binds a temporal-deictic expression to a reference time, and whether that internal anchoring is decoupled from how the deixis is behaviorally resolved across languages — in particular, whether the model silently defaults to a dominant-language or training-cutoff 'now' in some languages. We hypothesize that models anchor deictic expressions similarly across languages internally, but the query language gates whether the correct anchor is surfaced, so the SAME expression ('recently', 'this year', 'the current X') is resolved to a systematically different, often stale reference time in lower-resource, typologically distant languages. We build DeixisProbe, parallel passages across languages in which a context establishes an explicit reference time (e.g. a stated event date), followed by a deictic expression whose correct resolution depends on that anchor, with anchor-resolution probes ('recently' relative to when? 'the current president' as of when?), an anchor-shift control (the same expression under a different established 'now'), and a matched EXPLICIT-DATE control. Behaviorally we measure per-language deixis-resolution accuracy and anchor-drift (defaulting to a stale/dominant 'now') and test whether it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond comprehension. We train a linear deictic-anchor probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the resolution gap into a shared anchoring component versus a language-set expression gate — verifying the correct anchor is internally present even where resolution drifts. Via activation and path patching we localize a deictic-anchor signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to surface (or shift) the reference time while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual temporal-deixis failures as a steerable gate over a shared reference-time representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Swahili). MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (DeixisProbe): ~500 short passages, each ESTABLISHING an explicit reference time (a stated event with a date, e.g. 'It is March 2019. A meeting was held...') followed by a TEMPORAL-DEICTIC expression whose correct resolution depends on that established 'now': (A) RELATIVE-DEIXIS ('recently', 'last year', 'nowadays', 'these days') — probe: to roughly what time does this refer, given the context?; (B) CURRENT-STATE-DEIXIS ('the current president', 'the present situation') — probe: as of when should this be evaluated?; (C) ANCHOR-SHIFT variants where the SAME expression appears under a DIFFERENT established 'now' (e.g. 'It is 2005...' vs 'It is 2022...'), so correct resolution must FOLLOW the established anchor, not a fixed default. Include a matched EXPLICIT-DATE control (the reference time is stated directly at the deictic point, where resolution needs no anchoring) to bound the effect and separate deixis-resolution from comprehension, and a NO-DEIXIS control. Keep the established 'now', the deictic expression, and the correct answer fixed across languages; translate/native-verify; render deictic forms naturally per language. Record tokenization fertility; screen base-passage comprehension via the explicit-date control. Answers scored as resolved time-buckets (language-agnostic normalized matching).
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (passage, language) record whether the deictic expression is resolved to the CONTEXT-ESTABLISHED anchor vs an anchor-drift default (a stale/training-cutoff or dominant-language-typical 'now'). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME passage and established 'now', deixis-resolution accuracy is systematically lower (anchor-drift higher) in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond comprehension and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of anchor-drift on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, deixis type, comprehension indicator), passage as random effect; compare against the explicit-date control (language-flatter). Report per-language resolution profiles, anchor-shift-tracking (does resolution follow the different established 'now' across languages?), and cross-lingual disagreement on identical deictic passages.
4) SHARED DEICTIC-ANCHOR PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the deictic-expression/pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode the ESTABLISHED REFERENCE TIME the expression is bound to (the context 'now') on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC/accuracy as evidence of a language-independent deictic-anchor representation. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the anchor representation for the same passage. CRITICAL: on ANCHOR-DRIFT (mis-resolved) items, test whether the correct context-established anchor is still internally decodable across ALL languages even when the emitted resolution drifts — the signature of language-gated expression over an intact anchor.
5) ANCHORING-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: For each passage, compare the shared mid-layer anchor signal across languages (should be similar if anchoring is shared) versus behavioral resolution (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal anchor to surfaced resolution per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar anchor signal rather than weaker anchoring. Correlate per-language gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE DEICTIC-ANCHOR SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that resolves to the established anchor and one that drifts on the SAME passage, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer surfaces the correct reference-time resolution WITHOUT changing the decoded passage content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the anchor representation FROM a high-resolution language into a drifting run. Attention analysis: does the deictic-expression position attend to the established-date token, more so in high-resolution languages?
7) CAUSAL DEICTIC-ANCHOR STEERING (decisive): Derive a deictic-anchor steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (correct-anchor runs minus drift runs, and anchor-A vs anchor-B contrasts from the anchor-shift design). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to drift-prone languages increases correct anchor resolution toward high-resolution levels; (ii) SHIFT: steering toward a different established 'now' (anchor-A -> anchor-B) makes the model re-resolve 'recently/current' to the other reference time on well-anchored items; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where resolution was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY the reference-time resolution, not the decoded passage content or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the explicit-date/no-deixis controls, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: resolution-gap closure, anchor-shift-flip rate (reverse/dose-response), anchor-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes deixis resolution but not explicit-date-control or unrelated answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: deixis-type breakdown (relative vs current-state); does anchor-drift default toward the training cutoff or a dominant-language-typical 'now'?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the drift?); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single anchor vector generalizes across passages and languages; robustness across resolution-vs-anchor-shift formats and templates; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal anchor and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces the anchor without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language deixis-resolution accuracy and anchor-drift rate, resolution regression controlling for comprehension/fertility/resource, anchor-shift-tracking across languages, cross-lingual deictic-anchor probe transfer AUROC/accuracy and anchor-present-under-drift, cross-lingual anchor-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), anchoring-similarity vs resolution-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized deictic-anchor layer and attention-to-established-date evidence, cross-lingual anchor transplant recovery rate, causal steering resolution-gap closure and anchor-shift-flip rates, anchor-signal/output fidelity, explicit-date/no-deixis controls and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The anchoring-vs-expression split could be confounded if the deictic-anchor signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying correct-anchor decodability across all languages on drift items via probe transfer rather than assuming, and report how much of the gap is anchoring vs gate. 2) Deixis mis-resolution could reflect passage-comprehension failure rather than an expression gate; we use the matched EXPLICIT-DATE control and comprehension screening so residual anchor-drift reflects deixis resolution, not reading. 3) Anchor resolution can be genuinely graded ('recently' relative to 2019 spans a range); we score into coarse time-buckets with clear correct/incorrect boundaries, restrict to items with a native-consensus resolution, and analyze ambiguous ones separately. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal anchor, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet surfaces the anchor, dissociating the gate from length. 5) Some models may resolve deixis uniformly across languages (no gap) or drift everywhere (uniform training-cutoff default); either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual deixis anchoring and dominant-language 'now'-defaulting, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 6) Realizing deictic expressions naturally and equivalently across languages is delicate (relative-time adverbials and 'current' constructions differ); we native-verify, treat deixis type as a factor, and flag forms with no natural equivalent. 7) The anchor probe could latch onto surface date tokens rather than a genuine reference-time binding; the anchor-shift design (same expression, different established 'now'), the anchor-present-under-drift test, cross-lingual invariance, the attention-to-established-date analysis, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report anchor-signal/output fidelity, control retention, and general-QA retention rather than claiming a free lunch, and use the anchor-shift (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine deictic-anchor gate. 10) The gate/anchor signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my temporal-staleness (recency of stored facts), aspect-completion (single-event completion), timeline-reconstruction (order of multiple events), and event-duration proposals is essential; here the object is the binding of a TEMPORAL-DEICTIC expression ('now/recently/current/last year') to an implicit reference-time anchor and the decoupling of that anchoring from its behavioral resolution across languages, with direct time-sensitive-answer stakes.

Name: crosslingual_self_verification_gating
Title: Catching Your Own Mistake, in Every Language? A Shared Self-Error-Detection Signal Whose Expression Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: Self-verification—catching that one's OWN just-generated answer is wrong—is a capability distinct from generation, and it is language-dependent in a specific dissociable way: a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal 'self-error' signal that registers whether its own produced answer is correct, but whether that signal is behaviorally EXPRESSED (flagging/revising the wrong answer when asked to verify) is gated by the query language. For the SAME self-generated error, the model internally 'knows it is wrong' across languages yet fails to flag it far more often in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so cross-lingual self-verification failure decomposes into a shared self-error-detection signal versus a language-set verification-expression gate, and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable gate signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Self-verification is heavily studied but (a) monolingual/English, (b) method-building (using verification to boost accuracy via RL/self-consistency/self-refine: Zhang 2025, Chen 2026, FABSVer 2026, SSR 2025), and (c) treats verification as an accuracy tool. Chen et al. (2026) establish a generation-vs-self-verification capability asymmetry but monolingually and behaviorally. 'Verification Mirage' (Jin 2026, medical VQA) shows verifier-generator capacity coupling and a 'lazy verifier' but is monolingual, offers no internal representation, and no cross-lingual decomposition. Phalod (2026) shows same-model self-verification is a conditional confidence signal that varies by model/task, again monolingually. Multilingual work concerns cross-lingual reasoning transfer (COPSD 2026) or fact-checking accuracy (Singhal 2024), never self-verification of the model's OWN answer. My prior crosslingual_error_monitoring proposal concerns detecting errors in EXTERNALLY-PRESENTED steps/claims; this is distinct because the object is the generation-vs-self-verification asymmetry—whether the model catches its OWN just-produced error—and whether that self-checking competence is language-gated. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never for self-verification. No prior work (i) tests whether self-verification ability is language-dependent beyond generation ability, (ii) decomposes it into a shared self-error signal versus a language-set verification-expression gate, or (iii) causally localizes and steers a self-verification gate.
Abstract: A model that produces a wrong answer is more useful if it can catch its own mistake—yet self-verification is a capability distinct from generation, and it is studied almost entirely in English. We ask whether a model's ability to catch its OWN just-generated error is language-dependent, and how it is implemented internally. We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal self-error signal registering whether its own produced answer is correct, but the query language gates whether that signal is expressed as a flag or revision, so the SAME self-generated error is internally recognized across languages yet caught far less often in lower-resource, typologically distant languages—a self-verification gap dissociable from generation ability. We build SelfVerifyProbe: for each of several open models we elicit the model's own answer to parallel factual and reasoning questions across typologically and resource-diverse languages, retain items where the model is WRONG, then ask it in a fresh context to verify its own answer, measuring per-language catch-rate. We train a linear self-error probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the catch-rate gap into a shared self-error-detection component versus a language-set verification-expression gate—verifying the error is internally decodable even where it is not flagged. Via activation and path patching we localize a self-verification signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model flag and revise its own error in low-catch languages—or, in reverse, suppress catching—while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual self-verification failure as a steerable gate over a shared self-error signal.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (SelfVerifyProbe): ~500 short-answer FACTUAL items (mLAMA/BMLAMA/Wikidata) and ~200 multi-step REASONING items (MGSM-style), parallel and native-verified across 10 languages. STEP 1: elicit the model's OWN answer per (item, language) with gold-based correctness labeling. STEP 2: retain items the model answers WRONG (the self-verification target), plus a matched set it answers CORRECT (to measure false-flagging). STEP 3: in a FRESH context, present the question with the model's own answer and ask it to verify ('Is this answer correct? If not, give the correct one'); measure whether it CATCHES the error (flags wrong / revises to correct) vs endorses its own wrong answer. Keep item content and the presented (own) answer fixed across languages; record tokenization fertility.
3) BEHAVIORAL SELF-VERIFICATION-GAP TEST: Per (item, language) record self-error catch-rate (on wrong items) and false-flag rate (on correct items). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME self-generated error, catch-rate is systematically lower in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, and—crucially—this gap is SEPARABLE from generation: condition on items wrong in ALL compared languages so generation ability is matched, and show the verification gap persists. Mixed-effects logistic regression of catch-failure on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, item type), item as random effect; report per-language self-verification profiles, cross-lingual disagreement on identical self-errors, and the generation-vs-verification dissociation (does improving generation across languages predict verification? — replicate Chen et al.'s asymmetry cross-lingually).
4) SHARED SELF-ERROR PROBE & TRANSFER: At the pre-verdict position pool the hidden state; train a linear probe to decode whether the model's own presented answer is CORRECT vs WRONG on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent self-error signal. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on CATCH-FAILURE items, test whether the self-error is still strongly decodable across languages (the model 'knows it is wrong' internally) even where it endorses its own wrong answer—the signature of language-gated expression over intact detection.
5) DETECTION-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: For each catch-failure, classify via the probe as (A) DETECTION FAILURE (self-error not internally decodable) vs (B) EXPRESSION-GATE FAILURE (error internally present but not flagged). Report the proportion of A vs B per language and correlate with resource tier and typological distance (predict expression-gate failures dominate for typologically close languages, detection failures for distant/low-resource ones). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping the internal self-error signal to behavioral flagging; test whether cross-lingual catch-rate differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar detection signal. Anchor mid-vs-output split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE SELF-VERIFICATION SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that catches and one that misses on the SAME self-error item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer makes the error surface WITHOUT changing the decoded question/answer content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the self-error representation FROM a high-catch language into a missing low-catch run.
7) CAUSAL EXPRESSION STEERING (decisive): Derive a self-verification-expression steering vector via difference-of-means (catch/revise runs minus miss runs at matched internal detection). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to low-catch languages increases correct catching and self-revision toward high-catch levels; (ii) NULL ON DETECTION FAILURES: it does not help items where the self-error was never internally detected, validating the decomposition; (iii) SUPPRESS: subtracting it makes high-catch languages endorse their own errors; (iv) it changes ONLY self-verification flagging, does NOT inflate false-flagging on CORRECT items (specificity—the model must not start rejecting its own correct answers), does not change the decoded content or surface language (fidelity), and does not degrade general QA. Metrics: catch-rate-gap closure, correct-answer-revision recovery, false-flag change on correct items, suppression-induction rate (reverse), self-error-signal/output fidelity, general-QA (multilingual MMLU subset) retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes self-verification but not unrelated or correct-item answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: factual vs reasoning items; is English/high-resource the high-catch reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the gap?); does verification-in-English (translate-then-verify) recover the gap?; probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single expression vector generalizes across items and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal detection and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces self-errors without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language self-error catch-rate and false-flag rate, catch-failure regression controlling for generation/fertility/resource, generation-vs-self-verification dissociation, cross-lingual self-error probe transfer AUROC and self-error-present-under-catch-failure, detection-vs-expression-gate failure proportions with probe validation, patch-localized self-verification layer, cross-lingual self-error transplant recovery rate (and null on detection failures), causal steering catch-rate-gap closure and suppression-induction rates with false-flag specificity, self-error-signal/output fidelity, correct-item and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The detection-vs-expression split is the crux and could be confounded if the self-error signal itself differs by language (the model genuinely fails to recognize its own error in some languages); we test this directly by verifying self-error decodability across languages on catch-failure items via probe transfer, and report the split rather than assuming it—either outcome is informative. 2) The verification gap must be separable from generation ability; we condition on items wrong in all compared languages (matched generation failure) so residual catch-rate differences reflect verification, not generation, and explicitly test the Chen et al. generation-vs-verification asymmetry cross-lingually. 3) Verifier-generator capacity coupling / 'lazy verifier' and agreement bias (Jin 2026) could drive endorsement of one's own wrong answer; the internal-self-error-present-under-catch-failure probe and the null-on-detection-failures causal test dissociate a genuine expression gate from mere detection incapacity, and the false-flag control guards against a trivial 'reject-everything' shift. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal detection, and content-invariant steering surfaces self-errors without changing tokenization. 5) Some models/languages may self-verify uniformly (no gap) or never catch errors (pure detection failure everywhere); either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often each regime occurs. 6) Correctness/flagging scoring is noisy, especially for reasoning; we validate scorers against human labels, use gold-based labels, and report reliability. 7) The self-error probe could latch onto surface cues rather than a genuine self-error representation; the cross-lingual invariance test, the self-error-present-under-failure check, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 8) The key specificity guard: steering must NOT make the model reject its own correct answers; we report false-flag change on correct items as a primary metric and use the null-on-detection-failures, suppression (reverse), and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine verification-expression gate. 9) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 10) The gate/self-error signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my error-monitoring proposal (detecting errors in externally-presented content) is essential; here the object is the generation-vs-self-verification asymmetry—catching the model's OWN just-generated error—and its language-gating over a shared self-error signal, with direct reliability stakes for self-verification-based safety layers deployed multilingually.

Name: crosslingual_switch_cost_inhibition
Title: The Cost of Switching Tongues Mid-Sentence: A Language-Inhibition Signal at Code-Switch Points and Its Asymmetric, Steerable Processing Cost in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM reads an intra-sentential code-switch (the language flips mid-utterance), it incurs a measurable internal PROCESSING COST at the switch point—a transient disruption in next-token predictability and representational coherence—carried by a language-inhibition mechanism that must suppress the just-active language and activate the incoming one; and, mirroring human bilingual psycholinguistics, this switch cost is DIRECTIONALLY ASYMMETRIC (switching from a weaker/lower-resource language into the model's dominant language is cheaper than the reverse, because a dominant language is harder to inhibit) and scales with typological/script distance. The switch cost is causally driven by a localizable language-inhibition signal that can be steered to raise or lower the cost, and reducing it improves comprehension of code-switched text.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows multilingual LLMs are poor code-switchers (Zhang et al. 2023) and that code-switching in pretraining data aids language alignment (Wang et al. 2025, 'Investigating and Scaling up Code-Switching'); embedding studies show language becomes sharply linearly separable in early layers (Kim & Lee 2025). Human bilingual psycholinguistics robustly documents an intra-sentential SWITCH COST and its DIRECTIONAL ASYMMETRY driven by language inhibition—it is harder to inhibit the dominant language, so switching INTO the dominant language is costlier in production but comprehension shows the reverse advantage, and n-2 language-repetition costs evidence inhibitory control (Zhong et al. 2024; Green's inhibitory-control model). My prior codeswitch_concept_binding proposal concerned which language OWNS a switched concept for fact retrieval/agreement; homograph_concept_binding concerned same-form cross-language words. NEITHER addresses the PROCESSING COST of the switch itself (a transient predictability/representational disruption at the switch token), whether an internal language-inhibition signal drives it, whether the cost is directionally asymmetric as in humans, or whether it is causally localizable and steerable. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies switch-point processing cost or language inhibition. This is the first mechanistic, causal account of the code-switch processing cost in LLMs, transferring the human switch-cost/inhibition finding into a model-internal, steerable mechanism.
Abstract: Bilinguals pay a cost when they switch languages mid-sentence, and that cost is asymmetric: it is harder to suppress a dominant language than a weaker one, so switch direction matters. We ask whether a multilingual LLM incurs an analogous processing cost at intra-sentential code-switch points, whether it arises from an internal language-inhibition mechanism, and whether it shows the human directional asymmetry. We operationalize the switch cost as a transient disruption at the switch token—a spike in next-token surprisal and a drop in representational coherence relative to matched non-switching baselines. We build SwitchCostProbe, minimal-pair sentences that are identical in meaning but either continue monolingually or switch language at a controlled point, across language pairs varying in dominance and typological/script distance. Behaviorally we measure the per-switch cost and test whether it is directionally asymmetric and scales with distance. Mechanistically, we train a linear probe to decode a 'language-inhibition' signal (the suppression of the outgoing language and activation of the incoming one) at the switch, and test whether its strength predicts the switch cost. Via activation and path patching we localize the inhibition signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to raise or lower the switch cost and show that reducing it improves downstream comprehension of code-switched text—while leaving monolingual processing unchanged. We reframe the LLM code-switch penalty as a measurable, asymmetric, steerable consequence of a language-inhibition mechanism.
Experiments: 1) MODELS & LANGUAGE PAIRS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). Language pairs varying in dominance and distance: English<->Spanish (close script, dominance gap), English<->Chinese (script gap), English<->Hindi, English<->Arabic, Spanish<->Italian (close), plus a low-resource pair (English<->Swahili). 2) DATASET (SwitchCostProbe): ~500 base sentences, each rendered as (a) MONOLINGUAL (fully language A or fully language B) and (b) CODE-SWITCHED variants where the language flips at a controlled, grammatically-natural switch point (noun/verb-phrase boundary), in BOTH directions (A->B and B->A). Meaning is held fixed; switch content is matched. Native-verify naturalness of switches; record per-token tokenization fertility and per-language frequency of the words around the switch. Include a WITHIN-LANGUAGE control where a matched word is substituted with no language change (to separate switch cost from lexical-substitution surprise). 3) BEHAVIORAL SWITCH-COST TEST: Define SWITCH COST = increase in next-token surprisal (and drop in representational coherence, measured as cosine/CKA discontinuity between pre- and post-switch hidden states) at the switch token, relative to the within-language control at the matched position. KEY hypotheses: (i) a positive switch cost exists at intra-sentential switch points; (ii) it is DIRECTIONALLY ASYMMETRIC (switching INTO the dominant/higher-resource language differs systematically from the reverse, on the SAME word pair); (iii) it scales with typological/script distance. Mixed-effects regression of switch cost on (switch direction, dominance gap, typological/script distance via URIEL, tokenization fertility, local word frequency), sentence as random effect; test the direction effect and distance scaling, controlling for lexical surprise via the within-language control. Report per-pair switch-cost profiles. 4) SHARED LANGUAGE-INHIBITION PROBE: At the switch token, pool hidden states and train a linear probe to decode the LANGUAGE-INHIBITION state—operationalized as the simultaneous SUPPRESSION of the outgoing language and ACTIVATION of the incoming language (using the per-layer language-ID direction, Kim & Lee 2025 / Wang 2025): measure how sharply the outgoing-language direction is down-weighted and the incoming one up-weighted across the switch. Test cross-pair transfer (AUROC) to evidence a shared, language-pair-independent inhibition signal. 5) INHIBITION-PREDICTS-COST LINK: Correlate per-item inhibition-signal strength (how much suppression/activation is required) with the behavioral switch cost, within and across pairs. Test the human-motivated prediction that inhibiting the DOMINANT language requires stronger suppression (larger inhibition signal), explaining the directional asymmetry. 6) LOCALIZE THE INHIBITION SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a code-switched run and its matched within-language control at the switch token, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer changes the switch cost (surprisal spike / representational discontinuity). Report layer distribution relative to the early language-separation band (Kim & Lee 2025); cross-check activation vs path patching. Attention analysis: do specific heads down-weight prior-language tokens at the switch? 7) CAUSAL SWITCH-COST STEERING (decisive): Derive a language-inhibition steering vector via difference-of-means (high-inhibition switch runs minus smooth within-language runs, or outgoing-language-suppression direction). Test (i) LOWER-COST: steering to sharpen incoming-language activation / cleanly suppress the outgoing language at the switch reduces the surprisal spike and representational discontinuity; (ii) RAISE-COST: reverse steering increases it; (iii) DOSE-RESPONSE and cross-pair generality; (iv) DOWNSTREAM: reducing the switch cost improves comprehension of code-switched text (measured on a code-switched QA / NLI / sentiment set, e.g. SwitchEmbed/CS-SNLI-style items) toward monolingual levels, WITHOUT degrading monolingual processing or general QA (multilingual MMLU subset), and without changing surface language. Metrics: switch-cost change with dose-response, code-switched-comprehension gain, monolingual-control and general-QA retention, output fidelity. Reverse-consistency: steering changes switch-point processing but not monolingual or unrelated tokens. 8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: switch-position effects (early vs late in sentence, single-word insertion vs alternation); n-2 language-repetition analog (does a recently-suppressed language cost more to reactivate, mirroring Zhong 2024?); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the asymmetry?); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank inhibition subspace; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility switches at matched inhibition and by showing content-invariant steering lowers cost without changing tokenization. EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-pair per-direction switch cost (surprisal spike + representational discontinuity) and directional asymmetry, switch-cost regression on direction/dominance/distance controlling for lexical surprise/fertility/frequency, cross-pair language-inhibition probe transfer AUROC, inhibition-strength-vs-switch-cost correlation (and dominant-language-harder-to-inhibit test), patch-localized inhibition layer and prior-language-suppressing attention heads, n-2 repetition-cost analog, causal steering switch-cost change with dose-response and downstream code-switched-comprehension gain, monolingual-control/general-QA retention and output fidelity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The switch cost must be separated from ordinary lexical-substitution surprise (any word change raises surprisal); the WITHIN-LANGUAGE control (matched word swap, no language change) isolates the language-switch component, and we report switch cost as the excess over this control. 2) Tokenization fertility strongly affects surprisal at script/word boundaries; we control for fertility and local frequency, compare high- vs low-fertility switches at matched inhibition, and—crucially—the content-invariant causal steering lowers the switch cost without changing tokenization, dissociating the inhibition mechanism from tokenization artifacts. 3) The inhibition-predicts-cost link and its asymmetry could be confounded by frequency (dominant-language words are more frequent); we control for local word frequency and test the asymmetry on matched word pairs across directions. 4) Some models may show negligible switch cost or no directional asymmetry (especially balanced-multilingual Aya)—either is an informative, publishable finding about whether LLMs recapitulate the human switch cost and inhibitory asymmetry, and we quantify effect sizes rather than assuming them. 5) The language-inhibition probe could latch onto surface language-ID cues rather than a genuine suppression/activation dynamic; we validate it via cross-pair transfer, the inhibition-strength-vs-cost correlation, the prior-language-suppressing attention analysis, and causal patching. 6) Representational-coherence (CKA/cosine discontinuity) is one operationalization of cost; we triangulate with surprisal and downstream comprehension so the claim does not rest on a single metric. 7) The human switch-cost asymmetry differs between production and comprehension; since LLM reading is comprehension-like, we frame the predicted asymmetry accordingly and report where the model matches or deviates from the human comprehension pattern rather than assuming identity. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and pair-specific; we test five models and multiple language pairs, cross-check activation vs path patching, and report low-rank subspace variants. 9) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic surprisal lever; we report monolingual-control and general-QA retention, output fidelity, and use dose-response, raise-cost (reverse), and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine inhibition mechanism rather than a global surprisal shift. 10) Distinguishing from my prior codeswitch_concept_binding (which language owns a concept) and homograph_concept_binding (same-form words) proposals is essential; here the object is the PROCESSING COST of the language switch itself and the language-inhibition mechanism that produces it, grounded in the human switch-cost/inhibitory-control literature.

Name: crosslingual_attention_sink_reliance_gating
Title: Anchored to the Void, in Some Tongues More Than Others: Cross-Lingual Variation in Attention-Sink Reliance and Its Causal Effect on Multilingual Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: Decoder-only multilingual LLMs route a large fraction of attention onto content-empty 'sink' tokens (BOS, language tags, delimiters), and—mirroring the sink artifact recently documented in multilingual NMT—the DEGREE of this sink reliance is systematically LANGUAGE-DEPENDENT: for the SAME task the model dumps more attention mass onto sinks (and correspondingly less onto genuine content) in lower-resource / typologically distant / high-fertility languages, and this excess sink reliance causally degrades comprehension and reasoning. Sink reliance is a shared, localizable attention mechanism whose per-language over-allocation is measurable, predicts the cross-lingual performance gap beyond tokenization, and can be causally relieved (redistributing sink mass to content) to recover accuracy without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Attention sinks—the concentration of attention on the first/BOS token and other non-content tokens—are established in decoder LLMs (Xiao et al. 2023 StreamingLLM) and were just shown to be a systematic, vocabulary-design-driven artifact capturing 83-91% of cross-attention mass in multilingual NMT, with attention-entropy clustering by language family (Mutisya & Mugane 2026). My prior crosslingual_positional_bias proposal concerns lost-in-the-middle positional accuracy curves driven by attention sinks for single-item RETRIEVAL BY POSITION; this proposal is distinct: the object is the LANGUAGE-DEPENDENT FRACTION of attention mass dumped on content-empty sink tokens on the SAME task, whether that fraction predicts and CAUSES the cross-lingual comprehension/reasoning gap, and whether relieving sink over-reliance recovers accuracy—not a U-shaped positional curve. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies sink reliance or its language modulation as a causal driver of performance. Tokenization work (Limisiewicz 2023) ties vocabulary allocation to downstream gaps behaviorally. NO prior work (i) measures per-language attention-sink reliance in decoder LLMs across a controlled task battery, (ii) tests whether excess sink reliance predicts the cross-lingual performance gap beyond tokenization fertility, or (iii) causally redistributes sink mass to content and shows accuracy recovery. This converts the NMT sink artifact into a mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of a driver of multilingual under-performance in decoder LLMs.
Abstract: Transformer language models waste much of their attention on content-empty 'sink' tokens—the start token, language tags, punctuation—that carry no meaning, and recent work on multilingual machine translation shows this artifact is not uniform: it clusters by language family and swallows most attention mass. We ask whether decoder-only multilingual LLMs exhibit a language-dependent attention-sink reliance that causally drives their uneven performance across languages. We hypothesize that, for the SAME task, the model dumps a larger fraction of attention onto sinks (and less onto genuine content) in lower-resource, typologically distant, higher-fertility languages, and that this excess sink reliance causally degrades comprehension and reasoning beyond what tokenization alone explains. We build SinkReliance, parallel comprehension and multi-step reasoning items across typologically and resource-diverse languages, with content held fixed. For each layer and head we measure per-language sink-mass fraction (attention to BOS/language-tag/delimiter tokens) and its complement, content-mass fraction. Behaviorally we test whether per-language sink reliance predicts the cross-lingual accuracy gap after controlling for tokenization fertility and item difficulty. Mechanistically we localize the heads that carry sink mass and test whether they are shared across languages but over-engaged in weaker ones. In a decisive causal test we redistribute a controlled fraction of sink attention back onto content tokens at those heads (via attention re-normalization / sink-mass suppression) and show it recovers accuracy in high-sink-reliance languages—or, in reverse, induces degradation by amplifying sink reliance—while leaving the surface language and easy-item behavior unchanged. We reframe part of the multilingual performance gap as a language-modulated, mechanistically shared, and relievable attention-sink phenomenon.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + attention analysis + light steering on 1-2 A6000 GPUs; all RoPE decoder LLMs with a clear BOS/first-token sink). 10 typologically/script/resource/fertility-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (SinkReliance): parallel, content-fixed items in three strata—(A) READING COMPREHENSION (short passage + question), (B) MULTI-STEP REASONING (MGSM-style math word problems, multi-hop factual reasoning), (C) an EASY/SHORT-ANSWER control where accuracy is near-ceiling in all languages (to bound the effect and provide a difficulty-matched baseline). Native-verify translations; record per-language tokenization fertility (tokens/word) and item difficulty (English accuracy, hop-count). Identify per-model sink tokens: BOS/first token, language/system tags, and delimiter/punctuation tokens.
3) MEASURE ATTENTION-SINK RELIANCE: For each (item, language, layer, head) compute SINK-MASS FRACTION = attention mass to sink tokens, and CONTENT-MASS FRACTION = mass to genuine content tokens, at the answer/decision position (using content-only renormalization as in Mutisya & Mugane to separate sink from content). Aggregate to a per-(item,language) sink-reliance score and a per-layer/head sink profile. Also compute attention-entropy per language.
4) BEHAVIORAL SINK-ASYMMETRY TEST: KEY hypothesis—for the SAME item, sink-mass fraction is systematically higher in lower-resource/typologically distant/higher-fertility languages. Mixed-effects regression of sink reliance on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, item difficulty), item as random effect; test the language effect beyond fertility and difficulty. Report per-language sink-reliance profiles, attention-entropy clustering by family (replicating Mutisya & Mugane in decoder LLMs), and the EASY control (should show smaller language-driven sink gaps).
5) SINK-PREDICTS-GAP LINK (core): Regress per-(item,language) accuracy on sink reliance, controlling for tokenization fertility, item difficulty, and resource tier. Hypothesis: higher sink reliance predicts lower accuracy, and this holds WITHIN a language (item-level) and predicts the cross-lingual accuracy gap beyond fertility/difficulty (incremental R^2 / partial correlation). Contrast reasoning/comprehension (should show a strong sink-accuracy link) vs the easy control (weak link).
6) LOCALIZE SINK HEADS: Rank heads/layers by sink-mass carried; test whether the SAME heads carry sink mass across languages (shared mechanism) but are OVER-ENGAGED (higher sink fraction) in weaker languages. Report the head/layer distribution and whether a small set of heads accounts for most sink mass and most of the cross-lingual sink variance.
7) CAUSAL SINK-RELIEF INTERVENTION (decisive): At the identified sink-carrying heads, REDISTRIBUTE a controlled fraction of attention mass from sink tokens back onto content tokens (attention re-normalization that zeroes/down-weights sink-token attention and renormalizes over content, dose-controlled). Test (i) RELIEVE: in high-sink-reliance languages, sink relief recovers comprehension/reasoning accuracy toward high-resource levels, with dose-response; (ii) AMPLIFY (reverse): forcing MORE sink mass degrades accuracy, confirming the causal direction; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where sink reliance was highest; (iv) SPECIFICITY: it does not change the EASY control or already-content-focused (high-resource) items, does not alter the surface output language (fidelity), and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset); (v) verify the relief actually redistributes mass to content (attention check). Baselines: raising decoding temperature, translate-to-English, and a random-head control (relieving non-sink heads should not help). Metrics: cross-lingual accuracy-gap closure, dose-response, content-mass increase, easy-control/general-QA/output-language retention.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: stratum breakdown (comprehension vs reasoning vs easy); which sink-token type (BOS vs language tag vs delimiter) dominates per language; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training reduce sink asymmetry?); model scale; head-set size needed; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched sink reliance and by showing content-invariant sink relief (which does not change tokenization) recovers accuracy; whether one relief recipe generalizes across tasks and languages.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language sink-mass/content-mass fractions and attention-entropy clustering, sink-reliance regression controlling for fertility/difficulty/resource, sink-predicts-accuracy incremental R^2 (within-language and cross-lingual), shared-but-over-engaged sink-head localization, causal sink-relief accuracy-gap closure with dose-response and reverse (amplify) degradation, content-mass redistribution verification, easy-control/random-head specificity, output-language fidelity, general-QA retention, comparison to temperature and translate-to-English baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Sink reliance is heavily confounded with tokenization fertility (more/rarer tokens change attention patterns); the whole design controls for fertility in regression, compares high- vs low-fertility languages at matched sink reliance, and—crucially—the content-invariant causal sink-relief intervention does NOT change tokenization yet recovers accuracy, dissociating sink reliance from the token tax. 2) Some models/languages may show uniform sink reliance (no asymmetry)—this is itself an informative, publishable finding about whether the NMT sink artifact transfers as a language-dependent effect to decoder LLMs, and we quantify the asymmetry rather than assuming it. 3) The sink-predicts-gap link could be correlational; the causal relief (recover) and amplify (degrade) interventions with dose-response and the random-head/easy-control specificity checks are designed to establish causation, not mere correlation. 4) Attention mass is not a perfect proxy for causal information flow; we cross-check attention-based sink relief with its effect on content-mass and downstream accuracy, and treat the causal intervention (not the attention correlation) as the load-bearing evidence. 5) Aggressively zeroing sink attention can destabilize generation (sinks are known to stabilize attention, StreamingLLM); we dose-control the relief, cap the redistributed fraction, monitor fluency and general-QA retention, and report the accuracy-vs-stability trade-off rather than claiming a free lunch. 6) Defining which tokens are 'sinks' vs content is model-specific; we identify sink tokens empirically (top attention-receiving non-content tokens: BOS, tags, delimiters) per model and report sensitivity to the sink-token set. 7) Patching/attention-analysis results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and report aggregate and per-model results. 8) Distinguishing from my prior positional-bias proposal is essential; there the object was retrieval accuracy as a function of item POSITION (a U-curve) driven by positional attention bias, whereas here it is the language-dependent FRACTION of attention wasted on content-empty sink tokens on a fixed task and its causal effect on comprehension/reasoning—and from the NMT sink work (Mutisya & Mugane 2026) by moving to decoder-only LLMs, tying sink reliance causally to the cross-lingual performance gap, and intervening to relieve it.

Name: crosslingual_basic_level_category_gating
Title: Dog, Animal, or Labrador? A Shared Taxonomic-Level Representation Whose Basic-Level Default Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When naming or reasoning about an entity, a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of WHERE that entity sits in a conceptual taxonomy (subordinate/basic/superordinate, e.g. Labrador < dog < animal), and it defaults to the cognitively-privileged BASIC LEVEL ('dog') as humans do; but whether that basic-level default is behaviorally EXPRESSED is gated by the query language: the SAME entity is placed at the correct taxonomic level internally across languages yet named/reasoned about at a systematically over-general (superordinate) or over-specific level in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so the model internally 'knows the basic level' while behaviorally mislabeling. The taxonomic-level signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated categorization failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: The basic-level advantage—that humans preferentially name and reason at an intermediate taxonomic level ('dog', not 'animal' or 'Labrador')—is one of the most robust findings in cognitive psychology (Rosch et al. 1976; Murphy). In NLP, taxonomy/hypernymy is studied as a supervised extraction task (hypernym detection, WordNet-based probing) and monolingual work notes LLM embeddings encode hypernymy, but this is behavioral/representational, not a study of the basic-level DEFAULT, its cross-lingual structure, or its mechanism. My prior proposals cover colexification (two concepts fused in one word), kinship granularity (relational fineness), bridging (entity-to-scene links), and figure-ground (spatial roles); NONE address the vertical TAXONOMIC LEVEL at which an entity is categorized, whether a shared cross-lingual level representation exists, whether the basic-level default's behavioral expression is language-gated, or whether the level signal is causally steerable. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never for taxonomic level. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of basic-level categorization.
Abstract: Asked what an animal is, people say 'dog', not 'animal' or 'Labrador'—the basic-level advantage, a hallmark of human categorization at an intermediate taxonomic level. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal representation of an entity's taxonomic level (subordinate/basic/superordinate) and defaults to the basic level, and whether that internal placement is decoupled from how the entity is behaviorally categorized across languages. We hypothesize that models place entities at the correct level similarly across languages internally, but the query language gates whether the basic-level default is surfaced (naming, category-membership, and level-appropriate inference), so the SAME entity is categorized at an over-general or over-specific level far more in lower-resource, typologically distant languages—even though the model 'knows the basic level'. We build LevelProbe, parallel entity-naming and taxonomic-reasoning items across languages, each with subordinate/basic/superordinate options and a matched control where only one level is appropriate. Behaviorally we measure per-language basic-level preference and level-drift and test whether it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond entity knowledge. We train a linear taxonomic-level probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the categorization gap into a shared level component versus a language-set expression gate—verifying the correct level is internally present even where naming drifts. Via activation and path patching we localize a taxonomic-level signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to surface (or shift) the categorization level while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual categorization gaps as a steerable gate over a shared taxonomic-level representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Swahili). MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (LevelProbe): ~500 entities organized into subordinate<basic<superordinate triples (Labrador<dog<animal; oak<tree<plant; sedan<car<vehicle), sourced from WordNet/concept norms + native verification, chosen to translate cleanly. Item types: (A) NAMING ('What is this most naturally called?' with the three levels as options), (B) CATEGORY-MEMBERSHIP ('Is a Labrador a dog? an animal?'), (C) LEVEL-APPROPRIATE INFERENCE (a context requiring the basic level for a natural answer). Include a control where only ONE level is contextually appropriate (to separate level-drift from comprehension) and screen that the model knows the entity per language. Translate/native-verify; keep entities fixed; record tokenization fertility; use short scoreable options.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (entity, language) record basic-level vs superordinate/subordinate choice. KEY hypothesis: basic-level preference is systematically weaker (over-general or over-specific drift higher) in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond entity knowledge and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of level-drift on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, knowledge indicator), entity as random effect; compare against the single-appropriate-level control. Report per-language level profiles, replicate the English basic-level advantage as a sanity check, and quantify cross-lingual disagreement on identical entities.
4) SHARED TAXONOMIC-LEVEL PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the entity/pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode the entity's taxonomic LEVEL on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report macro-F1/AUROC as evidence of a language-independent level representation. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on DRIFT items, test whether the correct basic level is still internally decodable across ALL languages even when naming drifts.
5) LEVEL-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer level signal across languages (should be similar if placement is shared) versus behavioral categorization (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal level to surfaced categorization per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar level signal. Correlate gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes.
6) LOCALIZE THE LEVEL SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that surfaces the basic level and one that drifts on the SAME entity, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer surfaces the correct level WITHOUT changing the decoded entity identity. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the level representation FROM a high-expression language into a drifting run.
7) CAUSAL LEVEL STEERING (decisive): Derive a taxonomic-level steering vector via difference-of-means (basic-level runs minus drifted runs, plus level-shift contrasts). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to drift-prone languages increases basic-level preference toward high-expression levels; (ii) SHIFT: steering along the level axis moves categorization toward superordinate/subordinate on well-placed items (dose-response); (iii) it works cross-lingually, stronger where expression was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY the taxonomic level, not the decoded entity identity or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the single-appropriate-level control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: level-drift-gap closure, level-shift-flip rate (reverse), level-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes level judgments but not unrelated answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: item-type breakdown; drift direction (over-general vs over-specific) by language; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single level vector generalizes across categories and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal level and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces the basic level without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language basic-level preference and level-drift, expression regression controlling for knowledge/fertility/resource, English basic-level-advantage replication, cross-lingual level-probe transfer F1/AUROC and level-present-under-drift, cross-lingual level-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), level-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized taxonomic-level layer, cross-lingual level transplant recovery rate, causal steering drift-gap closure and level-shift-flip rates, level-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The level-vs-expression split could be confounded if the level signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying basic-level decodability across all languages on drift items via probe transfer, and report how much of the gap is placement vs gate. 2) Level-drift could reflect entity-knowledge ignorance rather than an expression gate; we screen per-language entity knowledge and restrict the gate analysis to known entities. 3) The basic level can be culture-dependent (what counts as 'basic' varies); we restrict to cross-culturally stable triples (native-verified) and analyze culture-variable ones separately, treating basic-level as the human-consensus level per language where possible. 4) Naming naturally varies by language (some languages lack a distinct basic-level term); we native-verify that all three levels have natural terms and flag gaps. 5) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal level, and content-invariant steering surfaces the basic level without changing tokenization. 6) Some models may categorize uniformly across languages (no gap) or drift everywhere; either is an informative finding, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 7) The level probe could latch onto surface cues rather than a genuine taxonomic representation; the cross-lingual invariance, level-present-under-drift test, single-appropriate-level control, and cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report level-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention, and use the level-shift (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine taxonomic-level gate. 10) The level signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my colexification, kinship-granularity, bridging, and figure-ground proposals is essential; here the object is the VERTICAL taxonomic level (subordinate/basic/superordinate) at which an entity is categorized and the language-gating of the basic-level default, grounded in the basic-level-advantage literature.

Name: crosslingual_integration_cost_gating
Title: Feeling the Hard Word, in Every Language: A Shared Human-Aligned Integration-Cost Signal Whose Behavioral Expression Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs compute a largely language-independent internal 'integration-cost' signal that registers how hard an incoming word is to integrate into its context (mirroring the per-word processing difficulty that drives human reading times / garden-path slowdowns), but whether that cost is behaviorally EXPRESSED—as extra allocated computation and human-aligned surprisal spikes—is gated by the query language: the SAME high-cost word is internally flagged as difficult across languages yet under-expressed (weaker cost-to-slowdown coupling, mirroring the documented L1>L2 surprisal effect) in lower-resource / typologically distant languages. The integration-cost signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated under-processing of hard words can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: A large body of work shows LLM surprisal robustly PREDICTS human reading times across languages (Hollenstein et al. 2021; de Varda & Marelli 2022 on MECO; CMCL 2022 shared tasks; Buggy et al. 2026), that L2 surprisal effects are WEAKER than L1 (de Varda & Marelli 2022), and that early-layer representations predict early-pass reading measures while scalar surprisal predicts late-pass (Tsipidi et al. 2026 'Probing for Reading Times'). ALL of this treats the model as a PREDICTOR of human data and is correlational: it never asks whether the model internally computes a shared, language-independent integration-DIFFICULTY representation, whether that representation's behavioral expression (allocated computation / human-aligned surprisal) is language-GATED, whether the L1>L2 asymmetry reflects a shared cost signal under a weaker expression gate rather than a weaker cost signal, or whether the cost signal is causally localizable and steerable. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never an integration-cost signal. My prior step-level-error, computational-depth, and code-switch-cost proposals target other objects (per-step correctness, vertical layer-commitment, switch-point cost); NONE address a shared human-aligned per-word integration-cost signal validated against cross-lingual eye-tracking (MECO) and decomposed into a shared cost representation versus a language-set expression gate. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of integration cost, converting a purely correlational reading-time literature into an internal, steerable mechanism.
Abstract: Reading a word that is hard to integrate into its context—a garden-path continuation, a low-predictability noun—slows human readers down, and language-model surprisal famously tracks this slowdown across many languages, though more weakly in a reader's second language. All of this evidence is correlational: it shows models PREDICT human difficulty, not that they internally REPRESENT it. We ask whether a multilingual LLM computes a shared, language-independent internal integration-cost signal registering how hard an incoming word is to integrate, and whether that internal cost is decoupled from how strongly it is behaviorally expressed across languages—mirroring the human L1>L2 asymmetry as a gating effect rather than a weaker signal. Using MECO and CMCL cross-lingual eye-tracking corpora, we operationalize behavioral expression as human-aligned surprisal and as allocated internal computation (layer-of-commitment / representational updating) at each word. We train a linear integration-cost probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the cross-lingual coupling gap (how well internal cost tracks human reading times per language) into a shared cost signal versus a language-set expression gate: a weak human-alignment in some languages should coincide with an intact internal cost signal. Via activation and path patching we localize the integration-cost signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model allocate extra computation to hard words and produce more human-aligned processing in low-expression languages—or, in reverse, flatten it—while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual reading-time misalignment as a steerable gate over a shared integration-cost representation.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B, plus XLM-R/mBERT for comparability with prior reading-time work (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). Languages covered by public cross-lingual eye-tracking corpora (MECO: 13 languages incl. English, Spanish, German, Russian, Greek, Hebrew, Turkish, Finnish, etc.; CMCL 2022 multilingual set), spanning scripts/families/resource tiers.
2) DATA: MECO and CMCL eye-tracking corpora provide per-word human reading-time measures (first fixation, gaze duration, total reading time) in parallel-genre naturalistic texts across languages, giving a ground-truth per-word integration-difficulty signal. Compute per-word LLM surprisal and per-word tokenization fertility; align to word-level human measures.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION / HUMAN-ALIGNMENT TEST: Per language, quantify how strongly the model's surprisal (and allocated internal computation, below) predicts human reading times (regression coefficient / delta-log-likelihood), replicating and extending de Varda & Marelli. KEY hypothesis: this cost-to-slowdown COUPLING is systematically weaker in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond tokenization fertility. Mixed-effects models of reading time on (surprisal x language, fertility, word frequency, length), word/subject as random effects; test the surprisal x language interaction and its dependence on resource tier (URIEL) and script.
4) SHARED INTEGRATION-COST PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer, pool the hidden state at each word position and train a linear probe to decode INTEGRATION COST—targeting the human per-word difficulty (z-scored total reading time) and, as a model-internal proxy, next-word surprisal—on ENGLISH data; apply zero-shot cross-lingually and report R^2/rank-correlation as evidence of a language-independent cost representation. Measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the cost representation for matched hard/easy words. CRITICAL: in LOW-COUPLING languages (weak human alignment), test whether the internal cost signal is still strong and still predicts the HUMAN difficulty—the signature of an intact cost signal under weak behavioral expression.
5) ALLOCATED-COMPUTATION MEASURE: Using logit-lens/tuned-lens, define per-word ALLOCATED COMPUTATION = layer-of-commitment (how deep the model processes before its next-word prediction stabilizes) and representational updating magnitude across layers. Test whether hard (high-human-cost) words recruit more allocated computation, and whether this cost-to-computation coupling is weaker in low-expression languages—an internal analog of the human reading-time slowdown.
6) SIGNAL-vs-GATE DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer cost signal across languages (should be similar / human-aligned if shared) versus the behavioral expression (surprisal-to-reading-time coupling and cost-to-computation coupling, which diverge). Define a per-language EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal cost to allocated computation/human-aligned surprisal; test whether cross-lingual coupling differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar cost signal rather than a weaker signal. Correlate gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes.
7) LOCALIZE THE INTEGRATION-COST SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a high-cost (garden-path/low-predictability) word run and a matched low-cost run (from controlled minimal-pair sentences, e.g. IMPPRES/garden-path stimuli translated cross-lingually), sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer changes the model's surprisal spike and allocated computation WITHOUT changing the decoded word content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching. Test patching the cost representation FROM a high-expression language into a low-expression run.
8) CAUSAL INTEGRATION-COST STEERING (decisive): Derive a cost-expression steering vector via difference-of-means (high-cost/high-computation runs minus low-cost runs at matched internal cost). Test (i) EXPRESS: adding it in low-expression languages increases allocated computation on hard words and improves human-alignment of surprisal (stronger reading-time coupling) toward high-expression levels; (ii) FLATTEN: subtracting it reduces human-alignment in high-expression languages; (iii) DOSE-RESPONSE and cross-lingual generality; (iv) it changes ONLY cost expression, not the decoded word content or surface language (fidelity checks), and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset) or next-word accuracy on easy words (specificity). Metrics: human-alignment (reading-time coupling) gap closure, allocated-computation-on-hard-words gain, flatten-induction (reverse), cost-signal/output fidelity, easy-word and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes hard-word processing but not easy-word or unrelated tokens.
9) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: measure breakdown (first-fixation/early-pass vs total/late-pass—relate to Tsipidi et al.'s early-layer vs surprisal finding cross-lingually); is a high-resource language the high-expression reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the L1>L2-style asymmetry?); probe layer/dimensionality; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal cost and by showing content-invariant steering improves human-alignment without changing tokenization; garden-path minimal-pair vs naturalistic-corpus consistency.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language surprisal-to-reading-time and cost-to-computation coupling and its resource/typology regression controlling for fertility/frequency, cross-lingual integration-cost probe transfer R^2/rank-correlation and cost-predicts-human-difficulty in low-coupling languages, signal-similarity vs coupling-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized integration-cost layer, cross-lingual cost transplant human-alignment gain, causal steering coupling-gap closure with dose-response and flatten-induction, cost-signal/output fidelity, easy-word and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The signal-vs-gate split could be confounded if the internal cost signal itself differs by language (the model genuinely computes weaker integration cost in some languages, not a weaker expression gate); we test this directly by checking whether the internal cost signal still predicts HUMAN per-word difficulty in low-coupling languages via probe transfer, and report how much of the coupling gap is signal vs gate—either outcome is informative and directly bears on why L2 surprisal effects are weaker. 2) Tokenization fertility is a major confound (surprisal and word-level alignment are affected by subword splitting); we control for fertility and word frequency/length, align at the word level, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal cost, and—crucially—the content-invariant causal steering improves human-alignment without changing tokenization, dissociating the gate from tokenization. 3) Eye-tracking data is noisy and subject-variable; we use established, widely-cited corpora (MECO, CMCL), mixed-effects models with subject random effects, and multiple reading-time measures. 4) Some models/languages may show uniform human-alignment (no gap) or a uniformly weak cost signal; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of integration-cost representation, and we quantify how often a gap occurs. 5) 'Allocated computation' (layer-of-commitment / representational updating) is an imperfect internal analog of reading time; we validate it against surprisal and human data and use it as one of several convergent measures rather than the sole claim. 6) The cost probe could latch onto surface frequency/length cues rather than a genuine integration-difficulty representation; we control for frequency/length, use garden-path minimal pairs where cost is dissociated from surface features, and validate via cross-lingual transfer and the cost-predicts-human-difficulty test. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models (plus encoder baselines), multiple stimuli, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic surprisal lever; we report cost-signal/output fidelity, easy-word and general-QA retention, and use dose-response, flatten (reverse), and reverse-consistency (hard-word-only effect) tests to ensure a genuine integration-cost gate rather than a global surprisal shift. 9) The cost signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction;
