we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from the correlational reading-time-prediction literature (de Varda & Marelli 2022; Tsipidi et al. 2026) is essential; our contribution is the shared, language-independent integration-cost REPRESENTATION, its decomposition into a shared signal versus a language-set expression gate (reframing the L1>L2 asymmetry), and its causal localization and steering—none of which prior correlational work provides.

Name: crosslingual_use_mention_gating
Title: Talking About the Word vs Using It: A Shared Use/Mention Representation Whose Expression Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When a linguistic form is MENTIONED (referred to as an object: 'How many letters are in the word cat?', 'The word bank has two meanings') rather than USED (deployed for its meaning), a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal 'use/mention' representation that quarantines the mentioned form from ordinary semantic processing, but whether that quarantine is behaviorally EXPRESSED—treating the form as an object (counting its letters, discussing its ambiguity, translating it as a token) rather than acting on its meaning—is gated by the query language: the SAME mentioned form is internally tagged as mentioned across languages yet processed semantically (as if used) far more often in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so the model internally 'knows it is being talked about' while behaviorally reacting to its meaning. The use/mention signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated use/mention failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: The use/mention distinction (deploying a form for its meaning vs referring to the form itself, typically via quotation) is foundational in philosophy of language and semantics (Quine; Cappelen & Lepore's theory of quotation) and central to metalinguistic competence. In NLP it is barely studied: monolingual English work notes LLMs conflate use and mention (e.g., processing a quoted slur as if used, or failing to treat a quoted word as an object), and metalinguistic-ability benchmarks (Song, Hu & Mahowald 2025; Arcon et al. 2026 WALS-based) measure metalinguistic knowledge but neither the use/mention distinction specifically nor its cross-lingual structure or mechanism. My prior crosslingual_metalinguistic_competence proposal concerns USING vs DESCRIBING a grammatical RULE (procedural competence vs metalinguistic rule-statement); my crosslingual_quotation_firewall proposal concerns attributing a SOURCE'S reported CLAIM and whether the model endorses it. NEITHER addresses the use/mention distinction of a linguistic FORM itself—whether a mentioned word is treated as an object vs acted on for its meaning—which is a distinct semantic phenomenon (object-of-reference vs meaning-carrier, not rule-description or claim-attribution). Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for use/mention. No prior work asks whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent use/mention representation, whether its internal quarantine is decoupled from behavioral expression across languages, whether use/mention expression tracks language resource level, or whether the signal is causally localizable and steerable—with direct safety stakes (a mentioned slur/harmful phrase processed as if used, unevenly across languages).
Abstract: There is a deep difference between using a word and merely mentioning it: 'cats are mammals' uses 'cats' for its meaning, but 'cat has three letters' refers to the word itself. Handling this use/mention distinction is essential to metalinguistic understanding and to safety (a quoted slur is mentioned, not endorsed), yet it is barely studied in language models and never cross-lingually. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal representation that quarantines a mentioned form from ordinary semantic processing, and whether that internal quarantine is decoupled from how reliably it is behaviorally expressed across languages. We hypothesize that models tag a form as mentioned similarly across languages internally, but the query language gates whether the mention is honored—treating the form as an object (counting its letters, discussing its ambiguity, translating it as a token, not endorsing a quoted slur) rather than acting on its meaning—so the SAME mentioned form is processed semantically (as if used) far more often in lower-resource, typologically distant languages. We build UseMentionProbe, parallel items across languages that MENTION a form (metalinguistic questions, quotation, discussion of a word's properties) alongside matched USE items and a safety stratum (quoted vs asserted harmful phrases). Behaviorally we measure per-language use/mention accuracy and mention-collapse (reacting to meaning when the form is mentioned) and test whether it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond comprehension. We train a linear use/mention probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the failure into a shared quarantine component versus a language-set expression gate—verifying the mention is internally tagged even where processing collapses to meaning. Via activation and path patching we localize a use/mention signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to surface (or flip) the use/mention status while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual metalinguistic and safety failures as a steerable gate over a shared use/mention representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Swahili). MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (UseMentionProbe): ~500 items in strata, each with a MENTION form and a matched USE form of the SAME word/phrase (content fixed). (A) METALINGUISTIC-PROPERTY: the word is mentioned and a question probes a form property ('How many letters/syllables are in the word X?', 'What letter does X start with?', 'Is X a noun?'), where correct behavior treats X as an object; the USE counterpart deploys X for meaning. (B) QUOTATION/DISCUSSION: a sentence discusses a word ('The word X is ambiguous / is borrowed from Latin / is considered old-fashioned'), where correct behavior reasons about the word, not its referent; matched USE items assert the referent's properties. (C) MENTION-TRANSLATION: 'How do you say X in language L?' / 'Translate the word X' where X should be treated as a lexical token (correct: give its translation-as-a-word), vs a USE context where X is part of a meaningful sentence. (D) SAFETY: a harmful phrase QUOTED/MENTIONED ('The sentence "[harmful phrase]" contains a slur; is that word offensive?') vs the same phrase USED, testing whether the model treats the mentioned form as an object of discussion rather than endorsing/acting on it. Include a control where use and mention coincide (bounds the effect) and screen that the model knows the base word per language (so failure is not lexical ignorance). Translate/native-verify; realize quotation/mention naturally per language (quotative particles, metalinguistic constructions); record tokenization fertility; use short scoreable answers.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (item, language) record MENTION-honoring (treats the form as an object) vs MENTION-COLLAPSE (reacts to meaning as if used). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME mentioned form, mention-collapse is systematically higher in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond comprehension and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of mention-collapse on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, stratum, knowledge indicator), item as random effect; compare against the use/mention-coincide control. Report per-language and per-stratum profiles, cross-lingual disagreement on identical mentioned forms, and replicate a monolingual English use/mention baseline.
4) SHARED USE/MENTION PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the form/pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode MENTION vs USE (is the form being referred to as an object vs deployed for meaning) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent use/mention representation. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on MENTION-COLLAPSE items, test whether the form is still internally tagged as MENTIONED across ALL languages even when processed semantically—the signature of language-gated expression over an intact quarantine.
5) QUARANTINE-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer use/mention signal across languages (should be similar if the tag is shared) versus behavioral honoring (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal use/mention tag to surfaced behavior per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar tag signal rather than a weaker tag. Correlate gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE USE/MENTION SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that honors the mention and one that collapses on the SAME item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer surfaces mention-honoring WITHOUT changing the decoded form identity. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the use/mention representation FROM a high-expression language into a collapsing run.
7) CAUSAL USE/MENTION STEERING (decisive): Derive a use/mention steering vector via difference-of-means (mention-honored runs minus collapsed runs, plus use-vs-mention contrasts). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to collapse-prone languages increases mention-honoring toward high-expression levels; (ii) FLIP: steering along the axis makes the model treat a USED form as mentioned (and vice versa) on well-handled items; (iii) it works cross-lingually, stronger where expression was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY use/mention status, not the decoded form or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the coincide control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset); (v) SAFETY: surfacing mention on stratum D makes the model discuss (not endorse/act on) quoted harmful phrases without over-refusing legitimately-mentioned ones. Metrics: mention-collapse-gap closure, use/mention-flip rate (reverse), tag-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention, safety-stratum specificity. Reverse-consistency: steering changes use/mention judgments but not unrelated answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: stratum breakdown (metalinguistic-property vs quotation vs mention-translation vs safety); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single use/mention vector generalizes across strata and languages; robustness across templates; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal tag and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces mention without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language use/mention accuracy and mention-collapse rate, expression regression controlling for comprehension/fertility/resource, English use/mention replication, cross-lingual use/mention probe transfer AUROC and mention-tag-present-under-collapse, cross-lingual tag-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), quarantine-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized use/mention layer, cross-lingual tag transplant recovery rate, causal steering collapse-gap closure and use/mention-flip rates, tag-signal/output fidelity, control/safety-stratum and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The quarantine-vs-expression split could be confounded if the use/mention signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying mention-tag decodability across all languages on collapse items via probe transfer rather than assuming, and report how much of the gap is quarantine vs gate. 2) Mention-collapse could reflect comprehension failure rather than an expression gate; we use the use/mention-coincide control and comprehension screening so residual collapse reflects use/mention processing, not reading. 3) Some words are genuinely ambiguous between use and mention without explicit quotation; we use clear metalinguistic constructions/quotation (native-verified) and analyze borderline items separately. 4) Realizing quotation/mention naturally and equivalently across languages is delicate (quotative particles, metalinguistic markers differ); we native-verify, treat stratum as a factor, and flag constructions with no natural equivalent. 5) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy (form-property questions depend on subword splitting, e.g. letter-counting); we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal tag, and content-invariant steering surfaces mention without changing tokenization—though metalinguistic form-property items (letter counts) are inherently tokenization-sensitive, so we analyze them separately and rely more on quotation/discussion and safety strata for the core claim. 6) Some models may honor use/mention uniformly across languages (no gap) or collapse everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual metalinguistic competence, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 7) The use/mention probe could latch onto surface quotation-mark cues rather than a genuine quarantine representation; the cross-lingual invariance test, the mention-tag-present-under-collapse check, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this, and we include mention items without explicit quotation marks. 8) The safety stratum guard: surfacing mention must NOT make the model over-refuse legitimately-mentioned harmful phrases nor under-refuse genuinely-used ones; we report safety-stratum specificity as a primary metric and use the flip (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine use/mention gate. 9) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 10) The gate/tag signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my metalinguistic-competence (using vs describing a grammatical RULE) and quotation-firewall (attributing a source's CLAIM) proposals is essential; here the object is the use/mention distinction of a linguistic FORM itself—whether a mentioned word is treated as an object of reference vs acted on for its meaning—a distinct semantic phenomenon with metalinguistic and safety stakes.

Name: crosslingual_illocutionary_force_gating
Title: Asking, Ordering, or Just Saying? A Shared Illocutionary-Force Representation Whose Recovery From Indirect Speech Acts Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: A multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of an utterance's ILLOCUTIONARY FORCE (whether it asserts, asks, commands, or commits/promises), distinct from its surface sentence form, but whether the model correctly recovers force from INDIRECT speech acts (a request phrased as a question, 'Can you close the window?'; a command phrased as a statement) is gated by the query language: the SAME indirect utterance is internally represented with the correct force across languages yet behaviorally mis-read as its literal surface force far more often in lower-resource / typologically distant / higher-directness-norm languages, so the model internally 'knows it is a request' while behaviorally treating it as a mere question. The force signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated force-recovery failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Speech-act / illocutionary-force work in NLP is behavioral and classification-oriented: multilingual speech-act annotation and XLM-R-style classifiers (Grattan et al. 2026; disinformation speech-act pipelines), and philosophical critiques of LLM pragmatic competence (Ozdil 2026; Sadigzada 2026) argue LLMs mishandle illocutionary force but supply no internal representation, no cross-lingual decomposition, and no mechanism. My prior crosslingual_pragmatics proposal targeted truth-conditional IMPLICATURE enrichment (scalar 'some'->'not all', indirect refusals as informativeness); this is distinct because the object is the SPEECH-ACT FORCE type of an utterance (assert/ask/command/commit) and the recovery of INTENDED force from indirect forms whose surface sentence type mismatches their force, not conversational-implicature enrichment. My detection-vs-expression and honorific/status proposals target other objects. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for illocutionary force. No prior work asks whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent force representation, whether indirect-force recovery is language-gated over that shared representation, whether it tracks directness typology, or whether the force signal is causally localizable and steerable—with direct stakes for assistants that must act on indirect requests/commands, unevenly across languages.
Abstract: Understanding what a speaker is DOING with an utterance—asserting, asking, commanding, or committing—is illocutionary force, and it often diverges from surface form: 'Can you pass the salt?' is a request dressed as a question, and 'You'll want to leave now' is a command dressed as a statement. Recovering this intended force is essential for assistants that must act, yet languages differ sharply in how directly they encode force. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal representation of illocutionary force, and whether that internal representation is decoupled from how reliably force is behaviorally recovered from INDIRECT speech acts across languages. We hypothesize that models represent force similarly across languages internally, but the query language gates whether the intended (non-literal) force is surfaced, so the SAME indirect utterance is treated as its literal surface act far more in lower-resource, typologically distant, higher-directness-norm languages. We build ForceProbe, parallel utterances across languages instantiating four forces (assertion, question, directive, commissive), each in a DIRECT form (surface type matches force) and a matched INDIRECT form (surface type mismatches force, e.g. a request as a question), with force-identification and act-response probes and a directness control. Behaviorally we measure per-language indirect-force recovery and literal-force collapse and test whether it tracks resource level, typological distance, and directness norms beyond comprehension. We train a linear force probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the recovery gap into a shared force representation versus a language-set expression gate—verifying the intended force is internally present even where behavior collapses to the literal act. Via activation and path patching we localize a force signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to surface (or flip) the illocutionary force while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual pragmatic-failure as a steerable gate over a shared illocutionary-force representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically/culturally/resource-diverse languages spanning directness norms (English, German, Russian [direct] vs Japanese, Korean, Hindi, Arabic [indirect/high-context] vs Spanish [mixed]), coded for directness/indirectness norms (Hall high/low-context; politeness typology) plus URIEL typological/resource distance (graded predictors). MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (ForceProbe): ~500 utterances instantiating four ILLOCUTIONARY FORCES (ASSERTION, QUESTION, DIRECTIVE/request-command, COMMISSIVE/promise-offer). Each utterance has a DIRECT form (surface sentence type matches force, e.g. imperative for a directive) and a matched INDIRECT form (surface type mismatches force, e.g. a directive as an interrogative 'Could you close the window?', a directive as a declarative 'It's cold in here', a commissive as a question). Probes: (A) FORCE-IDENTIFICATION ('Is the speaker asking, telling you to do something, stating a fact, or committing to do something?' MC over the four forces), (B) ACT-RESPONSE (does the model RESPOND to the intended act—e.g. take the requested action / answer as if commanded—vs respond to the literal surface act, e.g. merely answering yes/no to 'Can you...?'), (C) a DIRECT-CONTROL where surface type matches force (bounds the effect; separates force-recovery from comprehension). Include a NEUTRAL non-speech-act filler. Keep utterance content and intended force fixed across languages; translate/native-verify, realizing indirect forms naturally per language; record tokenization fertility; screen literal comprehension via the direct control. Short scoreable answers.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (utterance, language) record correct-intended-force recovery vs LITERAL-FORCE COLLAPSE (treating an indirect directive as a mere question, etc.). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME indirect utterance, literal-force collapse is systematically higher in lower-resource/typologically distant/higher-directness-norm languages, beyond comprehension and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of force-collapse on (directness-norm code, force type, direct-vs-indirect, language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, comprehension indicator), utterance as random effect; test the directness x indirectness interaction. Compare against the direct control (near-ceiling, language-flatter). Report per-language and per-force collapse profiles, cross-lingual disagreement on identical indirect utterances, and replicate an English indirect-speech-act baseline.
4) SHARED FORCE PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the utterance/pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode the INTENDED illocutionary force (assert/ask/direct/commit) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report macro-F1/AUROC as evidence of a language-independent force representation, and show it DISSOCIATES from a SURFACE-SENTENCE-TYPE probe (the force signal is distinct from declarative/interrogative/imperative surface form). Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on LITERAL-COLLAPSE items, test whether the correct intended force is still internally decodable across ALL languages even when the emitted behavior follows the literal act—the signature of language-gated expression over an intact force representation.
5) FORCE-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer force signal across languages (should be similar if force is shared) versus behavioral recovery (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal force to surfaced act per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar force signal. Correlate gate strength with directness norms, resource tier, and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE FORCE SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that recovers the intended force and one that collapses to literal on the SAME indirect utterance, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer surfaces the correct force WITHOUT changing the decoded propositional content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the force representation FROM a high-recovery language into a collapsing run.
7) CAUSAL FORCE STEERING (decisive): Derive a force steering vector via difference-of-means (intended-force-recovered runs minus literal-collapse runs, plus force-type contrasts, e.g. directive vs question). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to collapse-prone languages increases correct indirect-force recovery / act-response toward high-recovery levels; (ii) FLIP: steering along the force axis makes the model treat an indirect directive as a question (and vice versa) on well-recovered items; (iii) it works cross-lingually, stronger where recovery was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY illocutionary force, not the decoded propositional content or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the direct control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: collapse-gap closure, force-flip rate (reverse), force-signal/content/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes force interpretation but not propositional content or unrelated answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: force-type breakdown (which forces collapse most—directives vs commissives); indirect-form breakdown (directive-as-question vs directive-as-statement); is a high-resource/direct language the high-recovery reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the collapse?); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single force vector generalizes across forces and languages; robustness across identification-vs-act-response formats and templates; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal force and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces force without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language per-force indirect-force recovery and literal-collapse rate, collapse regression controlling for comprehension/fertility/resource with directness-norm interaction, English indirect-speech-act replication, cross-lingual force probe transfer F1/AUROC and its dissociation from a surface-sentence-type probe, force-present-under-collapse check, cross-lingual force-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), force-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-directness/resource/typology correlation, patch-localized force layer, cross-lingual force transplant recovery rate, causal steering collapse-gap closure and force-flip rates, force-signal/content/output fidelity, direct-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The force-vs-expression split could be confounded if the force signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying intended-force decodability across all languages on collapse items via probe transfer rather than assuming, and report how much of the gap is force-representation vs gate. 2) Literal-force collapse could reflect comprehension failure rather than an expression gate; we use the matched DIRECT control and comprehension screening so residual collapse reflects force recovery, not reading. 3) Illocutionary force can be genuinely ambiguous (an indirect utterance may license multiple forces); we restrict scored items to clear-consensus intended forces (native-verified, drawing on validated indirect-speech-act stimuli) and analyze ambiguous ones separately. 4) Realizing indirect speech acts naturally and equivalently across languages is delicate (conventionalized indirectness differs—'Can you X?' as a request is highly conventional in English but may differ elsewhere); we native-verify naturalness, treat force type and indirect-form type as factors, and flag forms with no natural equivalent. 5) The force probe could latch onto surface sentence-type cues rather than a genuine force representation; the explicit dissociation from a surface-sentence-type probe, cross-lingual invariance, the force-present-under-collapse test, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 6) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal force, and content-invariant steering surfaces force without changing tokenization. 7) Some models may recover force uniformly across languages (no gap) or collapse everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual pragmatic competence, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 8) Directness-norm coding is coarse and debated; we treat it as a graded predictor and report sensitivity to alternative codings. 9) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 10) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report force-signal/content/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention, and use the force-flip (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine force gate. 11) The gate/force signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 12) Distinguishing from my prior pragmatics (truth-conditional implicature enrichment) and honorific/status proposals is essential; here the object is the ILLOCUTIONARY FORCE type of an utterance (assert/ask/command/commit) and the recovery of intended force from indirect forms whose surface type mismatches their force, grounded in speech-act theory, with direct stakes for assistants that must act on indirect requests/commands unevenly across languages.

Name: crosslingual_deliberation_benefit_gating
Title: Should It Think, or Just Answer? Whether the Query Language Determines When Deliberate Reasoning Helps or Hurts in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Whether explicit deliberate reasoning (chain-of-thought / 'thinking mode') HELPS or HURTS accuracy is systematically query-language-dependent: for the SAME problem, forcing deliberation improves accuracy in some languages but causally DEGRADES it in others (often lower-resource or morphologically-distant), because deliberation induces a language-specific failure mode (drift to an unstable reasoning language, error compounding, or answer-format collapse) rather than a knowledge deficit. We hypothesize (1) a per-problem, per-language 'deliberation benefit' that is predictable from language typology/resource and problem type, and often NEGATIVE; (2) the harm arises from a localizable reasoning-drift/instability signal that fires more in harmed languages; and (3) a small, localizable 'deliberation-mode' signal can be causally steered per-language to enable deliberation where it helps and suppress it where it hurts, recovering accuracy without changing the surface answer language.
Related Work: Multilingual-reasoning work overwhelmingly treats deliberation as globally beneficial and seeks to make it work everywhere: XLT (Huang et al. 2023), cross-lingual prompting/self-consistency (Qin et al. 2023), xCoT (Chai et al. 2024), SoT (Qi et al. 2025), and steering toward a shared reasoning language (Wang 2025; Mahmoud 2025), while cross-lingual collapse/language-drift is studied as a uniform degradation (Park et al. 2025; Lim et al. 2025). Crucially, applied audits report an unexplained SIGN-FLIP where deliberation is CATASTROPHIC in specific languages: Swastik (2026) shows CoT DEGRADES Bengali (-14.4pp) and Kannada (-11.4pp) VLM accuracy while helping others, and Gu et al. (2026) show reasoning paradigms are not universally transferable across scales. All of this is behavioral/benchmark-level. NO prior work (i) frames the HELP-vs-HURT sign of deliberation as a query-language-dependent, per-problem property, (ii) predicts when deliberation is net-negative, (iii) attributes the harm to a localizable instability signal, or (iv) causally gates deliberation per-language via steering. This is distinct from my prior reasoning-language-steering (which language to think IN, assuming thinking helps) and computational-depth (vertical layer-commitment without explicit CoT) proposals: here the object is whether to deliberate AT ALL and the causal sign of that choice by language.
Abstract: Chain-of-thought and 'thinking modes' are assumed to make language models smarter, and multilingual research has focused on which language a model should reason in. But a striking, unexplained observation cuts against the assumption: enabling deliberate reasoning can collapse accuracy to near-chance in specific languages (e.g., Bengali/Kannada CoT) while helping in others. We reframe this as a fundamental phenomenon: whether deliberate reasoning helps or hurts is query-language-dependent, and for many problem-language pairs its causal effect is NEGATIVE. We first quantify a per-problem, per-language 'deliberation benefit' (accuracy with forced deliberation minus direct answering) across typologically and resource-diverse languages and problem types, testing whether it is predictable from language typology/resource and whether it is systematically negative for certain languages—ruling out a mere knowledge deficit by showing direct answering succeeds where deliberation fails. We then diagnose the harm mechanistically: using per-layer language-ID probes and logit-lens we test whether deliberation in harmed languages triggers reasoning-language drift, error compounding, or answer-format collapse, and we train a linear 'reasoning-instability' probe that fires more where deliberation hurts. Finally, via activation and path patching we localize a 'deliberation-mode' signal and, in a decisive causal test, steer it per-language—suppressing deliberation where it hurts and enabling it where it helps—recovering accuracy while leaving the surface answer language unchanged. We reframe deliberate reasoning as a language-gated, sometimes-harmful, steerable degree of freedom rather than a universal good.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Qwen3-14B (native thinking mode), Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Bengali, Kannada, Greek), chosen to include reported harm cases (Bengali, Kannada, Greek).
2) DATA: Parallel problems where deliberation MIGHT help—MGSM (math word problems), multilingual MMLU subsets, multi-hop factual reasoning (Wikidata-derived), and multiple-choice exam items (FinMMEval-style) with short scoreable answers. Native-verified translations; record tokenization fertility and per-language direct-answer accuracy.
3) DELIBERATION-BENEFIT MEASUREMENT: For each (problem, language) run TWO conditions: DIRECT (answer immediately / thinking-off) and DELIBERATE (forced CoT or thinking-on). Define deliberation benefit = DELIBERATE minus DIRECT accuracy, per problem and language. KEY behavioral test: identify problem-language cells where benefit is significantly NEGATIVE, replicating/generalizing the Bengali/Kannada/Greek collapse. Mixed-effects regression of benefit on (language typology/resource via URIEL, problem type, tokenization fertility), problem as random effect; test that the SIGN of benefit is predictable from language and that harm is not explained by knowledge (condition on DIRECT-correct items).
4) HARM-MECHANISM DIAGNOSIS: In harmed cells, use per-layer language-ID probes and logit-lens on the deliberation trace to test three failure modes: (a) REASONING-DRIFT (CoT switches to an unstable/wrong reasoning language mid-chain), (b) ERROR-COMPOUNDING (early wrong steps propagate), (c) ANSWER-FORMAT COLLAPSE (final answer fails to conform after long reasoning). Quantify each mode's prevalence per language and correlate with negative benefit.
5) REASONING-INSTABILITY PROBE: Train a linear probe on hidden states during deliberation to predict whether the deliberation ends in a wrong answer; test whether it fires more in harmed languages and transfers zero-shot across languages (a shared instability signal).
6) LOCALIZE THE DELIBERATION-MODE SIGNAL: Via activation/path patching between a DIRECT run and a DELIBERATE run on the same problem, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components that engage the deliberation trajectory; cross-check activation vs path patching; report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band.
7) CAUSAL PER-LANGUAGE GATING (decisive): Derive a deliberation-mode steering vector (deliberate runs minus direct runs). Test (i) SUPPRESS: in harmed problem-language cells, steering toward the direct mode recovers accuracy toward DIRECT levels; (ii) ENABLE: in helped cells, keeping deliberation preserves gains; (iii) build a per-problem GATE that predicts the benefit sign from language/problem features and applies suppress/enable, comparing against always-deliberate, always-direct, best-fixed-policy, and force-English-CoT (Wang 2025) baselines; (iv) verify surface answer language unchanged and general QA unharmed. Metrics: gated-policy accuracy vs baselines, harm-recovery rate in negative cells, retained gains in positive cells, output-language fidelity.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: which failure mode dominates per language; native thinking-mode (Qwen3) vs prompted CoT; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); problem-type breakdown (math vs factual vs MC); gate predictability (AUC for predicting benefit sign); robustness across templates.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-(problem,language) deliberation benefit and its sign-predictability, negative-benefit cell prevalence, failure-mode prevalence (drift/compounding/format-collapse), instability-probe AUC and cross-lingual transfer, patch-localized deliberation-mode layer, causal gating harm-recovery and retained-gain rates, gated-policy accuracy vs baselines, output-language fidelity, general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The DIRECT vs DELIBERATE contrast must be fair; we control prompt format, use both prompted-CoT and native thinking modes, and match answer-extraction so harm is not a parsing artifact (though answer-format collapse is a hypothesized mechanism we measure explicitly). 2) Negative benefit could reflect a weak base rather than genuine harm; we condition on DIRECT succeeding to show deliberation actively destroys correct answers. 3) Some models/languages may show uniformly positive benefit, leaving little harm to study—this is itself informative and we quantify how often the sign flips. 4) The instability probe may be noisy; we validate on English with gold labels and confirm findings causally via patching. 5) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test multiple models (including a native-thinking model where collapse was reported) and cross-check activation vs path patching. 6) Per-language gating may trade some gains for harm-avoidance; we report the full trade-off (harm recovered vs gains retained) rather than claiming a free lunch. 7) Distinguishing from my reasoning-language-steering and computational-depth proposals is essential; here the object is the HELP-vs-HURT sign of engaging explicit deliberation at all, its language-dependence, and its causal per-language gating, not which language to reason in or vertical layer-commitment depth. 8) The deliberation-mode signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank variants.

Name: crosslingual_backtranslation_attractor
Title: The Meaning Fixed Point: Do Iterated Cross-Lingual Round-Trips Collapse Toward a Shared Canonical Form, and Is the Attractor a Language-Independent Representation?
Short Hypothesis: Repeatedly translating a sentence out to another language and back (round-trip back-translation), iterated many times, is a dynamical process that converges to a stable ATTRACTOR (a canonical paraphrase the model stops changing), and this attractor is largely language-independent: the SAME source sentence, round-tripped through typologically different pivot languages, converges to nearby fixed points because convergence is driven by the model's shared meaning representation, not by per-pivot translation quality. The convergence RATE and the residual meaning-drift at the fixed point are predictable from how strongly the sentence's meaning aligns to the model's shared concept-space manifold, and can be causally slowed or accelerated by steering that manifold, revealing that round-trip collapse is a property of a shared semantic fixed point rather than accumulated translation noise.
Related Work: Back-translation is used for data augmentation and translation evaluation, and Li & Brom (2025) note a 'paradox of poetic intent' where iterated/repeated back-translation preserves surface fluency but loses metaphorical depth and even produces 'verbatim BT' (the output stops changing). But this is behavioral/quality-focused, single-pivot, and offers no account of round-trip as a DYNAMICAL SYSTEM, no notion of a language-independent attractor, and no mechanism. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies iterated round-trip dynamics or fixed points. Paraphrase-diversity and self-consistency work is single-pass. NO prior work (i) characterizes iterated back-translation as convergence to an attractor, (ii) tests whether the attractor is shared across typologically distinct pivots (evidencing a language-independent meaning fixed point), (iii) predicts convergence rate / fixed-point drift from shared-manifold alignment, or (iv) causally modulates convergence by steering the shared representation. This is a behavioral-dynamics phenomenon with a mechanistic explanation, distinct from quality-of-translation studies and from single-pass gating/leakage work.
Abstract: Translate a sentence into French and back to English, then do it again, and again: what happens? We show that iterated cross-lingual round-trip translation is a dynamical process that converges to an attractor—a canonical paraphrase the model ceases to alter—and we ask whether that fixed point is a language-independent property of the model's shared meaning representation. We hypothesize that the SAME source sentence, round-tripped through typologically diverse pivot languages, converges to NEARBY attractors because collapse is driven by the model's shared concept-space manifold, not by per-pivot translation noise; that the convergence rate and the residual meaning-drift at the fixed point are predicted by how strongly the sentence's meaning aligns to that manifold; and that steering the shared representation causally slows or accelerates convergence. Using open multilingual models, we iterate round-trip translation to convergence for parallel source sentences across many pivot languages, measuring per-iteration paraphrase change (edit/semantic distance) and total semantic drift from the source. Behaviorally we characterize convergence dynamics, test whether attractors coincide across pivots, and test whether convergence rate and fixed-point drift track pivot typological distance and content type (literal vs figurative). Mechanistically, we relate convergence to a pre-iteration shared-manifold alignment measure and, in a causal test, steer the sentence toward or away from the shared manifold to modulate how fast it collapses and how far it drifts. We reframe back-translation collapse as convergence to a shared semantic fixed point, offering a measurable, predictable, and steerable account of a phenomenon previously described only as quality loss.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + light steering on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). ~10 typologically/script-diverse PIVOT languages (Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili, Indonesian), with English as the fixed anchor language for the round-trip endpoints (and a robustness run anchoring in other languages).
2) DATASET (RoundTripAttractor): ~500 English source sentences spanning strata: (A) LITERAL/factual, (B) FIGURATIVE (idioms, metaphors, drawing on the poetic-intent cases), (C) STRUCTURALLY COMPLEX (nested clauses), (D) SHORT/simple control. For each source, run ITERATED ROUND-TRIP: English -> pivot -> English -> pivot -> ... for N iterations (N up to ~15) per pivot language, recording the English endpoint at each iteration.
3) CONVERGENCE DYNAMICS (behavioral): Per (sentence, pivot) measure per-iteration CHANGE = edit distance and semantic distance (multilingual sentence-embedding cosine) between successive English endpoints; define CONVERGENCE (attractor reached) when change drops below a threshold and stabilizes ('verbatim BT'). Extract CONVERGENCE RATE (iterations-to-fixed-point) and RESIDUAL DRIFT = semantic distance of the fixed point from the original source. Report convergence curves per stratum; test whether nearly all sentences converge to a stable attractor (a dynamical-systems characterization).
4) SHARED-ATTRACTOR TEST (core): For the SAME source, compare the fixed points reached through DIFFERENT pivot languages. KEY hypothesis: attractors are NEARBY across typologically distinct pivots (low pairwise semantic distance among pivot-specific fixed points), far more than expected if collapse were pivot-specific noise. Statistics: mixed-effects model of cross-pivot fixed-point agreement vs a shuffled-pivot null; test whether agreement decreases with pivot-pivot typological distance (URIEL) but remains high overall, evidencing a largely language-independent meaning fixed point.
5) RATE/DRIFT PREDICTORS: Regress convergence rate and residual drift on (pivot typological/script distance to the anchor via URIEL, content stratum, sentence length/complexity, tokenization fertility), sentence as random effect. Hypothesis: figurative/complex sentences drift more and converge slower; distant pivots increase drift; literal short sentences converge fastest with least drift.
6) SHARED-MANIFOLD ALIGNMENT MECHANISM: Identify shared vs language-specific layers via per-layer language-ID probes (Wang 2025). For each source sentence, compute a PRE-ITERATION shared-manifold alignment = how cleanly its meaning representation sits on the model's shared concept-space manifold (e.g., cross-lingual representation stability of the sentence's meaning: cosine/CKA of its mid-layer representation across the anchor and pivot renderings). Test whether this alignment predicts convergence rate and residual drift (a sentence already near the shared manifold should converge fast with little drift), beyond the surface predictors in (5).
7) CAUSAL MODULATION (decisive): Derive a shared-manifold steering direction (difference-of-means pulling a sentence's mid-layer representation toward the centroid of its cross-lingual renderings). Apply it (or its negation) during the translation steps and test whether (i) steering TOWARD the shared manifold ACCELERATES convergence and REDUCES residual drift, and (ii) steering AWAY SLOWS convergence / increases drift, with dose-response, while preserving output fluency and the anchor language. This shows collapse is governed by the shared representation, not merely accumulated noise. Metrics: iterations-to-fixed-point change, residual-drift change, dose-response, fluency/language fidelity.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: stratum breakdown (literal vs figurative attractor drift—does the attractor systematically strip metaphor, quantifying the 'poetic-intent' loss as fixed-point drift?); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—do attractors coincide more tightly across pivots for balanced models?); decoding temperature (does greedy vs sampled translation change whether a stable attractor exists?); anchor-language robustness (attractors in non-English anchors); whether attractor sentences are higher-frequency / more 'templatey' than sources.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-sentence convergence curves and iterations-to-attractor, fraction reaching a stable fixed point, cross-pivot fixed-point agreement vs shuffled null and vs typological distance, convergence-rate/residual-drift regression on pivot distance and content stratum, shared-manifold-alignment vs convergence-rate/drift correlation (incremental over surface predictors), causal steering acceleration/deceleration of convergence and drift with dose-response and fluency/language-fidelity retention, figurative-vs-literal attractor-drift and model-family comparisons.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Some models/decoding settings may not converge (endless paraphrase churn) rather than reaching a fixed point; whether a stable attractor exists is itself the empirical question, and non-convergence for some strata/models is an informative, publishable characterization—we quantify convergence prevalence rather than assuming it. 2) Convergence could be a trivial artifact of greedy decoding memorizing a canonical phrasing; we test greedy vs sampled decoding and report whether the attractor is decoding-robust, and check whether attractors are simply higher-frequency templates. 3) The shared-attractor claim could be confounded if English (the anchor) dominates and all pivots collapse to an English-centric canonical form regardless of meaning; we test non-English anchors, compare English-centric vs multilingual-centric models, and measure cross-pivot agreement relative to a shuffled-pivot null so agreement reflects meaning, not a fixed anchor phrasing. 4) Semantic-drift and fixed-point-agreement metrics depend on the sentence encoder; we use multiple multilingual encoders plus edit distance and validate drift against small human meaning-preservation ratings on a subset. 5) Tokenization fertility and pivot translation quality confound convergence rate; we control for fertility and include per-pivot single-pass translation-quality (COMET) as a covariate, and—crucially—the shared-manifold-alignment predictor and the causal steering (which does not change tokenization) dissociate a shared-representation fixed point from mere per-pivot noise accumulation. 6) The steering may harm fluency or leak languages; we cap strength, monitor output-language fidelity and fluency, and report dose-response rather than a free lunch. 7) The manifold-alignment measure is an imperfect proxy for 'distance to the fixed point'; we validate it against observed convergence and report where it fails. 8) Results may be model-specific; we test four models spanning English-centric and multilingual-centric pretraining and report per-model results. 9) Distinguishing from Li & Brom (2025) is essential; our contribution is the DYNAMICAL-SYSTEMS characterization (attractor/fixed point), the language-independence test across pivots, the manifold-alignment prediction of convergence, and the causal steering of collapse—none of which the quality-focused back-translation literature provides.

Name: grammatical_gender_concept_leakage
Title: Is a Bridge Masculine? Arbitrary Grammatical Gender Leaking Into the Conceptual Representation of Objects in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs do not represent inanimate object concepts in a fully gender-neutral, language-independent way. The arbitrary grammatical gender a language assigns to a noun leaks into the model's internal conceptual representation of that object, biasing (1) the associative/adjectival attributes ascribed to it and (2) downstream pronoun/anaphora and inference choices, in ways that (3) systematically differ across languages assigning opposite genders to the same object and vanish for genderless languages, and (4) can be isolated as a low-dimensional 'gender-leakage' direction that is causally steerable and correctable without harming factual knowledge about the object.
Related Work: Classic psycholinguistics (Boroditsky et al. 2003; Maciuszek et al. 2019 in Polish) shows humans describe objects with gender-stereotyped attributes consistent with their language's grammatical gender, and Nicoladis et al. 2021 show this cross-linguistic influence is mediated by semantic/embedding-level gender connotations. In ML, gender-bias work overwhelmingly targets SOCIAL/animate gender (occupations, coreference: WinoMT/WinoBias) and representation/frequency bias (Derner et al. 2024). The closest LLM work: Brinkmann et al. 2025 train SAEs and show grammatical gender/number/tense are encoded as SHARED cross-lingual morphosyntactic features and causally used in translation, but do not test whether that grammatical-gender feature CONTAMINATES the object's SEMANTIC/conceptual representation; and Saeed et al. 2025 (EMNLP) show grammatical gender shifts TEXT-TO-IMAGE outputs behaviorally, without an internal/mechanistic account. NONE test whether arbitrary (inanimate) grammatical gender leaks into the CONCEPTUAL representation of the object itself inside a text LLM, whether it reproduces the Boroditsky effect cross-lingually, whether it is a localizable low-dimensional direction, or whether it can be causally steered and removed while preserving factual knowledge. Our proposal reframes a linguistic-relativity question as a mechanistic, causal probe of language-specific interference in an otherwise shared concept space, exploiting opposite-gender language pairs and genderless-language controls that no prior LLM study uses.
Abstract: Grammatical gender assigns an arbitrary gender to inanimate nouns (German 'Bridge' is feminine, Spanish 'Puente' is masculine), a purely formal property with no semantic content. Classic psycholinguistics found this arbitrary assignment nonetheless shapes how humans conceptualize objects, and recent work shows grammatical gender even shifts text-to-image outputs. We ask whether the same leakage occurs inside multilingual text LLMs: does a noun's grammatical gender contaminate the model's internal conceptual representation of the object, and can we isolate and causally control it? We assemble GenderLeak, inanimate objects with documented opposite grammatical genders across language pairs (e.g., Spanish vs German) plus genderless-language controls (English, Turkish, Finnish, Hungarian). Behaviorally, we test whether the model ascribes stereotypically masculine/feminine attributes, pronouns, and inferences to an object as predicted by that language's grammatical gender, whether the effect flips across opposite-gender languages, and vanishes in genderless ones. Representationally, we probe for a 'grammatical-gender' direction at the object's hidden state and measure how strongly an inanimate concept's representation is displaced along it, contrasting shared mid-layer concept-space layers with language-specific layers. In a decisive causal test, we steer along the gender-leakage direction to flip an object's ascribed attributes and pronouns, and derive a corrective projection that removes the leakage while preserving factual knowledge about the object. We relate leakage strength to typological distance and gender-system type, turning a linguistic-relativity question into a mechanistic, causal account of language-specific interference in a shared concept space.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: Gendered languages with contrasting assignments (Spanish, French, Italian, German, Russian, Hindi) and GENDERLESS controls (English, Turkish, Finnish, Hungarian). MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (GenderLeak): ~300 concrete inanimate objects (bridge, key, spoon, moon, sun, table, clock, apple...). For each, record the grammatical gender of its noun in every gendered language (from dictionaries), creating OPPOSITE-GENDER pairs (masculine in one language, feminine in another) and AGREE pairs (same gender across languages) as within-item contrasts. Build three probe types per object per language: (A) ATTRIBUTE elicitation (list adjectives describing the object), each adjective scored on a masculine/feminine axis via an independently pre-rated adjective lexicon; (B) FORCED-CHOICE gendered-attribute minimal pairs ('Is the {object} more like a warrior or a ballerina?'); (C) PRONOUN/ANAPHORA (in genderless-language prompts about the object primed in a gendered language, measure he/she/it tendency). Native-verify all templates.
3) BEHAVIORAL BORODITSKY TEST: For each object, test whether ascribed-attribute masculinity correlates with the noun's grammatical gender in the query language. KEY within-item design: for OPPOSITE-GENDER objects, does the SAME object flip its ascribed gender-stereotyped attributes across the masculine- vs feminine-assigning language? Genderless controls should show no systematic shift. Mixed-effects regression of attribute-masculinity on (grammatical gender, language, object), object as random effect; test the gender coefficient and the opposite-pair flip.
4) CROSS-LINGUAL LEAKAGE MAGNITUDE: Quantify per-object cross-lingual DISAGREEMENT in ascribed gender attributes and relate it to whether languages assign the noun opposite (predicted high) vs same (low) gender; genderless languages should cluster near neutral.
5) REPRESENTATIONAL GENDER DIRECTION: Extract hidden states at the object noun/last-content position. Train a linear probe to decode grammatical gender of the noun -> the per-layer 'grammatical-gender direction'. Measure the object concept's projection onto it and test whether it (i) tracks the noun's gender, (ii) is stronger in language-specific late layers than the shared mid-layer concept space (relate to the language-transition band via per-layer language-ID probes), and (iii) per-object projection predicts the behavioral attribute shift. Cross-check with an SAE/ICA gender feature (a la Brinkmann et al.).
6) LEAKAGE-PREDICTS-BEHAVIOR LINK: Correlate per-object representational projection onto the gender direction with per-object behavioral attribute-masculinity, within and across languages. A positive link supports genuine conceptual leakage rather than surface lexical priming.
7) CAUSAL STEERING (decisive): Derive a gender-leakage steering vector via difference-of-means (masculine-noun object states minus feminine-noun object states, controlling for the shared concept). (a) FLIP: add/subtract it on held-out objects and test whether ascribed attributes and pronouns flip masculine<->feminine while the object's IDENTITY and factual knowledge stay intact. (b) CORRECT: derive a projection removing the gender direction and test whether it neutralizes cross-lingual attribute disagreement (a bridge described the same regardless of query language) WITHOUT degrading factual QA about the object ('What is a bridge used for?'). Metrics: attribute-flip rate, pronoun-flip rate, cross-lingual disagreement reduction after correction, factual-QA retention, off-target damage.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: regress leakage strength on URIEL typological distance and gender-system type (2-gender vs 3-gender vs noun-class); English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); layer/dimension sensitivity; token-pooling; robustness across templates; whether a single gender direction generalizes across objects and languages.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: attribute-masculinity gender coefficient and opposite-pair flip, cross-lingual attribute disagreement vs gender-agreement, gender-direction probe accuracy and per-object projection, projection-behavior correlation, causal flip/pronoun-flip rates, correction-induced disagreement reduction, factual-QA retention, off-target damage, typology/gender-system regression coefficients.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The effect may be driven by surface lexical priming (gendered articles/agreement in the prompt) rather than a deep conceptual representation; we mitigate with a critical control that primes the object concept in a gendered language but ELICITS attributes in a genderless language (English), removing surface gender cues, and by using the representational-projection-predicts-behavior link (step 6) as evidence beyond surface form. 2) Adjective gender-stereotype ratings are subjective; we use independently pre-rated lexicons, report inter-rater agreement, and include forced-choice minimal pairs (type B) as a rating-free complement. 3) Some models may show no leakage (gender-neutral concept space); this is itself an informative, publishable finding about the cleanliness of the shared concept space, and we quantify how often leakage is present. 4) Grammatical-gender assignment is confounded with word frequency and morphology; the within-item opposite-gender design and genderless controls remove object-identity confounds, and we report frequency proxies. 5) Probing linearity assumptions may not hold; we validate the gender direction on animate nouns with natural gender as a positive control and report low-dimensional (SAE/ICA) structure. 6) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 7) The corrective projection may harm fluency or factual knowledge; we explicitly report factual-QA retention and off-target damage rather than claiming a free lunch. 8) Distinguishing from social-gender-bias work and from Brinkmann et al. (shared morphosyntactic features) and Saeed et al. (T2I behavioral) is essential; we focus exclusively on INANIMATE arbitrary grammatical gender leaking into the CONCEPTUAL representation inside a text LLM, making any systematic effect clear evidence of leakage and providing the internal, causal account those works lack.

Name: crosslingual_comparison_class_gating
Title: Tall for a Building or Tall for a Person? A Shared Comparison-Class Representation for Gradable Adjectives Whose Threshold Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When interpreting a gradable adjective applied to a noun ('a tall building', 'an expensive coffee', 'a heavy dog'), a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of the implicit COMPARISON CLASS and the threshold it induces (tall-for-a-building differs from tall-for-a-person), but the query language causally recalibrates that threshold: for the SAME adjective-noun pair the model grounds the vague predicate to a systematically higher or lower cutoff depending on the query language, tracking typological/resource distance, in a way separable from the shared comparison-class representation and causally repairable by shifting a localizable threshold signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Gradable adjectives and the comparison-class-relative threshold that makes 'tall' context-dependent are foundational in degree semantics (Kennedy; the tall-for-a-building vs tall-for-a-person contrast; vague-predicate threshold theory). In NLP, monolingual work probes whether LLMs know adjective scales and gradable-adjective norms, but is English-centric and behavioral. My prior crosslingual_vague_quantifier proposal concerns FREQUENCY/PROBABILITY/QUANTITY scalars ('a few', 'often', 'likely') grounded to a numeric scale independent of any comparison class; this is distinct because the object is the NOUN-RELATIVE comparison class and threshold of a GRADABLE ADJECTIVE (the standard shifts with the noun the predicate applies to), a different semantic mechanism. My precision, ANS, number-naming, and generic-force proposals concern numeric magnitude, ratio acuity, number-word structure, and exception-tolerance respectively, not comparison-class-relative predicate thresholds. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never for comparison-class thresholds. No prior work asks whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent comparison-class representation, whether the threshold it induces is language-gated, whether cross-lingual threshold drift tracks typology, or whether the threshold signal is causally localizable and steerable.
Abstract: How tall is 'a tall building' versus 'a tall person'? Gradable adjectives are interpreted relative to an implicit comparison class fixed by the noun they modify, and a listener must ground the vague predicate to a threshold on the fly. As multilingual models increasingly reason about sizes, prices, and quantities for users worldwide, we ask whether the query language shifts where that threshold sits. We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of the comparison class and its induced threshold, but the query language causally recalibrates the threshold, so the SAME adjective-noun pair is grounded to a systematically different cutoff across languages, tracking typological and resource distance. We build GradableProbe, parallel items across languages that ground gradable adjectives applied to specific nouns to numeric thresholds (via estimation, forced-choice boundary, and downstream inference), with adjective-noun content held fixed and a comparison-class-shift design (the same adjective across nouns of very different scales, e.g. tall-for-a-building vs tall-for-a-person). Behaviorally we measure per-language grounded thresholds and test whether cross-lingual drift tracks resource level and typological distance beyond translation, while verifying the model still correctly SHIFTS the threshold with the noun (comparison-class sensitivity is shared). We train a linear comparison-class/threshold probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the drift into a shared comparison-class representation versus a language-set threshold gain. Via activation and path patching we localize a threshold signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to shift the grounded threshold of a predicate (or equalize it across languages) while leaving the surface language and the adjective-noun content unchanged. We reframe multilingual vague-predicate inconsistency as a shared comparison class under a steerable, language-dependent threshold gate.
Experiments: 1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili). 2) DATASET (GradableProbe): ~500 gradable-adjective-noun pairs spanning dimensions (SIZE: tall/big/long; PRICE: expensive/cheap; WEIGHT: heavy/light; SPEED: fast/slow), each with a documented consensus numeric threshold in a fixed cultural-neutral unit context (from human norms + native verification). Probes: (A) DIRECT ESTIMATION ('About how tall must a building be to count as tall?' -> a number), (B) FORCED-CHOICE BOUNDARY (given two heights, which counts as 'tall for a building?'), (C) DOWNSTREAM INFERENCE where the grounded threshold determines the answer. CRITICAL comparison-class-shift design: pair the SAME adjective with nouns of very different scales (tall building vs tall person; heavy dog vs heavy truck) so a correct model must shift the threshold with the noun. Include a NUMERIC control (explicit numbers, no vague predicate; language-flat). Keep adjective-noun content fixed across languages; translate/native-verify the surrounding request; record tokenization fertility. Optionally collect small per-language human norms on a subset. 3) BEHAVIORAL DRIFT TEST: Per (pair, language) record the grounded threshold. KEY hypotheses: (i) cross-lingual DRIFT exists (the same adjective-noun pair grounds to a systematically different threshold across languages); (ii) drift tracks resource level and typological distance beyond translation; (iii) comparison-class SENSITIVITY (the model shifts the threshold with the noun) is preserved across languages even where the absolute threshold drifts. Mixed-effects regression of grounded log-threshold on (language, noun-scale, adjective, tokenization fertility, resource tier via URIEL), pair as random effect; test the language main effect and confirm the noun-scale effect (comparison-class sensitivity) holds in all languages. Compare against the NUMERIC control (language-flat). 4) SHARED COMPARISON-CLASS/THRESHOLD PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode (i) the COMPARISON CLASS / noun-scale the adjective is relativized to and (ii) the induced THRESHOLD (regress to log-threshold) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC/R^2 as evidence of a language-independent comparison-class representation, plus cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the representation for the same pair. Show the comparison class is internally similar across languages even when the emitted threshold differs. 5) GAIN-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer comparison-class/threshold representation across languages (should be similar if shared) versus the emitted threshold (which drifts). Define a per-language THRESHOLD GAIN (an affine shift/scale from the shared representation to the emitted cutoff); test whether cross-lingual drift is explained by a language-set gain on a similar comparison-class representation rather than a different comparison class. Correlate per-language gain with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens. 6) LOCALIZE THE THRESHOLD SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that grounds a predicate high and one that grounds it low on the SAME pair, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer shifts the emitted threshold WITHOUT changing the decoded comparison-class representation. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the threshold components from one language into another's run. 7) CAUSAL THRESHOLD STEERING (decisive): Derive a threshold steering vector via difference-of-means over localized components (high-threshold runs minus low-threshold runs at matched comparison class). Test (i) SHIFT: adding/subtracting it moves the grounded threshold up/down in a graded (dose-response) way on held-out pairs; (ii) EQUALIZE: per-language threshold gains make the same adjective-noun pair ground to the same cutoff across languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually and can override a language's default; (iv) it changes ONLY the threshold, not the decoded comparison class (the model still shifts with the noun), the adjective-noun content, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the NUMERIC control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: cross-lingual drift closure, dose-response of grounded threshold, comparison-class/content/output fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts vague-predicate thresholds but not explicit-number or unrelated answers. 8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: dimension breakdown (size vs price vs weight vs speed); is English/high-resource the reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank threshold subspace; robustness across estimation-vs-forced-choice-vs-downstream formats; whether one threshold vector generalizes across pairs and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched comparison class and by showing content-invariant steering shifts thresholds without changing tokenization; model-vs-human threshold comparison on the subset. EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language grounded thresholds and cross-lingual drift with resource/typology regression, comparison-class sensitivity (noun-scale effect) preserved across languages, cross-lingual comparison-class/threshold probe transfer AUROC/R^2 and representation similarity, representation-similarity vs threshold-drift (gain) decomposition, gain-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized threshold layer, cross-lingual threshold transplant shift, causal steering drift closure with dose-response, comparison-class/content/output fidelity, numeric-control and general-QA retention, model-vs-human comparison.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Gradable-adjective thresholds are inherently fuzzy and culturally variable; we avoid claiming a single correct value, use human per-language norms descriptively where available, focus on relative cross-lingual drift and on preserved comparison-class sensitivity (the noun-scale shift), and use the numeric control to anchor. 2) The gain-vs-signal split could be confounded if the comparison-class representation itself differs by language; we test this directly by comparing the shared-probe comparison-class/threshold representation across languages rather than assuming, and report how much drift is representation vs gain. 3) Drift could be a mere translation effect (the translated adjective genuinely implies a different standard); we hold adjective-noun content fixed via native-verified parallels, and the internal-representation-predicts-threshold link plus content-preserving steering (which shifts the threshold without changing the adjective or noun) dissociate a genuine internal threshold gate from lexical translation. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds numeric output; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched comparison class, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts thresholds. 5) Instruction-tuned models may refuse or give ranges; we use both numeric generation and log-probability over threshold buckets, and report refusal/range rates. 6) Some models may ground gradable predicates uniformly across languages (no drift), lack a coherent comparison-class representation, or fail comparison-class sensitivity entirely; any of these is an informative, publishable finding about whether LLMs build noun-relative vague-predicate thresholds, and we quantify how often drift occurs and whether the shared comparison-class representation exists. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic numeric lever; we report comparison-class/content/output fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention, and use dose-response and reverse-consistency to ensure a genuine threshold gate rather than a global numeric shift. 9) The threshold signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my vague-quantifier (frequency/probability/quantity scalars grounded to a numeric scale), precision, ANS, and generic-force proposals is essential; here the object is the NOUN-RELATIVE comparison class and threshold of a gradable ADJECTIVE (the standard shifts with the modified noun) and its language-set threshold gate over a shared comparison-class representation.

Name: crosslingual_classifier_category_gating
Title: One Bottle, One Long-Thin Thing: A Shared Classifier-Category Representation for Nouns Whose Expression Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: Numeral-classifier languages (Chinese, Japanese, Korean) obligatorily categorize a noun by a semantic dimension (shape, animacy, function) when counting it (e.g. a long-thin classifier for pencils, a flat classifier for paper), while classifier-less languages (English, Russian) do not. We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of a noun's classifier-relevant semantic category (its shape/animacy/function class), but whether that categorization is behaviorally EXPRESSED—selecting the correct classifier when counting, judging a mismatched classifier as odd—is gated by the query language: the SAME noun's category is internally represented across languages yet the correct classifier is surfaced far less reliably in lower-resource / typologically distant classifier languages, so the model internally 'knows the object's shape class' while behaviorally mis-classifying. The classifier-category signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated classifier failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Numeral classifiers—obligatory morphemes that categorize a counted noun by shape, animacy, or function—are a canonical typological phenomenon (Aikhenvald's classifiers; Allan's classifier semantics), sharply dividing classifier languages (Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Thai, Vietnamese) from classifier-less ones (English, Russian). In NLP, numeral-classifier prediction/generation is a supervised or MT-quality task studied monolingually (Chinese/Japanese classifier selection), and my prior number-focused proposals concern number-word magnitude distortion, dynamic tallies, approximate-number acuity, measurement units, reported precision, and vague-quantifier grounding—NONE address the SEMANTIC CATEGORIZATION of a noun that classifiers impose (which shape/animacy/function class an object belongs to for counting). My colexification, kinship-granularity, and basic-level proposals concern sense conflation within a word, relational fineness, and taxonomic level respectively, not the classifier-category dimension. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never for classifier categories. No prior work asks whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent representation of a noun's classifier-relevant category, whether its behavioral expression (classifier selection) is language-gated over that shared representation, whether it tracks resource/typological distance, or whether the classifier-category signal is causally localizable and steerable. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of numeral-classifier categorization.
Abstract: To count a pencil in Chinese you must call it a long-thin thing, and a sheet of paper a flat thing: numeral classifiers force speakers to categorize every counted noun by its shape, animacy, or function, a categorization English speakers never make. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal representation of a noun's classifier-relevant semantic category, and whether that internal categorization is decoupled from how reliably the correct classifier is behaviorally expressed across languages. We hypothesize that models represent a noun's shape/animacy/function class similarly across languages internally, but the query language gates whether the correct classifier is surfaced when counting, so the SAME noun is mis-classified far more in lower-resource, typologically distant classifier languages—even though the model 'knows the object's category'. We build ClassifierProbe, parallel counting expressions across classifier languages (Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Thai) plus classifier-less controls (English, Russian), where the model must select or judge the classifier for nouns spanning classifier categories (long-thin, flat, round, animate, functional), with a mismatched-classifier anomaly probe and a control where category is unambiguous.
