Behaviorally we measure per-language classifier accuracy and category-mismatch tolerance and test whether it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond noun knowledge. We train a linear classifier-category probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer—including from classifier-less languages—then decompose the failure into a shared categorization component versus a language-set expression gate, verifying the correct category is internally present even where classifier selection fails. Via activation and path patching we localize a classifier-category signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to surface (or flip) the classifier while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual classifier failures as a steerable gate over a shared semantic-category representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 4 classifier languages spanning resource/typological distance (Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Thai) plus 2 classifier-less controls (English, Russian), coded for classifier-system richness from typological references (Aikhenvald) plus URIEL distance. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (ClassifierProbe): ~500 concrete nouns spanning classifier categories (LONG-THIN: pencil, rope; FLAT: paper, blanket; ROUND/small: ball, egg; ANIMATE: dog, person; FUNCTIONAL: machine, book), each labeled with its correct classifier per classifier language (from dictionaries + native verification), chosen to translate cleanly. Item types: (A) CLASSIFIER-SELECTION ('How do you count three {noun}?' with correct-classifier and mismatched-classifier options), (B) MISMATCH-ANOMALY ('Is it natural to count {noun} with {wrong-category classifier}?'), (C) CATEGORY-INFERENCE (identify the object's shape/animacy class, a language-neutral probe). Include a control where only one classifier is appropriate (bounds the effect) and screen that the model knows the noun per language. Translate/native-verify; keep nouns fixed; record tokenization fertility; short scoreable options.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (noun, language) record correct-classifier vs mismatch selection and mismatch-anomaly tolerance. KEY hypothesis: classifier accuracy is systematically lower (mismatch tolerance higher) in lower-resource/typologically distant classifier languages (e.g. Thai/Korean vs Chinese), beyond noun knowledge and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of classifier error on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, classifier category, knowledge indicator), noun as random effect; compare against the single-appropriate-classifier control. Report per-language and per-category profiles, cross-lingual disagreement on identical nouns, and replicate a monolingual classifier-selection baseline in the strongest language.
4) SHARED CLASSIFIER-CATEGORY PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the noun/pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode the noun's CLASSIFIER-RELEVANT CATEGORY (shape/animacy/function class) on data from the strongest classifier language (Chinese), apply zero-shot to other classifier languages AND to the classifier-less controls (English/Russian); report macro-F1/AUROC. CRITICAL: high transfer FROM classifier-less languages (whose speakers never overtly classify) would evidence a shared, language-independent categorization even absent overt marking. Measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine; on CLASSIFIER-FAILURE items, test whether the correct category is still internally decodable across ALL languages even when classifier selection fails.
5) CATEGORY-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer category signal across languages (should be similar if categorization is shared) versus behavioral classifier selection (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal category to surfaced classifier per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar category signal. Correlate gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes.
6) LOCALIZE THE CLASSIFIER-CATEGORY SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that surfaces the correct classifier and one that fails on the SAME noun, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer surfaces the correct classifier WITHOUT changing the decoded noun identity. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the category representation FROM a high-accuracy classifier language (or from a classifier-less language's shared category signal) into a failing run.
7) CAUSAL CLASSIFIER STEERING (decisive): Derive a classifier-category steering vector via difference-of-means (correct-classifier runs minus mismatch runs, plus category contrasts). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to failing languages increases correct classifier selection toward high-accuracy levels; (ii) FLIP: steering toward a different category makes the model select a different-category classifier (long-thin -> flat) on well-classified items; (iii) it works cross-lingually, stronger where expression was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY the classifier/category, not the decoded noun identity or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the single-appropriate control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: classifier-accuracy-gap closure, category-flip rate (reverse), category-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes classifier judgments but not unrelated answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: category breakdown (which categories—shape vs animacy vs function—leak most); does the shared category signal transfer from classifier-less languages?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single category vector generalizes across nouns and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal category and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces the classifier without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language per-category classifier accuracy and mismatch tolerance, expression regression controlling for noun knowledge/fertility/resource, monolingual classifier-selection replication, cross-lingual classifier-category probe transfer F1/AUROC (including from classifier-less languages) and category-present-under-failure, cross-lingual category-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), category-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized classifier-category layer, cross-lingual category transplant recovery rate, causal steering accuracy-gap closure and category-flip rates, category-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The category-vs-expression split could be confounded if the category signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying category decodability across all languages on failure items via probe transfer, and report how much of the gap is categorization vs gate. 2) Classifier failure could reflect noun-knowledge ignorance rather than an expression gate; we screen per-language noun knowledge and restrict the gate analysis to known nouns. 3) Classifier assignment can be genuinely variable (some nouns take multiple classifiers, register-dependent); we use dictionary + native-verified canonical classifiers, restrict scored items to clear-consensus assignments, and analyze variable ones separately. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal category, and content-invariant steering surfaces the classifier without changing tokenization. 5) Some models may classify uniformly across languages (no gap) or fail everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual classifier categorization, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 6) The transfer-from-classifier-less-languages test is the strongest novelty but could fail if the category is only represented in classifier languages (an equally informative result about whether classification is genuinely shared vs classifier-language-specific); we report it either way. 7) The category probe could latch onto surface classifier tokens rather than a genuine semantic-category representation; the transfer from classifier-less languages, the category-inference probe (type C), cross-lingual invariance, the category-present-under-failure test, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report category-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention, and use the category-flip (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine classifier-category gate. 10) The gate/category signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my colexification, kinship-granularity, and basic-level proposals is essential; here the object is the CLASSIFIER-RELEVANT semantic category (shape/animacy/function) that numeral classifiers impose on a counted noun and the language-gating of its expression, grounded in numeral-classifier typology.

Name: crosslingual_individuation_gating
Title: What Counts as One? A Shared Object-vs-Substance Individuation Representation Whose Expression Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: Languages carve the world into countable INDIVIDUALS versus unbounded STUFF very differently (English 'furniture' is a mass noun though it denotes discrete objects; many languages treat 'hair', 'rice', 'advice' as count where others treat them as mass). We hypothesize a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal 'individuation' representation of an entity (is it an object with natural units vs a substance without them), but whether that representation is behaviorally EXPRESSED—answering 'how many?' vs 'how much?', selecting count vs mass syntax, judging pluralization/quantifier felicity—is gated by the query language: the SAME entity is individuated consistently internally across languages yet processed with the wrong count/mass status far more often in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so the model internally 'knows whether it is a thing or stuff' while behaviorally mis-individuating. The individuation signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: The mass/count distinction and the object-vs-substance individuation it encodes is a core topic in semantics and cognitive science (Quine's individuation; Chierchia's mass/count semantics; Barner & Snedeker on quantity judgments; the cross-linguistic finding that languages differ sharply in which entities are grammatically countable). In NLP, mass/count is studied as a supervised lexical-classification or countability-prediction task, monolingually and behaviorally. My prior crosslingual_classifier_category proposal concerns the shape/animacy/function CLASS a numeral classifier assigns to an already-countable noun; crosslingual_basic_level concerns taxonomic LEVEL; crosslingual_colexification concerns sense conflation within a word; crosslingual_running_state concerns maintaining a numeric tally. NONE address the prior, more fundamental question of whether an entity is INDIVIDUATED at all (object with natural units vs unbounded substance)—the count/mass status—whether that individuation is a shared cross-lingual representation, whether its behavioral expression is language-gated, whether it tracks resource/typological distance, or whether the individuation signal is causally localizable and steerable. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never for individuation/count-mass status. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of object-vs-substance individuation in language models.
Abstract: A basic act of understanding is deciding whether something comes in countable units—three chairs, two apples—or is unbounded stuff you measure rather than count—water, advice, furniture. Languages disagree strikingly about which entities are countable, yet the underlying object-vs-substance individuation is largely shared across human cognition. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal representation of whether an entity is individuated (an object with natural units) or a substance (without them), and whether that internal individuation is decoupled from how reliably it is behaviorally expressed across languages. We hypothesize that models individuate entities similarly across languages internally, but the query language gates whether the correct count/mass status is surfaced—answering 'how many?' vs 'how much?', selecting count vs mass syntax, judging pluralization and quantifier felicity—so the SAME entity is processed with the wrong individuation status far more in lower-resource, typologically distant languages, even though the model 'knows whether it is a thing or stuff'. We build IndividuationProbe, parallel items across languages that require count/mass reasoning about entities whose grammatical countability differs cross-linguistically, plus entities that are count (or mass) in all languages as controls. Behaviorally we measure per-language individuation accuracy and mis-individuation (treating stuff as countable or objects as uncountable) and test whether it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond entity knowledge. We train a linear individuation probe and test whether a single probe transfers zero-shot across languages—including from languages that grammatically disagree—then decompose the failure into a shared individuation component versus a language-set expression gate, verifying the correct status is internally present even where behavior mis-individuates. Via activation and path patching we localize an individuation signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to surface (or flip) count/mass status while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual quantity-reasoning failures as a steerable gate over a shared individuation representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages that differ in the countability of many entities (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese [classifier language, largely mass-like nouns], Japanese), coded for how mass-oriented their nominal system is (from typological references) plus URIEL distance. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (IndividuationProbe): ~500 entities in three strata by cross-linguistic agreement: (A) DISAGREE entities whose grammatical countability differs across the 8 languages (furniture, hair, rice, advice, luggage, fruit, bread), (B) UNIVERSAL-COUNT controls (chair, apple, dog—count everywhere), (C) UNIVERSAL-MASS controls (water, gold, sand—mass everywhere), sourced from mass/count lexicons + native verification. Item types: (i) QUANTITY-QUESTION selection ('Do we ask HOW MANY or HOW MUCH {entity}?'), (ii) COUNT/MASS SYNTAX felicity ('Is "three {entity}s" natural? "a little {entity}"?'), (iii) INDIVIDUATION-INFERENCE (a context requiring counting discrete units vs measuring an amount), (iv) OBJECT-vs-SUBSTANCE category probe (language-neutral: does this come in natural discrete units in the world?). Translate/native-verify, realizing count/mass syntax naturally per language; keep entities fixed; screen that the model knows the entity per language (so failure is not lexical ignorance); record tokenization fertility; short scoreable answers.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (entity, language) record correct count/mass handling vs mis-individuation. KEY hypothesis: for DISAGREE (and even for world-consistent) entities, individuation accuracy is systematically lower (mis-individuation higher) in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond entity knowledge and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of mis-individuation on (language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, stratum, knowledge indicator), entity as random effect; compare against UNIVERSAL-COUNT/MASS controls (should be language-flatter). Report per-language and per-stratum profiles, cross-lingual disagreement on identical entities, and replicate a monolingual mass/count baseline in the strongest language.
4) SHARED INDIVIDUATION PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the entity/pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode OBJECT/INDIVIDUATED vs SUBSTANCE/UNINDIVIDUATED (the world-level individuation, distinct from any language's grammatical countability) on ENGLISH data, apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent individuation representation. CRITICAL: test transfer to and from languages that grammatically DISAGREE with English on the entity (e.g., a Chinese/Japanese run for 'furniture') — high transfer despite grammatical disagreement evidences a shared, world-grounded individuation representation beneath the surface count/mass grammar. Measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine; on MIS-INDIVIDUATION items, test whether the correct individuation is still internally decodable across ALL languages even when behavior mis-individuates.
5) INDIVIDUATION-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer individuation signal across languages (should be similar if individuation is shared) versus behavioral count/mass handling (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal individuation to surfaced count/mass behavior per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar individuation signal rather than weaker individuation. Correlate gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes.
6) LOCALIZE THE INDIVIDUATION SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that surfaces the correct count/mass status and one that mis-individuates on the SAME entity, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer surfaces correct individuation WITHOUT changing the decoded entity identity. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the individuation representation FROM a high-accuracy language (or from a grammatically-disagreeing language's shared signal) into a failing run.
7) CAUSAL INDIVIDUATION STEERING (decisive): Derive an individuation steering vector via difference-of-means (object/count runs minus substance/mass runs). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to mis-individuating languages increases correct count/mass handling toward high-accuracy levels; (ii) FLIP: steering along the axis makes the model treat an object as a substance (mass) and vice versa on well-handled items (e.g., pluralization/quantifier felicity flips); (iii) it works cross-lingually, stronger where expression was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY individuation status, not the decoded entity identity or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the UNIVERSAL controls, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: mis-individuation-gap closure, individuation-flip rate (reverse), individuation-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes count/mass judgments but not unrelated answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: stratum breakdown (disagree vs universal-count vs universal-mass); does the shared individuation signal transfer across grammatically-disagreeing languages?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single individuation vector generalizes across entities and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal individuation and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces correct status without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language per-stratum individuation accuracy and mis-individuation rate, expression regression controlling for entity knowledge/fertility/resource, monolingual mass/count replication, cross-lingual individuation probe transfer AUROC (including across grammatically-disagreeing languages) and individuation-present-under-mis-individuation, cross-lingual individuation-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), individuation-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized individuation layer, cross-lingual individuation transplant recovery rate, causal steering mis-individuation-gap closure and individuation-flip rates, individuation-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The individuation-vs-expression split could be confounded if the individuation signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying individuation decodability across all languages (especially grammatically-disagreeing ones) on mis-individuation items via probe transfer, and report how much of the gap is individuation vs gate. 2) Mis-individuation could reflect entity-knowledge ignorance rather than an expression gate; we screen per-language entity knowledge and restrict the gate analysis to known entities. 3) The DISAGREE stratum blurs 'world-level individuation' vs 'grammatical countability'; we anchor the probe target on WORLD-level object/substance status (does it come in natural units) and use the object-vs-substance category probe (type iv) to separate it from grammar, treating grammatical count/mass as the behavioral expression to be predicted. 4) Count/mass status can be genuinely gradient or register-dependent for some entities; we use clear-consensus items (native-verified), include universal-count/mass controls, and analyze borderline entities separately. 5) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal individuation, and content-invariant steering surfaces correct status without changing tokenization. 6) Some models may individuate uniformly across languages (no gap) or mis-individuate everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual individuation, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 7) The transfer-across-grammatically-disagreeing-languages test is the strongest novelty but could fail if individuation is only represented as surface grammatical countability (an equally informative result about whether individuation is world-grounded vs grammar-bound); we report it either way. 8) The individuation probe could latch onto surface count/mass syntax cues rather than a genuine world-grounded representation; the transfer across disagreeing languages, the object-vs-substance category probe, cross-lingual invariance, the individuation-present-under-failure test, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 9) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 10) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report individuation-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention, and use the flip (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine individuation gate. 11) The gate/individuation signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 12) Distinguishing from my classifier-category (shape/function class for counting an already-countable noun), basic-level (taxonomic level), colexification (sense conflation), and running-state (numeric tally) proposals is essential; here the object is the prior, more fundamental OBJECT-vs-SUBSTANCE individuation (count/mass status—whether an entity is countable at all) and the language-gating of its expression, grounded in mass/count semantics and Quinean individuation.

Name: crosslingual_facethreat_mitigation_gating
Title: Softening the Blow, in Some Tongues More Than Others: A Shared Face-Threat Signal Whose Politeness Mitigation Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When asked to deliver a face-threatening act (a refusal, criticism, bad news, a correction, a disagreement), a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of HOW face-threatening the content is (a shared face-threat estimate), but the query language causally sets how much politeness MITIGATION it wraps around that content: for the SAME face-threatening message with the SAME internal threat estimate, the model softens/hedges/apologizes far more in some languages—especially higher-power-distance / high-context / indirectness-favoring ones—and delivers it bluntly in others, producing a cross-lingual politeness-mitigation asymmetry that is separable from the propositional content and from the internal threat estimate, and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable mitigation-gate signal without changing the message content or surface language.
Related Work: Face-Threatening Acts and politeness/redress strategies (Brown & Levinson's politeness theory; power-distance and high/low-context communication) are foundational in pragmatics and cross-cultural communication, and vary sharply across languages/cultures in how much mitigation accompanies a face threat. In NLP this is barely studied and only behaviorally: multilingual politeness-transfer and honorific-generation work, and socio-normative benchmarks (Ghanbari Haez 2026) note cross-lingual variation in advice/role framing, with no internal representation, no decomposition, and no causal intervention. My prior crosslingual_hedging proposal concerns verbal hedging of a FACTUAL ANSWER decoupled from correctness; crosslingual_honorific_status concerns register keyed to the interlocutor's relative STATUS; crosslingual_pragmatics concerns truth-conditional implicature; crosslingual_illocutionary_force concerns recovering the FORCE of indirect speech acts. NONE address the DELIVERY of a face-threatening act—how much politeness mitigation the model volunteers around inherently face-threatening content—its decomposition into a shared face-threat estimate versus a language-set mitigation gain, or its causal steering. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies face-threat mitigation. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of politeness mitigation of face-threatening acts, with direct fairness/user-experience stakes: the SAME refusal or criticism can read as curt or gracious purely as a function of the query language.
Abstract: Delivering bad news, a refusal, or a criticism is a face-threatening act, and cultures differ enormously in how much softening—hedges, apologies, positive framing—they expect around it. As LLMs increasingly refuse, correct, and critique users worldwide, we ask whether the query language changes how gently the same hard message is delivered, and how this is implemented internally. We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of how face-threatening a message is, but the query language causally sets a mitigation gain on it, so the SAME face-threatening content is heavily softened in some languages—especially higher-power-distance, high-context ones—and delivered bluntly in others, independent of the propositional content and of the internal threat estimate. We build FaceThreatProbe, parallel scenarios across languages requiring a face-threatening act (refusals, criticisms, corrections, bad news, disagreements) with the core message held fixed, scored for a validated politeness-mitigation metric (density of hedges, apologies, positive framing, indirectness) and for whether the core content is preserved. Behaviorally we measure per-language mitigation and test whether it tracks power-distance and indirectness norms beyond content and internal threat. We train a linear face-threat probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the mitigation gap into a shared threat estimate versus a language-set mitigation gain—heavy softening should coincide with a similar internal threat estimate. Via activation and path patching we localize a mitigation-gate signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to equalize politeness mitigation across languages—or, in reverse, blunt or amplify it—while preserving the core message and surface language. We reframe cross-lingual politeness inequality as a shared face-threat signal under a steerable, language-dependent mitigation gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/culturally/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili, Korean), coded for documented power-distance / high-low-context / indirectness norms plus URIEL typological/resource distance (graded predictors).
2) DATASET (FaceThreatProbe): ~500 scenarios each requiring a FACE-THREATENING ACT with a FIXED core message: REFUSAL (decline a request), CRITICISM (negative feedback on work), CORRECTION (tell the user they are wrong), BAD NEWS (deliver an unwelcome fact), DISAGREEMENT (oppose a stated view). The propositional content (what must be conveyed) is held constant across languages; the model chooses how to deliver it. Vary THREAT SEVERITY (mild vs strong face threat) as a graded factor. Include a NEUTRAL control (non-face-threatening messages of matched length) to bound baseline politeness. Translate/native-verify scenarios; record tokenization fertility. Define a language-robust MITIGATION metric: per-language native-verified inventories of hedges, apology/softening markers, positive-framing and indirectness devices, plus a validated mitigation classifier calibrated against human politeness ratings on a subset; and a CONTENT-PRESERVATION check (is the core message—the refusal/criticism/correction—still clearly conveyed).
3) BEHAVIORAL MITIGATION-ASYMMETRY TEST: Per (scenario, language) measure mitigation density and content-preservation. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME face-threatening message, mitigation is systematically higher in higher-power-distance / high-context / indirectness-favoring languages, beyond content and threat severity. Mixed-effects regression of mitigation on (language, threat severity, act type, power-distance/indirectness codes, tokenization fertility, resource tier via URIEL), scenario as random effect; test the language effect and its cultural-norm dependence. Compare against the NEUTRAL control (should show smaller language-driven differences). Report per-language mitigation profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical hard messages; verify core content is preserved across languages (so the effect is mitigation, not content deletion).
4) SHARED FACE-THREAT PROBE & TRANSFER: At the pre-generation / early-answer position pool the hidden state; train a linear probe to decode how FACE-THREATENING the message is (graded threat severity, and act type) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report R^2/AUROC as evidence of a language-independent face-threat estimate. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on HEAVILY-MITIGATED and BLUNTLY-DELIVERED items, test whether the internal face-threat estimate is SIMILAR across languages—the signature of language modulating the mitigation GAIN, not the threat detection.
5) GAIN-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer face-threat estimate across languages (should be similar on matched items) versus the emitted mitigation (which diverges). Define a per-language MITIGATION GAIN mapping the threat estimate to realized softening; test whether cross-lingual mitigation differences are explained by a language-set gain on a similar threat signal rather than differing threat estimates. Correlate per-language gain with power-distance/indirectness norms, resource tier, and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE MITIGATION-GATE SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a high-mitigation language and a blunt-delivery language on the SAME face-threatening scenario, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer changes realized mitigation WITHOUT changing the decoded face-threat estimate or the core content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gate components from a high-mitigation language into a blunt run.
7) CAUSAL MITIGATION STEERING (decisive): Derive a mitigation-gate steering vector via difference-of-means (high-mitigation runs minus blunt runs at matched threat estimate). Test (i) SOFTEN: adding it in blunt languages increases politeness mitigation toward a reference level; (ii) BLUNT: subtracting it reduces mitigation in high-mitigation languages; (iii) EQUALIZE: per-language gains make the same hard message equally mitigated across languages; (iv) DOSE-RESPONSE: scaling produces graded softening; (v) it changes ONLY the amount of mitigation, NOT the core message / content-preservation, the decoded face-threat estimate, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the NEUTRAL control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Baselines: prompting for 'a polite/direct delivery', per-language style instructions, translate-to-English. Metrics: mitigation-gap closure, content-preservation retention (the refusal/criticism must remain clearly conveyed), blunt-induction rate (reverse), face-threat-signal/content/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes mitigation but not the core content or unrelated tasks.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: act-type breakdown (refusal vs criticism vs correction vs bad news vs disagreement); is a high-directness (e.g. German/English) or high-mitigation (e.g. Japanese/Korean) language the reference?; does mitigation track power-distance/indirectness beyond resource level?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the asymmetry?); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank mitigation subspace; whether one gate vector generalizes across acts and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched threat estimate and by showing content-invariant steering changes mitigation without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language mitigation density and content-preservation, mitigation regression controlling for content/threat/fertility/resource with cultural-norm correlation, cross-lingual face-threat probe transfer R^2/AUROC and threat-estimate-similarity-under-divergent-mitigation, signal-similarity vs mitigation-divergence (gain) decomposition, gain-vs-norm/resource/typology correlation, patch-localized mitigation-gate layer, cross-lingual gate transplant equalization rate, causal steering mitigation-gap closure with dose-response and blunt-induction rate, content-preservation and face-threat-signal/output fidelity, neutral-control and general-QA retention, comparison to prompt/style-instruction/translate baselines, model-vs-human politeness-rating agreement.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Cross-lingual mitigation metrics are hard to make comparable (politeness devices differ syntactically and pragmatically across languages); we build native-verified per-language mitigation inventories, use a mitigation classifier validated against human politeness ratings on a subset, analyze device categories separately, and report reliability. 2) The gain-vs-signal split could be confounded if the internal face-threat estimate itself differs by language; we test this directly via cross-lingual probe transfer and the threat-estimate-similarity-under-divergent-mitigation check, reporting how much of the mitigation gap is threat-signal vs gain—either outcome is informative. 3) The most important guard: steering must change SOFTENING, not delete the hard message; we score content-preservation (the refusal/criticism/correction must remain clearly conveyed) as a primary metric and treat mitigation gains that erase content as a null, not a success, and blunt-steering that adds rudeness beyond removing mitigation as off-target. 4) Mitigation could partly be a length artifact (more softening = more tokens); we normalize by content-matched neutral controls, control for length/fertility, and show content-invariant steering changes mitigation without proportional content change. 5) Some models/languages may show no mitigation asymmetry (uniform politeness or uniform bluntness); either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual face-threat mitigation, and we quantify how often a gap exists. 6) Power-distance/indirectness norm coding is coarse and debated; we treat it as a graded predictor, report sensitivity to alternative codings, and note a language effect is establishable even if its cultural correlate is weak. 7) Instruction-tuned models' RLHF may impose a global politeness prior that interacts with language; we compare base vs instruction-tuned and English-centric vs multilingual-centric models and report the interaction. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic politeness lever; we report content-preservation, face-threat-signal/output fidelity, neutral-control and general-QA retention, and use dose-response, blunt-induction (reverse), and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine mitigation gate rather than a global positivity/politeness knob. 10) The mitigation signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my hedging (verbal qualifiers on a factual answer decoupled from correctness), honorific/status (register keyed to interlocutor status), pragmatics (truth-conditional implicature), and illocutionary-force (recovering indirect-act force) proposals is essential; here the object is the DELIVERY of an inherently face-threatening act—how much politeness mitigation the model volunteers around fixed hard content—and its language-set mitigation gain over a shared face-threat estimate, grounded in politeness theory.

Name: crosslingual_deontic_force_gating
Title: Must, Should, or May? A Shared Deontic-Force Representation for Rules Whose Strength Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When interpreting a rule or instruction, a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of its DEONTIC FORCE (the strength of obligation/permission: must vs should vs may vs must-not), but the query language causally recalibrates how strongly it commits to that force: for the SAME rule the model reads it as a firmer obligation or a weaker suggestion depending on the query language, tracking each language's modal-marking typology and typological/resource distance, separably from the shared force representation and causally repairable by shifting a localizable deontic-strength signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Deontic modality (obligation/permission/prohibition strength) is a core linguistic category (Palmer's Mood and Modality; Kratzer's modal semantics; corpus studies such as Cepani & Rushiti 2025 on Albanian administrative deontic marking) and languages vary sharply in how they grammaticalize modal force (dedicated modal verbs, obligatory subjunctive/imperative moods, particles, or lexical periphrasis). In NLP, modality is studied as supervised modal-sense classification, monolingually and behaviorally; no work studies whether an LLM builds a shared internal deontic-force representation, whether the force it commits to is language-modulated, or its mechanism. My prior crosslingual_evidentiality proposal concerns information SOURCE (witnessed/inferred/hearsay), crosslingual_illocutionary_force concerns speech-act TYPE (assert/ask/command), crosslingual_moral_valence concerns normative right/wrong of an action, and crosslingual_hedging concerns qualifiers wrapping a factual answer. NONE address DEONTIC FORCE—the strength of an obligation/permission a rule imposes—its decomposition into a shared force representation versus a language-set strength gain, or its causal steering. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never for deontic force. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of deontic-force calibration, with direct compliance/safety stakes: the SAME rule can read as mandatory or optional purely as a function of query language.
Abstract: Rules come in strengths: 'you must submit the form' is an obligation, 'you should submit it' a recommendation, 'you may submit it' a permission. Getting this deontic force right is essential for compliance, safety instructions, and policy reasoning, yet languages grammaticalize obligation very differently. As LLMs interpret and enforce rules for users worldwide, we ask whether the query language changes how strongly the model reads the same rule. We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of a rule's deontic force, but the query language causally recalibrates how strongly it commits to that force, so the SAME rule is read as a firmer obligation or a weaker suggestion across languages, tracking modal-marking typology and typological distance. We build DeonticProbe, parallel rules across languages, each with a fixed intended force (must / should / may / must-not), probed for force strength via graded-strength rating, forced-choice force selection, and downstream compliance inference, with rule content held fixed and an explicit-force control. Behaviorally we measure per-language force ratings and test whether cross-lingual force drift tracks resource level and typological distance beyond translation. We train a linear deontic-force probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the drift into a shared force representation versus a language-set strength gain—a firmer/weaker reading should coincide with a similar internal force. Via activation and path patching we localize a deontic-strength signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to shift a rule's read force (or equalize it across languages) while leaving the rule content and surface language unchanged. We reframe multilingual rule-interpretation inconsistency as a shared deontic-force representation under a steerable, language-dependent strength gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages spanning modal-marking typology (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili), coded for how force is grammaticalized (dedicated modal verbs vs obligatory mood vs particles vs periphrasis) plus URIEL distance (graded predictors).
2) DATASET (DeonticProbe): ~500 rules/instructions, each with a fixed INTENDED deontic force on an ordinal scale—PROHIBITION (must-not), STRONG OBLIGATION (must), WEAK OBLIGATION (should), PERMISSION (may). Domains: institutional/procedural rules, safety instructions, everyday norms. Probes: (A) GRADED-STRENGTH rating ('How mandatory is this? 1-7'), (B) FORCED-CHOICE force selection (must/should/may/must-not), (C) DOWNSTREAM COMPLIANCE inference (does an agent HAVE to do X? is X permitted?). Keep rule content fixed across languages; translate/native-verify, realizing force naturally per language. Include an EXPLICIT-FORCE control where the strength is stated numerically/unambiguously (language-flat) to bound the effect, and a NEUTRAL non-deontic control. Record tokenization fertility.
3) BEHAVIORAL DRIFT TEST: Per (rule, language) record the force rating/selection. KEY hypotheses: (i) cross-lingual FORCE DRIFT exists (the same rule reads as firmer/weaker across languages); (ii) drift tracks modal-marking typology, resource level, and typological distance beyond translation; (iii) the ORDINAL ordering (must-not < ... < may, or force ranking) is preserved across languages even where absolute force drifts (a shared force scale). Mixed-effects ordinal regression of force on (language, intended force, modal-typology code, tokenization fertility, resource tier via URIEL), rule as random effect; test the language main effect and confirm ordinal preservation. Compare against the EXPLICIT-FORCE control (language-flat). Report per-language force profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical rules.
4) SHARED DEONTIC-FORCE PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the rule/pre-answer position; train a linear/ordinal probe to decode the deontic FORCE (the ordinal strength) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report ordinal-accuracy/rank-correlation as evidence of a language-independent force representation, and show it DISSOCIATES from a SURFACE-MODAL-MARKER probe (force distinct from which modal word appears). Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on firm-reading and weak-reading items, test whether the internal force representation is SIMILAR across languages even where the emitted rating diverges (language modulates a GAIN, not the force).
5) GAIN-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer force representation across languages (should be similar if shared) versus the emitted force (which drifts). Define a per-language FORCE GAIN (affine shift/scale from shared representation to emitted strength); test whether cross-lingual drift is explained by a language-set gain on a similar force representation rather than a different force. Correlate per-language gain with modal-typology, resource tier, and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE DEONTIC-STRENGTH SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that reads a rule firmly and one that reads it weakly on the SAME rule, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer shifts emitted force WITHOUT changing the decoded force representation or rule content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the strength components from one language into another's run.
7) CAUSAL DEONTIC-STRENGTH STEERING (decisive): Derive a deontic-strength steering vector via difference-of-means (firm-reading runs minus weak-reading runs at matched force). Test (i) SHIFT: adding/subtracting it moves the read force up/down in a graded (dose-response) way on held-out rules; (ii) EQUALIZE: per-language gains make the same rule read at the same force across languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually and can override a language's default; (iv) it changes ONLY force strength, not the decoded force representation, the rule content, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the EXPLICIT-FORCE/NEUTRAL controls, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: cross-lingual drift closure, dose-response of read force, force-representation/content/output fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts deontic force but not unrelated or non-deontic answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: force-level breakdown (prohibition vs strong vs weak vs permission—which drift most); is English/high-resource the reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank force subspace; robustness across rating-vs-forced-choice-vs-compliance formats; whether one strength vector generalizes across rules and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched force and by showing content-invariant steering shifts force without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language force ratings and cross-lingual drift with typology/resource regression, ordinal-force preservation across languages, cross-lingual deontic-force probe transfer ordinal-accuracy/rank-correlation and its dissociation from a surface-modal-marker probe, representation-similarity vs force-drift (gain) decomposition, gain-vs-typology/resource correlation, patch-localized deontic-strength layer, cross-lingual strength transplant shift, causal steering drift closure with dose-response, force-representation/content/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Deontic force can be genuinely graded and context-dependent; we use rules with clear consensus intended force, focus on relative cross-lingual drift and ordinal preservation rather than absolute correctness, and use the explicit-force control to anchor. 2) The gain-vs-signal split could be confounded if the force representation itself differs by language; we test this directly by comparing the shared-probe force representation across languages rather than assuming, and report how much drift is representation vs gain. 3) Drift could be a mere translation effect (the translated modal genuinely carries a different force); we hold rule content fixed via native-verified parallels, dissociate the force probe from a surface-modal-marker probe, and use content-preserving steering (which shifts force without changing the modal word) to distinguish a genuine internal strength gate from lexical translation. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched force, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts force. 5) Instruction-tuned models may refuse graded ratings; we use both ratings and log-probability over force options, and report refusal rates. 6) Some models may read force uniformly across languages (no drift) or lack a coherent force representation; either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often drift occurs and whether a shared force scale exists. 7) Modal-typology coding is coarse; we treat it as a graded predictor and report sensitivity. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic lever; we report force-representation/content/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention, and use dose-response and reverse-consistency to ensure a genuine deontic-strength gate. 10) The force signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my evidentiality (information source), illocutionary-force (speech-act type), moral-valence (right/wrong of an action), and hedging (qualifiers on a factual answer) proposals is essential; here the object is DEONTIC FORCE—the strength of obligation/permission a rule imposes—and its language-set strength gate over a shared force representation, with direct compliance/safety stakes.

Name: crosslingual_cognitive_map_gating
Title: Building the Map From the Directions, in Every Language: A Shared Cognitive-Map Representation Whose Survey-Level Expression Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When a text describes a route ('walk north two blocks, turn east, the library is on your right'), a multilingual LLM integrates it into a largely language-independent internal COGNITIVE MAP—a survey-level representation of the relative positions of landmarks that supports novel spatial-relation queries never stated in the text (e.g. 'is the library north or south of the start?'). But whether that integrated map is behaviorally EXPRESSED—answering survey-knowledge queries requiring inference beyond the literal route—is gated by the query language: the SAME route yields the same internal map across languages yet is answered at only route-level (echoing stated steps) far more often in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so the model internally 'has the map' while behaviorally failing to read it. The cognitive-map signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated survey-inference failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: The distinction between route knowledge (an ordered sequence of egocentric turns) and survey knowledge (an integrated allocentric cognitive map supporting novel-inference shortcuts) is one of the most robust findings in spatial cognition (Tolman's cognitive map; Siegel & White's landmark-route-survey progression; O'Keefe & Nadel). In NLP, spatial reasoning in LLMs is studied behaviorally and mostly multimodally (VLN/BEVBert, VSR, COMFORT, SpatialEval), and text-only spatial-reasoning benchmarks test static relations, not the INTEGRATION of a route description into a survey map. My prior crosslingual_spatial_frame_of_reference proposal concerns the COORDINATE SYSTEM (egocentric/intrinsic/absolute) a model reasons in, and crosslingual_figure_ground concerns which object is figure vs ground; NEITHER addresses constructing a cognitive MAP from a route and reading novel survey relations off it, whether that map is a shared cross-lingual representation, whether its survey-level expression is language-gated, or whether the map signal is causally localizable and steerable. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS but never for an integrated spatial map. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of cognitive-map construction from text, grounded in the route-vs-survey-knowledge literature and distinct from coordinate-frame and figure-ground work.
Abstract: Following directions and building a map from them are different skills: 'go two blocks north, then east to the library' can be repeated step by step (route knowledge) or integrated into a mental map that answers a question never stated—'is the library northeast of where I started?' (survey knowledge). Constructing such a cognitive map from language is a hallmark of spatial cognition, yet whether text-only LLMs do it, whether they do so equally across languages, and how it is implemented internally are unknown. We ask whether a multilingual LLM integrates a route description into a shared, language-independent internal cognitive map, and whether that internal map is decoupled from how reliably survey-level relations are behaviorally read off it across languages. We hypothesize that models build the same map across languages internally, but the query language gates whether survey-level queries (novel inferences beyond the stated route) are answered, so the SAME route is answered at only route level far more in lower-resource, typologically distant languages—even though the model 'has the map'. We build MapProbe, parallel route descriptions across languages, each with SURVEY probes (relative bearing/distance between landmarks not stated in the text), matched ROUTE probes (facts directly stated), and a control where survey and route coincide. Behaviorally we measure per-language survey-inference accuracy and route-level collapse and test whether it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond literal comprehension. We train a linear cognitive-map probe (decoding landmark positions on an inferred coordinate grid) and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the failure into a shared map component versus a language-set expression gate, verifying the correct map is internally present even where survey answering collapses. Via activation and path patching we localize a cognitive-map signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to surface survey-level answers while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual spatial-reasoning gaps as a steerable gate over a shared cognitive-map representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Swahili). MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (MapProbe): ~500 procedurally-generated route descriptions on a grid, each visiting 3-6 landmarks via a sequence of egocentric moves (directions + distances/turns), with a KNOWN ground-truth allocentric layout. Item types: (A) SURVEY probes requiring novel inference not stated in the text ('Which landmark is furthest north?', 'Is A northeast of B?', 'What is the straight-line direction from start to the last landmark?'); (B) matched ROUTE probes answerable by echoing stated steps ('Which way did you turn after the park?'); (C) a SURVEY=ROUTE control where the survey answer coincides with a stated step (bounds the effect and separates survey inference from comprehension). Vary route complexity (number of landmarks/turns) as a load factor. Keep the layout and route fixed across languages; translate/native-verify directional/spatial terms; record tokenization fertility; screen literal comprehension via ROUTE probes so survey failure is not reading failure. Short scoreable answers.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (route, language) record SURVEY-inference accuracy vs ROUTE-LEVEL COLLAPSE (giving a route-echo answer where a survey inference is required). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME route, survey accuracy is systematically lower (route collapse higher) in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond literal comprehension and tokenization; the gap grows with route complexity. Mixed-effects logistic regression of survey error on (language, route complexity, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, ROUTE-probe comprehension indicator), route as random effect; compare against ROUTE probes (should be language-flatter) and the SURVEY=ROUTE control. Report per-language survey-vs-route profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical routes; replicate an English survey>route baseline.
4) SHARED COGNITIVE-MAP PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer, at the post-route / pre-answer position, train a linear probe to decode each landmark's inferred allocentric POSITION (coordinates on the grid, or pairwise relative bearings) on ENGLISH data; apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report position-decoding accuracy/AUROC as evidence of a language-independent integrated map. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the map representation for the same route. CRITICAL: on ROUTE-COLLAPSE (survey-failed) items, test whether the correct landmark layout is still internally decodable across ALL languages even when the emitted answer is route-level—the signature of language-gated expression over an intact map.
5) MAP-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer map signal across languages (should be similar if map-building is shared) versus behavioral survey accuracy (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping the internal map to surfaced survey answering per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar map signal rather than weaker map-building. Correlate gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes.
6) LOCALIZE THE COGNITIVE-MAP SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that answers survey queries correctly and one that collapses to route on the SAME route, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer surfaces the correct survey answer WITHOUT changing the decoded route facts. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the map representation FROM a high-expression language into a collapsing run.
7) CAUSAL COGNITIVE-MAP STEERING (decisive): Derive a map-expression steering vector via difference-of-means (survey-answered runs minus route-collapse runs at matched internal map). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to collapse-prone languages increases correct survey-inference toward high-expression levels; (ii) NULL ON MAP FAILURES: it does NOT help routes where the layout was never internally built (validating a map-building vs expression-gate decomposition), where those exist; (iii) SUPPRESS: subtracting it makes high-expression languages collapse to route; (iv) it changes ONLY survey-level answering, not the decoded route facts or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the SURVEY=ROUTE control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: survey-accuracy-gap closure, per-mode recovery (expression-gate vs map-building), suppression-induction rate (reverse), map-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes survey answers but not route-probe or unrelated answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: probe-type breakdown (bearing vs distance vs furthest-landmark); route-complexity x language interaction; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the collapse?); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single map vector generalizes across routes and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal map and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces survey answers without changing tokenization; frame-of-reference control (does the model's map use a consistent allocentric frame across languages?).
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language survey-inference and route-collapse rates and accuracy-vs-complexity curves, expression regression controlling for comprehension/fertility/resource, English survey>route replication, cross-lingual cognitive-map probe transfer accuracy/AUROC and map-present-under-collapse, cross-lingual map-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), map-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized cognitive-map layer, cross-lingual map transplant recovery rate (and null on map-building failures), causal steering survey-gap closure and suppression-induction rates, map-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The map-vs-expression split could be confounded if the map signal itself differs by language (the model genuinely fails to integrate the route in some languages); we test this directly by verifying landmark-position decodability across all languages on collapse items via probe transfer, and report the split (map-building vs gate)—either outcome is informative, and the causal null-on-map-building-failures test confirms the decomposition. 2) Survey failure could reflect literal route-comprehension failure rather than an expression gate; we use matched ROUTE probes and comprehension screening so residual survey collapse reflects map-reading, not reading. 3) Some survey inferences depend on the assumed frame of reference (egocentric vs allocentric); we generate routes with an unambiguous allocentric ground truth, include a frame-of-reference control, and restrict scored items to frame-independent survey relations where possible. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy (directional terms and multi-step routes fragment differently); we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal map, and content-invariant steering surfaces survey answers without changing tokenization. 5) Some models may build and read the map uniformly across languages (no gap) or fail to build it everywhere (pure map-building failure); either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual cognitive-map construction, and we quantify how often each regime occurs. 6) Procedurally-generated routes may be unnatural; we native-verify directional phrasing, vary templates, and validate that findings persist on a held-out set of naturalistic human-written directions. 7) The map probe could latch onto surface directional tokens rather than a genuine integrated layout; the requirement that survey probes need NOVEL inference not stated in the text, the map-present-under-collapse test, cross-lingual invariance, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report map-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention, and use the null-on-map-building-failures, suppression (reverse), and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine map-expression gate. 10) The gate/map signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my spatial-frame-of-reference (coordinate system) and figure-ground (object roles) proposals is essential; here the object is the INTEGRATION of a route description into an allocentric COGNITIVE MAP and the reading of novel survey-level relations off it, grounded in the route-vs-survey-knowledge literature.

Name: pre_commitment_rationalization_signal
Title: Decided Before Thinking: A Pre-Reasoning Answer-Commitment Signal That Determines Whether Chain-of-Thought Derives or Rationalizes the Answer
Short Hypothesis: Before generating any chain-of-thought (CoT), an LLM often computes an internal 'answer-commitment' signal that already encodes its final answer; the STRENGTH of this pre-CoT commitment causally determines whether the ensuing reasoning is DERIVATIONAL (the CoT drives the answer) or RATIONALIZING (the CoT is a post-hoc justification of a pre-decided answer). This commitment signal is linearly decodable at the pre-reasoning position, predicts the final answer above chance before a single reasoning token is produced, its magnitude predicts per-item CoT unfaithfulness, and it can be causally steered to convert rationalizing traces into derivational ones (making the CoT load-bearing) and vice versa.
Related Work: Kumaran (2026) shows verbalized confidence tracks COMMITMENT more than correctness and that a post-answer state encodes a future abstention decision, but studies confidence/abstention, not whether a PRE-CoT commitment predicts the answer or governs CoT faithfulness. Gottesman & Geva (2024, KEEN) estimate knowledge from internal subject representations before generation, but predict knowledge/factuality, not a committed ANSWER or its effect on reasoning. Lee et al. (2026, 'Answer-Conditioned CoT') and Zelikman et al. (STaR) show answer-conditioned chains rationalize backward and degrade reasoning behaviorally, with an 'early final-answer statement' symptom, but offer no internal pre-CoT commitment representation, no per-item faithfulness prediction, and no causal steering. CoT-faithfulness work (Lanham 2023; Turpin 2023) measures whether English CoT reflects the true reason via perturbation, but never decodes a pre-reasoning commitment or ties its magnitude to a derive-vs-rationalize dichotomy. My prior answer_length_budget and crosslingual_cot_faithfulness proposals concern length pre-commitment and cross-lingual trace-answer coupling respectively; NEITHER decodes a pre-CoT ANSWER-commitment signal, decomposes CoT into derivational vs rationalizing based on its magnitude, or causally steers commitment to flip faithfulness. This is the first mechanistic, causal account of pre-reasoning answer commitment as the driver of rationalization.
Abstract: Chain-of-thought is trusted because it appears to show the work behind an answer, and it is increasingly used to audit models. But is the reasoning load-bearing, or has the model already decided and the reasoning merely rationalizes that decision? We hypothesize that before generating any reasoning, an LLM often computes an internal answer-commitment signal that already encodes its final answer, and that the strength of this pre-CoT commitment causally governs whether the subsequent reasoning derives the answer or post-hoc justifies a pre-decided one. First, we train a linear probe at the pre-reasoning position (immediately before any CoT token) and show it predicts the model's eventual final answer well above chance, evidencing pre-reasoning commitment. Second, we show this commitment's MAGNITUDE predicts per-item CoT unfaithfulness: on high-commitment items, perturbing or corrupting the reasoning barely moves the answer (rationalizing), whereas on low-commitment items the answer tracks the reasoning (derivational). Third, in a decisive causal test, we derive a difference-of-means commitment steering vector and show that suppressing pre-CoT commitment makes the reasoning causally load-bearing (the answer follows corrupted steps, faithfulness rises) while amplifying it forces rationalization (the answer ignores the reasoning), with dose-response and specificity. We localize the commitment signal via activation and path patching. Across factual, commonsense, and multi-step reasoning benchmarks and several open models, we reframe unfaithful chain-of-thought as a steerable consequence of pre-reasoning answer commitment, with direct implications for the trustworthiness of reasoning-based oversight.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & DATA: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Qwen3-14B (native thinking mode), Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). Datasets with verifiable answers: multiple-choice factual/commonsense (MMLU, CommonsenseQA, ARC), multi-step math (GSM8K), and multi-hop factual reasoning, all elicited with a CoT prompt so a pre-reasoning position (just after the question, before the first CoT token) is well-defined.
2) PRE-COT COMMITMENT PROBE: At the pre-reasoning position (before any CoT token), pool hidden states per layer and train a linear probe to predict the model's EVENTUAL final answer (the answer it will give after full CoT). KEY test: does the probe predict the final answer above chance BEFORE any reasoning is produced? Report per-layer accuracy, earliest layer where commitment is decodable, and calibration. Baselines: predicting from the prompt/question-difficulty features only (the probe must beat this), and a control probe predicting a random label. Cross-check with logit-lens: does an early representation already rank the eventual answer highly? Define a continuous COMMITMENT MAGNITUDE = probe margin / confidence that the eventual answer is committed at the pre-reasoning position.
3) COMMITMENT-PREDICTS-UNFAITHFULNESS (core dissociation): Apply established CoT-faithfulness perturbations per item: (a) STEP-CORRUPTION (inject an error into an intermediate reasoning step and measure whether the final answer follows the corrupted step), (b) EARLY-ANSWERING (truncate CoT at successive fractions and force an answer; a derivational trace should build toward the answer), (c) BIASING-STEP (prepend a plausible-but-wrong step). Define per-item FAITHFULNESS = how much the answer tracks the reasoning content. KEY hypothesis: pre-CoT commitment MAGNITUDE negatively predicts faithfulness—high-commitment items are rationalizing (answer ignores corrupted/truncated reasoning), low-commitment items are derivational. Mixed-effects regression of faithfulness on (commitment magnitude, item difficulty, model), item as random effect; condition on correct-answer items to dissociate from accuracy. Replicate the STaR/Lee et al. 'early final-answer statement' symptom and correlate it with commitment magnitude.
4) LOCALIZE THE COMMITMENT SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a high-commitment run and a low-commitment run on matched items, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer changes how much the final answer depends on the reasoning. Report layer distribution; cross-check activation vs path patching. Test whether patching the pre-CoT commitment representation forward changes downstream trace-answer coupling.
5) CAUSAL COMMITMENT STEERING (decisive): Derive a commitment steering vector via difference-of-means (high-commitment pre-CoT states minus low-commitment states). Test (i) SUPPRESS: subtracting it before reasoning makes the answer FOLLOW corrupted/truncated reasoning (faithfulness rises; re-run step-corruption and show the answer now tracks the trace, even into error) and shifts the internal commitment later; (ii) AMPLIFY: adding it forces rationalization (answer ignores the reasoning); (iii) DOSE-RESPONSE and specificity (a random/matched-control vector does nothing; general QA and output fluency preserved); (iv) verify the commitment probe reads lower/higher after suppression/amplification (mediation). Metrics: faithfulness change (step-corruption-following rate), commitment-magnitude shift, accuracy retention, general-QA (held-out) retention, output fidelity. Reverse-consistency: steering changes how much the trace matters, not unrelated answers.
6) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: task-type breakdown (factual/commonsense vs multi-step math—does math show more genuine derivation?); native thinking mode (Qwen3) vs prompted CoT; model scale (does larger scale increase pre-commitment/rationalization?); base vs instruction/RL-tuned models; probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank commitment subspace; whether commitment magnitude predicts which items are 'answer-conditioned-degradable' (link to Lee et al. distillation harm); robustness across templates.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: pre-CoT commitment probe accuracy and incremental predictive power over prompt-only baseline, earliest commitment layer, commitment-magnitude vs per-item faithfulness correlation (controlling for difficulty/accuracy), early-final-answer-symptom correlation, patch-localized commitment layer, causal steering faithfulness change with dose-response (suppress raises faithfulness including following corrupted steps; amplify forces rationalization), commitment-magnitude mediation under steering, accuracy/general-QA/output-fidelity retention, task/scale/tuning-stage breakdowns.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Pre-CoT commitment decodability could reflect the prompt/difficulty rather than a genuine internal answer commitment; we control by requiring the probe to beat a prompt-only baseline and by dissociating commitment from accuracy (conditioning on correct items) and from difficulty in regression. 2) Faithfulness metrics are indirect proxies; we use three complementary perturbations (step-corruption, early-answering, biasing-step) and require convergence, treating agreement as evidence rather than any single metric. 3) The commitment-vs-faithfulness link could be confounded by item difficulty (easy items are both high-commitment and answer-insensitive); we control for difficulty and, crucially, the causal steering (which changes commitment while holding the item fixed) dissociates commitment from difficulty. 4) The steering could act as a generic accuracy/format lever rather than a commitment dial; the decisive guard is that SUPPRESSING commitment should make the model follow CORRUPTED (wrong) reasoning into error—a genuine faithfulness increase—while amplification makes it ignore even correct-but-perturbed reasoning; we report these plus reverse-consistency and specificity (matched-control vector). 5) Some models/tasks may show little pre-commitment (reasoning is genuinely load-bearing)—this is itself an informative, publishable finding about when CoT is trustworthy, and we quantify how often pre-commitment occurs rather than assuming it. 6) Logit-lens/probe estimates are noisy for multi-token answers; we prefer short/decodable answers (multiple-choice, single-number) and validate probe reliability. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test multiple models (including a native-thinking model) and templates and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) The commitment signal may be low-rank or entangled with a confidence signal; we test low-rank variants and check whether commitment dissociates from a KEEN-style knowledge/confidence probe (Kumaran 2026 shows commitment and correctness lie in near-orthogonal directions, supporting separability). 9) Safety framing: the amplification direction could make traces more deceptive; we use it strictly as an interpretability probe to demonstrate causality, and the applied contribution is the suppression direction that makes reasoning load-bearing and the commitment-magnitude signal as a per-item rationalization detector for reasoning-based oversight.

Name: crosslingual_categorical_perception_warping
Title: Goluboy vs Siniy in the Weights: Do Lexical Color Boundaries Warp a Multilingual Model's Representational Geometry, and Is the Warp Causally Set by the Category?
Short Hypothesis: A multilingual LLM's internal representation of a continuous perceptual-semantic dimension (color) is WARPED by the lexical category boundaries of the query language: pairs of colors straddling a language's category boundary are held farther apart in representation (and judged more different) than equidistant within-category pairs, reproducing the human categorical-perception effect (e.g. Russian's obligatory light-blue 'goluboy' vs dark-blue 'siniy' boundary vs English's single 'blue'), and this warp is language-dependent, larger where the query language lexicalizes the boundary. The warp is causally driven by a localizable 'category-boundary' representation: it appears/disappears when queried in a boundary-lexicalizing vs non-lexicalizing language, and can be steered to install or erase the categorical warp without changing the surface colors.
Related Work: Winawer et al. (2007, PNAS) established the canonical Whorfian categorical-perception effect: Russian speakers discriminate cross-boundary blues (goluboy/siniy) faster than within-category blues, an advantage absent in English speakers and abolished under verbal interference; categorical perception at lexical color boundaries is one of the most robust findings in the language-and-thought literature (Regier & Kay; Thierry et al. on lexical influence on early perception).
