In NLP, color-term representation is probed monolingually (embeddings encode color similarity) and a recent unpublished student project touches cross-lingual grounded structures, but no work tests whether LEXICAL CATEGORY BOUNDARIES warp a multilingual model's REPRESENTATIONAL GEOMETRY of a continuous dimension (expanded between-category / compressed within-category distances), whether this warp is language-dependent (present when queried in a boundary-lexicalizing language, absent otherwise), or whether it is causally localizable and steerable. My prior colexification proposal concerns two DISTINCT concepts fused into one word (discrete sense conflation); this is distinct because the object is a CONTINUOUS perceptual dimension and the categorical WARPING of its geometry by a lexical boundary—a different phenomenon (Whorfian categorical perception) with a decisive human benchmark and minimal-pair design. My comparison-class (gradable-adjective threshold), vague-quantifier, and individuation proposals concern thresholds/counting, not categorical warping of a perceptual continuum. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies categorical-perception warping. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual transfer of the Winawer categorical-perception effect into LLMs.
Abstract: One of the strongest claims that language shapes thought is categorical perception: Russian, which obligatorily splits blue into light 'goluboy' and dark 'siniy', makes speakers see two colors straddling that boundary as more different than two equidistant colors within a category—an effect English speakers lack. We ask whether a multilingual language model, which never sees color, nonetheless warps its internal geometry of the color continuum along the lexical boundaries of the query language, reproducing this Whorfian effect. We hypothesize that (1) for the SAME pair of colors, the model represents and judges a CROSS-BOUNDARY pair as more different than an equidistant WITHIN-CATEGORY pair, but only when queried in a language that lexicalizes the boundary (Russian, Greek's two-blues, Turkish blue/green splits), and not in a language with a single term (English 'blue'); (2) this warp is a measurable expansion of between-category and compression of within-category representational distances at the color positions, larger where the boundary is lexicalized and scaling with the language's category structure; and (3) the warp is causally set by a localizable category-boundary representation—steering it into an English run installs the Russian-style categorical warp, and steering it out of a Russian run erases it, without changing the described colors. Using color-difference judgments and hidden-state geometry across languages with contrasting color lexicons, minimal-pair cross-boundary vs within-category color triples calibrated in a perceptual space, and activation/path patching, we transfer the categorical-perception effect into a model, decompose it into a shared color representation versus a language-imposed categorical warp, and causally install and remove it.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: Languages with contrasting color-category structure: boundary-lexicalizing (Russian [goluboy/siniy], Greek [ghalazio/ble], Turkish [blue/green splits], Korean) vs single-term (English, Spanish, German) for the target boundary; coded per boundary from color-naming references (World Color Survey; Winawer) plus URIEL. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (ColorWarpProbe): ~500 color triples defined by hex/RGB and calibrated distances in a perceptual space (CIELAB dE), each with an anchor color and two comparison colors EQUIDISTANT from it in perceptual space, one CROSS-BOUNDARY (straddling the target lexical boundary, e.g. light-blue vs dark-blue) and one WITHIN-CATEGORY (same side). Probes: (A) DIFFERENCE JUDGMENT ('How different are these two colors? 1-7' / forced-choice 'which pair is more different?'), (B) SAME-DIFFERENT / oddity, (C) representational readout (hidden states at the color tokens). Present colors as names+values (native color terms where they exist; hex values held identical across languages so surface perceptual input is fixed). Include control boundaries lexicalized in ALL languages (e.g. red/green, a clear category cut everywhere) to bound the effect and a VERBAL-INTERFERENCE analog (a concurrent verbal-load prompt) mirroring Winawer's abolition test. Native-verify color terms; record tokenization fertility.
3) BEHAVIORAL CATEGORICAL-PERCEPTION TEST: Per (triple, language) compute CATEGORICAL ADVANTAGE = (judged/decoded difference for the cross-boundary pair) minus (for the equidistant within-category pair). KEY hypothesis: the categorical advantage is POSITIVE and LARGER in boundary-lexicalizing languages than single-term languages on the SAME triples, replicating Winawer's Russian>English pattern; it is reduced/abolished under the verbal-interference analog; and control boundaries lexicalized everywhere show a language-flat advantage. Mixed-effects regression of categorical advantage on (boundary-lexicalization status, language, perceptual distance held constant, tokenization fertility, resource tier via URIEL), triple as random effect; test the lexicalization x language interaction.
4) SHARED COLOR-GEOMETRY & WARP PROBE: At each layer pool hidden states at the color tokens; measure the representational distance between the two colors of each pair (cosine/Mahalanobis). Test whether, for the SAME physical pair, between-category representational distance is EXPANDED and within-category COMPRESSED in boundary-lexicalizing-language runs relative to single-term runs—the geometric signature of categorical perception. Train a linear probe to decode the color's CATEGORY (which side of the boundary) and test whether category-decodability is high only in lexicalizing languages. Correlate per-triple representational warp with the behavioral categorical advantage (link test). Decompose: is the underlying color-position representation SHARED across languages (a language-independent color line) with the warp applied on top (a language-imposed categorical boundary)? Measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine of the color-line geometry and whether the warp is an added language-specific component.
5) LOCALIZE THE CATEGORY-BOUNDARY SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a lexicalizing-language run (warped) and a single-term-language run (unwarped) on the SAME color pair, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer installs/removes the categorical warp (expanded cross-boundary distance / category-decodability) WITHOUT changing the decoded color values. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band (per-layer language-ID probes); cross-check activation vs path patching.
6) CAUSAL WARP STEERING (decisive): Derive a category-boundary steering vector via difference-of-means (lexicalizing-language color states minus single-term-language states, or cross-boundary vs within-category contrasts). Test (i) INSTALL: adding it in an ENGLISH (single-term) run installs a Russian-style categorical warp—cross-boundary pairs judged/decoded as more different than equidistant within-category pairs—on held-out triples; (ii) ERASE: subtracting it in a Russian run removes the categorical advantage (colors judged by perceptual distance alone); (iii) DOSE-RESPONSE and cross-boundary generality; (iv) it changes ONLY the categorical warp, not the decoded color values/hex or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the all-languages-lexicalized control boundary, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: warp install/erase rate (behavioral + representational), dose-response, color-value/output fidelity, control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts near-boundary color-difference judgments but not far-apart or unrelated judgments.
7) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: boundary breakdown (blue-blue vs blue-green vs green-green across languages); does the warp track the language's number of basic color terms / World-Color-Survey category structure?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training install multiple languages' warps simultaneously?); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank warp subspace; robustness across name-based vs hex-based color presentation; whether a single warp vector generalizes across boundaries; comparison of the model categorical-advantage magnitude to the human Winawer effect.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language categorical advantage (cross-boundary minus within-category difference) and its lexicalization-x-language interaction controlling for perceptual distance/fertility, Winawer Russian>English replication and verbal-interference abolition, representational warp (between-category expansion / within-category compression) and category-decodability by language, warp-vs-behavior correlation, shared color-line vs language-imposed warp decomposition (cross-lingual CKA), patch-localized category-boundary layer, causal steering warp-install and warp-erase rates with dose-response, color-value/output fidelity, control-boundary and general-QA retention, model-vs-human effect-size comparison.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Text-only models never see color, so any categorical warp is recovered from distributional co-occurrence of color terms/values; a null (no warp, or warp only from surface term identity) is itself an informative, publishable finding about whether Whorfian categorical perception emerges in a text model, and we quantify how often the warp is present. 2) The effect could be a trivial surface artifact of the language having two color WORDS (the boundary is lexically obvious from the prompt) rather than a genuine representational warp; we mitigate by (a) presenting IDENTICAL hex values across languages so physical input is fixed, (b) a critical control that PRIMES the color category in a lexicalizing language but ELICITS the difference judgment with hex-only (no color words), and (c) the representational-warp-predicts-behavior link, testing warping beyond surface term presence. 3) Perceptual-distance calibration (CIELAB dE) is an imperfect proxy for how the MODEL scales color; we calibrate triples in CIELAB, verify equidistance also under the model's own decoded color-line where possible, and report sensitivity. 4) The shared-line-vs-warp decomposition could be confounded if the underlying color representation itself differs by language; we test this directly via cross-lingual CKA of the color-line geometry rather than assuming, and report how much of the effect is a shared line plus an added warp vs a genuinely different geometry. 5) Tokenization fertility confounds (color terms/hex split differently); we control for it, and content-invariant steering (which does not change the presented colors) installs/erases the warp without changing tokenization, dissociating the warp from surface factors. 6) Some models may install multiple languages' warps at once or none; either is informative, and Aya vs Llama contrasts this. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic difference-inflation lever; we report color-value/output fidelity, control-boundary and general-QA retention, and use erase (reverse), dose-response, and reverse-consistency (near-boundary-only effect) tests to ensure a genuine categorical-boundary warp rather than a global difference knob. 9) The warp signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my colexification (two discrete concepts fused in one word), comparison-class (gradable-adjective thresholds), and individuation (count/mass) proposals is essential; here the object is the categorical WARPING of a CONTINUOUS perceptual dimension's representational geometry by a lexical category boundary—Whorfian categorical perception—with a decisive human benchmark (Winawer et al. 2007) and a minimal-pair, causally-steerable design.

Name: crosslingual_information_structure_gating
Title: What's Given, What's New, in Every Language? A Shared Information-Structure Representation Whose Focus/Given Expression Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: A multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of a sentence's INFORMATION STRUCTURE—which element is the discourse-new FOCUS and which is GIVEN/backgrounded—but whether that structure is behaviorally EXPRESSED (resolving focus-sensitive operators like 'only'/'even', answering what-is-new questions, choosing the felicitous continuation, tracking contrastive focus) is gated by the query language: the SAME sentence is assigned the same focus/given partition internally across languages yet processed with the wrong focus far more often in lower-resource / typologically distant languages—especially those whose focus-marking typology (word order, cleft, prosody-substituting particles) differs from the model's dominant languages—so the model internally 'knows what is new' while behaviorally mis-partitioning. The information-structure signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated focus failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Information structure—the partition of a sentence into focus (discourse-new, contrastively highlighted) versus given/topic (backgrounded)—is a core topic in linguistics (Halliday; Rooth's alternative semantics of focus; Krifka; Büring), and languages mark it very differently (English via prosody/it-clefts, Hungarian/Turkish via a dedicated preverbal focus position, Japanese/Korean via particles wa/ga, many via word order). Focus is truth-conditionally consequential through focus-sensitive operators ('only [JOHN] left' vs 'only John [LEFT]'). In NLP, information structure / focus is studied as a supervised annotation task (question-under-discussion, focus detection) and is overwhelmingly monolingual/English and behavioral; no work studies whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared internal focus/given representation, whether its behavioral expression is language-gated, or its mechanism. My prior crosslingual_discourse_relation proposal concerns the RELATION LABEL (cause/contrast) linking two CLAUSES; crosslingual_bridging concerns linking a new ENTITY to an implicit scene anchor; crosslingual_illocutionary_force concerns speech-act TYPE; crosslingual_presupposition concerns accepting backgrounded PRESUPPOSED content. NONE address the FOCUS/GIVEN partition WITHIN a sentence (which element is discourse-new and contrastively highlighted), which is a distinct information-structural object with a decisive truth-conditional test via focus-sensitive operators, its own cross-linguistic marking typology, and its own detection-vs-expression decomposition. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never for information structure. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of focus/given representation.
Abstract: Every sentence divides into what is already known and what is newly asserted—its information structure—and this focus/given partition is not decorative: 'only JOHN passed' and 'John only PASSED' mean different things depending on which element carries focus. Languages mark focus very differently—English by prosody and clefts, Hungarian and Turkish by a dedicated preverbal position, Japanese and Korean by particles—so recovering the intended partition demands language-specific cues over a shared communicative function. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal representation of which element is focus and which is given, and whether that internal partition is decoupled from how reliably it is behaviorally expressed across languages. We hypothesize that models compute the same focus/given partition across languages internally, but the query language gates whether it is surfaced—resolving focus-sensitive operators, answering what-is-new questions, choosing felicitous continuations—so the SAME sentence is mis-partitioned far more in lower-resource, typologically distant languages, even though the model 'knows what is new'. We build FocusProbe, parallel sentences across languages in which context fixes the focus, each with a focus-sensitive-operator truth-value probe, a what-is-new question probe, and a contrastive-continuation felicity probe, plus a control where focus is unambiguous. Behaviorally we measure per-language focus-resolution accuracy and focus-drift and test whether it tracks resource level, typological distance, and focus-marking typology beyond comprehension. We train a linear focus/given probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer—including across languages with different focus-marking devices—then decompose the failure into a shared partition component versus a language-set expression gate, verifying the correct focus is internally present even where behavior drifts. Via activation and path patching we localize a focus signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to surface (or shift) the focus while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual pragmatic-comprehension gaps as a steerable gate over a shared information-structure representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages spanning focus-marking typology (English, German [prosody/clefts], Russian [word order], Hindi, Arabic, Chinese, Japanese/Korean-style [focus particles], Turkish/Hungarian-style [dedicated focus position]), coded for focus-marking device and richness from typological references (Rooth; Büring; WALS-related sources) plus URIEL distance. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (FocusProbe): ~500 sentences, each embedded in a CONTEXT (a preceding question-under-discussion or contrast) that FIXES which element is focus (discourse-new/contrastive) vs given. Item types: (A) FOCUS-SENSITIVE OPERATOR truth-value: sentences with 'only'/'even'/'also' where the truth conditions depend on which element is focused ('John only introduced BILL to Sue' vs 'John only introduced Bill to SUE'), with a truth-value or entailment probe whose correct answer requires the context-fixed focus; (B) WHAT-IS-NEW question ('Given the context, what is the newly asserted/highlighted information in this sentence?'); (C) CONTRASTIVE-CONTINUATION felicity (which continuation is coherent given the focus, e.g., '...not MARY' is felicitous only under subject focus). Include a matched FOCUS-UNAMBIGUOUS control (only one partition is possible; bounds the effect and separates focus resolution from comprehension) and a NEUTRAL filler. Keep sentence content and context-fixed focus fixed across languages; translate/native-verify, realizing focus naturally per language (word order, cleft, particle); flag constructions with no natural equivalent. Record tokenization fertility; screen literal comprehension via the unambiguous control. Short scoreable answers.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (item, language) record correct focus-based resolution vs FOCUS-DRIFT (defaulting to a canonical/subject focus or the model's dominant-language-typical partition). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME context-fixed focus, focus-drift is systematically higher in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, and worst where the language's focus-marking device differs most from the dominant languages, beyond comprehension and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of focus-drift on (focus-marking typology, language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, item type, comprehension indicator), item as random effect; compare against the unambiguous control (language-flatter). Report per-language and per-item-type profiles, cross-lingual disagreement on identical sentences, and replicate an English focus-sensitivity baseline.
4) SHARED FOCUS/GIVEN PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the focused-element / pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode WHICH element is FOCUS vs GIVEN on ENGLISH data, apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent information-structure representation. CRITICAL: test transfer ACROSS languages with DIFFERENT focus-marking devices (e.g., train on English prosody/cleft focus, test on Japanese-particle or Turkish-position focus)—high transfer despite different surface marking evidences a shared partition beneath language-specific cues. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. On FOCUS-DRIFT items, test whether the correct focus is still internally decodable across ALL languages even when behavior drifts—the signature of language-gated expression over an intact partition.
5) PARTITION-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer focus signal across languages (should be similar if the partition is shared) versus behavioral focus resolution (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal partition to surfaced behavior per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar partition signal. Correlate gate strength with focus-marking typology, resource tier, and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes.
6) LOCALIZE THE FOCUS SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that surfaces the correct focus and one that drifts on the SAME sentence, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer surfaces the correct focus WITHOUT changing the decoded propositional content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the focus representation FROM a high-expression language into a drifting run. Attention analysis: does the focus-sensitive operator attend to the context-fixed focused element, more so in high-expression languages?
7) CAUSAL FOCUS STEERING (decisive): Derive a focus steering vector via difference-of-means (correct-focus runs minus drifted runs, plus focus-position contrasts, e.g., subject-focus vs object-focus). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to drift-prone languages increases correct focus-based resolution toward high-expression levels; (ii) SHIFT: steering along the focus axis makes the model treat a different element as focus (subject-focus -> object-focus), flipping the truth value of a focus-sensitive-operator sentence on well-handled items; (iii) it works cross-lingually, stronger where expression was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY the focus partition, not the decoded propositional content or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the unambiguous control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: focus-drift-gap closure, focus-shift-flip rate (reverse), focus-signal/content/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes focus judgments but not unambiguous-control or unrelated answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: item-type breakdown (operator vs what-is-new vs continuation); focus-marking-device breakdown (prosody/cleft vs particle vs position); does the shared focus signal transfer across differently-marking languages?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the drift?); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single focus vector generalizes across constructions and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal partition and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces focus without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language per-item-type focus-resolution accuracy and focus-drift rate, drift regression controlling for comprehension/fertility/resource with focus-marking-typology effect, English focus-sensitivity replication, cross-lingual focus/given probe transfer AUROC (including across differently-marking languages) and focus-present-under-drift, cross-lingual partition-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), partition-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-typology/resource correlation, patch-localized focus layer and operator-to-focus attention evidence, cross-lingual focus transplant recovery rate, causal steering drift-gap closure and focus-shift-flip rates, focus-signal/content/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The partition-vs-expression split could be confounded if the focus signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying correct-focus decodability across all languages (especially differently-marking ones) on drift items via probe transfer, and report how much of the gap is partition vs gate. 2) Focus-drift could reflect comprehension failure rather than an expression gate; we use the matched FOCUS-UNAMBIGUOUS control and comprehension screening so residual drift reflects focus resolution, not reading. 3) Focus can be genuinely ambiguous without prosody (text lacks the intonation English uses to mark focus); we FIX focus via explicit context (question-under-discussion / contrast) and restrict scored items to clear context-determined focus, analyzing ambiguous ones separately—this also makes the cross-lingual design fair since all languages rely on textual cues. 4) Realizing focus naturally and equivalently across languages is delicate (word order, cleft, particle, dedicated position differ); we native-verify, treat focus-marking device as a factor, and flag constructions with no natural equivalent (using them for transfer-limit analysis). 5) The transfer-across-differently-marking-languages test is the key novelty but could fail if focus is only represented via each language's surface device (an equally informative result about whether the partition is genuinely shared vs marking-specific); we report it either way. 6) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal partition, and content-invariant steering surfaces focus without changing tokenization. 7) Some models may resolve focus uniformly across languages (no gap) or drift everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual information structure, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 8) The focus probe could latch onto surface cues (cleft words, particles) rather than a genuine partition representation; the transfer across differently-marking languages, the focus-present-under-drift test, the operator-to-focus attention analysis, cross-lingual invariance, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 9) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 10) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report focus-signal/content/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention, and use the focus-shift (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine focus gate. 11) The gate/focus signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 12) Distinguishing from my discourse-relation (inter-clausal relation label), bridging (entity-to-scene link), illocutionary-force (speech-act type), and presupposition (backgrounded presupposed content) proposals is essential; here the object is the FOCUS/GIVEN partition WITHIN a sentence (which element is discourse-new and contrastively highlighted), a distinct information-structural object with a decisive truth-conditional test via focus-sensitive operators and its own cross-linguistic marking typology.

Short Hypothesis: A multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of a sentence's INFORMATION STRUCTURE—which element is discourse-new FOCUS and which is GIVEN—but whether that partition is behaviorally EXPRESSED (resolving focus-sensitive operators like 'only'/'even', answering what-is-new questions, choosing felicitous continuations) is gated by the query language: the SAME sentence is assigned the same focus/given partition internally across languages yet processed with the wrong focus far more often in lower-resource / typologically distant languages—especially those whose focus-marking typology (word order, cleft, particles) differs from the model's dominant languages. The information-structure signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated focus failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Information structure—the focus (discourse-new, contrastively highlighted) vs given/topic partition—is core to linguistics (Rooth's alternative semantics; Krifka; Büring) and is truth-conditionally consequential via focus-sensitive operators ('only [JOHN] left' vs 'only John [LEFT]'). Languages mark it very differently (English prosody/clefts, Hungarian/Turkish preverbal focus position, Japanese/Korean particles). In NLP, focus/information structure is a supervised annotation task, monolingual and behavioral. Recent multilingual-geometry work is correlational and about other objects: Civelli et al. (2026) show a shared-then-language-specific geometry of problem DIFFICULTY; Freenor & Alvarez (RISE, 2025) show negation/conditionality map to consistent geometric rotations; Mathewson (2026) probes NLLB conceptual geometry. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for FACTS. My prior proposals cover discourse RELATION labels (cause/contrast) between clauses, BRIDGING (entity-to-scene links), ILLOCUTIONARY FORCE (speech-act type), and PRESUPPOSITION accommodation. NONE address the FOCUS/GIVEN partition WITHIN a sentence, whether a shared cross-lingual focus representation exists, whether its behavioral expression is language-gated (a shared-signal-plus-gate decomposition), whether it transfers across languages with different focus-marking devices, or whether the focus signal is causally localizable and steerable via focus-sensitive-operator truth values. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of information-structure representation.
Abstract: Every sentence divides into what is already known and what is newly asserted—its information structure—and this focus/given partition is not decorative: 'only JOHN passed' and 'John only PASSED' mean different things depending on which element carries focus. Languages mark focus very differently, so recovering the intended partition demands language-specific cues over a shared communicative function. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal representation of which element is focus and which is given, and whether that internal partition is decoupled from how reliably it is behaviorally expressed across languages. We hypothesize that models compute the same partition across languages internally, but the query language gates whether it is surfaced—resolving focus-sensitive operators, answering what-is-new questions, choosing felicitous continuations—so the SAME sentence is mis-partitioned far more in lower-resource, typologically distant languages, even though the model 'knows what is new'. We build FocusProbe, parallel context-plus-sentence items across languages in which context fixes the focus, each with a focus-sensitive-operator truth-value probe, a what-is-new question probe, and a contrastive-continuation felicity probe, plus a focus-unambiguous control. Behaviorally we measure per-language focus-resolution accuracy and focus-drift and test whether it tracks resource level, typological distance, and focus-marking typology beyond comprehension. We train a linear focus/given probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer—including across languages with different focus-marking devices—then decompose the failure into a shared partition component versus a language-set expression gate, verifying the correct focus is internally present even where behavior drifts. Via activation and path patching we localize a focus signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to surface or shift the focus (flipping the truth value of a focus-sensitive-operator sentence) while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual pragmatic-comprehension gaps as a steerable gate over a shared information-structure representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages spanning focus-marking typology (English, German [prosody/clefts], Russian [word order], Hindi, Arabic, Chinese, Japanese [wa/ga particles], Turkish [preverbal focus position]), coded for focus-marking device/richness (Rooth; Büring; WALS-related sources) plus URIEL distance. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (FocusProbe): ~500 sentences, each in a CONTEXT (a preceding question-under-discussion or contrast) that FIXES which element is focus vs given. Item types: (A) FOCUS-SENSITIVE OPERATOR truth-value: sentences with 'only'/'even'/'also' whose truth conditions depend on which element is focused ('John only introduced BILL to Sue' vs 'John only introduced Bill to SUE'), with a truth-value/entailment probe requiring the context-fixed focus; (B) WHAT-IS-NEW question ('what is the newly asserted/highlighted information?'); (C) CONTRASTIVE-CONTINUATION felicity ('...not MARY' is felicitous only under subject focus). Include a matched FOCUS-UNAMBIGUOUS control (only one partition possible; bounds the effect, separates focus resolution from comprehension) and a NEUTRAL filler. Keep sentence content and context-fixed focus fixed across languages; translate/native-verify, realizing focus naturally per language (word order, cleft, particle); flag constructions with no natural equivalent. Record tokenization fertility; screen literal comprehension via the unambiguous control. Short scoreable answers.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (item, language) record correct focus-based resolution vs FOCUS-DRIFT (defaulting to canonical/subject focus or a dominant-language-typical partition). Hypothesis: for the SAME context-fixed focus, focus-drift is higher in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, worst where the language's focus-marking device differs most from the dominant languages, beyond comprehension and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of focus-drift on (focus-marking typology, language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, item type, comprehension indicator), item as random effect; compare against the unambiguous control. Report per-language/item-type profiles, cross-lingual disagreement, and replicate an English focus-sensitivity baseline.
4) SHARED FOCUS/GIVEN PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the focused-element/pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode WHICH element is FOCUS vs GIVEN on ENGLISH data, apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC. CRITICAL: test transfer ACROSS languages with DIFFERENT focus-marking devices (train on English cleft/prosody focus, test on Japanese-particle or Turkish-position focus)—high transfer despite different surface marking evidences a shared partition. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. On FOCUS-DRIFT items, test whether the correct focus is still internally decodable across ALL languages even when behavior drifts.
5) PARTITION-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer focus signal across languages (should be similar if the partition is shared) vs behavioral resolution (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal partition to surfaced behavior per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar partition signal. Correlate gate strength with focus-marking typology, resource tier, typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes.
6) LOCALIZE THE FOCUS SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that surfaces the correct focus and one that drifts on the SAME sentence, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for minimal components whose transfer surfaces the correct focus WITHOUT changing the decoded propositional content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the focus representation FROM a high-expression language into a drifting run. Attention analysis: does the focus-sensitive operator attend to the context-fixed focused element, more in high-expression languages?
7) CAUSAL FOCUS STEERING (decisive): Derive a focus steering vector via difference-of-means (correct-focus runs minus drifted runs, plus subject-focus vs object-focus contrasts). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to drift-prone languages increases correct focus-based resolution; (ii) SHIFT: steering along the focus axis makes the model treat a different element as focus (subject->object), flipping the truth value of a focus-sensitive-operator sentence on well-handled items; (iii) it works cross-lingually, stronger where expression was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY the focus partition, not the decoded propositional content or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the unambiguous control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: focus-drift-gap closure, focus-shift-flip rate (reverse), focus-signal/content/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes focus judgments but not unambiguous-control or unrelated answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: item-type breakdown (operator vs what-is-new vs continuation); focus-marking-device breakdown (prosody/cleft vs particle vs position); does the shared focus signal transfer across differently-marking languages?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single focus vector generalizes across constructions and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal partition and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces focus without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language per-item-type focus-resolution accuracy and focus-drift rate, drift regression controlling for comprehension/fertility/resource with focus-marking-typology effect, English focus-sensitivity replication, cross-lingual focus/given probe transfer AUROC (including across differently-marking languages) and focus-present-under-drift, cross-lingual partition-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), partition-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-typology/resource correlation, patch-localized focus layer and operator-to-focus attention evidence, cross-lingual focus transplant recovery rate, causal steering drift-gap closure and focus-shift-flip rates, focus-signal/content/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The partition-vs-expression split could be confounded if the focus signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying correct-focus decodability across all languages (especially differently-marking ones) on drift items via probe transfer, and report how much of the gap is partition vs gate. 2) Focus-drift could reflect comprehension failure rather than an expression gate; we use the matched FOCUS-UNAMBIGUOUS control and comprehension screening so residual drift reflects focus resolution, not reading. 3) Focus can be genuinely ambiguous without prosody (text lacks intonation); we FIX focus via explicit context (question-under-discussion/contrast), restrict scored items to clear context-determined focus, and analyze ambiguous ones separately—this also makes the cross-lingual design fair since all languages rely on textual cues. 4) Realizing focus naturally and equivalently across languages is delicate (word order, cleft, particle, dedicated position differ); we native-verify, treat focus-marking device as a factor, and flag constructions with no natural equivalent (using them for transfer-limit analysis). 5) The transfer-across-differently-marking-languages test is the key novelty but could fail if focus is only represented via each language's surface device (an equally informative result about whether the partition is genuinely shared vs marking-specific); we report it either way. 6) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal partition, and content-invariant steering surfaces focus without changing tokenization. 7) Some models may resolve focus uniformly across languages (no gap) or drift everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual information structure, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 8) The focus probe could latch onto surface cues (cleft words, particles) rather than a genuine partition representation; the transfer across differently-marking languages, the focus-present-under-drift test, the operator-to-focus attention analysis, cross-lingual invariance, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 9) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 10) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report focus-signal/content/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention, and use the focus-shift (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine focus gate. 11) The gate/focus signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 12) Distinguishing from my discourse-relation (inter-clausal relation label), bridging (entity-to-scene link), illocutionary-force (speech-act type), and presupposition (backgrounded presupposed content) proposals is essential; here the object is the FOCUS/GIVEN partition WITHIN a sentence (which element is discourse-new and contrastively highlighted), a distinct information-structural object with a decisive truth-conditional test via focus-sensitive operators and its own cross-linguistic marking typology.

Name: crosslingual_answer_community_structure
Title: Answer Basins: Does a Multilingual Model's Factual Knowledge Cluster Into Mutual-Intelligibility Communities, and Is the Community Structure a Causally Steerable Routing Property?
Short Hypothesis: For a fixed factual question asked across many languages, a multilingual LLM's per-language answers are not independent and are not a single universal answer; instead they organize into a small number of 'answer basins' — graph communities of languages that agree with each other — and this community structure is governed by MUTUAL INTELLIGIBILITY / dialect-cluster relatedness (mutually intelligible or same-cluster languages fall in the same basin) far more than by raw resource level or writing system. The basin a language falls into is a causally steerable routing property: steering a query's language-identity representation toward another basin's language flips its answer into that basin, and the number and sharpness of basins predicts per-fact cross-lingual inconsistency.
Related Work: Prior work documents that multilingual LLMs give DIFFERENT factual answers across languages (Qi et al. 2023; Wang 2025 'Lost in Multilinguality'; Aggarwal et al. 2025 'Factuality Depends on the Language of Inquiry'; Ifergan et al. 2024 show knowledge-sharing scales with script/typological similarity) and that facts live in a shared concept space with language-specific decoding (Wang 2025; Lim 2025). All of this treats cross-lingual inconsistency as a per-language accuracy scalar or a pairwise transfer/similarity quantity. NO prior work characterizes the GLOBAL STRUCTURE of per-language answers as a small set of answer BASINS (graph communities of mutual agreement), tests whether that community structure is governed specifically by MUTUAL INTELLIGIBILITY / dialect-cluster relatedness (a linguistically-grounded relation distinct from typological distance or resource tier), or shows that basin membership is a causally steerable routing property (steering a query into another basin flips its answer). My prior proposals concern per-fact gating, native-language imprint, and language-relationship routing as a transfer key; none characterize answer-basin community structure or tie it to mutual intelligibility. This reframes cross-lingual factual inconsistency from a scalar gap into a discoverable, predictable, and steerable graph structure.
Abstract: When a multilingual language model is asked the same factual question in fifty languages, we usually summarize the result as an accuracy number per language. We instead ask about the global structure of those answers: do the languages that agree with each other form a small number of coherent 'answer basins', and what governs which basin a language falls into? We hypothesize that per-language answers organize into graph communities of mutual agreement, that this community structure is driven by mutual intelligibility and dialect-cluster relatedness (mutually intelligible languages share a basin) more than by resource level or script, and that basin membership is a causally steerable routing property. For each of many factual questions we query the model in a large, typologically and genealogically diverse language set, build a language-by-language answer-agreement graph, and apply community detection to recover answer basins. We test whether the recovered communities align with documented mutual-intelligibility clusters (e.g., Slavic, Romance, Turkic, Hindi-Urdu, Scandinavian) beyond URIEL typological distance and resource tier, and whether the number/sharpness of basins predicts a fact's cross-lingual inconsistency. Mechanistically, we relate basin membership to the model's internal language-identity representation, and in a decisive causal test we steer a query's language-identity vector toward a target basin's language and show the emitted answer flips into that basin, while the surface answer language is unchanged. We reframe multilingual factual inconsistency as a mutual-intelligibility-governed, causally steerable answer-community structure.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + light steering on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). ~40 languages chosen to include known MUTUAL-INTELLIGIBILITY clusters and dialect continua (Slavic: Russian/Ukrainian/Belarusian/Polish/Czech; Romance: Spanish/Italian/Portuguese/French; Turkic: Turkish/Azerbaijani; Hindi-Urdu; Scandinavian: Danish/Norwegian/Swedish; plus genealogically isolated controls: Basque, Swahili, Chinese, Japanese, Arabic, Finnish), so mutual intelligibility, typological distance (URIEL), script, and resource tier are dissociable. Code per-pair mutual-intelligibility from documented linguistic sources (dialectology/intelligibility studies) as a graded predictor.
2) DATASET: ~600 factual questions with short decodable answers (mLAMA/BMLAMA/Wikidata), especially items known to be cross-lingually contested/variable, translated/native-verified into all ~40 languages. For each (fact, language) obtain the model's answer via normalized matching; record per-language tokenization fertility.
3) BUILD THE ANSWER-AGREEMENT GRAPH: For each fact, build a language-by-language graph with edge weight = whether two languages produce the same answer; aggregate across facts into a weighted co-agreement graph (and keep per-fact graphs). Apply community detection (Louvain / Leiden / modularity clustering) to recover ANSWER BASINS. Report the number of basins, modularity, and basin sizes per model.
4) BEHAVIORAL BASIN-STRUCTURE TEST: KEY hypothesis — answers organize into a SMALL number of coherent basins rather than being independent per language or a single universal answer. Compare recovered modularity/community count against a null of independent per-language answers (permutation test) and against a single-community null. Report per-fact basin count distribution and how often multiple basins exist (cross-lingual inconsistency as multi-basin structure).
5) MUTUAL-INTELLIGIBILITY-GOVERNS-BASINS TEST (core): Test whether basin co-membership is predicted by mutual intelligibility BEYOND URIEL typological distance, script identity, and resource tier. Mixed-effects logistic regression of same-basin membership on (mutual-intelligibility score, URIEL distance, script match, resource-tier match), language-pair as unit; test incremental predictive power of mutual intelligibility (likelihood-ratio / AUC) and whether documented intelligibility clusters (Slavic, Romance, Scandinavian, Hindi-Urdu) recover as communities, while isolated controls form singletons. Compare English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya).
6) BASIN-SHARPNESS-PREDICTS-INCONSISTENCY: Test whether the number/sharpness of basins for a fact predicts its overall cross-lingual inconsistency and its per-language accuracy variance, and whether facts with a single dominant basin are more likely correct (consensus) than multi-basin facts.
7) INTERNAL BASIN REPRESENTATION: Using per-layer language-ID probes (Wang 2025), test whether the model's internal language-identity geometry (cosine/CKA of per-language language-identity vectors) recovers the same community structure as the behavioral answer basins — i.e., languages in the same answer basin sit closer in language-identity space — beyond typology/script.
8) CAUSAL BASIN-ROUTING TEST (decisive): Derive a language-identity steering vector (difference-of-means between languages) and add the TARGET-basin language's identity vector to a query posed in a SOURCE-basin language (surface tokens kept in the source language). Test whether the emitted ANSWER flips from the source basin's answer to the target basin's answer on facts where the two basins disagree, with dose-response and specificity (a random/other-basin vector does not reroute; the fact changes only where basins genuinely differ), while the surface output language is unchanged. Cross-check with activation patching of the language-identity representation. Metrics: basin-flip rate, dose-response, specificity, output-language fidelity, general-QA (multilingual MMLU subset) retention.
9) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: robustness of communities to the agreement threshold and community-detection algorithm; per-fact vs aggregate graphs; dialect-continuum languages (do they bridge basins?); English/high-resource basin dominance; model scale; whether a single steering recipe generalizes across facts.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: number/modularity of answer basins vs independence and single-community nulls, same-basin-membership regression with incremental predictive power of mutual intelligibility beyond typology/script/resource, recovery of documented intelligibility clusters as communities, basin-sharpness vs cross-lingual inconsistency correlation, internal language-identity community recovery, causal basin-routing flip rate with dose-response/specificity, output-language fidelity, general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Answer basins might not exist (answers uniform, or idiosyncratically per-language) — either is an informative, publishable characterization of whether cross-lingual factual inconsistency has community structure, and we quantify modularity vs nulls rather than assuming basins. 2) Mutual-intelligibility scores are coarse, asymmetric, and debated; we use documented intelligibility/dialectology sources, treat intelligibility as a graded predictor, report sensitivity to alternative codings, and note the effect is establishable even if the exact intelligibility metric is imperfect. 3) Mutual intelligibility is correlated with typological distance, script, and shared training data (mutually intelligible languages often share corpora); we control for URIEL distance, script match, and resource-tier match in regression to test incremental predictive power, but cannot fully rule out shared-corpus confounds — we report per-pair corpus-overlap proxies where available and treat the causal steering (which routes by internal language identity, not corpus) as the load-bearing evidence that basins are a routing property. 4) Answer-matching across languages is noisy (translation-equivalent answers, transliteration); we use normalized/translation-aware matching validated against human checks on a subset and restrict to short decodable answers. 5) Community-detection results depend on threshold/algorithm; we report robustness across Louvain/Leiden/modularity and multiple thresholds. 6) The causal steering may only partially reroute answers, may change the surface output language, or may act as a generic accuracy lever; we report basin-flip rate with dose-response, specificity (random/other-basin vector null; fact changes only where basins disagree), output-language fidelity, and general-QA retention, cross-checking with activation patching. 7) Results may be model-specific; we test four models spanning English-centric and multilingual-centric pretraining and report per-model community structures. 8) Distinguishing from my prior language-relationship-routing (transfer key) and native-language-imprint proposals is essential; here the object is the emergent GLOBAL COMMUNITY STRUCTURE of per-language factual ANSWERS and its governance by mutual intelligibility, characterized behaviorally as a graph and validated causally as a steerable routing property, not per-fact transfer or acquisition-language imprint.

Name: crosslingual_agreement_domain_gating
Title: Agreeing Across the Gap: A Shared Long-Distance Agreement Representation Whose Robustness Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When a controller and a target that must grammatically agree (subject-verb number, noun-adjective gender/case) are separated by an intervening dependency, a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of the correct agreement feature the target should carry, but whether that feature is behaviorally EXPRESSED at increasing agreement-domain LENGTH (more intervening material/attractors) is gated by the query language: the SAME agreement dependency is internally represented correctly across languages yet realized as an agreement error far more often, and at shorter distances, in lower-resource / typologically distant languages, so the model internally 'knows the controller's features' while behaviorally failing to carry them across the gap. The agreement signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated long-distance agreement failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Long-distance agreement and agreement-attraction are classic probes of syntactic competence (Linzen et al. 2016; BLiMP/CLiMP; targeted-syntactic evaluation), and my prior crosslingual_grammaticality_illusion proposal studied susceptibility to a grammatical ILLUSION (a local attractor overriding a correct dependency) within a single language. This proposal is distinct: the causal variable is agreement-domain LENGTH/robustness—how far the correct feature can be CARRIED across an intervening gap before it decays—and its cross-lingual decomposition into a shared feature representation versus a language-set expression gate, not attractor-induced illusion susceptibility. Multilingual acceptability work (CLiMP, multilingual BLiMP-style suites) reports per-language accuracy behaviorally, never testing whether a shared internal agreement feature is carried across the gap, whether its behavioral expression decays with distance in a language-gated way, or whether it is causally steerable. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never for long-distance agreement carrying. No prior work (i) tests whether agreement-carrying robustness across distance is language-dependent beyond feature knowledge, (ii) decomposes it into a shared feature signal versus a language-set carrying gate, or (iii) causally localizes and steers an agreement-carrying signal.
Abstract: Grammatical agreement often spans a gap: 'the KEY to the cabinets IS...' requires carrying the singular of 'key' across intervening words to the verb, and gender/case agreement over embedded phrases makes similar demands. Languages differ enormously in how richly they mark agreement (morphology-rich Russian/Turkish vs morphology-poor Chinese/English) and in how they order the agreeing elements. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal representation of the feature an agreement target should carry, and whether that internal feature is decoupled from how robustly it is behaviorally carried across an intervening gap in different languages. We hypothesize that models represent the controller's agreement feature similarly across languages internally, but the query language gates how far that feature can be carried before an agreement error emerges, so the SAME dependency fails at shorter distances far more often in lower-resource, typologically distant languages—even though the model 'knows the controller's features'. We build AgreeSpanProbe, parallel controller-target agreement dependencies across languages with the agreement-domain LENGTH (number of intervening words/attractors) varied as a controlled factor, each with an agreement-acceptability probe, plus an adjacent-agreement control where no gap must be spanned. Behaviorally we measure per-language agreement accuracy as a function of distance and test whether the accuracy-vs-distance decay is steeper in some languages beyond feature knowledge and tokenization. We train a linear agreement-feature probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the decay into a shared feature representation versus a language-set carrying gate, verifying the correct feature is internally present even where agreement fails. Via activation and path patching we localize an agreement-carrying signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to restore correct long-distance agreement in high-decay languages—or, in reverse, induce failure—while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual syntactic fragility as a steerable gate over a shared agreement representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 languages spanning agreement-morphology richness and word-order typology (rich: Russian, Turkish, Spanish, German; moderate: Hindi; poor/analytic: English, Chinese, Indonesian), coded for agreement-marking richness (number/gender/case on verbs/adjectives) from WALS-related sources plus URIEL distance. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (AgreeSpanProbe): ~500 controller-target agreement dependencies (subject-verb number; noun-adjective/article gender/case where the language has it) in minimal-pair form (grammatical vs ungrammatical agreement), with a controlled AGREEMENT-DOMAIN LENGTH factor: 0 (adjacent) up to ~5 intervening words (relative clauses, PP modifiers, coordinated NPs), including attractor and non-attractor intervening material as a sub-factor. Include an ADJACENT-AGREEMENT control (distance 0; establishes baseline agreement competence) to bound the effect and separate carrying from base knowledge. Probes: (A) acceptability forced-choice (grammatical vs ungrammatical target), (B) log-prob preference for the correct target form. Realize each construction naturally per language with native verification; flag constructions with no natural equivalent (e.g. agreement absent in an analytic language) for transfer-limit analysis; record per-length tokenization fertility.
3) BEHAVIORAL DECAY TEST: For each language, plot agreement accuracy (log-prob preference for the correct form) vs agreement-domain length; fit each language's accuracy-vs-distance DECAY (slope / distance at which accuracy falls below threshold). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME dependency, the decay is steeper (correct feature carried a shorter distance) in lower-resource / typologically distant / morphology-poorer languages, beyond baseline (distance-0) competence and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of agreement error on (distance x language, agreement-morphology richness, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, distance-0 baseline), item as random effect; test the distance x language interaction. Compare against the adjacent control (should be language-flatter). Report per-language decay curves and cross-lingual disagreement at matched distances; replicate a monolingual long-distance-agreement baseline in the strongest language.
4) SHARED AGREEMENT-FEATURE PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer, at the target/pre-answer position, train a linear probe to decode the CORRECT agreement feature (the number/gender/case the target SHOULD take, determined by the controller, not by any attractor) on data from a morphology-rich language (Russian), apply zero-shot cross-lingually including to analytic languages; report AUROC/macro-F1 as evidence of a language-independent agreement-feature representation. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on AGREEMENT-FAILURE items (long-distance errors), test whether the correct feature is still internally decodable across ALL languages even where the emitted agreement is wrong—the signature of language-gated carrying over an intact feature representation.
5) FEATURE-vs-CARRYING DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer agreement-feature signal across languages (should be similar/correct if the feature is shared) versus behavioral agreement (which decays with distance). Define a language-set CARRYING GATE mapping the internal feature to a correct target across the gap; test whether cross-lingual decay differences are explained by a weaker carrying gate on a similar (correct) internal feature rather than a weaker feature signal. Correlate per-language carrying strength with agreement-morphology richness, resource tier, and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes.
6) LOCALIZE THE AGREEMENT-CARRYING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that carries the feature correctly at distance and one that fails on the SAME dependency, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer restores correct agreement WITHOUT changing the decoded controller feature. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the feature representation FROM a robust language into a failing run. Attention analysis: does the target position attend to the controller across the gap, more so in low-decay languages?
7) CAUSAL AGREEMENT-CARRYING STEERING (decisive): Derive a carrying steering vector via difference-of-means (correct-long-distance-agreement runs minus failed runs at matched internal feature). Test (i) RESTORE: adding it to high-decay languages restores correct long-distance agreement toward robust-language levels; (ii) INDUCE: subtracting it induces long-distance agreement failure in robust languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, stronger where decay was steepest; (iv) it changes ONLY agreement carrying, not the decoded controller feature, baseline (adjacent) agreement, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the adjacent control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: decay-gap closure (extended carrying distance), agreement-failure-induction rate (reverse), feature-signal/output fidelity, adjacent-control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes long-distance agreement but not adjacent-control or unrelated answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: agreement-type breakdown (number vs gender vs case); attractor vs non-attractor intervening material (does the language-gating interact with attraction?); does the shared feature signal transfer to analytic languages that lack overt agreement?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the decay asymmetry?); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single carrying vector generalizes across agreement types and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal feature and by showing content-invariant steering extends carrying without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language accuracy-vs-distance decay curves and their distance x language interaction controlling for baseline competence/fertility/resource with agreement-morphology effect, monolingual long-distance-agreement replication, cross-lingual agreement-feature probe transfer AUROC (including to analytic languages) and correct-feature-present-under-failure, cross-lingual feature-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), feature-similarity vs carrying-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-morphology/resource/typology correlation, patch-localized agreement-carrying layer and controller-to-target attention evidence, cross-lingual feature transplant restoration rate, causal steering decay-gap closure and agreement-failure-induction rates, feature-signal/output fidelity, adjacent-control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The feature-vs-carrying split could be confounded if the agreement-feature signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying correct-feature decodability across all languages on failure items via probe transfer rather than assuming, and report how much of the decay is feature-representation vs carrying gate. 2) Decay could reflect a baseline agreement-knowledge gap rather than a carrying gate; we condition on the adjacent (distance-0) control so residual distance-dependent decay reflects carrying, not base competence. 3) Realizing long-distance agreement naturally and equivalently across languages is delicate, especially in analytic languages (Chinese/Indonesian) with little/no overt agreement—we native-verify, treat agreement-morphology richness as a graded predictor, flag constructions with no natural equivalent (using them for transfer-limit analysis), and for languages lacking a given agreement analyze the applicable agreement types only; the shared-feature transfer test to analytic languages is itself informative about whether agreement features are represented even without overt marking. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy at longer distances (more intervening tokens); we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal feature and matched intervening-word count, and content-invariant steering extends carrying without changing tokenization, dissociating the gate from length. 5) Some models may carry agreement uniformly across languages (no decay asymmetry) or fail everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual syntactic robustness, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 6) Acceptability judgments can be prompt-sensitive (acquiescence bias); we use both forced-choice and log-prob preference, counterbalance grammaticality, and validate against a monolingual long-distance-agreement baseline. 7) The agreement-feature probe could latch onto surface controller cues rather than a genuine carried-feature representation; the correct-feature-present-under-failure test, the controller-to-target attention analysis, cross-lingual invariance, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report feature-signal/output fidelity, adjacent-control and general-QA retention, and use the agreement-failure-induction (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine agreement-carrying gate. 10) The gate/feature signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my crosslingual_grammaticality_illusion proposal is essential; there the object was attractor-induced ILLUSION susceptibility (a local distractor overriding a correct dependency), whereas here it is agreement-domain LENGTH ROBUSTNESS—how far a correct agreement feature can be carried across an intervening gap before it decays—and its cross-lingual feature-vs-carrying decomposition, a distinct, distance-parametrized syntactic phenomenon.

Name: crosslingual_npi_licensing_gating
Title: Licensed by the Negation, in Every Language? A Shared NPI-Licensing Representation Whose Expression Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: Negative polarity items (NPIs like English 'any', 'ever', 'yet') are grammatical only when licensed by a downward-entailing operator (negation, 'few', 'without', questions). We hypothesize a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal 'licensing' representation that registers whether an NPI's licensing environment is present and c-commands it, but whether that licensing is behaviorally EXPRESSED (judging an unlicensed NPI as ungrammatical, resolving the scope that licenses it, blocking an NPI when the licensor is outside its domain) is gated by the query language: the SAME NPI-licensing configuration is internally represented across languages yet mis-judged far more often in lower-resource / typologically distant languages—especially those whose polarity-sensitivity typology (negative concord, NPI-strictness) differs from the dominant languages. The licensing signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated NPI failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Negative polarity items and their licensing by downward-entailing / negative operators are a cornerstone of formal semantics (Ladusaw's downward-entailment condition; Giannakidou; Zwarts), and languages vary sharply in polarity-sensitivity typology: negative-concord languages (Spanish, Italian, Russian, Greek) where multiple negatives yield one negation, NPI-licensing languages (English, German) with c-command and strict/non-strict NPIs, and languages with distinct polarity systems. In NLP, monolingual English work probes whether LLMs respect NPI licensing (BLiMP includes NPI/licensor items; 'NPI-illusion' garden-path studies), but this is English-centric and behavioral. My prior crosslingual_logical_operator proposal concerned truth-conditional polarity of negation/negative-concord (does the sentence mean affirmative or negated); crosslingual_grammaticality_illusion concerned attractor-induced illusion susceptibility; crosslingual_agreement_domain concerned carrying an agreement feature across a gap. NONE address NPI LICENSING—the grammatical dependency between a polarity-sensitive item and a c-commanding downward-entailing licensor—whether that licensing relation is a shared cross-lingual representation, whether its behavioral expression is language-gated, whether it tracks polarity-sensitivity typology, or whether the licensing signal is causally localizable and steerable. NPI licensing offers a decisive grammaticality/scope test (an NPI is ungrammatical without a c-commanding licensor) and clean typological variation, distinct from truth-conditional negation meaning, agreement, or illusion susceptibility. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never for NPI licensing.
Abstract: Some words are grammatical only in the shadow of a negation: 'I didn't see anyone' is fine, but '*I saw anyone' is not, because the negative polarity item 'anyone' must be licensed by a c-commanding negative or downward-entailing operator. This licensing dependency is a hallmark of grammatical competence, and languages differ strikingly in their polarity-sensitivity systems—from negative concord in Spanish and Russian to strict NPI licensing in English. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal representation of whether an NPI is licensed, and whether that internal representation is decoupled from how reliably licensing is behaviorally expressed across languages. We hypothesize that models represent NPI licensing similarly across languages internally, but the query language gates whether it is surfaced—judging an unlicensed NPI as ungrammatical, respecting that a licensor must c-command and scope over the NPI, blocking licensing when the negation is embedded outside the NPI's domain—so the SAME configuration is mis-judged far more in lower-resource, typologically distant languages. We build NPIProbe, minimal-pair sentences across languages crossing NPI presence with licensor presence, position (c-commanding vs non-c-commanding), and licensor type (negation, 'few', 'without', questions), with a grammaticality-acceptability probe and a licensing-scope probe, plus a licensed control. Behaviorally we measure per-language licensing accuracy and licensing-drift (accepting unlicensed NPIs or rejecting licensed ones) and test whether it tracks resource level, typological distance, and polarity-sensitivity typology beyond comprehension. We train a linear NPI-licensing probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer—including across differing polarity systems—then decompose the failure into a shared licensing component versus a language-set expression gate, verifying the correct licensing status is internally present even where behavior drifts. Via activation and path patching we localize a licensing signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to surface (or flip) NPI licensing while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual syntactic-semantic fragility as a steerable gate over a shared NPI-licensing representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 languages spanning polarity-sensitivity typology: negative-concord (Spanish, Italian, Russian, Greek), NPI-licensing non-concord (English, German), plus distinct-system languages (Japanese with mo/-shika NPIs, Hindi), coded for negative-concord vs NPI-strict status and NPI inventory from typological/semantic references (Giannakidou; Zeijlstra) plus URIEL distance. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (NPIProbe): ~500 minimal-pair sentences crossing NPI PRESENCE (an NPI vs a non-polarity-sensitive counterpart) x LICENSOR PRESENCE (a downward-entailing licensor present vs absent) x LICENSOR POSITION (c-commanding/scoping over the NPI vs present-but-non-c-commanding/embedded-elsewhere) x LICENSOR TYPE (clausal negation, 'few', 'without', question). The signature: an NPI is grammatical iff a licensor c-commands it; '*He saw anyone' (no licensor) and '*The man who didn't come saw anyone' (licensor present but not c-commanding the NPI) are ungrammatical, while 'He didn't see anyone' is fine. Probes: (A) ACCEPTABILITY forced-choice / log-prob preference for the licensed vs unlicensed target; (B) LICENSING-SCOPE probe (does the negation scope over / license the NPI here?). Include a LICENSED control (unambiguously grammatical) to bound the effect and separate licensing from comprehension. Realize NPIs and licensors naturally per language with native verification, adapting from BLiMP-style NPI paradigms; flag languages/constructions with no natural NPI equivalent (using them for transfer-limit analysis); handle negative-concord languages carefully (where 'n-words' are concord items, not free NPIs) with native-designed items. Record tokenization fertility; screen literal comprehension via the licensed control. Short scoreable answers.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (item, language) record correct licensing judgment vs LICENSING-DRIFT (accepting an unlicensed NPI or rejecting a licensed one, or ignoring the c-command requirement). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME configuration, licensing-drift is systematically higher in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, and interacts with polarity-sensitivity typology (concord vs strict), beyond comprehension and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of licensing-drift on (polarity-sensitivity typology, licensor type, licensor position, language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, comprehension indicator), item as random effect; test the position (c-command) effect and its language interaction. Compare against the licensed control (language-flatter). Report per-language and per-licensor-type profiles, cross-lingual disagreement, and replicate an English NPI-licensing baseline (BLiMP).
4) SHARED NPI-LICENSING PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the NPI/pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode whether the NPI is LICENSED (a c-commanding downward-entailing licensor is present in its domain) on ENGLISH data, apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC. CRITICAL: test transfer ACROSS differing polarity systems (train on English NPI-licensing, test on negative-concord Spanish/Russian and Japanese -shika)—high transfer despite different surface systems evidences a shared licensing representation. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. On LICENSING-DRIFT items, test whether correct licensing status is still internally decodable across ALL languages even when behavior drifts—the signature of language-gated expression over an intact licensing signal.
5) LICENSING-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer licensing signal across languages (should be similar if licensing is shared) versus behavioral acceptability (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal licensing to surfaced judgment per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar licensing signal. Correlate gate strength with polarity-sensitivity typology, resource tier, and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes.
6) LOCALIZE THE LICENSING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that judges licensing correctly and one that drifts on the SAME item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer surfaces correct licensing WITHOUT changing the decoded propositional content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the licensing representation FROM a high-expression language into a drifting run. Attention analysis: does the NPI attend to its licensor, more so in high-expression languages?
7) CAUSAL LICENSING STEERING (decisive): Derive an NPI-licensing steering vector via difference-of-means (licensed/correct-judgment runs minus unlicensed/drift runs, plus c-command-present vs absent contrasts).
