Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to drift-prone languages increases correct licensing judgments toward high-expression levels; (ii) FLIP: steering along the licensing axis makes the model accept an unlicensed NPI or reject a licensed one on well-handled items (a targeted grammaticality flip); (iii) it works cross-lingually, stronger where expression was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY licensing judgments, not the decoded propositional content or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the licensed control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: licensing-drift-gap closure, licensing-flip rate (reverse), licensing-signal/content/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes NPI-licensing judgments but not licensed-control or unrelated answers, guarding against a generic acceptability lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: licensor-type breakdown (negation vs 'few' vs 'without' vs question—which downward-entailing licensors leak most); c-command/position sensitivity; does the shared licensing signal transfer across concord vs strict systems?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; whether a single licensing vector generalizes across licensor types and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal licensing and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces licensing without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language per-licensor-type licensing accuracy and licensing-drift rate, drift regression controlling for comprehension/fertility/resource with polarity-typology and c-command effects, English NPI-licensing (BLiMP) replication, cross-lingual NPI-licensing probe transfer AUROC (including across differing polarity systems) and licensing-present-under-drift, cross-lingual licensing-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), licensing-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-typology/resource correlation, patch-localized licensing layer and NPI-to-licensor attention evidence, cross-lingual licensing transplant recovery rate, causal steering drift-gap closure and licensing-flip rates, licensing-signal/content/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The licensing-vs-expression split could be confounded if the licensing signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying correct-licensing decodability across all languages (especially differing-polarity-system ones) on drift items via probe transfer, and report how much of the gap is licensing-representation vs gate. 2) Licensing-drift could reflect comprehension failure rather than an expression gate; we use the matched LICENSED control and comprehension screening so residual drift reflects licensing, not reading. 3) Constructing NPI-licensing minimal pairs equivalently across languages is delicate: negative-concord languages treat 'n-words' as concord items rather than free NPIs, and NPI inventories differ (English 'any/ever' vs Japanese -shika/mo); we native-design items per language, treat polarity-sensitivity typology as a factor, flag constructions with no natural equivalent (using them for transfer-limit analysis), and analyze concord vs strict systems separately—where a language lacks a comparable NPI, we rely on the applicable licensor types. 4) The transfer-across-differing-systems test is the key novelty but could fail if licensing is only represented via each language's surface polarity system (an equally informative result about whether the licensing relation is genuinely shared vs system-specific); we report it either way. 5) The c-command/position manipulation must be genuinely diagnostic; we use minimal pairs where the licensor is present but structurally outside the NPI's domain, verified by native syntacticians, so acceptance there reflects ignoring the structural licensing condition, not lexical presence. 6) Tokenization fertility confounds accuracy; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal licensing, and content-invariant steering surfaces licensing without changing tokenization. 7) Acceptability judgments can be prompt-sensitive (acquiescence bias); we use both forced-choice and log-prob preference, counterbalance grammaticality, and validate against the English BLiMP NPI baseline. 8) Some models may judge licensing uniformly across languages (no gap) or drift everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual NPI licensing, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 9) The licensing probe could latch onto surface negation-word cues rather than a genuine c-command-sensitive licensing representation; the c-command position manipulation, the transfer across differing systems, the licensing-present-under-drift test, the NPI-to-licensor attention analysis, cross-lingual invariance, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 10) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 11) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic acceptability lever; we report licensing-signal/content/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention, and use the licensing-flip (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine licensing gate. 12) The gate/licensing signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 13) Distinguishing from my crosslingual_logical_operator (truth-conditional polarity/meaning of negation and negative concord), grammaticality-illusion (attractor-induced illusion susceptibility), and agreement-domain (carrying an agreement feature across a gap) proposals is essential; here the object is NPI LICENSING—the grammatical dependency between a polarity-sensitive item and a c-commanding downward-entailing licensor—with a decisive grammaticality/scope test and clean polarity-sensitivity typology, a distinct syntactic-semantic phenomenon.

Name: crosslingual_counting_ensemble_gating
Title: Counting the Crowd, in Every Language: A Shared Set-Cardinality Estimate Whose Enumeration-vs-Estimation Strategy Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When asked how many items satisfy a condition in a described scene/list (e.g. 'how many of these ten animals are mammals?'), a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of the true set cardinality, but the query language causally sets WHICH strategy it uses to report it: precise item-by-item ENUMERATION versus coarse gist ESTIMATION. For the SAME counting problem the model enumerates accurately in some languages and defaults to a systematically biased quick estimate in others (typically lower-resource / higher-fertility / typologically distant), producing a cross-lingual counting-accuracy asymmetry that is separable from the shared cardinality signal and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable strategy-gating signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Multilingual math is studied only behaviorally at the benchmark level (MGSM), reporting per-language accuracy without a mechanism. My prior number-focused proposals concern distinct objects: number-naming distortion (magnitude of a single spelled number), running-state tracking (maintaining a numeric TALLY across a discourse as items are added/removed), the approximate-number system (ratio-dependent COMPARISON acuity / Weber's law), reported PRECISION (rounding granularity), vague-quantifier grounding, individuation (count/mass status), and classifier categories. NONE address SET-CARDINALITY COUNTING—determining how many items in a static presented set satisfy a condition—nor whether the ENUMERATION-vs-ESTIMATION strategy (a documented human dual-process for cardinality: exact subitizing/counting vs approximate estimation) is language-gated over a shared cardinality signal, nor causally localize/steer such a strategy gate. This differs from running-state (dynamic tally over turns, not counting a static set), from the ANS (which is ratio COMPARISON acuity, not set counting or strategy selection), and from precision (rounding a known value, not choosing whether to count exactly). Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never for counting strategy. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of set-cardinality counting and its enumeration-vs-estimation strategy gate, grounded in the human dual-process counting literature (Feigenson, Dehaene & Spelke).
Abstract: Asked how many of ten listed items are edible, a careful reader counts one by one; a hurried one eyeballs a rough number. Humans switch between exact enumeration and approximate estimation for set cardinality, and the choice determines accuracy. As multilingual models answer counting questions for users worldwide, we ask whether the query language changes which strategy the model uses on the same problem. We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal estimate of a set's true cardinality, but the query language causally sets a strategy gate—precise enumeration versus coarse estimation—so the SAME counting problem is enumerated accurately in some languages and answered with a biased quick estimate in others, worst in lower-resource, typologically distant, higher-fertility languages. This predicts a cross-lingual counting-accuracy asymmetry dissociable from the model's underlying cardinality representation. We build CountGateProbe, parallel set-counting items across languages (count how many listed/described items satisfy a property), with the item set and target count held fixed and set size varied to trace an accuracy-vs-size curve, plus an explicit-total control. Behaviorally we measure per-language counting accuracy and estimation-bias (systematic under/over-shoot indicative of gist estimation) and test whether it tracks resource level, fertility, and typological distance beyond the model's cardinality signal. We train a linear cardinality probe and a strategy probe (enumeration vs estimation trajectory) and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the accuracy gap into a shared cardinality estimate versus a language-set strategy gate—verifying the correct count is internally decodable even where the emitted answer is a biased estimate. Via activation and path patching we localize a strategy-gating signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model enumerate (recovering accuracy) in estimation-prone languages—or, in reverse, force estimation—while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual counting gaps as a shared cardinality estimate under a steerable, language-dependent strategy gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 10 typologically/script/resource/fertility-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Swahili).
2) DATASET (CountGateProbe): ~500 SET-COUNTING items: a static list/description of N items (N varied 3..15 to trace accuracy-vs-size), and a question asking how many satisfy a property (how many animals are mammals / foods are fruits / numbers are even). The item set and the ground-truth count are fixed across languages; translate/native-verify the items and question. Include (a) an EXPLICIT-TOTAL control (the count is stated directly; language-flat) to bound the effect and (b) a SINGLE-ITEM-CLASSIFICATION screen (verify the model can correctly classify each individual item's property per language) so counting error is not per-item misclassification but a counting/strategy issue. Record per-language tokenization fertility; short single-token-decodable numeric answers.
3) BEHAVIORAL ASYMMETRY TEST: Per (item, language) record counting accuracy and, on errors, the SIGNED bias (systematic under/over-shoot, a signature of gist estimation) and its dependence on set size N. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME counting problem, accuracy is systematically lower and estimation-bias larger in lower-resource / higher-fertility / typologically distant languages, and this gap GROWS with N (estimation dominates for larger sets), beyond per-item classification ability. Mixed-effects regression of counting error / bias on (language, set size N, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, single-item-classification accuracy), item as random effect; test the language x N interaction. Compare against the explicit-total control (language-flat). Report per-language accuracy-vs-size curves and cross-lingual disagreement on identical problems.
4) SHARED CARDINALITY & STRATEGY PROBES + TRANSFER: At the pre-answer position pool the hidden state; train (i) a linear CARDINALITY probe to regress the true count on ENGLISH data, applied zero-shot cross-lingually (report R^2/rank-correlation as a language-independent cardinality estimate; cross-lingual CKA/cosine), and (ii) a STRATEGY probe distinguishing ENUMERATION vs ESTIMATION (target from whether the model produced/attended to an item-by-item trace vs a direct guess, and from allocated computation via layer-of-commitment). CRITICAL: on ERROR (biased-estimate) items, test whether the correct cardinality is still strongly decodable across languages—the signature of 'knows the count, reports an estimate'.
5) GATE-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer cardinality estimate across languages (should be similar on matched items) versus the emitted answer (which diverges). Define a per-language STRATEGY GATE mapping cardinality to enumeration-vs-estimation; test whether cross-lingual accuracy differences are explained by a language-set strategy gate on a similar cardinality signal rather than a weaker signal. Correlate per-language gate (enumeration propensity) with resource tier, fertility, and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE STRATEGY-GATING SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that enumerates and one that estimates on the SAME problem, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips estimate->enumerate WITHOUT changing the decoded cardinality signal. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gating components from an enumeration-prone language into an estimating run.
7) CAUSAL STRATEGY STEERING (decisive): Derive a strategy-gating steering vector via difference-of-means (enumeration runs minus estimation runs at matched cardinality). Test (i) ENUMERATE: adding it in estimation-prone languages recovers counting accuracy toward a reference; (ii) ESTIMATE: subtracting it induces biased estimation in enumeration-prone languages; (iii) DOSE-RESPONSE and cross-lingual generality; (iv) it changes ONLY the strategy, not the decoded cardinality, the item set, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the explicit-total control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Baselines: prompt-based 'count carefully step by step', per-language temperature, translate-to-English. Metrics: accuracy-gap closure, estimation-bias reduction, estimation-induction rate (reverse), cardinality-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts strategy but not per-item classification or unrelated answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: set-size breakdown (small/subitizable vs large sets); is English/high-resource the enumeration reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the asymmetry?); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank strategy subspace; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched cardinality and by showing content-invariant steering recovers accuracy without changing tokenization; whether one gating vector generalizes across problems and languages.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language counting accuracy and estimation-bias with language x set-size interaction controlling for per-item classification/fertility/resource, explicit-total control, cross-lingual cardinality-probe transfer R^2/rank-correlation and cardinality-present-under-error, strategy-probe transfer, signal-similarity vs strategy-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/fertility/typology correlation, patch-localized strategy-gating layer, cross-lingual gating transplant repair rate, causal steering accuracy-gap closure with dose-response and estimation-induction rate, cardinality-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention, comparison to count-carefully/temperature/translate baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Counting errors could reflect per-item misclassification rather than a strategy gate; the single-item-classification screen and the requirement that the cardinality is internally decodable on error items dissociate these, restricting the sharp test to items where each element is correctly classified. 2) The gate-vs-signal split could be confounded if the internal cardinality estimate itself differs by language; we test this directly via cross-lingual cardinality-probe transfer and the cardinality-present-under-error check, reporting how much of the gap is signal vs gate—either outcome is informative. 3) Tokenization fertility strongly confounds counting (longer lists split into more/rarer tokens); we control for fertility, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched cardinality and matched set size, and—crucially—the content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet recovers accuracy, dissociating the strategy gate from the token tax. 4) The enumeration-vs-estimation strategy label is an operationalization; we triangulate it via emitted item-by-item traces, allocated computation (layer-of-commitment), and the signed estimation-bias signature, and treat convergence rather than a single measure as evidence. 5) Some models/languages may count uniformly (no asymmetry) or estimate everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often a gap exists. 6) For very large N the model may estimate in ALL languages; we focus the strategy-gate claim on the mid-range where the two strategies dissociate and report the size regime explicitly. 7) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 8) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report cardinality-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention, and use the estimation-induction (reverse), reverse-consistency, and dose-response tests to ensure a genuine strategy dial rather than a global accuracy boost. 9) The strategy signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 10) Distinguishing from my running-state (dynamic tally over turns), ANS (ratio comparison acuity), number-naming (single-number magnitude), and precision (rounding) proposals is essential; here the object is SET-CARDINALITY COUNTING of a static presented set and its enumeration-vs-estimation strategy gate over a shared cardinality representation, grounded in the human dual-process counting literature.

Name: crosslingual_semantic_map_recovery
Title: Does a Model Redraw the Typological Semantic Map? Whether Multilingual LLMs Internally Recover the Universal Connectivity of Polyfunctional Meaning Spaces
Short Hypothesis: Linguistic typology's SEMANTIC MAPS posit that related functions of a polyfunctional gram (e.g. the many uses of the dative: recipient, beneficiary, experiencer, purpose; or of 'get'/reflexive/indefinite pronouns) occupy a universal connectivity graph where any single language's morpheme covers only a CONNECTED subgraph. We hypothesize a multilingual LLM internally recovers this universal semantic-map connectivity: (1) the model's internal representations of the distinct functions of a polyfunctional form are arranged so that cross-lingually co-lexified (adjacent-on-the-map) functions are closer than non-adjacent ones, reconstructing the human-attested map from text alone; (2) the recovered geometry predicts, better than surface co-occurrence, which function-pairs a HELD-OUT language will co-lexify (the connectedness constraint); and (3) the map is a causally real structure: interpolating a form's representation along a map edge shifts the model between adjacent functions, whereas jumping a non-edge does not.
Related Work: Semantic maps (Haspelmath 2003; the dative/indefinite-pronoun/reflexive maps; CLICS colexification networks, Rzymski et al. 2020) are an authoritative typological framework: cross-linguistic co-expression patterns constrain related functions to a universal connectivity graph on which each language covers a connected region. In NLP, colexification networks have been used to build/improve multilingual embeddings behaviorally (e.g. colexification-informed lexical typology), and my prior crosslingual_colexification proposal studied whether a query language's colexification of two concepts blurs their internal separability (a per-pair sense-conflation phenomenon). This proposal is fundamentally distinct: the object is the GLOBAL CONNECTIVITY STRUCTURE of a polyfunctional form's many functions (a graph over 4-8+ functions, e.g. the dative map), whether the model's internal geometry RECONSTRUCTS the human-attested semantic map, whether that geometry predicts the connectedness constraint on a held-out language's co-lexification, and whether map edges are causally real interpolation paths. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never tests recovery of typological semantic-map connectivity. No prior work asks whether an LLM internally redraws a semantic map, predicts co-lexification connectedness from its geometry, or treats map edges as causal interpolation directions. This is a structure-discovery + causal proposal grounded in an authoritative typological framework, not another shared-signal-plus-gate gating study.
Abstract: Linguistic typology's semantic maps encode a deep universal: the many functions a single morpheme can express—the dative's recipient, beneficiary, experiencer, and purpose uses, or the shared uses of reflexives, 'get'-passives, and indefinite pronouns—are not arbitrary but lie on a universal connectivity graph, and every language's form covers only a CONNECTED region of it. We ask whether a multilingual LLM, trained only on text, internally redraws these maps. We hypothesize that the model arranges the distinct functions of a polyfunctional form so that functions cross-lingually co-expressed (adjacent on the attested map) are represented closer than non-adjacent ones, reconstructing the human semantic map; that this internal geometry predicts, better than surface co-occurrence, which function-pairs a held-out language will co-lexify (the connectedness constraint); and that map edges are causally real—interpolating a form's representation along an edge moves the model between adjacent functions, while a non-edge jump does not. Using canonical semantic maps (dative, reflexive/middle, indefinite-pronoun series, instrumental-comitative) and CLICS colexification networks as ground truth, we extract per-function internal representations across many languages, recover the model's function-connectivity graph, and compare it to the typological map. We test whether the geometry forecasts held-out-language co-lexification connectedness, and causally probe map edges via representation interpolation. We reframe cross-lingual polyfunctionality as a recoverable, predictive, causally-structured semantic map inside the model, offering a mechanistic test of a foundational typological universal.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + light steering on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). ~15 typologically/genealogically diverse languages spanning families and scripts.
2) SEMANTIC MAPS & GROUND TRUTH: Use canonical, well-documented semantic maps with 4-8+ functions each: (A) DATIVE map (recipient, beneficiary, experiencer, purpose, direction, predicative possessor), (B) REFLEXIVE/MIDDLE map (reflexive, reciprocal, anticausative, passive, potential), (C) INDEFINITE-PRONOUN map (Haspelmath's specific-known/specific-unknown/irrealis/question/conditional/comparative/free-choice series), (D) INSTRUMENTAL-COMITATIVE map. Ground-truth connectivity from typological literature; supplement/validate co-lexification data with CLICS. For each function build ~30-50 native-verified example sentences per language that instantiate that function.
3) EXTRACT PER-FUNCTION REPRESENTATIONS: For each (function, language), pool hidden states at the polyfunctional form / relevant position across its example sentences to get a function centroid. Identify shared vs language-specific layers via per-layer language-ID probes (Wang 2025).
4) RECOVER THE MODEL'S CONNECTIVITY GRAPH: In representation space, compute pairwise function distances (cosine / CKA) aggregated across languages, and build the model's function-adjacency graph (e.g. via a minimum spanning graph / k-NN / distance threshold). CORE STRUCTURE TEST: does the recovered graph match the human-attested semantic map above chance? Metrics: graph edit distance to the typological map, edge-precision/recall vs a permuted-map null, and whether adjacent-on-map function pairs are significantly closer in representation than non-adjacent pairs (mixed-effects model of representational distance on map-adjacency, controlling for surface lexical co-occurrence frequency).
5) GEOMETRY-PREDICTS-CONNECTEDNESS (held-out languages): For each held-out language, the set of functions its polyfunctional form covers should form a CONNECTED region of the map. Test whether the MODEL's recovered geometry predicts which function-pairs that language co-lexifies (are covered by one form) better than (a) surface co-occurrence frequency and (b) a random map. Fit a predictor from representational adjacency to held-out co-lexification and report AUC / incremental predictive power over the surface baselines; test the connectedness constraint (predicted covered regions are connected in the recovered graph).
6) CAUSAL MAP-EDGE INTERPOLATION (decisive): For a polyfunctional form, derive function-centroid representations and INTERPOLATE the form's representation along a putative MAP EDGE (function A -> adjacent function B) vs a NON-EDGE jump (A -> non-adjacent function C), at the shared layer. Test whether edge-interpolation smoothly shifts the model's interpretation/behavior from A toward B (measured by function-disambiguation probes / continuation felicity), with graded dose-response, whereas non-edge interpolation does not produce a coherent intermediate reading. This treats map edges as causally real transition directions. Metrics: interpolation-induced function-shift rate along edges vs non-edges, dose-response, specificity, output fidelity.
7) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: per-map breakdown (dative vs reflexive vs indefinite-pronoun); does map recovery improve at shared mid-layers vs language-specific late layers?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training recover cleaner maps?); model scale; dissociation from surface co-occurrence (control for lexical-form frequency so recovery reflects function geometry, not string co-occurrence); robustness across distance metrics and graph-construction thresholds; comparison of recovered maps to CLICS colexification network structure.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: recovered-graph match to the typological semantic map (edit distance, edge P/R vs permuted null), adjacent-vs-non-adjacent representational-distance test controlling for surface co-occurrence, held-out-language co-lexification prediction AUC and connectedness-constraint satisfaction vs surface/random baselines, causal edge-vs-non-edge interpolation function-shift with dose-response and specificity, per-map/model/scale breakdowns, comparison to CLICS.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The model may NOT recover the typological map (functions arranged by surface co-occurrence rather than universal connectivity); this is itself an informative, publishable finding about whether LLMs internalize semantic-map universals, and we quantify recovery vs nulls rather than assuming it. 2) The central confound is surface lexical co-occurrence: functions co-expressed by one frequent form may be close simply because they share a string; we control for lexical-form frequency and string identity, aggregate representations across MANY languages (so any single language's form is not the driver), and treat the held-out-language prediction and causal interpolation (which do not depend on shared strings) as the load-bearing evidence. 3) Instantiating each function cleanly and equivalently across languages is delicate; we use native-verified example sets, canonical well-documented maps, and CLICS to validate ground-truth connectivity, and report sensitivity. 4) Semantic maps themselves are debated and some are non-planar / probabilistic; we use the best-attested maps, report which maps recover well, and treat map disagreements as analyzable rather than fatal. 5) Graph-recovery results depend on distance metric and thresholds; we report robustness across cosine/CKA and multiple graph-construction methods against a permuted-map null. 6) The causal interpolation may not yield coherent intermediate readings even along true edges (representations may not be linearly interpolable); a null here still tests whether edges are causal, and we report edge-vs-non-edge contrasts and dose-response rather than assuming smoothness. 7) Results may be model- and map-specific; we test four models and four maps and report per-condition results. 8) Distinguishing from my prior crosslingual_colexification proposal is essential; there the object was per-PAIR sense-conflation (do two concepts fused in one word become less separable), whereas here it is the GLOBAL CONNECTIVITY STRUCTURE of a polyfunctional form's many functions, its recovery of the human semantic map, its prediction of the connectedness constraint on held-out languages, and the causal reality of map edges—a structure-discovery account grounded in an authoritative typological framework.

Name: crosslingual_shortcut_reliance_gating
Title: Right Answer, Wrong Reason, in Some Tongues More Than Others: A Shared Task-Feature Representation Whose Shortcut-vs-Genuine Reliance Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When a task can be solved either by a genuine task-relevant feature or by a spurious shortcut cue (lexical overlap in NLI, position/first-mention bias, sentiment-word heuristics), a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of BOTH the genuine feature and the shortcut cue, but the query language causally sets how much it RELIES on the shortcut: for the SAME item the model uses the genuine feature in some languages and defaults to the spurious shortcut in others (typically lower-resource / typologically distant), producing a cross-lingual robustness asymmetry that is separable from the underlying feature representation and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable shortcut-reliance signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Shortcut/spurious-correlation reliance is heavily studied MONOLINGUALLY (HANS lexical-overlap heuristics in NLI; McCoy et al.; shortcut-learning surveys), and causal/invariant-representation work for low-resource NLP (Aminu et al. 2025; DINER debiasing) removes spurious features via training-side augmentation/invariance, treating shortcut reliance as an aggregate robustness scalar to be reduced. My prior gating-template proposals target distinct objects: leading-question framing (suggestive wording), anchoring (irrelevant numeric prime), credential-deference (authoritative source), analogy (relational vs surface association in analogies), and confabulation. NONE frame SHORTCUT-vs-GENUINE-FEATURE reliance as a shared internal representation gated by a language-DEPENDENT reliance threshold, dissociate the shortcut-reliance gate from the co-present genuine-feature representation, or causally localize and steer a shortcut-reliance signal to equalize robustness across languages while preserving genuine-feature use. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies shortcut reliance or its language modulation. This differs from my analogy proposal (relational mapping vs surface association within analogies specifically) by targeting general task-solving shortcuts (lexical-overlap NLI, position bias, sentiment heuristics) and their internal shared-feature-vs-gate decomposition, and from training-side debiasing by giving an inference-time, mechanistic, causal account.
Abstract: Language models often reach the right answer for the wrong reason—exploiting a spurious shortcut (surface lexical overlap, first-mention position, a sentiment keyword) instead of the genuine task-relevant feature. We ask whether this shortcut reliance is language-dependent, and how it is implemented internally. We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of BOTH the genuine task feature and the co-present shortcut cue, but the query language causally sets how strongly it relies on the shortcut, so for the SAME item the model uses the genuine feature in some languages and defaults to the shortcut in others—worst in lower-resource, typologically distant languages—independent of whether it can represent the genuine feature. This predicts a cross-lingual robustness asymmetry dissociable from the shared feature representation. We build ShortcutGateProbe from parallel diagnostic sets across 12 languages: HANS-style NLI where lexical overlap and true entailment are decorrelated, position-bias QA where the answer's position and correctness are decorrelated, and sentiment items where a salient sentiment word conflicts with the true label. Behaviorally we measure per-language shortcut-reliance (accuracy on shortcut-CONSISTENT minus shortcut-CONFLICTING items) and test whether it tracks resource level and typological distance beyond genuine-feature competence. We train a linear probe for both the genuine feature and the shortcut cue and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the robustness gap into a shared genuine-feature representation versus a language-set shortcut-reliance gate—high shortcut reliance should coincide with an intact internal genuine-feature signal. Via activation and path patching we localize a shortcut-reliance signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model use the genuine feature across languages—or, in reverse, induce shortcut reliance—while leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual robustness disparity as a shared feature representation under a steerable, language-dependent shortcut-reliance gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili, Yoruba).
2) DATASET (ShortcutGateProbe): three diagnostic tasks each with a clean shortcut-vs-genuine decorrelation. (A) LEXICAL-OVERLAP NLI (HANS-style): premise-hypothesis pairs where surface word overlap and true entailment are crossed, so overlap is a shortcut; ~250 items with SHORTCUT-CONSISTENT (overlap predicts correct) and SHORTCUT-CONFLICTING (overlap predicts wrong) subsets. (B) POSITION-BIAS QA / multiple-choice: items where the correct option's position (first/last) and correctness are decorrelated, so position is a shortcut. (C) SENTIMENT-KEYWORD: items where a salient sentiment word's polarity conflicts with the true label. Keep item content and gold labels fixed across languages; translate/native-verify. Include a NEUTRAL control where shortcut and genuine feature agree (bounds the effect). Screen GENUINE-FEATURE competence per language (accuracy on shortcut-CONSISTENT items and a genuine-feature-only probe) so shortcut reliance is measured given the model CAN represent the feature. Record tokenization fertility. Short scoreable answers.
3) BEHAVIORAL SHORTCUT-RELIANCE ASYMMETRY TEST: Per (item, language) compute SHORTCUT RELIANCE = accuracy on shortcut-CONSISTENT minus shortcut-CONFLICTING items (a positive gap = reliance on the shortcut). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME items, shortcut reliance is systematically higher in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond genuine-feature competence and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of conflicting-item error on (language, task, resource tier via URIEL, typological distance, tokenization fertility, consistent-item accuracy), item as random effect; test the language effect. Report per-language shortcut-reliance profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical items; replicate the English HANS-style shortcut effect as a sanity check.
4) SHARED FEATURE & SHORTCUT PROBES + TRANSFER: At the pre-answer position pool the hidden state; train linear probes to decode (i) the GENUINE task feature (true entailment / correct-option content / true polarity) and (ii) the SHORTCUT cue (overlap level / option position / sentiment-keyword polarity) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, and apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC for both as evidence of language-independent representations of both the genuine feature and the shortcut. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on shortcut-CONFLICTING ERROR items, test whether the internal GENUINE-feature signal still points to the correct answer across languages—the signature of 'knows the right feature, follows the shortcut'.
5) GATE-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer genuine-feature signal across languages (should be similar on matched items) versus the emitted answer (which follows the shortcut in some languages). Define a per-language SHORTCUT-RELIANCE GATE mapping (genuine-feature signal, shortcut signal) to the emitted answer; test whether cross-lingual robustness differences are explained by a shifted gate (more weight on the shortcut) on a similar genuine-feature signal rather than a weaker genuine signal. Correlate per-language gate strength with resource tier and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-decision split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE SHORTCUT-RELIANCE SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that uses the genuine feature and one that follows the shortcut on the SAME conflicting item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips shortcut->genuine WITHOUT changing the decoded genuine-feature or shortcut signals. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gating components from a robust language into a shortcut-reliant run. Attention analysis: does the shortcut-reliant response over-attend to the shortcut cue (overlapping words / option position / sentiment word), more so in high-reliance languages?
7) CAUSAL SHORTCUT-RELIANCE STEERING (decisive): Derive a shortcut-reliance steering vector via difference-of-means (genuine-feature-using runs minus shortcut-following runs on matched conflicting items). Test (i) DEBIAS: adding it in shortcut-reliant languages makes the model use the genuine feature toward a reference (robust) level; (ii) INDUCE: subtracting it makes robust languages follow the shortcut; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where reliance was worst; (iv) DOSE-RESPONSE: scaling produces graded reliance shifts; (v) it changes ONLY shortcut-vs-genuine reliance, NOT the decoded genuine-feature/shortcut signals, item content, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not harm the NEUTRAL control (where shortcut and feature agree), and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Baselines: prompt-based 'ignore surface cues', per-language threshold tuning, translate-to-English, and a training-side invariance/DINER-style baseline for comparison. Metrics: shortcut-reliance-gap closure, genuine-feature-accuracy recovery on conflicting items, shortcut-induction rate (reverse), genuine/shortcut-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts reliance but not the underlying feature/shortcut readouts or unrelated answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: task breakdown (lexical-overlap NLI vs position bias vs sentiment keyword); is English/high-resource the robust reference?; does reliance track resource beyond genuine competence?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the asymmetry?); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank shortcut-reliance subspace; whether one gating vector generalizes across tasks and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched genuine-feature signal and by showing content-invariant steering shifts reliance without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language shortcut reliance and its resource/typology regression controlling for genuine-feature competence/fertility, English HANS-style replication, cross-lingual genuine-feature and shortcut probe transfer AUROC and genuine-signal-correct-under-shortcut-error, signal-similarity vs reliance-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized shortcut-reliance layer and attention-to-shortcut evidence, cross-lingual gating transplant repair rate, causal steering shortcut-reliance-gap closure with dose-response and shortcut-induction rate, genuine-feature-accuracy recovery, NEUTRAL-control and general-QA retention, comparison to prompt/threshold-tuning/translate/training-side-debiasing baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The gate-vs-signal split could be confounded if the genuine-feature signal itself differs by language (the model genuinely fails to represent the feature in some languages rather than knowing-it-but-shortcutting); we test this directly by verifying the genuine-feature signal still points correct on shortcut-error items across languages via probe transfer, screen genuine-feature competence, and report how much of the gap is signal vs gate—either outcome is informative. 2) Shortcut reliance could reflect a genuine-feature-competence gap; we condition on items where the model succeeds on shortcut-CONSISTENT versions (feature is usable) so residual conflicting-item error reflects shortcut reliance, not incapacity. 3) Tokenization fertility confounds (lexical-overlap and position cues interact with subword splitting); we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched genuine-feature signal, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts reliance, dissociating the gate from the token tax. 4) The shortcut/genuine probes could latch onto surface cues; the genuine-signal-correct-under-shortcut-error test, the attention-to-shortcut analysis, cross-lingual invariance, and the cross-lingual gating transplant guard against this. 5) The key specificity guard: debiasing steering must NOT harm cases where the shortcut is legitimately aligned with the answer; we include the NEUTRAL control (shortcut and feature agree) and report its retention, using it to ensure the steering reduces undue shortcut reliance rather than suppressing a useful cue—if entangled, that is itself a publishable finding. 6) Some models/languages may show no shortcut-reliance asymmetry (uniformly robust or uniformly shortcut-reliant); either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often a gap exists, replicating the English shortcut effect first. 7) Constructing clean shortcut-vs-genuine decorrelation equivalently across languages is delicate (lexical overlap and word order differ); we native-verify, keep gold labels and item structure fixed, adapt HANS-style templates cross-lingually, and analyze each task separately. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report genuine/shortcut-signal/output fidelity, NEUTRAL-control and general-QA retention, and use the shortcut-induction (reverse), reverse-consistency, and dose-response tests to ensure a genuine shortcut-reliance dial. 10) The shortcut-reliance signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my leading-question, anchoring, credential-deference, and analogy proposals is essential; here the object is general task-solving SHORTCUT-vs-GENUINE-FEATURE reliance (lexical-overlap NLI, position bias, sentiment heuristics) and its language-set reliance gate over a co-present shared genuine-feature representation, and from training-side debiasing (Aminu 2025, DINER) by providing an inference-time, mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account those methods lack.
