Test (i) DEBIAS: adding it in shortcut-reliant languages makes the model use the genuine feature toward a reference level; (ii) INDUCE: subtracting it makes robust languages follow the shortcut; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where reliance was worst; (iv) DOSE-RESPONSE: scaling produces graded reliance shifts; (v) it changes ONLY shortcut-vs-genuine reliance, NOT the decoded genuine-feature/shortcut signals, item content, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not harm the NEUTRAL control (where shortcut and feature agree), and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Baselines: prompt-based 'ignore surface cues', per-language threshold tuning, translate-to-English, and a training-side invariance/DINER-style baseline for comparison. Metrics: shortcut-reliance-gap closure, genuine-feature-accuracy recovery on conflicting items, shortcut-induction rate (reverse), genuine/shortcut-signal/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts reliance but not the underlying feature/shortcut readouts or unrelated answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: task breakdown (lexical-overlap NLI vs position bias vs sentiment keyword); is English/high-resource the robust reference?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the asymmetry?); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank shortcut-reliance subspace; whether one gating vector generalizes across tasks and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched genuine-feature signal and by showing content-invariant steering shifts reliance without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language shortcut reliance and its resource/typology regression controlling for genuine-feature competence/fertility, English HANS-style replication, cross-lingual genuine-feature and shortcut probe transfer AUROC and genuine-signal-correct-under-shortcut-error, signal-similarity vs reliance-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-resource/typology correlation, patch-localized shortcut-reliance layer and attention-to-shortcut evidence, cross-lingual gating transplant repair rate, causal steering shortcut-reliance-gap closure with dose-response and shortcut-induction rate, genuine-feature-accuracy recovery, NEUTRAL-control and general-QA retention, comparison to prompt/threshold-tuning/translate/training-side-debiasing baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The gate-vs-signal split could be confounded if the genuine-feature signal itself differs by language (the model genuinely fails to represent the feature in some languages rather than knowing-it-but-shortcutting); we test this directly by verifying the genuine-feature signal still points correct on shortcut-error items across languages via probe transfer, screen genuine-feature competence, and report how much of the gap is signal vs gate—either outcome is informative. 2) Shortcut reliance could reflect a genuine-feature-competence gap; we condition on items where the model succeeds on shortcut-CONSISTENT versions (feature is usable) so residual conflicting-item error reflects shortcut reliance, not incapacity. 3) Tokenization fertility confounds (lexical-overlap and position cues interact with subword splitting); we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched genuine-feature signal, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts reliance, dissociating the gate from the token tax. 4) The shortcut/genuine probes could latch onto surface cues; the genuine-signal-correct-under-shortcut-error test, the attention-to-shortcut analysis, cross-lingual invariance, and the cross-lingual gating transplant guard against this. 5) The key specificity guard: debiasing steering must NOT harm cases where the shortcut is legitimately aligned with the answer; we include the NEUTRAL control and report its retention, ensuring the steering reduces undue shortcut reliance rather than suppressing a useful cue—if entangled, that is itself a publishable finding. 6) Some models/languages may show no shortcut-reliance asymmetry (uniformly robust or uniformly shortcut-reliant); either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often a gap exists, replicating the English shortcut effect first. 7) Constructing clean shortcut-vs-genuine decorrelation equivalently across languages is delicate (lexical overlap and word order differ); we native-verify, keep gold labels and item structure fixed, adapt HANS-style templates cross-lingually, and analyze each task separately. 8) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 9) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report genuine/shortcut-signal/output fidelity, NEUTRAL-control and general-QA retention, and use the shortcut-induction (reverse), reverse-consistency, and dose-response tests to ensure a genuine shortcut-reliance dial. 10) The shortcut-reliance signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 11) Distinguishing from my leading-question, anchoring, credential-deference, and analogy proposals is essential; here the object is general task-solving SHORTCUT-vs-GENUINE-FEATURE reliance (lexical-overlap NLI, position bias, sentiment heuristics) and its language-set reliance gate over a co-present shared genuine-feature representation, and from training-side debiasing (Aminu 2025, DINER) by providing an inference-time, mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account those methods lack.

Name: crosslingual_clarification_seeking_gating
Title: Should It Ask, or Just Guess? A Shared Ambiguity-Detection Signal Whose Clarification-Seeking Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When a user request is genuinely UNDER-SPECIFIED or AMBIGUOUS (multiple valid interpretations, a missing critical parameter), a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal 'ambiguity' signal that registers that the request cannot be resolved without more information, but whether it behaviorally EXPRESSES that by ASKING A CLARIFYING QUESTION (vs silently guessing one interpretation) is gated by the query language: for the SAME ambiguous request the model asks in some languages and silently commits to a guess in others (typically lower-resource / typologically distant / higher-power-distance), producing a cross-lingual clarification asymmetry that is separable from the model internally detecting the ambiguity and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable clarification-gate signal without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Clarification-question generation and ambiguity detection are studied in NLP (task-oriented dialogue, ambiguous-QA like AmbigQA, 'ask-vs-guess' behavior of assistants), but this is English-centric and behavioral, treating clarification as a capability to be improved, with no internal representation, no cross-lingual decomposition, and no causal intervention. My prior gating-template proposals target distinct objects: abstention concerns attempt-vs-abstain on ANSWERABLE-vs-UNANSWERABLE questions (a factual-knowledge gate, not ambiguity), confabulation concerns fabricating detail about NONEXISTENT entities, and default-referent concerns silently filling an UNDER-SPECIFIED category referent to continue. This proposal is distinct because the object is recognizing that a request is AMBIGUOUS/UNDER-SPECIFIED and ASKING for clarification (an interactive cooperation behavior with a clear normative benchmark: genuinely ambiguous requests should elicit a clarifying question, unambiguous ones should not), decomposed into a shared ambiguity-detection signal versus a language-set clarification-expression gate, and causally localized/steered. Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies clarification-seeking or its language modulation. No prior work (i) tests whether clarification-seeking is language-dependent beyond the model's internal ambiguity detection, (ii) decomposes it into a shared ambiguity signal versus a language-set expression gate, or (iii) causally localizes and steers a clarification gate.
Abstract: A cooperative assistant, faced with an ambiguous request, asks a clarifying question instead of guessing; a poor one silently commits to one interpretation and may do the wrong thing. As LLMs serve users worldwide, we ask whether the query language changes whether the model asks or guesses on the same ambiguous request, and how this is implemented internally. We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal ambiguity signal that registers when a request is under-specified, but the query language causally gates whether that ambiguity is behaviorally expressed as a clarifying question, so the SAME ambiguous request elicits a clarification in some languages and a silent guess in others—worst in lower-resource, typologically distant, higher-power-distance languages—independent of whether the model internally detects the ambiguity. This predicts a cross-lingual clarification asymmetry dissociable from ambiguity detection. We build ClarifyGateProbe, parallel requests across 12 languages, split into genuinely AMBIGUOUS/UNDER-SPECIFIED items (a critical parameter is missing or multiple interpretations are valid) and matched UNAMBIGUOUS controls, with content held fixed. Behaviorally we measure per-language clarification rate on ambiguous items and over-asking on unambiguous ones, and test whether under-asking tracks resource level, typological distance, and power-distance norms beyond ambiguity detection. We train a linear ambiguity probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the clarification gap into a shared ambiguity-detection component versus a language-set expression gate—verifying the ambiguity is internally detected even where the model silently guesses. Via activation and path patching we localize a clarification-gate signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to make the model ask across languages—or, in reverse, suppress asking—while verifying it does not over-ask on unambiguous items and leaving the surface language unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual cooperation disparity as a shared ambiguity signal under a steerable, language-dependent clarification gate.
Experiments:
1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/culturally/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili, Yoruba), coded for documented power-distance/directness norms plus URIEL typological/resource distance (graded predictors).
2) DATASET (ClarifyGateProbe): ~500 requests, half GENUINELY AMBIGUOUS/UNDER-SPECIFIED (a critical parameter is missing—'book me a flight' without dates/destination; multiple valid referents—'summarize the report' when several were mentioned; a term with distinct task-relevant meanings) where the cooperative behavior is to ASK a clarifying question, and half matched UNAMBIGUOUS controls (the same request type but fully specified) where asking would be over-asking. Keep request content fixed across languages; translate/native-verify. Screen that the model can, when asked directly, IDENTIFY what is missing/ambiguous per language (so under-asking is not failure to comprehend the request). Record tokenization fertility. Classify responses as ASK (clarifying question) vs GUESS (silently commits to an interpretation) via a validated classifier + human checks on a subset.
3) BEHAVIORAL ASYMMETRY TEST: Per (item, language) record clarification rate on ambiguous items and over-ask rate on unambiguous controls. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME ambiguous request, clarification rate is systematically lower in lower-resource/typologically distant/higher-power-distance languages, beyond ambiguity detection and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of under-asking on (language, resource tier via URIEL, typological distance, power-distance code, tokenization fertility, ambiguity-identification screen), item as random effect; test the language effect. Compare against unambiguous controls (over-asking should be language-flatter). Report per-language clarification profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical ambiguous requests; replicate an English ask-vs-guess baseline.
4) SHARED AMBIGUITY PROBE & TRANSFER: At the pre-response position pool the hidden state; train a linear probe to decode AMBIGUOUS/UNDER-SPECIFIED vs FULLY-SPECIFIED on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC as evidence of a language-independent ambiguity-detection signal. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on GUESS (under-asking) items, test whether the internal ambiguity signal is still strong across languages—the signature of 'detects the ambiguity, guesses anyway'.
5) GATE-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer ambiguity signal across languages (should be similar on matched items) versus the emitted ask/guess decision (which diverges). Define a per-language CLARIFICATION GATE mapping the ambiguity signal to asking; test whether cross-lingual under-asking differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar ambiguity signal rather than weaker detection. Correlate per-language gate strength with power-distance norms, resource tier, and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-decision split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens.
6) LOCALIZE THE CLARIFICATION-GATE SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that asks and one that guesses on the SAME ambiguous item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer flips guess->ask WITHOUT changing the decoded ambiguity signal or request content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gating components from an ask-prone language into a guessing run.
7) CAUSAL CLARIFICATION STEERING (decisive): Derive a clarification-gate steering vector via difference-of-means (ask runs minus guess runs at matched ambiguity). Test (i) ASK: adding it in under-asking languages makes the model ask clarifying questions on ambiguous items toward a reference level; (ii) SUPPRESS: subtracting it induces silent guessing in ask-prone languages; (iii) it works cross-lingually, more strongly where the gap was largest; (iv) DOSE-RESPONSE and cross-lingual generality; (v) it changes ONLY ask-vs-guess on AMBIGUOUS items, NOT over-asking on UNAMBIGUOUS controls (specificity—the model must not start pestering with questions on clear requests), the decoded ambiguity signal, request content, or surface language (fidelity checks), and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Baselines: prompt-based 'ask if anything is unclear', per-language threshold tuning, translate-to-English. Metrics: clarification-gap closure, unambiguous-control over-asking retention, guess-induction rate (reverse), ambiguity-signal/output fidelity, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts clarification but not unrelated or unambiguous-control answers.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: ambiguity-type breakdown (missing-parameter vs multiple-referent vs term-ambiguity); is English/high-resource the ask-prone reference?; does under-asking track power-distance/directness beyond resource level?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten the asymmetry?); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank clarification subspace; whether one gating vector generalizes across items and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched ambiguity signal and by showing content-invariant steering shifts clarification without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language clarification and over-ask rates and their power-distance/resource/typology regression controlling for ambiguity identification, English ask-vs-guess replication, cross-lingual ambiguity probe transfer AUROC and ambiguity-signal-present-under-guessing, signal-similarity vs decision-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-norm/resource/typology correlation, patch-localized clarification-gate layer, cross-lingual gating transplant repair rate, causal steering clarification-gap closure with dose-response and guess-induction rate, unambiguous-control specificity, ambiguity-signal/output fidelity, general-QA retention, comparison to prompt/threshold-tuning/translate baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The gate-vs-signal split could be confounded if the ambiguity signal itself differs by language (the model genuinely fails to detect the ambiguity in some languages rather than detecting-but-guessing); we test this directly by verifying an intact internal ambiguity signal on guessing items across languages via probe transfer, screen ambiguity identification, and report how much of the gap is detection vs gate—either outcome is informative. 2) Under-asking could reflect an ambiguity-detection gap; we screen that the model can identify what is missing when asked directly and restrict the sharp test to such items, so residual guessing reflects the gate. 3) The key specificity guard: any ask-inducing intervention must NOT make the model over-ask on unambiguous requests; we include unambiguous controls and report over-asking retention as a primary metric, ensuring the steering targets genuine under-asking, not questioning in general—if entangled, that is itself a publishable finding. 4) Tokenization fertility confounds; we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched ambiguity signal, and content-invariant steering does not change tokenization yet shifts clarification. 5) Ask-vs-guess classification is noisy across languages (hedged answers, partial clarification); we validate the classifier against human labels per language and report reliability. 6) Some models/languages may show no clarification asymmetry (uniformly ask or uniformly guess); either is an informative, publishable finding, and we quantify how often a gap exists, replicating the English effect first. 7) What counts as 'genuinely ambiguous' can be graded; we use items with clear native-consensus ambiguity (missing a critical parameter) and analyze borderline items separately. 8) Power-distance/directness norm coding is coarse; we treat it as a graded predictor and report sensitivity. 9) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 10) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic questioning lever; we report ambiguity-signal/output fidelity, unambiguous-control and general-QA retention, and use the guess-induction (reverse), reverse-consistency, and dose-response tests to ensure a genuine clarification gate. 11) The clarification signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 12) Distinguishing from my abstention (answerable-vs-unanswerable factual gate), confabulation (nonexistent entities), and default-referent (silently filling an under-specified category to continue) proposals is essential; here the object is recognizing that a request is AMBIGUOUS/UNDER-SPECIFIED and ASKING for clarification (an interactive cooperation behavior with a clear normative benchmark) and its language-set clarification gate over a shared ambiguity-detection signal, with direct assistant-usability stakes.

Name: crosslingual_punctuation_prosody_gating
Title: Reading the Tone in Punctuation, in Every Language: A Shared Prosodic-Intent Representation Whose Expression Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: Text carries prosodic/emotional intent through punctuation and typographic cues (exclamation marks, ellipses, ALL-CAPS, repeated letters/marks, question marks used for irony/incredulity). We hypothesize a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal 'prosodic-intent' representation of such cues (registering the intended emphasis, incredulity, excitement, or hesitancy a written cue conveys), but whether that intent is behaviorally EXPRESSED (interpreting an exclamation as excitement/urgency, an ironic '?' as incredulity, ellipsis as hesitation, ALL-CAPS as emphasis/shouting) is gated by the query language: the SAME punctuated text is assigned the same prosodic intent internally across languages yet processed at face value (ignoring the cue) far more often in lower-resource / typologically distant languages whose punctuation-and-typographic conventions differ from the dominant languages. The prosodic-intent signal is causally localizable and its expression steerable, so language-gated failures can be repaired without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Prosody and intonation in language processing are studied almost entirely in SPEECH (Fujisaki F0 modeling, emotion recognition from pitch/intensity; the search returned only speech-synthesis and speech-emotion work, e.g. Zervas et al. 2006, Hirst 2000, and multilingual speech/prosody reviews), never in text-only LLMs and their reading of WRITTEN prosodic cues. In NLP, emoji/punctuation-sentiment is a supervised classification task, monolingual and behavioral. My prior proposals cover figurative meaning (metaphor/idiom), pragmatic implicature, illocutionary force, information structure (focus), and affective-intensity reweighting of DESCRIBED emotion; NONE address WRITTEN PROSODY—the emphasis/emotion/irony conveyed by punctuation and typographic cues (!, ..., ALL-CAPS, repeated marks, ironic ?)—whether it is a shared cross-lingual representation, whether its behavioral expression is language-gated, whether it tracks punctuation-convention typology, or whether the prosodic-intent signal is causally localizable and steerable. My affective-intensity proposal reweights the intensity of an emotion the TEXT DESCRIBES; here the object is the prosodic/emphatic intent CARRIED BY the punctuation/typography itself (a written-prosody cue), a distinct signal with cross-linguistic convention variation (e.g. ellipsis/exclamation usage, CJK vs Latin punctuation, script-specific emphasis devices). Mechanistic multilingual work (Wang 2025; Lim 2025) locates a shared concept space with language-specific decoding for facts but never studies written prosody. This is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual account of how LLMs read prosodic intent from punctuation and typography.
Abstract: Writing conveys tone without sound: an exclamation mark shouts, an ellipsis trails off, ALL-CAPS emphasizes, and a lone question mark can signal incredulity rather than a question. Reading this written prosody is essential to understanding intent, yet languages differ in their punctuation and typographic conventions. We ask whether a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-independent internal representation of the prosodic/emotional intent carried by such cues, and whether that internal representation is decoupled from how reliably it is behaviorally expressed across languages. We hypothesize that models register the same prosodic intent across languages internally, but the query language gates whether it is surfaced—interpreting an exclamation as excitement/urgency, an ironic '?' as incredulity, ellipsis as hesitation, ALL-CAPS as emphasis—so the SAME punctuated text is read at face value (ignoring the cue) far more in lower-resource, typologically distant languages, even though the model 'gets the tone'. We build ProsodyProbe, parallel sentences across languages that carry a prosodic cue via punctuation/typography (exclamation, ellipsis, ALL-CAPS, repeated marks, ironic question mark), each with a tone/intent probe, a cue-vs-no-cue minimal pair, and a control where the cue is absent. Behaviorally we measure per-language prosodic-intent accuracy and face-value drift and test whether it tracks resource level, typological distance, and punctuation-convention typology beyond literal comprehension. We train a linear prosodic-intent probe and test whether a single probe transfers zero-shot across languages, then decompose the failure into a shared intent component versus a language-set expression gate, verifying the correct intent is internally present even where behavior drifts to face value. Via activation and path patching we localize a prosodic-intent signal, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to surface (or flip) the read tone while leaving the surface language and the cue unchanged. We reframe cross-lingual tone-reading gaps as a steerable gate over a shared written-prosody representation.
Experiments:
1) LANGUAGES & MODELS: 8 typologically/script/resource-diverse languages spanning punctuation-convention variation (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese [CJK punctuation], Japanese), coded for punctuation/typographic-emphasis conventions (exclamation/ellipsis usage, full-width vs Latin marks, script-specific emphasis devices) plus URIEL distance. MODELS: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B; inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs.
2) DATASET (ProsodyProbe): ~500 base sentences, each rendered with a PROSODIC CUE via punctuation/typography and in a matched NO-CUE (plain) version: (A) EXCLAMATION (excitement/urgency: 'The house is on fire!'), (B) ELLIPSIS (hesitation/trailing/implication: 'Well... I guess so'), (C) ALL-CAPS/repeated letters (emphasis/shouting: 'I said NO'), (D) IRONIC/INCREDULOUS QUESTION MARK ('You did WHAT?' / a statement + '?' signaling disbelief), (E) REPEATED MARKS ('really???'). Probes: (i) TONE/INTENT identification ('What tone/emotion does the writer convey?' MC: excited/urgent vs neutral, incredulous vs genuine-question, hesitant vs confident, emphatic vs plain), (ii) DOWNSTREAM INFERENCE where the cue's intent determines the answer (e.g. does the writer accept? is the writer surprised?), (iii) CUE-vs-NO-CUE minimal-pair judgment (does the punctuation change the intent?). Include a NO-CUE control (bounds the effect and separates prosody-reading from literal comprehension). Keep sentence content and cue fixed across languages; translate/native-verify, realizing the cue naturally per language (respecting each language's punctuation conventions); flag cues with no natural equivalent (e.g. ALL-CAPS in non-cased scripts — use script-appropriate emphasis or exclude). Record tokenization fertility; screen literal comprehension via the no-cue control. Short scoreable answers.
3) BEHAVIORAL EXPRESSION TEST: Per (item, language) record correct prosodic-intent reading vs FACE-VALUE DRIFT (ignoring the cue, e.g. treating an ironic '?' as a genuine question, ellipsis as a mere pause, ALL-CAPS as neutral). KEY hypothesis: for the SAME cue, face-value drift is systematically higher in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, and worst where the language's punctuation conventions differ most from the dominant languages, beyond literal comprehension and tokenization. Mixed-effects logistic regression of face-value drift on (punctuation-convention typology, cue type, language, resource tier via URIEL, tokenization fertility, comprehension indicator), item as random effect; compare against the no-cue control (language-flatter). Report per-language and per-cue-type profiles, cross-lingual disagreement on identical punctuated sentences, and replicate an English written-prosody baseline.
4) SHARED PROSODIC-INTENT PROBE & TRANSFER: At each layer pool the hidden state at the cue/pre-answer position; train a linear probe to decode the PROSODIC INTENT (excited/urgent, incredulous, hesitant, emphatic vs neutral) on ENGLISH data, apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report macro-F1/AUROC as evidence of a language-independent written-prosody representation. CRITICAL: test transfer ACROSS languages with different punctuation conventions (train on English exclamation/ellipsis, test on CJK-punctuation Chinese/Japanese) — high transfer despite different surface marks evidences a shared intent representation. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. On FACE-VALUE-DRIFT items, test whether the correct prosodic intent is still internally decodable across ALL languages even when behavior drifts — the signature of language-gated expression over an intact intent signal.
5) INTENT-vs-EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer intent signal across languages (should be similar if the intent is shared) versus behavioral reading (which diverges). Define an EXPRESSION GATE mapping internal intent to surfaced behavior per language; test whether cross-lingual differences are explained by a weaker gate on a similar intent signal rather than weaker intent detection. Correlate gate strength with punctuation-convention typology, resource tier, and typological distance (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split with per-layer language-ID probes.
6) LOCALIZE THE PROSODIC-INTENT SIGNAL: Via activation and path patching between a language that surfaces the correct tone and one that drifts to face value on the SAME item, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer surfaces the correct prosodic intent WITHOUT changing the decoded propositional content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the intent representation FROM a high-expression language into a drifting run. Attention analysis: does the answer attend to the punctuation-cue token, more so in high-expression languages?
7) CAUSAL PROSODIC-INTENT STEERING (decisive): Derive a prosodic-intent steering vector via difference-of-means (correct-intent runs minus face-value-drift runs, plus cue-vs-no-cue contrasts). Test (i) SURFACE: adding it to drift-prone languages increases correct tone reading toward high-expression levels; (ii) FLIP: steering along the axis makes the model read a plain statement as emphatic/incredulous (and vice versa) on well-handled items; (iii) it works cross-lingually, stronger where expression was weakest; (iv) it changes ONLY the read prosodic intent, not the decoded propositional content or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the no-cue control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Metrics: face-value-drift-gap closure, intent-flip rate (reverse), intent-signal/content/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering changes tone judgments but not no-cue-control or unrelated answers, guarding against a generic accuracy lever.
8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: cue-type breakdown (exclamation vs ellipsis vs ALL-CAPS vs ironic-? vs repeated marks — which leak most); does the shared intent signal transfer across differing-punctuation languages?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya); probe layer/dimensionality; token-pooling (punctuation/typographic cues tokenize differently across scripts); whether a single intent vector generalizes across cue types and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal intent and by showing content-invariant steering surfaces tone without changing tokenization.
EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language per-cue-type prosodic-intent accuracy and face-value-drift rate, drift regression controlling for comprehension/fertility/resource with punctuation-convention-typology effect, English written-prosody replication, cross-lingual prosodic-intent probe transfer F1/AUROC (including across differing-punctuation languages) and intent-present-under-drift, cross-lingual intent-representation similarity (CKA/cosine), intent-similarity vs expression-divergence (gate) decomposition, gate-vs-typology/resource correlation, patch-localized prosodic-intent layer and cue-token attention evidence, cross-lingual intent transplant recovery rate, causal steering drift-gap closure and intent-flip rates, intent-signal/content/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The intent-vs-expression split could be confounded if the prosodic-intent signal itself differs by language; we test this directly by verifying correct-intent decodability across all languages (especially differing-punctuation ones) on drift items via probe transfer, and report how much of the gap is intent-detection vs gate. 2) Face-value drift could reflect literal-comprehension failure rather than an expression gate; we use the matched NO-CUE control and comprehension screening so residual drift reflects prosody reading, not reading. 3) Prosodic cues can be genuinely ambiguous (an exclamation may signal excitement or anger; ellipsis has many uses); we restrict scored items to cues with a clear context-determined intent (native-verified) and analyze ambiguous ones separately. 4) Punctuation/typographic conventions differ sharply across scripts (CJK full-width marks, non-cased scripts lack ALL-CAPS, some languages use different emphasis devices); we native-verify natural realization, treat cue type and convention as factors, flag cues with no natural equivalent (using them for transfer-limit analysis), and use script-appropriate emphasis where the Latin device is unavailable. 5) The transfer-across-differing-punctuation-languages test is the key novelty but could fail if intent is only represented via each language's surface marks (an equally informative result about whether written prosody is genuinely shared vs convention-specific); we report it either way. 6) Tokenization fertility strongly interacts with punctuation (marks/caps tokenize differently across scripts); we control for it, compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched internal intent, use multiple token-pooling schemes, and content-invariant steering surfaces tone without changing tokenization, dissociating the gate from tokenization. 7) Some models may read written prosody uniformly across languages (no gap) or drift everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding about the universality of cross-lingual written-prosody reading, and we quantify how often the gap occurs. 8) The intent probe could latch onto surface punctuation-token cues rather than a genuine intent representation; the transfer across differing-punctuation languages, the intent-present-under-drift test, the cue-token attention analysis, cross-lingual invariance, and the cross-lingual transplant guard against this. 9) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 10) Steering may harm fluency or act as a generic accuracy lever; we report intent-signal/content/output fidelity, control and general-QA retention, and use the intent-flip (reverse) and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine prosodic-intent gate. 11) The gate/intent signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 12) Distinguishing from my affective-intensity (reweighting the intensity of a DESCRIBED emotion), metaphor/idiom, illocutionary-force, and information-structure proposals is essential; here the object is the prosodic/emphatic intent CARRIED BY punctuation and typographic cues (written prosody) and the language-gating of its expression, a distinct signal with cross-linguistic convention variation, and—being text-only—distinct from the entirely speech-based prosody literature the search surfaced.

Name: crosslingual_trait_expression_gating
Title: Same Disposition, Different Tone: A Shared Personality-Trait Representation Whose Behavioral Expression Is Gated by the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: A multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of its dispositional TRAIT tendency along interpretable axes (agreeableness/warmth, assertiveness, cautiousness/risk-aversion, honesty-modesty), but whether that trait is behaviorally EXPRESSED in open interaction (a helpful reply's warmth, an advisory answer's assertiveness, a recommendation's caution) is gated by the query language: for the SAME situation the model expresses the same internal trait more strongly in some languages and is flattened toward a narrow, socially-desirable default in others (typically lower-resource / typologically distant), producing a cross-lingual trait-expression asymmetry that is separable from the shared trait representation and from surface style, and is causally repairable by shifting a localizable trait-expression gate without changing the surface language.
Related Work: Behavioral work documents that aligned LLMs cluster in a narrow, normatively positive personality-response region across languages with only localized facet variation (Heierli et al. 2026, HEXACO in four languages; Hashimoto & Oshio 2025 structural compression), that self-reports dissociate from behavior (Han et al. 2025), and that personality measurements are unstable (Tosato et al. 2025). Neuron-based trait induction / persona-steering (NPTI; Chen et al. 2026) and MBTI-fine-tuning (Machine Mindset) manipulate traits but are MONOLINGUAL/English and treat traits as a global knob. GlobalTrait (Siddique 2018) aligns trait embeddings for RECOGNITION, not the model's own expression. NONE (i) test whether the model's behaviorally-expressed disposition in open interaction is language-dependent BEYOND self-report and surface style, (ii) decompose cross-lingual trait expression into a shared internal trait representation versus a language-set expression gate (verifying the trait is internally present even where behavior flattens), or (iii) causally localize and steer a trait-expression gate to equalize disposition across languages while preserving the underlying trait. This differs from my prior hedging (qualifiers on a factual answer), affect-intensity (rating a described emotion), face-threat-mitigation (softening a hard message), and moral-valence (right/wrong of an action) proposals: the object here is the model's own dispositional TRAIT tendency expressed in ordinary behavior and its language-set expression gate over a shared trait representation.
Abstract: Aligned language models tend to sound uniformly agreeable and cautious, and recent work shows their personality-style responses collapse into a narrow, positive band across languages. But is the model's underlying disposition actually the same across languages and merely voiced differently, and if so, is that voicing gated by the query language? We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a largely language-independent internal representation of its trait tendency along interpretable axes (warmth/agreeableness, assertiveness, cautiousness, honesty-modesty), but the query language causally sets how strongly that trait is behaviorally expressed in open interaction, so the SAME situation elicits a warmer/more assertive/more cautious response in some languages and a flattened, socially-desirable default in others—worst in lower-resource, typologically distant languages—independent of the shared trait representation. We build TraitExpressProbe, parallel open-ended interaction scenarios across 12 languages (advice-giving, disagreement, recommendation, help requests) scored for behaviorally-expressed trait level via validated trait-behavior rubrics, with situation content held fixed and surface-style controls. Behaviorally we measure per-language expressed-trait level and test whether flattening tracks resource level and typological distance beyond surface fluency. We train a linear trait probe and test zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, then decompose the expression gap into a shared trait representation versus a language-set expression gate—a flattened behavior should coincide with an intact internal trait signal. Via activation and path patching we localize a trait-expression gate, and in a decisive causal test we steer it to equalize disposition across languages—or, in reverse, flatten or amplify it—while preserving the underlying trait and surface language. We reframe cross-lingual personality flattening as a shared trait representation under a steerable, language-dependent expression gate.
Experiments: 1) MODELS & LANGUAGES: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23-8B (inference + probing + patching on 1-2 A6000 GPUs). 12 typologically/culturally/resource-diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili, Yoruba), coded for cultural-response-style norms plus URIEL typological/resource distance (graded predictors). 2) DATASET (TraitExpressProbe): ~500 open-ended interaction scenarios that pull on interpretable trait axes: WARMTH/AGREEABLENESS (respond to a distressed user), ASSERTIVENESS (advise on a decision / give feedback), CAUTIOUSNESS/RISK-AVERSION (recommend under uncertainty), HONESTY-MODESTY (whether to acknowledge limits / avoid overclaiming). The situation content is held fixed across languages; the model chooses HOW to respond. Score behaviorally-expressed trait level via validated trait-behavior rubrics (e.g., warmth markers, assertiveness/hedging balance, risk-recommendation direction) using a classifier calibrated against human ratings on a subset, plus HEXACO/behavioral anchors from human reference data (Heierli et al.). Include a matched TRAIT-NEUTRAL control (situations where trait axes are irrelevant) to bound baseline, and a SURFACE-STYLE control (measure lexical politeness/formality separately, so expressed-trait is not merely style). Translate/native-verify; record tokenization fertility; screen that the model comprehends each scenario per language. 3) BEHAVIORAL FLATTENING TEST: Per (scenario, language) measure expressed-trait level along each axis. KEY hypothesis: for the SAME situation, expressed-trait is systematically FLATTENED (compressed toward a positive/cautious default, reduced range) in lower-resource/typologically distant languages, beyond surface fluency and tokenization. Mixed-effects regression of expressed-trait (and per-language trait RANGE/variance) on (language, resource tier via URIEL, typological distance, tokenization fertility, cultural-norm code), scenario as random effect; test the language effect and range-compression. Compare against human HEXACO reference range per language and the surface-style control. Report per-language trait-expression profiles and cross-lingual disagreement on identical situations. 4) SHARED TRAIT PROBE & TRANSFER: At the pre-generation/early-response position pool the hidden state; train a linear probe to decode the model's internal TRAIT tendency along each axis (target from expressed-trait in the least-flattened/reference language and from self-report anchors) on ENGLISH data, select the best layer on English validation, apply zero-shot cross-lingually; report AUROC/R^2 as evidence of a language-independent trait representation. Compare to per-language probes; measure cross-lingual CKA/cosine. CRITICAL: on FLATTENED items, test whether the internal trait signal is still SIMILAR across languages—the signature of language modulating the expression GAIN, not the disposition. 5) GATE-vs-SIGNAL DECOMPOSITION: Compare the shared mid-layer trait signal across languages (should be similar on matched items) versus emitted expressed-trait (which flattens). Define a per-language EXPRESSION GAIN mapping the trait signal to realized behavior; test whether cross-lingual flattening is explained by a language-set gain on a similar trait signal rather than a differing signal. Correlate per-language gain with resource tier, typological distance, and cultural norms (Spearman); anchor mid-vs-output split via per-layer language-ID probes / logit-lens. 6) LOCALIZE THE TRAIT-EXPRESSION GATE: Via activation and path patching between a full-expression language and a flattened language on the SAME scenario, sweep layers/heads/MLPs for the minimal components whose transfer changes expressed-trait WITHOUT changing the decoded trait signal or the propositional content. Report layer distribution relative to the language-transition band; cross-check activation vs path patching; test patching the gate components from a full-expression language into a flattened run. 7) CAUSAL TRAIT-EXPRESSION STEERING (decisive): Derive a trait-expression steering vector via difference-of-means (full-expression runs minus flattened runs at matched trait signal). Test (i) EQUALIZE: adding it in flattened languages restores expressed-trait toward a reference level; (ii) FLATTEN/AMPLIFY: subtracting/scaling it flattens or amplifies expression in full-expression languages, with DOSE-RESPONSE; (iii) it works cross-lingually, stronger where flattening was worst; (iv) it changes ONLY expressed-trait, not the decoded trait signal, the propositional content/task-correctness, or surface language (fidelity checks), does not move the TRAIT-NEUTRAL control, and does not degrade general QA (multilingual MMLU subset). Baselines: prompt-based persona instructions, per-language style prompts, translate-to-English, and NPTI-style monolingual trait induction. Metrics: cross-lingual expression-gap/range-compression closure, dose-response, content/task fidelity, trait-signal/output fidelity, neutral-control retention, general-QA retention. Reverse-consistency: steering shifts expressed-trait but not propositional content or unrelated tasks. 8) ANALYSIS/ABLATIONS: trait-axis breakdown (warmth vs assertiveness vs cautiousness vs honesty-modesty—which flatten most); is English/high-resource the full-expression reference?; does flattening track cultural response-style norms beyond resource level?; English-centric (Llama) vs multilingual-centric (Aya—does balanced training flatten less?); probe layer/dimensionality; single-direction vs low-rank trait-expression subspace; whether one gate vector generalizes across axes and languages; dissociation from tokenization by comparing high- vs low-fertility languages at matched trait signal and by showing content-invariant steering changes expression without changing tokenization; dissociation from self-report by comparing behaviorally-expressed vs self-reported trait per language (extending Han et al. cross-lingually). EVAL METRICS SUMMARY: per-language expressed-trait level and range-compression with resource/typology/norm regression controlling for surface style/fluency/fertility, human-HEXACO-range replication, cross-lingual trait probe transfer AUROC/R^2 and trait-signal-similarity-under-flattening, signal-similarity vs expression-divergence (gain) decomposition, gain-vs-resource/typology/norm correlation, patch-localized trait-expression-gate layer, cross-lingual gate transplant equalization rate, causal steering expression-gap/range closure with dose-response and flatten/amplify induction, content/task/trait-signal/output fidelity, neutral-control and general-QA retention, self-report-vs-behavior dissociation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The gate-vs-signal split could be confounded if the internal trait signal itself differs by language (the model genuinely has a different disposition, not a flattened expression); we test this directly via cross-lingual trait-probe transfer and the trait-signal-similarity-under-flattening check, reporting how much of the gap is signal vs gain—either outcome is informative. 2) Expressed-trait must be separable from surface style/fluency; we measure lexical politeness/formality separately (surface-style control), score trait via behavioral rubrics (assertiveness = advice directedness, cautiousness = recommendation direction under uncertainty) not word counts, and show content-invariant steering changes trait expression without proportional style change. 3) The most important guard: steering must change DISPOSITION expression, not degrade task correctness or delete content; we score content/task fidelity as a primary metric and treat trait changes that harm correctness as off-target. 4) Cross-lingual trait rubrics are hard to make comparable; we build native-verified per-language behavioral anchors, calibrate the trait classifier against human ratings and human HEXACO reference ranges (Heierli et al.), analyze each axis separately, and report reliability. 5) Some models/languages may show no flattening asymmetry (uniform expression) or uniform flattening everywhere; either is an informative, publishable finding about cross-lingual personality flattening, and we quantify how often a gap exists. 6) Tokenization fertility confounds; we control for it and compare high- vs low-fertility languages at matched trait signal. 7) Instruction-tuning/RLHF imposes a global socially-desirable prior that may interact with language; we compare base vs instruction-tuned and English-centric vs multilingual-centric models. 8) 'Personality' in LLMs is contested and unstable (Tosato 2025); we scope claims to behaviorally-expressed trait tendencies on interpretable axes, not stable human personality, and use repeated elicitation to estimate expression reliably. 9) Cultural-norm coding is coarse; we treat it as a graded predictor and report sensitivity. 10) Patching/steering results can be model- and template-specific; we test five models, multiple templates, and cross-check activation vs path patching. 11) Causal steering may harm fluency or act as a generic positivity lever; we report content/task/trait-signal/output fidelity, neutral-control and general-QA retention, and use flatten/amplify (reverse), dose-response, and reverse-consistency tests to ensure a genuine trait-expression gate rather than a global tone knob. 12) The trait-expression signal may be low-rank rather than a single direction; we test low-rank subspace variants. 13) Distinguishing from behavioral cross-lingual personality work (Heierli 2026; Hashimoto 2025), monolingual self-report/behavior dissociation (Han 2025), and monolingual persona-steering (NPTI, Chen 2026) is essential; our contribution is the internal, causal, cross-lingual account—a shared trait representation under a language-set behavioral-expression gate, localized and steerable—and the cross-lingual self-report-vs-behavior dissociation, none of which prior work provides.
